What is chemistry?
docs.text: According to Britannica, chemistry is the science that deals with the properties, composition, and structure of substances (defined as elements and compounds), the transformations they undergo, and the energy that is released or absorbed during these processes.

docs.title: Chemical Bonding | Hybridisation
docs.text:
Hybridisation is the process of intermixing of the orbitals of slightly different energies so as to redistribute their energies, resulting in the formation of a new set of orbitals of equivalent energies and shape.

  • The concept was introduced by Pauling to explain the shapes of polyatomic molecules like CH4, NH3 and H2O.
  • The new orbitals are called hybrid orbitals. Unlike pure orbitals, hybrid orbitals are used in bond formation.
  • Example: one 2s and three 2p orbitals of carbon hybridise to form four new sp3 hybrid orbitals.

docs.title: Salient Features of Hybridisation
docs.text:
• The number of hybrid orbitals is equal to the number of atomic orbitals that get hybridised.
  • Hybrid orbitals are always equivalent in energy and shape.
  • Hybrid orbitals form more stable bonds than pure atomic orbitals.
  • Hybrid orbitals point in preferred directions in space so that repulsion between electron pairs is minimum. So the type of hybridisation indicates the geometry of the molecule.

docs.title: Important Conditions for Hybridisation
docs.text:
• Only the orbitals of the valence shell are hybridised.
  • The orbitals undergoing hybridisation should have almost equal energy.
  • Promotion of an electron is not an essential condition before hybridisation.
  • Not only half-filled orbitals take part; in some cases even filled valence orbitals hybridise.

docs.title: 1. sp Hybridisation
docs.text:
• One s and one p orbital mix to form two equivalent sp hybrid orbitals. If the hybrids lie along the z-axis, the s and pz orbitals are used.
  • Each sp hybrid has 50% s-character and 50% p-character.
  • The two hybrids point in opposite directions along the axis (180°), with large positive lobes and very small negative lobes, which gives effective overlap and strong bonds.
  • Molecules with an sp hybridised central atom are linear. It is also called diagonal hybridisation.

BeCl2

  • Ground state of Be: 1s22s2. In the excited state, one 2s electron is promoted to a vacant 2p orbital.
  • One 2s and one 2p orbital hybridise to form two sp orbitals at 180°.
  • Each sp orbital overlaps axially with a 2p orbital of Cl to form two Be-Cl sigma bonds. BeCl2 is linear.

docs.title: 2. sp<sup>2</sup> Hybridisation
docs.text:
• One s and two p orbitals mix to form three equivalent sp2 hybrid orbitals.
  • The three hybrids are arranged in a trigonal planar manner at 120°.

BCl3

  • Ground state of B: 1s22s22p1. In the excited state, one 2s electron is promoted to a 2p orbital, giving three unpaired electrons.
  • One 2s and two 2p orbitals hybridise to form three sp2 orbitals.
  • They overlap with 2p orbitals of Cl to form three B-Cl bonds. BCl3 is trigonal planar with Cl-B-Cl angle of 120°.

docs.title: 3. sp<sup>3</sup> Hybridisation
docs.text:
• One s and three p orbitals of the valence shell mix to form four equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals.
  • Each sp3 orbital has 25% s-character and 75% p-character.
  • The four hybrids are directed towards the four corners of a tetrahedron, at 109.5° to each other.

CH4

The four sp3 orbitals of carbon overlap with the 1s orbitals of four H atoms to form four C-H sigma bonds. CH4 is tetrahedral with H-C-H angle of 109.5°.

NH3

  • N has the configuration 2s22px12py12pz1. After sp3 hybridisation, three hybrid orbitals have one electron each and the fourth has a lone pair.
  • The three singly occupied orbitals overlap with 1s orbitals of H to form three N-H sigma bonds.
  • Since lp-bp repulsion > bp-bp repulsion, the angle reduces from 109.5° to 107°. NH3 is pyramidal.

H2O

  • The four sp3 orbitals of O include two with one electron each and two with a lone pair each.
  • Two H atoms occupy two corners of the tetrahedron and the lone pairs occupy the other two.
  • The bond angle reduces from 109.5° to 104.5°, and the molecule is V-shaped (angular).

docs.title: Other Examples of sp<sup>3</sup>, sp<sup>2</sup> and sp Hybridisation
1. Ethane, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> (sp<sup>3</sup>)
docs.text:
• Both C atoms are sp3 hybridised. One sp3 orbital of each C overlaps axially with that of the other C to form the sp3-sp3 C-C sigma bond.
  • The other three sp3 orbitals of each C form sp3-s sigma bonds with H atoms.
  • C-C bond length = 154 pm and C-H bond length = 109 pm.

docs.title: 2. Ethene, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (sp<sup>2</sup>)
docs.text:
• Each C atom is sp2 hybridised. One sp2 orbital of each C overlaps axially to form a C-C sigma bond, and the other two form sp2-s sigma bonds with H atoms.
  • The unhybridised 2p orbital (2px or 2py) of each C overlaps sideways with that of the other C to form a weak pi bond, made of two electron clouds above and below the plane of the molecule.
  • So the C=C double bond consists of one sp2-sp2 sigma bond and one pi bond.
  • C=C bond length = 134 pm, C-H bond length = 108 pm, H-C-H angle = 117.6° and H-C-C angle = 121°.

docs.title: 3. Ethyne, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> (sp)
docs.text:
• Both C atoms are sp hybridised, with two unhybridised orbitals each: 2py and 2px.
  • One sp orbital of each C overlaps axially to form the C-C sigma bond. The other sp orbital of each C forms a sigma bond with the 1s orbital of H.
  • The two unhybridised p orbitals of each C overlap sideways to form two pi bonds.
  • So the C≡C triple bond is made up of one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The molecule is linear.

docs.title: Hybridisation Involving d Orbitals
docs.text:
• Third period elements have 3d orbitals in addition to 3s and 3p. The energy of 3d orbitals is comparable to 3s and 3p, and also to 4s and 4p.
  • So hybridisation involving 3s, 3p and 3d, or 3d, 4s and 4p, is possible. But since 3p and 4s differ significantly in energy, hybridisation involving 3p, 3d and 4s is not possible.
Shape of molecule/ion Hybridisation type Atomic orbitals Examples Square planar dsp2 d + s + p(2) [Ni(CN)4]2-, [PtCl4]2- Trigonal bipyramidal sp3d s + p(3) + d PF5, PCl5 Square pyramidal sp3d2 s + p(3) + d(2) BrF5, XeOF4 Octahedral sp3d2 or d2sp3 s + p(3) + d(2) or d(2) + s + p(3) SF6, [CrF6]3-, [Co(NH3)6]3+

docs.title: 1. PCl<sub>5</sub> (sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridisation)
docs.text:
\[P\ (ground\ state):\ 3s^2\ 3p^3\ 3d^0\] \[P\ (excited\ state):\ 3s^1\ 3p^3\ 3d^1\]
  • One 3s, three 3p and one 3d orbital hybridise to give five sp3d orbitals directed towards the corners of a trigonal bipyramid.
  • These overlap with singly occupied p orbitals of five Cl atoms to form five P-Cl sigma bonds.
  • All bond angles are not equal:
    • Three equatorial P-Cl bonds lie in one plane at 120° to each other.
    • Two axial P-Cl bonds lie above and below this plane, at 90° to it.
  • The axial bond pairs suffer more repulsion from the equatorial bond pairs. So the axial bonds are slightly longer and weaker than the equatorial bonds, which makes PCl5 more reactive.

docs.title: 2. SF<sub>6</sub> (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridisation)
docs.text:
\[S\ (ground\ state):\ 3s^2\ 3p^4\ 3d^0\] \[S\ (excited\ state):\ 3s^1\ 3p^3\ 3d^2\]
  • In the excited state, six orbitals (one s, three p and two d) are singly occupied. They hybridise to form six sp3d2 orbitals pointing to the six corners of a regular octahedron.
  • These overlap with singly occupied orbitals of six F atoms to form six S-F sigma bonds. SF6 is octahedral.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What is meant by hybridisation of atomic orbitals? Describe the shapes of sp, sp2 and sp3 hybrid orbitals.

  • Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies of the same atom to form an equal number of new, equivalent hybrid orbitals.
  • sp: two hybrid orbitals, linear, at 180°.
  • sp2: three hybrid orbitals, trigonal planar, at 120°.
  • sp3: four hybrid orbitals, tetrahedral, at 109.5°.
  • Each hybrid orbital has one large lobe and one very small lobe, pointing away from the nucleus in its own direction.

Describe the change in hybridisation (if any) of the Al atom in the following reaction: AlCl3 + Cl- → AlCl4-

  • In AlCl3, Al (excited state 3s13p2) uses one 3s and two 3p orbitals, so it is sp2 hybridised and trigonal planar.
  • In AlCl4-, the empty 3p orbital of Al also takes part, accepting a lone pair from Cl-. Al becomes sp3 hybridised and the ion is tetrahedral.

Is there any change in the hybridisation of B and N atoms as a result of the following reaction? BF3 + NH3 → F3B.NH3

  • Before the reaction, B in BF3 is sp2 hybridised (trigonal planar) and N in NH3 is sp3 hybridised.
  • In the product, N donates its lone pair to the empty orbital of B. B now has four electron pairs and becomes sp3 hybridised.
  • N remains sp3 hybridised; its lone pair simply becomes a bond pair.

What is the total number of sigma and pi bonds in the following molecules? (a) C2H2 (b) C2H4

  • (a) C2H2 (H-C≡C-H): Two C-H sigma bonds + one C-C sigma bond = 3 sigma bonds, and 2 pi bonds.
  • (b) C2H4 (H2C=CH2): Four C-H sigma bonds + one C-C sigma bond = 5 sigma bonds, and 1 pi bond.

Which hybrid orbitals are used by carbon atoms in the following molecules? (a) CH3-CH3 (b) CH3-CH=CH2 (c) CH3-CH2-OH (d) CH3-CHO (e) CH3COOH

  • A carbon with only single bonds is sp3, a carbon with one double bond is sp2, and a carbon with a triple bond (or two double bonds) is sp.
  • (a) Both C atoms are sp3.
  • (b) CH3 carbon is sp3; the CH and CH2 carbons of the double bond are sp2.
  • (c) Both C atoms are sp3.
  • (d) CH3 carbon is sp3; CHO carbon is sp2.
  • (e) CH3 carbon is sp3; COOH carbon is sp2.

Describe the hybridisation in case of PCl5. Why are the axial bonds longer as compared to equatorial bonds?

  • P (3s23p3) promotes one 3s electron to a 3d orbital, giving five unpaired electrons (3s13p33d1).
  • These five orbitals form five sp3d hybrids arranged in a trigonal bipyramid, which overlap with p orbitals of five Cl atoms.
  • Each axial bond pair is at 90° to three equatorial bond pairs, while each equatorial bond pair is at 90° to only two axial bond pairs. So the axial bonds suffer more repulsion and become slightly longer (and weaker) than the equatorial bonds.

docs.title: Chemical Bonding | Hydrogen Bonding
docs.text:
Hydrogen bond can be defined as the attractive force which binds the hydrogen atom of one molecule with the electronegative atom (F, O or N) of another molecule.

  • Nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine are highly electronegative elements.
  • When one of them is covalently bonded to hydrogen, the shared electrons shift towards the more electronegative atom. The H atom gets a partial positive charge.
  • This partially positive H atom then forms a bond with the electronegative atom of another molecule. This bond is called a hydrogen bond, and it is weaker than a covalent bond.
  • A hydrogen bond is shown by a dotted line (- - -), while a covalent bond is shown by a solid line.

Hydrogen bonding in HF

\[- - - \overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{F} - - - \overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{F} - - - \overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{F} - - -\]

Here, each H atom acts as a bridge: it is held to one F atom by a covalent bond and to another F atom by a hydrogen bond.

docs.title: Cause of Formation of Hydrogen Bond
docs.text:
• When hydrogen is bonded to a strongly electronegative element X, the shared electron pair moves far away from the hydrogen atom.
  • The H atom becomes highly electropositive with respect to X. H acquires a fractional positive charge (δ+) and X acquires a fractional negative charge (δ-).
  • This gives a polar molecule with an electrostatic force of attraction to neighbouring molecules:
\[\overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{X} - - - \overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{X}\]
  • The magnitude of hydrogen bonding depends on the physical state of the compound. It is maximum in the solid state and minimum in the gaseous state.
  • Hydrogen bonds have a strong influence on the structure and properties of compounds.

docs.title: 1. Intermolecular Hydrogen Bond
docs.text:
• It is formed between two different molecules of the same or different compounds.
  • Examples: hydrogen bonding in HF, in water and in alcohols.
\[- - - \overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{O}(H) - - - \overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{O}(H) - - -\]

docs.title: 2. Intramolecular Hydrogen Bond
docs.text:
• It is formed when a hydrogen atom lies between two highly electronegative atoms (F, O, N) present within the same molecule.
  • Example: In o-nitrophenol, the H of the -OH group is hydrogen bonded to an O atom of the neighbouring -NO2 group, forming a ring within the molecule.
Intermolecular hydrogen bond Intramolecular hydrogen bond Formed between two or more molecules Formed within the same molecule Molecules get associated, so boiling point increases No association between molecules, so boiling point is lower Examples: HF, H2O, alcohols, p-nitrophenol Example: o-nitrophenol

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Define hydrogen bond. Is it weaker or stronger than the van der Waals forces?

  • A hydrogen bond is the attractive force which binds the hydrogen atom of one molecule (or part of a molecule) with a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) of another molecule (or another part of the same molecule).
  • A hydrogen bond is stronger than van der Waals forces, because it involves attraction between a strongly positive H and a strongly negative atom, while van der Waals forces are weak attractions between temporary or permanent dipoles. However, it is much weaker than a covalent bond.

docs.title: Chemical Bonding | Ionic Bond and Bond Parameters
Chemical Bonding | Ionic Bond and Bond Parameters
Ionic or Electrovalent Bond
docs.text:
An ionic or electrovalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions, produced by transfer of electrons from one atom to another.

  • The formation of an ionic compound depends mainly on:
    • The ease of formation of the positive and negative ions from the neutral atoms.
    • The arrangement of the ions in the solid, that is, the lattice of the crystalline compound.
  • Formation of a positive ion involves ionization (removal of electrons), and formation of a negative ion involves addition of electrons.
\[M_{(g)} → M^+_{(g)} + e^- \qquad (Ionization\ enthalpy)\] \[X_{(g)} + e^- → X^-_{(g)} \qquad (Electron\ gain\ enthalpy)\] \[M^+_{(g)} + X^-_{(g)} → MX_{(s)}\]
  • The electron gain enthalpy, ΔegH, is the enthalpy change when a gaseous atom in its ground state gains an electron. It may be exothermic or endothermic.
  • Ionization is always endothermic.
  • Electron affinity is the negative of the energy change accompanying electron gain.

Conclusion

Ionic bonds are formed more easily between elements with comparatively low ionization enthalpies and elements with comparatively high negative electron gain enthalpy.

  • Most ionic compounds have cations from metals and anions from non-metals. The ammonium ion, NH4+ (made of two non-metals) is an exception; it is the cation of many ionic compounds.
  • In the crystalline state, ionic compounds are orderly three-dimensional arrangements of cations and anions held together by coulombic forces. Example: NaCl has the rock salt structure.

docs.title: Why ionic compounds are stable
docs.text:
• The sum of ionization enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy may be positive, yet the crystal is stable because of the energy released when the crystal lattice forms.

Energetics of NaCl

\[Na_{(g)} → Na^+_{(g)} + e^-;\ \ ΔH = +495.8\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\] \[Cl_{(g)} + e^- → Cl^-_{(g)};\ \ ΔH = -348.7\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\] \[Sum = +147.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

This is more than compensated by the enthalpy of lattice formation of NaCl(s) (-788 kJ mol-1). So the energy released is more than the energy absorbed.

  • Thus, the stability of an ionic compound is measured by its enthalpy of lattice formation, and not simply by achieving an octet around the ions in the gaseous state.

docs.title: Lattice Enthalpy
docs.text:
The lattice enthalpy of an ionic solid is defined as the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into gaseous constituent ions.

  • Example: The lattice enthalpy of NaCl is 788 kJ mol-1. This means 788 kJ of energy is needed to separate one mole of solid NaCl into one mole of Na+(g) and one mole of Cl-(g) to an infinite distance.
  • This involves both attraction between opposite charges and repulsion between like charges. As the crystal is three-dimensional, lattice enthalpy cannot be calculated from these forces alone; the crystal geometry must also be taken into account.

docs.title: 1. Bond Length
docs.text:
Bond length is defined as the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms in a molecule.

  • It is measured by spectroscopic, X-ray diffraction and electron-diffraction methods.
  • In a covalent bond A-B, each atom contributes its covalent radius to the bond length:
\[R = r_A + r_B\]

Where, R = bond length and rA, rB = covalent radii of A and B.

  • Covalent radius is roughly the radius of an atom's core which is in contact with the core of an adjacent atom in a bonded situation. It is half the distance between two similar atoms joined by a covalent bond.
  • van der Waals radius is the overall size of the atom, including its valence shell, in a non-bonded situation. It is half the distance between two similar atoms in separate molecules in a solid.
  • For chlorine, covalent radius = 99 pm (Cl-Cl bond length = 198 pm) and van der Waals radius = 180 pm.

Average bond lengths for some single, double and triple bonds:

Bond Type Covalent Bond Length (pm) O-H 96 C-H 107 N-O 136 C-O 143 C-N 143 C-C 154 C=O 121 N=O 122 C=C 133 C=N 138 C≡N 116 C≡C 120

Bond lengths in some common molecules:

Molecule Bond Length (pm) H2 (H-H) 74 F2 (F-F) 144 Cl2 (Cl-Cl) 199 Br2 (Br-Br) 228 I2 (I-I) 267 N2 (N≡N) 109 O2 (O=O) 121 HF (H-F) 92 HCl (H-Cl) 127 HBr (H-Br) 141 HI (H-I) 160

docs.title: 2. Bond Angle
docs.text:
Bond angle is defined as the angle between the orbitals containing bonding electron pairs around the central atom in a molecule or complex ion.

  • It is expressed in degrees and determined by spectroscopic methods.
  • It gives an idea of the distribution of orbitals around the central atom and hence helps to find the shape of the molecule. Example: the H-O-H bond angle in water is 104.5°.

docs.title: 3. Bond Enthalpy
docs.text:
Bond enthalpy is defined as the amount of energy required to break one mole of bonds of a particular type between two atoms in the gaseous state. Its unit is kJ mol-1.

\[H_{2(g)} → H_{(g)} + H_{(g)};\ \ Δ_aH^0 = 435.8\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\] \[O_{2(g)} → O_{(g)} + O_{(g)};\ \ Δ_aH^0 = 498\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\] \[N_{2(g)} → N_{(g)} + N_{(g)};\ \ Δ_aH^0 = 946.0\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\] \[HCl_{(g)} → H_{(g)} + Cl_{(g)};\ \ Δ_aH^0 = 431.0\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • Larger the bond dissociation enthalpy, stronger is the bond.
  • In polyatomic molecules, the same type of bond may need different energies to break. In H2O, the second O-H bond is in a changed chemical environment:
\[H_2O_{(g)} → H_{(g)} + OH_{(g)};\ \ Δ_aH_1^0 = 502\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\] \[OH_{(g)} → H_{(g)} + O_{(g)};\ \ Δ_aH_2^0 = 427\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • So, for polyatomic molecules we use the mean or average bond enthalpy, obtained by dividing the total bond dissociation enthalpy by the number of bonds broken:
\[Average\ bond\ enthalpy\ of\ O-H = {502 + 427 \over 2} = 464.5\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

docs.title: 4. Bond Order
docs.text:
In the Lewis description of a covalent bond, the bond order is given by the number of bonds between the two atoms in a molecule.

  • Bond order of H2 = 1, O2 = 2, N2 = 3 and CO = 3.
  • Isoelectronic molecules and ions have identical bond orders. Example: F2 and O22- have bond order 1, while N2, CO and NO+ have bond order 3.

Conclusion

With increase in bond order, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases.

docs.title: 5. Resonance Structures
docs.text:
Whenever a single Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule accurately, a number of structures with similar energy, positions of nuclei, bonding and non-bonding pairs of electrons are taken as the canonical structures of the hybrid, which describes the molecule accurately.

  • Example: Ozone, O3. A single Lewis structure shows one O-O single bond (148 pm) and one O=O double bond (121 pm). But experimentally, both O-O bonds in O3 are equal (128 pm), which is between a single and a double bond.
  • So O3 is represented by two canonical (resonance) structures, and the actual molecule is their resonance hybrid. Resonance is shown by a double-headed arrow.
\[O=O^+-O^- \longleftrightarrow\ ^-O-O^+=O\]
  • Carbonate ion, CO32-: A single structure with two C-O single bonds and one C=O double bond gives unequal bonds, but experimentally all C-O bonds are equivalent. So CO32- is a resonance hybrid of three canonical forms, with the double bond on each of the three O atoms in turn.
  • Carbon dioxide, CO2: The experimental C-O bond length is 115 pm, which lies between C=O (121 pm) and C≡O (110 pm). So CO2 is a hybrid of three canonical forms:
\[O=C=O \longleftrightarrow\ ^-O-C\equiv O^+ \longleftrightarrow\ ^+O\equiv C-O^-\]

Important points about resonance

  • Resonance stabilises the molecule, because the energy of the resonance hybrid is less than that of any single canonical structure.
  • Resonance averages the bond characteristics as a whole.
  • The canonical forms have no real existence.
  • The molecule does not exist in one canonical form for some fraction of time and in other forms for other fractions of time.
  • There is no equilibrium between canonical forms like there is between keto and enol forms in tautomerism.
  • The molecule has a single structure, the resonance hybrid, which cannot be shown by a single Lewis structure.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Write the favourable factors for the formation of an ionic bond.

  • Low ionization enthalpy of the metal atom, so that it easily loses electrons to form a cation.
  • High negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal atom, so that it easily gains electrons to form an anion.
  • High lattice enthalpy of the resulting solid, so that the energy released in forming the crystal lattice more than compensates for the energy needed to form the gaseous ions.

How do you express the bond strength in terms of bond order?

  • Bond strength (bond enthalpy) increases as bond order increases, while bond length decreases.
  • Example: N2 (bond order 3) has bond enthalpy 946 kJ mol-1, O2 (bond order 2) has 498 kJ mol-1, and H2 (bond order 1) has 435.8 kJ mol-1.

Explain the structure of the CO32- ion in terms of resonance.

  • A single Lewis structure with two C-O single bonds and one C=O double bond would give unequal bonds.
  • Experimentally, all three carbon-oxygen bonds in CO32- are equivalent.
  • So the carbonate ion is a resonance hybrid of three canonical forms. In each form the double bond is on a different O atom and the other two O atoms carry a negative charge each:
\[O=C(O^-)_2\ \longleftrightarrow\ ^-O-C(=O)-O^-\ \longleftrightarrow\ (^-O)_2C=O\]
  • In the hybrid, each C-O bond has a bond order of about 1.33 and the negative charge is spread over all three O atoms.

H3PO3 can be drawn as (1) with one H bonded directly to P and two P-OH groups, or (2) with three P-OH groups. Can these be taken as canonical forms of a resonance hybrid?

  • No. Canonical structures must have the same positions of nuclei and differ only in the arrangement of electrons.
  • In structure (1), one H atom is attached to P, while in structure (2), that H atom is attached to O. The positions of atoms are different.
  • So these are two different structures, not resonance forms of H3PO3.

Write the resonance structures for SO3, NO2 and NO3-.

  • SO3: The S=O double bond can be with any of the three O atoms (the other two being S-O single bonds with formal charges), giving three equivalent canonical forms.
\[O=S^{2+}(O^-)_2\ \longleftrightarrow\ ^-O-S^{2+}(=O)-O^-\ \longleftrightarrow\ (^-O)_2S^{2+}=O\]
  • NO2: The double bond can be with either O atom; the odd electron stays on N.
\[O=\dot{N}^+-O^-\ \longleftrightarrow\ ^-O-\dot{N}^+=O\]
  • NO3-: Like carbonate, the N=O double bond can be with any of the three O atoms.
\[O=N^+(O^-)_2\ \longleftrightarrow\ ^-O-N^+(=O)-O^-\ \longleftrightarrow\ (^-O)_2N^+=O\]

docs.title: Chemical Bonding | Kössel-Lewis Approach
docs.text:
The attractive force which holds the constituents (atoms, ions, etc.) together in different chemical species is called a chemical bond.

  • Apart from noble gases, no element normally exists as a free, independent atom. Atoms group together to form molecules.
  • Atoms combine because bonding lowers the energy of the system, and a system with lower energy is more stable.
  • Different theories have been put forward to explain why atoms combine and why molecules have definite shapes: the Kössel-Lewis approach, VSEPR theory, Valence Bond (VB) theory and Molecular Orbital (MO) theory.

docs.title: Kössel-Lewis Approach
docs.text:
In 1916, Kössel and Lewis independently explained chemical bonding on the basis of the inertness of noble gases.

  • Lewis pictured an atom as a positively charged kernel (nucleus + inner electrons) surrounded by an outer shell that can hold a maximum of eight electrons.
  • An outer shell with eight electrons (an octet) is a particularly stable arrangement.
  • Lewis proposed that atoms achieve a stable octet when they are linked by chemical bonds, either by transfer of electrons (as in NaCl) or by sharing a pair of electrons (as in Cl2, H2, F2).

docs.title: Lewis Symbols
docs.text:
• Only the outer shell (valence) electrons take part in chemical combination. These are called valence electrons.
  • In a Lewis symbol, the valence electrons are shown as dots around the symbol of the element.
  • For second period elements: Li has 1 dot, Be has 2, B has 3, C has 4, N has 5, O has 6, F has 7 and Ne has 8 dots.
\[Li\cdot \qquad \cdot Be \cdot \qquad \cdot \dot{B} \cdot \qquad \cdot \dot{C} \cdot \qquad \cdot \ddot{N} \cdot \qquad :\ddot{O} \cdot \qquad :\ddot{F} \cdot \qquad :\ddot{Ne}:\]
  • Significance: The number of dots gives the number of valence electrons, which helps to find the group valence of an element.
  • The group valence is generally either equal to the number of dots or 8 minus the number of dots.

docs.title: Kössel's Postulates (Electrovalent Bond)
docs.text:
• In the periodic table, the highly electronegative halogens and the highly electropositive alkali metals are separated by the noble gases.
  • A negative ion is formed when a halogen atom gains an electron, and a positive ion is formed when an alkali metal atom loses an electron.
  • The ions formed attain the stable noble gas configuration, ns2np6 (helium has a duplet, 1s2).
  • The positive and negative ions are held together by electrostatic attraction.

Formation of NaCl and CaF2

\[Na → Na^+ + e^- \qquad [Ne]3s^1 → [Ne]\] \[Cl + e^- → Cl^- \qquad [Ne]3s^2 3p^5 → [Ne]3s^2 3p^6\ or\ [Ar]\] \[Na^+ + Cl^- → NaCl\ or\ Na^+Cl^-\] \[Ca → Ca^{2+} + 2e^- \qquad [Ar]4s^2 → [Ar]\] \[F + e^- → F^- \qquad [He]2s^2 2p^5 → [He]2s^2 2p^6\ or\ [Ne]\] \[Ca^{2+} + 2F^- → CaF_2\ or\ Ca^{2+}(F^-)_2\]
  • The bond formed by electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions is called an electrovalent bond.
  • The electrovalence is equal to the number of unit charges on the ion. So calcium has an electrovalence of +2 and chlorine has an electrovalence of -1.

docs.title: Octet Rule
docs.text: According to the electronic theory of chemical bonding (Kössel and Lewis, 1916), atoms combine either by transfer of valence electrons from one atom to another or by sharing of valence electrons, in order to have an octet in their valence shells. This is known as the octet rule.

docs.title: Covalent Bond
docs.text:
• Langmuir (1919) refined Lewis's ideas and introduced the term covalent bond.
  • In Cl2, each Cl atom ([Ne]3s23p5) is one electron short of the argon configuration. Each Cl contributes one electron to a shared pair, and both atoms attain an octet.
\[:\ddot{\underset{..}{Cl}}\cdot + \cdot\ddot{\underset{..}{Cl}}: → :\ddot{\underset{..}{Cl}}:\ddot{\underset{..}{Cl}}:\ \ or\ \ Cl-Cl\]
  • Conditions for writing Lewis dot structures of covalent molecules:
    • Each bond is formed by sharing one electron pair between the atoms.
    • Each combining atom contributes at least one electron to the shared pair.
    • The combining atoms attain the outer shell noble gas configuration by sharing electrons.
  • In H2O, each H atom attains a duplet and O attains an octet. In CCl4, C and all four Cl atoms attain an octet.

docs.title: Single, Double and Triple Bonds
docs.text:
• When two atoms share one electron pair, they are joined by a single covalent bond. Example: Cl-Cl, H-H.
  • When two atoms share two electron pairs, a double bond is formed. Example: O=C=O in CO2 and C=C in ethene (C2H4).
  • When two atoms share three electron pairs, a triple bond is formed. Example: N≡N in N2 and H-C≡C-H in ethyne (C2H2).

docs.title: Lewis Structures
docs.text: Lewis dot structures show the bonding in molecules and ions in terms of shared pairs of electrons and the octet rule. They can be written using these steps:

docs.title: 1. Count the total electrons
docs.text:
• Add the valence electrons of all the combining atoms. Example: CH4 has 4 (from C) + 4 × 1 (from H) = 8 valence electrons.
  • For an anion, add one electron for each negative charge. CO32- has 2 extra electrons.
  • For a cation, subtract one electron for each positive charge. NH4+ has 1 electron less.

docs.title: 2. Write the skeletal structure
docs.text: • The least electronegative atom usually occupies the central position. In NF3 and CO32-, N and C are central, while F and O are terminal.

docs.title: 3. Distribute the electrons
docs.text:
• First place one shared pair for each single bond.
  • Use the remaining electron pairs either for multiple bonds or as lone pairs, so that each bonded atom gets an octet (H gets a duplet).

Lewis structures of some molecules

\[H_2:\quad H:H\quad or\quad H-H\] \[O_2:\quad \ddot{O}::\ddot{O}\quad or\quad \ddot{O}=\ddot{O}\] \[N_2:\quad :N:::N:\quad or\quad :N\equiv N:\] \[NF_3:\quad F-\underset{\underset{F}{|}}{\ddot{N}}-F\quad (each\ F\ carries\ three\ lone\ pairs)\] \[CO_3^{2-}:\quad \left[O=\underset{\underset{O}{|}}{C}-O\right]^{2-}\]

docs.title: Formal Charge
docs.text:
• In a polyatomic ion, the net charge belongs to the ion as a whole, not to a particular atom. However, it is useful to assign a formal charge to each atom.
  • The formal charge of an atom is the difference between the number of valence electrons in the free atom and the number of electrons assigned to it in the Lewis structure.
\[Formal\ charge\ (F.C.) = V - L - {1 \over 2}S\]

Where, V = total valence electrons in the free atom, L = total non-bonding (lone pair) electrons and S = total bonding (shared) electrons.

  • The counting assumes that the atom owns one electron of each shared pair and both electrons of a lone pair.

Formal charges in ozone, O3

In the Lewis structure of O3, the central O (1) has one lone pair, one double bond and one single bond. The end O (2) is double bonded with two lone pairs and the end O (3) is single bonded with three lone pairs.

\[Central\ O\ (1):\ 6 - 2 - {1 \over 2}(6) = +1\] \[End\ O\ (2):\ 6 - 4 - {1 \over 2}(4) = 0\] \[End\ O\ (3):\ 6 - 6 - {1 \over 2}(2) = -1\]

So O3 is written as O=O+-O-.

  • Formal charges do not indicate real charge separation in the molecule. They only help keep track of valence electrons.
  • Formal charges help to select the best Lewis structure: generally the lowest energy structure is the one with the smallest formal charges on the atoms.

docs.title: Limitations of the Octet Rule
docs.text: The octet rule is useful, especially for organic compounds and second period elements, but it is not universal. There are three types of exceptions.

docs.title: 1. Incomplete octet of the central atom
docs.text:
• In some compounds the central atom has fewer than eight electrons. This is common for elements with fewer than four valence electrons.
  • Examples: LiCl (Li has 2 electrons around it), BeH2 (Be has 4) and BCl3 (B has 6). AlCl3 and BF3 are similar.

docs.title: 2. Odd-electron molecules
docs.text: • Molecules with an odd number of electrons, like nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2), cannot satisfy the octet rule for all atoms.

docs.title: 3. Expanded octet
docs.text:
• Elements of the third period and beyond have 3d orbitals available (besides 3s and 3p) for bonding. So they can have more than eight electrons around the central atom.
  • Examples: PF5 (10 electrons around P), SF6 (12 electrons around S) and H2SO4 (12 electrons around S), and many coordination compounds.
  • Interestingly, sulphur also forms compounds that obey the octet rule. In SCl2, S has an octet around it.

docs.title: Other drawbacks of the octet theory
docs.text:
• The octet rule is based on the inertness of noble gases, but some noble gases (like xenon and krypton) do form compounds such as XeF2, KrF2 and XeOF2.
  • It does not explain the shape of molecules.
  • It says nothing about the energy of a molecule, so it cannot explain the relative stability of molecules.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Explain the formation of a chemical bond.

  • Atoms combine to attain a stable noble gas configuration (octet, or duplet for H) and to lower their energy.
  • They do this either by transfer of electrons, forming ions held by electrostatic attraction (ionic bond, e.g. NaCl), or by sharing electron pairs (covalent bond, e.g. Cl2).
  • The attractive force that holds the atoms or ions together in the resulting species is the chemical bond.

Write Lewis dot symbols for atoms of the following elements: Mg, Na, B, O, N, Br.

  • The number of dots equals the number of valence electrons.
\[Mg:\ \cdot Mg \cdot \quad (2) \qquad Na:\ Na\cdot \quad (1) \qquad B:\ \cdot\dot{B}\cdot \quad (3)\] \[O:\ :\ddot{O}\cdot \quad (6) \qquad N:\ \cdot\ddot{N}\cdot \quad (5) \qquad Br:\ :\ddot{\underset{..}{Br}}\cdot \quad (7)\]

Write Lewis symbols for the following atoms and ions: S and S2-; Al and Al3+; H and H-.

\[S:\ :\ddot{S}\cdot \qquad S^{2-}:\ \left[:\ddot{\underset{..}{S}}:\right]^{2-}\] \[Al:\ \cdot\dot{Al}\cdot \qquad Al^{3+}:\ [Al]^{3+}\] \[H:\ H\cdot \qquad H^-:\ [H:]^-\]

Define octet rule. Write its significance and limitations.

  • Octet rule: Atoms combine by transfer or sharing of valence electrons so as to have eight electrons (an octet) in their valence shells.
  • Significance: It explains why atoms combine, and helps to write the structures of most organic compounds and compounds of second period elements.
  • Limitations: It cannot explain compounds with an incomplete octet (BeH2, BCl3), odd-electron molecules (NO, NO2) and expanded octets (PF5, SF6). It also fails for compounds of noble gases (XeF2), and says nothing about the shapes of molecules or their relative stability.

Use Lewis symbols to show electron transfer between the following atoms to form cations and anions: (a) K and S (b) Ca and O (c) Al and N.

\[(a)\ 2K\cdot + \cdot\ddot{S}: → 2K^+ + [:\ddot{\underset{..}{S}}:]^{2-}\ \ or\ \ K_2S\] \[(b)\ Ca: + \cdot\ddot{O}: → Ca^{2+} + [:\ddot{\underset{..}{O}}:]^{2-}\ \ or\ \ CaO\] \[(c)\ \cdot\dot{Al}\cdot + \cdot\ddot{N}\cdot → Al^{3+} + [:\ddot{\underset{..}{N}}:]^{3-}\ \ or\ \ AlN\]

Write the correct Lewis structure for acetic acid, CH3COOH.

  • Acetic acid has 24 valence electrons (2 C × 4 + 4 H × 1 + 2 O × 6).
  • The methyl carbon forms four single bonds (three C-H and one C-C). There is no C=C double bond.
  • The carboxyl carbon forms one C=O double bond and one C-O single bond. Each O atom has two lone pairs.
\[H_3C-\underset{\underset{:O:}{||}}{C}-\ddot{O}-H\]

Write the Lewis dot structure of the CO molecule.

  • Step 1: Valence shell configurations are C: 2s22p2 and O: 2s22p4.
\[Total\ valence\ electrons = 4 + 6 = 10\]

  • Step 2: The skeletal structure is C O.

  • Step 3: A single bond between C and O, with the octet of O completed, leaves two electrons as a lone pair on C. Then carbon has only 4 electrons, so its octet is incomplete.

\[:C-\ddot{\underset{..}{O}}:\ \ (octet\ of\ C\ incomplete)\]
  • So we need a triple bond between C and O, which completes the octet of both atoms:
\[:C\equiv O:\]

Write the Lewis structure of the nitrite ion, NO2-.

  • Step 1: Count valence electrons of N (2s22p3), two O (2s22p4) and one extra electron for the negative charge.
\[Total = 5 + (2 \times 6) + 1 = 18\ electrons\]

  • Step 2: The skeletal structure is O N O.

  • Step 3: With two N-O single bonds and the octets of both O atoms completed, only two electrons remain as a lone pair on N. So N does not get an octet.

  • Hence a double bond is required between N and one of the O atoms. This gives two equivalent Lewis structures:

\[\left[\ddot{O}=\ddot{N}-\ddot{\underset{..}{O}}:\right]^- \quad or \quad \left[:\ddot{\underset{..}{O}}-\ddot{N}=\ddot{O}\right]^-\]

docs.title: Chemical Bonding | Molecular Orbital Theory
docs.text:
Molecular orbital theory describes bonding in terms of molecular orbitals that belong to the molecule as a whole, formed by the combination of atomic orbitals of comparable energies and proper symmetry.

  • Molecular orbital (MO) theory was developed by F. Hund and R.S. Mulliken in 1932.

docs.title: Salient Features of MO Theory
docs.text:
• Electrons in a molecule are present in molecular orbitals, just as electrons of atoms are present in atomic orbitals.
  • Atomic orbitals of comparable energies and proper symmetry combine to form molecular orbitals.
  • An electron in an atomic orbital is influenced by one nucleus, while an electron in a molecular orbital is influenced by two or more nuclei. So an atomic orbital is monocentric and a molecular orbital is polycentric.
  • The number of molecular orbitals formed is equal to the number of combining atomic orbitals. Two atomic orbitals form two molecular orbitals: a bonding molecular orbital and an antibonding molecular orbital.
  • The bonding MO has lower energy and greater stability than the corresponding antibonding MO.
  • A molecular orbital gives the electron probability distribution around the group of nuclei in a molecule.
  • Molecular orbitals are filled according to the aufbau principle, Pauli's exclusion principle and Hund's rule.

docs.title: Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO)
docs.text:
• Atomic orbitals are wave functions (\(\psi\)) obtained from the Schrödinger wave equation. Since this equation cannot be solved exactly for systems with more than one electron, an approximate method called linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO) is used.
  • For H2, the 1s orbitals of atoms A and B are represented by \(\psi_A\) and \(\psi_B\). Molecular orbitals form by addition and subtraction of these wave functions:
\[\psi_{MO} = \psi_A \pm \psi_B\] \[\sigma = \psi_A + \psi_B \quad (bonding\ MO)\] \[\sigma^* = \psi_A - \psi_B \quad (antibonding\ MO)\]
  • In a bonding MO, the electron waves of the two atoms reinforce each other (constructive interference). Electron density is concentrated between the nuclei, which reduces repulsion between the nuclei and holds them together. So a bonding MO has lower energy than the atomic orbitals.
  • In an antibonding MO, the electron waves cancel each other (destructive interference). Most of the electron density is away from the space between the nuclei, and there is a nodal plane (zero electron density) between them. Electrons in an antibonding MO destabilise the molecule.
  • The energy of the antibonding orbital is raised above the parent atomic orbitals, and the energy of the bonding orbital is lowered by the same amount. The total energy of the two MOs is the same as that of the two original atomic orbitals.

docs.title: Conditions for the Combination of Atomic Orbitals
1. Same or nearly the same energy
docs.text: • A 1s orbital can combine with another 1s orbital, but not with a 2s orbital, because the energy of 2s is much higher. (This is not true if the atoms are very different.)

docs.title: 2. Same symmetry about the molecular axis
docs.text:
• By convention, the z-axis is taken as the molecular axis. Orbitals with the same energy but different symmetry do not combine.
  • Example: 2pz of one atom can combine with 2pz of the other, but not with 2px or 2py.

docs.title: 3. Maximum overlap
docs.text: • Greater the extent of overlap, greater is the electron density between the nuclei in the molecular orbital.

docs.title: Types of Molecular Orbitals
docs.text:
• Molecular orbitals of diatomic molecules are named σ (sigma), π (pi), δ (delta), etc.
  • Sigma (σ) molecular orbitals are symmetrical around the bond axis. Examples: σ1s and σ*1s from 1s orbitals; σ2pz and σ*2pz from 2pz orbitals.
  • Pi (π) molecular orbitals are not symmetrical around the bond axis, because they have positive lobes above and negative lobes below the molecular plane. 2px and 2py orbitals form π and π* orbitals.
  • A π bonding MO has larger electron density above and below the internuclear axis. A π* antibonding MO has a node between the nuclei.

docs.title: Energy Level Diagram for Molecular Orbitals
docs.text:
The 2s and 2p atomic orbitals (eight atomic orbitals on two atoms) form eight molecular orbitals:

\[Antibonding\ MOs:\ \sigma^*2s,\ \sigma^*2p_z,\ \pi^*2p_x,\ \pi^*2p_y\] \[Bonding\ MOs:\ \sigma2s,\ \sigma2p_z,\ \pi2p_x,\ \pi2p_y\]
  • The order of energies was found experimentally from spectroscopic data.

docs.title: For O<sub>2</sub> and F<sub>2</sub>
docs.text: \[\sigma1s < \sigma^*1s < \sigma2s < \sigma^*2s < \sigma2p_z < (\pi2p_x = \pi2p_y) < (\pi^*2p_x = \pi^*2p_y) < \sigma^*2p_z\]

docs.title: For Li<sub>2</sub>, Be<sub>2</sub>, B<sub>2</sub>, C<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>
docs.text:
\[\sigma1s < \sigma^*1s < \sigma2s < \sigma^*2s < (\pi2p_x = \pi2p_y) < \sigma2p_z < (\pi^*2p_x = \pi^*2p_y) < \sigma^*2p_z\]
  • The key difference is that for these lighter molecules, the energy of σ2pz is higher than that of π2px and π2py. This is due to 2s-2p mixing.

docs.title: Electronic Configuration and Molecular Behaviour
docs.text: The distribution of electrons among the various molecular orbitals is called the electronic configuration of the molecule. Let Nb be the number of electrons in bonding orbitals and Na the number in antibonding orbitals.

docs.title: 1. Stability of molecules
docs.text:
• If Nb > Na, the bonding influence is stronger and the molecule is stable.
  • If Nb < Na, the antibonding influence is stronger and the molecule is unstable.

docs.title: 2. Bond order
docs.text:
Bond order (b.o.) is defined as one half the difference between the number of electrons present in the bonding and the antibonding orbitals.

\[Bond\ order\ (b.o.) = {1 \over 2}(N_b - N_a)\]
  • A positive bond order (Nb > Na) means a stable molecule. A negative or zero bond order (Nb ≤ Na) means an unstable molecule.

docs.title: 3. Nature of the bond
docs.text: • Bond order values of 1, 2 and 3 correspond to single, double and triple bonds.

docs.title: 4. Bond length
docs.text: • Bond length decreases as bond order increases.

docs.title: 5. Magnetic nature
docs.text:
• If all molecular orbitals are doubly occupied, the substance is diamagnetic (repelled by a magnetic field).
  • If one or more molecular orbitals are singly occupied, it is paramagnetic (attracted by a magnetic field). Example: O2.

docs.title: Bonding in Some Homonuclear Diatomic Molecules
1. Hydrogen molecule (H<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
\[H_2:\ (\sigma1s)^2\] \[Bond\ order = {2 - 0 \over 2} = 1\]
  • The two H atoms are joined by a single covalent bond. Bond dissociation energy = 438 kJ mol-1 and bond length = 74 pm.
  • There is no unpaired electron, so H2 is diamagnetic.

docs.title: 2. Helium molecule (He<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
\[He_2:\ (\sigma1s)^2(\sigma^*1s)^2\] \[Bond\ order = {1 \over 2}(2 - 2) = 0\]
  • He2 is unstable and does not exist. Similarly, Be2, with configuration (σ1s)2(σ*1s)2(σ2s)2(σ*2s)2, also does not exist.

docs.title: 3. Lithium molecule (Li<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
\[Li_2:\ (\sigma1s)^2(\sigma^*1s)^2(\sigma2s)^2\ \ or\ \ KK(\sigma2s)^2\] \[Bond\ order = {1 \over 2}(4 - 2) = 1\]
  • KK represents the closed K shell structure (σ1s)2(σ*1s)2.
  • Li2 is stable and diamagnetic. Li2 molecules are known to exist in the vapour phase.

docs.title: 4. Carbon molecule (C<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
\[C_2:\ (\sigma1s)^2(\sigma^*1s)^2(\sigma2s)^2(\sigma^*2s)^2(\pi2p_x^2 = \pi2p_y^2)\] \[or\ \ KK(\sigma2s)^2(\sigma^*2s)^2(\pi2p_x^2 = \pi2p_y^2)\] \[Bond\ order = {1 \over 2}(8 - 4) = 2\]
  • C2 is diamagnetic and has been detected in the vapour phase.
  • Interestingly, the double bond in C2 consists of two pi bonds, because the four bonding electrons are in two pi molecular orbitals. In most other molecules, a double bond is one sigma + one pi bond.

docs.title: 5. Oxygen molecule (O<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
• Each O atom (1s22s22p4) has 8 electrons, so O2 has 16 electrons.
\[O_2:\ (\sigma1s)^2(\sigma^*1s)^2(\sigma2s)^2(\sigma^*2s)^2(\sigma2p_z)^2(\pi2p_x^2 = \pi2p_y^2)(\pi^*2p_x^1 = \pi^*2p_y^1)\] \[or\ \ KK(\sigma2s)^2(\sigma^*2s)^2(\sigma2p_z)^2(\pi2p_x^2 = \pi2p_y^2)(\pi^*2p_x^1 = \pi^*2p_y^1)\] \[Bond\ order = {1 \over 2}(10 - 6) = 2\]
  • So the O atoms are held by a double bond.
  • O2 has two unpaired electrons in π*2px and π*2py. So MO theory correctly predicts that O2 is paramagnetic, which matches experiment. (The Lewis structure cannot explain this.)

docs.title: MO occupancy for B<sub>2</sub> to Ne<sub>2</sub>
docs.text:
Molecule Valence electron configuration Bond order Magnetic nature Bond energy (kJ mol-1) Bond length (pm) B2 (σ2s)2(σ*2s)2(π2p)2 1 Paramagnetic 290 159 C2 (σ2s)2(σ*2s)2(π2p)4 2 Diamagnetic 620 131 N2 (σ2s)2(σ*2s)2(π2p)4(σ2p)2 3 Diamagnetic 945 110 O2 (σ2s)2(σ*2s)2(σ2p)2(π2p)4(π*2p)2 2 Paramagnetic 498 121 F2 (σ2s)2(σ*2s)2(σ2p)2(π2p)4(π*2p)4 1 Diamagnetic 159 143 Ne2 (σ2s)2(σ*2s)2(σ2p)2(π2p)4(π*2p)4(σ*2p)2 0 - - -

Conclusion

From B2 to N2, bond order rises from 1 to 3, bond energy increases and bond length decreases. From N2 to Ne2, the extra electrons enter antibonding orbitals, so bond order falls to 0 and Ne2 does not exist.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Write the important conditions required for the linear combination of atomic orbitals to form molecular orbitals.

  • The combining atomic orbitals must have the same or nearly the same energy.
  • They must have the same symmetry about the molecular axis.
  • They must overlap to the maximum extent.

Use molecular orbital theory to explain why the Be2 molecule does not exist.

  • Be (1s22s2) has 4 electrons, so Be2 has 8 electrons.
\[Be_2:\ (\sigma1s)^2(\sigma^*1s)^2(\sigma2s)^2(\sigma^*2s)^2\] \[Bond\ order = {1 \over 2}(4 - 4) = 0\]
  • A bond order of zero means there is no net bonding. So Be2 does not exist.

Compare the relative stability of the following species and indicate their magnetic properties: O2, O2+, O2- (superoxide), O22- (peroxide).

  • O2 has 16 electrons: KK(σ2s)2(σ*2s)2(σ2pz)2(π2p)4(π*2p)2. Removing or adding electrons changes only the π* occupancy.
\[O_2^+\ (15\ e^-):\ b.o. = {1 \over 2}(10 - 5) = 2.5\] \[O_2\ (16\ e^-):\ b.o. = {1 \over 2}(10 - 6) = 2\] \[O_2^-\ (17\ e^-):\ b.o. = {1 \over 2}(10 - 7) = 1.5\] \[O_2^{2-}\ (18\ e^-):\ b.o. = {1 \over 2}(10 - 8) = 1\]
  • Stability increases with bond order: O22- < O2- < O2 < O2+.
  • O2+ (1 unpaired electron), O2 (2 unpaired) and O2- (1 unpaired) are paramagnetic. O22- has all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic.

What is meant by the term bond order? Calculate the bond order of: N2, O2, O2+ and O2-.

  • Bond order is one half of the difference between the number of electrons in bonding (Nb) and antibonding (Na) molecular orbitals.
\[N_2:\ KK(\sigma2s)^2(\sigma^*2s)^2(\pi2p_x^2 = \pi2p_y^2)(\sigma2p_z)^2\] \[b.o.(N_2) = {1 \over 2}(8 - 2) = 3\] \[b.o.(O_2) = {1 \over 2}(8 - 4) = 2\] \[b.o.(O_2^+) = {1 \over 2}(8 - 3) = 2.5\] \[b.o.(O_2^-) = {1 \over 2}(8 - 5) = 1.5\]

(Here only valence electrons are counted; the KK electrons cancel out.)

Write the significance of a plus and a minus sign shown in representing the orbitals.

  • The signs show the phase (sign of the wave function, \(\psi\)) of the orbital lobes; they do not represent electric charge.
  • When lobes of the same sign overlap, the waves add (constructive interference) and a bonding MO forms. When lobes of opposite sign overlap, the waves cancel and an antibonding MO forms.

docs.title: Chemical Bonding | Polarity of Bonds and Dipole Moment
Chemical Bonding | Polarity of Bonds and Dipole Moment
Polarity of Bonds
docs.text:
• A 100% ionic or 100% covalent bond is an ideal situation. In reality, no bond or compound is completely ionic or completely covalent.
  • When a covalent bond is formed between two similar atoms (H2, O2, Cl2, N2, F2), the shared pair is equally attracted by both atoms. It lies exactly between the two nuclei. Such a bond is a non-polar covalent bond.
  • In a heteronuclear molecule like HF, the shared pair shifts towards fluorine, because the electronegativity of F is much greater than that of H. Such a bond is a polar covalent bond.
\[\overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{F}\]

docs.title: Dipole Moment
docs.text:
As a result of polarisation, the molecule possesses a dipole moment, which is defined as the product of the magnitude of the charge and the distance between the centres of positive and negative charge.

\[Dipole\ moment\ (\mu) = Charge\ (Q) \times Distance\ of\ separation\ (r)\] \[1\ D = 3.33564 \times 10^{-30}\ C\ m\]

Where, D = Debye, C = coulomb and m = metre.

  • Dipole moment is usually expressed in Debye (D) units, named after Peter Debye.
  • Dipole moment is a vector quantity. It is shown by a crossed arrow (\(+\!\!\rightarrow\)) above the Lewis structure, with the tail at the positive centre and the head pointing towards the negative centre. For HF, the arrow points from H to F.

docs.title: Dipole moment of polyatomic molecules
docs.text:
• In polyatomic molecules, the dipole moment depends on the individual bond dipoles and also on the spatial arrangement of the bonds.
  • The dipole moment of the molecule is the vector sum of the bond dipoles.

docs.title: 1. H<sub>2</sub>O
docs.text:
• H2O is bent, with the two O-H bonds at 104.5°. The bond dipoles do not cancel and give a net dipole moment:
\[\mu = 1.85\ D = 1.85 \times 3.33564 \times 10^{-30}\ C\ m = 6.17 \times 10^{-30}\ C\ m\]

docs.title: 2. BeF<sub>2</sub>
docs.text: • BeF2 is linear. The two equal Be-F bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel each other. So the dipole moment of BeF2 is zero.

docs.title: 3. BF<sub>3</sub>
docs.text: • BF3 is trigonal planar with B-F bonds at 120°. The resultant of any two bond dipoles is equal and opposite to the third, so the net dipole moment is zero.

docs.title: 4. NH<sub>3</sub> and NF<sub>3</sub>
docs.text:
• Both are pyramidal with one lone pair on nitrogen. Even though F is more electronegative than N, the dipole moment of NH3 (4.90 × 10-30 C m) is much greater than that of NF3 (0.80 × 10-30 C m).
  • In NH3, the N-H bond dipoles point towards N, in the same direction as the orbital dipole of the lone pair. They add up.
  • In NF3, the N-F bond dipoles point away from N, opposite to the lone pair dipole. The lone pair dipole cancels part of the bond moments, giving a low dipole moment.

docs.title: Dipole moments of some molecules
docs.text:
Type of Molecule Example Dipole Moment, μ (D) Geometry AB HF 1.78 linear AB HCl 1.07 linear AB HBr 0.79 linear AB HI 0.38 linear AB H2 0 linear AB2 H2O 1.85 bent AB2 H2S 0.95 bent AB2 CO2 0 linear AB3 NH3 1.47 trigonal pyramidal AB3 NF3 0.23 trigonal pyramidal AB3 BF3 0 trigonal planar AB4 CH4 0 tetrahedral AB4 CHCl3 1.04 tetrahedral AB4 CCl4 0 tetrahedral

Conclusion

Symmetrical molecules (linear AB2, trigonal planar AB3, tetrahedral AB4) with identical bonds have zero dipole moment. So dipole moment helps us predict the shape of molecules and the polarity of bonds.

docs.title: Fajans' Rules (Covalent Character of Ionic Bonds)
docs.text:
Just as all covalent bonds have some partial ionic character, ionic bonds also have partial covalent character. Fajans explained this with the following rules:

  • Size of ions: The smaller the size of the cation and the larger the size of the anion, the greater is the covalent character of the ionic bond.
  • Charge on cation: The greater the charge on the cation, the greater is the covalent character.

  • Electronic configuration of cation: For cations of the same size and charge, a cation with configuration (n-1)dnns0 (typical of transition metals) is more polarising than one with a noble gas configuration ns2np6 (typical of alkali and alkaline earth metal cations).

  • The cation polarises the anion: it pulls electron density of the anion towards itself, increasing electron density between the two nuclei. This is just what happens in a covalent bond.

  • The polarising power of the cation, the polarisability of the anion and the extent of distortion of the anion decide the percentage covalent character of an ionic bond.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Although both CO2 and H2O are triatomic molecules, the shape of H2O is bent while that of CO2 is linear. Explain this on the basis of dipole moment.

  • CO2 has zero dipole moment. Since C=O bonds are polar, the two bond dipoles must be equal and opposite, which is possible only if the molecule is linear (O=C=O at 180°).
  • H2O has a dipole moment of 1.85 D. The two O-H bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule must be bent (bond angle 104.5°).

Write the significance/applications of dipole moment.

  • It helps to decide whether a molecule is polar or non-polar.
  • It helps to predict the shape of molecules. Example: zero dipole moment of CO2 and BF3 shows they are linear and trigonal planar respectively.
  • It helps to find the percentage ionic character of a bond.
  • It helps to distinguish between cis and trans isomers; the cis isomer usually has a higher dipole moment.

Explain with the help of a suitable example a polar covalent bond.

  • When a covalent bond is formed between two atoms with different electronegativities, the shared pair shifts towards the more electronegative atom.
  • Example: In HCl, chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen. The shared pair lies closer to Cl, so Cl gets a partial negative charge (δ-) and H gets a partial positive charge (δ+). This bond is a polar covalent bond.
\[\overset{\delta+}{H} - \overset{\delta-}{Cl}\]

Define electronegativity. How does it differ from electron gain enthalpy?

  • Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a chemical compound to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself.
  • Electron gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron.
Electronegativity Electron gain enthalpy Property of a bonded atom Property of an isolated atom Relative number with no units Measurable energy in kJ mol-1 Relates to attraction for a shared pair Relates to gain of an extra electron

Arrange the bonds in order of increasing ionic character in the molecules: LiF, K2O, N2, SO2 and ClF3.

  • Ionic character increases with increase in electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms. N2 has zero difference, and K-O has the largest difference.
\[N_2 < SO_2 < ClF_3 < LiF < K_2O\]

Explain why BeH2 molecule has a zero dipole moment although the Be-H bonds are polar.

  • BeH2 is a linear molecule (H-Be-H, 180°).
  • The two Be-H bond dipoles are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel each other. Hence the net dipole moment is zero.

Which out of NH3 and NF3 has higher dipole moment and why?

  • NH3 has the higher dipole moment.
  • In NH3, the lone pair dipole on N and the resultant of the N-H bond dipoles are in the same direction, so they add up.
  • In NF3, the N-F bond dipoles point towards F, opposite to the lone pair dipole, so they partly cancel.

docs.title: Chemical Bonding | Valence Bond Theory
docs.text:
Valence bond theory explains the formation of a covalent bond in terms of the overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals of the bonding atoms, with pairing of electrons of opposite spins.

  • The Lewis approach helps to write structures but does not explain how a bond forms. It also cannot explain why H2 (435.8 kJ mol-1, 74 pm) and F2 (150.6 kJ mol-1, 144 pm) differ in bond enthalpy and bond length, even though both have a single bond.
  • VSEPR theory predicts shapes but does not explain them theoretically.
  • To overcome these limitations, two quantum mechanical theories were introduced: Valence Bond (VB) theory and Molecular Orbital (MO) theory.
  • VB theory was introduced by Heitler and London (1927) and developed further by Pauling and others.

docs.title: Formation of the Hydrogen Molecule
docs.text:
• Consider two hydrogen atoms A and B with nuclei NA, NB and electrons eA, eB.
  • When they are far apart, there is no interaction. As they approach each other, new attractive and repulsive forces begin to act.

docs.title: Attractive forces
docs.text:
• Between the nucleus of an atom and its own electron: NA-eA and NB-eB.
  • Between the nucleus of one atom and the electron of the other: NA-eB and NB-eA.

docs.title: Repulsive forces
docs.text:
• Between the electrons of the two atoms: eA-eB.

  • Between the nuclei of the two atoms: NA-NB.

  • Experimentally, the new attractive forces are stronger than the new repulsive forces. So as the atoms come closer, the potential energy decreases.

  • At a certain distance, attraction balances repulsion and the system reaches minimum energy. The two H atoms are now bonded, with a bond length of 74 pm.
  • The energy released when the bond forms is the bond enthalpy. Conversely, 435.8 kJ is needed to dissociate one mole of H2:
\[H_{2(g)} + 435.8\ kJ\ mol^{-1} → H_{(g)} + H_{(g)}\]
  • If the nuclei are brought still closer than 74 pm, the energy rises sharply and the molecule becomes unstable.

docs.title: Orbital Overlap Concept
docs.text:
• When two H atoms are close enough at the minimum energy state, their atomic orbitals partially interpenetrate. This partial merging of atomic orbitals is called overlapping of atomic orbitals, and it results in pairing of electrons.
  • The extent of overlap decides the strength of a covalent bond. Greater the overlap, stronger the bond.

Conclusion

According to the orbital overlap concept, a covalent bond is formed by pairing of electrons of opposite spins present in half-filled valence shell orbitals of the two atoms.

docs.title: Directional Properties of Bonds
docs.text:
• In polyatomic molecules like CH4, NH3 and H2O, the shape of the molecule is also important. VB theory explains shapes using overlap and hybridisation of atomic orbitals.
  • Overlap of orbitals can be positive (same sign of lobes overlapping, forms a bond), negative (opposite signs, no bond) or zero (orbitals perpendicular, no net overlap).

docs.title: Why simple overlap cannot explain the shape of CH<sub>4</sub>
docs.text:
• Carbon in its ground state is [He]2s22p2, and in the excited state [He]2s12px12py12pz1. The energy for this excitation is compensated by the energy released on bond formation.
  • These four half-filled orbitals can overlap with the 1s orbitals of four H atoms to form four C-H bonds.
  • But the three p orbitals are at 90° to each other, so three H-C-H angles would be 90°. The 2s orbital is spherical, so the direction of the fourth bond cannot be fixed.
  • This does not fit the actual tetrahedral angle of 109.5°. Similarly, simple overlap predicts 90° for NH3 and H2O, while the actual angles are 107° and 104.5°. This problem is solved by hybridisation.

docs.title: Types of Overlapping: Sigma and Pi Bonds
1. Sigma (σ) Bond
docs.text:
A sigma bond is formed by the end to end (head-on) overlap of bonding orbitals along the internuclear axis. It is also called axial overlap.

  • s-s overlap: Two half-filled s orbitals overlap along the internuclear axis. Example: H2.
  • s-p overlap: A half-filled s orbital of one atom overlaps with a half-filled p orbital of another atom. Example: HF, HCl.
  • p-p overlap: Half-filled p orbitals of two atoms overlap end to end. Example: Cl2, F2.

docs.title: 2. Pi (π) Bond
docs.text:
A pi bond is formed when the atomic orbitals overlap sideways, with their axes parallel to each other and perpendicular to the internuclear axis.

  • The pi bond consists of two saucer-shaped charge clouds, above and below the plane of the participating atoms.

docs.title: Strength of Sigma and Pi Bonds
docs.text:
• In a sigma bond, orbitals overlap to a larger extent. In a pi bond, overlap is smaller.
  • So a sigma bond is stronger than a pi bond.
  • A pi bond between two atoms is always formed in addition to a sigma bond. It is present in molecules with double or triple bonds.
Sigma (σ) bond Pi (π) bond Formed by axial (head-on) overlap Formed by sideways overlap Can form from s-s, s-p, p-p or hybrid orbitals Forms only from unhybridised p (or d) orbitals Overlap is large, so bond is strong Overlap is small, so bond is weaker Electron density lies along the internuclear axis Electron density lies above and below the internuclear axis Can exist alone (single bond) Always exists along with a sigma bond Free rotation about the bond is possible Free rotation is restricted

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Explain the formation of H2 molecule on the basis of valence bond theory.

  • As two H atoms approach each other, the attraction between each nucleus and the electron of the other atom increases, along with nucleus-nucleus and electron-electron repulsion.
  • Since the new attractive forces are greater than the repulsive forces, the energy of the system decreases.
  • At an internuclear distance of 74 pm, the energy is minimum (435.8 kJ mol-1 lower than the separate atoms). Here the 1s orbitals overlap and the two electrons of opposite spin pair up to form the H-H sigma bond.

Considering x-axis as the internuclear axis, which of the following will not form a sigma bond and why? (a) 1s and 1s (b) 1s and 2px (c) 2py and 2py (d) 1s and 2s.

  • (c) 2py and 2py will not form a sigma bond.
  • With x as the internuclear axis, the 2py orbitals are perpendicular to the axis. They can only overlap sideways and form a pi bond.
  • The pairs (a), (b) and (d) can overlap along the x-axis and form sigma bonds.

What do you understand by bond pairs and lone pairs of electrons? Illustrate by giving one example of each type.

  • Bond pair: An electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond. Example: each O-H bond in H2O has one bond pair.
  • Lone pair: A valence electron pair on an atom that is not shared in bonding. Example: O in H2O has two lone pairs and N in NH3 has one lone pair.

docs.title: Chemical Bonding | VSEPR Theory
docs.text:
The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory predicts the shapes of covalent molecules from the repulsions between electron pairs in the valence shell of the central atom.

  • The Lewis concept cannot explain the shapes of molecules. VSEPR theory gives a simple way to predict them.
  • It was proposed by Sidgwick and Powell (1940) and further developed by Nyholm and Gillespie (1957).

docs.title: Postulates of VSEPR Theory
docs.text:
• The shape of a molecule depends on the number of valence shell electron pairs (bonded or non-bonded) around the central atom.
  • Electron pairs in the valence shell repel one another because their electron clouds are negatively charged.
  • These electron pairs occupy positions in space that minimise repulsion and so maximise the distance between them.
  • The valence shell is taken as a sphere, with the electron pairs placed on its surface at maximum distance from one another.
  • A multiple bond is treated as if it were a single electron pair. The two or three electron pairs of a multiple bond act as a single super pair.
  • Where two or more resonance structures can represent a molecule, VSEPR applies to any of them.

docs.title: Order of repulsion
docs.text:
\[lone\ pair\ (lp) - lone\ pair\ (lp) > lone\ pair\ (lp) - bond\ pair\ (bp) > bond\ pair\ (bp) - bond\ pair\ (bp)\]
  • A lone pair is localised on the central atom, while a bond pair is shared between two atoms.
  • So a lone pair occupies more space than a bond pair. This causes greater repulsion involving lone pairs, which distorts the ideal shape and changes bond angles.

docs.title: Molecules with No Lone Pair on the Central Atom
docs.text:
• For molecules of type ABx (A = central atom, B = surrounding atoms), the shape is the same as the arrangement of electron pairs.
Number of electron pairs Arrangement / Geometry Bond angle Examples 2 Linear 180° BeCl2, HgCl2 3 Trigonal planar 120° BF3 4 Tetrahedral 109.5° CH4, NH4+ 5 Trigonal bipyramidal 120° and 90° PCl5 6 Octahedral 90° SF6

docs.title: Molecules with Lone Pairs on the Central Atom
docs.text:
• For molecules of type ABxEy (E = lone pair), the arrangement of electron pairs is decided by the total number of pairs, but the shape is described by the positions of the atoms only.
Molecule type Bond pairs Lone pairs Arrangement of electron pairs Shape Examples AB2E 2 1 Trigonal planar Bent SO2, O3 AB3E 3 1 Tetrahedral Trigonal pyramidal NH3 AB2E2 2 2 Tetrahedral Bent H2O AB4E 4 1 Trigonal bipyramidal See-saw SF4 AB3E2 3 2 Trigonal bipyramidal T-shape ClF3 AB5E 5 1 Octahedral Square pyramid BrF5 AB4E2 4 2 Octahedral Square planar XeF4

docs.title: 1. SO<sub>2</sub> (AB<sub>2</sub>E)
docs.text:
• With three electron "pairs" (two S=O super pairs and one lone pair), the shape should be trigonal planar with 120° angles.
  • Because lp-bp repulsion is greater than bp-bp repulsion, the O-S-O angle reduces to 119.5° and the molecule is bent (V-shaped).

docs.title: 2. NH<sub>3</sub> (AB<sub>3</sub>E)
docs.text:
• With four electron pairs, NH3 would be tetrahedral if all were bond pairs.
  • The one lone pair repels the bond pairs more strongly, so the H-N-H angle reduces from 109.5° to 107° and the shape is trigonal pyramidal.

docs.title: 3. H<sub>2</sub>O (AB<sub>2</sub>E<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
• With two lone pairs and two bond pairs, the arrangement is tetrahedral.
  • Since lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp, the H-O-H angle reduces from 109.5° to 104.5°. The shape is bent (angular), a distorted tetrahedron.

docs.title: 4. SF<sub>4</sub> (AB<sub>4</sub>E)
docs.text:
• The five electron pairs have a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement. The lone pair can sit at an axial or an equatorial position.
  • At an axial position, the lone pair has three lp-bp repulsions at 90°. At an equatorial position, it has only two lp-bp repulsions at 90°.
  • So the lone pair takes the equatorial position. The shape is a distorted tetrahedron, also called a folded square or see-saw.

docs.title: 5. ClF<sub>3</sub> (AB<sub>3</sub>E<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
• The five electron pairs again have a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement.
  • When both lone pairs are at equatorial positions, there are the fewest lp-lp and lp-bp repulsions at 90°. So this arrangement is the most stable, and the shape is T-shaped.

Note

VSEPR theory predicts the geometry of a large number of molecules, especially compounds of p-block elements, quite accurately, even when the energy difference between possible structures is very small. However, its theoretical basis is still a subject of discussion.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Discuss the shape of the following molecules using the VSEPR model: BeCl2, BCl3, SiCl4, AsF5, H2S, PH3.

Molecule Bond pairs Lone pairs Type Shape BeCl2 2 0 AB2 Linear (180°) BCl3 3 0 AB3 Trigonal planar (120°) SiCl4 4 0 AB4 Tetrahedral (109.5°) AsF5 5 0 AB5 Trigonal bipyramidal H2S 2 2 AB2E2 Bent PH3 3 1 AB3E Trigonal pyramidal
  • Be, B, Si and As use all their valence electrons in bonding, so there is no lone pair and the shape matches the electron pair arrangement.
  • S in H2S has 6 valence electrons: 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs. P in PH3 has 5 valence electrons: 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair. The lone pairs distort the tetrahedral arrangement.

Although geometries of NH3 and H2O molecules are distorted tetrahedral, bond angle in water is less than that of ammonia. Discuss.

  • In NH3, N has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair. The lp-bp repulsion reduces the angle from 109.5° to 107°.
  • In H2O, O has 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs. Now there is lp-lp repulsion as well, which is the strongest repulsion.
  • The two lone pairs push the bond pairs closer together, so the angle reduces further to 104.5°.

Apart from tetrahedral geometry, another possible geometry for CH4 is square planar with the four H atoms at the corners of the square and the C atom at its centre. Explain why CH4 is not square planar.

  • In a square planar arrangement, the H-C-H bond angle would be 90°. In a tetrahedral arrangement it is 109.5°.
  • The four bond pairs are farther apart in the tetrahedral arrangement, so repulsion between them is less and the molecule is more stable.
  • Also, carbon in CH4 is sp3 hybridised, and sp3 hybrid orbitals point towards the corners of a tetrahedron. Square planar geometry would need dsp2 hybridisation, which is not possible for carbon as it has no d orbitals.

docs.title: Coordination Compounds | Crystal Field Theory
docs.text: The crystal field theory (CFT) is an electrostatic model which considers the metal-ligand bond to be ionic, arising purely from electrostatic interactions between the metal ion and the ligand.

docs.title: Basic Idea of Crystal Field Theory
docs.text:
• Ligands are treated as point charges (if they are anions) or dipoles (if they are neutral molecules).
  • The five d orbitals of an isolated gaseous metal atom/ion have the same energy, i.e., they are degenerate.
  • This degeneracy is kept if a spherically symmetrical field of negative charges surrounds the metal ion.
  • When the negative field is due to ligands (anions or negative ends of dipoles like NH3 and H2O), it becomes asymmetrical and the degeneracy of the d orbitals is lifted. The d orbitals split into groups of different energy.
  • The pattern of splitting depends on the nature (geometry) of the crystal field.

docs.title: Crystal Field Splitting in Octahedral Complexes
docs.text:
• In an octahedral complex, six ligands approach the metal ion along the x, y and z axes.
  • The electrons in the metal d orbitals are repelled by the electrons (negative charges) of the ligands. This repulsion is more when the d orbital points towards the ligands.
  • The dx2-y2 and dz2 orbitals point along the axes, towards the ligands. They experience more repulsion and are raised in energy. This set of two orbitals is called the eg set.
  • The dxy, dyz and dxz orbitals point between the axes. They are lowered in energy relative to the average energy in a spherical field. This set of three orbitals is called the t2g set.
  • The splitting of the degenerate levels due to ligands in a definite geometry is called crystal field splitting. The energy separation is denoted by Δo (o for octahedral).
  • The average energy (barycentre) is kept the same:
\[Energy\ of\ e_g\ orbitals = +{3 \over 5}Δ_o = +0.6Δ_o\] \[Energy\ of\ t_{2g}\ orbitals = -{2 \over 5}Δ_o = -0.4Δ_o\] \[2(+0.6Δ_o) + 3(-0.4Δ_o) = 0\]
  • The magnitude of Δo depends on the field produced by the ligand and the charge on the metal ion. Strong field ligands produce a large splitting; weak field ligands produce a small splitting.

docs.title: Spectrochemical Series
docs.text:
The ligands arranged in order of increasing field strength (increasing Δo) form the spectrochemical series. It is an experimentally determined series, based on the absorption of light by complexes with different ligands.

\[I^- < Br^- < SCN^- < Cl^- < S^{2-} < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O\] \[< NCS^- < edta^{4-} < NH_3 < en < CN^- < CO\]
  • Ligands at the left end (I-, Br-, Cl-, F-) are weak field ligands.
  • Ligands at the right end (en, CN-, CO) are strong field ligands.

docs.title: Filling of Electrons: High Spin and Low Spin Complexes
docs.text:
• In d1, d2 and d3 ions, electrons occupy the t2g orbitals singly, according to Hund's rule.
  • For a d4 ion, there are two choices for the fourth electron:
    1. Enter the t2g level and pair with an existing electron. This costs the pairing energy, P (energy required for pairing electrons in a single orbital).
    2. Avoid pairing by entering the higher eg level. This costs energy Δo.
  • Which one occurs depends on the relative magnitudes of Δo and P:
\[If\ Δ_o < P:\ t_{2g}^3 e_g^1\ (weak\ field\ ligand,\ high\ spin\ complex)\] \[If\ Δ_o > P:\ t_{2g}^4 e_g^0\ (strong\ field\ ligand,\ low\ spin\ complex)\]
  • Calculations show that d4 to d7 coordination entities are more stable for the strong field case than the weak field case.
d electrons Weak field (Δo < P), high spin Unpaired Strong field (Δo > P), low spin Unpaired d1 t2g1 1 t2g1 1 d2 t2g2 2 t2g2 2 d3 t2g3 3 t2g3 3 d4 t2g3eg1 4 t2g4 2 d5 t2g3eg2 5 t2g5 1 d6 t2g4eg2 4 t2g6 0 d7 t2g5eg2 3 t2g6eg1 1 d8 t2g6eg2 2 t2g6eg2 2 d9 t2g6eg3 1 t2g6eg3 1 d10 t2g6eg4 0 t2g6eg4 0

Note

High spin and low spin arrangements differ only for d4 to d7 ions. For d1-d3 and d8-d10, both fields give the same arrangement.

  • The energy gained by the electrons due to splitting is called the crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE). For an octahedral complex:
\[CFSE = (-0.4\ n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6\ n_{e_g})Δ_o + (number\ of\ extra\ pairs)P\]

docs.title: Crystal Field Splitting in Tetrahedral Complexes
docs.text:
• In tetrahedral complexes, the d orbital splitting is inverted compared with octahedral splitting. The e set (dx2-y2, dz2) is lower and the t2 set (dxy, dyz, dxz) is higher in energy.
  • The splitting is smaller than in octahedral complexes. For the same metal, same ligands and same metal-ligand distances:
\[Δ_t = {4 \over 9}Δ_o\]
  • Since Δt is small, it is usually less than the pairing energy. Therefore, low spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely observed.

docs.title: Colour in Coordination Compounds
docs.text:
• Transition metal complexes show a wide range of colours. When white light passes through a complex, some part of the visible spectrum is absorbed.
  • The colour of the complex is complementary to the colour absorbed. For example, if green light is absorbed, the complex appears red.
Coordination entity Wavelength absorbed (nm) Colour of light absorbed Colour of complex [CoCl(NH3)5]2+ 535 Yellow Violet [Co(NH3)5(H2O)]3+ 500 Blue green Red [Co(NH3)6]3+ 475 Blue Yellow orange [Co(CN)6]3- 310 Ultraviolet Pale yellow [Cu(H2O)4]2+ 600 Red Blue [Ti(H2O)6]3+ 498 Blue green Purple

docs.title: Explanation by CFT: d-d transition
docs.text:
• Consider [Ti(H2O)6]3+, which is violet. It is octahedral and Ti3+ is a 3d1 system.
  • In the ground state, the single electron is in the t2g level. The next higher level available is the empty eg level.
  • When light of the yellow-green region is absorbed, the electron is excited from t2g to eg:
\[t_{2g}^1 e_g^0 \xrightarrow{hν} t_{2g}^0 e_g^1\]
  • Hence, the complex appears violet. CFT attributes the colour of coordination compounds to this d-d transition of electrons.
  • In the absence of ligands, crystal field splitting does not occur and the substance is colourless:
    • Removing water from [Ti(H2O)6]Cl3 by heating makes it colourless.
    • Anhydrous CuSO4 is white, but CuSO4.5H2O is blue.

docs.title: Effect of ligand on colour
docs.text:
• When ethane-1,2-diamine (en) is gradually added to a green solution of [Ni(H2O)6]2+ in en:Ni ratios 1:1, 2:1 and 3:1, water is replaced step by step and the colour changes:
\[[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}_{(aq)}\ (green) + en → [Ni(H_2O)_4(en)]^{2+}_{(aq)}\ (pale\ blue) + 2H_2O\] \[[Ni(H_2O)_4(en)]^{2+}_{(aq)} + en → [Ni(H_2O)_2(en)_2]^{2+}_{(aq)}\ (blue/purple) + 2H_2O\] \[[Ni(H_2O)_2(en)_2]^{2+}_{(aq)} + en → [Ni(en)_3]^{2+}_{(aq)}\ (violet) + 2H_2O\]
  • en is a stronger field ligand than H2O. As more en is attached, Δo increases, so light of higher energy (shorter wavelength) is absorbed and the observed colour changes.

docs.title: Colour of some gem stones
docs.text:
• Ruby is aluminium oxide (Al2O3) containing about 0.5-1% Cr3+ ions (d3) randomly placed at positions normally occupied by Al3+. These are octahedral chromium(III) complexes in the alumina lattice, and d-d transitions at these centres give the colour.
  • In emerald, Cr3+ ions occupy octahedral sites in the mineral beryl (Be3Al2Si6O18). The absorption bands are shifted to longer wavelengths (yellow-red and blue) compared to ruby, so emerald transmits light in the green region.

docs.title: Limitations of Crystal Field Theory
docs.text:
• CFT explains the formation, structures, colour and magnetic properties of coordination compounds to a large extent. However:
    1. If ligands are point charges, anionic ligands should exert the greatest splitting. But anionic ligands are actually found at the low end of the spectrochemical series.
    2. It does not take into account the covalent character of the bonding between the ligand and the central atom.
  • These weaknesses are explained by ligand field theory (LFT) and molecular orbital theory.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The hexaquo manganese(II) ion contains five unpaired electrons, while the hexacyano ion contains only one unpaired electron. Explain using Crystal Field Theory.

Mn2+ has the configuration 3d5.

  • H2O is a weak field ligand (Δo < P). The electrons do not pair and the configuration is t2g3eg2, giving five unpaired electrons (high spin).

  • CN- is a strong field ligand (Δo > P). The electrons pair up in t2g and the configuration is t2g5eg0, giving only one unpaired electron (low spin).

What is crystal field splitting energy? How does the magnitude of Δo decide the actual configuration of d orbitals in a coordination entity?

  • When ligands approach the metal ion, the degenerate d orbitals split into two sets of different energy. The energy difference between the two sets (t2g and eg in an octahedral field) is called the crystal field splitting energy, Δo.

  • If Δo < P (weak field ligand), electrons enter the eg orbitals before pairing, giving a high spin configuration (e.g. d4: t2g3eg1).

  • If Δo > P (strong field ligand), electrons pair in the t2g orbitals first, giving a low spin configuration (e.g. d4: t2g4eg0).

What is spectrochemical series? Explain the difference between a weak field ligand and a strong field ligand.

The arrangement of ligands in order of increasing crystal field splitting (field strength) is called the spectrochemical series:

\[I^- < Br^- < SCN^- < Cl^- < S^{2-} < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < edta^{4-} < NH_3 < en < CN^- < CO\]

  • Weak field ligand: Produces small splitting, Δo < P. Forms high spin complexes. Examples: Cl-, F-.

  • Strong field ligand: Produces large splitting, Δo > P. Forms low spin complexes. Examples: CN-, CO.

A solution of [Ni(H2O)6]2+ is green but a solution of [Ni(CN)4]2- is colourless. Explain.

  • In [Ni(H2O)6]2+, Ni2+ (3d8) has two unpaired electrons with weak field H2O. A d-d transition absorbs red light and the complementary colour, green, is seen.
