  • In [Ni(CN)4]2-, CN- is a strong field ligand. All electrons are paired (square planar, dsp2) and the splitting is large, so no d-d transition occurs in the visible region. Hence the solution is colourless.

[Fe(CN)6]4- and [Fe(H2O)6]2+ are of different colours in dilute solutions. Why?

In both, Fe is in the +2 state (3d6). But CN- is a strong field ligand and H2O is a weak field ligand, so the magnitudes of Δo are different. The complexes therefore absorb light of different wavelengths in the d-d transition and show different (complementary) colours.

What will be the correct order for the wavelengths of absorption in the visible region for the following: [Ni(NO2)6]4-, [Ni(NH3)6]2+, [Ni(H2O)6]2+?

  • The order of field strength of the ligands is NO2- > NH3 > H2O, so Δo follows the same order.

  • Energy absorbed is inversely proportional to wavelength:

\[E = {hc \over λ}\ ⇒\ λ ∝ {1 \over Δ_o}\]

Hence, the order of wavelength of absorption is:

\[[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+} > [Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+} > [Ni(NO_2)_6]^{4-}\]

Calculate the CFSE (in terms of Δo) and the spin-only magnetic moment of [Co(NH3)6]3+ (low spin) and [CoF6]3- (high spin).

Co3+ is 3d6.

  • [Co(NH3)6]3+: t2g6eg0, n = 0
\[CFSE = 6(-0.4Δ_o) = -2.4Δ_o\ (+\ pairing\ energy)\] \[μ = 0\ BM\ (diamagnetic)\]
  • [CoF6]3-: t2g4eg2, n = 4
\[CFSE = 4(-0.4Δ_o) + 2(0.6Δ_o) = -0.4Δ_o\] \[μ = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = 4.90\ BM\]

docs.title: Coordination Compounds | Important Terms
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the important terms used in coordination chemistry like coordination entity, ligand, denticity, coordination number and oxidation number.

docs.title: 1. Coordination Entity
docs.text:
• A coordination entity constitutes a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules.
  • Example: In [CoCl3(NH3)3], the cobalt ion is surrounded by three ammonia molecules and three chloride ions.
  • Other examples: [Ni(CO)4], [PtCl2(NH3)2], [Fe(CN)6]4-, [Co(NH3)6]3+.

docs.title: 2. Central Atom/Ion
docs.text:
• The atom or ion to which a fixed number of ions/groups are bound in a definite geometrical arrangement is called the central atom or ion.
  • Example: The central atoms/ions in [NiCl2(H2O)4], [CoCl(NH3)5]2+ and [Fe(CN)6]3- are Ni2+, Co3+ and Fe3+ respectively.
  • The central atom accepts electron pairs from the ligands. Hence, central atoms/ions are also called Lewis acids.

docs.title: 3. Ligands
docs.text:
• The ions or molecules bound to the central atom/ion in a coordination entity are called ligands.
  • Ligands can be simple ions (Cl-), small molecules (H2O, NH3), larger molecules (H2NCH2CH2NH2, N(CH2CH2NH2)3) or even macromolecules such as proteins.
  • Ligands donate electron pairs to the metal, so they act as Lewis bases.

docs.title: Classification of ligands based on number of donor atoms
(a) Unidentate ligands
docs.text:
• A ligand bound to the metal through a single donor atom is called a unidentate ligand.
  • Examples: Cl-, H2O, NH3.

docs.title: (b) Didentate ligands
docs.text:
• A ligand which binds through two donor atoms is called a didentate ligand.
  • Examples: H2NCH2CH2NH2 (ethane-1,2-diamine, 'en') binds through two N atoms; C2O42- (oxalate, 'ox') binds through two O atoms.

docs.title: (c) Polydentate ligands
docs.text:
• A ligand with several donor atoms is called a polydentate ligand.
  • Example: N(CH2CH2NH2)3 has four N donor atoms.
  • Ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion (EDTA4-) is an important hexadentate ligand. It binds to a metal ion through two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms.
\[EDTA^{4-}:\ (^-OOCCH_2)_2N-CH_2-CH_2-N(CH_2COO^-)_2\]

docs.title: Denticity and Chelate Ligands
docs.text:
• The number of donor (ligating) groups in a ligand is called its denticity. Example: denticity of NH3 = 1, en = 2, EDTA4- = 6.
  • When a di- or polydentate ligand uses two or more donor atoms to bind a single metal ion, it is called a chelate ligand.
  • The ring formed by a chelate ligand and the metal is called a chelate ring.
  • Chelate complexes are more stable than similar complexes containing unidentate ligands. This extra stability is called the chelate effect.

docs.title: Ambidentate Ligands
docs.text:
• A ligand which can bind through two different donor atoms (but only one at a time) is called an ambidentate ligand.
  • Examples: NO2- and SCN-.
Ligand Binding atom Linkage Name NO2- N M ← NO2 nitrito-N NO2- O M ← ONO nitrito-O SCN- S M ← SCN thiocyanato SCN- N M ← NCS isothiocyanato

docs.title: 4. Coordination Number
docs.text:
• The coordination number (CN) of a metal ion in a complex is the number of ligand donor atoms to which the metal is directly bonded.
  • The coordination number is determined only by the number of sigma bonds formed between the ligands and the central atom. Pi bonds, if present, are not counted.

Examples

  • In [PtCl6]2-, CN of Pt = 6

  • In [Ni(NH3)4]2+, CN of Ni = 4

  • In [Fe(C2O4)3]3- and [Co(en)3]3+, CN of Fe and Co is 6, because C2O42- and en are didentate ligands (3 × 2 = 6).

\[Coordination\ number = \sum (Number\ of\ ligands \times Denticity)\]

docs.title: 5. Coordination Sphere
docs.text:
• The central atom/ion and the ligands attached to it are enclosed in a square bracket. This is collectively called the coordination sphere.
  • The ionisable groups written outside the bracket are called counter ions.
  • Example: In K4[Fe(CN)6], the coordination sphere is [Fe(CN)6]4- and the counter ion is K+.

docs.title: 6. Coordination Polyhedron
docs.text:
• The spatial arrangement of the ligand atoms directly attached to the central atom/ion defines a coordination polyhedron.
  • The most common coordination polyhedra are octahedral, square planar and tetrahedral.
  • Examples: [Co(NH3)6]3+ is octahedral, [Ni(CO)4] is tetrahedral and [PtCl4]2- is square planar.

Here, M represents the central atom/ion and L a unidentate ligand.

docs.title: 7. Oxidation Number of Central Atom
docs.text:
• The oxidation number of the central atom is the charge it would carry if all the ligands were removed along with the electron pairs they share with the central atom.
  • It is written as a Roman numeral in parentheses after the name of the coordination entity.
  • Example: The oxidation number of copper in [Cu(CN)4]3- is +1, written as Cu(I).
  • To calculate it, equate the sum of the charges on the metal and the ligands to the charge on the complex.

Example

Oxidation number of Cu in [Cu(CN)4]3-:

\[x + 4(-1) = -3\] \[x = +1\]

Oxidation number of Fe in K3[Fe(C2O4)3]:

\[3(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0\] \[x = +3\]

docs.title: 8. Homoleptic and Heteroleptic Complexes
docs.text:
• Homoleptic complexes: The metal is bound to only one kind of donor group. Example: [Co(NH3)6]3+.
  • Heteroleptic complexes: The metal is bound to more than one kind of donor group. Example: [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Specify the oxidation numbers of the metals in the following coordination entities: (i) [Co(H2O)(CN)(en)2]2+ (ii) [CoBr2(en)2]+ (iii) [PtCl4]2- (iv) K3[Fe(CN)6] (v) [Cr(NH3)3Cl3]

H2O, en and NH3 are neutral; CN-, Br- and Cl- carry -1 charge.

\[(i)\ x + 0 + (-1) + 0 = +2,\ x = +3\] \[(ii)\ x + 2(-1) + 0 = +1,\ x = +3\] \[(iii)\ x + 4(-1) = -2,\ x = +2\] \[(iv)\ 3(+1) + x + 6(-1) = 0,\ x = +3\] \[(v)\ x + 0 + 3(-1) = 0,\ x = +3\]

What is meant by unidentate, didentate and ambidentate ligands? Give two examples of each.

  • Unidentate: Ligand binding through a single donor atom. Examples: NH3, Cl-.

  • Didentate: Ligand binding through two donor atoms. Examples: ethane-1,2-diamine (en), oxalate (C2O42-).

  • Ambidentate: Ligand which can bind through either of two different donor atoms. Examples: NO2- (through N or O), SCN- (through S or N).

Find the coordination number and denticity of each ligand in [Co(en)2Cl2]+.

Denticity of en = 2 and denticity of Cl- = 1.

\[CN = 2 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 = 6\]

It is a heteroleptic complex with coordination number 6 (octahedral).

docs.title: Coordination Compounds | Introduction and Werner's Theory
Coordination Compounds | Introduction and Werner's Theory
docs.text: Coordination compounds are compounds in which a central metal atom or ion is bonded to a fixed number of anions or neutral molecules. They were earlier called complex compounds.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• Transition metals form a large number of complex compounds in which the metal atom is bound to a number of anions or neutral molecules. In modern terminology, these are called coordination compounds.
  • Coordination compounds are the backbone of modern inorganic chemistry, bio-inorganic chemistry and the chemical industry.
  • Many vital components of biological systems are coordination compounds:
    • Chlorophyll - coordination compound of magnesium
    • Haemoglobin - coordination compound of iron
    • Vitamin B12 - coordination compound of cobalt
  • They are also used in metallurgical processes, industrial catalysts, analytical reagents, electroplating, textile dyeing and medicinal chemistry.

docs.title: Werner's Experiments
docs.text:
• Alfred Werner (1866-1919), a Swiss chemist, was the first to explain the structures of coordination compounds. He prepared and studied a large number of them using simple experimental techniques.
  • Werner proposed that a metal ion shows two kinds of valence - a primary valence and a secondary valence.
  • Binary compounds such as CrCl3, CoCl2 and PdCl2 have a primary valence of 3, 2 and 2 respectively.
  • Werner studied a series of compounds of cobalt(III) chloride with ammonia. On adding excess silver nitrate solution in cold, only some of the chloride ions were precipitated as AgCl; the rest remained in solution.
Compound (1 mol) Colour Moles of AgCl precipitated CoCl3.6NH3 Yellow 3 CoCl3.5NH3 Purple 2 CoCl3.4NH3 Green 1 CoCl3.4NH3 Violet 1
  • These observations, together with conductivity measurements, can be explained if:
    1. Six groups in all (chloride ions, ammonia molecules or both) remain bonded to the cobalt ion during the reaction.
    2. The compounds are formulated with the bonded groups inside a square bracket. The atoms within the square bracket form a single entity which does not dissociate under the reaction conditions.
Colour Formula Conductivity corresponds to Yellow [Co(NH3)6]3+ 3Cl- 1:3 electrolyte Purple [CoCl(NH3)5]2+ 2Cl- 1:2 electrolyte Green [CoCl2(NH3)4]+ Cl- 1:1 electrolyte Violet [CoCl2(NH3)4]+ Cl- 1:1 electrolyte
  • Only the chloride ions outside the square bracket are free to precipitate as AgCl.
  • The number of groups bound directly to the metal ion was termed the secondary valence by Werner. In all the above compounds, the secondary valence of cobalt is 6.
  • The last two compounds have the same empirical formula, CoCl3.4NH3, but different properties (green and violet). Such compounds are called isomers.

docs.title: Postulates of Werner's Theory
docs.text: Werner put forward his theory of coordination compounds in 1898. Its main postulates are:

docs.title: 1. Two types of valences
docs.text: • In coordination compounds, metals show two types of linkages (valences) - primary and secondary.

docs.title: 2. Primary valence
docs.text:
• Primary valences are normally ionisable.
  • They are satisfied by negative ions.
  • In modern terms, the primary valence corresponds to the oxidation state of the metal.

docs.title: 3. Secondary valence
docs.text:
• Secondary valences are non-ionisable.
  • They are satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions.
  • The secondary valence is equal to the coordination number and is fixed for a metal.

docs.title: 4. Spatial arrangement
docs.text:
• The ions or groups bound to the metal by secondary linkages have characteristic spatial arrangements corresponding to different coordination numbers.
  • In modern language, such spatial arrangements are called coordination polyhedra.
  • The species inside the square bracket is called the coordination entity or complex, and the ions outside the square bracket are called counter ions.
  • Werner further proposed that octahedral, tetrahedral and square planar shapes are the most common in coordination compounds of transition metals.

Example

  • Octahedral: [Co(NH3)6]3+, [CoCl(NH3)5]2+, [CoCl2(NH3)4]+

  • Tetrahedral: [Ni(CO)4]

  • Square planar: [PtCl4]2-

Conclusion

In modern language, Werner's primary and secondary linkages are recognised as the ionisable (ionic) and non-ionisable (covalent) bonds respectively.

docs.title: Difference between a Double Salt and a Complex
docs.text:
• Both double salts and complexes are formed by combining two or more stable compounds in a fixed (stoichiometric) ratio.
  • Double salts dissociate completely into simple ions when dissolved in water. Examples: carnallite, KCl.MgCl2.6H2O; Mohr's salt, FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O; potash alum, KAl(SO4)2.12H2O.
  • Complexes do not dissociate completely. For example, the complex ion [Fe(CN)6]4- of K4[Fe(CN)6] does not dissociate into Fe2+ and CN- ions.
\[Mohr's\ salt:\ FeSO_4.(NH_4)_2SO_4.6H_2O_{(aq)} → Fe^{2+} + 2NH_4^+ + 2SO_4^{2-} + 6H_2O\] \[K_4[Fe(CN)_6]_{(aq)} → 4K^+ + [Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
On the basis of the following observations made with aqueous solutions, assign secondary valences to the metals: (i) PdCl2.4NH3 - 2 mol AgCl (ii) NiCl2.6H2O - 2 mol AgCl (iii) PtCl4.2HCl - 0 mol AgCl (iv) CoCl3.4NH3 - 1 mol AgCl (v) PtCl2.2NH3 - 0 mol AgCl (moles of AgCl precipitated per mole of compound with excess AgNO3)

The chlorides that precipitate are outside the coordination sphere. The remaining chlorides and the neutral molecules are bonded to the metal, and their total gives the secondary valence.

Compound Formulation Secondary valence PdCl2.4NH3 [Pd(NH3)4]Cl2 4 NiCl2.6H2O [Ni(H2O)6]Cl2 6 PtCl4.2HCl H2[PtCl6] 6 CoCl3.4NH3 [CoCl2(NH3)4]Cl 6 PtCl2.2NH3 [PtCl2(NH3)2] 4

FeSO4 solution mixed with (NH4)2SO4 solution in 1:1 molar ratio gives the test of Fe2+ ion, but CuSO4 solution mixed with aqueous ammonia in 1:4 molar ratio does not give the test of Cu2+ ion. Explain why.

  • FeSO4 and (NH4)2SO4 in 1:1 ratio form a double salt, Mohr's salt (FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O), which dissociates completely in water. So free Fe2+ ions are present.

  • CuSO4 and NH3 in 1:4 ratio form a complex which does not dissociate into Cu2+ ions:

\[CuSO_4 + 4NH_3 → [Cu(NH_3)_4]SO_4\]

Hence, free Cu2+ ions are not available and the test for Cu2+ is negative.

docs.title: Coordination Compounds | Isomerism
docs.text: Isomers are two or more compounds that have the same chemical formula but a different arrangement of atoms. Because of the different arrangement, they differ in one or more physical or chemical properties.

docs.title: Types of Isomerism
docs.text:
Coordination compounds show two main types of isomerism:

  • Stereoisomerism: Same chemical formula and same chemical bonds, but different spatial arrangement.
    1. Geometrical isomerism
    2. Optical isomerism
  • Structural isomerism: Different bonds.
    1. Linkage isomerism
    2. Coordination isomerism
    3. Ionisation isomerism
    4. Solvate isomerism

docs.title: 1. Geometrical Isomerism
docs.text:
• Geometrical isomerism arises in heteroleptic complexes due to different possible geometrical arrangements of the ligands.
  • It is mainly seen in complexes with coordination numbers 4 (square planar) and 6 (octahedral).
  • When two identical ligands are adjacent to each other, the isomer is called cis. When they are opposite to each other, it is called trans.

docs.title: (a) Square planar complexes
docs.text:
• In a square planar complex of formula [MX2L2] (X and L are unidentate), the two X ligands can be cis or trans to each other.
  • A square planar complex of type [MABXL] (A, B, X, L are unidentate) shows three geometrical isomers - two cis and one trans.
  • Geometrical isomerism is not possible for tetrahedral complexes, because all four positions are adjacent to each other.

docs.title: (b) Octahedral complexes
docs.text:
• Octahedral complexes of formula [MX2L4] show cis and trans isomers. Example: [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+.
  • Complexes of formula [MX2(L-L)2], where L-L is a didentate ligand like en, also show cis and trans isomers. Example: [CoCl2(en)2].

docs.title: (c) Facial and meridional isomers
docs.text:
• Octahedral entities of type [Ma3b3], like [Co(NH3)3(NO2)3], show another type of geometrical isomerism.
  • Facial (fac) isomer: The three donor atoms of the same ligand occupy adjacent positions at the corners of one octahedral face.
  • Meridional (mer) isomer: The three donor atoms of the same ligand lie around the meridian of the octahedron.
Complex type Geometry Number of geometrical isomers [MA4], [MA3B] Square planar 0 [MA2B2] Square planar 2 (cis, trans) [MABCD] Square planar 3 Any [MAnBm] Tetrahedral 0 [MA4B2] Octahedral 2 (cis, trans) [MA3B3] Octahedral 2 (fac, mer) [M(AA)2B2] Octahedral 2 (cis, trans)

docs.title: 2. Optical Isomerism
docs.text:
• Optical isomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed on one another. They are called enantiomers.
  • Molecules or ions that cannot be superimposed on their mirror images are called chiral.
  • The two forms are called dextro (d) and laevo (l), depending on whether they rotate the plane of polarised light to the right (d) or to the left (l) in a polarimeter.
  • Optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes containing didentate ligands.

[Co(en)3]3+

The complex has no plane of symmetry, so the d and l forms are non-superimposable mirror images.

  • In entities of type [MX2(L-L)2], such as [PtCl2(en)2]2+ or [CoCl2(en)2]+, only the cis isomer is optically active. The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and its mirror image is superimposable on it.

Conclusion

  • Tetrahedral complexes: no geometrical isomerism.

  • Square planar complexes: generally no optical isomerism, because the plane of the molecule is a plane of symmetry.

  • Octahedral complexes with didentate ligands: show both geometrical and optical isomerism.

docs.title: 3. Linkage Isomerism
docs.text:
• Linkage isomerism arises in a coordination compound containing an ambidentate ligand.
  • Example: The thiocyanate ligand NCS- may bind through nitrogen (M-NCS) or through sulphur (M-SCN).
  • Jorgensen discovered this behaviour in [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2:
    • Red form: the nitrite ligand is bound through oxygen (-ONO)
    • Yellow form: the nitrite ligand is bound through nitrogen (-NO2)
\[[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]Cl_2\ (red)\ \ and\ \ [Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl_2\ (yellow)\]

docs.title: 4. Coordination Isomerism
docs.text:
• Coordination isomerism arises from the interchange of ligands between the cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions in a complex.
  • Example: In [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6], NH3 ligands are bound to Co3+ and CN- ligands to Cr3+. In its coordination isomer [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6], NH3 is bound to Cr3+ and CN- to Co3+.

docs.title: 5. Ionisation Isomerism
docs.text:
• Ionisation isomerism arises when the counter ion in a complex salt is itself a potential ligand. It can displace a ligand, which then becomes the counter ion.
  • The isomers give different ions in solution.
  • Example: [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br and [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4.
\[[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4 + Ba^{2+} → BaSO_4 ↓\ (white\ ppt.)\] \[[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br + Ag^+ → AgBr ↓\ (pale\ yellow\ ppt.)\]

docs.title: 6. Solvate Isomerism
docs.text:
• Solvate isomers differ in whether a solvent molecule is directly bonded to the metal ion or is merely present as a free solvent molecule in the crystal lattice.
  • When the solvent is water, it is called hydrate isomerism. It is similar to ionisation isomerism.
  • Example: [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 (violet) and its solvate isomer [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O (grey-green).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Why is geometrical isomerism not possible in tetrahedral complexes having two different types of unidentate ligands coordinated with the central metal ion?

In a tetrahedral complex, every position is adjacent to every other position. The relative positions of the unidentate ligands attached to the central metal atom are therefore the same with respect to each other, so cis and trans arrangements cannot exist.

Draw structures of geometrical isomers of [Fe(NH3)2(CN)4]-.

It is an octahedral complex of type [MA2B4], so it shows two geometrical isomers:

  • cis isomer: The two NH3 ligands are at adjacent positions (90° apart), and the four CN- occupy the remaining positions.

  • trans isomer: The two NH3 ligands are at opposite positions (180° apart, one above and one below Fe), and the four CN- lie in the square plane around Fe.

These arrangements are exactly like the cis and trans forms of [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ shown above, with NH3 in place of Cl and CN in place of NH3.

Out of the following two coordination entities, which is chiral (optically active)? (a) cis-[CrCl2(ox)2]3- (b) trans-[CrCl2(ox)2]3-

The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry (containing the two oxalate ligands), so it is superimposable on its mirror image. The cis isomer has no plane of symmetry.

Hence, (a) cis-[CrCl2(ox)2]3- is chiral (optically active).

Indicate the types of isomerism exhibited by the following complexes: (i) K[Cr(H2O)2(C2O4)2] (ii) [Co(en)3]Cl3 (iii) [Co(NH3)5(NO2)](NO3)2 (iv) [Pt(NH3)(H2O)Cl2]

  • (i) Type [M(AA)2B2]: both geometrical (cis, trans) and optical isomerism. The cis form exists as d and l isomers.

  • (ii) Type [M(AA)3]: two optical isomers (d and l).

  • (iii) It shows ionisation isomerism (NO2- and NO3- can exchange places), linkage isomerism (NO2- can bind through N or O) and geometrical isomerism. There are 10 possible isomers in all.

  • (iv) Square planar [MABX2]: geometrical (cis and trans) isomers.

Give evidence that [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Cl are ionisation isomers.

The two compounds give different ions in solution and so react differently with reagents:

  • [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 gives free SO42- ions, so it forms a white precipitate of BaSO4 with BaCl2 solution but gives no precipitate with AgNO3.

  • [Co(NH3)5SO4]Cl gives free Cl- ions, so it forms a white precipitate of AgCl with AgNO3 solution but gives no precipitate with BaCl2.

How many geometrical isomers are possible in the following coordination entities? (i) [Cr(C2O4)3]3- (ii) [Co(NH3)3Cl3]

  • (i) [Cr(C2O4)3]3- is of type [M(AA)3]. It shows no geometrical isomers (only optical isomers).

  • (ii) [Co(NH3)3Cl3] is of type [MA3B3]. It shows two geometrical isomers - fac and mer.

Write all the geometrical isomers of [Pt(NH3)(Br)(Cl)(py)] and how many of these will exhibit optical isomerism?

It is a square planar complex of type [MABCD], which has three geometrical isomers. Fixing NH3 at one corner, the ligand trans (opposite) to it can be Br, Cl or py:

  • Isomer 1: NH3 trans to Br (Cl trans to py)

  • Isomer 2: NH3 trans to Cl (Br trans to py)

  • Isomer 3: NH3 trans to py (Br trans to Cl)

Square planar complexes are planar and have a plane of symmetry, so none of these isomers shows optical isomerism.

Draw all the isomers (geometrical and optical) of [CoCl2(en)2]+.

[CoCl2(en)2]+ shows two geometrical isomers, cis and trans (shown in the figure for [CoCl2(en)2] above).

  • The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

  • The cis isomer is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers (d and l).

Hence, there are three isomers in total: trans, d-cis and l-cis.

docs.title: Coordination Compounds | Metal Carbonyls, Stability and Applications
Coordination Compounds | Metal Carbonyls, Stability and Applications
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss bonding in metal carbonyls, stability of coordination compounds in solution and the importance of coordination compounds.

docs.title: Metal Carbonyls
docs.text:
• Homoleptic carbonyls are compounds containing only carbonyl (CO) ligands. Most transition metals form them.
  • These carbonyls have simple, well defined structures:
Carbonyl Name Structure [Ni(CO)4] Tetracarbonylnickel(0) Tetrahedral [Fe(CO)5] Pentacarbonyliron(0) Trigonal bipyramidal [Cr(CO)6] Hexacarbonylchromium(0) Octahedral [Mn2(CO)10] Decacarbonyldimanganese(0) Two square pyramidal Mn(CO)5 units joined by a Mn-Mn bond [Co2(CO)8] Octacarbonyldicobalt(0) Co-Co bond bridged by two CO groups

docs.title: Bonding in Metal Carbonyls
docs.text: The metal-carbon bond in metal carbonyls has both σ and π character.

docs.title: 1. M-C σ bond
docs.text: • It is formed by donation of the lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of the metal (ligand to metal donation).

docs.title: 2. M-C π bond
docs.text: • It is formed by donation of a pair of electrons from a filled d orbital of the metal into the vacant antibonding π* orbital of carbon monoxide (metal to ligand donation). This is called back bonding (or back donation).

docs.title: Synergic bonding
docs.text:
• σ donation from CO increases the electron density on the metal, which helps the metal donate electrons back to CO through π bonding. The π back donation, in turn, removes electron density from the metal and makes it a better acceptor for σ donation. Each bond strengthens the other.
  • This mutual reinforcement is called the synergic effect. It strengthens the bond between CO and the metal and gives stability to metal carbonyls.

Note

Since electrons enter the antibonding π* orbital of CO during back bonding, the C-O bond order decreases slightly. So the C-O bond in a metal carbonyl is a little longer (weaker) than in free CO, while the M-C bond gets stronger.

docs.title: Stability of Coordination Compounds
docs.text:
• The stability of a complex in solution refers to the degree of association between the two species involved in the state of equilibrium.
  • It is expressed quantitatively by the magnitude of the stability (or formation) constant. The larger the stability constant, the higher the proportion of the complex in solution.
\[M + 4L ⇌ ML_4\]

docs.title: Stepwise stability constants
docs.text:
• Free metal ions rarely exist in solution; they are surrounded by solvent molecules, which are replaced step by step by the ligands L. Ignoring the solvent, the formation can be written in steps:
\[M + L ⇌ ML,\ \ K_1 = {[ML] \over [M][L]}\] \[ML + L ⇌ ML_2,\ \ K_2 = {[ML_2] \over [ML][L]}\] \[ML_2 + L ⇌ ML_3,\ \ K_3 = {[ML_3] \over [ML_2][L]}\] \[ML_3 + L ⇌ ML_4,\ \ K_4 = {[ML_4] \over [ML_3][L]}\]
  • K1, K2, etc. are called stepwise stability constants.

docs.title: Overall stability constant
docs.text:
\[M + 4L ⇌ ML_4,\ \ β_4 = {[ML_4] \over [M][L]^4}\] \[β_4 = K_1 \times K_2 \times K_3 \times K_4\] \[In\ general:\ β_n = K_1 \times K_2 \times K_3 \times ... \times K_n\]
  • β is called the overall stability constant.

Formation of cuprammonium ion

\[Cu^{2+} + NH_3 ⇌ [Cu(NH_3)]^{2+},\ \ K_1 = {[Cu(NH_3)^{2+}] \over [Cu^{2+}][NH_3]}\] \[[Cu(NH_3)]^{2+} + NH_3 ⇌ [Cu(NH_3)_2]^{2+},\ \ K_2 = {[Cu(NH_3)_2^{2+}] \over [Cu(NH_3)^{2+}][NH_3]}\] \[β_4 = {[Cu(NH_3)_4^{2+}] \over [Cu^{2+}][NH_3]^4}\] \[log K_1 = 4.0,\ log K_2 = 3.2,\ log K_3 = 2.7,\ log K_4 = 2.0\] \[log β_4 = 4.0 + 3.2 + 2.7 + 2.0 = 11.9\]

The successive stability constants decrease, a pattern found for most formation constants.

  • The instability constant or dissociation constant of a coordination compound is the reciprocal of its formation constant.
\[Overall\ dissociation\ constant = {1 \over β_n}\]

docs.title: Chelate effect
docs.text:
• Complexes formed by chelating (di- or polydentate) ligands are more stable than similar complexes with unidentate ligands. The extra stability due to chelation is called the chelate effect.
  • Example: [Ni(en)3]2+ is more stable than [Ni(NH3)6]2+, though both have six Ni-N bonds.
  • The stability of coordination compounds is related to Gibbs energy, enthalpy and entropy terms. Replacing several unidentate ligands by one chelating ligand increases the number of free particles, so entropy increases and the complex is favoured.

docs.title: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds
1. Analytical chemistry
docs.text:
• Many qualitative and quantitative analyses are based on the colour reactions given by metal ions with ligands (especially chelating ligands), which form coordination entities.
  • Examples of such reagents: EDTA, DMG (dimethylglyoxime), α-nitroso-β-naphthol, cupron.
  • Hardness of water is estimated by simple titration with Na2EDTA. Ca2+ and Mg2+ form stable complexes with EDTA. They can be estimated selectively because their complexes have different stability constants.

docs.title: 2. Metallurgy
docs.text:
• Extraction of silver and gold uses complex formation. Gold combines with cyanide in the presence of oxygen and water to form [Au(CN)2]-. Gold is recovered as metal by adding zinc.
\[4Au + 8CN^- + 2H_2O + O_2 → 4[Au(CN)_2]^- + 4OH^-\] \[2[Au(CN)_2]^- + Zn → [Zn(CN)_4]^{2-} + 2Au\]
  • Purification of metals: impure nickel is converted to [Ni(CO)4], which is decomposed to give pure nickel (Mond process).

docs.title: 3. Biological systems
docs.text:
• Chlorophyll, the pigment of photosynthesis, is a coordination compound of magnesium.
  • Haemoglobin, the red pigment of blood which carries oxygen, is a coordination compound of iron.
  • Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamine), the anti-pernicious anaemia factor, is a coordination compound of cobalt.
  • Enzymes like carboxypeptidase A and carbonic anhydrase contain coordinated metal ions.

docs.title: 4. Industrial catalysts
docs.text: • Coordination compounds are used as catalysts in many industrial processes. Example: the rhodium complex [(Ph3P)3RhCl], Wilkinson catalyst, is used for hydrogenation of alkenes.

docs.title: 5. Electroplating
docs.text: • Articles are electroplated with silver and gold more smoothly and evenly from solutions of [Ag(CN)2]- and [Au(CN)2]- than from solutions of simple metal ions.

docs.title: 6. Photography
docs.text:
• In black and white photography, the developed film is fixed by washing with hypo solution. It dissolves the undecomposed AgBr by forming the complex ion [Ag(S2O3)2]3-.
\[AgBr + 2Na_2S_2O_3 → Na_3[Ag(S_2O_3)_2] + NaBr\]

docs.title: 7. Medicinal chemistry
docs.text:
• Chelate therapy: Excess of metals in toxic amounts is removed by chelating ligands. Excess copper and iron are removed by D-penicillamine and desferrioxime B. EDTA is used in the treatment of lead poisoning.
  • Some coordination compounds of platinum effectively inhibit the growth of tumours. Example: cis-platin, cis-[PtCl2(NH3)2], and related compounds.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the overall complex dissociation equilibrium constant for the [Cu(NH3)4]2+ ion, given that β4 for this complex is 2.1 × 1013.

The overall dissociation constant is the reciprocal of the overall stability constant:

\[K_d = {1 \over β_4} = {1 \over 2.1 \times 10^{13}}\] \[K_d = 4.7 \times 10^{-14}\]

Discuss the nature of bonding in metal carbonyls.

  • The M-C bond has both σ and π character.

  • σ bond: The carbon of CO donates its lone pair into a vacant orbital of the metal.

  • π bond: The metal donates a pair of electrons from a filled d orbital into the vacant antibonding π* orbital of CO (back bonding).

  • The two interactions reinforce each other (synergic effect), which strengthens the M-CO bond and makes metal carbonyls stable.

What is meant by the chelate effect? Give an example.

When a didentate or polydentate ligand binds to the same metal ion through two or more donor atoms, a ring (chelate) is formed. Such complexes are more stable than similar complexes with unidentate ligands. This is called the chelate effect.

Example: [Ni(en)3]2+ is more stable than [Ni(NH3)6]2+. Similarly, EDTA4- forms very stable complexes with Ca2+ and Mg2+.

Amongst the following, the most stable complex is: (i) [Fe(H2O)6]3+ (ii) [Fe(NH3)6]3+ (iii) [Fe(C2O4)3]3- (iv) [FeCl6]3-

Oxalate is a didentate (chelating) ligand and forms three five-membered chelate rings with Fe3+. Due to the chelate effect, the most stable complex is (iii) [Fe(C2O4)3]3-.

docs.title: Coordination Compounds | IUPAC Nomenclature
docs.text: The formulas and names of coordination entities are based on the recommendations of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC). A systematic method is needed so that every formula and name describes exactly one compound, which is especially important when dealing with isomers.

docs.title: Writing Formulas of Mononuclear Coordination Entities
docs.text:
Mononuclear coordination entities contain a single central metal atom. The following rules are used while writing their formulas:

  1. The central atom is listed first.
  2. The ligands are then listed in alphabetical order. The placement of a ligand in the list does not depend on its charge.
  3. Polydentate ligands are also listed alphabetically. For an abbreviated ligand, the first letter of the abbreviation decides its position.
  4. The formula of the entire coordination entity, charged or not, is enclosed in square brackets. Polyatomic ligands and ligand abbreviations are enclosed in parentheses.
  5. There is no space between the ligands and the metal within a coordination sphere.
  6. When the formula of a charged coordination entity is written without the counter ion, the charge is shown outside the square bracket as a right superscript, with the number before the sign. Example: [Co(CN)6]3-, [Cr(H2O)6]3+.
  7. The charge of the cation(s) is balanced by the charge of the anion(s).

docs.title: Naming Mononuclear Coordination Compounds
docs.text:
Names are built using additive nomenclature: the groups around the central atom are written as prefixes to the name of the central atom, with suitable multipliers. The rules are:

  1. The cation is named first, whether the complex part is the cation or the anion.
  2. The ligands are named in alphabetical order before the name of the central atom (this is the reverse of writing the formula). Multiplying prefixes (di, tri, etc.) are ignored while alphabetising.
  3. Names of anionic ligands end in -o (the 2004 IUPAC recommendation uses -ido, so chloro becomes chlorido). Neutral and cationic ligands keep their usual names, except aqua for H2O, ammine for NH3, carbonyl for CO and nitrosyl for NO.
  4. Prefixes mono, di, tri, tetra, etc. show the number of each ligand. If the ligand name already contains a numerical prefix, the terms bis, tris, tetrakis are used and the ligand name is put in parentheses. Example: [NiCl2(PPh3)2] is dichloridobis(triphenylphosphine)nickel(II).
  5. The oxidation state of the metal is shown by a Roman numeral in parentheses after the metal name.
  6. If the complex ion is a cation, the metal is named as the element (Co - cobalt, Pt - platinum). If the complex ion is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate (Co in [Co(SCN)4]2- is cobaltate). For some metals, the Latin names are used in anions.
  7. A neutral complex molecule is named like a complex cation.
  8. The number of cations and anions in an ionic compound is never stated in the name.

docs.text:
Metal Name in anion Iron (Fe) ferrate Copper (Cu) cuprate Silver (Ag) argentate Gold (Au) aurate Lead (Pb) plumbate Tin (Sn) stannate

Other metals simply add -ate: cobaltate, nickelate, chromate, zincate, aluminate, platinate, palladate, manganate.

docs.title: Worked Examples
docs.text:
1. [Cr(NH3)3(H2O)3]Cl3

Name: triamminetriaquachromium(III) chloride

  • The complex ion inside the square bracket is a cation.

  • The ammine ligands are named before aqua ligands (alphabetical order).

  • There are three Cl- counter ions, so the complex ion has a charge of +3. All the ligands are neutral, so the oxidation number of Cr is +3.

2. [Co(H2NCH2CH2NH2)3]2(SO4)3

Name: tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) sulphate

  • Three sulphate ions (total charge -6) balance two complex cations, so each complex cation has a charge of +3.

  • Ethane-1,2-diamine is neutral, so the oxidation number of Co is +3.

  • 'tris' is used because the ligand name already contains the prefix 'di'.

3. [Ag(NH3)2][Ag(CN)2]

Name: diamminesilver(I) dicyanoargentate(I)

  • Both the cation and the anion are complex ions. The cation is named first.

  • Silver in the anion is named argentate. Notice how the name of the metal differs in the cation and the anion even though both contain Ag+.

docs.title: Steps to Name a Complex
docs.text:
Steps

  1. Identify the cation and the anion; decide which one is the complex.

  2. Find the oxidation number of the metal from the charges.

  3. List ligand names alphabetically with multiplying prefixes.

  4. Add the metal name (with -ate if the complex is an anion) and the oxidation number in Roman numerals.

  5. Name the counter ion separately (cation first, then anion).

docs.title: Coordination Compounds | Questions
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some questions on coordination compounds covering nomenclature, isomerism, valence bond theory, crystal field theory and stability.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Explain the bonding in coordination compounds in terms of Werner's postulates.

  • Metals show two types of valences - primary and secondary.

  • Primary valences are ionisable and are satisfied by negative ions. They correspond to the oxidation state of the metal.

  • Secondary valences are non-ionisable and are satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions. The secondary valence equals the coordination number and is fixed for a metal.

  • The groups bound by secondary valences have a characteristic spatial arrangement (coordination polyhedron).

Example: In [Co(NH3)6]Cl3, the primary valence of Co is 3 (satisfied by three Cl-) and the secondary valence is 6 (satisfied by six NH3), with an octahedral arrangement.

Aqueous copper sulphate solution (blue in colour) gives: (i) a green precipitate with aqueous potassium fluoride and (ii) a bright green solution with aqueous potassium chloride. Explain these experimental results.

Aqueous CuSO4 contains the blue complex [Cu(H2O)4]2+. The water ligands are weak and are easily replaced by F- and Cl-:

\[[Cu(H_2O)_4]^{2+} + 4F^- → [CuF_4]^{2-}\ (green\ ppt.) + 4H_2O\] \[[Cu(H_2O)_4]^{2+} + 4Cl^- → [CuCl_4]^{2-}\ (bright\ green\ solution) + 4H_2O\]

The change of ligand changes the crystal field splitting and hence the colour.

What is the coordination entity formed when excess of aqueous KCN is added to an aqueous solution of copper sulphate? Why is it that no precipitate of copper sulphide is obtained when H2S(g) is passed through this solution?

With excess KCN, Cu2+ is reduced and forms the very stable complex [Cu(CN)4]3-:

\[2CuSO_4 + 10KCN → 2K_3[Cu(CN)_4] + 2K_2SO_4 + (CN)_2\]

This complex has a very high stability constant and does not dissociate to give free copper ions. Hence, when H2S is passed, no precipitate of copper sulphide is formed.

Give the oxidation state, d orbital occupation and coordination number of the central metal ion in the following complexes: (i) K3[Co(C2O4)3] (ii) cis-[Cr(en)2Cl2]Cl (iii) (NH4)2[CoF4] (iv) [Mn(H2O)6]SO4

\[(i)\ 3(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0,\ x = +3\] \[(ii)\ x + 0 + 2(-1) = +1,\ x = +3\] \[(iii)\ 2(+1) + x + 4(-1) = 0,\ x = +2\] \[(iv)\ x + 0 = +2,\ x = +2\] Complex Oxidation state d electrons d orbital occupation CN K3[Co(C2O4)3] +3 3d6 t2g6eg0 6 cis-[Cr(en)2Cl2]Cl +3 3d3 t2g3eg0 6 (NH4)2[CoF4] +2 3d7 e4t23 (tetrahedral) 4 [Mn(H2O)6]SO4 +2 3d5 t2g3eg2 6

Write down the IUPAC name for each of the following complexes and indicate the oxidation state, electronic configuration and coordination number. Also give the stereochemistry and magnetic moment of the complex: (i) K[Cr(H2O)2(C2O4)2].3H2O (ii) [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 (iii) CrCl3(py)3 (iv) Cs[FeCl4] (v) K4[Mn(CN)6]

(i) Potassium diaquadioxalatochromate(III) trihydrate

  • Oxidation state = +3, configuration 3d3 (t2g3), CN = 6, octahedral

  • Shows geometrical isomerism (cis, trans); the cis form is optically active

\[μ = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = 3.87\ BM\]

(ii) Pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride

  • Oxidation state = +3, configuration 3d6 (t2g6, low spin), CN = 6, octahedral

  • No stereoisomers; diamagnetic, μ = 0

(iii) Trichloridotripyridinechromium(III)

  • Oxidation state = +3, configuration 3d3 (t2g3), CN = 6, octahedral

  • Type [MA3B3], shows fac and mer isomers

\[μ = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = 3.87\ BM\]

(iv) Caesium tetrachloridoferrate(III)

  • Oxidation state = +3, configuration 3d5 (e2t23), CN = 4, tetrahedral (sp3)

  • No stereoisomers

\[μ = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = 5.92\ BM\]

(v) Potassium hexacyanomanganate(II)

  • Oxidation state = +2, configuration 3d5 (t2g5, low spin since CN- is a strong ligand), CN = 6, octahedral (d2sp3)

  • No stereoisomers

\[μ = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = 1.73\ BM\]

Draw all the isomers (geometrical and optical) of: (i) [Co(NH3)Cl(en)2]2+ (ii) [Co(NH3)2Cl2(en)]+

(i) [Co(NH3)Cl(en)2]2+

  • NH3 and Cl can be trans (opposite) or cis (adjacent) to each other - two geometrical isomers.

  • The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive. The cis isomer is chiral and exists as d and l forms.

  • Total isomers = 3 (trans, d-cis, l-cis).

(ii) [Co(NH3)2Cl2(en)]+

  • Two Cl trans to each other (both NH3 cis) - optically inactive.

  • Two NH3 trans to each other (both Cl cis) - optically inactive.

  • Both Cl cis and both NH3 cis - chiral, exists as d and l forms.

  • Total = 3 geometrical isomers, 4 isomers in all.

What is meant by stability of a coordination compound in solution? State the factors which govern stability of complexes.

The stability of a complex in solution is the degree of association between the metal ion and the ligands at equilibrium. It is expressed by the stability (formation) constant; a larger value means a more stable complex.

\[M + nL ⇌ ML_n,\ \ β_n = {[ML_n] \over [M][L]^n}\]

Factors governing stability:

  • Charge on the central metal ion: Higher charge gives a more stable complex.

  • Size of the metal ion: Smaller size (higher charge density) gives a more stable complex.

  • Nature of the ligand: More basic ligands (better electron pair donors) form more stable complexes.

  • Chelation: Chelating ligands form more stable complexes than unidentate ligands (chelate effect).

Discuss briefly, giving an example in each case, the role of coordination compounds in: (i) biological systems (ii) medicinal chemistry (iii) analytical chemistry (iv) extraction/metallurgy of metals

  • (i) Biological systems: Chlorophyll (Mg complex) is responsible for photosynthesis; haemoglobin (Fe complex) carries oxygen in blood; vitamin B12 is a cobalt complex.

  • (ii) Medicinal chemistry: EDTA is used to treat lead poisoning; cis-platin is used as an anti-tumour drug; D-penicillamine removes excess copper.

  • (iii) Analytical chemistry: Hardness of water is estimated by titration with Na2EDTA; DMG is used to detect Ni2+.

  • (iv) Metallurgy: Gold and silver are extracted as cyanide complexes ([Au(CN)2]-); nickel is purified via [Ni(CO)4].

How many ions are produced from the complex Co(NH3)6Cl2 in solution? (i) 6 (ii) 4 (iii) 3 (iv) 2

\[[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_2 → [Co(NH_3)_6]^{2+} + 2Cl^-\]

Three ions are produced. Answer: (iii) 3

Amongst the following ions, which one has the highest magnetic moment value? (i) [Cr(H2O)6]3+ (ii) [Fe(H2O)6]2+ (iii) [Zn(H2O)6]2+

  • Cr3+: 3d3, 3 unpaired electrons

  • Fe2+: 3d6, H2O is weak field (t2g4eg2), 4 unpaired electrons

  • Zn2+: 3d10, 0 unpaired electrons

Maximum unpaired electrons give the highest magnetic moment. Answer: (ii) [Fe(H2O)6]2+

\[μ = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = 4.90\ BM\]

The oxidation number of cobalt in K[Co(CO)4] is: (i) +1 (ii) +3 (iii) -1 (iv) -3

CO is a neutral ligand.

\[(+1) + x + 4(0) = 0\] \[x = -1\]

Answer: (iii) -1

Write the name, hybridisation, shape and magnetic behaviour of [Ni(CO)4], [Fe(CN)6]3- and [CoF6]3-.

Complex IUPAC name Hybridisation Shape Unpaired e- Magnetic nature [Ni(CO)4] Tetracarbonylnickel(0) sp3 Tetrahedral 0 Diamagnetic [Fe(CN)6]3- Hexacyanoferrate(III) ion d2sp3 Octahedral 1 Paramagnetic (1.73 BM) [CoF6]3- Hexafluoridocobaltate(III) ion sp3d2 Octahedral 4 Paramagnetic (4.90 BM)

docs.title: Bonding in Coordination Compounds
docs.text:
Werner was the first to describe bonding in coordination compounds, but his theory could not answer some basic questions:

  • Why do only certain elements form coordination compounds?
  • Why do the bonds in coordination compounds have directional properties?
  • Why do coordination compounds have characteristic magnetic and optical properties?

Several theories explain bonding in coordination compounds - Valence Bond Theory (VBT), Crystal Field Theory (CFT), Ligand Field Theory (LFT) and Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT). Here we will study VBT; CFT is discussed in the next article.

docs.title: Valence Bond Theory
docs.text:
• According to VBT, the metal atom or ion, under the influence of ligands, uses its (n-1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation.
  • This gives a set of equivalent hybrid orbitals of definite geometry such as octahedral, tetrahedral or square planar.
  • These hybrid orbitals overlap with ligand orbitals that donate electron pairs, forming coordinate bonds.
Coordination number Type of hybridisation Distribution of hybrid orbitals in space 4 sp3 Tetrahedral 4 dsp2 Square planar 5 sp3d Trigonal bipyramidal 6 sp3d2 Octahedral 6 d2sp3 Octahedral
  • It is usually possible to predict the geometry of a complex if its magnetic behaviour is known.
  • In the orbital diagrams below, each column is one orbital, ↑↓ are the metal's own electrons, and xx is an electron pair donated by a ligand.

docs.title: 1. [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> - inner orbital complex
docs.text:
• Cobalt is in the +3 oxidation state. Co3+ has the configuration 3d6.
  • NH3 causes the 3d electrons to pair up, leaving two 3d orbitals empty. These two 3d orbitals, one 4s and three 4p orbitals hybridise to give six d2sp3 hybrid orbitals.
Species 3d 3d 3d 3d 3d 4s 4p 4p 4p Co3+ ion ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ d2sp3 hybridised Co3+ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ [Co(NH3)6]3+ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ xx xx xx xx xx xx
  • Six pairs of electrons, one from each NH3, occupy the six hybrid orbitals. The complex is octahedral and diamagnetic (no unpaired electron).
  • Since the inner d orbitals (3d) are used in hybridisation, [Co(NH3)6]3+ is called an inner orbital or low spin or spin paired complex.

docs.title: 2. [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3-</sup> - outer orbital complex
docs.text:
• Co3+ is again 3d6, but F- does not cause pairing of the 3d electrons.
  • The outer 4d orbitals are used: one 4s, three 4p and two 4d orbitals give six sp3d2 hybrid orbitals.
Species 3d 3d 3d 3d 3d 4s 4p 4p 4p 4d 4d Co3+ ion ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ [CoF6]3- ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ xx xx xx xx xx xx
  • The complex is octahedral and paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons.
  • Since the outer d orbitals (4d) are used, [CoF6]3- is called an outer orbital or high spin or spin free complex.

Inner vs Outer Orbital Complexes

  • Inner orbital (low spin): d2sp3 hybridisation using (n-1)d orbitals; electrons paired as far as possible. Example: [Co(NH3)6]3+.

  • Outer orbital (high spin): sp3d2 hybridisation using nd orbitals; maximum number of unpaired electrons. Example: [CoF6]3-.

docs.title: [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>
docs.text:
• In tetrahedral complexes, one s and three p orbitals hybridise to give four sp3 orbitals oriented tetrahedrally.
  • Nickel is in the +2 oxidation state with configuration 3d8.
Species 3d 3d 3d 3d 3d 4s 4p 4p 4p Ni2+ ion ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ [NiCl4]2- ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ xx xx xx xx
  • Each Cl- donates one electron pair. The complex is tetrahedral and paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons (high spin).
  • Similarly, [Ni(CO)4] is tetrahedral, but it is diamagnetic because nickel is in the zero oxidation state (3d10 after rearrangement of the 4s electrons) and has no unpaired electron.

docs.title: [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>
docs.text:
• In square planar complexes, the hybridisation is dsp2 (one 3d, one 4s and two 4p orbitals).
  • Nickel is in the +2 oxidation state (3d8). CN- forces the two unpaired 3d electrons to pair up, making one 3d orbital empty.
Species 3d 3d 3d 3d 3d 4s 4p 4p 4p Ni2+ ion ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ dsp2 hybridised Ni2+ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ [Ni(CN)4]2- ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ xx xx xx xx
  • Each hybrid orbital receives an electron pair from a cyanide ion. The complex is diamagnetic (low spin).

Note

Hybrid orbitals do not actually exist. Hybridisation is only a mathematical manipulation of the wave equation for the atomic orbitals involved.

docs.title: Magnetic Properties of Coordination Compounds
docs.text:
• The magnetic moment of a coordination compound can be measured by magnetic susceptibility experiments. The results tell us about the structure of the complex.
  • The spin-only magnetic moment is related to the number of unpaired electrons (n):
\[μ = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ BM\] Unpaired electrons (n) 1 2 3 4 5 μ (BM) 1.73 2.83 3.87 4.90 5.92

docs.title: Magnetic behaviour and the number of d electrons
docs.text:
• For metal ions with up to three 3d electrons, like Ti3+ (d1), V3+ (d2) and Cr3+ (d3), two 3d orbitals are already vacant for d2sp3 hybridisation. Their free ions and complexes have similar magnetic behaviour.
  • When more than three 3d electrons are present, a vacant pair of 3d orbitals is obtained only by pairing electrons against Hund's rule. For d4 (Cr2+, Mn3+), d5 (Mn2+, Fe3+) and d6 (Fe2+, Co3+), this pairing leaves two, one and zero unpaired electrons respectively.
  • The magnetic data agree with maximum spin pairing in many cases, especially for d6 ions. But for d4 and d5 ions, there are complications, which VBT explains using inner and outer orbital complexes:
Complex Metal ion Hybridisation Type Unpaired electrons [Mn(CN)6]3- Mn3+ (d4) d2sp3 Inner orbital 2 [MnCl6]3- Mn3+ (d4) sp3d2 Outer orbital 4 [Fe(CN)6]3- Fe3+ (d5) d2sp3 Inner orbital 1 [FeF6]3- Fe3+ (d5) sp3d2 Outer orbital 5 [Co(C2O4)3]3- Co3+ (d6) d2sp3 Inner orbital 0 (diamagnetic) [CoF6]3- Co3+ (d6) sp3d2 Outer orbital 4

docs.title: Limitations of Valence Bond Theory
docs.text:
VBT explains the formation, structures and magnetic behaviour of coordination compounds to a large extent, but it has the following shortcomings:

  1. It involves a number of assumptions.
  2. It does not give a quantitative interpretation of magnetic data.
  3. It does not explain the colour exhibited by coordination compounds.
  4. It does not give a quantitative interpretation of the thermodynamic or kinetic stabilities of coordination compounds.
  5. It does not make exact predictions about tetrahedral and square planar structures of 4-coordinate complexes.
  6. It does not distinguish between weak and strong ligands.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The spin only magnetic moment of [MnBr4]2- is 5.9 BM. Predict the geometry of the complex ion.

  • The coordination number of Mn2+ is 4, so the complex is either tetrahedral (sp3) or square planar (dsp2).
\[5.9 = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ ⇒\ n = 5\]
  • Mn2+ is 3d5, and all five electrons remain unpaired. No 3d orbital is vacant for dsp2 hybridisation, so sp3 hybridisation occurs.

Hence, [MnBr4]2- is tetrahedral.

Explain on the basis of valence bond theory that [Ni(CN)4]2- ion with square planar structure is diamagnetic and the [NiCl4]2- ion with tetrahedral geometry is paramagnetic.

In both complexes, Ni is in the +2 state with 3d8 configuration (two unpaired electrons).

  • CN- is a strong ligand. It pairs up the two unpaired 3d electrons, leaving one 3d orbital empty. dsp2 hybridisation gives a square planar complex with no unpaired electrons - diamagnetic.

  • Cl- is a weak ligand and cannot pair up the 3d electrons. sp3 hybridisation (4s + 4p) gives a tetrahedral complex with two unpaired electrons - paramagnetic.

[NiCl4]2- is paramagnetic while [Ni(CO)4] is diamagnetic though both are tetrahedral. Why?

  • In [Ni(CO)4], Ni is in the zero oxidation state (3d84s2). In the presence of CO, the 4s electrons move into 3d and all d electrons pair up (3d10). sp3 hybridisation gives a tetrahedral complex with no unpaired electron - diamagnetic.

  • In [NiCl4]2-, Ni is in the +2 state (3d8). Cl- is a weak ligand and cannot pair up the two unpaired electrons - paramagnetic.

[Fe(H2O)6]3+ is strongly paramagnetic whereas [Fe(CN)6]3- is weakly paramagnetic. Explain.

In both, Fe is in the +3 state (3d5).

  • CN- is a strong ligand. The 3d electrons pair up, leaving only one unpaired electron. d2sp3 hybridisation gives an inner orbital complex - weakly paramagnetic.

  • H2O is a weak ligand. The 3d electrons do not pair up. sp3d2 hybridisation gives an outer orbital complex with five unpaired electrons - strongly paramagnetic.

Explain why [Co(NH3)6]3+ is an inner orbital complex whereas [Ni(NH3)6]2+ is an outer orbital complex.

  • In [Co(NH3)6]3+, Co3+ is 3d6. In the presence of NH3, the 3d electrons pair up, leaving two 3d orbitals empty for d2sp3 hybridisation. So it is an inner orbital complex.

  • In [Ni(NH3)6]2+, Ni2+ is 3d8. Even after pairing, only one 3d orbital can be emptied, so two vacant 3d orbitals are not available. The outer 4d orbitals are used, giving sp3d2 hybridisation. So it is an outer orbital complex.

Predict the number of unpaired electrons in the square planar [Pt(CN)4]2- ion.

Pt2+ has the configuration 5d8. For a square planar shape, the hybridisation is dsp2. The two unpaired electrons in 5d pair up to make one 5d orbital empty for dsp2 hybridisation.

Hence, there is no unpaired electron in [Pt(CN)4]2-.

Discuss the nature of bonding in the following coordination entities on the basis of valence bond theory: (i) [Fe(CN)6]4- (ii) [FeF6]3- (iii) [Co(C2O4)3]3- (iv) [CoF6]3-

Complex Metal ion Ligand Hybridisation Geometry Unpaired e- Nature [Fe(CN)6]4- Fe2+, 3d6 Strong d2sp3 Octahedral 0 Inner orbital, diamagnetic [FeF6]3- Fe3+, 3d5 Weak sp3d2 Octahedral 5 Outer orbital, paramagnetic [Co(C2O4)3]3- Co3+, 3d6 Pairs electrons d2sp3 Octahedral 0 Inner orbital, diamagnetic [CoF6]3- Co3+, 3d6 Weak sp3d2 Octahedral 4 Outer orbital, paramagnetic

[Cr(NH3)6]3+ is paramagnetic while [Ni(CN)4]2- is diamagnetic. Explain why.

  • Cr3+ is 3d3. Two 3d orbitals are already empty, so d2sp3 hybridisation takes place without any pairing. The three unpaired electrons remain, so [Cr(NH3)6]3+ is paramagnetic.
\[μ = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = 3.87\ BM\]
  • Ni2+ is 3d8. CN- pairs up the two unpaired electrons, and dsp2 hybridisation gives a square planar complex with no unpaired electrons - diamagnetic.

docs.title: d-block Elements | Atomic and Ionic Sizes
d-block Elements | Atomic and Ionic Sizes
Atomic and Ionic sizes of d-block elements
docs.text:
• In general, the atomic and ionic radius decreased in 3d series with increase in atomic number.

  • Reason: The new electron enters a d-orbital due to which nuclear charge increases. The shielding effect of a d-electron is not effective and hence the net electrostatic attraction between the nuclear charge and the outermost electron increases and the ionic radius decreases.

  • The 4d and 5d series elements exhibit similar radii due to lanthonoid contraction.

Lanthanoid contraction

It occurs because of the poorest shielding effect of f-electrons. Lanthanoid contraction is associated with the intervention of the 4f-orbitals which must be filled before the 5d-series of elements begin. The filling of 4f-orbitals before 5d-orbitals results in a regular decrease in atomic radii which essentially compensates for the expected increase in atomic size with increasing atomic number.

docs.title: Density of d-block elements
docs.text:
• The decrease in metallic radius along with increase in atomic mass results in a general increase in density of these elements along the series.

Density

\[Sc < Ti < V < Zn < Cr < Mn < Fe < Co < Ni < Cu\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Zr belongs to 2nd d-series and Hf belongs to 3rd d-series but they have very similar physical and chemical properties. Why?

It is because they exhibit similar atomic radii due to lanthanoid contraction.

In the series from Ti (Z = 22) to Cu (Z = 29), copper has the highest density. Explain.

It is because density increases in the series due to decrease in atomic radius and increase in atomic mass.

docs.title: Ionization Enthalpy
docs.text:
• The energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state is known as ionization enthalpy. It is depicted by ΔiH. It is expressed in Kilojoules per mole (KJ mol-1).

  • It is the quantitative measure of the tendency of an atom to lose electron.

  • Energy is always required to remove electron(s) from an atom. Hence, it is always positive.

  • In general, ionization enthalpy increases along each series from left to right due to increase in nuclear charge.

docs.title: Irregular trend in first ionization enthalpy of 3d elements
docs.text:
• Removal of one electron alters the relative energies of 4s and 3d-orbitals. Due to reorganization of energy, the irregular trend is observed in first ionization enthalpy of 3-d metals.

The first ionization enthalpy of Cr is lower while that of Zn is higher. Explain.

The first ionization enthalpy of Cr is lower because of absence of any change in the d-configuration.

Electronic configuration of Cr: 1s22s22p63s23p63d54s1. The last electron in 4s can be easily removed.

The first ionization enthalpy of Zn is higher as electron has to be removed from completely filled 4s-orbital. (Electronic configuration of Zn: 1s22s22p63s23p63d104s2)

docs.title: Second ionization enthalpy of 3d elements
docs.text:
• Second ionization enthalpy is the energy required to remove second outermost electron from a cation (with +1 charge) in gaseous state.
  • The second ionization enthalpy also shows very irregular trend in 3d metals.

The second ionization enthalpy of Cr and Cu are very high. Explain.

In case of Cr, second electron has to be removed from stable 3d5 configuration and in case of Cu, second electron has to be removed from stable 3d10 configuration.

The second ionization enthalpy of Zn is low. Why?

Electronic configuration of Zn+: 1s22s22p63s23p63d104s1

Second electron has to be removed from 4s shell, which is much easier and it will allow the formation of stable completely filled d10 configuration.

docs.title: Third ionization enthalpy of 3d elements
docs.text:
• The third ionization enthalpy of these elements is very high because it is very difficult to remove electron from d-orbitals.

Why is it difficult to obtain oxidation state greater than 2 for transition elements?

It is difficult to obtain oxidation state greater than 2 for transition elements due to high value of third ionization enthalpy.

Generally, ionization enthalpy increases across a series. But third ionization enthalpy of Fe is less than that of Mn. Explain.

Electronic configuration of Mn2+: 1s2222p63s23p63d5

Electronic configuration of Fe2+: 1s22s22p63s23p63d6

Fe2+ readily loses electron to achieve stable d5 configuration while Mn2+ does not give electron easily due to presence of stable d5 configuration.

docs.title: d-block Elements | Magnetic, Catalytic and Other Properties
d-block Elements | Magnetic, Catalytic and Other Properties
Magnetic Properties of d-block Elements
docs.text:
• Diamagnetic Substances: Diamagnetic substances are repelled by the applied magnetic field.

  • Paramagnetic Substances: Paramagnetic substances are weakly attracted by the applied magnetic field.

  • Ferromagnetic Substances: Ferromagnetic substances are strongly attracted by the applied magnetic field.

  • In d-block elements , paramagnetism arises due to presence of unpaired electrons, each electron having a dipole moment.

  • Magnetic moment is calculated by "spin only" formula:

\[μ = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\]

where, n = Number of unpaired electrons

  • The unit of spin only magnetic moment is Bohr Magneton (B.M).

docs.title: Formation of Coloured Compounds by d-block Elements
docs.text:
• When an electron from a lower energy d-orbital is excited to a higher energy d-orbital, the energy of excitation corresponds to the frequency of light absorbed. This frequency generally lies in the visible region.
  • The colour observed corresponds to the complimentary colour of the light absorbed.
  • The frequency of light absorbed is determined by the nature of ligand.
Ion Sc+3 Ti+4 Ti+3 V+4 V+3 V+2 Cr+3 Cr+2 Mn+3 Mn+2 Fe+3 Fe+2 Co+3 Co+2 Ni+2 Cu+2 Zn+2 Colour Colourless Colourless Purple Blue Green Violet Violet Blue Violet Pink Yellow Green Blue Pink Green Blue Colourless

docs.title: Formation of Complex Compounds by d-block Elements
docs.text:
Complex Compounds

Complex compounds are those in which the metal ions bind a number of anions or neutral molecules giving complex species.

Transition elements form a large number of coordination compounds due to:

  • Smaller sizes of metal ions.
  • Availability of d-orbitals for bond formation.
  • High ionic charges.

Examples

  1. \({[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\)
  2. \([Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}\)

docs.title: Catalytic Properties of d-block Elements
docs.text:
Transition elements are effective as catalysts due to their ability to:

  • adopt multiple oxidation states.
  • form complexes.
Reaction Catalyst Contact Process Vanadium(V) Oxide Haber Process Finely divided iron Catalytic hydrogenation Nickel

Example

Iron(III) catalyzes reaction between iodide and persulphate ion.

\[2I^- + S_2O_8^{2-} → I_2 + 2SO_4^{2-}\]

Step 1.

\[2Fe^{3+} + 2I^- → 2Fe^{2+} + I_2\]

Step 2.

\[2Fe^{2+} + S_2O_8^{2-} → 2Fe^{3+} + 2SO_4^{2-}\]

docs.title: Formation of Interstitial Compounds by d-block Elements
docs.text:
• Interstitial compounds are those which are formed when small atoms like H, C or N are trapped inside the crystal lattices of metals. They are usually non-stoichiometric and are neither typically ionic or covalent.
  • Examples: TiC, Mn4N, Fe3H, VH0.56, TiH1.7
  • Interstitial compounds are very hard and have high melting points than pure metals.
  • Interstitial compounds are chemically inert and have metallic conductivity.

docs.title: Alloy Formation by d-block Elements
docs.text:
• An alloy is a blend of metals prepared by mixing the components.
  • Alloys are formed by atoms with metallic radii that are within about 15% of each other.
  • Because of similar radii and other characteristics of transition metals, alloys are readily formed by these metals. The alloys so formed are hard and have high melting points. Example: Stainless steel
  • Alloys of transition metals with non transition metals are also made. Example: Brass (Copper + Zinc) and Bronze (Copper + Tin).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the magnetic moment of a divalent ion in aqueous solution if its atomic number is 25.

Electronic Configuration of divalent ion with Z = 25 is: 1s22s22p63s23p63d5.

Number of unpaired electrons, n = 5

\[μ = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\] \[μ = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = 5.92\ BM\]

Calculate the spin only magnetic moment of M2+(aq) ion (Z = 27).

Electronic configuration of M2+(aq): 1s22s22p63s23p63d7.

Number of unpaired electrons, n = 3

\[μ = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\] \[μ = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = 3.87\ BM\]

Hence, spin only magnetic moment obtained for the given ion is 3.87 BM.

docs.title: Oxidation states of d-block elements
docs.text:
• +2 is the most stable oxidation state among d-block elements due to high value of third ionization enthalpy.
  • The elements which show large number of oxidation states occur in or near the middle of the series. For example, manganese exhibits all oxidation states from +2 to +7.
  • Transition elements show oxidation states which differ by unity due to incompletely filled d-orbitals.
  • The elements at the extreme ends exhibit lesser number of oxidation states due to: (i) too few electrons to lose or share and (ii) too many d-electrons (fewer orbitals available for sharing of electrons).
  • Heavier elements favour higher oxidation states.
  • Low oxidation states are found when a complex has ligands capable of π-acceptor character in addition to σ- bonding. For example, in Ni(CO)4 and Fe(CO5), oxidation states of Ni and Fe = 0.

docs.title: Trends in stability of higher oxidation states
docs.text:
• The highest oxidation numbers are achieved in case of TiX4 (tetrahalides), VF5 and CrF6.

  • The +7 oxidation state for Mn is not represented in simple halides but MnO3F is known, and beyond Mn no metal has a trihalide except FeX3 and CoF3.

  • Fluorine has the ability to stabilize higher oxidation state due to: (i) high lattice energy (in case of CoF3) and (ii) higher bond enthalpy terms for higher covalent compounds (VF5 and CrF6).

  • Fluorides are unstable in low oxidation states. Example: VX2, X = Cl, Br or I

  • Cu(II) halides are known except iodide. In this case, Cu2+ oxidizes I- to I2.

\[2Cu^{2+} + 4I^- → Cu_2I_{2(s)} + I_2\]
  • Many copper(I) compounds are unstable in aqueous solution and undergo disproportionation.
\[2Cu^+ → Cu^{2+} + Cu\]

  • Cu2+ is more stable than Cu+ due to more negative value of hydration enthalpy of Cu2+ which more than compensates for the second ionization enthalpy of copper.

  • The ability of oxygen to stabilize higher oxidation states is more than fluorine. It is because oxygen has the ability to form multiple bonds to metals.

docs.title: Trends in M<sup>2+</sup>/M Standard Electrode Potentials
docs.text:
• The E0 value of M2+/M becomes less negative across the series due to increase in the sum of first and second ionization enthalpies.

  • The value of E0(M2+/M) for Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than expected. For Mn and Zn, it is due to stability of half filled and fully filled d-orbitals respectively. For Ni, it is due to the highest negative hydration enthalpy.

  • The value of E0(M2+/M) for copper is positive because hydration energy and lattice energy of Cu2+ is more than that of Cu.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Name a transition element which does not exhibit variable oxidation states.

Scandium (Z = 21) does not exhibit variable oxidation states.

Note: Zn also does not exhibit variable oxidation state but it is not a transition element.

Which of the 3d series of the transition metal exhibits the largest number of oxidation states and why?

Mn exhibits the largest number of oxidation states because it has total 7 electrons in s- and d-orbitals which can take part in bonding.

Cr(VI) in the form of dichromate in acidic medium is a strong oxidizing agent whereas MoO3 and WO3 are not. Explain.

It is because Mo(VI) and W(VI) are found to be more stable than Cr(VI). [Heavier elements favour higher oxidation state.]

The E0(M2+/M) value of copper is positive (+0.34 V). What is possible reason for this?

The E0(M2+/M) value of copper is positive (+0.34 V) because hydration energy and lattice energy of Cu2+ is more than that of Cu.

Only oxidizing acids like HNO3 and hot conc. H2SO4 react with Cu, the acids being reduced. Explain.

Because of positive E0 value of Cu, it cannot liberate H2 from acids. So, only oxidizing acids like HNO3 and hoyt conc. H2SO4 react with Cu, the acids being reduced.

Why E0 values for Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than expected?

The value of E0(M2+/M) for Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than expected. For Mn and Zn, it is due to stability of half filled and fully filled d-orbitals respectively. For Ni, it is due to highest negative hydration enthalpy.

Why is Cr2+ reducing and Mn3+ oxidizing when both have d4 configuration?

Cr2+ is reducing as its configuration changes from d4 to d3, the latter having a half filled t2g level. On the other hand, the change from Mn2+ to Mn3+ results in the half filled d5 configuration which has extra stability.

How would you account for the irregular variation of ionization enthalpies (first and second) in the first series of the transition elements?

It is due to different stability of their electronic configuration.

How would you account for the increasing oxidizing power in the series VO2+ < Cr2O72- < MnO4-?

This is due to the increasing stability of the lower species to which they are reduced.

The highest Mn fluoride known is MnF4 whereas the highest oxide is Mn2O7. Explain.

It is due to the fact that the ability of oxygen to stabilize the high oxidation states exceeds that of fluorine.

Why is the highest oxidation state of a metal exhibited in its oxide or fluoride only?

It is because O2 and F2 are strong oxidizing agents due to high electronegativity.

Which is a stronger reducing agent Cr2+ or Fe2+ and why?

Fe2+ is strong reducing agent because it will get oxidized to Fe3+ which has half filled d-orbitals which is more stable.

For the first row of transition metals, the E0 values are: ElementVCrMnFeCoNiCuE0(M2+/M)-1.18-0.91-1.18-0.44-0.28-0.25+0.34 Explain the irregularity in above values.

The E0(M2+/M) values are not regular which can be explained from the irregular variation of ionization enthalpies and also the sublimation enthalpies which are relatively much less for manganese and vanadium.

Why is the E0 values for the Mn3+/Mn2+ couple much more positive than that of Cr3+/Cr2+ or Fe3+/Fe2+?

It is due to much larger third ionization energy of Mn (where the required change is d5 to d4). This also explains why the +3 oxidation state of Mn is of little importance.

What is meant by disproportionation of an oxidation state? Give an example.

When a particular oxidation state becomes less stable relative to other oxidation states: one lower and one higher, it is said to undergo disproportionation.

Example: Manganese (VI) becomes unstable relative to Manganese (VII) and Manganese (IV) in acidic solution.

\[3MnO_4^{2-} → 2MnO_4^- + MnO_2 + 2H_2O\]

Explain why Cu+ ion is not stable in aqueous solutions?

It is because Cu2+ ion is more stable as hydration energy overcomes second ionization energy.

docs.title: d-block Elements | Transition Elements and Their Physical Properties
d-block Elements | Transition Elements and Their Physical Properties
docs.text:
• The d-block of the periodic table contains the elements of the groups 3-12 in which the d-orbitals are progressively filled in each of the four long periods.
  • d-block consists of four series: 3d series, 4d series, 5d series and 6d series. 6d series is incomplete.
  • In this chapter, we will mainly focus on 3d series of d-block elements.

docs.title: Transition Element
docs.text:
• A transition element is defined as the one which has incompletely filled d-orbitals in its ground state or in any of its oxidation states.
  • The d-block element which has completely filled d-orbitals in ground state as well as in oxidation state cannot be classified as transition element. Example: Zinc

docs.title: Electronic Configuration
docs.text:
• General electronic configuration: (n-1)d1-10ns1-2

Exceptions in Electronic Configuration

  • \(Cr:\ 3d^54s^1\)

  • \(Cu:\ 3d^{10}4s^1\)

  • \(Hg:\ 5d^{10}6s^2\)

  • \(Cd:\ 4d^{10}5s^2\)

  • The electronic configuration of Zinc(Zn), Cadmium(Cd) and Mercury(Hg) is represented by the general formula (n-1)d10ns2.
  • The d orbitals in Zn, Cd and Hg are completely filled in the ground state as well as in their common oxidation states. Therefore, they are not regarded as transition elements.
  • Completely filled d-orbitals do not participate in bonding.

docs.title: 1. Metallic Properties
docs.text:
• High tensile strength, ductile, malleable, high thermal and electrical conductivity, metallic lustre, hard and low volatility.
  • d-block elements are very hard except Cd, Hg and Zn.

docs.title: 2. Melting Points
docs.text:
• The melting points of d-block elements are high due to involvement of greater number of electrons (both from ns and (n-1)d orbitals) in inter-atomic metallic bonding.
  • Cr has the highest melting point while Cu has the lowest melting point in 3d series.

docs.title: 3. Metallic Bond
docs.text: • 3d and 4d series elements of d-block are more frequent in forming metallic bonding due to high enthalpies of atomization and very high boiling point.

docs.title: 4. Enthalpy of Atomization
docs.text:
• The enthalpy change when one mole atoms of an element in gaseous state are formed from the most stable form of that element is known as enthalpy of atomization.
  • Since d-block elements are strongly bonded by metallic bond, they have high enthalpy of atomization.
  • Enthalpy of atomization of Zn is lowest as it has completely filled d-orbitals. Completely filled d-orbitals do not participate in bonding.
\[Enthalpy\ of\ atomization ∝ Valence\ electrons\ in\ bonding\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
On what ground can you say that Scandium (Z = 21) is a transition element but zinc (Z = 30) is not?

On the basis of incompletely filled 3d orbitals in case of Scandium in its ground state (3d1), it is regarded as a transition element. On the other hand, Zinc atom has completely filled d-orbitals (3d10) in its ground state as well as in its oxidized state, hence it is not regarded as a transition element.

Silver atom has completely filled d-orbitals (4d10) in its ground state. How can you say that it is a transition element?

Silver is regarded as a transition element because it can exhibit +2 oxidation state which has incompletely filled d-orbitals.

Why do transition elements exhibit higher enthalpies of atomization?

Because of large number of unpaired electrons in their atoms, transition elements have stronger inter-atomic interactions and hence stronger bonding between atoms resulting in higher enthalpies of atomization.

docs.title: f-block Elements | Actinoids and their Properties
f-block Elements | Actinoids and their Properties
Actinoids
docs.text:
• The actinoids include fourteen elements from Thorium (Th) to Lawrencium (Lr).

General Electronic Configuration

\[(n-2)f^{0-14} (n-1)d^{0-1}ns^2\]
  • The irregularities in the electronic configuration of actinoids are related to stability of f0, f7 and f14 configuration of the 5f orbitals.
  • The chemistry of actinoids is much complicated due to: (a) wide range of oxidation states (b) Radioactive property

docs.title: Atomic and Ionic Sizes
docs.text:
Actinoid Contraction

The gradual decrease in the size of atoms or M3+ ions across the actinoid series is called actinoid contraction.

Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction due to very poor shielding of 5f-electrons as compared to 4f-electrons.

docs.title: Oxidation States
docs.text:
• In general, actinoids show +3 oxidation state.
  • However, they exhibit a very wide range of oxidation states, which makes their chemistry complicated.

docs.title: Similarities between Lanthanoids and Actinoids
docs.text:
• In both, f-orbitals are progressively filled.
  • Both form coloured ions.
  • Both are paramagnetic in nature.
  • Both show contraction, ie, lanthanoid contraction and actinoid contraction.

docs.title: Differences between Lanthanoids and Actinoids
docs.text: S.No. Lanthanoids Actinoids 1. 4-f orbital is progressively filled. 5-f orbital is progressively filled. 2. +3 oxidation state is the most common along with +2 and +4. They show +2, +3, +4, +5, +6, +7 oxidation states. 3. Only promethium (Pm) is radioactive. All are radioactive. 4. They are less reactive than actinoid. They are more reactive. 5. The magnetic properties are less complex. The magnetic properties are more complex.

docs.title: Applications of d and f block Elements
docs.text:
• Tungsten (W) is used in making electrical filaments.
  • Titanium is used in nuclear reactions.
  • Iron is used as a catalyst in Haber's process.

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction. Why?

It is due to very poor shielding of 5f electrons as compared to 4f electrons.

docs.title: f-block Elements | Lanthanoids and their Properties
f-block Elements | Lanthanoids and their Properties
Lanthanoids
docs.text:
• The fourteen elements following lanthanum are called lanthanoids.
  • Because lanthanum closely resembles the lanthanoids, it is usually included in the discussion of lanthanoids.
  • Promethium (Z=61) is the only lanthanoid which is radioactive.

docs.title: Electronic configuration of lanthanoids
docs.text:
• Atoms of these elements have electronic configuration with 6s2 common but with variable occupancy of 4f level.

General Electronic Configuration of lanthanoids

\[(n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-1}ns^{2},\ where\ n = 6\] Atomic Number Name Electronic configuration 57 Lanthanum (La) 5d16s2 58 Cerium (Ce) 4f15d16s2 59 Praseodymium (Pr) 4f36s2 60 Neodymium (Nd) 4f46s2 61 Promethium (Pm) 4f56s2 62 Samarium (Sm) 4f66s2 63 Europium (Eu) 4f76s2 64 Gadolinium (Gd) 4f75d16s2 65 Terbium (Tb) 4f96s2 66 Dysprosium (Dy) 4f106s2 67 Holmium (Ho) 4f116s2 68 Erbium (Er) 4f126s2 69 Thulium (Tm) 4f136s2 70 Ytterbium (Yb) 4f146s2 71 Lutetium (Lu) 4f145d16s2

docs.title: Atomic and Ionic Sizes
docs.text:
Lanthanoid Contraction

The overall decrease in atomic and ionic radii from lanthanum to lutetium is called lanthanoid contraction. For every additional proton in the nucleus, the corresponding electron goes into the 4f shell which is too diffused to screen the nucleus as effectively as more localized inner shell.

Consequence of lanthanoid contraction: It causes the radii of the members of the third transition series to be very similar to those of the corresponding members of the second series.

docs.title: Oxidation States
docs.text:
• The most common oxidation state is +3. For lanthanum (La), it is +2.
  • However, occasionally +2 and +4 ions in solution or in solid compounds are also obtained. This irregularity arises mainly due to extra stability of empty, half-filled or completely filled f-subshell.
  • Cem Pm, Nd, Tb and Dy show both +3 and +4 oxidation states.
  • Eu and Sm show both +2 and +3 oxidation states.
  • Eu2+ is a strong reducing agent.
  • Yb2+ which has f14 configuration is a reactant.
  • TbIV has half filled f-orbital and is an oxidant.
  • Ce4+ can oxidize water as the E0 value for Ce4+/Ce3+ is +1.74 V.

docs.title: Colour
docs.text:
• Many trivalent lanthanoids ions except La3+ and Lu3+ are coloured both in solid state and in aqueous solutions.
  • Colour of these ions may be attributed to the presence of f-electrons. However, absorption bands are narrow probably because of the excitation within f-level.

docs.title: Magnetic Property
docs.text:
• The lanthanoid ions other than f0 type (La3+ and Ce4+) and the f14 type (Yb2+ and Lu3+) are all paramagnetic.
  • The paramagnetism rises to maximum in neodymium(Nd).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Name a member of the lanthanoid series which is well known to exhibit +4 oxidation state.

Cerium (Z = 58) is well known to exhibit +4 oxidation state.

Name two members of the lanthanoid series which exhibit: (a) +2 oxidation state (b) +4 oxidation state.

(a) Europium (Z = 63) and Ytterbium (Z = 70) (b) Cerium (Z = 58) and Neodymium (Z = 60)

Name a member of the lanthanoid series which has: (a) maximum paramagnetic property (b) no paramagnetic property.

(a) Neodymium (Z = 60) has maximum paramagnetic property. (b) La3+ and Ce4+ have no paramagnetic property.

Name a member of the lanthanoid series which is radioactive.

Promethium (Z = 61) is the only lanthanoid, which is radioactive.

docs.title: Environmental Chemistry | Pollution Control and Green Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry | Pollution Control and Green Chemistry
docs.text: Controlling environmental pollution needs two things: proper management of the wastes we already produce, and new ways of doing chemistry that produce fewer pollutants in the first place.

docs.title: Strategies to Control Environmental Pollution
docs.text:
• Waste management, i.e., reduction of waste and its proper disposal, and recycling of materials and energy.
  • Adopting methods in day-to-day life which reduce environmental pollution.
  • Green chemistry, which uses existing knowledge and practices to reduce the production of pollutants.
