docs.title: Waste Management
docs.text:
• Besides household solid waste, there are medical, agricultural, industrial and mining wastes.
  • Improper disposal of wastes is one of the major causes of environmental degradation, so waste management is very important.

docs.title: Collection and Disposal
docs.text:
• Domestic wastes are collected in small bins and transferred to community bins by private or municipal workers. From there they are carried to the disposal site.
  • At the site, garbage is sorted into biodegradable and non-biodegradable materials:
    • Non-biodegradable materials such as plastic, glass and metal scraps are sent for recycling.
    • Biodegradable wastes are deposited in land fills and converted into compost.
  • Waste not collected in bins finds its way into sewers. Some of it is eaten by cattle. Polythene bags and metal scraps choke sewers, and polythene swallowed by cattle can kill them.
  • Poor waste management causes health problems and epidemics due to contamination of ground water. It is especially hazardous for rag pickers and waste workers who handle waste without gloves, waterproof boots or gas masks.

docs.title: Waste Recycling
docs.text:
• Fuel obtained from plastic waste has a high octane rating and contains no lead. It is known as "green fuel".
  • Clothes can be made from recycled plastic waste.
  • Electricity can be produced from garbage: after removing ferrous metals, plastic, glass and paper, the garbage is mixed with water and cultured with bacteria that produce methane (biogas). The biogas is used to generate electricity and the remaining product is used as manure.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• India achieved self-sufficiency in food by the late 20th century using fertilizers, pesticides and improved farming methods. But over-exploitation of soil and excessive use of fertilizers and pesticides have degraded soil, water and air.
  • The solution is not to stop development but to find methods that reduce damage to the environment.

Definition

Green chemistry is a way of thinking that uses the existing knowledge and principles of chemistry and other sciences to reduce the adverse impact on the environment. It is a production process that brings about minimum pollution or deterioration of the environment.

  • By-products of a process, if not used gainfully, add to environmental pollution. Such processes are environmentally unfriendly and also cost-ineffective, since both waste generation and its disposal are economically unsound.

docs.title: Principles of Green Chemistry
docs.text:
• A chemical reaction involves reactants, attacking reagents and the medium. Its extent depends on temperature, pressure and catalyst.
  • If reactants are fully converted into useful, environment-friendly products using an environment-friendly medium, no chemical pollutants enter the environment.
  • Choose starting materials that can be converted into end products with a yield of about 100 per cent, by arriving at optimum conditions of synthesis.
  • Prefer water as the reaction medium wherever possible. Water has high specific heat and low volatility, and is cost effective, non-inflammable and free of carcinogenic effects.
  • Organic solvents such as benzene, toluene and carbon tetrachloride are highly toxic and should be used with care.

Note

Yves Chauvin, Robert H. Grubbs and Richard R. Schrock won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the metathesis method in organic synthesis, a way to rearrange groups of atoms within molecules. It reduces hazardous waste through smarter production and is used in the pharmaceutical, biotechnology and food industries and in making environment-friendlier polymers.

docs.title: 1. Dry Cleaning of Clothes
docs.text:
• Tetrachloroethene (Cl2C=CCl2) was earlier used as a dry cleaning solvent. It contaminates ground water and is a suspected carcinogen.
  • It is being replaced by liquefied carbon dioxide with a suitable detergent. Replacing halogenated solvents with liquid CO2 causes less harm to ground water.
  • Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is now used for bleaching clothes in laundry. It gives better results and uses less water.

docs.title: 2. Bleaching of Paper
docs.text:
• Chlorine gas was earlier used for bleaching paper.
  • Now hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is used with a suitable catalyst that promotes its bleaching action.

docs.title: 3. Synthesis of Chemicals
docs.text:
• Ethanal (CH3CHO) is now prepared commercially by one-step oxidation of ethene using an ionic catalyst in aqueous medium, with a yield of 90%:
\[CH_2{=}CH_2 + O_2 \xrightarrow[Pd(II)/Cu(II)\ (in\ water)]{Catalyst} CH_3CHO\ (90\%)\]

Conclusion

Green chemistry, in a nutshell, is a cost-effective approach which involves reduction in material, energy consumption and waste generation.

Our responsibility

  • Set up a compost tin at home and use it to make manure, reducing the use of fertilizers.
  • Use a cloth bag and avoid plastic carry bags.
  • Make sure newspapers, glass, aluminium and other items are recycled.

docs.title: Environmental Chemistry | Introduction
docs.text:
Environmental chemistry deals with the study of the origin, transport, reactions, effects and fates of chemical species in the environment.

  • Environmental studies cover all the social, economical, biological, physical and chemical interrelations with our surroundings.
  • Environmental chemistry focuses only on the chemical side of this picture: where a chemical comes from, how it moves, what it reacts with and what finally happens to it.

docs.title: Environmental Pollution
docs.text:
Environmental pollution is the effect of undesirable changes in our surroundings that have harmful effects on plants, animals and human beings.

  • A substance which causes pollution is called a pollutant.
  • Pollutants can be solid, liquid or gaseous. They are substances present in a concentration greater than their natural abundance, produced either by human activities or by natural happenings.
  • An average human being needs nearly 12-15 times more air than food. So even small amounts of pollutants in the air become significant compared to similar levels in food.

docs.title: 1. Degradable Pollutants
docs.text:
• These are broken down rapidly by natural processes.
  • Example: Discarded vegetables.

docs.title: 2. Slowly Degradable / Non-Degradable Pollutants
docs.text:
• These remain in the environment in an unchanged form for many decades and are difficult to remove once released.
  • They cannot be degraded by natural processes and are harmful to living organisms.
  • Examples: Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT), plastic materials, heavy metals, many chemicals and nuclear wastes.

Note

In the process of environmental pollution, pollutants originate from a source and are then transported by air or water, or are dumped into the soil by human beings.

docs.title: Regions of the Atmosphere
docs.text: The atmosphere around the earth does not have the same thickness at all heights. It consists of concentric layers of air, each with a different density.

docs.title: 1. Troposphere
docs.text:
• It is the lowest region of the atmosphere in which human beings and other organisms live.
  • It extends up to a height of about 10 km from sea level.
  • It is a turbulent, dusty zone containing air, much water vapour and clouds. Strong air movement and cloud formation take place here.

docs.title: 2. Stratosphere
docs.text:
• It lies between 10 km and 50 km above sea level.
  • It contains dinitrogen, dioxygen, ozone and little water vapour.
  • The ozone present in the stratosphere prevents about 99.5 per cent of the sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from reaching the earth's surface, thereby protecting humans and other animals.
Region Height above sea level Main constituents Troposphere 0 to ~10 km Air, much water vapour, clouds, dust Stratosphere 10 to 50 km N2, O2, O3, little water vapour

docs.title: Atmospheric Pollution
docs.text:
Atmospheric pollution is generally studied under two heads:

  • Tropospheric pollution: caused by undesirable solid or gaseous particles in the lower atmosphere (oxides of sulphur, nitrogen and carbon, hydrocarbons, particulates, smog).
  • Stratospheric pollution: mainly the depletion of the protective ozone layer by chemicals such as chlorofluorocarbons.

The following pages discuss tropospheric pollution, smog and particulates, stratospheric pollution, water and soil pollution, and finally the strategies to control pollution, including green chemistry.

docs.title: Environmental Chemistry | Particulate Pollutants and Smog
Environmental Chemistry | Particulate Pollutants and Smog
docs.text: Particulate pollutants are the minute solid particles or liquid droplets in air. They are present in vehicle emissions, smoke particles from fires, dust particles and ash from industries.

docs.title: Particulate Pollutants
docs.text: Particulates in the atmosphere may be viable or non-viable.

docs.title: 1. Viable Particulates
docs.text:
• These are minute living organisms dispersed in the atmosphere, e.g., bacteria, fungi, moulds, algae etc.
  • Human beings are allergic to some of the fungi found in air. These particulates can also cause plant diseases.

docs.title: 2. Non-Viable Particulates
docs.text: Non-viable particulates are classified according to their nature and size:

docs.title: (a) Smoke
docs.text:
• Solid particles, or a mixture of solid and liquid particles, formed during combustion of organic matter.
  • Examples: Cigarette smoke, smoke from burning of fossil fuel, garbage and dry leaves, oil smoke.

docs.title: (b) Dust
docs.text:
• Fine solid particles (over 1 μm in diameter) produced during crushing, grinding and attrition of solid materials.
  • Examples: Sand from sand blasting, saw dust from wood works, pulverized coal, cement and fly ash from factories, dust storms.

docs.title: (c) Mists
docs.text:
• Produced by particles of spray liquids and by condensation of vapours in air.
  • Examples: Sulphuric acid mist, and herbicides and insecticides that miss their targets and travel through air to form mists.

docs.title: (d) Fumes
docs.text:
• Obtained by condensation of vapours during sublimation, distillation, boiling and several other chemical reactions.
  • Generally, organic solvents, metals and metallic oxides form fume particles.

docs.title: Effects of Particulate Pollutants
docs.text:
• The effect depends largely on particle size. Air-borne particles such as dust, fumes and mist are dangerous for human health.
  • Particles bigger than 5 microns are likely to lodge in the nasal passage, whereas particles of about 1.0 micron enter the lungs easily.
  • Lead used to be a major air pollutant from vehicles running on leaded petrol. It interferes with the development and maturation of red blood cells. This problem has largely been overcome in Indian cities by using unleaded petrol.

docs.title: Smog
docs.text:
The word smog is derived from smoke and fog. It is the most common example of air pollution in many cities throughout the world. There are two types of smog:

Property Classical smog Photochemical smog Climate Cool, humid Warm, dry and sunny Composition Smoke, fog and SO2 O3, NO, acrolein, formaldehyde, PAN Origin Burning of coal and fuels in humid air Action of sunlight on unsaturated hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides from automobiles and factories Chemical nature Reducing mixture High concentration of oxidising agents Also called Reducing smog Oxidising smog

docs.title: Formation of Photochemical Smog
docs.text:
• Burning of fossil fuels releases hydrocarbons (unburnt fuels) and nitric oxide (NO) into the troposphere.
  • When these build up to sufficiently high levels, a chain reaction occurs due to their interaction with sunlight, in which NO is converted into NO2.
  • NO2 absorbs energy from sunlight and breaks up into nitric oxide and a free oxygen atom:
\[NO_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{h\nu} NO_{(g)} + O_{(g)}\ \ \ ...(i)\]
  • Oxygen atoms are very reactive and combine with O2 in air to produce ozone:
\[O_{(g)} + O_{2(g)} ⇌ O_{3(g)}\ \ \ ...(ii)\]
  • The ozone formed reacts rapidly with the NO formed in reaction (i) to regenerate NO2. NO2 is a brown gas and at high enough levels it contributes to haze:
\[NO_{(g)} + O_{3(g)} → NO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)}\ \ \ ...(iii)\]
  • Ozone is a toxic gas. Both NO2 and O3 are strong oxidising agents and react with unburnt hydrocarbons in the polluted air to produce chemicals such as formaldehyde, acrolein and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN):
\[3CH_4 + 2O_3 → 3CH_2{=}O + 3H_2O\] \[Formaldehyde:\ HCHO\ \ \ \ Acrolein:\ CH_2{=}CH{-}CHO\ \ \ \ PAN:\ CH_3COOONO_2\]

Note

PAN is peroxyacetyl nitrate, CH3C(=O)OONO2. It contains an acetyl group joined through a peroxide (-O-O-) link to an NO2 group.

docs.title: Effects of Photochemical Smog
docs.text:
• The common components are ozone, nitric oxide, acrolein, formaldehyde and PAN.
  • Ozone and PAN are powerful eye irritants.
  • Ozone and nitric oxide irritate the nose and throat. Their high concentration causes headache, chest pain, dryness of the throat, cough and difficulty in breathing.
  • Photochemical smog causes cracking of rubber and extensive damage to plant life.
  • It also corrodes metals, stones, building materials, rubber and painted surfaces.

docs.title: Control of Photochemical Smog
docs.text:
• If the primary precursors (NO2 and hydrocarbons) are controlled, the secondary precursors (ozone and PAN) are automatically reduced.
  • Catalytic converters in automobiles prevent the release of nitrogen oxide and hydrocarbons into the atmosphere.
  • Certain plants, e.g., Pinus, Juniparus, Quercus, Pyrus and Vitis, can metabolise nitrogen oxide. Planting them can help.

docs.title: Environmental Chemistry | Questions
docs.text: Short-answer questions with solutions on environmental chemistry covering tropospheric pollution, smog, ozone depletion, water pollution, BOD, pesticides and green chemistry.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Define environmental chemistry.

Environmental chemistry is the branch of chemistry which deals with the study of the origin, transport, reactions, effects and fates of chemical species in the environment.

Explain tropospheric pollution in brief.

  • Tropospheric pollution occurs due to undesirable solid or gaseous particles in the lowest layer of the atmosphere (up to about 10 km), where we live.
  • Gaseous pollutants: oxides of sulphur (SO2), nitrogen (NO, NO2) and carbon (CO, CO2), hydrogen sulphide, hydrocarbons, ozone and other oxidants. They come mainly from burning fossil fuels and automobile exhaust.
  • Particulate pollutants: dust, mist, fumes, smoke and smog.
  • They cause respiratory diseases, eye irritation, damage to plants, acid rain, smog and global warming.

Carbon monoxide gas is more dangerous than carbon dioxide gas. Why?

  • CO combines with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which is about 300 times more stable than the oxygen-haemoglobin complex.
\[Hb + CO → HbCO\]
  • So haemoglobin can no longer carry oxygen to the organs and tissues. At 3-4 per cent carboxyhaemoglobin in blood, the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood is greatly reduced, causing headache, weak eyesight, nervousness, cardiovascular disorder and even death.
  • CO2 does not bind to haemoglobin in this way. It is harmful mainly by contributing to global warming, not by direct poisoning.

List the gases which are responsible for the greenhouse effect.

Carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), water vapour, nitrous oxide (N2O), chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and ozone (O3). CO2 is the major contributor.

Statues and monuments in India are affected by acid rain. How?

  • SO2 and NO2 released from industries, power plants and domestic fuels get oxidised and react with water to form H2SO4 and HNO3:
\[2SO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O → 2H_2SO_4\] \[4NO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O → 4HNO_3\]
  • Statues and monuments made of marble (CaCO3) react with these acids:
\[CaCO_3 + H_2SO_4 → CaSO_4 + H_2O + CO_2\]
  • The marble slowly gets corroded, discoloured and lustreless. The Taj Mahal at Agra is a well-known example.

What is smog? How is classical smog different from photochemical smog?

Smog is a mixture of smoke and fog. It is the most common form of air pollution in cities.

Classical smog Photochemical smog Occurs in cool, humid climate Occurs in warm, dry and sunny climate Mixture of smoke, fog and SO2 Contains O3, NO, acrolein, formaldehyde and PAN Reducing in nature (reducing smog) Oxidising in nature (oxidising smog)

Write down the reactions involved during the formation of photochemical smog.

\[NO_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{h\nu} NO_{(g)} + O_{(g)}\] \[O_{(g)} + O_{2(g)} ⇌ O_{3(g)}\] \[NO_{(g)} + O_{3(g)} → NO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)}\]

O3 and NO2 then oxidise unburnt hydrocarbons to formaldehyde, acrolein and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN):

\[3CH_4 + 2O_3 → 3HCHO + 3H_2O\]

What are the harmful effects of photochemical smog and how can they be controlled?

Harmful effects:

  • Ozone and PAN are powerful eye irritants.
  • Ozone and NO irritate the nose and throat; high concentrations cause headache, chest pain, dryness of throat, cough and difficulty in breathing.
  • It cracks rubber, damages plant life and corrodes metals, stones, building materials and painted surfaces.

Control:

  • Control the primary precursors (NO2 and hydrocarbons) using catalytic converters in automobiles; the secondary precursors (O3 and PAN) then automatically decrease.
  • Plant trees such as Pinus, Juniparus, Quercus, Pyrus and Vitis, which can metabolise nitrogen oxide.

What are the reactions involved in ozone layer depletion in the stratosphere?

CFCs are broken down by UV radiation to give chlorine radicals, which destroy ozone in a chain reaction:

\[CF_2Cl_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{UV} \dot{Cl}_{(g)} + \dot{C}F_2Cl_{(g)}\] \[\dot{Cl}_{(g)} + O_{3(g)} → Cl\dot{O}_{(g)} + O_{2(g)}\] \[Cl\dot{O}_{(g)} + O_{(g)} → \dot{Cl}_{(g)} + O_{2(g)}\]

The chlorine radical is regenerated, so one CFC molecule can destroy many ozone molecules.

What do you mean by ozone hole? What are its consequences?

  • The depletion of the ozone layer over the South Pole (Antarctica), first reported in the 1980s, is called the ozone hole. It forms because polar stratospheric clouds in winter convert chlorine sinks (ClONO2, HCl) into HOCl and Cl2, which are photolysed in spring to give chlorine radicals.
  • Consequences: More UV radiation reaches the troposphere, causing ageing of skin, cataract, sunburn, skin cancer, death of phytoplanktons, reduced fish productivity, harmful mutation of cells, loss of soil moisture through increased evaporation from leaves, and fading of paints and fibres.

What are the major causes of water pollution? Explain.

  • Pathogens: bacteria and other organisms from domestic sewage and animal excreta, e.g., Escherichia coli and Streptococcus faecalis, which cause gastrointestinal diseases.
  • Organic wastes: leaves, grass, trash and excess phytoplankton. Their decomposition by bacteria uses up dissolved oxygen, killing aquatic life.
  • Chemical pollutants: heavy metals (Cd, Hg, Ni), acids from mine drainage, salts, petroleum products, pesticides, PCBs, detergents and fertilizers (phosphates cause eutrophication).

What do you mean by Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)?

  • The amount of oxygen required by bacteria to break down the organic matter present in a certain volume of a water sample is called BOD.
  • It measures the amount of organic matter in water. Clean water has BOD less than 5 ppm, while highly polluted water has BOD of 17 ppm or more.

What are pesticides and herbicides? Explain giving examples.

  • Pesticides are synthetic toxic chemicals used to kill insects, rodents and other pests that damage crops. Examples: DDT, Aldrin, Dieldrin (organo-chlorides), and organo-phosphates and carbamates. Organo-chlorides are non-biodegradable and accumulate in the food chain.
  • Herbicides are chemicals used to kill weeds. Examples: sodium chlorate (NaClO3) and sodium arsinite (Na3AsO3). They are toxic to mammals but decompose within a few months.

What do you mean by green chemistry? How will it help decrease environmental pollution?

  • Green chemistry is a way of thinking that uses existing knowledge and principles of chemistry and other sciences to reduce the adverse impact on the environment.
  • It helps by: choosing starting materials that give nearly 100% yield of useful products, so little by-product waste forms; using water instead of toxic organic solvents; replacing harmful reagents (e.g., liquid CO2 instead of tetrachloroethene in dry cleaning, H2O2 instead of Cl2 in bleaching paper); and reducing material and energy consumption.

What would have happened if the greenhouse gases were totally missing in the earth's atmosphere? Discuss.

  • Greenhouse gases trap part of the heat radiated by the earth's surface and keep the earth warm (natural greenhouse effect).
  • Without them, all this heat would escape into space. The earth's surface would become extremely cold, and life as we know it, including plants and animals, could not survive.

A large number of fish are suddenly found floating dead on a lake. There is no evidence of toxic dumping but you find an abundance of phytoplankton. Suggest a reason for the fish kill.

  • The abundant phytoplankton indicates eutrophication, caused by nutrients such as phosphates from fertilizers or detergents.
  • When the phytoplankton die, bacteria decompose them and use up the dissolved oxygen. The algal bloom also covers the surface, reducing oxygen in water.
  • When DO falls well below 6 ppm, fish cannot survive and die of oxygen deficiency.

How can domestic waste be used as manure?

  • Domestic waste is separated into biodegradable (vegetable peels, leftover food, leaves etc.) and non-biodegradable (plastic, glass, metal) parts.
  • The biodegradable part is put in a compost pit or land fill, where micro-organisms decompose it into compost, which is used as manure. Non-biodegradable materials are sent for recycling.

docs.title: Environmental Chemistry | Stratospheric Pollution
docs.text:
Stratospheric pollution mainly refers to the depletion of the protective ozone layer of the upper atmosphere by chemicals such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).

  • The upper stratosphere contains a considerable amount of ozone (O3).
  • It protects us from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation (λ 255 nm) coming from the sun. This radiation causes skin cancer (melanoma) in humans, so it is important to maintain the ozone shield.

docs.title: Formation and Breakdown of Ozone
docs.text:
• Ozone in the stratosphere is formed by the action of UV radiation on dioxygen (O2) molecules.
  • UV radiation splits molecular oxygen into free oxygen atoms, which then combine with molecular oxygen to form ozone:
\[O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{UV} O_{(g)} + O_{(g)}\] \[O_{(g)} + O_{2(g)} \overset{UV}{⇌} O_{3(g)}\]
  • Ozone is thermodynamically unstable and decomposes back to molecular oxygen.
  • So a dynamic equilibrium exists between the production and decomposition of ozone molecules. Any chemical that speeds up the decomposition reduces the ozone level.

docs.title: Depletion of Ozone by CFCs
docs.text:
• The main cause of ozone layer depletion is believed to be the release of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), also called freons.
  • CFCs are non-reactive, non-flammable, non-toxic organic molecules. So they are used in refrigerators, air conditioners, production of plastic foam and by the electronic industry for cleaning computer parts.
  • Once released, CFCs mix with the normal atmospheric gases and eventually reach the stratosphere.
  • In the stratosphere, powerful UV radiation breaks them down, releasing a chlorine free radical:
\[CF_2Cl_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{UV} \dot{Cl}_{(g)} + \dot{C}F_2Cl_{(g)}\ \ \ ...(i)\]
  • The chlorine radical reacts with stratospheric ozone to form a chlorine monoxide radical and molecular oxygen:
\[\dot{Cl}_{(g)} + O_{3(g)} → Cl\dot{O}_{(g)} + O_{2(g)}\ \ \ ...(ii)\]
  • The chlorine monoxide radical reacts with atomic oxygen and regenerates the chlorine radical:
\[Cl\dot{O}_{(g)} + O_{(g)} → \dot{Cl}_{(g)} + O_{2(g)}\ \ \ ...(iii)\]

Conclusion

  • Chlorine radicals are continuously regenerated in reactions (ii) and (iii), so a single chlorine radical can destroy a very large number of ozone molecules (a chain reaction).
  • Thus CFCs act as transporting agents that continuously generate chlorine radicals in the stratosphere and damage the ozone layer.

docs.title: The Ozone Hole
docs.text:
• In the 1980s, atmospheric scientists working in Antarctica reported depletion of the ozone layer over the South Pole, commonly known as the ozone hole.
  • A unique set of conditions is responsible for it.

docs.title: Summer: formation of chlorine sinks
docs.text:
• Chlorine monoxide reacts with nitrogen dioxide, and chlorine atoms react with methane. These form chlorine sinks (chlorine nitrate and HCl), which prevent much ozone depletion:
\[Cl\dot{O}_{(g)} + NO_{2(g)} → ClONO_{2(g)}\ \ \ ...(iv)\] \[\dot{Cl}_{(g)} + CH_{4(g)} → \dot{C}H_{3(g)} + HCl_{(g)}\ \ \ ...(v)\]

docs.title: Winter: polar stratospheric clouds
docs.text:
• In winter, a special type of cloud called polar stratospheric clouds forms over Antarctica.
  • These clouds provide a surface on which chlorine nitrate is hydrolysed to hypochlorous acid. Chlorine nitrate also reacts with HCl to give molecular chlorine:
\[ClONO_{2(g)} + H_2O_{(g)} → HOCl_{(g)} + HNO_{3(g)}\ \ \ ...(vi)\] \[ClONO_{2(g)} + HCl_{(g)} → Cl_{2(g)} + HNO_{3(g)}\ \ \ ...(vii)\]

docs.title: Spring: release of chlorine radicals
docs.text:
• When sunlight returns to Antarctica in spring, the sun's warmth breaks up the clouds, and HOCl and Cl2 are photolysed:
\[HOCl_{(g)} \xrightarrow{h\nu} \dot{O}H_{(g)} + \dot{Cl}_{(g)}\ \ \ ...(viii)\] \[Cl_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2\dot{Cl}_{(g)}\ \ \ ...(ix)\]
  • The chlorine radicals so formed start the chain reaction for ozone depletion described above. This is why the ozone hole appears over Antarctica in spring.

docs.title: Effects of Depletion of the Ozone Layer
docs.text:
With a thinner ozone layer, more UV radiation filters into the troposphere. This leads to:

  • Ageing of skin, cataract, sunburn and skin cancer.
  • Killing of many phytoplanktons and damage to fish productivity.
  • Harmful mutation of cells, since plant proteins are easily affected by UV radiation.
  • More evaporation of surface water through the stomata of leaves, decreasing the moisture content of the soil.
  • Damage to paints and fibres, causing them to fade faster.

docs.title: Environmental Chemistry | Tropospheric Pollution
docs.text:
Tropospheric pollution occurs due to the presence of undesirable solid or gaseous particles in the air of the lowest region of the atmosphere.

The major pollutants present in the troposphere are of two kinds:

  • Gaseous air pollutants: oxides of sulphur, nitrogen and carbon, hydrogen sulphide, hydrocarbons, ozone and other oxidants.
  • Particulate pollutants: dust, mist, fumes, smoke, smog etc. These are discussed on the next page.

docs.title: 1. Oxides of Sulphur
docs.text:
• Oxides of sulphur are produced when sulphur-containing fossil fuel is burnt. The most common one is sulphur dioxide (SO2).
  • SO2 is poisonous to both animals and plants.
  • Even a low concentration of SO2 causes respiratory diseases in humans such as asthma, bronchitis and emphysema. It also irritates the eyes, causing tears and redness.
  • A high concentration of SO2 makes flower buds stiff, and they eventually fall off the plants.
  • Uncatalysed oxidation of SO2 is slow. However, particulate matter in polluted air catalyses its oxidation to sulphur trioxide:
\[2SO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} → 2SO_{3(g)}\]
  • The oxidation can also be promoted by ozone and hydrogen peroxide:
\[SO_{2(g)} + O_{3(g)} → SO_{3(g)} + O_{2(g)}\] \[SO_{2(g)} + H_2O_{2(l)} → H_2SO_{4(aq)}\]

docs.title: 2. Oxides of Nitrogen
docs.text:
• Dinitrogen and dioxygen are the main constituents of air, but they do not react with each other at normal temperature.
  • At high altitudes, when lightning strikes, they combine to form oxides of nitrogen. NO2 is oxidised to nitrate ion (NO3-), which is washed into the soil where it serves as a fertilizer.
  • In an automobile engine, fossil fuel burns at a high temperature, and dinitrogen and dioxygen combine to give significant quantities of nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2):
\[N_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{1483\ K} 2NO_{(g)}\] \[2NO_{(g)} + O_{2(g)} → 2NO_{2(g)}\]
  • NO reacts instantly with oxygen to give NO2. The rate of production of NO2 is faster when NO reacts with ozone in the stratosphere:
\[NO_{(g)} + O_{3(g)} → NO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: Harmful effects of NO<sub>x</sub>
docs.text:
• The irritant red haze seen in traffic and congested places is due to oxides of nitrogen.
  • High concentrations of NO2 damage the leaves of plants and slow down photosynthesis.
  • NO2 is a lung irritant that can cause acute respiratory disease in children. It is toxic to living tissues.
  • It also harms textile fibres and metals.

docs.title: 3. Hydrocarbons
docs.text:
• Hydrocarbons are compounds of only hydrogen and carbon. They are formed by incomplete combustion of fuel used in automobiles.
  • They are carcinogenic, i.e., they cause cancer.
  • They harm plants by causing ageing, breakdown of tissues and shedding of leaves, flowers and twigs.

docs.title: (a) Carbon Monoxide (CO)
docs.text:
• CO is a colourless and odourless gas and one of the most serious air pollutants.
  • It is produced by incomplete combustion of carbon. It is mainly released by automobile exhaust; incomplete burning of coal, firewood and petrol also produces it.
  • Poorly maintained vehicles and vehicles with inadequate pollution control equipment release larger amounts of CO.
  • Why is CO poisonous? It binds to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which is about 300 times more stable than the oxygen-haemoglobin complex. So CO blocks the delivery of oxygen to the organs and tissues.
\[Hb + CO → HbCO\ (carboxyhaemoglobin)\]
  • When the concentration of carboxyhaemoglobin in blood reaches about 3-4 per cent, the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood is greatly reduced.
  • The resulting oxygen deficiency causes headache, weak eyesight, nervousness and cardiovascular disorders. This is one reason people are advised not to smoke.
  • In pregnant women who smoke, increased CO in blood may cause premature birth, spontaneous abortion and deformed babies.

docs.title: (b) Carbon Dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
• CO2 is released into the atmosphere by respiration, burning of fossil fuels, decomposition of limestone during cement manufacture and volcanic eruptions.
  • It is confined to the troposphere only. Normally it forms about 0.03 per cent by volume of the atmosphere.
  • Green plants use CO2 for photosynthesis and release oxygen, which keeps the CO2 level balanced.
  • Deforestation and burning of fossil fuel increase the CO2 level and disturb this balance. This excess CO2 is mainly responsible for global warming.

docs.title: Global Warming and Greenhouse Effect
docs.text:
• About 75% of the solar energy reaching the earth is absorbed by the earth's surface, which increases its temperature. The rest of the heat radiates back to the atmosphere.
  • Some of this heat is trapped by gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, ozone, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and water vapour. This adds to the heating of the atmosphere and causes global warming.

docs.title: Natural Greenhouse Effect
docs.text:
• In a greenhouse (a glass-covered area used to grow plants in cold places), visible sunlight passes through the transparent glass and heats the soil and plants.
  • The warm soil and plants emit infrared (heat) radiation. Glass is opaque to infrared radiation, so it partly reflects and partly absorbs it. The sun's energy stays trapped inside.
  • Similarly, CO2 molecules are transparent to sunlight but not to heat radiation. So the blanket of air around the earth traps the sun's heat near the surface and keeps the earth warm.
  • This is called the natural greenhouse effect. It maintains the temperature and makes the earth suitable for life.
  • If the amount of CO2 crosses its delicate proportion of 0.03 per cent, the natural greenhouse balance gets disturbed. CO2 is the major contributor to global warming.

docs.title: Other Greenhouse Gases
docs.text: Gas Main sources CO<sub>2</sub> Burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, respiration, cement manufacture Methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) Burning, digestion or rotting of vegetation in the absence of oxygen; paddy fields, coal mines, rotting garbage dumps, fossil fuels Nitrous oxide (N<sub>2</sub>O) Occurs naturally; increased by chemical fertilizers and burning of fossil fuels CFCs Man-made chemicals used in air conditioning etc.; also damage the ozone layer Ozone and water vapour Present naturally in the atmosphere

docs.title: Consequences of Global Warming
docs.text:
• If the present trend continues, the average global temperature may rise to a level which melts polar ice caps and floods low-lying areas all over the earth.
  • A rise in global temperature increases the incidence of infectious diseases like dengue, malaria, yellow fever and sleeping sickness.

How can we reduce global warming?

  • Use fossil fuels efficiently and judiciously, and minimise the use of automobiles (use bicycles, public transport or carpools).
  • Plant more trees to increase the green cover.
  • Avoid burning dry leaves, wood etc.
  • Avoid smoking, especially in public places.

docs.title: Acid Rain
docs.text:
• Normal rain water has a pH of about 5.6. This is because rain water reacts with atmospheric CO2 to form carbonic acid, which gives H+ ions:
\[H_2O_{(l)} + CO_{2(g)} ⇌ H_2CO_{3(aq)}\] \[H_2CO_{3(aq)} ⇌ H^+_{(aq)} + HCO^-_{3(aq)}\]
  • When the pH of rain water drops below 5.6, it is called acid rain.
  • Acid rain refers to the ways in which acid from the atmosphere is deposited on the earth's surface. Acidic oxides of nitrogen and sulphur, carried by wind along with solid particles, settle down:
    • on the ground as dry deposition, or
    • in water, fog and snow as wet deposition.

docs.title: Formation of Acid Rain
docs.text:
• Burning of fossil fuels containing sulphur and nitrogenous matter (coal and oil in power stations and furnaces, petrol and diesel in motor engines) produces SO2 and nitrogen oxides.
  • After oxidation and reaction with water, SO2 and NO2 become the major contributors to acid rain. Particulate matter in polluted air catalyses this oxidation:
\[2SO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → 2H_2SO_{4(aq)}\] \[4NO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → 4HNO_{3(aq)}\]
  • Ammonium salts are also formed and appear as an atmospheric haze (aerosol of fine particles). Aerosol particles of oxides or ammonium salts in rain drops cause wet deposition.
  • SO2 is also absorbed directly on solid and liquid ground surfaces and is thus deposited as dry deposition.

docs.title: Harmful Effects of Acid Rain
docs.text:
• It is harmful for agriculture, trees and plants because it dissolves and washes away the nutrients they need.
  • It causes respiratory ailments in humans and animals.
  • When it reaches rivers and lakes as ground water, it affects plant and animal life in the aquatic ecosystem.
  • It corrodes water pipes, leading to leaching of heavy metals such as iron, lead and copper into drinking water.
  • It damages buildings and structures made of stone or metal.

docs.title: Taj Mahal and Acid Rain
docs.text:
• The air around Agra contains fairly high levels of sulphur and nitrogen oxides due to many industries and power plants, and the use of poor quality coal, kerosene and firewood as domestic fuel.
  • The resulting acid rain reacts with the marble (CaCO3) of the Taj Mahal, slowly making it discoloured and lustreless:
\[CaCO_3 + H_2SO_4 → CaSO_4 + H_2O + CO_2\]
  • Under an action plan announced in 1995 for the 'Taj Trapezium' (Agra, Firozabad, Mathura and Bharatpur), more than 2000 polluting industries were to switch from coal or oil to natural gas or LPG, and vehicles near the Taj were encouraged to use low sulphur diesel.

docs.title: Controlling Acid Rain
docs.text:
• Reduce the emission of SO2 and NO2: use fewer vehicles driven by fossil fuels, use low-sulphur fuels in power plants and industries, and prefer natural gas over coal.
  • Use catalytic converters in cars. The converter is a ceramic honeycomb coated with precious metals Pd, Pt and Rh. When exhaust gases containing unburnt fuel, CO and NOx pass through it at 573 K, they are converted into CO2 and N2.
  • The acidity of soil can be reduced by adding powdered limestone to neutralise it.

docs.title: Environmental Chemistry | Water and Soil Pollution
Environmental Chemistry | Water and Soil Pollution
docs.text: Water pollution is the contamination of surface or ground water by pathogens, organic wastes and chemicals. It originates mostly from human activities.

docs.title: Sources of Water Pollution
docs.text:
• Point source: an easily identified source or place of pollution. Example: municipal and industrial discharge pipes where pollutants enter the water source.
  • Non-point source: a source that cannot be easily identified. Examples: agricultural run-off (from farms, animals and crop lands), acid rain, storm-water drainage (from streets, parking lots and lawns).
Pollutant Source Micro-organisms Domestic sewage Organic wastes Domestic sewage, animal excreta and waste, decaying animals and plants, discharge from food processing factories Plant nutrients Chemical fertilizers Toxic heavy metals Industries and chemical factories Sediments Erosion of soil by agriculture and strip mining Pesticides Chemicals used for killing insects, fungi and weeds Radioactive substances Mining of uranium containing minerals Heat Water used for cooling in industries

docs.title: 1. Pathogens
docs.text:
• These are the most serious water pollutants. Pathogens are disease-causing agents, including bacteria and other organisms, that enter water from domestic sewage and animal excreta.
  • Human excreta contain bacteria such as Escherichia coli and Streptococcus faecalis, which cause gastrointestinal diseases.

docs.title: 2. Organic Wastes
docs.text:
• Organic matter such as leaves, grass and trash pollutes water as a result of run-off. Excessive phytoplankton growth within water is also a cause. These wastes are biodegradable.
  • Bacteria decompose this organic matter and consume the oxygen dissolved in water.
  • The amount of oxygen water can hold is limited. In cold water, dissolved oxygen (DO) can reach up to 10 ppm, whereas oxygen in air is about 200,000 ppm. So even a moderate amount of decomposing organic matter can deplete water of its dissolved oxygen.
  • If the DO of water falls below 6 ppm, the growth of fish gets inhibited.
  • Oxygen reaches water from the atmosphere and from photosynthesis by aquatic plants during daylight. At night, photosynthesis stops but plants continue to respire, which lowers the DO.
  • If too much organic matter is added, all the available oxygen is used up and oxygen-dependent aquatic life dies. Anaerobic bacteria then break down the waste and produce foul-smelling chemicals harmful to human health.

docs.title: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)
docs.text:
• The amount of oxygen required by bacteria to break down the organic matter present in a certain volume of a water sample is called Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD).
  • BOD is a measure of the amount of organic material in water, in terms of how much oxygen is needed to break it down biologically.
Water quality BOD value Clean water Less than 5 ppm Highly polluted water 17 ppm or more

docs.title: 3. Chemical Pollutants
docs.text:
• Heavy metals: Water-soluble inorganic chemicals including heavy metals such as cadmium, mercury and nickel are important pollutants. The body cannot excrete them, so over time they cross the tolerance limit and damage kidneys, the central nervous system, liver etc.
  • Acids and salts: Acids (like sulphuric acid) from mine drainage and salts from many sources, including raw salt (sodium and calcium chloride) used to melt snow and ice in colder climates, are water-soluble pollutants.
  • Organic chemicals: Petroleum products (e.g., major oil spills in oceans), pesticides drifting from sprays or run-off, and industrial chemicals like polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) used as cleansing solvents. PCBs are suspected to be carcinogenic.
  • Detergents: Most detergents today are biodegradable, but the bacteria that degrade them grow rapidly and may use up all the dissolved oxygen, killing fish and plants.
  • Fertilizers: They contain phosphates as additives, which enhance algae growth.

docs.title: Eutrophication
docs.text:
• Profuse growth of algae covers the water surface and reduces the oxygen concentration in water.
  • This leads to anaerobic conditions, with accumulation of obnoxious decay and animal death. Bloom-infested water inhibits the growth of other living organisms.
  • The process in which nutrient-enriched water bodies support a dense plant population, which kills animal life by depriving it of oxygen and results in loss of biodiversity, is called eutrophication.

docs.title: 1. Fluoride
docs.text:
• Drinking water should be tested for fluoride ion concentration. Its deficiency causes diseases such as tooth decay.
  • Soluble fluoride is often added to drinking water to bring its concentration up to 1 ppm or 1 mg dm-3.
  • F- ions make tooth enamel much harder by converting hydroxyapatite into the much harder fluorapatite:
\[Hydroxyapatite:\ [3(Ca_3(PO_4)_2).Ca(OH)_2]\ →\ Fluorapatite:\ [3(Ca_3(PO_4)_2).CaF_2]\]
  • F- above 2 ppm causes brown mottling of teeth. Excess fluoride (over 10 ppm) harms bones and teeth, as reported from some parts of Rajasthan.

docs.title: 2. Lead
docs.text:
• Water gets contaminated with lead when lead pipes are used to transport it.
  • The prescribed upper limit of lead in drinking water is about 50 ppb. Lead can damage the kidney, liver and reproductive system.

docs.title: 3. Sulphate
docs.text: • Excessive sulphate (> 500 ppm) causes a laxative effect. At moderate levels it is harmless.

docs.title: 4. Nitrate
docs.text:
• The maximum limit of nitrate in drinking water is 50 ppm.
  • Excess nitrate can cause methemoglobinemia ('blue baby' syndrome).

docs.title: 5. Other Metals
docs.text:
Metal Maximum concentration (ppm or mg dm-3) Fe 0.2 Mn 0.05 Al 0.2 Cu 3.0 Zn 5.0 Cd 0.005

What can we do?

  • Do not dump waste into drains that lead directly to a river, pond, stream or lake.
  • Use compost instead of chemical fertilizers in gardens.
  • Avoid pesticides like DDT and malathion at home; dried neem leaves help keep insects away.
  • Add a few crystals of potassium permanganate (KMnO4) or bleaching powder to the household water tank.

docs.title: Soil Pollution
docs.text:
• India gives high priority to agriculture, and the surplus produce is stored for the lean season. Crops and stored food must be protected from insects, rodents, weeds and crop diseases.
  • Insecticides, pesticides and herbicides used for this purpose cause soil pollution. Hence their judicious use is needed.

docs.title: Pesticides
docs.text:
• Before World War II, naturally occurring chemicals like nicotine (by planting tobacco in the crop field) were used as pest controllers.
  • During World War II, DDT was found very useful for controlling malaria and other insect-borne diseases. After the war it was used in agriculture. Due to its adverse effects, it has been banned in India.
  • Pesticides are synthetic toxic chemicals with ecological repercussions. Repeated use of the same pesticides gives rise to resistant pests, making the pesticides ineffective.
  • As insects became resistant to DDT, other organic toxins such as Aldrin and Dieldrin were introduced. Most of these are water insoluble and non-biodegradable.
  • These highly persistent toxins are transferred from lower to higher trophic levels through the food chain. Over time, their concentration in higher animals reaches a level that causes serious metabolic and physiological disorders.

Note

At each trophic level, the pollutant gets about 10 times more concentrated. So the organism at the top of the food chain (human beings) receives the highest concentration.

  • Because chlorinated organic toxins are so persistent, less persistent, more biodegradable organo-phosphates and carbamates were introduced. But these are severe nerve toxins and more harmful to humans; deaths of agricultural field workers have been reported. Insects have become resistant to these too.

docs.title: Herbicides
docs.text:
• The pesticide industry has now shifted its attention to herbicides such as sodium chlorate (NaClO3) and sodium arsinite (Na3AsO3).
  • Most herbicides are toxic to mammals but are not as persistent as organo-chlorides; they decompose in a few months.
  • Like organo-chlorides, they too become concentrated in the food web. Some herbicides cause birth defects.
  • Corn fields sprayed with herbicides are more prone to insect attack and plant disease than fields weeded manually.

docs.title: Industrial Waste
docs.text:
Industrial solid wastes are sorted into biodegradable and non-degradable wastes.

Type Source / Examples Biodegradable Cotton mills, food processing units, paper mills, textile factories Non-biodegradable Fly ash from thermal power plants; blast furnace slag and steel melting slag from iron and steel plants; mud and tailings from Al, Zn and Cu industries; gypsum from fertilizer industries Hazardous Inflammables, composite explosives and highly reactive substances from industries dealing in metals, chemicals, drugs, pharmaceuticals, dyes, pesticides, rubber goods etc.
  • Improper disposal of non-degradable industrial waste is a serious threat to the environment.
  • Nowadays fly ash and slag from the steel industry are used by the cement industry.
  • Large quantities of toxic waste are usually destroyed by controlled incineration, whereas small quantities are burnt along with factory garbage in open bins.

docs.title: Hydrogen | Dihydrogen - Preparation, Properties and Uses
Hydrogen | Dihydrogen - Preparation, Properties and Uses
docs.text: Dihydrogen, H2, is a colourless, odourless, tasteless and combustible gas. In this article, we will discuss how dihydrogen is prepared in the laboratory and on a commercial scale, its physical and chemical properties and its uses.

docs.title: 1. From zinc and dilute acid
docs.text:
• Dihydrogen is usually prepared in the laboratory by the reaction of granulated zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid.
\[Zn + 2H^+ → Zn^{2+} + H_2\]

docs.title: 2. From zinc and aqueous alkali
docs.text:
• It can also be prepared by the reaction of zinc with aqueous alkali. Sodium zincate is formed.
\[Zn + 2NaOH → Na_2ZnO_2 + H_2\]

docs.title: 1. Electrolysis of acidified water
docs.text:
• Electrolysis of water containing traces of acid or base, using platinum electrodes, gives dihydrogen.
\[2H_2O_{(l)} \xrightarrow[Traces\ of\ acid/base]{Electrolysis} 2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)}\]
  • The acid or base is added because pure water is a very poor conductor. The electrolyte makes water conducting so that electrolysis can occur.

docs.title: 2. Electrolysis of barium hydroxide solution
docs.text: • High purity dihydrogen (> 99.95%) is obtained by electrolysing warm aqueous barium hydroxide solution between nickel electrodes.

docs.title: 3. By-product of the chlor-alkali process
docs.text:
• Dihydrogen is obtained as a by-product in the manufacture of sodium hydroxide and chlorine by electrolysis of brine (aqueous NaCl).
\[At\ anode:\ 2Cl^-_{(aq)} → Cl_{2(g)} + 2e^-\] \[At\ cathode:\ 2H_2O_{(l)} + 2e^- → H_{2(g)} + 2OH^-_{(aq)}\] \[Overall:\ 2Na^+_{(aq)} + 2Cl^-_{(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → Cl_{2(g)} + H_{2(g)} + 2Na^+_{(aq)} + 2OH^-_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: 4. From hydrocarbons or coke (syngas)
docs.text:
• Reaction of steam with hydrocarbons or coke at high temperature in the presence of a catalyst gives dihydrogen.
\[C_nH_{2n+2} + nH_2O \xrightarrow[Ni]{1270\ K} nCO + (3n+1)H_2\] \[CH_{4(g)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow[Ni]{1270\ K} CO_{(g)} + 3H_{2(g)}\]
  • The mixture of CO and H2 is called water gas.
  • Since this mixture is used for the synthesis of methanol and many hydrocarbons, it is also called synthesis gas or syngas.
  • Nowadays, syngas is also produced from sewage, saw-dust, scrap wood, newspapers, etc.
  • The process of producing syngas from coal is called coal gasification.
\[C_{(s)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow{1270\ K} CO_{(g)} + H_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: 5. Water-gas shift reaction
docs.text:
• The yield of dihydrogen can be increased by reacting the carbon monoxide of syngas with steam in the presence of iron chromate as catalyst. This is called the water-gas shift reaction.
\[CO_{(g)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow[catalyst]{673\ K} CO_{2(g)} + H_{2(g)}\]
  • The CO2 formed is removed by scrubbing with sodium arsenite solution.

Note

At present, about 77% of industrial dihydrogen is produced from petrochemicals, 18% from coal, 4% from electrolysis of aqueous solutions and 1% from other sources.

docs.title: Physical Properties of Dihydrogen
docs.text:
• It is a colourless, odourless, tasteless and combustible gas.
  • It is lighter than air and insoluble in water.
  • Its melting point is 13.96 K, boiling point is 20.39 K and density is 0.09 g L-1.

docs.title: Chemical Properties of Dihydrogen
docs.text:
• The H-H bond dissociation enthalpy (435.88 kJ mol-1) is the highest for a single bond between two atoms of any element.
  • Because of this, dissociation of H2 into atoms is only about 0.081% at around 2000 K, rising to 95.5% at 5000 K. For the same reason, dihydrogen is relatively inert at room temperature.
  • Atomic hydrogen is produced at high temperature in an electric arc or under ultraviolet radiation.
  • Since its 1s orbital is incomplete, hydrogen combines with almost all elements. It does so by:
    • losing its electron to give H+,
    • gaining an electron to form H-, or
    • sharing electrons to form a single covalent bond.

docs.title: 1. Reaction with halogens
docs.text:
• Dihydrogen reacts with halogens to give hydrogen halides. The reaction with fluorine occurs even in the dark, while that with iodine needs a catalyst.
\[H_{2(g)} + X_{2(g)} → 2HX_{(g)}\ \ (X = F, Cl, Br, I)\]

docs.title: 2. Reaction with dioxygen
docs.text:
• It reacts with dioxygen to form water. The reaction is highly exothermic.
\[2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{catalyst\ or\ heating} 2H_2O_{(l)};\ \ ΔH^0 = -285.9\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

docs.title: 3. Reaction with dinitrogen
docs.text:
• With dinitrogen it forms ammonia. This is the basis of the Haber process for the manufacture of ammonia.
\[3H_{2(g)} + N_{2(g)} \xrightarrow[Fe]{673\ K,\ 200\ atm} 2NH_{3(g)};\ \ ΔH^0 = -92.6\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

docs.title: 4. Reaction with metals
docs.text:
• With many metals it combines at high temperature to give the corresponding hydrides.
\[H_{2(g)} + 2M_{(g)} → 2MH_{(s)}\ \ (M = alkali\ metal)\]

docs.title: 5. Reaction with metal ions and metal oxides
docs.text:
• It reduces some metal ions in aqueous solution, and oxides of metals less active than iron, into the corresponding metals.
\[H_{2(g)} + Pd^{2+}_{(aq)} → Pd_{(s)} + 2H^+_{(aq)}\] \[yH_{2(g)} + M_xO_{y(s)} → xM_{(s)} + yH_2O_{(l)}\]

docs.title: 6. Reaction with organic compounds
docs.text:
• In the presence of catalysts, it reacts with many organic compounds to give useful hydrogenated products.
  • Hydrogenation of vegetable oils, using nickel as catalyst, gives edible fats (margarine and vanaspati ghee).
  • Hydroformylation of olefins gives aldehydes, which are further reduced to alcohols.
\[H_2 + CO + RCH=CH_2 → RCH_2CH_2CHO\] \[H_2 + RCH_2CH_2CHO → RCH_2CH_2CH_2OH\]

docs.title: Uses of Dihydrogen
docs.text:
• The largest single use is in the synthesis of ammonia, which is used to make nitric acid and nitrogenous fertilizers.
  • It is used to manufacture vanaspati fat by hydrogenation of polyunsaturated vegetable oils like soyabean and cotton seed oils.
  • It is used to manufacture bulk organic chemicals, particularly methanol.
\[CO_{(g)} + 2H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{cobalt\ catalyst} CH_3OH_{(l)}\]
  • It is widely used to manufacture metal hydrides.
  • It is used to prepare hydrogen chloride, a very useful chemical.
  • In metallurgy, it is used to reduce heavy metal oxides to metals.
  • Atomic hydrogen and oxy-hydrogen torches are used for cutting and welding. Dihydrogen is dissociated into atoms in an electric arc, and the atoms are allowed to recombine on the surface to be welded. The energy released on recombination produces a temperature of about 4000 K.
  • It is used as a rocket fuel in space research.
  • It is used in fuel cells to generate electrical energy. It produces no pollution and releases more energy per unit mass than gasoline and other fuels.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Comment on the reactions of dihydrogen with (i) chlorine, (ii) sodium, and (iii) copper(II) oxide.

(i) Dihydrogen reduces chlorine to chloride (Cl-) ion and is itself oxidised to H+, forming hydrogen chloride. An electron pair is shared between H and Cl, so a covalent molecule is formed.

\[H_2 + Cl_2 → 2HCl\]

(ii) Dihydrogen is reduced by sodium to form NaH. An electron is transferred from Na to H, giving an ionic compound, Na+H-.

\[2Na + H_2 → 2NaH\]

(iii) Dihydrogen reduces copper(II) oxide to copper in the zero oxidation state and is itself oxidised to H2O, a covalent molecule.

\[CuO + H_2 → Cu + H_2O\]

How can the production of dihydrogen, obtained from 'coal gasification', be increased?

The CO present in the syngas obtained from coal gasification is reacted with steam at 673 K in the presence of iron chromate catalyst (water-gas shift reaction). This converts CO into CO2 and produces more H2. The CO2 is then removed by scrubbing with sodium arsenite solution.

\[CO_{(g)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow[catalyst]{673\ K} CO_{2(g)} + H_{2(g)}\]

Describe the bulk preparation of dihydrogen by electrolytic method. What is the role of an electrolyte in this process?

Dihydrogen is prepared in bulk by electrolysis of water containing traces of acid or alkali, using platinum electrodes. H2 is liberated at the cathode and O2 at the anode.

\[2H_2O_{(l)} \xrightarrow[Traces\ of\ acid/base]{Electrolysis} 2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)}\]

Pure water is a very poor conductor of electricity. The added acid or alkali (electrolyte) provides ions that make water conducting, so that electrolysis can take place.

Complete the following reactions:(i) H2(g) + MmOo(s) → (heat)(ii) CO(g) + H2(g) → (heat, catalyst)(iii) C3H8(g) + 3H2O(g) → (heat, catalyst)(iv) Zn(s) + NaOH(aq) → (heat)

\[(i)\ oH_{2(g)} + M_mO_{o(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} mM_{(s)} + oH_2O_{(l)}\] \[(ii)\ CO_{(g)} + 2H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow[cobalt\ catalyst]{\Delta} CH_3OH_{(l)}\] \[(iii)\ C_3H_{8(g)} + 3H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow[Ni]{\Delta} 3CO_{(g)} + 7H_{2(g)}\] \[(iv)\ Zn_{(s)} + 2NaOH_{(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} Na_2ZnO_{2(aq)} + H_{2(g)}\]

Discuss the consequences of high enthalpy of H-H bond in terms of chemical reactivity of dihydrogen.

The H-H bond dissociation enthalpy (435.88 kJ mol-1) is the highest for a single bond between two atoms of any element. As a result:

  • Dihydrogen dissociates into atoms only to a very small extent (about 0.081% at 2000 K).
  • It is relatively inert at room temperature, and most of its reactions need high temperature, catalysts or electric discharge.

How does the atomic hydrogen or oxy-hydrogen torch function for cutting and welding purposes? Explain.

In an atomic hydrogen torch, dihydrogen is dissociated into hydrogen atoms with the help of an electric arc. This absorbs a large amount of energy because the H-H bond is very strong. The hydrogen atoms are then allowed to recombine on the metal surface to be welded. Recombination releases the same large amount of energy, producing a temperature of about 4000 K, which is enough to cut and weld metals.

docs.title: Hydrogen | Hard and Soft Water
docs.text:
Rain water is almost pure, though it may contain some dissolved gases from the atmosphere. Being a good solvent, water dissolves many salts as it flows over the surface of the earth.

  • Water containing calcium and magnesium salts in the form of hydrogencarbonate, chloride and sulphate is called hard water. Hard water does not give lather with soap.
  • Water free from soluble salts of calcium and magnesium is called soft water. It gives lather with soap easily.

docs.title: Why is Hard Water Undesirable?
docs.text:
• Hard water forms scum (a precipitate) with soap. Soap, which contains sodium stearate (C17H35COONa), reacts with hard water to precipitate calcium or magnesium stearate.
\[2C_{17}H_{35}COONa_{(aq)} + M^{2+}_{(aq)} → (C_{17}H_{35}COO)_2M ↓ + 2Na^+_{(aq)}\] \[[M = Ca\ or\ Mg]\]
  • So, hard water is unsuitable for laundry, as soap is wasted.
  • It is also harmful for boilers, because salts get deposited as scale. This reduces the efficiency of the boiler.

Hardness of water is of two types:

  • Temporary hardness
  • Permanent hardness

docs.title: Temporary Hardness
docs.text: Temporary hardness is due to the presence of hydrogencarbonates of magnesium and calcium. It can be removed by the following methods.

docs.title: 1. Boiling
docs.text:
• On boiling, soluble Mg(HCO3)2 is converted into insoluble Mg(OH)2, and Ca(HCO3)2 into insoluble CaCO3.
  • Mg(OH)2 (and not MgCO3) is precipitated because the solubility product of Mg(OH)2 is lower than that of MgCO3.
  • The precipitates are removed by filtration. The filtrate is soft water.
\[Mg(HCO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{Heating} Mg(OH)_2 ↓ + 2CO_2 ↑\] \[Ca(HCO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{Heating} CaCO_3 ↓ + H_2O + CO_2 ↑\]

docs.title: 2. Clark's method
docs.text:
• A calculated amount of lime (Ca(OH)2) is added to hard water. It precipitates calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide, which are filtered off.
\[Ca(HCO_3)_2 + Ca(OH)_2 → 2CaCO_3 ↓ + 2H_2O\] \[Mg(HCO_3)_2 + 2Ca(OH)_2 → 2CaCO_3 ↓ + Mg(OH)_2 ↓ + 2H_2O\]

docs.title: Permanent Hardness
docs.text: Permanent hardness is due to the presence of soluble salts of magnesium and calcium in the form of chlorides and sulphates. It is not removed by boiling. It can be removed by the following methods.

docs.title: 1. Treatment with washing soda (sodium carbonate)
docs.text:
• Washing soda reacts with soluble calcium and magnesium chlorides and sulphates to form insoluble carbonates.
\[MCl_2 + Na_2CO_3 → MCO_3 ↓ + 2NaCl\] \[MSO_4 + Na_2CO_3 → MCO_3 ↓ + Na_2SO_4\] \[[M = Mg,\ Ca]\]

docs.title: 2. Calgon's method
docs.text:
• Sodium hexametaphosphate (Na6P6O18), commercially called calgon, is added to hard water.
\[Na_6P_6O_{18} → 2Na^+ + Na_4P_6O_{18}^{2-}\] \[M^{2+} + Na_4P_6O_{18}^{2-} → [Na_2MP_6O_{18}]^{2-} + 2Na^+\] \[[M = Mg,\ Ca]\]
  • The complex anion keeps the Mg2+ and Ca2+ ions in solution, so they cannot react with soap.

docs.title: 3. Ion-exchange method (zeolite/permutit process)
docs.text:
• Hydrated sodium aluminium silicate is called zeolite or permutit. For simplicity, sodium aluminium silicate (NaAlSiO4) is written as NaZ.
  • When it is added to hard water, Na+ ions are exchanged for Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions.
\[2NaZ_{(s)} + M^{2+}_{(aq)} → MZ_{2(s)} + 2Na^+_{(aq)}\] \[[M = Mg,\ Ca]\]
  • Permutit/zeolite is said to be exhausted when all its sodium is used up. It is regenerated by treating it with aqueous sodium chloride solution.
\[MZ_{2(s)} + 2NaCl_{(aq)} → 2NaZ_{(s)} + MCl_{2(aq)}\]

docs.title: 4. Synthetic resins method
docs.text:
• Nowadays, hard water is softened using synthetic cation exchangers. This method is more efficient than the zeolite process.
  • Cation exchange resins are large, water-insoluble organic molecules containing the -SO3H group.
  • The resin RSO3H is first changed to RNa by treating it with NaCl. Here R is the resin anion. The resin then exchanges its Na+ ions with Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions of hard water.
\[2RNa_{(s)} + M^{2+}_{(aq)} → R_2M_{(s)} + 2Na^+_{(aq)}\]
  • The resin can be regenerated by adding aqueous NaCl solution.

docs.title: Demineralised (De-ionised) Water
docs.text:
Pure demineralised water, free from all soluble mineral salts, is obtained by passing water successively through a cation exchange resin (in the H+ form) and an anion exchange resin (in the OH- form).

  • Cation exchange: H+ of the resin is exchanged for Na+, Ca2+, Mg2+ and other cations present in water. This releases protons and makes the water acidic.
\[2RH_{(s)} + M^{2+}_{(aq)} ⇌ MR_{2(s)} + 2H^+_{(aq)}\]
  • Anion exchange: OH- of the resin is exchanged for anions like Cl-, HCO3-, SO42-, etc. present in water.
\[RNH_{2(s)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ RNH_3^+.OH^-_{(s)}\] \[RNH_3^+.OH^-_{(s)} + X^-_{(aq)} ⇌ RNH_3^+.X^-_{(s)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\]
  • The OH- ions released neutralise the H+ ions set free in the cation exchange.
\[H^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)} → H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • The exhausted cation and anion exchange resin beds are regenerated by treatment with dilute acid and dilute alkali solutions respectively.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What causes the temporary and permanent hardness of water?

  • Temporary hardness is caused by the presence of soluble hydrogencarbonates of calcium and magnesium, Ca(HCO3)2 and Mg(HCO3)2. It is removed by boiling.
  • Permanent hardness is caused by the presence of soluble chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium (CaCl2, MgCl2, CaSO4, MgSO4). It is not removed by boiling.

Discuss the principle and method of softening of hard water by synthetic ion-exchange resins.

Principle: Ion-exchange resins are insoluble, giant organic molecules that can exchange their own ions for the ions present in water.

Method: Water is passed through a cation exchange resin (RSO3H, or its sodium form RNa). The Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions are retained by the resin and Na+ (or H+) ions are released into water.

\[2RNa_{(s)} + M^{2+}_{(aq)} → R_2M_{(s)} + 2Na^+_{(aq)}\]

For complete demineralisation, the water is then passed through an anion exchange resin (RNH3+OH-), which removes anions and releases OH-. The OH- neutralises the H+ released by the cation exchanger to form water. The exhausted resins are regenerated with NaCl solution (or dilute acid) and dilute alkali respectively.

What is meant by 'demineralised' water and how can it be obtained?

Demineralised water is water free from all soluble mineral salts (both cations and anions). It is obtained by passing water successively through a cation exchange resin in the H+ form and an anion exchange resin in the OH- form. Cations are replaced by H+, anions by OH-, and H+ and OH- combine to form water.

Is demineralised or distilled water useful for drinking purposes? If not, how can it be made useful?

No. Demineralised and distilled water lack the essential minerals (such as calcium, magnesium and potassium salts) that the body needs, and it also tastes flat. It can be made useful for drinking by adding the required minerals in proper amounts.

docs.title: Hydrogen | Heavy Water and Hydrogen as a Fuel
Hydrogen | Heavy Water and Hydrogen as a Fuel
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss heavy water (D2O) and the use of dihydrogen as a fuel, including the idea of a hydrogen economy.

docs.title: Heavy Water, D<sub>2</sub>O
docs.text: Heavy water, D2O, is water in which both protium atoms are replaced by deuterium.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• It is prepared by exhaustive electrolysis of ordinary water. Since H2 is liberated faster than D2, the remaining water gets gradually enriched in D2O.
  • It is also obtained as a by-product in some fertilizer industries.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Heavy water has a higher molecular mass, melting point, boiling point, density and viscosity than ordinary water.
Property H2O D2O Molecular mass (g mol-1) 18.0151 20.0276 Melting point (K) 273.0 276.8 Boiling point (K) 373.0 374.4 Density at 298 K (g cm-3) 1.0000 1.1059 Temperature of maximum density (K) 276.98 284.2 Viscosity (centipoise) 0.8903 1.107

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• It is extensively used as a moderator in nuclear reactors.
  • It is used in exchange reactions to study reaction mechanisms.
  • It is used to prepare other deuterium compounds, for example:
\[CaC_2 + 2D_2O → C_2D_2 + Ca(OD)_2\] \[SO_3 + D_2O → D_2SO_4\] \[Al_4C_3 + 12D_2O → 3CD_4 + 4Al(OD)_3\]

docs.title: Dihydrogen as a Fuel
docs.text:
Dihydrogen releases a large amount of heat on combustion. The energy released by burning different fuels is compared below.

Energy released on combustion (kJ) Dihydrogen (gas) Dihydrogen (liquid) LPG CH4 gas Octane (liquid) per mole 286 285 2220 880 5511 per gram 143 142 50 53 47 per litre 12 9968 25590 35 34005

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• On a mass basis, dihydrogen releases about three times more energy than petrol.
  • It burns to give only water, so pollution is much lower than with petrol. The only pollutants are oxides of nitrogen, formed because dinitrogen is present as an impurity.
  • Even this can be minimised by injecting a small amount of water into the cylinder. This lowers the temperature so that dinitrogen and dioxygen do not react.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• A cylinder of compressed dihydrogen weighs about 30 times as much as a tank of petrol containing the same amount of energy.
  • To liquefy dihydrogen it must be cooled to 20 K, which requires expensive insulated tanks.
  • Tanks of metal alloys like NaNi5, Ti-TiH2 and Mg-MgH2 are used to store dihydrogen, but only in small quantities.

These limitations have led researchers to search for better ways of storing and using dihydrogen.

docs.title: Hydrogen Economy
docs.text:
• The basic principle of the hydrogen economy is the transportation and storage of energy in the form of liquid or gaseous dihydrogen.
  • Its advantage is that energy is transmitted as dihydrogen and not as electric power.
  • In India, a pilot project using dihydrogen as a fuel for automobiles was launched in October 2005. Initially, 5% dihydrogen was mixed with CNG for four-wheeler vehicles, and the percentage is to be raised gradually to an optimum level.
  • Dihydrogen is also used in fuel cells to generate electric power.
  • It is expected that economically viable and safe sources of dihydrogen will be found in the coming years, making it a common source of energy.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Knowing the properties of H2O and D2O, do you think that D2O can be used for drinking purposes?

No. D2O has different physical properties (higher density, viscosity, melting and boiling points) from H2O, and reactions involving D are slower than those involving H because the bond with D is stronger. Heavy water therefore slows down the biochemical reactions in living cells, so it is harmful and not suitable for drinking.

What do you understand by the terms:(i) hydrogen economy (ii) hydrogenation (iii) 'syngas' (iv) water-gas shift reaction (v) fuel-cell?

(i) Hydrogen economy: A system in which energy is stored and transported in the form of liquid or gaseous dihydrogen instead of electric power or fossil fuels.

(ii) Hydrogenation: Addition of dihydrogen to a compound, usually an unsaturated one, in the presence of a catalyst. Example: hydrogenation of vegetable oils using nickel to make vanaspati ghee.

(iii) Syngas: The mixture of CO and H2, obtained by reacting steam with hydrocarbons or coke. It is used to synthesise methanol and many hydrocarbons.

\[CH_{4(g)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow[Ni]{1270\ K} CO_{(g)} + 3H_{2(g)}\]

(iv) Water-gas shift reaction: Reaction of the CO in syngas with steam over iron chromate catalyst to produce more dihydrogen.

\[CO_{(g)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow[catalyst]{673\ K} CO_{2(g)} + H_{2(g)}\]

(v) Fuel cell: A device that converts the chemical energy of a fuel such as dihydrogen directly into electrical energy. In a H2-O2 fuel cell, dihydrogen and dioxygen combine to form water, producing electricity without pollution.

docs.title: Hydrogen | Hydrides
docs.text:
Under suitable conditions, dihydrogen combines with almost all elements except noble gases to form binary compounds called hydrides. If E is the symbol of an element, its hydride can be written as EHx (e.g., MgH2) or EmHn (e.g., B2H6).

Hydrides are classified into three categories:

  • Ionic or saline or saltlike hydrides
  • Covalent or molecular hydrides
  • Metallic or non-stoichiometric hydrides

docs.title: 1. Ionic or Saline Hydrides
docs.text:
• These are stoichiometric compounds of hydrogen formed with most of the s-block elements, which are highly electropositive.
  • The lighter metal hydrides such as LiH, BeH2 and MgH2 show significant covalent character. In fact, BeH2 and MgH2 are polymeric in structure.
  • Ionic hydrides are crystalline, non-volatile and non-conducting in the solid state.
  • Their melts conduct electricity, and on electrolysis liberate dihydrogen at the anode. This confirms the presence of the H- ion.
\[2H^-_{(melt)} \xrightarrow{anode} H_{2(g)} + 2e^-\]
  • Saline hydrides react violently with water, producing dihydrogen gas.
\[NaH_{(s)} + H_2O_{(aq)} → NaOH_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)}\]
  • Lithium hydride is rather unreactive towards O2 or Cl2 at moderate temperatures. It is therefore used to synthesise other useful hydrides.
\[8LiH + Al_2Cl_6 → 2LiAlH_4 + 6LiCl\] \[2LiH + B_2H_6 → 2LiBH_4\]

docs.title: 2. Covalent or Molecular Hydrides
docs.text:
• Dihydrogen forms molecular compounds with most p-block elements. Familiar examples are CH4, NH3, H2O and HF.
  • Being covalent, they are volatile compounds.
  • Based on the relative number of electrons and bonds in their Lewis structures, molecular hydrides are classified into three types:

docs.title: (a) Electron-deficient hydrides
docs.text:
• These have too few electrons to write a conventional Lewis structure.
  • Example: diborane (B2H6). In fact, all elements of group 13 form electron-deficient compounds.
  • They act as Lewis acids, i.e., electron acceptors.

docs.title: (b) Electron-precise hydrides
docs.text:
• These have exactly the required number of electrons to write conventional Lewis structures.
  • All elements of group 14 form such compounds (e.g., CH4). They are tetrahedral in geometry.

docs.title: (c) Electron-rich hydrides
docs.text:
• These have excess electrons, present as lone pairs.
  • Elements of groups 15-17 form such compounds. NH3 has 1 lone pair, H2O has 2 and HF has 3 lone pairs.
  • They behave as Lewis bases, i.e., electron donors.
  • Lone pairs on highly electronegative atoms like N, O and F lead to hydrogen bonding between molecules, which causes association of molecules.
Type Group Example Behaviour Electron-deficient 13 B2H6 Lewis acid Electron-precise 14 CH4 Neither (tetrahedral) Electron-rich 15-17 NH3, H2O, HF Lewis base

docs.title: 3. Metallic or Non-stoichiometric (Interstitial) Hydrides
docs.text:
• These are formed by many d-block and f-block elements.
  • Metals of groups 7, 8 and 9 do not form hydrides. From group 6, only chromium forms a hydride (CrH).
  • They conduct heat and electricity, though not as efficiently as their parent metals.
  • Unlike saline hydrides, they are almost always non-stoichiometric, being deficient in hydrogen. For these hydrides, the law of constant composition does not hold.

Examples

LaH2.87, YbH2.55, TiH1.5-1.8, ZrH1.3-1.75, VH0.56, NiH0.6-0.7, PdH0.6-0.8

  • Earlier it was believed that hydrogen occupies interstices in the metal lattice, causing distortion without changing the lattice type. So they were called interstitial hydrides.
  • Recent studies show that, except for hydrides of Ni, Pd, Ce and Ac, the other hydrides of this class have a lattice different from that of the parent metal.
  • The ability of transition metals to absorb hydrogen is widely used in catalytic reduction and hydrogenation reactions.
  • Some metals (e.g., Pd, Pt) can absorb a very large volume of hydrogen. So, they can be used as hydrogen storage media. This gives them high potential for hydrogen storage and as a source of energy.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Would you expect the hydrides of N, O and F to have lower boiling points than the hydrides of their subsequent group members? Give reasons.

On the basis of molecular masses alone, the boiling points of NH3, H2O and HF should be lower than those of the hydrides of the next members of their groups (PH3, H2S, HCl).

However, N, O and F are highly electronegative, so extensive hydrogen bonding exists in their hydrides. Extra energy is needed to break these hydrogen bonds. Hence, the boiling points of NH3, H2O and HF are actually higher than those of the hydrides of their subsequent group members.

Can phosphorus with outer electronic configuration 3s23p3 form PH5?

Although phosphorus shows +3 and +5 oxidation states, it cannot form PH5. Apart from other factors, the high ΔaH (atomisation enthalpy) of dihydrogen and the ΔegH (electron gain enthalpy) of hydrogen do not favour phosphorus showing its highest oxidation state with hydrogen. Hence PH5 is not formed.

What do you understand by (i) electron-deficient, (ii) electron-precise, and (iii) electron-rich compounds of hydrogen? Provide justification with suitable examples.

(i) Electron-deficient hydrides have too few electrons to write a conventional Lewis structure. Example: B2H6. Boron has only 3 valence electrons, so B2H6 has 12 electrons, which are not enough for 8 normal two-electron bonds.

(ii) Electron-precise hydrides have exactly enough electrons for a conventional Lewis structure. Example: CH4. Carbon's 4 valence electrons form 4 C-H bonds with no lone pair left.

(iii) Electron-rich hydrides have extra electrons present as lone pairs. Examples: NH3 (1 lone pair), H2O (2 lone pairs), HF (3 lone pairs).

What characteristics do you expect from an electron-deficient hydride with respect to its structure and chemical reactions?

  • Structure: Since there are not enough electrons for normal two-centre two-electron bonds, such hydrides exist in associated forms with bridging hydrogen atoms (e.g., B2H6 instead of BH3).
  • Reactions: They are electron acceptors, so they act as Lewis acids and readily react with Lewis bases (electron donors) such as NH3.

Do you expect the carbon hydrides of the type CnH2n+2 to act as 'Lewis' acid or base? Justify your answer.

No. CnH2n+2 hydrides are electron-precise. All the valence electrons of carbon are used in bonding and there are neither vacant orbitals nor lone pairs. So, they can neither accept nor donate electron pairs, and do not act as Lewis acids or bases.

What do you understand by the term 'non-stoichiometric hydrides'? Do you expect this type of hydrides to be formed by alkali metals? Justify your answer.

Non-stoichiometric hydrides are hydrides in which the ratio of metal to hydrogen is not a simple whole number and can vary, e.g., LaH2.87, TiH1.5-1.8. They are formed by d- and f-block elements and are deficient in hydrogen.

Alkali metals do not form such hydrides. Alkali metals are highly electropositive and transfer their electron completely to hydrogen, forming ionic hydrides (M+H-) of fixed, stoichiometric composition.

How do you expect the metallic hydrides to be useful for hydrogen storage? Explain.

In metallic hydrides, hydrogen is absorbed into the metal lattice. Some metals such as Pd and Pt can accommodate a very large volume of hydrogen. On heating, the absorbed hydrogen is released. Hence, these metals and their alloys can store hydrogen compactly and release it when needed, making them useful as hydrogen storage media.

Saline hydrides are known to react with water violently producing fire. Can CO2, a well known fire extinguisher, be used in this case? Explain.

No. Saline hydrides like NaH react with water to give H2, which catches fire due to the heat of the reaction. Hot metal hydrides (and the metals formed) are strong reducing agents and can reduce CO2, so the fire would not be put out. For example:

\[NaH + CO_2 → HCOONa\]

So, CO2 cannot be used. Such fires are extinguished with dry sand.

How can saline hydrides remove traces of water from organic compounds?

Saline hydrides react with water to form the metal hydroxide and dihydrogen gas. The H2 escapes and the hydroxide can be separated, leaving the organic compound dry.

\[NaH_{(s)} + H_2O_{(l)} → NaOH_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)}\]

Arrange the following:(i) CaH2, BeH2 and TiH2 in order of increasing electrical conductance.(ii) LiH, NaH and CsH in order of increasing ionic character.(iii) H-H, D-D and F-F in order of increasing bond dissociation enthalpy.(iv) NaH, MgH2 and H2O in order of increasing reducing property.

(i) BeH2 is covalent and non-conducting, CaH2 is ionic (conducts only when molten) and TiH2 is metallic.

\[BeH_2 < CaH_2 < TiH_2\]

(ii) Ionic character increases as electropositive character of the metal increases down the group.

\[LiH < NaH < CsH\]

(iii) F-F bond is weak due to repulsion between lone pairs; D-D is slightly stronger than H-H.

\[F-F < H-H < D-D\]

(iv) Ionic hydrides are the strongest reducing agents; H2O is a very weak one.

\[H_2O < MgH_2 < NaH\]

What do you expect the nature of hydrides to be, if formed by elements of atomic numbers 15, 19, 23 and 44 with dihydrogen? Compare their behaviour towards water.

  • Z = 15 (P): forms covalent hydride PH3. It does not react appreciably with water.
  • Z = 19 (K): forms ionic hydride KH. It reacts violently with water.
\[KH_{(s)} + H_2O_{(l)} → KOH_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)}\]
  • Z = 23 (V): forms metallic (non-stoichiometric) hydride, e.g., VH0.56. It does not react with water.
  • Z = 44 (Ru): belongs to group 8, which does not form hydrides.

docs.title: Hydrogen | Hydrogen Peroxide
docs.text: Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, is an important chemical used in pollution control treatment of domestic and industrial effluents. In this article, we will discuss its preparation, physical properties, structure, chemical properties, storage and uses.

docs.title: 1. From barium peroxide
docs.text:
• Acidifying barium peroxide and removing excess water by evaporation under reduced pressure gives hydrogen peroxide.
\[BaO_2.8H_2O_{(s)} + H_2SO_{4(aq)} → BaSO_{4(s)} + H_2O_{2(aq)} + 8H_2O_{(l)}\]

docs.title: 2. From peroxodisulphate
docs.text:
• Peroxodisulphate is obtained by electrolytic oxidation of acidified sulphate solutions at high current density. Its hydrolysis gives hydrogen peroxide.
\[2HSO^-_{4(aq)} \xrightarrow{Electrolysis} HO_3SOOSO_3H_{(aq)} \xrightarrow{Hydrolysis} 2HSO^-_{4(aq)} + 2H^+_{(aq)} + H_2O_{2(aq)}\]
  • This method is now used for the laboratory preparation of D2O2.
\[K_2S_2O_{8(s)} + 2D_2O_{(l)} → 2KDSO_{4(aq)} + D_2O_{2(l)}\]

docs.title: 3. Industrial method: auto-oxidation of 2-alkylanthraquinols
docs.text:
• Industrially, H2O2 is prepared by auto-oxidation of 2-alkylanthraquinols, e.g., 2-ethylanthraquinol. The oxidised product is reduced back with H2/Pd and reused.
\[2\text{-}ethylanthraquinol \underset{H_2/Pd}{\overset{O_2\ (air)}{\rightleftharpoons}} H_2O_2 + oxidised\ product\]
  • This gives about 1% H2O2. It is extracted with water and concentrated to about 30% (by mass) by distillation under reduced pressure.
  • It can be further concentrated to about 85% by careful distillation under low pressure. The remaining water is frozen out to obtain pure H2O2.

docs.title: Physical Properties of Hydrogen Peroxide
docs.text:
• In the pure state, H2O2 is an almost colourless (very pale blue) liquid.
  • It is miscible with water in all proportions and forms a hydrate, H2O2.H2O (mp 221 K).
