Property Value Melting point (K) 272.4 Boiling point, extrapolated (K) 423 Vapour pressure at 298 K (mm Hg) 1.9 Density of solid at 268.5 K (g cm-3) 1.64 Density of liquid at 298 K (g cm-3) 1.44 Viscosity at 290 K (centipoise) 1.25 Dielectric constant at 298 K (C2/N m2) 70.7 Electrical conductivity at 298 K (Ω-1 cm-1) 5.1 × 10-8

docs.title: Volume strength of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
docs.text:
• The strength of H2O2 solutions is commonly expressed as volume strength.
  • A 30% solution of H2O2 is marketed as '100 volume' hydrogen peroxide. It means that 1 mL of this solution gives 100 mL of oxygen at STP.
  • Commercially it is marketed as '10 volume', which means it contains about 3% H2O2.

Calculate the strength of 10 volume solution of hydrogen peroxide.

10 volume H2O2 means that 1 L of this solution gives 10 L of O2 at STP.

\[2H_2O_{2(l)} → O_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}\] \[2 \times 34\ g = 68\ g\ H_2O_2\ gives\ 22.4\ L\ O_2\ at\ STP\] \[∴\ 10\ L\ O_2\ is\ given\ by = {68 \times 10 \over 22.4}\ g = 30.36\ g\ H_2O_2\]

Therefore, the strength of 10 volume H2O2 = 30.36 g/L.

docs.title: Structure of Hydrogen Peroxide
docs.text:
• H2O2 has a non-planar (open book) structure. The two O-H bonds lie in different planes.
  • The angle between the two planes is called the dihedral angle. It is 111.5° in the gas phase and 90.2° in the solid phase (at 110 K).
Parameter Gas phase Solid phase O-O bond length 147.5 pm 145.8 pm O-H bond length 95.0 pm 98.8 pm O-O-H bond angle 94.8° 101.9° Dihedral angle 111.5° 90.2°

docs.title: Chemical Properties of Hydrogen Peroxide
docs.text: H2O2 acts as an oxidising agent as well as a reducing agent in both acidic and alkaline media. The oxidation state of oxygen in H2O2 is -1, which lies between 0 (in O2) and -2 (in H2O). So it can be either oxidised or reduced.

docs.title: 4. Reducing action in basic medium
docs.text:
\[I_2 + H_2O_2 + 2OH^- → 2I^- + 2H_2O + O_2\] \[2MnO_4^- + 3H_2O_2 → 2MnO_2 + 3O_2 + 2H_2O + 2OH^-\]

Conclusion

When H2O2 acts as an oxidising agent, it is reduced to H2O (or OH-). When it acts as a reducing agent, it is oxidised to O2.

docs.title: Storage of Hydrogen Peroxide
docs.text:
• H2O2 decomposes slowly on exposure to light.
\[2H_2O_{2(l)} → 2H_2O_{(l)} + O_{2(g)}\]
  • The decomposition is catalysed by metal surfaces or traces of alkali (present in glass containers).
  • Therefore, it is stored in wax-lined glass or plastic vessels in the dark.
  • Urea can be added as a stabiliser.
  • It is kept away from dust, because dust can cause explosive decomposition.

docs.title: Uses of Hydrogen Peroxide
docs.text:
• In daily life, it is used as a hair bleach and as a mild disinfectant. As an antiseptic it is sold as perhydrol.
  • It is used to manufacture chemicals like sodium perborate and per-carbonate, which are used in high quality detergents.
  • It is used in the synthesis of hydroquinone, tartaric acid, certain food products and pharmaceuticals (cephalosporin), etc.
  • It is used in industry as a bleaching agent for textiles, paper pulp, leather, oils, fats, etc.
  • It is used in environmental (green) chemistry, for example in pollution control treatment of domestic and industrial effluents, oxidation of cyanides and restoring aerobic conditions to sewage wastes.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Compare the structures of H2O and H2O2.

  • H2O is a bent, planar molecule with an H-O-H bond angle of 104.5° and O-H bond length 95.7 pm.
  • H2O2 is a non-planar (open book) molecule containing an O-O single bond. The two O-H bonds lie in different planes, with a dihedral angle of 111.5° in the gas phase and 90.2° in the solid phase. The O-O-H angle is 94.8° (gas phase) and the O-H bond length is 95.0 pm.

Write chemical reactions to justify that hydrogen peroxide can function as an oxidising as well as reducing agent.

As oxidising agent (H2O2 is reduced to H2O or OH-):

\[2Fe^{2+} + 2H^+ + H_2O_2 → 2Fe^{3+} + 2H_2O\ \ (acidic)\] \[Mn^{2+} + H_2O_2 → Mn^{4+} + 2OH^-\ \ (basic)\]

As reducing agent (H2O2 is oxidised to O2):

\[2MnO_4^- + 6H^+ + 5H_2O_2 → 2Mn^{2+} + 8H_2O + 5O_2\ \ (acidic)\] \[I_2 + H_2O_2 + 2OH^- → 2I^- + 2H_2O + O_2\ \ (basic)\]

How does H2O2 behave as a bleaching agent?

H2O2 bleaches by oxidation. It releases nascent oxygen, which oxidises the coloured matter into colourless products.

\[H_2O_2 → H_2O + [O]\] \[Coloured\ matter + [O] → Colourless\ matter\]

Since the action is mild, it is used to bleach delicate materials like hair, silk, wool, textiles and paper pulp.

Complete the following reactions:(i) PbS(s) + H2O2(aq) →(ii) MnO4-(aq) + H2O2(aq) →(iii) CaO(s) + H2O(g) →(iv) AlCl3(g) + H2O(l) →(v) Ca3N2(s) + H2O(l) →Classify the above into (a) hydrolysis, (b) redox and (c) hydration reactions.

\[(i)\ PbS_{(s)} + 4H_2O_{2(aq)} → PbSO_{4(s)} + 4H_2O_{(l)}\ \ (redox)\] \[(ii)\ 2MnO^-_{4(aq)} + 5H_2O_{2(aq)} + 6H^+_{(aq)} → 2Mn^{2+}_{(aq)} + 8H_2O_{(l)} + 5O_{2(g)}\ \ (redox)\] \[(iii)\ CaO_{(s)} + H_2O_{(g)} → Ca(OH)_{2(s)}\ \ (hydration)\] \[(iv)\ AlCl_{3(g)} + 3H_2O_{(l)} → Al(OH)_{3(s)} + 3HCl_{(aq)}\ \ (hydrolysis)\] \[(v)\ Ca_3N_{2(s)} + 6H_2O_{(l)} → 3Ca(OH)_{2(aq)} + 2NH_{3(g)}\ \ (hydrolysis)\]

docs.title: Hydrogen | Introduction
docs.text:
Hydrogen is the first element of the periodic table and has the simplest atomic structure of all elements: one proton and one electron. In elemental form it exists as a diatomic molecule, H2, called dihydrogen.

  • Hydrogen forms more compounds than any other element.
  • It is the most abundant element in the universe and the third most abundant element on the surface of the earth.
  • Since it burns cleanly and releases a lot of energy, hydrogen is seen as a major future source of energy.

In this article, we will discuss the position of hydrogen in the periodic table, its occurrence and its isotopes.

docs.title: Position of Hydrogen in the Periodic Table
docs.text:
• Electronic configuration of hydrogen is 1s1.
  • Hydrogen shows resemblance with both alkali metals (group 1) and halogens (group 17). At the same time it differs from both of them. That is why its position in the periodic table has long been debated.

docs.title: 1. Resemblance with alkali metals
docs.text:
• Its electronic configuration (1s1) is similar to the outer electronic configuration of alkali metals (ns1).
  • Like alkali metals, it can lose one electron to form a unipositive ion, H+.
  • Like alkali metals, it forms oxides, halides and sulphides.

docs.title: 2. Resemblance with halogens
docs.text:
• Like halogens (ns2np5), it is short of just one electron to attain the configuration of the nearest noble gas, helium (1s2).
  • Like halogens, it can gain one electron to form a uninegative ion, H-.
  • Like halogens, it forms a diatomic molecule and combines with elements to form hydrides and a large number of covalent compounds.
  • In terms of ionization enthalpy, hydrogen resembles halogens more than alkali metals:
Element Li H F ΔiH (kJ mol-1) 520 1312 1680

docs.title: 3. Differences from alkali metals and halogens
docs.text:
• Unlike alkali metals, hydrogen has a very high ionization enthalpy and shows no metallic character under normal conditions.
  • Unlike halogens, its reactivity is very low.
  • Loss of the electron leaves only a bare nucleus (H+) of size about 1.5 × 10-3 pm. This is extremely small compared to normal atomic and ionic sizes of 50 to 200 pm. As a result, H+ never exists freely and is always associated with other atoms or molecules.

Conclusion

Hydrogen is unique in its behaviour. Therefore, it is best placed separately in the periodic table.

docs.title: Occurrence of Dihydrogen
docs.text:
• Dihydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe (about 70% of the total mass of the universe) and is the principal element in the solar atmosphere.
  • The giant planets Jupiter and Saturn consist mostly of hydrogen.
  • Being very light, it is much less abundant (0.15% by mass) in the earth's atmosphere.
  • In the combined form, it makes up 15.4% of the earth's crust and the oceans.
  • Besides water, it occurs in plant and animal tissues, carbohydrates, proteins, hydrides including hydrocarbons and many other compounds.

docs.title: Isotopes of Hydrogen
docs.text:
Hydrogen has three isotopes:

\[Protium:\ {}^1_1H\] \[Deuterium:\ {}^2_1H\ or\ D\] \[Tritium:\ {}^3_1H\ or\ T\]
  • The isotopes differ only in the number of neutrons in the nucleus. Protium has no neutron, deuterium (also called heavy hydrogen) has one neutron and tritium has two neutrons.
  • Protium is the predominant form. Terrestrial hydrogen contains 0.0156% of deuterium, mostly in the form of HD.
  • Tritium is present only to the extent of about one atom per 1018 atoms of protium.
  • Only tritium is radioactive. It emits low energy β- particles with a half-life of 12.33 years.
  • In 1934, Harold C. Urey received the Nobel Prize for separating the hydrogen isotope of mass number 2 (deuterium) by physical methods.

Note

Since the isotopes have the same electronic configuration, they have almost the same chemical properties. They differ only in their rates of reaction, mainly because of their different bond dissociation enthalpies. Their physical properties, however, differ considerably due to the large differences in their masses.

docs.title: Atomic and Physical Properties of Hydrogen Isotopes
docs.text:
Property Hydrogen Deuterium Tritium Relative abundance (%) 99.985 0.0156 10-15 Relative atomic mass (g mol-1) 1.008 2.014 3.016 Melting point (K) 13.96 18.73 20.62 Boiling point (K) 20.39 23.67 25.0 Density (g L-1) 0.09 0.18 0.27 Enthalpy of fusion (kJ mol-1) 0.117 0.197 - Enthalpy of vaporization (kJ mol-1) 0.904 1.226 - Bond dissociation enthalpy at 298.2 K (kJ mol-1) 435.88 443.35 - Internuclear distance (pm) 74.14 74.14 - Ionization enthalpy (kJ mol-1) 1312 - - Electron gain enthalpy (kJ mol-1) -73 - - Covalent radius (pm) 37 - - Ionic radius, H- (pm) 208 - -
  • Notice that the D-D bond (443.35 kJ mol-1) is stronger than the H-H bond (435.88 kJ mol-1). This is why reactions involving D are slower than those involving H.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Justify the position of hydrogen in the periodic table on the basis of its electronic configuration.

Hydrogen has the configuration 1s1.

  • Like alkali metals (ns1), it has one electron in its valence shell and can lose it to form H+. So, it can be placed in group 1.
  • Like halogens (ns2np5), it is one electron short of the noble gas configuration (He, 1s2) and can gain one electron to form H-. So, it can also be placed in group 17.

However, it has a much higher ionization enthalpy than alkali metals, is non-metallic, and is much less reactive than halogens. Moreover, H+ is extremely small and cannot exist freely. Because of this unique behaviour, hydrogen is best placed separately in the periodic table.

Write the names of isotopes of hydrogen. What is the mass ratio of these isotopes?

The isotopes of hydrogen are protium (1H), deuterium (2H or D) and tritium (3H or T).

Their mass numbers are 1, 2 and 3. Hence:

\[Mass\ ratio\ (H : D : T) = 1 : 2 : 3\]

Why does hydrogen occur in a diatomic form rather than in a monoatomic form under normal conditions?

A hydrogen atom has only one electron (1s1), so its valence shell is incomplete. By sharing its electron with another hydrogen atom, each atom attains the stable helium configuration (1s2). The H-H bond formed is very strong (435.88 kJ mol-1), so the H2 molecule is far more stable than free H atoms. Therefore, hydrogen exists as H2 under normal conditions.

docs.title: Hydrogen | Water
docs.text:
Water is the most common and abundant compound of hydrogen. A major part of all living organisms is water: the human body has about 65% water and some plants have as much as 95%. It is a crucial compound for the survival of all life forms and a solvent of great importance.

In this article, we will discuss the physical properties, structure and chemical properties of water.

docs.title: Distribution of Water on Earth
docs.text: Source % of Total Oceans 97.33 Saline lakes and inland seas 0.008 Polar ice and glaciers 2.04 Ground water 0.61 Lakes 0.009 Soil moisture 0.005 Atmospheric water vapour 0.001 Rivers 0.0001

docs.title: Physical Properties of Water
docs.text:
• Water is a colourless and tasteless liquid.
  • Its unusual properties in the condensed phase (liquid and solid) are due to extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
  • Because of hydrogen bonding, water has a higher freezing point, boiling point, heat of vaporisation and heat of fusion than H2S and H2Se.
  • Compared to other liquids, water has a higher specific heat, thermal conductivity, surface tension, dipole moment and dielectric constant.
  • Its high heat of vaporisation and heat capacity moderate the climate and the body temperature of living beings.
  • It is an excellent solvent for transporting ions and molecules needed for plant and animal metabolism.
  • Due to hydrogen bonding with polar molecules, even covalent compounds like alcohol and carbohydrates dissolve in water.

docs.title: Physical properties of H<sub>2</sub>O and D<sub>2</sub>O
docs.text: Property H<sub>2</sub>O D<sub>2</sub>O Molecular mass (g mol<sup>-1</sup>) 18.0151 20.0276 Melting point (K) 273.0 276.8 Boiling point (K) 373.0 374.4 Enthalpy of formation (kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) -285.9 -294.6 Enthalpy of vaporisation at 373 K (kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) 40.66 41.61 Enthalpy of fusion (kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) 6.01 - Temperature of maximum density (K) 276.98 284.2 Density at 298 K (g cm<sup>-3</sup>) 1.0000 1.1059 Viscosity (centipoise) 0.8903 1.107 Dielectric constant (C<sup>2</sup>/N m<sup>2</sup>) 78.39 78.06 Electrical conductivity at 293 K (ohm<sup>-1</sup> cm<sup>-1</sup>) 5.7 × 10<sup>-8</sup> -

docs.title: Structure of Water
docs.text:
• In the gas phase, water is a bent molecule with a bond angle of 104.5° and an O-H bond length of 95.7 pm.
  • It is a highly polar molecule. Oxygen carries a partial negative charge (2δ-) and each hydrogen a partial positive charge (δ+).
  • In the liquid phase, water molecules are associated together by hydrogen bonds.

docs.title: Structure of Ice
docs.text:
• Ice is the crystalline form of water. At atmospheric pressure, ice crystallises in the hexagonal form, but at very low temperatures it condenses to the cubic form.
  • Ice has a highly ordered three-dimensional hydrogen-bonded structure. X-ray studies show that each oxygen atom is surrounded tetrahedrally by four other oxygen atoms at a distance of 276 pm.
  • Hydrogen bonding gives ice a rather open structure with wide holes. These holes can hold other molecules of suitable size interstitially.
  • Because of this open structure, the density of ice is less than that of water. That is why an ice cube floats on water.
  • In winter, the ice formed on the surface of a lake insulates the water below and ensures the survival of aquatic life. This fact is of great ecological significance.

docs.title: 1. Amphoteric nature
docs.text:
• Water can act both as an acid and as a base, i.e., it is amphoteric.
  • In the Bronsted sense, it acts as an acid with NH3 and as a base with H2S.
\[H_2O_{(l)} + NH_{3(aq)} ⇌ OH^-_{(aq)} + NH^+_{4(aq)}\] \[H_2O_{(l)} + H_2S_{(aq)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + HS^-_{(aq)}\]
  • Auto-protolysis (self-ionization) of water: one water molecule donates a proton to another.
\[H_2O_{(l)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\] \[acid_1\ \ \ \ base_2\ \ \ \ conjugate\ acid_2\ \ \ \ conjugate\ base_1\]

docs.title: 2. Redox reactions involving water
docs.text:
• Water is easily reduced to dihydrogen by highly electropositive metals. So, it is a great source of dihydrogen.
\[2H_2O_{(l)} + 2Na_{(s)} → 2NaOH_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)}\]
  • Water is oxidised to O2 during photosynthesis.
\[6CO_{2(g)} + 12H_2O_{(l)} → C_6H_{12}O_{6(aq)} + 6H_2O_{(l)} + 6O_{2(g)}\]
  • Water is also oxidised to O2 by fluorine.
\[2F_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → 4H^+_{(aq)} + 4F^-_{(aq)} + O_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: 3. Hydrolysis reactions
docs.text:
• Due to its high dielectric constant, water has a very strong hydrating tendency and dissolves many ionic compounds.
  • However, some covalent and some ionic compounds are hydrolysed (decomposed) by water.
\[P_4O_{10(s)} + 6H_2O_{(l)} → 4H_3PO_{4(aq)}\] \[SiCl_{4(l)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → SiO_{2(s)} + 4HCl_{(aq)}\] \[N^{3-}_{(s)} + 3H_2O_{(l)} → NH_{3(g)} + 3OH^-_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: 4. Hydrate formation
docs.text:
• Many salts crystallise from aqueous solution as hydrated salts. The water in them is associated in different ways:
  1. Coordinated water, e.g., [Cr(H2O)6]3+3Cl-
  2. Interstitial water, e.g., BaCl2.2H2O
  3. Hydrogen-bonded water, e.g., [Cu(H2O)4]2+SO42-.H2O in CuSO4.5H2O

How many hydrogen-bonded water molecule(s) are associated in CuSO4.5H2O?

CuSO4.5H2O is written as [Cu(H2O)4]2+SO42-.H2O. Only one water molecule, which is outside the brackets (coordination sphere), is hydrogen-bonded. The other four are coordinated to Cu2+.

Hydrolysis vs Hydration

  • Hydrolysis is a reaction in which water breaks a compound into new products, e.g., SiCl4 + 2H2O → SiO2 + 4HCl.
  • Hydration is the attachment of water molecules to a substance without decomposing it, e.g., formation of CuSO4.5H2O or hydrated ions like [Cr(H2O)6]3+.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Among NH3, H2O and HF, which would you expect to have highest magnitude of hydrogen bonding and why?

The strength of a single hydrogen bond depends on the electronegativity of the atom attached to hydrogen. Since F is the most electronegative element, a single H...F hydrogen bond in HF is the strongest.

However, each H2O molecule has two H atoms and two lone pairs, so it can form up to four hydrogen bonds, while HF and NH3 are limited (HF has only one H; NH3 has only one lone pair). Hence, the overall magnitude (extent) of hydrogen bonding is highest in H2O, which is also why water has the highest boiling point of the three.

What do you understand by the term 'auto-protolysis' of water? What is its significance?

Auto-protolysis (self-ionization) is the transfer of a proton from one water molecule to another, forming H3O+ and OH- ions.

\[H_2O_{(l)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\]

Significance: It shows that water is amphoteric, i.e., it can act both as an acid and as a base. Because of this, water can react with both acids and bases, and the small concentration of ions it produces explains its very low electrical conductivity.

Consider the reaction of water with F2 and suggest, in terms of oxidation and reduction, which species are oxidised/reduced.

\[2F_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → 4H^+_{(aq)} + 4F^-_{(aq)} + O_{2(g)}\]
  • Oxidation state of O changes from -2 (in H2O) to 0 (in O2). So, water is oxidised.
  • Oxidation state of F changes from 0 (in F2) to -1 (in F-). So, fluorine is reduced.

Write chemical reactions to show the amphoteric nature of water.

Water acts as an acid with NH3 (donates a proton):

\[H_2O_{(l)} + NH_{3(aq)} ⇌ OH^-_{(aq)} + NH^+_{4(aq)}\]

Water acts as a base with H2S (accepts a proton):

\[H_2O_{(l)} + H_2S_{(aq)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + HS^-_{(aq)}\]

Describe the structure of the common form of ice.

The common form of ice is hexagonal ice, formed at atmospheric pressure. It has a highly ordered three-dimensional hydrogen-bonded structure in which each oxygen atom is surrounded tetrahedrally by four other oxygen atoms at a distance of 276 pm. Hydrogen bonding gives ice an open structure with wide holes, which is why ice is less dense than water.

What properties of water make it useful as a solvent? What types of compound can it (i) dissolve, and (ii) hydrolyse?

Water has a high dielectric constant (78.39), a high dipole moment and the ability to form hydrogen bonds. These make it an excellent solvent.

(i) It dissolves most ionic compounds (e.g., NaCl) and polar covalent compounds that can form hydrogen bonds with it (e.g., alcohols, carbohydrates).

(ii) It hydrolyses many covalent compounds (e.g., P4O10, SiCl4) and some ionic compounds such as nitrides.

\[SiCl_{4(l)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → SiO_{2(s)} + 4HCl_{(aq)}\]

Describe the usefulness of water in biosphere and biological systems.

  • Water makes up a major part of living organisms (about 65% of the human body) and is essential for all life forms.
  • Its high specific heat and heat of vaporisation moderate the climate and the body temperature of living beings.
  • It is an excellent solvent and transports ions and molecules needed for plant and animal metabolism.
  • It takes part in photosynthesis, where it is oxidised to O2.
  • Ice floats on water and insulates the water below, which helps aquatic life survive in winter.

Do you expect different products in solution when aluminium(III) chloride and potassium chloride are treated separately with (i) normal water (ii) acidified water, and (iii) alkaline water? Write equations wherever necessary.

KCl is a salt of a strong acid and strong base. It is not hydrolysed and simply dissociates into K+ and Cl- ions in all three cases.

\[KCl_{(s)} + H_2O → K^+_{(aq)} + Cl^-_{(aq)}\]

AlCl3 is a salt of a weak base and strong acid, so it behaves differently:

(i) In normal water, it is hydrolysed, giving an acidic solution:

\[AlCl_3 + 3H_2O → Al(OH)_3 + 3HCl\]

(ii) In acidified water, hydrolysis is suppressed and it stays in solution as hydrated ions:

\[AlCl_3 + 6H_2O → [Al(H_2O)_6]^{3+} + 3Cl^-\]

(iii) In alkaline water, Al(OH)3 first forms and then dissolves in excess alkali, giving tetrahydroxoaluminate ions:

\[AlCl_3 + 4OH^- → [Al(OH)_4]^- + 3Cl^-\]

docs.title: Metallurgy | Concentration of Ores
docs.text:
Removal of the unwanted materials (gangue) like sand and clay from the ore is known as concentration, dressing or benefaction of the ore.

  • Concentration involves several steps. The choice of steps depends on the differences in physical properties of the metal compound and the gangue.
  • The type of metal, the available facilities and environmental factors are also taken into consideration.
  • The important methods of concentration are:
    • Hydraulic washing
    • Magnetic separation
    • Froth floatation
    • Leaching

docs.title: 1. Hydraulic Washing
docs.text:
• It is based on the difference in densities (specific gravities) of the ore particles and the gangue particles. Hence, it is a type of gravity separation.
  • An upward stream of running water is used to wash the powdered ore.
  • The lighter gangue particles are washed away and the heavier ore particles are left behind.

Note

This method works well for heavy oxide and carbonate ores, e.g., haematite and tin stone, where the ore is much heavier than the gangue.

docs.title: 2. Magnetic Separation
docs.text:
• It is based on the difference in magnetic properties of the ore components.
  • It is used when either the ore or the gangue (one of the two) is attracted by a magnetic field, e.g., in case of iron ores.
  • The ground ore is carried on a conveyer belt which passes over a magnetic roller.
  • The magnetic particles are attracted by the roller and fall close to it, while the non-magnetic particles are thrown farther away. Thus they collect in two separate heaps.

Example

Ores containing iron such as haematite, magnetite, siderite and iron pyrites can be concentrated by magnetic separation.

docs.title: 3. Froth Floatation Method
docs.text:
• This method is used for removing gangue from sulphide ores.
  • It is based on the principle that the mineral (ore) particles are preferentially wetted by oil, while the gangue particles are wetted by water.
  • A suspension of the powdered ore is made with water. To it, collectors and froth stabilisers are added.

docs.title: Collectors
docs.text:
• Collectors enhance the non-wettability of the mineral particles by water, so that they stick to the oil.
  • Examples: pine oils, fatty acids, xanthates.

docs.title: Froth Stabilisers
docs.text:
• Froth stabilisers stabilise the froth so that it does not collapse.
  • Examples: cresols, aniline.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
• A rotating paddle agitates the mixture and draws air into it.
  • As a result, a froth is formed which carries the mineral particles with it.
  • The froth is light and is skimmed off. It is then dried to recover the ore particles.
  • The gangue particles, wetted by water, settle at the bottom.

docs.title: Depressants
docs.text:
• It is possible to separate two sulphide ores from each other by adjusting the proportion of oil to water or by using depressants.
  • A depressant selectively prevents one of the sulphides from coming into the froth.

Example

In an ore containing ZnS and PbS, NaCN is used as a depressant. It selectively prevents ZnS from coming to the froth but allows PbS to come with the froth.

Note

The froth floatation method made copper mining profitable even from low grade ores. Before it was invented, only ores containing large amounts of copper could be used. As a result, world production of copper rose sharply and the metal became cheaper.

docs.title: 4. Leaching
docs.text: Leaching is used when the ore is soluble in some suitable solvent while the impurities are not.

docs.title: (a) Leaching of alumina from bauxite
docs.text:
• Bauxite, the principal ore of aluminium, usually contains SiO2, iron oxides and titanium oxide (TiO2) as impurities.
  • The powdered ore is digested with a concentrated solution of NaOH at 473 – 523 K and 35 – 36 bar pressure.
  • Al2O3 is leached out as sodium aluminate (and SiO2 too as sodium silicate), leaving the other impurities behind.
\[Al_2O_{3(s)} + 2NaOH_{(aq)} + 3H_2O_{(l)} → 2Na[Al(OH)_4]_{(aq)}\]
  • The aluminate in solution is neutralised by passing CO2 gas, and hydrated Al2O3 is precipitated.
  • At this stage, the solution is seeded with freshly prepared samples of hydrated Al2O3, which induces the precipitation.
\[2Na[Al(OH)_4]_{(aq)} + CO_{2(g)} → Al_2O_3.xH_2O_{(s)} + 2NaHCO_{3(aq)}\]
  • Sodium silicate remains in the solution. The hydrated alumina is filtered, dried and heated to give back pure Al2O3.
\[Al_2O_3.xH_2O_{(s)} \xrightarrow{1470\ K} Al_2O_{3(s)} + xH_2O_{(g)}\]

docs.title: (b) Leaching of silver and gold
docs.text:
• In the metallurgy of silver and gold, the metal is leached with a dilute solution of NaCN or KCN in the presence of air (for O2).
  • The metal goes into solution as a soluble cyano complex. It is later recovered by displacement with a more reactive metal like zinc.
\[4M_{(s)} + 8CN^-_{(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(aq)} + O_{2(g)} → 4[M(CN)_2]^-_{(aq)} + 4OH^-_{(aq)}\] \[(M = Ag\ or\ Au)\] \[2[M(CN)_2]^-_{(aq)} + Zn_{(s)} → [Zn(CN)_4]^{2-}_{(aq)} + 2M_{(s)}\]

docs.title: Metallurgy | Conversion to Oxide and Reduction
Metallurgy | Conversion to Oxide and Reduction
docs.text:
The concentrated ore must be converted into a form which is suitable for reduction. Usually it is first converted into its oxide by calcination or roasting, and the oxide is then reduced to the metal.

  • Isolation of a crude metal from the concentrated ore involves two major steps:
    • Conversion of the ore to oxide
    • Reduction of the oxide to metal
  • Sulphide and carbonate ores are converted to oxides before reduction because oxides are easier to reduce.

Why are oxides easier to reduce?

The standard Gibbs energy of formation of most metal sulphides is more negative than that of CS2 and H2S (CS2 is in fact an endothermic compound). So the reduction of a sulphide by carbon or hydrogen has a positive ΔG0 and is not feasible. For oxides, the formation of CO or CO2 can make the overall ΔG0 negative. Hence, sulphide ores are roasted to oxides before reduction.

docs.title: 1. Calcination
docs.text:
• Calcination is heating the ore (usually in the absence or limited supply of air) so that the volatile matter escapes, leaving behind the metal oxide.
  • It is used for hydrated oxide ores and carbonate ores. Water and CO2 are removed.
\[Fe_2O_3.xH_2O_{(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} Fe_2O_{3(s)} + xH_2O_{(g)}\] \[ZnCO_{3(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} ZnO_{(s)} + CO_{2(g)}\] \[CaCO_3.MgCO_{3(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} CaO_{(s)} + MgO_{(s)} + 2CO_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: 2. Roasting
docs.text:
• In roasting, the ore is heated in a regular supply of air in a furnace at a temperature below the melting point of the metal.
  • It is mainly used for sulphide ores, which are oxidised to oxides.
\[2ZnS + 3O_2 → 2ZnO + 2SO_2\] \[2PbS + 3O_2 → 2PbO + 2SO_2\] \[2Cu_2S + 3O_2 → 2Cu_2O + 2SO_2\]
  • The SO2 produced is utilised for manufacturing H2SO4.

docs.title: Roasting of copper ores
docs.text:
• The sulphide ores of copper are heated in a reverberatory furnace.
  • If the ore contains iron, it is mixed with silica (SiO2) before heating.
  • Silica acts as a flux: iron oxide forms a slag of iron silicate, and copper is produced in the form of copper matte, which contains Cu2S and FeS.
\[FeO + SiO_2 → FeSiO_3\ (slag)\]

docs.title: Difference between Calcination and Roasting
docs.text: Calcination Roasting Ore is heated in absence or limited supply of air. Ore is heated in a regular supply of air. Used for carbonate and hydrated oxide ores. Used for sulphide ores. Moisture, CO<sub>2</sub> and other volatile matter are removed. The sulphide is oxidised; SO<sub>2</sub> is given off. Example: ZnCO<sub>3</sub> → ZnO + CO<sub>2</sub> Example: 2ZnS + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2ZnO + 2SO<sub>2</sub>

docs.title: Reduction of Oxide to the Metal
docs.text:
• Reduction of the metal oxide usually involves heating it with some other substance which acts as a reducing agent, like C, CO or even another metal.
  • The reducing agent (e.g., carbon) combines with the oxygen of the metal oxide.
\[M_xO_y + yC → xM + yCO\]
  • Some metal oxides get reduced easily while others are very difficult to reduce. In every case, heating is required.
  • Extraction of metals by thermal reduction at high temperature is called pyrometallurgy.
  • To understand the temperature needed for a reduction, and to predict which element will be a suitable reducing agent for a given metal oxide (MxOy), we use the thermodynamic concept of Gibbs energy. This is discussed in the next part.

docs.title: Metallurgy | Electrochemical Principles and Oxidation-Reduction
docs.text: Metal ions in solution or in the molten state can be reduced by electrolysis or by adding a more reactive metal. The same thermodynamic principles used in pyrometallurgy apply here, through the relation between Gibbs energy and electrode potential.

docs.title: Gibbs Energy and Electrode Potential
docs.text:
\[\Delta G^0 = -nE^0F\]

Where, n is the number of electrons exchanged and E0 is the electrode potential of the redox couple formed in the system.

  • More reactive metals have large negative electrode potentials, so their reduction is difficult.
  • If the difference of two E0 values gives a positive E0, then ΔG0 is negative. The less reactive metal then comes out of the solution and the more reactive metal goes into the solution.

Example

\[Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + Fe_{(s)} → Cu_{(s)} + Fe^{2+}_{(aq)}\]

Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution.

  • In simple electrolysis, the Mn+ ions are discharged at the negative electrode (cathode) and deposited there.
  • Precautions are taken considering the reactivity of the metal produced, and suitable materials are used as electrodes.
  • Sometimes a flux is added to make the molten mass more conducting.

docs.title: Extraction of Aluminium (Hall-Heroult Process)
docs.text:
• Purified Al2O3 (obtained by leaching bauxite) is mixed with Na3AlF6 (cryolite) or CaF2.
  • Cryolite lowers the melting point of the mixture and increases its electrical conductivity.
  • The fused mixture is electrolysed in an electrolytic cell using carbon electrodes:
    • Cathode: steel vessel with a carbon lining.
    • Anode: graphite rods dipped in the melt.
  • The overall reaction may be taken as:
\[2Al_2O_3 + 3C → 4Al + 3CO_2\]
  • The electrode reactions are:
\[Cathode:\ Al^{3+}_{(melt)} + 3e^- → Al_{(l)}\] \[Anode:\ C_{(s)} + O^{2-}_{(melt)} → CO_{(g)} + 2e^-\] \[C_{(s)} + 2O^{2-}_{(melt)} → CO_{2(g)} + 4e^-\]
  • The oxygen liberated at the anode reacts with the carbon of the anode, producing CO and CO2.
  • So the graphite anode is slowly burnt away. For each kg of aluminium produced, about 0.5 kg of carbon anode is consumed, and the anodes have to be replaced from time to time.
  • The graphite anode is useful here because it helps in the reduction of the oxide to the metal.

Note

A large amount of electricity is needed for this process, so a cheap and good source of electricity is essential.

docs.title: Copper from Low Grade Ores and Scraps
docs.text:
• Copper is extracted from low grade ores by hydrometallurgy.
  • The copper is leached out using acid or bacteria. The solution containing Cu2+ is then treated with scrap iron or H2:
\[Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + Fe_{(s)} → Cu_{(s)} + Fe^{2+}_{(aq)}\] \[Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)} → Cu_{(s)} + 2H^+_{(aq)}\]

At a site, low grade copper ores are available and zinc and iron scraps are also available. Which of the two scraps would be more suitable for reducing the leached copper ore and why?

Zinc lies above iron in the electrochemical series (zinc is the more reactive metal), so the reduction will be faster with zinc scraps. But zinc is a costlier metal than iron, so using iron scraps is more advisable and economical.

docs.title: Oxidation-Reduction
docs.text: Besides reductions, some extractions are based on oxidation, particularly for non-metals.

docs.title: 1. Extraction of chlorine from brine
docs.text:
• Chlorine is abundant in sea water as common salt. It is obtained by the oxidation of Cl- ions:
\[2Cl^-_{(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → 2OH^-_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)} + Cl_{2(g)}\]
  • ΔG0 for this reaction is +422 kJ. Converting it into E0:
\[E^0 = -{\Delta G^0 \over nF} = -{422000 \over 2 \times 96500} = -2.2\ V\]
  • So the reaction needs an external emf greater than 2.2 V. In practice, electrolysis needs an extra potential to overcome some other hindering reactions.
  • Thus, Cl2 is obtained by electrolysis, with H2 and aqueous NaOH as by-products.
  • Molten NaCl can also be electrolysed. But in that case, Na metal is produced and not NaOH.

docs.title: 2. Extraction of gold and silver
docs.text:
• Leaching of gold and silver with CN- is also an oxidation reaction (Ag → Ag+ or Au → Au+).
  • The metal is later recovered by displacement, in which zinc acts as the reducing agent.
\[4Au_{(s)} + 8CN^-_{(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(aq)} + O_{2(g)} → 4[Au(CN)_2]^-_{(aq)} + 4OH^-_{(aq)}\] \[2[Au(CN)_2]^-_{(aq)} + Zn_{(s)} → 2Au_{(s)} + [Zn(CN)_4]^{2-}_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: Metallurgy | Extraction of Iron, Copper and Zinc
Metallurgy | Extraction of Iron, Copper and Zinc
docs.text: Iron, copper and zinc are extracted by reducing their oxides with coke or carbon monoxide. The Ellingham diagram explains the choice of reducing agent and the temperature used in each case.

docs.title: 1. Extraction of Iron from its Oxides
docs.text:
• Oxide ores of iron are first concentrated and then calcined or roasted to remove water, decompose carbonates and oxidise sulphides.
  • They are then mixed with limestone and coke and fed into a blast furnace from its top. Here the oxide is reduced to the metal.
  • One of the main reduction steps is:
\[FeO_{(s)} + C_{(s)} → Fe_{(s/l)} + CO_{(g)}\]
  • It can be seen as a coupling of two simpler reactions: the reduction of FeO and the oxidation of C to CO.
\[FeO_{(s)} → Fe_{(s)} + {1 \over 2}O_{2(g)}\ \ \ [\Delta G_{(FeO,\ Fe)}]\] \[C_{(s)} + {1 \over 2}O_{2(g)} → CO_{(g)}\ \ \ [\Delta G_{(C,\ CO)}]\] \[\Delta_rG = \Delta G_{(C,\ CO)} + \Delta G_{(FeO,\ Fe)}\]
  • The overall reaction takes place when \(\Delta_rG\) is negative.
  • In the ΔG0 vs T plot, the line for Fe → FeO goes upward while the line for C → CO goes downward.
  • Above about 1073 K, the C, CO line comes below the Fe, FeO line [\(\Delta G_{(C,\ CO)} < \Delta G_{(Fe,\ FeO)}\)]. So in this range, coke reduces FeO and is itself oxidised to CO.
  • Similarly, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 are reduced by CO at relatively lower temperatures, because their curves intersect the CO, CO2 curve at lower temperatures.

docs.title: Reactions in the Blast Furnace
docs.text:
• Hot air is blown in from the bottom of the furnace and coke is burnt to give a temperature up to about 2200 K in the lower portion. The burning of coke supplies most of the heat needed.
  • The CO and heat move to the upper part of the furnace. Here the temperature is lower, and the iron oxides (Fe2O3 and Fe3O4) coming from the top are reduced in steps to FeO.

docs.title: (a) At 500 – 800 K (lower temperature range)
docs.text: \[3Fe_2O_3 + CO &rarr; 2Fe_3O_4 + CO_2\] \[Fe_3O_4 + 4CO &rarr; 3Fe + 4CO_2\] \[Fe_2O_3 + CO &rarr; 2FeO + CO_2\]

docs.title: (b) At 900 – 1500 K (higher temperature range)
docs.text: \[C + CO_2 &rarr; 2CO\] \[FeO + CO &rarr; Fe + CO_2\]

docs.title: (c) Role of limestone
docs.text:
• Limestone decomposes to CaO, which acts as a flux and removes the silicate impurity of the ore as slag.
  • The slag is in the molten state and separates out from the iron.
\[CaCO_3 → CaO + CO_2\] \[CaO + SiO_2 → CaSiO_3\ (slag)\]

docs.title: 1. Pig iron
docs.text:
• The iron obtained from the blast furnace contains about 4% carbon and smaller amounts of many impurities (e.g., S, P, Si, Mn).
  • It is known as pig iron and can be cast into a variety of shapes.

docs.title: 2. Cast iron
docs.text:
• Cast iron is made by melting pig iron with scrap iron and coke using a hot air blast.
  • It has a slightly lower carbon content (about 3%) and is extremely hard and brittle.

docs.title: 3. Wrought iron (malleable iron)
docs.text:
• It is the purest form of commercial iron.
  • It is prepared from cast iron by oxidising the impurities in a reverberatory furnace lined with haematite. The haematite oxidises carbon to carbon monoxide:
\[Fe_2O_3 + 3C → 2Fe + 3CO\]
  • Limestone is added as a flux. Sulphur, silicon and phosphorus are oxidised and pass into the slag.
  • The metal is removed and freed from the slag by passing it through rollers.

docs.title: 2. Extraction of Copper from Cuprous Oxide
docs.text:
• In the Ellingham diagram, the Cu2O line is almost at the top. So it is quite easy to reduce oxide ores of copper directly to the metal by heating with coke.
  • The lines for C, CO and C, CO2 lie much lower in the diagram, particularly after 500 – 600 K.
  • However, most copper ores are sulphides and some also contain iron. The sulphide ores are roasted or smelted to give oxides:
\[2Cu_2S + 3O_2 → 2Cu_2O + 2SO_2\]
  • The oxide is then easily reduced to metallic copper using coke:
\[Cu_2O + C → 2Cu + CO\]

docs.title: Actual process
docs.text:
• The ore is heated in a reverberatory furnace after mixing with silica.
  • Iron oxide forms a slag of iron silicate, and copper is produced in the form of copper matte, which contains Cu2S and FeS.
\[FeO + SiO_2 → FeSiO_3\ (slag)\]
  • The copper matte is then charged into a silica lined converter. Some silica is also added and a hot air blast is blown in.
  • The remaining FeS, FeO and Cu2S/Cu2O are converted to metallic copper:
\[2FeS + 3O_2 → 2FeO + 2SO_2\] \[FeO + SiO_2 → FeSiO_3\] \[2Cu_2S + 3O_2 → 2Cu_2O + 2SO_2\] \[2Cu_2O + Cu_2S → 6Cu + SO_2\]
  • The last reaction is a self-reduction (auto-reduction): Cu2S itself reduces Cu2O, and no external reducing agent is needed.
  • The solidified copper has a blistered appearance due to the evolution of SO2, so it is called blister copper.

docs.title: 3. Extraction of Zinc from Zinc Oxide
docs.text:
• Zinc blende (ZnS) is first roasted to ZnO, and calamine (ZnCO3) is calcined to ZnO.
  • The reduction of zinc oxide is done using coke. The temperature needed is higher than that for copper.
  • For heating, the oxide is made into brickettes with coke and clay.
\[ZnO + C \xrightarrow{\Delta} Zn + CO\]
  • At this high temperature zinc is formed as a vapour. The metal is distilled off and collected by rapid chilling.

docs.title: Metallurgy | Introduction
docs.text:
Metallurgy is the entire scientific and technological process used for the isolation of a metal from its ores.

  • Only a few elements like carbon, sulphur, gold and the noble gases occur in the free (native) state in nature.
  • Most other elements occur in combined form, i.e., as compounds such as oxides, sulphides, carbonates and silicates.
  • Extracting an element from its combined form needs a process that is both chemically feasible and commercially viable.
  • Every metal has its own extraction route, but a few general principles are common to all of them.

docs.title: 1. Mineral
docs.text: Minerals are naturally occurring chemical substances in the earth's crust which can be obtained by mining.

docs.title: 2. Ore
docs.text:
• A metal may be found in many minerals, but only a few of them are viable sources of that metal.
  • A mineral from which a metal can be extracted conveniently and profitably is called an ore.
  • Hence, all ores are minerals but all minerals are not ores.

Example

Aluminium occurs in many minerals like mica and clays, but it is extracted only from bauxite. So bauxite is an ore of aluminium, while clay is just a mineral of aluminium.

docs.title: 3. Gangue
docs.text: An ore rarely contains only the desired compound. It is usually contaminated with earthy or undesired materials like sand, clay and rocks, which are known as gangue (or matrix).

docs.title: 4. Flux and Slag
docs.text:
• A flux is a substance added during metallurgy which combines with the gangue to form a fusible material called slag.
  • Slag separates more easily from the ore than the gangue does, so the removal of gangue becomes easier.
\[Flux + Gangue → Slag\] \[FeO + SiO_2 → FeSiO_3\ (slag)\]

docs.title: Major Steps in Metallurgy
docs.text:
The extraction and isolation of a metal from its ore involves three major steps:

  • Concentration of the ore: removal of gangue from the ore.
  • Isolation of the metal from the concentrated ore: conversion of the ore into oxide followed by reduction of the oxide to metal.
  • Purification (refining) of the metal: removal of the remaining minor impurities.

Note

Before concentration, ores are graded and crushed to a reasonable size.

docs.title: Occurrence of Metals
docs.text:
• Elements vary greatly in their abundance in the earth's crust.
  • Aluminium is the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element in the earth's crust (about 8.3% by weight).
  • Aluminium is a major component of many igneous minerals including mica and clays.
  • Many gemstones are impure forms of Al2O3. The impurities range from Cr (in ruby) to Co (in sapphire).
  • Iron is the second most abundant metal in the earth's crust. It forms a variety of compounds and is also one of the essential elements in biological systems.

docs.title: Principal Ores of Some Important Metals
docs.text: Metal Ore Composition Aluminium Bauxite AlO<sub>x</sub>(OH)<sub>3-2x</sub> [where 0 < x < 1] Aluminium Kaolinite (a form of clay) [Al<sub>2</sub>(OH)<sub>4</sub>Si<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>] Iron Haematite Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> Iron Magnetite Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> Iron Siderite FeCO<sub>3</sub> Iron Iron pyrites FeS<sub>2</sub> Copper Copper pyrites CuFeS<sub>2</sub> Copper Malachite CuCO<sub>3</sub>.Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> Copper Cuprite Cu<sub>2</sub>O Copper Copper glance Cu<sub>2</sub>S Zinc Zinc blende or Sphalerite ZnS Zinc Calamine ZnCO<sub>3</sub> Zinc Zincite ZnO

docs.title: Choice of Ore for Extraction
docs.text:
• Aluminium: bauxite is chosen.
  • Iron: usually the oxide ores (haematite, magnetite) are used. They are abundant and do not produce polluting gases like SO2, which is produced when iron pyrites is used.
  • Copper and Zinc: any of the listed ores may be used, depending upon availability and other relevant factors.

docs.title: Extraction at a Glance
docs.text: Metal Common ores Method of extraction Remarks Aluminium Bauxite, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O; Cryolite, Na<sub>3</sub>AlF<sub>6</sub> Electrolysis of Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> dissolved in molten Na<sub>3</sub>AlF<sub>6</sub> A good source of electricity is required. Iron Haematite, Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>; Magnetite, Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> Reduction of the oxide with CO and coke in a blast furnace Temperature approaching 2170 K is required. Copper Copper pyrites, CuFeS<sub>2</sub>; Copper glance, Cu<sub>2</sub>S; Malachite; Cuprite, Cu<sub>2</sub>O Partial roasting of sulphide followed by reduction Self-reduction in a converter; acid leaching is used for low grade ores (hydrometallurgy). Zinc Zinc blende, ZnS; Calamine, ZnCO<sub>3</sub>; Zincite, ZnO Roasting followed by reduction with coke The metal may be purified by fractional distillation.

docs.title: Metallurgy | Questions
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some important questions based on the general principles and processes of isolation of elements.

docs.title: Concentration of Ores
docs.text:
Which of the ores of aluminium, iron, copper and zinc can be concentrated by magnetic separation method?

Ores in which one of the components (either the impurity or the actual ore) is magnetic can be concentrated by this method. For example, the iron ores: haematite (Fe2O3), magnetite (Fe3O4), siderite (FeCO3) and iron pyrites (FeS2).

What is the significance of leaching in the extraction of aluminium?

Leaching of bauxite with concentrated NaOH dissolves Al2O3 as sodium aluminate. This removes impurities like SiO2, Fe2O3 and TiO2 from the bauxite ore, giving pure alumina for electrolysis.

What is the role of depressant in froth floatation process?

A depressant selectively prevents one sulphide ore from coming into the froth, so that two sulphide ores present together can be separated. For example, in an ore containing ZnS and PbS, NaCN acts as a depressant. It prevents ZnS from forming froth but allows PbS to come with the froth.

How can you separate alumina from silica in a bauxite ore associated with silica? Give equations, if any.

The powdered ore is digested with concentrated NaOH at 473 – 523 K and 35 – 36 bar. Al2O3 dissolves as sodium aluminate and SiO2 as sodium silicate:

\[Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH + 3H_2O → 2Na[Al(OH)_4]\] \[SiO_2 + 2NaOH → Na_2SiO_3 + H_2O\]

CO2 is passed through the solution (seeded with fresh hydrated alumina). Only hydrated alumina precipitates, while sodium silicate stays in solution:

\[2Na[Al(OH)_4] + CO_2 → Al_2O_3.xH_2O ↓ + 2NaHCO_3\]

The precipitate is filtered and heated to get pure alumina:

\[Al_2O_3.xH_2O \xrightarrow{1470\ K} Al_2O_3 + xH_2O\]

How is leaching carried out in case of low grade copper ores?

Low grade copper ores are leached with acid (or bacteria) in the presence of air. Copper goes into solution as Cu2+ ions:

\[Cu_{(s)} + 2H^+_{(aq)} + {1 \over 2}O_{2(g)} → Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)}\]

The solution is then treated with scrap iron or H2 to recover copper:

\[Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + Fe_{(s)} → Cu_{(s)} + Fe^{2+}_{(aq)}\] \[Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)} → Cu_{(s)} + 2H^+_{(aq)}\]

Differentiate between minerals and ores.

Minerals are naturally occurring chemical substances in the earth's crust obtainable by mining. Ores are those minerals from which a metal can be extracted conveniently and profitably. Thus, all ores are minerals but all minerals are not ores. Example: aluminium occurs in clay and bauxite, but only bauxite is an ore of aluminium.

Giving examples, differentiate between roasting and calcination.

  • Calcination: the ore is heated in absence or limited supply of air to remove volatile matter like water and CO2. Used for carbonate and hydrated ores.
\[ZnCO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} ZnO + CO_2\] \[Fe_2O_3.xH_2O \xrightarrow{\Delta} Fe_2O_3 + xH_2O\]
  • Roasting: the ore is heated in a regular supply of air below the melting point of the metal. Used for sulphide ores.
\[2ZnS + 3O_2 → 2ZnO + 2SO_2\] \[2Cu_2S + 3O_2 → 2Cu_2O + 2SO_2\]

docs.title: Thermodynamic Principles
docs.text:
The reaction Cr2O3 + 2Al → Al2O3 + 2Cr (ΔG0 = -421 kJ) is thermodynamically feasible as is apparent from the Gibbs energy value. Why does it not take place at room temperature?

A negative ΔG0 only shows that the reaction is possible. It says nothing about its rate. All the reactants are solids, and a certain amount of activation energy is needed even for a thermodynamically feasible reaction. Therefore heating is required to start the reaction.

Is it true that under certain conditions, Mg can reduce Al2O3 and Al can reduce MgO? What are those conditions?

Yes. The MgO and Al2O3 lines in the Ellingham diagram cross at about 1350 °C (point A).

  • Below 1350 °C, the MgO line lies lower, so Mg can reduce Al2O3.
  • Above 1350 °C, the Al2O3 line lies lower, so Al can reduce MgO.

Predict conditions under which Al might be expected to reduce MgO.

Above the point of intersection of the Al2O3 and MgO curves in the Ellingham diagram (about 1350 °C), ΔfG0 of Al2O3 is more negative than that of MgO. So above this temperature, the reaction below has a negative ΔG0:

\[3MgO + 2Al → Al_2O_3 + 3Mg\]

The value of ΔfG0 for formation of Cr2O3 is -540 kJ mol-1 and that of Al2O3 is -827 kJ mol-1. Is the reduction of Cr2O3 possible with Al?

\[Cr_2O_3 + 2Al → Al_2O_3 + 2Cr\] \[\Delta_rG^0 = \Delta_fG^0(Al_2O_3) - \Delta_fG^0(Cr_2O_3)\] \[\Delta_rG^0 = -827 - (-540) = -287\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

Since ΔrG0 is negative, the reduction of Cr2O3 by Al is possible.

Out of C and CO, which is a better reducing agent at 673 K?

At 673 K, the line for CO → CO2 lies below the line for C → CO in the Ellingham diagram, i.e., the oxidation of CO to CO2 has the more negative ΔG0. Hence CO is a better reducing agent than C at 673 K. (Above about 983 K, carbon becomes the better reducing agent.)

Out of C and CO, which is a better reducing agent for ZnO?

The ZnO line lies below the CO → CO2 line at all temperatures, so CO cannot reduce ZnO. The C → CO line slopes downwards and crosses below the ZnO line at high temperature (above about 1270 K). Hence carbon is the better reducing agent for ZnO.

\[ZnO + C → Zn + CO\]

Why is zinc not extracted from zinc oxide through reduction using CO?

For reduction by CO, the sum of ΔG0 for ZnO → Zn and CO → CO2 must be negative. In the Ellingham diagram, the line for 2CO + O2 → 2CO2 lies above the line for 2Zn + O2 → 2ZnO, so the overall ΔG0 stays positive. Hence CO cannot reduce ZnO, and coke is used instead at a high temperature.

The choice of a reducing agent in a particular case depends on thermodynamic factor. How far do you agree with this statement? Support your opinion with two examples.

The statement is largely true. A reducing agent works only if the overall ΔG0 of the coupled reaction is negative, i.e., the line for its oxide lies below that of the metal oxide in the Ellingham diagram at the chosen temperature.

  • Cu2O lies near the top of the diagram, so it is easily reduced by coke even at low temperatures.
  • ZnO is reduced by coke only at high temperatures where the C → CO line falls below the ZnO line; CO cannot reduce it.
  • Cr2O3 is reduced by Al, since ΔfG0 of Al2O3 is much more negative.

However, kinetic and economic factors (rate, cost, temperature required) also matter. For example, Mg is not used to reduce alumina even though it is feasible.

docs.title: Extraction of Metals
docs.text:
Copper can be extracted by hydrometallurgy but not zinc. Explain.

In hydrometallurgy, the metal ion in solution is displaced by a more reactive metal.

\[E^0_{Cu^{2+}/Cu} = +0.34\ V,\ \ E^0_{Zn^{2+}/Zn} = -0.76\ V\]

Cu2+ is easily displaced by a cheap metal like iron (E0 = -0.44 V). Zinc is itself a highly reactive metal, so displacing Zn2+ would need still more reactive metals like Al, Mg, Ca or K. These are costlier, and many of them also react with water. So zinc cannot be extracted by hydrometallurgy economically.

Why is the extraction of copper from pyrites more difficult than that from its oxide ore through reduction?

The ΔfG0 of Cu2S is not compensated by the oxidation of carbon or hydrogen, because CS2 and H2S have less negative (CS2 even positive) Gibbs energies of formation. So copper sulphide cannot be reduced directly by C or H2. Pyrites must first be roasted to the oxide, and its iron must be removed as slag. On the other hand, Cu2O lies near the top of the Ellingham diagram and is easily reduced by coke.

Write down the reactions taking place in different zones in the blast furnace during the extraction of iron.

  • Lower temperature zone (500 – 800 K):
\[3Fe_2O_3 + CO → 2Fe_3O_4 + CO_2\] \[Fe_3O_4 + 4CO → 3Fe + 4CO_2\] \[Fe_2O_3 + CO → 2FeO + CO_2\]
  • Higher temperature zone (900 – 1500 K):
\[C + CO_2 → 2CO\] \[FeO + CO → Fe + CO_2\]
  • Slag formation:
\[CaCO_3 → CaO + CO_2\] \[CaO + SiO_2 → CaSiO_3\]
  • Bottom (combustion) zone, about 2170 K:
\[C + O_2 → CO_2\] \[FeO + C → Fe + CO\]

Write chemical reactions taking place in the extraction of zinc from zinc blende.

  • Concentration by froth floatation, followed by roasting:
\[2ZnS + 3O_2 → 2ZnO + 2SO_2\]
  • Reduction with coke at high temperature:
\[ZnO + C → Zn + CO\]
  • The zinc vapour is distilled off and collected by rapid chilling. It may be purified by fractional distillation.

State the role of silica in the metallurgy of copper.

Silica acts as a flux. It removes the iron oxide present in the copper ore as a fusible slag of iron silicate, both in the reverberatory furnace and in the converter:

\[FeO + SiO_2 → FeSiO_3\ (slag)\]

Why is copper matte put in silica lined converter?

Copper matte contains Cu2S and FeS. In the silica lined converter, a hot air blast converts FeS to FeO, which combines with silica to form FeSiO3 slag. Cu2S is partly oxidised to Cu2O, which then reacts with the remaining Cu2S to give copper:

\[2FeS + 3O_2 → 2FeO + 2SO_2\] \[FeO + SiO_2 → FeSiO_3\] \[2Cu_2S + 3O_2 → 2Cu_2O + 2SO_2\] \[2Cu_2O + Cu_2S → 6Cu + SO_2\]

How is cast iron different from pig iron?

Pig iron, obtained from the blast furnace, contains about 4% carbon and many impurities (S, P, Si, Mn). Cast iron is made by melting pig iron with scrap iron and coke using a hot air blast. It has a slightly lower carbon content (about 3%) and is extremely hard and brittle.

What is the role of cryolite in the metallurgy of aluminium?

Cryolite (Na3AlF6) is mixed with purified alumina before electrolysis. It lowers the melting point of the mixture and increases its electrical conductivity, so the electrolysis can be carried out at a lower temperature with less energy.

What is the role of graphite rod in the electrometallurgy of aluminium?

The graphite rod acts as the anode. The oxygen liberated at the anode reacts with the carbon to form CO and CO2, so the graphite helps in the reduction of alumina to aluminium. Without it, the liberated oxygen could re-oxidise some of the aluminium. In the process the anode is burnt away (about 0.5 kg per kg of Al) and must be replaced periodically.

\[C + O^{2-} → CO + 2e^-\] \[C + 2O^{2-} → CO_2 + 4e^-\]

Name the processes from which chlorine is obtained as a by-product. What will happen if an aqueous solution of NaCl is subjected to electrolysis?

Chlorine is obtained as a by-product in the electrolysis of molten NaCl (manufacture of sodium metal). It is also a product of the electrolysis of brine.

On electrolysis of aqueous NaCl, Cl2 is liberated at the anode, H2 at the cathode, and NaOH remains in the solution:

\[2Cl^-_{(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → 2OH^-_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)} + Cl_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: Refining
docs.text:
Name the common elements present in the anode mud in electrolytic refining of copper. Why are they so present?

Anode mud contains antimony, selenium, tellurium, silver, gold and platinum. These elements are less reactive (less electropositive) than copper, so they are not oxidised at the anode and do not dissolve in the electrolyte. They simply fall below the anode as the anode dissolves.

Describe a method for refining nickel.

Nickel is refined by the Mond process (vapour phase refining). Impure nickel is heated in a stream of CO to form volatile nickel tetracarbonyl. The vapour is taken to another chamber and heated to a higher temperature, where it decomposes to give pure nickel:

\[Ni + 4CO \xrightarrow{330 - 350\ K} Ni(CO)_4\] \[Ni(CO)_4 \xrightarrow{450 - 470\ K} Ni + 4CO\]

Explain: (i) Zone refining (ii) Column chromatography.

  • Zone refining: Impurities are more soluble in the melt than in the solid metal. A mobile heater moves along a rod of impure metal; the pure metal crystallises behind the molten zone while impurities move with it. After several passes, impurities collect at one end, which is cut off. Used for Ge, Si, B, Ga and In.
  • Column chromatography: A column of adsorbent like Al2O3 is packed in a glass tube. The mixture is passed through it in a liquid medium. Components are adsorbed to different extents and form separate bands, which are eluted one by one with suitable solvents. It is used for elements present in minute amounts whose impurities have similar chemical properties.

Outline the principles of refining of metals by the following methods: (i) Zone refining (ii) Electrolytic refining (iii) Vapour phase refining

  • Zone refining: impurities are more soluble in the molten state than in the solid state of the metal.
  • Electrolytic refining: impure metal is the anode and pure metal the cathode in a solution of its salt. The metal dissolves at the anode and deposits in pure form at the cathode; more reactive impurities stay in solution and less reactive ones form anode mud.
\[Anode:\ M → M^{n+} + ne^-\] \[Cathode:\ M^{n+} + ne^- → M\]
  • Vapour phase refining: the metal is converted into a volatile compound, which is collected and then decomposed to give pure metal. Examples: Mond process for Ni and van Arkel method for Zr and Ti.
\[Zr + 2I_2 → ZrI_4 \xrightarrow{1800\ K} Zr + 2I_2\]

What is meant by the term chromatography?

Chromatography is a technique for separating the components of a mixture, based on the fact that different components are adsorbed (or distributed) to different extents between a stationary phase and a mobile phase. As the mobile phase moves through the stationary phase, the components travel at different rates and get separated.

What criterion is followed for the selection of the stationary phase in chromatography?

The stationary phase is chosen such that the components of the mixture have different solubilities (or different extents of adsorption) in it. A component more strongly held by the stationary phase moves slowly, while a component less strongly held moves faster with the mobile phase, so the components get separated. The stationary phase must also be immobile and immiscible with the mobile phase.

docs.title: Metallurgy | Refining and Uses of Metals
Metallurgy | Refining and Uses of Metals
docs.text:
A metal extracted by any method is usually contaminated with some impurity. Refining is the process of removing these impurities to obtain the metal in a highly pure form. The technique chosen depends on the differences in properties of the metal and the impurity.

The common refining methods are:

  • Distillation
  • Liquation
  • Electrolytic refining
  • Zone refining
  • Vapour phase refining
  • Chromatographic methods

docs.title: 1. Distillation
docs.text:
• It is useful for low boiling metals like zinc and mercury.
  • The impure metal is evaporated and the pure metal is obtained as the distillate. The non-volatile impurities are left behind.

docs.title: 2. Liquation
docs.text:
• In this method, a low melting metal like tin is made to flow on a sloping surface.
  • The metal melts and flows down, and is thus separated from the higher melting impurities.

docs.title: 3. Electrolytic Refining
docs.text:
• The impure metal is made the anode, and a strip of the same metal in pure form is used as the cathode.
  • Both are put in a suitable electrolytic bath containing a soluble salt of the same metal.
  • The more basic (more reactive) metal impurities remain in the solution, and the less basic ones fall below the anode as anode mud.
  • The process is explained using the concepts of electrode potential, overpotential and Gibbs energy.
\[Anode:\ M → M^{n+} + ne^-\] \[Cathode:\ M^{n+} + ne^- → M\]

docs.title: Electrolytic refining of copper
docs.text:
• Anode: impure (blister) copper. Cathode: pure copper strips.
  • Electrolyte: acidified solution of copper sulphate.
  • The net result is the transfer of copper in pure form from the anode to the cathode.
\[Anode:\ Cu → Cu^{2+} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ Cu^{2+} + 2e^- → Cu\]
  • Impurities from the blister copper deposit as anode mud, which contains antimony, selenium, tellurium, silver, gold and platinum. Recovery of these elements may meet the cost of refining.
  • Zinc may also be refined this way.

docs.title: 4. Zone Refining
docs.text:
• It is based on the principle that the impurities are more soluble in the melt than in the solid state of the metal.
  • A circular mobile heater is fixed at one end of a rod of the impure metal, and a molten zone is formed.
  • The molten zone moves along with the heater. As the heater moves forward, the pure metal crystallises out of the melt, and the impurities pass into the adjacent molten zone.
  • The process is repeated several times with the heater moving in the same direction. The impurities get concentrated at one end, which is finally cut off.
  • The process is carried out in an inert (noble gas) atmosphere.
  • It is very useful for producing semiconductors and other metals of very high purity, e.g., germanium, silicon, boron, gallium and indium.

docs.title: 5. Vapour Phase Refining
docs.text:
In this method, the metal is converted into its volatile compound, which is collected elsewhere and then decomposed to give the pure metal. The two requirements are:

  • The metal should form a volatile compound with an available reagent.
  • The volatile compound should be easily decomposable, so that the recovery is easy.

docs.title: (a) Mond process for refining nickel
docs.text:
• Nickel is heated in a stream of carbon monoxide, forming a volatile complex, nickel tetracarbonyl.
  • The carbonyl is then heated to a higher temperature, where it decomposes to give pure nickel.
\[Ni + 4CO \xrightarrow{330 - 350\ K} Ni(CO)_4\] \[Ni(CO)_4 \xrightarrow{450 - 470\ K} Ni + 4CO\]

docs.title: (b) van Arkel method for refining zirconium or titanium
docs.text:
• This method is very useful for removing all the oxygen and nitrogen present as impurities in metals like Zr and Ti.
  • The crude metal is heated with iodine in an evacuated vessel. The metal iodide, being more covalent, volatilises.
  • The metal iodide is decomposed on a tungsten filament electrically heated to about 1800 K. The pure metal is deposited on the filament.
\[Zr + 2I_2 → ZrI_4\] \[ZrI_4 \xrightarrow{1800\ K} Zr + 2I_2\]

docs.title: 6. Chromatographic Methods
docs.text:
• This method is based on the principle that different components of a mixture are adsorbed to different extents on an adsorbent.
  • The mixture is put in a liquid or gaseous medium (mobile phase), which is moved through the adsorbent (stationary phase).
  • Different components are adsorbed at different levels on the column. Later, the adsorbed components are removed (eluted) using suitable solvents called eluants.
  • The method gets its name from the physical state of the moving medium, the adsorbent material and the way the medium passes. Examples are paper chromatography, column chromatography and gas chromatography.

docs.title: Column chromatography
docs.text:
• A column of Al2O3 (stationary phase) is prepared in a glass tube, and the moving medium containing a solution of the components is in liquid form.
  • It is very useful for purifying elements which are available in minute quantities and whose impurities are not very different in chemical properties from the element to be purified.

Mobile and stationary phases

  • The mobile phase may be a gas, a liquid or a supercritical fluid. The sample is dissolved in it.
  • The stationary phase is immobile and immiscible, like the Al2O3 column.
  • The two phases are chosen such that the components of the sample have different solubilities in them.
  • A component which is quite soluble in the stationary phase takes longer to travel through it than a component which is not very soluble in the stationary phase but very soluble in the mobile phase. Thus, the components get separated as they travel through the stationary phase.

docs.title: Uses of Aluminium, Copper, Zinc and Iron
1. Aluminium
docs.text:
• Aluminium foils are used as wrappers for chocolates.
  • The fine dust of the metal is used in paints and lacquers.
  • Being highly reactive, it is used in the extraction of chromium and manganese from their oxides.
  • Wires of aluminium are used as electricity conductors.
  • Alloys containing aluminium, being light, are very useful.

docs.title: 2. Copper
docs.text:
• Copper is used for making wires in the electrical industry and for water and steam pipes.
  • It is used in several alloys that are tougher than the metal itself, e.g., brass (with zinc), bronze (with tin) and coinage alloy (with nickel).

docs.title: 3. Zinc
docs.text:
• Zinc is used for galvanising iron.
  • It is used in large quantities in batteries.
  • It is a constituent of many alloys, e.g., brass (Cu 60%, Zn 40%) and german silver (Cu 25-30%, Zn 25-30%, Ni 40-50%).
  • Zinc dust is used as a reducing agent in the manufacture of dye-stuffs, paints, etc.

docs.title: 4. Iron
docs.text:
• Cast iron, the most important form of iron, is used for casting stoves, railway sleepers, gutter pipes, toys, etc. It is also used to make wrought iron and steel.
  • Wrought iron is used in making anchors, wires, bolts, chains and agricultural implements.
  • Steel finds a number of uses. Alloy steel is obtained when other metals are added to it:
    • Nickel steel: cables, automobile and aeroplane parts, pendulums, measuring tapes.
    • Chrome steel: cutting tools and crushing machines.
    • Stainless steel: cycles, automobiles, utensils, pens, etc.

docs.title: Metallurgy | Thermodynamic Principles and Ellingham Diagram
Metallurgy | Thermodynamic Principles and Ellingham Diagram
docs.text: Thermodynamics explains why only a certain reducing agent and a minimum specific temperature are suitable for the reduction of a metal oxide to the metal. Gibbs energy is the most important quantity here.

docs.title: Gibbs Energy and Feasibility
docs.text:
• The change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, for any process at a given temperature is:
\[\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\]

Where, \(\Delta H\) is the enthalpy change and \(\Delta S\) is the entropy change of the process.

  • ΔG0 is also related to the equilibrium constant K of the reaction at temperature T:
\[\Delta G^0 = -RT\ lnK\]
  • A negative ΔG gives a large positive value of ln K, i.e., K > 1. This happens only when the reaction proceeds towards the products.

From these relations we get two important conclusions:

docs.title: 1. Effect of temperature
docs.text:
• A reaction proceeds only when ΔG is negative.
  • If ΔS is positive, increasing the temperature increases TΔS. When TΔS becomes greater than ΔH, ΔG becomes negative.

docs.title: 2. Coupling of reactions
docs.text:
• If two reactions are put together in a system and the net ΔG of the two is negative, the overall reaction will occur.
  • So we add up the ΔG values of the two reactions and look at the sign of the sum. Such coupling is easily understood through plots of ΔG0 vs T for the formation of oxides.

docs.title: Ellingham Diagram
docs.text:
The graphical representation of Gibbs energy of formation of oxides against temperature was first used by H.J.T. Ellingham, and it is known as the Ellingham diagram. It provides a sound basis for choosing a reducing agent and predicting the feasibility of thermal reduction of an ore.

  • The criterion of feasibility is that at the given temperature, the Gibbs energy of the reaction must be negative.

docs.title: Features of the Ellingham Diagram
docs.text:
• It consists of plots of ΔfG0 vs T for the formation of oxides of elements, i.e., for the reaction:
\[2xM_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} → 2M_xO_{(s)}\]
  • Positive slope: In this reaction, a gas (O2) is consumed, so the randomness decreases and ΔS is negative. This makes the term -TΔS positive, so ΔG becomes less negative as T increases. Hence most of the MxO lines slope upwards.
  • Change in slope: Each plot is a straight line except where a phase change (s → l or l → g) takes place. At that temperature the slope increases on the positive side. For example, in the Zn, ZnO plot, melting is shown by an abrupt change in the curve.
  • Decomposition of oxide: There is a point in a curve below which ΔG is negative (MxO is stable). Above this point, MxO will decompose on its own.
  • The diagram gives ΔfG0 values of the oxides of common metals and of some reducing agents (C, CO) at different temperatures, which makes interpretation easy.
  • Similar diagrams are drawn for sulphides and halides. They show why reduction of MxS is difficult: the ΔfG0 of MxS is not compensated by that of the oxidised reducing agent.

docs.title: Lines for carbon
docs.text:
• C → CO2: The number of gas molecules is unchanged, so ΔS is nearly zero and the line is almost horizontal.
  • C → CO: Gas molecules increase (1 mol O2 gives 2 mol CO), so ΔS is positive and the line slopes downwards. This is why carbon becomes a better reducing agent at high temperature.
  • CO → CO2: Gas molecules decrease, so the line slopes upwards like the metal lines.

docs.title: Limitations of Ellingham Diagram
docs.text:
• It only tells whether a reduction is possible or not, i.e., the tendency of reduction with a reducing agent. It is based only on thermodynamics and says nothing about the kinetics (rate) of the reduction.
  • The interpretation of ΔG0 is based on K (\(\Delta G^0 = -RT\ lnK\)). It is assumed that reactants and products are in equilibrium:
\[M_xO + A_{red} ⇌ xM + AO_{ox}\]
  • This is not always true because the reactants and products may be solids. However, it explains why reactions are sluggish when every species is in the solid state and smooth when the ore melts.

Note

ΔH and ΔS of a reaction remain nearly constant with temperature, so in \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) the dominant variable is T. However, ΔS depends greatly on the physical state. Entropy increases when a compound melts (s → l) or vaporises (l → g).

docs.title: Choice of Reducing Agent
docs.text:
• When a metal oxide is reduced, the reducing agent itself forms its oxide.
  • The role of the reducing agent is to provide a ΔG0 that is negative and large enough to make the sum of the two ΔG0 values (oxidation of the reducing agent + reduction of the metal oxide) negative.
  • During reduction, the metal oxide decomposes:
\[M_xO_{(s)} → xM_{(s\ or\ l)} + {1 \over 2}O_{2(g)}\]
  • This is the reverse of the formation of the oxide:
\[xM_{(s\ or\ l)} + {1 \over 2}O_{2(g)} → M_xO_{(s)}\ \ \ [\Delta G^0_{(M,\ M_xO)}]\]
  • At the same time, the reducing agent (C or CO) is oxidised:
\[C_{(s)} + {1 \over 2}O_{2(g)} → CO_{(g)}\ \ \ [\Delta G^0_{(C,\ CO)}]\] \[CO_{(g)} + {1 \over 2}O_{2(g)} → CO_{2(g)}\ \ \ [\Delta G^0_{(CO,\ CO_2)}]\] \[{1 \over 2}C_{(s)} + {1 \over 2}O_{2(g)} → {1 \over 2}CO_{2(g)}\ \ \ [{1 \over 2}\Delta G^0_{(C,\ CO_2)}]\]
  • Subtracting the metal oxide formation equation from each of these gives the actual reduction reactions:
\[M_xO_{(s)} + C_{(s)} → xM_{(s\ or\ l)} + CO_{(g)}\] \[M_xO_{(s)} + CO_{(g)} → xM_{(s\ or\ l)} + CO_{2(g)}\] \[M_xO_{(s)} + {1 \over 2}C_{(s)} → xM_{(s\ or\ l)} + {1 \over 2}CO_{2(g)}\]
  • The ΔrG0 of these reactions is obtained by a similar subtraction of the ΔfG0 values.

Conclusion

  • Heating favours a negative ΔrG0, so the temperature is chosen such that the sum of ΔrG0 of the two coupled reactions is negative.
  • On the Ellingham diagram, this is shown by the point of intersection of the two curves (the MxO curve and the curve for oxidation of the reducing substance).
  • Beyond that point, ΔrG0 for the combined process becomes negative.
  • An element whose line lies lower in the diagram can reduce the oxide of an element whose line lies higher. The larger the gap between the two lines, the easier the reduction.

docs.title: Solved Examples
docs.text:
Suggest a condition under which magnesium could reduce alumina.

The two equations are:

\[(a)\ {4 \over 3}Al + O_2 → {2 \over 3}Al_2O_3\] \[(b)\ 2Mg + O_2 → 2MgO\]

At the point of intersection of the Al2O3 and MgO curves (marked "A" in the Ellingham diagram), ΔG0 becomes zero for the reaction:

\[{2 \over 3}Al_2O_3 + 2Mg → 2MgO + {4 \over 3}Al\]

Below that temperature the MgO line lies lower, so magnesium can reduce alumina at temperatures below the point of intersection.

Although thermodynamically feasible, in practice magnesium metal is not used for the reduction of alumina in the metallurgy of aluminium. Why?

Magnesium can reduce alumina only in a certain temperature range given by the Ellingham diagram. Even in that range the gap between the two lines is small, and the temperature required is so high that the process would be uneconomic and technologically difficult. Magnesium is also a costlier metal.

Why is the reduction of a metal oxide easier if the metal formed is in liquid state at the temperature of reduction?

The entropy is higher if the metal is in liquid state than when it is in solid state. So the entropy change (ΔS) of the reduction is more positive when the metal formed is liquid and the metal oxide being reduced is solid. Thus the value of ΔG0 (\(\Delta H - T\Delta S\)) becomes more negative and the reduction becomes easier.

docs.title: Group 13 Elements | Chemical Properties
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss chemical properties of group 13 elements like oxidation states, inert pair effect, Lewis acid character, reactivity and the anomalous properties of boron.

docs.title: 1. Oxidation States and Trends in Chemical Reactivity
docs.text:
• Boron is very small, so the sum of its first three ionization enthalpies is very high. It cannot form B3+ ions and forms only covalent compounds.
  • From B to Al, the sum of the first three ionization enthalpies decreases considerably. So aluminium readily forms Al3+ ions and is a highly electropositive metal.
  • Ga, In and Tl show both +1 and +3 oxidation states.
  • The relative stability of the +1 oxidation state increases down the group:
\[Al\ <\ Ga\ <\ In\ <\ Tl\]
  • In thallium, the +1 oxidation state is predominant, whereas the +3 state is highly oxidising.
  • Compounds in the +1 oxidation state are more ionic than those in the +3 state.

docs.title: Inert Pair Effect
docs.text:
• Down the group, poor shielding by the intervening d and f orbitals increases the effective nuclear charge. This holds the ns electrons tightly and they do not readily take part in bonding.
  • As a result, only the p-orbital electron may be involved in bonding, giving the +1 oxidation state.
  • This reluctance of the ns2 electron pair to participate in bonding is called the inert pair effect.

docs.title: 2. Lewis Acid Character
docs.text:
• In the trivalent state, the central atom in a molecule such as BF3 has only six electrons around it. Such molecules are called electron deficient molecules.
  • Electron deficient molecules accept a pair of electrons to complete their octet and therefore behave as Lewis acids.
  • The tendency to behave as a Lewis acid decreases with increase in size down the group.
  • BCl3 easily accepts a lone pair of electrons from ammonia. The planar BCl3 becomes tetrahedral in the adduct:
\[BCl_3 + :NH_3 → BCl_3.NH_3\]
  • AlCl3 achieves stability by forming a dimer, Al2Cl6, through chlorine bridges. Each aluminium atom is tetrahedrally surrounded by four chlorine atoms.

docs.title: Hydrolysis of trihalides
docs.text:
• In the trivalent state, most compounds are covalent and are hydrolysed in water.
  • The trichlorides on hydrolysis form tetrahedral [M(OH)4]- species, in which M is sp3 hybridised.
  • Aluminium chloride in acidified aqueous solution forms the octahedral [Al(H2O)6]3+ ion. Here the 3d orbitals of Al are used and its hybridisation is sp3d2.

docs.title: 3. Reactivity Towards Air
docs.text:
• Crystalline boron is unreactive.
  • Aluminium forms a very thin oxide layer on its surface which protects the metal from further attack.
  • Amorphous boron and aluminium on heating in air form B2O3 and Al2O3 respectively. With dinitrogen at high temperature they form nitrides.
\[2E_{(s)} + 3O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2E_2O_{3(s)}\] \[2E_{(s)} + N_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2EN_{(s)}\] \[[E = element]\]
  • The nature of these oxides varies down the group:
Oxide Nature B2O3 Acidic (reacts with basic oxides to form metal borates) Al2O3, Ga2O3 Amphoteric In2O3, Tl2O3 Basic

docs.title: 4. Reactivity Towards Acids and Alkalies
docs.text:
• Boron does not react with acids and alkalies even at moderate temperature.
  • Aluminium dissolves in mineral acids as well as aqueous alkalies, and thus shows amphoteric character.
  • Aluminium dissolves in dilute HCl and liberates dihydrogen:
\[2Al_{(s)} + 6HCl_{(aq)} → 2Al^{3+}_{(aq)} + 6Cl^-_{(aq)} + 3H_{2(g)}\]
  • Concentrated nitric acid renders aluminium passive by forming a protective oxide layer on its surface.
  • Aluminium also reacts with aqueous alkali and liberates dihydrogen, forming sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate(III):
\[2Al_{(s)} + 2NaOH_{(aq)} + 6H_2O_{(l)} → 2Na^+[Al(OH)_4]^-_{(aq)} + 3H_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: 5. Reactivity Towards Halogens
docs.text:
• These elements react with halogens to form trihalides (except TlI3).
\[2E_{(s)} + 3X_{2(g)} → 2EX_{3(s)}\] \[[X = F,\ Cl,\ Br,\ I]\]

docs.title: 6. Important Trends and Anomalous Properties of Boron
docs.text:
• The trichlorides, tribromides and triiodides of all group 13 elements are covalent and are hydrolysed in water.
  • Species like tetrahedral [M(OH)4]- and octahedral [M(H2O)6]3+ exist in aqueous medium for all the elements except boron.
  • The monomeric trihalides, being electron deficient, are strong Lewis acids. Boron trifluoride easily reacts with Lewis bases such as NH3 to complete the octet around boron:
\[F_3B + :NH_3 → F_3B \leftarrow NH_3\]
  • Due to the absence of d orbitals, the maximum covalence of boron is 4. Since d orbitals are available with Al and the other elements, their maximum covalence can be expected to go beyond 4.
  • Most of the other metal halides (e.g., AlCl3) are dimerised through halogen bridging (e.g., Al2Cl6). The metal completes its octet by accepting electrons from the bridging halogen.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Standard electrode potential values, E0 for Al3+/Al is -1.66 V and that of Tl3+/Tl is +1.26 V. Predict about the formation of M3+ ion in solution and compare the electropositive character of the two metals.

  • The large negative E0 of Al3+/Al shows that aluminium has a high tendency to form Al3+(aq) ions.
  • The positive E0 of Tl3+/Tl shows that Tl3+ is unstable in solution and is a powerful oxidising agent. Thus Tl+ is more stable in solution than Tl3+.
  • Aluminium, being able to form +3 ions easily, is more electropositive than thallium.

White fumes appear around the bottle of anhydrous aluminium chloride. Give reason.

Anhydrous aluminium chloride is partially hydrolysed by atmospheric moisture, liberating HCl gas. Moist HCl appears white in colour, which is seen as white fumes.

Boron is unable to form BF63- ion. Explain.
