Boron has no d orbitals in its valence shell, so it cannot expand its octet. Its maximum covalence is 4 (as in BF4-), so it cannot bond with six fluoride ions.

Why does boron trifluoride behave as a Lewis acid?

In BF3, boron has only six electrons in its valence shell, so the molecule is electron deficient. It readily accepts a pair of electrons from a donor such as NH3 to complete its octet. A species that accepts an electron pair is a Lewis acid.

docs.title: Group 13 Elements | Important Compounds of Boron
Group 13 Elements | Important Compounds of Boron
docs.text: Some useful compounds of boron are borax, orthoboric acid and diborane. In this article, we will discuss their preparation, properties and structures, along with the uses of boron and aluminium.

docs.title: 1. Borax
docs.text:
• Borax is the most important compound of boron. It is a white crystalline solid with formula Na2B4O7.10H2O.
  • It actually contains the tetranuclear unit [B4O5(OH)4]2-, so its correct formula is Na2[B4O5(OH)4].8H2O.

docs.title: 1. Alkaline nature
docs.text:
• Borax dissolves in water to give an alkaline solution, because it forms the strong base NaOH and the weak acid H3BO3:
\[Na_2B_4O_7 + 7H_2O → 2NaOH + 4H_3BO_3\] \[[H_3BO_3 = Orthoboric\ acid]\]

docs.title: 2. Action of heat
docs.text:
• On heating, borax first loses water molecules and swells up. On further heating, it turns into a transparent liquid which solidifies into a glass-like material known as borax bead.
\[Na_2B_4O_7.10H_2O \xrightarrow{\Delta} Na_2B_4O_7 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2NaBO_2 + B_2O_3\] \[[NaBO_2 = Sodium\ metaborate,\ B_2O_3 = Boric\ anhydride]\]

docs.title: 3. Borax bead test
docs.text:
• The metaborates of many transition metals have characteristic colours. So the borax bead test is used to identify them in the laboratory.
  • For example, when borax is heated in a Bunsen burner flame with CoO on a loop of platinum wire, a blue coloured Co(BO2)2 bead is formed.

docs.title: 2. Orthoboric Acid
docs.text:
• Orthoboric acid, H3BO3 (or B(OH)3), is a white crystalline solid with a soapy touch.
  • It is sparingly soluble in cold water but highly soluble in hot water.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• It is prepared by acidifying an aqueous solution of borax:
\[Na_2B_4O_7 + 2HCl + 5H_2O → 2NaCl + 4B(OH)_3\]
  • It is also formed by the hydrolysis (reaction with water or dilute acid) of most boron compounds such as halides and hydrides.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text: • Boric acid has a layer structure in which planar BO3 units are joined together by hydrogen bonds (shown by dotted lines).

docs.title: 1. Acidic nature
docs.text:
• Boric acid is a weak monobasic acid.
  • It is not a protonic acid (it does not release H+ on its own). Instead, it acts as a Lewis acid by accepting electrons from a hydroxyl ion of water:
\[B(OH)_3 + 2HOH → [B(OH)_4]^- + H_3O^+\]

docs.title: 2. Action of heat
docs.text:
• On heating above 370 K, orthoboric acid forms metaboric acid (HBO2), which on further heating gives boric oxide (B2O3):
\[H_3BO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} HBO_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} B_2O_3\]

docs.title: 3. Diborane, B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>
docs.text: • Diborane is the simplest boron hydride known.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• By treating boron trifluoride with LiAlH4 in diethyl ether:
\[4BF_3 + 3LiAlH_4 → 2B_2H_6 + 3LiF + 3AlF_3\]
  • Laboratory method: Oxidation of sodium borohydride with iodine:
\[2NaBH_4 + I_2 → B_2H_6 + 2NaI + H_2\]
  • Industrial method: Reaction of BF3 with sodium hydride:
\[2BF_3 + 6NaH \xrightarrow{450\ K} B_2H_6 + 6NaF\]

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Diborane is a colourless, highly toxic gas with a boiling point of 180 K.
  • It catches fire spontaneously on exposure to air and burns in oxygen releasing an enormous amount of energy. Most of the higher boranes are also spontaneously flammable in air.
\[B_2H_6 + 3O_2 → B_2O_3 + 3H_2O;\ Δ_cH^0 = -1976\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • Boranes are readily hydrolysed by water to give boric acid:
\[B_2H_{6(g)} + 6H_2O_{(l)} → 2B(OH)_{3(aq)} + 6H_{2(g)}\]
  • Diborane undergoes cleavage reactions with Lewis bases (L) to give borane adducts, BH3.L:
\[B_2H_6 + 2NMe_3 → 2BH_3.NMe_3\] \[B_2H_6 + 2CO → 2BH_3.CO\]
  • Reaction with ammonia first gives B2H6.2NH3, formulated as [BH2(NH3)2]+[BH4]-. Further heating gives borazine, B3N3H6, known as "inorganic benzene" because of its ring structure with alternate BH and NH groups.
\[3B_2H_6 + 6NH_3 → 3[BH_2(NH_3)_2]^+[BH_4]^-\] \[3[BH_2(NH_3)_2]^+[BH_4]^- \xrightarrow{Heat} 2B_3N_3H_6 + 12H_2\]

docs.title: Structure of Diborane
docs.text:
• The four terminal hydrogen atoms and the two boron atoms lie in one plane.
  • Above and below this plane there are two bridging hydrogen atoms.
  • The four terminal B-H bonds (119 pm) are normal two-centre-two-electron (2c-2e) bonds.
  • The two bridge B-H-B bonds (134 pm) are different. Each is a three-centre-two-electron (3c-2e) bond, in which one pair of electrons holds three atoms (B, H, B) together. These are also called banana bonds.
  • Each boron atom is sp3 hybridised. Of its four sp3 hybrid orbitals, one is empty (shown by broken lines below). Two hybrids form terminal bonds, while the remaining two (one filled, one empty) take part in the bridges.

docs.title: Borohydrides
docs.text:
• Boron also forms a series of hydridoborates. The most important is the tetrahedral [BH4]- ion.
  • Lithium and sodium tetrahydridoborates, also known as borohydrides, are prepared by reacting metal hydrides with B2H6 in diethyl ether:
\[2MH + B_2H_6 → 2M^+[BH_4]^-\] \[[M = Li\ or\ Na]\]
  • Both LiBH4 and NaBH4 are used as reducing agents in organic synthesis and as starting materials for preparing other metal borohydrides.

docs.title: 4. Uses of Boron and its Compounds
docs.text:
• Boron is an extremely hard refractory solid with high melting point, low density and very low electrical conductivity.
  • Boron fibres are used in making bullet-proof vests and light composite materials for aircraft.
  • The boron-10 (10B) isotope has a high ability to absorb neutrons. So metal borides are used in the nuclear industry as protective shields and control rods.
  • Borax and boric acid are mainly used in the manufacture of heat resistant glasses (e.g., Pyrex), glass-wool and fibreglass.
  • Borax is used as a flux for soldering metals, for heat, scratch and stain resistant glazed coatings on earthenware, and as a constituent of medicinal soaps.
  • An aqueous solution of orthoboric acid is used as a mild antiseptic.

docs.title: 5. Uses of Aluminium and its Compounds
docs.text:
• Aluminium is a bright silvery-white metal with high tensile strength and high electrical and thermal conductivity.
  • On a weight-to-weight basis, the electrical conductivity of aluminium is twice that of copper.
  • It forms alloys with Cu, Mn, Mg, Si and Zn.
  • Aluminium and its alloys can be shaped into pipes, tubes, rods, wires, plates and foils. They are used in packing, utensil making, construction, aeroplane and transportation industries.
  • The use of aluminium and its compounds for domestic purposes is now much reduced because of their toxic nature.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Why is boric acid considered as a weak acid?

Boric acid cannot release H+ ions on its own. It accepts an OH- ion from a water molecule to complete its octet, and in turn releases an H+ (as H3O+) ion. Since very few H+ ions are produced this way, it is a weak acid.

Explain the structures of diborane and boric acid.

  • Diborane: Two boron atoms and four terminal hydrogen atoms lie in one plane; two bridging hydrogen atoms lie above and below this plane. The four terminal B-H bonds are normal 2c-2e bonds, while the two B-H-B bridge bonds are 3c-2e (banana) bonds. Each boron is sp3 hybridised.
  • Boric acid: It has a layer structure in which planar BO3 units are linked to each other by hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen bonding is the reason boric acid is polymeric.

docs.title: Group 13 Elements | Physical and Atomic Properties
Group 13 Elements | Physical and Atomic Properties
Introduction to p-Block Elements
docs.text:
• In p-block elements, the last electron enters the outermost p orbital. Since a set of p orbitals can hold a maximum of six electrons, there are six groups of p-block elements, numbered 13 to 18.
  • Boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine and helium head these groups.
  • The general valence shell electronic configuration of p-block elements is ns2np1-6 (except helium, which is 1s2).
  • The inner core of the electronic configuration differs from element to element. This difference strongly influences both physical properties (atomic and ionic radii, ionisation enthalpy, etc.) and chemical properties.

docs.title: Oxidation states of p-block elements
docs.text:
• The maximum oxidation state shown by a p-block element is equal to its total number of valence electrons (sum of s and p electrons). This is called the group oxidation state.
  • Many p-block elements also show oxidation states which differ from the group oxidation state by two units.
  • In the boron, carbon and nitrogen families, the group oxidation state is the most stable state for the lighter elements. For the heavier elements, the oxidation state two units less than the group oxidation state becomes progressively more stable. This is attributed to the inert pair effect.
Group 13 14 15 16 17 18 General electronic configuration ns2np1 ns2np2 ns2np3 ns2np4 ns2np5 ns2np6 (1s2 for He) First member of the group B C N O F He Group oxidation state +3 +4 +5 +6 +7 +8 Other oxidation states +1 +2, -4 +3, -3 +4, +2, -2 +5, +3, +1, -1 +6, +4, +2

docs.title: Metallic and non-metallic character
docs.text:
• Non-metals and metalloids exist only in the p-block. Non-metallic character decreases down a group; the heaviest element of each p-block group is the most metallic.
  • Non-metals have higher ionisation enthalpies and electronegativities than metals. So, non-metals readily form anions while metals form cations.
  • Compounds of highly reactive non-metals with highly reactive metals are generally ionic, whereas compounds formed between non-metals are largely covalent.
  • Non-metal oxides are acidic or neutral, whereas metal oxides are basic.

docs.title: How the first member differs
docs.text:
The first member of each p-block group differs from the rest of its group in two major ways:

  • Size: It is much smaller, so all size-dependent properties differ.
  • Absence of d orbitals: Second period elements have no d orbitals, so their maximum covalence is four (using one 2s and three 2p orbitals). Third period elements (3s23pn) have vacant 3d orbitals and can expand their covalence above four. For example, boron forms only [BF4]-, whereas aluminium forms [AlF6]3-.
  • pπ-pπ bonding: The first member can form strong pπ-pπ multiple bonds with itself (C=C, C≡C, N≡N) and with other second period elements (C=O, C=N, C≡N, N=O). Heavier elements form π bonds using d orbitals (dπ-pπ or dπ-dπ), which are weaker.
  • Heavier elements can have higher coordination numbers in the same oxidation state. For example, in the +5 state, N forms NO3- (three-coordinate) while P forms PO43- (four-coordinate).

docs.title: Introduction to Group 13 Elements
docs.text:
• The elements of group 13 are Boron(B), Aluminium(Al), Gallium(Ga), Indium(In) and Thallium(Tl). This group is known as the boron family.
  • The group shows a wide variation in properties. Boron is a typical non-metal, aluminium is a metal with many chemical similarities to boron, and gallium, indium and thallium are almost exclusively metallic.

docs.title: Occurrence
docs.text:
• Boron is a fairly rare element (less than 0.0001% by mass of the earth's crust). It mainly occurs as orthoboric acid (H3BO3), borax (Na2B4O7.10H2O) and kernite (Na2B4O7.4H2O).
  • In India, borax occurs in Puga Valley (Ladakh) and Sambhar Lake (Rajasthan).
  • Boron has two isotopes: 10B (19%) and 11B (81%).
  • Aluminium is the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element in the earth's crust (8.3% by mass), after oxygen (45.5%) and silicon (27.7%).
  • Bauxite (Al2O3.2H2O) and cryolite (Na3AlF6) are the important minerals of aluminium.
  • Gallium, indium and thallium are less abundant in nature.

docs.title: 1. Electronic Configuration
docs.text:
• General valence shell electronic configuration: ns2np1
  • Boron and aluminium have a noble gas core. Gallium and indium have a noble gas core plus 10 d-electrons, and thallium has a noble gas core plus 14 f-electrons and 10 d-electrons.
  • These more complex inner cores affect the properties of the heavier members.

docs.title: 2. Atomic Radii
docs.text:
• Atomic radius is expected to increase down the group as one extra shell of electrons is added at each step.
  • Exception: The atomic radius of Ga (135 pm) is less than that of Al (143 pm).

Reason

Gallium has 10 additional d-electrons in its inner core. d-electrons have poor screening effect, so the outer electrons of gallium experience a larger effective nuclear charge. As a result, the atomic radius of gallium is smaller than that of aluminium.

docs.title: 3. Ionization Enthalpy
docs.text:
• Ionization enthalpy does not decrease smoothly down the group.
  • The decrease from B to Al is due to increase in atomic size.
  • The discontinuity between Al and Ga, and between In and Tl, is due to the poor screening effect of d- and f-electrons, which fail to compensate for the increase in nuclear charge.
  • As expected, \(Δ_iH_1 < Δ_iH_2 < Δ_iH_3\). The sum of the first three ionization enthalpies is very high for every element of the group.

docs.title: 4. Electronegativity
docs.text: • Down the group, electronegativity first decreases from B to Al and then increases marginally. This is due to the irregular variation in atomic size of these elements.

docs.title: Physical Properties of Group 13 Elements
docs.text:
• Boron is non-metallic. It is an extremely hard, black coloured solid and exists in many allotropic forms.
  • Boron has an unusually high melting point due to its very strong crystalline lattice.
  • The rest of the members are soft metals with low melting points and high electrical conductivity.
  • Gallium has an unusually low melting point (303 K) and can exist as a liquid in summer. Its high boiling point (2676 K) makes it useful for measuring high temperatures.
  • Density increases down the group from boron to thallium.
