docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
How would you explain the lower atomic radius of Ga as compared to Al?

Gallium has 10 electrons in its inner 3d subshell, which aluminium does not have. d-electrons shield the outer electrons poorly from the nuclear charge. So the valence electrons of gallium feel a higher effective nuclear charge and are pulled closer to the nucleus. Hence the atomic radius of Ga (135 pm) is less than that of Al (143 pm).

Why does gallium, a metal, remain liquid on a hot summer day, and why is it used in high temperature thermometers?

Gallium has an unusually low melting point of 303 K, so it melts at summer temperatures. Its boiling point is very high (2676 K), so it stays liquid over a very wide range of temperature. This makes it useful for measuring high temperatures.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Discuss the pattern of variation in the oxidation states from B to Tl.

  • All group 13 elements have the valence configuration ns2np1, so the group oxidation state is +3.
  • Boron and aluminium show only the +3 oxidation state.
  • Ga, In and Tl show both +1 and +3 oxidation states. Due to the inert pair effect, the stability of the +1 state increases down the group:
\[Al\ <\ Ga\ <\ In\ <\ Tl\]
  • In thallium, +1 is the predominant oxidation state and Tl(III) compounds are strong oxidising agents.

How can you explain higher stability of BCl3 as compared to TlCl3?

Boron has no d or f electrons in its inner core, so both of its 2s electrons take part in bonding and the +3 state is stable. In thallium, poor shielding by the 4f and 5d electrons holds the 6s2 pair tightly (inert pair effect). So Tl prefers the +1 state, and TlCl3 tends to change into the more stable TlCl. Hence BCl3 is more stable than TlCl3.

Consider the compounds, BCl3 and CCl4. How will they behave with water? Justify.

  • BCl3 is electron deficient. Boron accepts a lone pair from the oxygen of water, and the compound is hydrolysed to boric acid:
\[BCl_3 + 3H_2O → B(OH)_3 + 3HCl\]
  • In CCl4, carbon already has a complete octet and has no vacant d orbitals to accept a lone pair from water. So CCl4 is not hydrolysed by water.

Is boric acid a protic acid? Explain.

No. Boric acid does not donate H+ ions by itself. It acts as a Lewis acid by accepting an OH- ion from water, which releases H3O+:

\[B(OH)_3 + 2HOH → [B(OH)_4]^- + H_3O^+\]

Explain what happens when boric acid is heated.

On heating above 370 K, orthoboric acid first forms metaboric acid, which on stronger heating forms boric oxide:

\[H_3BO_3 \xrightarrow{370\ K} HBO_2 + H_2O\] \[2HBO_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} B_2O_3 + H_2O\]

Describe the shapes of BF3 and BH4-. Assign the hybridisation of boron in these species.

  • BF3: Boron forms three bond pairs and has no lone pair. It is sp2 hybridised and the molecule is trigonal planar (bond angle 120°).
  • BH4-: Boron forms four bond pairs (one of them by accepting H-). It is sp3 hybridised and the ion is tetrahedral (bond angle 109.5°).

Write reactions to justify amphoteric nature of aluminium.

Aluminium dissolves both in acids and in alkalies, liberating dihydrogen:

\[2Al_{(s)} + 6HCl_{(aq)} → 2Al^{3+}_{(aq)} + 6Cl^-_{(aq)} + 3H_{2(g)}\] \[2Al_{(s)} + 2NaOH_{(aq)} + 6H_2O_{(l)} → 2Na^+[Al(OH)_4]^-_{(aq)} + 3H_{2(g)}\]

What are electron deficient compounds? Are BCl3 and SiCl4 electron deficient species? Explain.

  • Compounds in which the central atom has less than eight electrons in its valence shell are called electron deficient compounds.
  • BCl3 is electron deficient: boron has only six electrons around it and acts as a Lewis acid.
  • SiCl4 is not electron deficient: silicon has a complete octet (it is an electron precise molecule). However, it can still accept lone pairs because silicon has vacant 3d orbitals.

Suggest reasons why the B-F bond lengths in BF3 (130 pm) and BF4- (143 pm) differ.

  • In BF3, boron is sp2 hybridised and has a vacant 2p orbital. A filled 2p orbital of fluorine donates electron density into it (pπ-pπ back bonding). This gives the B-F bond partial double bond character, so it is shorter (130 pm).
  • In BF4-, boron is sp3 hybridised and has no vacant p orbital, so no back bonding is possible. The B-F bonds are pure single bonds and hence longer (143 pm).

If B-Cl bond has a dipole moment, explain why BCl3 molecule has zero dipole moment.

BCl3 is trigonal planar with three identical B-Cl bonds at 120° to each other. The three bond dipoles are equal in magnitude and point symmetrically, so they cancel each other. The resultant dipole moment is zero.

Aluminium trifluoride is insoluble in anhydrous HF but dissolves on addition of NaF. Aluminium trifluoride precipitates out of the resulting solution when gaseous BF3 is bubbled through. Give reasons.

  • Anhydrous HF is a covalent, hydrogen bonded liquid and provides almost no free F- ions, so AlF3 does not dissolve in it.
  • NaF supplies F- ions, which form the soluble complex Na3[AlF6]:
\[AlF_3 + 3NaF → Na_3[AlF_6]\]
  • Boron, being smaller and more electron deficient, has a stronger tendency to form BF4-. BF3 removes F- from the complex and AlF3 precipitates:
\[Na_3[AlF_6] + 3BF_3 → 3NaBF_4 + AlF_3↓\]

What happens when (a) Borax is heated strongly, (b) Boric acid is added to water, (c) Aluminium is treated with dilute NaOH, (d) BF3 is reacted with ammonia?

(a) Borax loses water, swells up and finally forms a glassy bead of sodium metaborate and boric anhydride:

\[Na_2B_4O_7.10H_2O \xrightarrow{\Delta} Na_2B_4O_7 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2NaBO_2 + B_2O_3\]

(b) Boric acid accepts OH- from water and acts as a weak monobasic acid:

\[B(OH)_3 + 2HOH → [B(OH)_4]^- + H_3O^+\]

(c) Dihydrogen is liberated and sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate(III) is formed:

\[2Al + 2NaOH + 6H_2O → 2Na^+[Al(OH)_4]^- + 3H_2\]

(d) BF3 (Lewis acid) accepts a lone pair from NH3 (Lewis base) to form an adduct:

\[F_3B + :NH_3 → F_3B \leftarrow NH_3\]

What happens when hydrated alumina is treated with aqueous NaOH solution?

Alumina is amphoteric, so it dissolves in NaOH to form soluble sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate(III):

\[Al_2O_{3(s)} + 2NaOH_{(aq)} + 3H_2O_{(l)} → 2Na[Al(OH)_4]_{(aq)}\]

Give reasons: (i) Conc. HNO3 can be transported in aluminium container. (ii) A mixture of dilute NaOH and aluminium pieces is used to open drain. (iii) Aluminium alloys are used to make aircraft body. (iv) Aluminium utensils should not be kept in water overnight. (v) Aluminium wire is used to make transmission cables.

(i) Concentrated HNO3 makes aluminium passive by forming a thin protective layer of Al2O3 on its surface, which stops further reaction.

(ii) Aluminium reacts with NaOH to liberate H2 gas with evolution of heat. The pressure of the gas and the heat help loosen and clear the clogging matter.

(iii) Aluminium alloys are light, strong and resistant to corrosion, which are ideal properties for an aircraft body.

(iv) Aluminium slowly reacts with water and dissolved oxygen (and salts in water) on long contact. The oxide/hydroxide formed dissolves partly, which corrodes the utensil and introduces aluminium, a toxic metal, into the water.

(v) On a weight-to-weight basis, aluminium conducts electricity about twice as well as copper. It is also light, cheap and corrosion resistant.

In some of the reactions thallium resembles aluminium, whereas in others it resembles group 1 metals. Support this statement by giving some evidences.

  • Like aluminium: Thallium shows the +3 oxidation state and forms compounds such as TlCl3 and Tl2O3, and complexes like [TlF6]3-, similar to AlCl3, Al2O3 and [AlF6]3-.
  • Like group 1 metals: Due to the inert pair effect, its most stable state is +1, like alkali metals. Tl2O and TlOH are strongly basic, and TlOH is soluble in water, just like NaOH and KOH. Tl+ compounds such as TlCl are largely ionic.

When metal X is treated with sodium hydroxide, a white precipitate (A) is obtained, which is soluble in excess of NaOH to give soluble complex (B). Compound (A) is soluble in dilute HCl to form compound (C). The compound (A) when heated strongly gives (D), which is used to extract metal. Identify (X), (A), (B), (C) and (D). Write suitable equations to support their identities.

  • X = Al, A = Al(OH)3, B = Na[Al(OH)4], C = AlCl3, D = Al2O3
\[Al^{3+} + 3OH^- → Al(OH)_3↓\ (white)\] \[Al(OH)_3 + NaOH → Na[Al(OH)_4]\] \[Al(OH)_3 + 3HCl → AlCl_3 + 3H_2O\] \[2Al(OH)_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} Al_2O_3 + 3H_2O\]
  • Alumina (D) is electrolysed to extract aluminium metal.

What do you understand by inert pair effect?

In the heavier p-block elements, poor shielding by the inner d and f electrons increases the effective nuclear charge on the ns2 electrons. These electrons are held tightly and do not participate in bonding. This reluctance of the ns2 pair to take part in bonding is called the inert pair effect. It makes the oxidation state two units less than the group oxidation state more stable down the group (e.g., Tl+ over Tl3+).

A certain salt X gives the following results. (i) Its aqueous solution is alkaline to litmus. (ii) It swells up to a glassy material Y on strong heating. (iii) When conc. H2SO4 is added to a hot solution of X, white crystal of an acid Z separates out. Write equations for all the above reactions and identify X, Y and Z.

  • X = Borax (Na2B4O7.10H2O), Y = glassy mass of NaBO2 + B2O3, Z = Orthoboric acid (H3BO3)
\[(i)\ Na_2B_4O_7 + 7H_2O → 2NaOH + 4H_3BO_3\] \[(ii)\ Na_2B_4O_7.10H_2O \xrightarrow{\Delta} Na_2B_4O_7 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2NaBO_2 + B_2O_3\] \[(iii)\ Na_2B_4O_7 + H_2SO_4 + 5H_2O → Na_2SO_4 + 4H_3BO_3\]

Write balanced equations for: (i) BF3 + LiH → (ii) B2H6 + H2O → (iii) NaH + B2H6 → (iv) H3BO3 on heating (v) Al + NaOH → (vi) B2H6 + NH3 →

\[(i)\ 8BF_3 + 6LiH → B_2H_6 + 6LiBF_4\] \[(ii)\ B_2H_6 + 6H_2O → 2B(OH)_3 + 6H_2\] \[(iii)\ 2NaH + B_2H_6 → 2Na^+[BH_4]^-\] \[(iv)\ H_3BO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} HBO_2 + H_2O;\ \ 2HBO_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} B_2O_3 + H_2O\] \[(v)\ 2Al + 2NaOH + 6H_2O → 2Na^+[Al(OH)_4]^- + 3H_2\] \[(vi)\ 3B_2H_6 + 6NH_3 → 3[BH_2(NH_3)_2]^+[BH_4]^- \xrightarrow{Heat} 2B_3N_3H_6 + 12H_2\]

docs.title: Multiple Choice Questions
docs.text:
An aqueous solution of borax is (a) neutral (b) amphoteric (c) basic (d) acidic

(c) basic. Borax hydrolyses to give the strong base NaOH and the weak acid H3BO3, so the solution is alkaline.

Boric acid is polymeric due to (a) its acidic nature (b) the presence of hydrogen bonds (c) its monobasic nature (d) its geometry

(b) the presence of hydrogen bonds. Planar BO3 units are linked into layers by hydrogen bonds.

The type of hybridisation of boron in diborane is (a) sp (b) sp2 (c) sp3 (d) dsp2

(c) sp3. Each boron atom uses four sp3 hybrid orbitals, one of which is empty.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• The existence of an element in two or more forms having different physical properties but similar chemical properties is called allotropy.
  • Carbon exhibits many allotropic forms, both crystalline and amorphous. This is possible because of its property of catenation and its ability to form pπ-pπ bonds.
  • Diamond and graphite are the two well-known crystalline forms of carbon.
  • A third form, fullerenes, was discovered in 1985 by H.W. Kroto, E. Smalley and R.F. Curl, who were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1996 for this discovery.

docs.title: 1. Diamond
docs.text:
• Diamond has a crystalline lattice in which each carbon atom is sp3 hybridised and linked to four other carbon atoms in a tetrahedral fashion.
  • The C-C bond length is 154 pm.
  • The structure extends in space to form a rigid three-dimensional network of carbon atoms, with directional covalent bonds throughout the lattice.
  • It is very difficult to break this extended covalent bonding, so diamond is the hardest substance on earth.

docs.title: Uses of diamond
docs.text:
• As an abrasive for sharpening hard tools.
  • In making dies and in the manufacture of tungsten filaments for electric light bulbs.
  • As a precious stone in jewellery. It is measured in carats (1 carat = 200 mg).

docs.title: 2. Graphite
docs.text:
• Graphite has a layered structure. Each layer is made up of planar hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.
  • The C-C bond length within a layer is 141.5 pm, and the distance between two layers is 340 pm.
  • The layers are held together by weak van der Waals forces.
  • Each carbon atom in a hexagonal ring is sp2 hybridised and forms three sigma bonds with three neighbouring carbon atoms. The fourth electron forms a π bond.
  • These π electrons are delocalised over the whole sheet. Since the electrons are mobile, graphite conducts electricity along the sheet.
  • Graphite cleaves easily between the layers, so it is very soft and slippery.

docs.title: Uses of graphite
docs.text:
• As a dry lubricant in machines running at high temperature, where oil cannot be used.
  • Graphite fibres embedded in plastic form high strength, lightweight composites used in tennis rackets, fishing rods, aircraft and canoes.
  • Being a good conductor, it is used for electrodes in batteries and industrial electrolysis.
  • Crucibles made from graphite are inert to dilute acids and alkalies.

docs.title: Diamond vs Graphite
docs.text: Property Diamond Graphite Hybridisation sp<sup>3</sup> sp<sup>2</sup> Structure Three-dimensional tetrahedral network Layers of hexagonal rings C-C bond length 154 pm 141.5 pm (within a layer) Hardness Hardest natural substance Soft and slippery Electrical conduction Non-conductor (no free electrons) Good conductor (delocalised π electrons) Density 3.51 g cm<sup>-3</sup> 2.22 g cm<sup>-3</sup>

docs.title: 3. Fullerenes
docs.text:
• Fullerenes are made by heating graphite in an electric arc in the presence of inert gases such as helium or argon.
  • The sooty material formed by condensation of vaporised Cn small molecules consists mainly of C60, with a smaller quantity of C70 and traces of fullerenes with an even number of carbon atoms up to 350 or above.
  • Fullerenes are the only pure form of carbon, because they have a smooth structure without any 'dangling' bonds.
  • Fullerenes are cage-like molecules. The C60 molecule has a shape like a soccer ball and is called Buckminsterfullerene. Spherical fullerenes are also called bucky balls.

docs.title: Structure of C<sub>60</sub>
docs.text:
• It contains twenty six-membered rings and twelve five-membered rings.
  • A six-membered ring is fused with six or five membered rings, but a five-membered ring can fuse only with six-membered rings.
  • All the carbon atoms are equal and are sp2 hybridised. Each carbon forms three sigma bonds with three other carbon atoms. The remaining electron on each carbon is delocalised in molecular orbitals, which gives the molecule aromatic character.
  • The ball-shaped molecule has 60 vertices, each occupied by one carbon atom.
  • It contains both single and double bonds, with C-C distances of 143.5 pm and 138.3 pm respectively.

docs.title: Thermodynamic Stability of Allotropes
docs.text:
• Graphite is the thermodynamically most stable allotrope of carbon. Therefore, ΔfH0 of graphite is taken as zero.
  • The ΔfH0 values of diamond and fullerene (C60) are 1.90 and 38.1 kJ mol-1 respectively.

docs.title: Amorphous Forms of Carbon
docs.text:
• Carbon black, coke and charcoal are impure forms of graphite or fullerenes.
  • Carbon black is obtained by burning hydrocarbons in a limited supply of air. It is used as a black pigment in black ink and as a filler in automobile tyres.
  • Charcoal and coke are obtained by heating wood or coal respectively at high temperatures in the absence of air.
  • Being highly porous, activated charcoal is used to adsorb poisonous gases, in water filters to remove organic contaminants, and in air conditioning systems to control odour.
  • Coke is used as a fuel and largely as a reducing agent in metallurgy.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Diamond is covalent, yet it has high melting point. Why?

Diamond has a three-dimensional network of strong C-C covalent bonds extending throughout the crystal. To melt diamond, a very large number of these strong bonds must be broken, which needs a lot of energy. Hence its melting point is very high.

Explain the difference in properties of diamond and graphite on the basis of their structures.

  • In diamond, each carbon is sp3 hybridised and bonded to four others in a rigid 3D network. All electrons are localised in bonds. So diamond is extremely hard and a non-conductor of electricity.
  • In graphite, each carbon is sp2 hybridised and bonded to three others in flat hexagonal layers. The fourth electron is delocalised over the layer, so graphite conducts electricity. The layers are held by weak van der Waals forces and slide over each other, so graphite is soft and slippery.

Thermodynamically the most stable form of carbon is (a) diamond (b) graphite (c) fullerenes (d) coal

(b) graphite. Its ΔfH0 is taken as zero, while diamond (1.90 kJ mol-1) and C60 (38.1 kJ mol-1) have positive values.

docs.title: Group 14 Elements | Chemical Properties
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss chemical properties of group 14 elements like oxidation states, reactivity towards oxygen, water and halogens, and the anomalous behaviour of carbon.

docs.title: 1. Oxidation States and Trends in Chemical Reactivity
docs.text:
• Group 14 elements have four electrons in the outermost shell. Their common oxidation states are +4 and +2. Carbon also exhibits negative oxidation states.
  • The sum of the first four ionization enthalpies is very high, so compounds in the +4 oxidation state are generally covalent.
  • In the heavier members, the tendency to show the +2 oxidation state increases in the order:
\[Ge\ <\ Sn\ <\ Pb\]
  • This is due to the inability of the ns2 electrons of the valence shell to participate in bonding (inert pair effect).

docs.title: Relative stability of +4 and +2 states
docs.text: Element Behaviour C, Si Mostly show the +4 oxidation state Ge Forms stable compounds in the +4 state and only a few in the +2 state Sn Forms compounds in both states; Sn(II) is a reducing agent Pb Pb(II) compounds are stable; Pb(IV) compounds are strong oxidising agents

docs.title: Electron precise molecules and expansion of covalence
docs.text:
• In the tetravalent state, the central atom (e.g., carbon in CCl4) has eight electrons around it. Such electron precise molecules are not normally expected to act as electron acceptors or donors.
  • Carbon cannot exceed a covalence of 4. The other elements of the group can, because they have d orbitals.
  • Due to this, their halides undergo hydrolysis and tend to form complexes by accepting electron pairs from donor species. For example, in SiF62-, [GeCl6]2- and [Sn(OH)6]2-, the central atom is sp3d2 hybridised.

docs.title: 2. Reactivity Towards Oxygen
docs.text:
• All members form oxides when heated in oxygen. There are two main types: monoxides (MO) and dioxides (MO2). SiO exists only at high temperature.
  • Oxides in higher oxidation states are generally more acidic than those in lower oxidation states.
Type Acidic Amphoteric Neutral Dioxides CO2, SiO2, GeO2 SnO2, PbO2 - Monoxides GeO SnO, PbO CO

docs.title: 3. Reactivity Towards Water
docs.text:
• Carbon, silicon and germanium are not affected by water.
  • Tin decomposes steam to form the dioxide and dihydrogen:
\[Sn + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{\Delta} SnO_2 + 2H_2\]
  • Lead is unaffected by water, probably because of a protective oxide film on its surface.

docs.title: 4. Reactivity Towards Halogens
docs.text:
• These elements form halides of formula MX2 and MX4 (X = F, Cl, Br, I).
  • Except carbon, all members react directly with halogens under suitable conditions.
  • Most MX4 are covalent. The central atom is sp3 hybridised and the molecule is tetrahedral. SnF4 and PbF4 are exceptions; they are ionic.
  • PbI4 does not exist, because the energy released in forming Pb-I bonds is not enough to unpair the 6s2 electrons and excite one of them to a higher orbital to give four unpaired electrons.
  • The heavier members Ge to Pb also form dihalides, MX2. The stability of dihalides increases down the group. Considering thermal and chemical stability, GeX4 is more stable than GeX2, whereas PbX2 is more stable than PbX4.

docs.title: Hydrolysis of tetrachlorides
docs.text:
• Except CCl4, all tetrachlorides are easily hydrolysed by water, because the central atom can accommodate a lone pair from the oxygen of water in its vacant d orbital.
  • For example, SiCl4 first accepts a lone pair from a water molecule in a d orbital of Si and loses HCl. Repetition of this step finally gives silicic acid, Si(OH)4:
\[SiCl_4 + H_2O → SiCl_3(OH) + HCl\] \[SiCl_3(OH) + 3H_2O → Si(OH)_4 + 3HCl\] \[Overall:\ SiCl_4 + 4H_2O → Si(OH)_4 + 4HCl\]
  • CCl4 is not hydrolysed because carbon has no d orbitals to accept the lone pair.

docs.title: 5. Important Trends and Anomalous Behaviour of Carbon
docs.text: Like the first member of other groups, carbon differs from the rest of its group. This is due to its smaller size, higher electronegativity, higher ionisation enthalpy and the unavailability of d orbitals.

docs.title: 1. Maximum covalence of four
docs.text: • Carbon has only s and p orbitals available for bonding, so it can accommodate only four pairs of electrons. Its maximum covalence is four, whereas the other members can expand their covalence due to d orbitals.

docs.title: 2. pπ-pπ multiple bonding
docs.text:
• Carbon has a unique ability to form pπ-pπ multiple bonds with itself and with other atoms of small size and high electronegativity. Examples: C=C, C≡C, C=O, C=S and C≡N.
  • Heavier elements do not form pπ-pπ bonds because their atomic orbitals are too large and diffuse for effective overlap.

docs.title: 3. Catenation
docs.text:
• The tendency of atoms of an element to link with one another through covalent bonds to form chains and rings is called catenation.
  • Carbon shows catenation to the greatest extent because C-C bonds are very strong.
  • Down the group, size increases and electronegativity decreases, so the tendency to catenate decreases. Lead does not show catenation.
\[Order\ of\ catenation:\ C >> Si > Ge \approx Sn\] Bond Bond enthalpy / kJ mol-1 C-C 348 Si-Si 297 Ge-Ge 260 Sn-Sn 240
  • Due to catenation and pπ-pπ bond formation, carbon is able to show allotropic forms.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Select the member(s) of group 14 that (i) forms the most acidic dioxide, (ii) is commonly found in +2 oxidation state, (iii) used as semiconductor.

(i) Carbon (CO2)

(ii) Lead

(iii) Silicon and germanium

[SiF6]2- is known whereas [SiCl6]2- not. Give possible reasons.

The main reasons are:

  • Six large chloride ions cannot be accommodated around the small Si4+ ion, whereas six small fluoride ions can.
  • The interaction between a lone pair of the chloride ion and Si4+ is not very strong.

Discuss the pattern of variation in the oxidation states from C to Pb.

  • All members have the configuration ns2np2 and show +4 and +2 oxidation states. Carbon also shows negative oxidation states (e.g., -4 in CH4).
  • C and Si show mainly +4. Going down the group, the inert pair effect makes the +2 state more stable in the order Ge < Sn < Pb.
  • Thus, Ge(IV) is more stable than Ge(II), Sn shows both states (Sn2+ is reducing), and Pb(II) is more stable than Pb(IV) (Pb4+ is oxidising).

Rationalise the given statements and give chemical reactions: (i) Lead(II) chloride reacts with Cl2 to give PbCl4. (ii) Lead(IV) chloride is highly unstable towards heat. (iii) Lead is known not to form an iodide, PbI4.

(i) Because of the inert pair effect, Pb(II) is more stable than Pb(IV), so PbCl2 reacts with Cl2 only with difficulty. PbCl4 formed is unstable:

\[PbCl_2 + Cl_2 → PbCl_4\]

(ii) Pb(IV) tends to change to the more stable Pb(II). On heating, PbCl4 decomposes:

\[PbCl_4 \xrightarrow{\Delta} PbCl_2 + Cl_2\]

(iii) Pb4+ is a strong oxidising agent and I- is a strong reducing agent, so they cannot coexist. Also, the Pb-I bond formed does not release enough energy to unpair the 6s2 electrons. Hence PbI4 does not exist.

What do you understand by catenation?

Catenation is the ability of atoms of an element to link with one another through covalent bonds to form long chains or rings. Carbon shows it to the maximum extent because of its strong C-C bonds (348 kJ mol-1). The tendency decreases down the group: C >> Si > Ge ≈ Sn, and Pb does not show catenation.

Elements of group 14 (a) exhibit oxidation state of +4 only (b) exhibit oxidation state of +2 and +4 (c) form M2- and M4+ ion (d) form M2+ and M4+ ions

(b) exhibit oxidation state of +2 and +4.

docs.title: Group 14 Elements | Important Compounds of Carbon and Silicon
Group 14 Elements | Important Compounds of Carbon and Silicon
docs.text: The two important oxides of carbon are carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO2). In this article, we will also discuss silicon dioxide, silicones, silicates and zeolites.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Direct oxidation of carbon in a limited supply of oxygen or air:
\[2C_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2CO_{(g)}\]
  • Laboratory method: On a small scale, pure CO is prepared by dehydration of formic acid with concentrated H2SO4 at 373 K:
\[HCOOH \xrightarrow[conc.\ H_2SO_4]{373\ K} H_2O + CO\]
  • Commercial method: By passing steam over hot coke. The mixture of CO and H2 produced is called water gas or synthesis gas:
\[C_{(s)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow{473-1273\ K} \underbrace{CO_{(g)} + H_{2(g)}}_{Water\ gas}\]
  • When air is used instead of steam, a mixture of CO and N2 called producer gas is formed:
\[2C_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} + 4N_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{1273\ K} \underbrace{2CO_{(g)} + 4N_{2(g)}}_{Producer\ gas}\]
  • Water gas and producer gas are very important industrial fuels. The CO in them burns further to CO2 with liberation of heat.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• CO is a colourless, odourless and almost water-insoluble gas.
  • It is a powerful reducing agent and reduces almost all metal oxides except those of the alkali and alkaline earth metals, aluminium and a few transition metals. This is used in the extraction of many metals from their oxide ores:
\[Fe_2O_{3(s)} + 3CO_{(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2Fe_{(s)} + 3CO_{2(g)}\] \[ZnO_{(s)} + CO_{(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} Zn_{(s)} + CO_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• In the CO molecule, there is one sigma bond and two π bonds between carbon and oxygen:
\[:C \equiv O:\]
  • Because of the lone pair on carbon, CO acts as a donor and reacts with certain metals on heating to form metal carbonyls.

docs.title: Poisonous nature of CO
docs.text:
• CO is highly poisonous because it forms a complex with haemoglobin which is about 300 times more stable than the oxygen-haemoglobin complex.
  • This prevents haemoglobin in red blood corpuscles from carrying oxygen around the body, ultimately resulting in death.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• By complete combustion of carbon and carbon-containing fuels in excess of air:
\[C_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} CO_{2(g)}\] \[CH_{4(g)} + 2O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} CO_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(g)}\]
  • Laboratory method: By the action of dilute HCl on calcium carbonate:
\[CaCO_{3(s)} + 2HCl_{(aq)} → CaCl_{2(aq)} + CO_{2(g)} + H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • Commercial method: By heating limestone.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• CO2 is a colourless and odourless gas. Its low solubility in water makes it of immense biochemical and geochemical importance.
  • With water, it forms carbonic acid, H2CO3, a weak dibasic acid which dissociates in two steps:
\[H_2CO_{3(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ HCO^-_{3(aq)} + H_3O^+_{(aq)}\] \[HCO^-_{3(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ CO^{2-}_{3(aq)} + H_3O^+_{(aq)}\]
  • The H2CO3/HCO3- buffer system helps to maintain the pH of blood between 7.26 and 7.42.
  • Being acidic, CO2 combines with alkalies to form metal carbonates.

docs.title: Photosynthesis and the greenhouse effect
docs.text:
• CO2 is present to the extent of about 0.03% by volume in the atmosphere. It is removed by photosynthesis, the process by which green plants convert atmospheric CO2 into carbohydrates such as glucose:
\[6CO_2 + 12H_2O \xrightarrow[Chlorophyll]{h\nu} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 + 6H_2O\]
  • Unlike CO, CO2 is not poisonous. However, increased combustion of fossil fuels and decomposition of limestone for cement manufacture seem to be increasing the CO2 content of the atmosphere. This may increase the greenhouse effect and raise the temperature of the atmosphere, with serious consequences.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Dry ice: Solid CO2, obtained by allowing liquified CO2 to expand rapidly. It is used as a refrigerant for ice-cream and frozen food.
  • Gaseous CO2 is used to carbonate soft drinks.
  • Being heavy and a non-supporter of combustion, it is used as a fire extinguisher.
  • A large amount of CO2 is used to manufacture urea.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• In CO2, the carbon atom is sp hybridised. Its two sp hybrid orbitals overlap with two p orbitals of the oxygen atoms to form two sigma bonds. The other two electrons of carbon form pπ-pπ bonds with the oxygen atoms.
  • This gives a linear molecule with both C-O bonds of equal length (115 pm) and no dipole moment.
  • CO2 is a resonance hybrid of the following structures:
\[^-:\ddot{O}-C \equiv O:^+ \leftrightarrow\ :\ddot{O}=C=\ddot{O}:\ \leftrightarrow\ ^+:O \equiv C-\ddot{O}:^-\]

docs.title: 3. Silicon Dioxide (SiO<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
• 95% of the earth's crust is made up of silica and silicates.
  • Silicon dioxide, commonly known as silica, occurs in several crystallographic forms. Quartz, cristobalite and tridymite are crystalline forms of silica, and they are interconvertible at suitable temperatures.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• SiO2 is a covalent, three-dimensional network solid.
  • Each silicon atom is covalently bonded in a tetrahedral manner to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom is in turn bonded to another silicon atom. Each corner is shared with another tetrahedron.
  • The entire crystal may be considered as a giant molecule in which eight-membered rings are formed with alternate silicon and oxygen atoms.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Silica in its normal form is almost non-reactive because of the very high Si-O bond enthalpy. It resists attack by halogens, dihydrogen and most acids and metals, even at elevated temperatures.
  • However, it is attacked by HF and NaOH:
\[SiO_2 + 2NaOH → Na_2SiO_3 + H_2O\] \[SiO_2 + 4HF → SiF_4 + 2H_2O\]

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Quartz is extensively used as a piezoelectric material. It has made possible extremely accurate clocks, modern radio and television broadcasting and mobile radio communications.
  • Silica gel is used as a drying agent and as a support for chromatographic materials and catalysts.
  • Kieselghur, an amorphous form of silica, is used in filtration plants.

docs.title: 4. Silicones
docs.text:
• Silicones are a group of organosilicon polymers which have \(-(R_2SiO)-\) as a repeating unit.
  • The starting materials are alkyl or aryl substituted silicon chlorides, RnSiCl(4-n), where R is an alkyl or aryl group.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• When methyl chloride reacts with silicon in the presence of copper as a catalyst at 573 K, various methyl substituted chlorosilanes (MeSiCl3, Me2SiCl2, Me3SiCl and small amounts of Me4Si) are formed.
  • Hydrolysis of dimethyldichlorosilane, (CH3)2SiCl2, followed by condensation polymerisation gives straight chain polymers:
\[2CH_3Cl + Si \xrightarrow[573\ K]{Cu\ powder} (CH_3)_2SiCl_2\] \[(CH_3)_2SiCl_2 + 2H_2O → (CH_3)_2Si(OH)_2 + 2HCl\] \[n(CH_3)_2Si(OH)_2 \xrightarrow{Polymerisation} -[O-Si(CH_3)_2]_n- + nH_2O\]
  • The chain length of the polymer can be controlled by adding (CH3)3SiCl, which blocks the ends. Its hydrolysis product (CH3)3SiOH has only one OH group, so the chain cannot grow beyond it:
\[n(CH_3)_2Si(OH)_2 + (CH_3)_3SiOH \xrightarrow{-H_2O} -O-[Si(CH_3)_2-O]_n-Si(CH_3)_3\]

docs.title: Properties and uses
docs.text:
• Silicones are surrounded by non-polar alkyl groups, so they are water repelling in nature.
  • They have high thermal stability, high dielectric strength and resistance to oxidation and chemicals.
  • They are used as sealants, greases, electrical insulators and for water proofing of fabrics.
  • Being biocompatible, they are also used in surgical and cosmetic plants.

docs.title: 5. Silicates
docs.text:
• A large number of silicate minerals exist in nature, for example feldspar, zeolites, mica and asbestos.
  • The basic structural unit of silicates is SiO44-, in which a silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms in a tetrahedral fashion.
  • In silicates, either the discrete unit is present or a number of such units are joined together via corners by sharing 1, 2, 3 or 4 oxygen atoms per silicate unit.
  • When silicate units are linked together, they form chain, ring, sheet or three-dimensional structures.
  • The negative charge on the silicate structure is neutralised by positively charged metal ions.
  • If all four corners are shared with other tetrahedral units, a three-dimensional network is formed.
  • Two important man-made silicates are glass and cement.

docs.title: 6. Zeolites
docs.text:
• If aluminium atoms replace a few silicon atoms in the three-dimensional network of silicon dioxide, the overall structure, known as an aluminosilicate, acquires a negative charge.
  • Cations such as Na+, K+ or Ca2+ balance this negative charge. Examples are feldspar and zeolites.
  • Zeolites are widely used as catalysts in the petrochemical industry for cracking of hydrocarbons and isomerisation. For example, ZSM-5 (a type of zeolite) is used to convert alcohols directly into gasoline.
  • Hydrated zeolites are used as ion exchangers in the softening of "hard" water.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What are silicones?

Simple silicones consist of \(-(R_2SiO)_n-\) chains in which alkyl or phenyl groups occupy the remaining bonding positions on each silicon. They are hydrophobic (water repellent) in nature.

Suggest a reason as to why CO is poisonous.

CO forms a complex with haemoglobin (carboxyhaemoglobin) which is about 300 times more stable than the oxygen-haemoglobin complex. So haemoglobin in red blood cells can no longer carry oxygen to the body tissues, which leads to suffocation and ultimately death.

docs.title: Group 14 Elements | Physical and Atomic Properties
Group 14 Elements | Physical and Atomic Properties
Introduction
docs.text: • The elements of group 14 are Carbon(C), Silicon(Si), Germanium(Ge), Tin(Sn) and Lead(Pb). This group is known as the carbon family.

docs.title: Occurrence
docs.text:
• Carbon is the seventeenth most abundant element by mass in the earth's crust. It occurs in the free state as coal, graphite and diamond, and in the combined state as metal carbonates, hydrocarbons and carbon dioxide (0.03% in air).
  • Carbon is the most versatile element. Combined with hydrogen, oxygen, chlorine and sulphur, it forms an enormous range of materials, from living tissues to drugs and plastics. Organic chemistry is devoted to carbon compounds.
  • Naturally occurring carbon contains two stable isotopes, 12C and 13C. A third, radioactive isotope 14C (half-life 5770 years) is used for radiocarbon dating.
  • Silicon is the second most abundant element (27.7% by mass) in the earth's crust. It occurs as silica and silicates and is an important component of ceramics, glass and cement.
  • Germanium exists only in traces. Tin occurs mainly as cassiterite (SnO2) and lead as galena (PbS).
  • Ultrapure germanium and silicon are used to make transistors and semiconductor devices.

docs.title: 1. Electronic Configuration
docs.text:
• General valence shell electronic configuration: ns2np2
  • As in group 13, the inner core of the electronic configuration differs from element to element.

docs.title: 2. Covalent Radius
docs.text:
• There is a considerable increase in covalent radius from C to Si.
  • From Si to Pb, only a small increase in radius is observed. This is due to the presence of completely filled d and f orbitals in the heavier members, which shield the outer electrons poorly.

docs.title: 3. Ionization Enthalpy
docs.text:
• The first ionization enthalpy of group 14 elements is higher than that of the corresponding group 13 elements.
  • In general, ionization enthalpy decreases down the group.
  • The small decrease in ΔiH from Si to Ge to Sn, and the slight increase from Sn to Pb, are due to the poor shielding effect of the intervening d and f orbitals together with the increase in atomic size.

docs.title: 4. Electronegativity
docs.text:
• Due to their smaller size, group 14 elements are slightly more electronegative than group 13 elements.
  • The electronegativity values of the elements from Si to Pb are almost the same.

docs.title: Physical Properties of Group 14 Elements
docs.text:
• All group 14 elements are solids.
  • Carbon and silicon are non-metals, germanium is a metalloid, whereas tin and lead are soft metals with low melting points.
  • The melting and boiling points of group 14 elements are much higher than those of the corresponding group 13 elements.
Property Carbon (C) Silicon (Si) Germanium (Ge) Tin (Sn) Lead (Pb) Atomic number 6 14 32 50 82 Atomic mass (g mol-1) 12.01 28.09 72.60 118.71 207.2 Electronic configuration [He]2s22p2 [Ne]3s23p2 [Ar]3d104s24p2 [Kr]4d105s25p2 [Xe]4f145d106s26p2 Covalent radius / pm 77 118 122 140 146 Ionic radius M4+ / pm - 40 53 69 78 Ionic radius M2+ / pm - - 73 118 119 ΔiH1 (kJ mol-1) 1086 786 761 708 715 ΔiH2 (kJ mol-1) 2352 1577 1537 1411 1450 ΔiH3 (kJ mol-1) 4620 3228 3300 2942 3081 ΔiH4 (kJ mol-1) 6220 4354 4409 3929 4082 Electronegativity (Pauling) 2.5 1.8 1.8 1.8 1.9 Density / g cm-3 (293 K) 3.51 (diamond), 2.22 (graphite) 2.34 5.32 7.26 11.34 Melting point / K 4373 1693 1218 505 600 Boiling point / K - 3550 3123 2896 2024 Electrical resistivity / ohm cm (293 K) 1014-1016 50 50 10-5 2 × 10-5

Note

The covalent radius is given for the M(IV) oxidation state and ionic radii for 6-coordination. The density of tin is for the β-form, which is stable at room temperature.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Explain why is there a phenomenal decrease in ionization enthalpy from carbon to silicon?

Carbon is very small (covalent radius 77 pm), so its valence electrons are held very strongly by the nucleus. In silicon, a new shell is added and the covalent radius jumps to 118 pm. The valence electrons are much farther from the nucleus and are also shielded by more inner electrons. Hence the ionization enthalpy drops sharply from 1086 kJ mol-1 (C) to 786 kJ mol-1 (Si).

Why are group 14 elements slightly more electronegative than group 13 elements?

In a period, the nuclear charge increases by one unit from group 13 to group 14 while the electrons enter the same shell. The atoms of group 14 are therefore smaller and attract shared electrons more strongly, making them slightly more electronegative.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Write the resonance structures of CO32- and HCO3-.

  • CO32-: Carbon is bonded to three oxygen atoms. In each structure, one oxygen is double bonded and the other two carry a negative charge. The double bond can be placed on any of the three oxygens, giving three equivalent structures:
\[O=C(-O^-)_2\ \leftrightarrow\ ^-O-C(=O)-O^-\ \leftrightarrow\ (^-O)_2C=O\]
  • HCO3-: One oxygen is attached to hydrogen and cannot take part in resonance. The double bond and the negative charge are shared by the other two oxygens, giving two structures:
\[HO-C(=O)-O^-\ \leftrightarrow\ HO-C(-O^-)=O\]

What is the state of hybridisation of carbon in (a) CO32- (b) diamond (c) graphite?

(a) CO32-: sp2 (trigonal planar, three σ bonds)

(b) Diamond: sp3 (each carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others)

(c) Graphite: sp2 (each carbon bonded to three others in a hexagonal layer)

How is excessive content of CO2 responsible for global warming?

CO2 allows sunlight to pass through but absorbs the infrared (heat) radiation given off by the earth's surface and re-emits part of it back to the earth. This traps heat in the atmosphere (the greenhouse effect). Burning of fossil fuels and decomposition of limestone for cement have increased atmospheric CO2, which increases the greenhouse effect and raises the temperature of the atmosphere, causing global warming.

Explain the following reactions: (a) Silicon is heated with methyl chloride at high temperature in the presence of copper; (b) Silicon dioxide is treated with hydrogen fluoride; (c) CO is heated with ZnO.

(a) A mixture of methyl substituted chlorosilanes (MeSiCl3, Me2SiCl2, Me3SiCl and a little Me4Si) is formed. These are the starting materials for silicones:

\[2CH_3Cl + Si \xrightarrow[573\ K]{Cu\ powder} (CH_3)_2SiCl_2\]

(b) SiO2 is attacked by HF to form silicon tetrafluoride; with excess HF, fluorosilicic acid is formed:

\[SiO_2 + 4HF → SiF_4 + 2H_2O\] \[SiF_4 + 2HF → H_2SiF_6\]

(c) CO reduces zinc oxide to zinc metal:

\[ZnO_{(s)} + CO_{(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} Zn_{(s)} + CO_{2(g)}\]

Give reasons: (i) Graphite is used as lubricant. (ii) Diamond is used as an abrasive.

(i) Graphite has a layered structure in which the layers are held by weak van der Waals forces. The layers slide easily over one another, making graphite soft and slippery. It is also stable at high temperatures, so it is used as a dry lubricant where oil cannot be used.

(ii) Diamond has a rigid three-dimensional network of strong C-C covalent bonds and is the hardest substance on earth. So it can grind and sharpen other hard materials and is used as an abrasive.

What are allotropes? Sketch the structure of two allotropes of carbon namely diamond and graphite. What is the impact of structure on physical properties of two allotropes?

  • Different forms of the same element having different physical properties but similar chemical properties are called allotropes.
  • Diamond: Each sp3 carbon is tetrahedrally bonded to four other carbons (C-C = 154 pm), forming a rigid 3D network. Hence it is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.
  • Graphite: Each sp2 carbon is bonded to three others in planar hexagonal layers (C-C = 141.5 pm), with layers 340 pm apart held by van der Waals forces. Hence it is soft, slippery, and conducts electricity due to delocalised π electrons.
  • The structures of diamond and graphite are shown on the Allotropes of Carbon page.

(a) Classify following oxides as neutral, acidic, basic or amphoteric: CO, B2O3, SiO2, CO2, Al2O3, PbO2, Tl2O3 (b) Write suitable chemical equations to show their nature.

(a) Neutral: CO; Acidic: B2O3, SiO2, CO2; Amphoteric: Al2O3, PbO2; Basic: Tl2O3

(b) Acidic oxides react with bases:

\[B_2O_3 + 2NaOH → 2NaBO_2 + H_2O\] \[SiO_2 + 2NaOH → Na_2SiO_3 + H_2O\] \[CO_2 + 2NaOH → Na_2CO_3 + H_2O\]

Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases:

\[Al_2O_3 + 6HCl → 2AlCl_3 + 3H_2O\] \[Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH + 3H_2O → 2Na[Al(OH)_4]\] \[PbO_2 + 4HCl → PbCl_2 + Cl_2 + 2H_2O\] \[PbO_2 + 2NaOH → Na_2PbO_3 + H_2O\]

Basic oxides react with acids:

\[Tl_2O_3 + 6HCl → 2TlCl_3 + 3H_2O\]

CO, being neutral, reacts with neither acids nor bases.

Give one method for industrial and one for laboratory preparation of CO and CO2 each.

  • CO (industrial): Passing steam over hot coke gives water gas:
\[C_{(s)} + H_2O_{(g)} \xrightarrow{473-1273\ K} CO_{(g)} + H_{2(g)}\]
  • CO (laboratory): Dehydration of formic acid with conc. H2SO4:
\[HCOOH \xrightarrow[conc.\ H_2SO_4]{373\ K} H_2O + CO\]
  • CO2 (industrial): Heating limestone:
\[CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} CaO + CO_2\]
  • CO2 (laboratory): Action of dilute HCl on calcium carbonate:
\[CaCO_{3(s)} + 2HCl_{(aq)} → CaCl_{2(aq)} + CO_{2(g)} + H_2O_{(l)}\]

If the starting material for the manufacture of silicones is RSiCl3, write the structure of the product formed.

  • Hydrolysis of RSiCl3 gives RSi(OH)3, which has three OH groups:
\[RSiCl_3 + 3H_2O → RSi(OH)_3 + 3HCl\]
  • Condensation can occur through all three OH groups, so the chains get linked to one another. The product is a cross-linked (three-dimensional) silicone, in which each silicon carries one R group and is bonded to three bridging oxygen atoms:
\[n\,RSi(OH)_3 \xrightarrow{-H_2O} [RSiO_{3/2}]_n\ \ (cross\ linked\ network)\]

What do you understand by allotropy?

The existence of an element in two or more forms which have different physical properties but similar chemical properties is called allotropy. For example, carbon exists as diamond, graphite and fullerenes.

docs.title: Group 15 Elements | Chemical Properties
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss chemical properties of group 15 elements like oxidation states, anomalous behaviour of nitrogen and reactivity towards hydrogen, oxygen, halogens and metals.

docs.title: 1. Oxidation States and Trends in Chemical Reactivity
docs.text:
• The common oxidation states of group 15 elements are -3, +3 and +5.
  • The tendency to show -3 oxidation state decreases down the group due to increase in size and metallic character. Bismuth hardly forms any compound in -3 oxidation state.
  • The stability of +5 oxidation state decreases down the group, while that of +3 oxidation state increases. This is due to the inert pair effect (reluctance of the ns2 electrons to take part in bonding).
  • The only well characterised Bi(V) compound is BiF5.
  • Nitrogen also shows +1, +2 and +4 oxidation states when it combines with oxygen. Phosphorus shows +1 and +4 oxidation states in some oxoacids.

docs.title: Disproportionation
docs.text:
• In the case of nitrogen, all oxidation states from +1 to +4 tend to disproportionate in acid solution. For example:
\[3HNO_2 → HNO_3 + H_2O + 2NO\]
  • In the case of phosphorus, nearly all intermediate oxidation states disproportionate into +5 and -3, both in alkali and in acid.
  • The +3 oxidation state of arsenic, antimony and bismuth becomes increasingly stable with respect to disproportionation.

docs.title: Covalency
docs.text:
• Nitrogen is restricted to a maximum covalency of 4, because only four orbitals (one s and three p) are available for bonding.
  • The heavier elements have vacant d orbitals in the outermost shell, so they can expand their covalence, as in PF6-.

docs.title: 2. Anomalous Properties of Nitrogen
docs.text:
Nitrogen differs from the rest of the members of the group due to its small size, high electronegativity, high ionisation enthalpy and non-availability of d orbitals.

  • pπ-pπ multiple bonding: Nitrogen can form pπ-pπ multiple bonds with itself and with other small, highly electronegative atoms like C and O. Heavier elements cannot do this because their atomic orbitals are too large and diffuse for effective sideways overlap.
  • Diatomic molecule: Because of this, nitrogen exists as a diatomic molecule with a triple bond (one σ and two π) between the two atoms. Its bond enthalpy is very high (941.4 kJ mol-1).
  • On the other hand, phosphorus, arsenic and antimony form single bonds (P-P, As-As, Sb-Sb), while bismuth forms metallic bonds in the elemental state.
  • Weak catenation: The single N-N bond is weaker than the single P-P bond. Owing to the small bond length, the non-bonding electrons on the two nitrogen atoms repel each other strongly. Hence, the catenation tendency of nitrogen is weaker.
  • No dπ-pπ bonding: Since nitrogen has no d orbitals, it cannot form dπ-pπ bonds as heavier elements do, for example in R3P=O or R3P=CH2 (R = alkyl group).
  • Phosphorus and arsenic can also form dπ-dπ bonds with transition metals when their compounds like P(C2H5)3 and As(C6H5)3 act as ligands.
  • Maximum covalency of 4: Nitrogen cannot expand its octet.

docs.title: 3. Reactivity towards Hydrogen
docs.text:
• All group 15 elements form hydrides of the type EH3 (E = N, P, As, Sb, Bi).
  • The hydrides show a regular gradation in their properties.
Property NH3 PH3 AsH3 SbH3 BiH3 Melting point (K) 195.2 139.5 156.7 185 - Boiling point (K) 238.5 185.5 210.6 254.6 290 E-H distance (pm) 101.7 141.9 151.9 170.7 - HEH angle (°) 107.8 93.6 91.8 91.3 - ΔfH0 (kJ mol-1) -46.1 13.4 66.4 145.1 278 ΔdissH0 (E-H) (kJ mol-1) 389 322 297 255 -
  • Thermal stability decreases from NH3 to BiH3, as seen from the decreasing E-H bond dissociation enthalpy.
  • Reducing character therefore increases down the group. Ammonia is only a mild reducing agent while BiH3 is the strongest reducing agent amongst all the hydrides.
  • Basicity decreases down the group:
\[Stability:\ NH_3\ >\ PH_3\ >\ AsH_3\ >\ SbH_3\ >\ BiH_3\] \[Reducing\ character:\ NH_3\ <\ PH_3\ <\ AsH_3\ <\ SbH_3\ <\ BiH_3\] \[Basicity:\ NH_3\ >\ PH_3\ >\ AsH_3\ >\ SbH_3\ \geq\ BiH_3\]
  • NH3 has an unusually high melting and boiling point because its molecules are associated through hydrogen bonding.

docs.title: 4. Reactivity towards Oxygen
docs.text:
• All these elements form two types of oxides: E2O3 and E2O5.
  • The oxide in the higher oxidation state of an element is more acidic than that in the lower oxidation state.
  • Acidic character of the oxides decreases down the group.
  • The E2O3 oxides of nitrogen and phosphorus are purely acidic, those of arsenic and antimony are amphoteric and those of bismuth are predominantly basic.

docs.title: 5. Reactivity towards Halogens
docs.text:
• These elements react with halogens to form two series of halides: EX3 and EX5.
  • Nitrogen does not form pentahalides because it has no d orbitals in its valence shell.
  • Pentahalides are more covalent than trihalides.
  • All the trihalides are stable except those of nitrogen. In the case of nitrogen, only NF3 is known to be stable.
  • Trihalides, except BiF3, are predominantly covalent in nature.

docs.title: 6. Reactivity towards Metals
docs.text:
• All these elements react with metals to form binary compounds in which they show -3 oxidation state. For example:
Compound Name Ca3N2 Calcium nitride Ca3P2 Calcium phosphide Na3As2 Sodium arsenide Zn3Sb2 Zinc antimonide Mg3Bi2 Magnesium bismuthide

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Though nitrogen exhibits +5 oxidation state, it does not form pentahalide. Give reason.

Nitrogen (n = 2) has only s and p orbitals in its valence shell. It has no d orbitals, so it cannot expand its covalence beyond four. That is why nitrogen does not form a pentahalide.

PH3 has lower boiling point than NH3. Why?

In the liquid state, NH3 molecules are associated through hydrogen bonding, but PH3 molecules are not (phosphorus is much less electronegative than nitrogen). Extra energy is needed to break the hydrogen bonds in NH3, so PH3 has a lower boiling point.

Why are pentahalides more covalent than trihalides?

In pentahalides the central atom is in the +5 oxidation state, while in trihalides it is in the +3 state. An atom in a higher oxidation state has a higher charge and smaller size, so it has greater polarising power. It distorts the electron cloud of the halide more strongly, which increases covalent character. Hence pentahalides are more covalent than trihalides.

Why is BiH3 the strongest reducing agent amongst all the hydrides of group 15 elements?

Down the group, the size of the central atom increases and the E-H bond becomes longer and weaker. BiH3 has the weakest E-H bond, so it is the least stable hydride and gives up hydrogen most easily. Therefore, it is the strongest reducing agent.

Why does nitrogen exist as N2 while phosphorus exists as P4?

Nitrogen is small and can form strong pπ-pπ multiple bonds, so two nitrogen atoms join by a triple bond to give N2. Phosphorus atoms are larger and their p orbitals are too diffuse for effective pπ-pπ overlap, so phosphorus forms P-P single bonds instead, giving the tetrahedral P4 molecule.

docs.title: (a) Commercial method
docs.text:
• Dinitrogen is produced commercially by the liquefaction and fractional distillation of air.
  • Liquid dinitrogen (b.p. 77.2 K) distils out first, leaving behind liquid oxygen (b.p. 90 K).

docs.title: (b) Laboratory method
docs.text:
• In the laboratory, dinitrogen is prepared by treating an aqueous solution of ammonium chloride with sodium nitrite.
\[NH_4Cl_{(aq)} + NaNO_{2(aq)} → N_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} + NaCl_{(aq)}\]
  • Small amounts of NO and HNO3 are also formed. These impurities are removed by passing the gas through aqueous sulphuric acid containing potassium dichromate.

docs.title: (c) From ammonium dichromate
docs.text: \[(NH_4)_2Cr_2O_7 \xrightarrow{Heat} N_2 + 4H_2O + Cr_2O_3\]

docs.title: (d) Very pure dinitrogen
docs.text:
• Very pure nitrogen is obtained by the thermal decomposition of sodium or barium azide.
\[Ba(N_3)_2 → Ba + 3N_2\] \[2NaN_3 → 2Na + 3N_2\]

docs.title: 2. Properties
docs.text:
• Dinitrogen is a colourless, odourless, tasteless and non-toxic gas.
  • It has two stable isotopes: 14N and 15N.
  • It has very low solubility in water (23.2 cm3 per litre of water at 273 K and 1 bar pressure) and low freezing and boiling points.
  • Dinitrogen is rather inert at room temperature because of the very high bond enthalpy of the N≡N bond.
  • Its reactivity increases rapidly with rise in temperature. At high temperatures it combines directly with some metals to form predominantly ionic nitrides, and with non-metals to form covalent nitrides.
\[6Li + N_2 \xrightarrow{Heat} 2Li_3N\] \[3Mg + N_2 \xrightarrow{Heat} Mg_3N_2\]
  • It combines with hydrogen at about 773 K in the presence of a catalyst (Haber's process) to form ammonia.
\[N_{2(g)} + 3H_{2(g)} \overset{773\ K}{⇌} 2NH_{3(g)};\ \ Δ_fH^0 = -46.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • It combines with dioxygen only at very high temperature (about 2000 K) to form nitric oxide.
\[N_2 + O_{2(g)} \overset{Heat}{⇌} 2NO_{(g)}\]

docs.title: 3. Uses
docs.text:
• The main use of dinitrogen is in the manufacture of ammonia and other industrial chemicals containing nitrogen (e.g., calcium cyanamide).
  • It is used where an inert atmosphere is needed (e.g., in the iron and steel industry, and as an inert diluent for reactive chemicals).
  • Liquid dinitrogen is used as a refrigerant to preserve biological materials and food items, and in cryosurgery.

docs.title: 1. Preparation
docs.text:
• Ammonia is present in small quantities in air and soil, where it is formed by the decay of nitrogenous organic matter such as urea.
\[NH_2CONH_2 + 2H_2O → (NH_4)_2CO_3 ⇌ 2NH_3 + H_2O + CO_2\]
  • On a small scale, ammonia is obtained by treating ammonium salts with caustic soda or lime.
\[2NH_4Cl + Ca(OH)_2 → 2NH_3 + 2H_2O + CaCl_2\] \[(NH_4)_2SO_4 + 2NaOH → 2NH_3 + 2H_2O + Na_2SO_4\]

docs.title: 2. Haber's Process
docs.text:
• On a large scale, ammonia is manufactured by Haber's process.
\[N_{2(g)} + 3H_{2(g)} ⇌ 2NH_{3(g)};\ \ Δ_fH^0 = -46.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • The forward reaction decreases the number of gaseous moles (4 → 2) and is exothermic. So, according to Le Chatelier's principle, high pressure favours the formation of ammonia.
  • The optimum conditions are:
    • Pressure: 200 × 105 Pa (about 200 atm)
    • Temperature: about 700 K
    • Catalyst: iron oxide with small amounts of K2O and Al2O3, used to increase the rate of attainment of equilibrium.
  • The temperature is a compromise: a lower temperature would give a better yield, but the reaction would be too slow.
  • The gas mixture coming out of the catalyst chamber is cooled so that ammonia liquefies, and the unreacted N2 and H2 are pumped back.

docs.title: 3. Properties
docs.text:
• Ammonia is a colourless gas with a pungent odour. Its freezing and boiling points are 198.4 K and 239.7 K respectively.
  • In the solid and liquid states, ammonia molecules are associated through hydrogen bonds, as in water. This accounts for its higher melting and boiling points than expected from its molecular mass.
  • Structure: The ammonia molecule is trigonal pyramidal with the nitrogen atom at the apex. It has three bond pairs and one lone pair of electrons. The N-H bond length is 101.7 pm and the H-N-H bond angle is 107.8°.

docs.title: (a) Basic nature
docs.text:
• Ammonia is highly soluble in water. Its aqueous solution is weakly basic due to the formation of OH- ions.
\[NH_{3(g)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ NH^+_{4(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\]
  • It forms ammonium salts with acids, e.g., NH4Cl, (NH4)2SO4.

docs.title: (b) Precipitation of metal hydroxides
docs.text:
• As a weak base, it precipitates the hydroxides of many metals from their salt solutions.
\[2FeCl_{3(aq)} + 3NH_4OH_{(aq)} → Fe_2O_3.xH_2O_{(s)} + 3NH_4Cl_{(aq)}\] \[[Brown\ ppt]\] \[ZnSO_{4(aq)} + 2NH_4OH_{(aq)} → Zn(OH)_{2(s)} + (NH_4)_2SO_{4(aq)}\] \[[White\ ppt]\]

docs.title: (c) Complex formation (Lewis base)
docs.text:
• The lone pair on nitrogen makes ammonia a Lewis base. It donates this electron pair to metal ions to form complexes. This is used to detect metal ions such as Cu2+ and Ag+.
\[Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + 4NH_{3(aq)} ⇌ [Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}_{(aq)}\] \[[Blue]\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ [Deep\ blue]\] \[Ag^+_{(aq)} + Cl^-_{(aq)} → AgCl_{(s)}\] \[[Colourless]\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ [White\ ppt]\] \[AgCl_{(s)} + 2NH_{3(aq)} → [Ag(NH_3)_2]Cl_{(aq)}\] \[[White\ ppt]\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ [Colourless]\]

docs.title: 4. Uses
docs.text:
• Ammonia is used to produce nitrogenous fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate, urea, ammonium phosphate and ammonium sulphate.
  • It is used in the manufacture of some inorganic nitrogen compounds, the most important being nitric acid.
  • Liquid ammonia is used as a refrigerant.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Write the reaction of thermal decomposition of sodium azide.

Thermal decomposition of sodium azide gives dinitrogen gas.

\[2NaN_3 → 2Na + 3N_2\]

Why is N2 less reactive at room temperature?

The two nitrogen atoms in N2 are joined by a triple bond (N≡N), which has a very high bond dissociation enthalpy (941.4 kJ mol-1). A lot of energy is needed to break this bond, so N2 is rather inert at room temperature.

Why does NH3 act as a Lewis base?

The nitrogen atom in NH3 has one lone pair of electrons which is available for donation. Therefore, it acts as a Lewis base.

Mention the conditions required to maximise the yield of ammonia.

\[N_{2(g)} + 3H_{2(g)} ⇌ 2NH_{3(g)};\ \ Δ_fH^0 = -46.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • The reaction proceeds with a decrease in gaseous moles, so a high pressure (about 200 atm) favours ammonia.
  • The reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature favours ammonia. In practice, about 700 K is used so that the rate is reasonable.
  • A catalyst of iron oxide with small amounts of K2O and Al2O3 is used to reach equilibrium quickly.
  • Removing ammonia as it forms (by liquefaction) also shifts the equilibrium forward.

How does ammonia react with a solution of Cu2+?

Ammonia acts as a Lewis base and forms a deep blue complex, tetraamminecopper(II) ion, with Cu2+.

\[Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + 4NH_{3(aq)} ⇌ [Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: Group 15 Elements | Oxides of Nitrogen and Nitric Acid
Group 15 Elements | Oxides of Nitrogen and Nitric Acid
Oxides of Nitrogen
docs.text:
• Nitrogen forms a number of oxides in which it shows different oxidation states, from +1 to +5.
  • Their names, formulas, common methods of preparation and physical appearance are given below.
Name Formula Oxidation state of N Common method of preparation Physical appearance and chemical nature Dinitrogen oxide [Nitrogen(I) oxide] N2O +1 NH4NO3 → N2O + 2H2O (on heating) Colourless gas, neutral Nitrogen monoxide [Nitrogen(II) oxide] NO +2 2NaNO2 + 2FeSO4 + 3H2SO4 → Fe2(SO4)3 + 2NaHSO4 + 2H2O + 2NO Colourless gas, neutral Dinitrogen trioxide [Nitrogen(III) oxide] N2O3 +3 2NO + N2O4 → 2N2O3 (at 250 K) Blue solid, acidic Nitrogen dioxide [Nitrogen(IV) oxide] NO2 +4 2Pb(NO3)2 → 4NO2 + 2PbO (at 673 K) Brown gas, acidic Dinitrogen tetroxide [Nitrogen(IV) oxide] N2O4 +4 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 (forms on cooling, reverts on heating) Colourless solid/liquid, acidic Dinitrogen pentoxide [Nitrogen(V) oxide] N2O5 +5 4HNO3 + P4O10 → 4HPO3 + 2N2O5 Colourless solid, acidic

docs.title: Preparation reactions
docs.text: \[NH_4NO_3 \xrightarrow{Heat} N_2O + 2H_2O\] \[2NaNO_2 + 2FeSO_4 + 3H_2SO_4 &rarr; Fe_2(SO_4)_3 + 2NaHSO_4 + 2H_2O + 2NO\] \[2NO + N_2O_4 \xrightarrow{250\ K} 2N_2O_3\] \[2Pb(NO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{673\ K} 4NO_2 + 2PbO\] \[2NO_2 \overset{Cool}{\underset{Heat}{&#8652;}} N_2O_4\] \[4HNO_3 + P_4O_{10} &rarr; 4HPO_3 + 2N_2O_5\]

docs.title: Structures of oxides of nitrogen
docs.text:
• The main resonance structures (Lewis dot) and bond parameters of the oxides of nitrogen are shown below.
  • N2O is linear, NO2 is angular (bond angle 134°) and N2O3, N2O4 and N2O5 are planar.
  • NO and NO2 contain an odd number of valence electrons, so they are odd-electron molecules (paramagnetic).

docs.title: Nitric Acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>)
docs.text: • Nitrogen forms oxoacids such as H2N2O2 (hyponitrous acid), HNO2 (nitrous acid) and HNO3 (nitric acid). Amongst them, HNO3 is the most important.

docs.title: 1. Laboratory Preparation
docs.text:
• In the laboratory, nitric acid is prepared by heating KNO3 or NaNO3 with concentrated H2SO4 in a glass retort.
\[NaNO_3 + H_2SO_4 → NaHSO_4 + HNO_3\]

docs.title: 2. Ostwald's Process
docs.text: • On a large scale, nitric acid is prepared mainly by Ostwald's process. This method is based on the catalytic oxidation of NH3 by atmospheric oxygen.

docs.title: Step 1: Catalytic oxidation of ammonia
docs.text: \[4NH_{3(g)} + 5O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow[500\ K,\ 9\ bar]{Pt/Rh\ gauze\ catalyst} 4NO_{(g)} + 6H_2O_{(g)}\]

docs.title: Step 3: Absorption of NO<sub>2</sub> in water
docs.text:
\[3NO_{2(g)} + H_2O_{(l)} → 2HNO_{3(aq)} + NO_{(g)}\]
  • The NO formed in step 3 is recycled.
  • The aqueous HNO3 can be concentrated by distillation up to about 68% by mass. Further concentration to 98% is achieved by dehydration with concentrated H2SO4.

docs.title: 3. Physical Properties
docs.text:
• Nitric acid is a colourless liquid (f.p. 231.4 K and b.p. 355.6 K).
  • Laboratory grade nitric acid contains about 68% HNO3 by mass and has a specific gravity of 1.504.
  • Structure: In the gaseous state, HNO3 exists as a planar molecule.

docs.title: (a) Acidic nature
docs.text:
• In aqueous solution, nitric acid behaves as a strong acid, giving hydronium and nitrate ions.
\[HNO_{3(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} → H_3O^+_{(aq)} + NO^-_{3(aq)}\]

docs.title: (b) Oxidising nature: reaction with metals
docs.text:
• Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent and attacks most metals except noble metals such as gold and platinum.
  • The products of oxidation depend on the concentration of the acid, the temperature and the nature of the material being oxidised.
\[3Cu + 8HNO_3(dilute) → 3Cu(NO_3)_2 + 2NO + 4H_2O\] \[Cu + 4HNO_3(conc.) → Cu(NO_3)_2 + 2NO_2 + 2H_2O\]
  • Zinc reacts with dilute nitric acid to give N2O and with concentrated acid to give NO2.
\[4Zn + 10HNO_3(dilute) → 4Zn(NO_3)_2 + 5H_2O + N_2O\] \[Zn + 4HNO_3(conc.) → Zn(NO_3)_2 + 2H_2O + 2NO_2\]
  • Some metals, like Cr and Al, do not dissolve in concentrated nitric acid because a passive film of oxide forms on their surface. This is called passivity.

docs.title: (c) Oxidising nature: reaction with non-metals
docs.text:
• Concentrated nitric acid oxidises non-metals and their compounds. Iodine is oxidised to iodic acid, carbon to carbon dioxide, sulphur to H2SO4 and phosphorus to phosphoric acid.
\[I_2 + 10HNO_3 → 2HIO_3 + 10NO_2 + 4H_2O\] \[C + 4HNO_3 → CO_2 + 2H_2O + 4NO_2\] \[S_8 + 48HNO_3(conc.) → 8H_2SO_4 + 48NO_2 + 16H_2O\] \[P_4 + 20HNO_3(conc.) → 4H_3PO_4 + 20NO_2 + 4H_2O\]

docs.title: 5. Brown Ring Test for Nitrates
docs.text:
• The brown ring test depends on the ability of Fe2+ to reduce nitrate to nitric oxide, which then combines with Fe2+ to form a brown coloured complex.
  • Procedure: Dilute ferrous sulphate solution is added to an aqueous solution containing nitrate ion. Then concentrated sulphuric acid is carefully added along the sides of the test tube.
  • A brown ring at the interface between the solution and the sulphuric acid layer indicates the presence of nitrate ion.
\[NO^-_3 + 3Fe^{2+} + 4H^+ → NO + 3Fe^{3+} + 2H_2O\] \[[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+} + NO → [Fe(H_2O)_5(NO)]^{2+} + H_2O\] \[[Brown]\]

docs.title: 6. Uses
docs.text:
• Manufacture of ammonium nitrate for fertilisers and of other nitrates for explosives and pyrotechnics.
  • Preparation of nitroglycerin, trinitrotoluene (TNT) and other organic nitro compounds.
  • Pickling of stainless steel, etching of metals, and as an oxidiser in rocket fuels.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Why does NO2 dimerise?

NO2 contains an odd number of valence electrons and behaves as a typical odd-electron molecule. On dimerisation, it is converted into the stable N2O4 molecule, which has an even number of electrons.

\[2NO_2 ⇌ N_2O_4\]

What is the covalency of nitrogen in N2O5?

In N2O5, each nitrogen atom forms one N=O double bond (2 shared pairs), one N-O single bond to the bridging oxygen (1 shared pair) and one coordinate bond to the other oxygen (1 shared pair). So each nitrogen shares four electron pairs, and the covalency of nitrogen in N2O5 is 4.

Why does copper give different products with dilute and concentrated nitric acid?

The product of reduction of HNO3 depends on its concentration. Concentrated HNO3 is reduced only to NO2, while dilute HNO3 is reduced further to NO.

\[3Cu + 8HNO_3(dilute) → 3Cu(NO_3)_2 + 2NO + 4H_2O\] \[Cu + 4HNO_3(conc.) → Cu(NO_3)_2 + 2NO_2 + 2H_2O\]

Why does aluminium not dissolve in concentrated nitric acid?

Concentrated nitric acid forms a thin, protective (passive) film of oxide on the surface of aluminium. This film prevents further reaction, so the metal does not dissolve.

docs.title: Group 15 Elements | Allotropes of Phosphorus and Phosphine
Group 15 Elements | Allotropes of Phosphorus and Phosphine
Allotropic Forms of Phosphorus
docs.text: • Phosphorus is found in many allotropic forms. The important ones are white, red and black phosphorus.

docs.title: 1. White Phosphorus
docs.text:
• White phosphorus is a translucent, white, waxy solid.
  • It is poisonous, insoluble in water but soluble in carbon disulphide (CS2).
  • It glows in the dark. This is called chemiluminescence.
  • It dissolves in boiling NaOH solution in an inert atmosphere to give phosphine.
\[P_4 + 3NaOH + 3H_2O → PH_3 + 3NaH_2PO_2\] \[[NaH_2PO_2 = Sodium\ hypophosphite]\]
  • Structure: It consists of discrete tetrahedral P4 molecules, with each P-P-P bond angle only 60°.
  • White phosphorus is less stable, and therefore more reactive, than the other solid forms under normal conditions. This is because of the angular strain in the P4 molecule, where the angles are only 60°.
  • It readily catches fire in air, giving dense white fumes of P4O10.
\[P_4 + 5O_2 → P_4O_{10}\]

docs.title: 2. Red Phosphorus
docs.text:
• Red phosphorus is obtained by heating white phosphorus at 573 K in an inert atmosphere for several days.
  • It has an iron grey lustre. It is odourless, non-poisonous and insoluble in water as well as in carbon disulphide.
  • Chemically, red phosphorus is much less reactive than white phosphorus. It does not glow in the dark.
  • Structure: It is polymeric, consisting of chains of P4 tetrahedra linked together.
  • When red phosphorus is heated under high pressure, a series of phases of black phosphorus are formed.

docs.title: 3. Black Phosphorus
docs.text:
• Black phosphorus has two forms: α-black phosphorus and β-black phosphorus.
  • α-Black phosphorus is formed when red phosphorus is heated in a sealed tube at 803 K. It can be sublimed in air and has opaque monoclinic or rhombohedral crystals. It does not oxidise in air.
  • β-Black phosphorus is prepared by heating white phosphorus at 473 K under high pressure. It does not burn in air up to 673 K.

docs.title: Comparison of White and Red Phosphorus
docs.text: Property White Phosphorus Red Phosphorus Appearance Translucent white waxy solid Iron grey lustre Toxicity Poisonous Non-poisonous Solubility in CS<sub>2</sub> Soluble Insoluble Glow in dark Glows (chemiluminescence) Does not glow Structure Discrete P<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra Polymeric chains of P<sub>4</sub> units Reactivity Very reactive, catches fire in air Much less reactive

docs.title: 1. Preparation
docs.text:
• Phosphine is prepared by the reaction of calcium phosphide with water or dilute HCl.
\[Ca_3P_2 + 6H_2O → 3Ca(OH)_2 + 2PH_3\] \[Ca_3P_2 + 6HCl → 3CaCl_2 + 2PH_3\]
  • Laboratory method: In the laboratory, it is prepared by heating white phosphorus with concentrated NaOH solution in an inert atmosphere of CO2.
\[P_4 + 3NaOH + 3H_2O → PH_3 + 3NaH_2PO_2\]
  • Purification: Pure phosphine is non-inflammable, but it becomes inflammable because of the presence of P2H4 or P4 vapours. To purify it, phosphine is absorbed in HI to form phosphonium iodide (PH4I), which on treatment with KOH gives off pure phosphine.
\[PH_4I + KOH → KI + H_2O + PH_3\]

docs.title: 2. Properties
docs.text:
• Phosphine is a colourless gas with a rotten fish smell and is highly poisonous.
  • It explodes in contact with traces of oxidising agents like HNO3, Cl2 and Br2 vapours.
  • It is slightly soluble in water. In the presence of light, its aqueous solution decomposes to give red phosphorus and H2.
  • When absorbed in copper sulphate or mercuric chloride solution, the corresponding phosphides are obtained.
\[3CuSO_4 + 2PH_3 → Cu_3P_2 + 3H_2SO_4\] \[3HgCl_2 + 2PH_3 → Hg_3P_2 + 6HCl\]
  • Basic nature: Phosphine is weakly basic and, like ammonia, gives phosphonium compounds with acids.
\[PH_3 + HBr → PH_4Br\]

docs.title: 3. Uses
docs.text:
• The spontaneous combustion of phosphine is used in Holme's signals. Containers holding calcium carbide and calcium phosphide are pierced and thrown into the sea. The gases evolved (acetylene and phosphine) catch fire and serve as a signal.
  • It is also used in smoke screens.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
In what way can it be proved that PH3 is basic in nature?

PH3 reacts with acids like HI to form PH4I, which shows that it is basic in nature.

\[PH_3 + HI → PH_4I\]

Due to the lone pair on the phosphorus atom, PH3 acts as a Lewis base in this reaction.

Bond angle in PH4+ is higher than that in PH3. Why?

In PH3, phosphorus has three bond pairs and one lone pair. The lone pair repels the bond pairs more strongly than bond pairs repel each other, so the bond angle is small (93.6°). In PH4+, the lone pair is used to bond with H+, so there are four bond pairs and no lone pair. The ion is regular tetrahedral with a bond angle of 109°28'. Hence the bond angle in PH4+ is higher.

What happens when white phosphorus is heated with concentrated NaOH solution in an inert atmosphere of CO2?

Phosphine gas is evolved along with sodium hypophosphite.

\[P_4 + 3NaOH + 3H_2O → PH_3 + 3NaH_2PO_2\]

Why is white phosphorus more reactive than red phosphorus?

White phosphorus consists of discrete P4 tetrahedra in which the P-P-P bond angle is only 60°. This causes large angular strain, which makes the molecule unstable and highly reactive. Red phosphorus is polymeric, with P4 units linked into chains, so it is more stable and much less reactive.

docs.title: Group 15 Elements | Phosphorus Halides and Oxoacids
Group 15 Elements | Phosphorus Halides and Oxoacids
Phosphorus Halides
docs.text: • Phosphorus forms two types of halides: PX3 (X = F, Cl, Br, I) and PX5 (X = F, Cl, Br).

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• It is obtained by passing dry chlorine over heated white phosphorus.
\[P_4 + 6Cl_2 → 4PCl_3\]
  • It is also obtained by the action of thionyl chloride on white phosphorus.
\[P_4 + 8SOCl_2 → 4PCl_3 + 4SO_2 + 2S_2Cl_2\]

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• It is a colourless oily liquid.
  • It hydrolyses in the presence of moisture, giving fumes of HCl.
\[PCl_3 + 3H_2O → H_3PO_3 + 3HCl\]
  • It reacts with organic compounds containing an -OH group, such as CH3COOH and C2H5OH, replacing -OH by -Cl.
\[3CH_3COOH + PCl_3 → 3CH_3COCl + H_3PO_3\] \[3C_2H_5OH + PCl_3 → 3C_2H_5Cl + H_3PO_3\]
  • Structure: PCl3 has a pyramidal shape. Phosphorus is sp3 hybridised, with three bond pairs and one lone pair.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• It is prepared by the reaction of white phosphorus with excess of dry chlorine.
\[P_4 + 10Cl_2 → 4PCl_5\]
  • It can also be prepared by the action of SO2Cl2 on phosphorus.
\[P_4 + 10SO_2Cl_2 → 4PCl_5 + 10SO_2\]

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• PCl5 is a yellowish white powder.
  • In moist air, it hydrolyses to POCl3 and finally gets converted to phosphoric acid.
\[PCl_5 + H_2O → POCl_3 + 2HCl\] \[POCl_3 + 3H_2O → H_3PO_4 + 3HCl\]
  • When heated, it sublimes but decomposes on stronger heating.
\[PCl_5 \xrightarrow{Heat} PCl_3 + Cl_2\]
  • It reacts with organic compounds containing an -OH group, converting them to chloro derivatives.
\[C_2H_5OH + PCl_5 → C_2H_5Cl + POCl_3 + HCl\] \[CH_3COOH + PCl_5 → CH_3COCl + POCl_3 + HCl\]
  • Finely divided metals on heating with PCl5 give the corresponding chlorides.
\[2Ag + PCl_5 → 2AgCl + PCl_3\] \[Sn + 2PCl_5 → SnCl_4 + 2PCl_3\]
  • It is used in the synthesis of some organic compounds, e.g., C2H5Cl and CH3COCl.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• In the gaseous and liquid phases, PCl5 has a trigonal bipyramidal structure (sp3d hybridisation of P).
  • The three equatorial P-Cl bonds (202 pm) are equivalent, while the two axial bonds (240 pm) are longer than the equatorial bonds. This is because the axial bond pairs suffer more repulsion than the equatorial bond pairs.
  • In the solid state, PCl5 exists as an ionic solid, [PCl4]+[PCl6]-, in which the cation [PCl4]+ is tetrahedral and the anion [PCl6]- is octahedral.

docs.title: Oxoacids of Phosphorus
docs.text:
• Phosphorus forms a number of oxoacids. The important ones, with their oxidation states, characteristic bonds and methods of preparation, are given below.
Name Formula Oxidation state of P Characteristic bonds and their number Preparation Hypophosphorous (Phosphinic) H3PO2 +1 One P-OH, Two P-H, One P=O White P4 + alkali Orthophosphorous (Phosphonic) H3PO3 +3 Two P-OH, One P-H, One P=O P2O3 + H2O Pyrophosphorous H4P2O5 +3 Two P-OH, Two P-H, Two P=O PCl3 + H3PO3 Hypophosphoric H4P2O6 +4 Four P-OH, Two P=O, One P-P Red P4 + alkali Orthophosphoric H3PO4 +5 Three P-OH, One P=O P4O10 + H2O Pyrophosphoric H4P2O7 +5 Four P-OH, Two P=O, One P-O-P Heat phosphoric acid Metaphosphoric (HPO3)n +5 Three P-OH, Three P=O, Three P-O-P (for (HPO3)3) Phosphorous acid + Br2, heat in a sealed tube
  • Metaphosphoric acid exists in polymeric forms only.
  • The compositions of the oxoacids are interrelated by the loss or gain of H2O molecules or O atoms.

docs.title: Important features
docs.text:
• In the oxoacids, phosphorus is tetrahedrally surrounded by other atoms.
  • All these acids contain one P=O bond and at least one P-OH bond.
  • Oxoacids in which phosphorus has an oxidation state less than +5 also contain either P-P bonds (e.g., in H4P2O6) or P-H bonds (e.g., in H3PO2), but not both.

docs.title: 1. Disproportionation
docs.text:
• Acids in the +3 oxidation state of phosphorus tend to disproportionate into higher and lower oxidation states. For example, orthophosphorous acid (phosphorous acid) on heating gives orthophosphoric acid (phosphoric acid) and phosphine.
\[4H_3PO_3 → 3H_3PO_4 + PH_3\]

docs.title: 2. Reducing nature
docs.text:
• Acids containing P-H bonds have strong reducing properties. Hypophosphorous acid, with two P-H bonds, is a good reducing agent. For example, it reduces AgNO3 to metallic silver.
\[4AgNO_3 + 2H_2O + H_3PO_2 → 4Ag + 4HNO_3 + H_3PO_4\]

docs.title: 3. Basicity
docs.text:
• The P-H bonds are not ionisable and play no role in basicity. Only the H atoms attached to oxygen (in P-OH) are ionisable and cause basicity.
Acid Number of P-OH bonds Basicity H3PO2 1 Monobasic H3PO3 2 Dibasic H3PO4 3 Tribasic

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Why does PCl3 fume in moisture?

PCl3 hydrolyses in the presence of moisture, giving fumes of HCl.

\[PCl_3 + 3H_2O → H_3PO_3 + 3HCl\]

Are all the five bonds in PCl5 molecule equivalent? Justify your answer.

No. PCl5 has a trigonal bipyramidal structure. The three equatorial P-Cl bonds are equivalent, while the two axial bonds are different and longer than the equatorial bonds, because the axial bond pairs suffer more repulsion from the other bond pairs.

What happens when PCl5 is heated?

On heating, PCl5 first sublimes, and on stronger heating it decomposes into phosphorus trichloride and chlorine.

\[PCl_5 \xrightarrow{Heat} PCl_3 + Cl_2\]

Write a balanced equation for the hydrolytic reaction of PCl5 in heavy water.

With a limited amount of heavy water (D2O), PCl5 gives POCl3 and DCl:

\[PCl_5 + D_2O → POCl_3 + 2DCl\]

With excess heavy water, complete hydrolysis takes place:

\[PCl_5 + 4D_2O → D_3PO_4 + 5DCl\]

How do you account for the reducing behaviour of H3PO2 on the basis of its structure?

In H3PO2, two H atoms are bonded directly to the P atom. These P-H bonds impart reducing character to the acid.

What is the basicity of H3PO4?

H3PO4 contains three P-OH bonds, and all three hydrogen atoms are ionisable. So, H3PO4 is tribasic.

What happens when H3PO3 is heated?

On heating, H3PO3 (phosphorus in +3 state) disproportionates to give orthophosphoric acid (+5) and phosphine (-3).

\[4H_3PO_3 → 3H_3PO_4 + PH_3\]

docs.title: Group 15 Elements | Physical and Atomic Properties
Group 15 Elements | Physical and Atomic Properties
Introduction
docs.text:
• The elements of group 15 are Nitrogen(N), Phosphorus(P), Arsenic(As), Antimony(Sb) and Bismuth(Bi).
  • Group 15 is also known as the nitrogen family.
  • On moving down the group, the character of the elements changes from non-metallic to metallic through metalloidic.
  • Nitrogen and phosphorus are non-metals, arsenic and antimony are metalloids and bismuth is a typical metal.

docs.title: Occurrence
docs.text:
• Nitrogen: Molecular nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere by volume. In the earth's crust, it occurs as sodium nitrate, NaNO3 (Chile saltpetre) and potassium nitrate, KNO3 (Indian saltpetre). It is also present in proteins of plants and animals.
  • Phosphorus: It occurs in minerals of the apatite family, Ca9(PO4)6.CaX2 (X = F, Cl or OH), for example fluorapatite Ca9(PO4)6.CaF2. These are the main components of phosphate rocks.
  • Phosphorus is an essential constituent of animal and plant matter. It is present in bones and in living cells. Phosphoproteins are present in milk and eggs.
  • Arsenic, antimony and bismuth are found mainly as sulphide minerals.
