  • BeO is amphoteric, while the oxides of the other elements are ionic and basic in nature.
  • All these oxides except BeO react with water to form sparingly soluble hydroxides.
\[MO + H_2O → M(OH)_2\]

docs.title: Hydroxides of alkaline earth metals
docs.text: • Hydroxides are obtained when the oxides react with water.

docs.title: Properties of hydroxides of alkaline earth metals
docs.text:
• The solubility, thermal stability and basic character of these hydroxides increase with increasing atomic number from Mg(OH)2 to Ba(OH)2.

Solubility, thermal stability and basic strength

\[Be(OH)_2 < Mg(OH)_2 < Ca(OH)_2 < Sr(OH)_2 < Ba(OH)_2\]
  • Alkaline earth metal hydroxides are less basic and less stable than alkali metal hydroxides.
  • Beryllium hydroxide is amphoteric in nature as it reacts with both acid and alkali.
\[Be(OH)_2 + 2OH^- → [Be(OH)_4]^{2-}\] \[(Beryllate\ ion)\] \[Be(OH)_2 + 2HCl + 2H_2O → [Be(OH)_4]Cl_2\]

docs.title: Halides of alkaline earth metals
docs.text:
• Except for beryllium halides, all other halides of alkaline earth metals are ionic in nature.
  • Beryllium halides are essentially covalent and soluble in organic solvents.

docs.title: Structure of Beryllium Chloride
docs.text:
• In the solid state, beryllium chloride has a chain structure in which each Be atom is bonded to four Cl atoms through chlorine bridges.
  • In the vapour phase, BeCl2 tends to form a chloro-bridged dimer, which dissociates into the linear monomer at high temperatures of the order of 1200 K.

Linear monomer in vapour phase

\[Cl - Be - Cl\]

docs.title: Properties of halides of alkaline earth metals
docs.text:
• The tendency to form halide hydrates gradually decreases down the group.

Example

MgCl2.8H2O, CaCl2.6H2O, SrCl2.6H2O and BaCl2.2H2O

  • The hydrated chlorides, bromides and iodides of Ca, Sr and Ba can be dehydrated by heating. However, the corresponding hydrated halides of Be and Mg undergo hydrolysis on heating.
  • The fluorides are relatively less soluble than the chlorides owing to their high lattice energies.

docs.title: Salts of oxoacids of alkaline earth metals
docs.text: • The alkaline earth metals also form salts of oxoacids, such as carbonates, sulphates and nitrates.

docs.title: 1. Carbonates
docs.text:
• Carbonates of alkaline earth metals are insoluble in water. They can be precipitated by adding a sodium or ammonium carbonate solution to a solution of a soluble salt of these metals.
  • The solubility of carbonates in water decreases as the atomic number of the metal ion increases.
  • All the carbonates decompose on heating to give carbon dioxide and the oxide.
\[MCO_3 + Heat → MO + CO_2\]
  • Beryllium carbonate is unstable and can be kept only in an atmosphere of CO2.
  • The thermal stability of carbonates increases with increasing cationic size.

Thermal stability

\[BeCO_3 < MgCO_3 < CaCO_3 < SrCO_3 < BaCO_3\]

docs.title: 2. Sulphates
docs.text:
• The sulphates of alkaline earth metals are all white solids and stable to heat.
  • BeSO4 and MgSO4 are readily soluble in water. The solubility decreases from CaSO4 to BaSO4.
  • The greater hydration enthalpies of Be2+ and Mg2+ ions overcome the lattice enthalpy factor and therefore their sulphates are soluble in water.

Solubility

\[BeSO_4 > MgSO_4 > CaSO_4 > SrSO_4 > BaSO_4\]

docs.title: 3. Nitrates
docs.text:
• Nitrates are made by dissolving the carbonates in dilute nitric acid.
  • Magnesium nitrate crystallizes with six molecules of water, whereas barium nitrate crystallizes as the anhydrous salt. This again shows the decreasing tendency to form hydrates with increasing size and decreasing hydration enthalpy.
  • All of them decompose on heating to give the oxide, like lithium nitrate.
\[2M(NO_3)_2 + Heat → 2MO + 4NO_2 + O_2\]

Here, M = Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Why does the solubility of alkaline earth metal hydroxides in water increase down the group?

  • Among alkaline earth metal hydroxides, the anion (OH-) is common. So the cationic radius decides the lattice enthalpy.
  • Lattice enthalpy decreases much more than the hydration enthalpy as the ionic size increases.
  • Since |hydration enthalpy| increasingly exceeds |lattice enthalpy| down the group, the solubility increases as we go down the group.

Why does the solubility of alkaline earth metal carbonates and sulphates in water decrease down the group?

  • The anions (CO32- and SO42-) are much larger than the cations. So the lattice enthalpy remains almost constant within the group.
  • Since the hydration enthalpies of the cations decrease down the group, the solubility of alkaline earth metal carbonates and sulphates decreases down the group.

Which one of the following alkaline earth metal carbonates is thermally the most stable?(a) MgCO3 (b) CaCO3 (c) SrCO3 (d) BaCO3

The thermal stability of carbonates increases with increasing cationic size. Ba2+ is the largest cation, so BaCO3 is thermally the most stable.

Answer: (d) BaCO3

docs.title: Alkaline Earth Metals | Some Important Compounds of Calcium
Alkaline Earth Metals | Some Important Compounds of Calcium
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss some important compounds of calcium like quick lime, slaked lime, calcium carbonate, plaster of paris and cement, and the biological importance of magnesium and calcium.

docs.title: Preparation of Calcium Oxide
docs.text:
• Calcium oxide is prepared on a commercial scale by heating limestone (CaCO3) in a rotary kiln at 1070-1270 K.
\[CaCO_3 + Heat ⇌ CaO + CO_2\]
  • The reaction is reversible, so carbon dioxide is removed as soon as it is produced. This allows the reaction to proceed to completion (Le Chatelier's principle).

docs.title: Properties of Calcium Oxide
docs.text:
• Calcium oxide is a white amorphous solid with a melting point of 2870 K.
  • On exposure to the atmosphere, it absorbs moisture and carbon dioxide.
\[CaO + H_2O → Ca(OH)_2\] \[CaO + CO_2 → CaCO_3\]
  • Adding a limited amount of water breaks up the lump of lime. This process is called slaking of lime.
  • Quick lime slaked with soda gives solid soda lime.
  • Being a basic oxide, CaO combines with acidic oxides at high temperature.
\[CaO + SiO_2 → CaSiO_3\] \[6CaO + P_4O_{10} → 2Ca_3(PO_4)_2\]

docs.title: Uses of Calcium Oxide
docs.text:
• It is an important primary material for manufacturing cement and is the cheapest form of alkali.
  • It is used in the manufacture of sodium carbonate from caustic soda.
  • It is used in the purification of sugar and in the manufacture of dye stuffs.

docs.title: Calcium Hydroxide or Slaked Lime (Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
• Calcium hydroxide is prepared by adding water to quick lime, CaO.
\[CaO + H_2O → Ca(OH)_2\]

docs.title: Properties of Calcium Hydroxide
docs.text:
• It is a white amorphous powder and is sparingly soluble in water.
  • Its aqueous solution is known as lime water and a suspension of slaked lime in water is known as milk of lime.
  • When carbon dioxide is passed through lime water, it turns milky due to the formation of insoluble calcium carbonate.
\[Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 → CaCO_3 ↓ + H_2O\]
  • On passing excess of carbon dioxide, the precipitate dissolves to form soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate and the milkiness disappears.
\[CaCO_3 + CO_2 + H_2O → Ca(HCO_3)_2\]
  • Milk of lime reacts with chlorine to form hypochlorite, a constituent of bleaching powder.
\[2Ca(OH)_2 + 2Cl_2 → CaCl_2 + Ca(OCl)_2 + 2H_2O\]

docs.title: Uses of Calcium Hydroxide
docs.text:
• It is used in the preparation of mortar, a building material.
  • It is used in white wash due to its disinfectant nature.
  • It is used in glass making, in the tanning industry, for the preparation of bleaching powder and for the purification of sugar.

docs.title: Calcium Carbonate (CaCO<sub>3</sub>)
docs.text: • Calcium carbonate occurs in nature in several forms like limestone, chalk and marble.

docs.title: Preparation of Calcium Carbonate
docs.text:
• It can be prepared by passing carbon dioxide through slaked lime or by adding sodium carbonate to calcium chloride.
\[Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 → CaCO_3 + H_2O\] \[CaCl_2 + Na_2CO_3 → CaCO_3 + 2NaCl\]
  • Excess of carbon dioxide should be avoided, since it leads to the formation of water soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate.

docs.title: Properties of Calcium Carbonate
docs.text:
• Calcium carbonate is a white fluffy powder which is almost insoluble in water.
  • When heated to 1200 K, it decomposes to evolve carbon dioxide.
\[CaCO_3 + Heat\ (1200\ K) → CaO + CO_2\]
  • It reacts with dilute acids to liberate carbon dioxide.
\[CaCO_3 + 2HCl → CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\] \[CaCO_3 + H_2SO_4 → CaSO_4 + H_2O + CO_2\]

docs.title: Uses of Calcium Carbonate
docs.text:
• It is used as a building material in the form of marble and in the manufacture of quick lime.
  • Calcium carbonate along with magnesium carbonate is used as a flux in the extraction of metals such as iron.
  • Specially precipitated CaCO3 is used extensively in the manufacture of high quality paper.
  • It is also used as an antacid, a mild abrasive in tooth paste, a constituent of chewing gum and a filler in cosmetics.

docs.title: Calcium Sulphate or Plaster of Paris (CaSO<sub>4</sub>.½H<sub>2</sub>O)
docs.text: • Plaster of Paris is a hemihydrate of calcium sulphate: one molecule of water is shared between two units of CaSO4.

docs.title: Preparation of Plaster of Paris
docs.text:
• It is obtained when gypsum, CaSO4.2H2O, is heated to 393 K.
\[2(CaSO_4.2H_2O) + Heat\ (393\ K) → 2(CaSO_4).H_2O + 3H_2O\]
  • Above 393 K, no water of crystallization is left and anhydrous calcium sulphate, CaSO4, is formed. This is known as dead burnt plaster.

docs.title: Properties of Plaster of Paris
docs.text: • It has a remarkable property of setting with water. On mixing with an adequate quantity of water, it forms a plastic mass that sets into a hard solid in 5 to 15 minutes.

docs.title: Uses of Plaster of Paris
docs.text:
• Its largest use is in the building industry as well as in plasters.
  • It is used for immobilizing the affected part of the body where there is a bone fracture or sprain.
  • It is also employed in dentistry, in ornamental work and for making casts of statues and busts.

docs.title: Cement
docs.text:
• Cement is an important building material. It was first introduced in England in 1824 by Joseph Aspdin.
  • It is also called Portland cement because it resembles the natural limestone quarried in the Isle of Portland, England.
  • Cement is obtained by combining a material rich in lime, CaO, with other material such as clay which contains silica, SiO2, along with the oxides of aluminium, iron and magnesium.

docs.title: Composition of Portland Cement
docs.text:
Constituent Percentage CaO 50-60% SiO2 20-25% Al2O3 5-10% MgO 2-3% Fe2O3 1-2% SO3 1-2%
  • For a good quality cement, the following ratios should be maintained:
\[{SiO_2 \over Al_2O_3} = 2.5\ to\ 4\] \[{CaO \over SiO_2 + Al_2O_3 + Fe_2O_3} ≈ 2\]

docs.title: Manufacture of Cement
docs.text:
• The raw materials for the manufacture of cement are limestone and clay.
  • When clay and lime are strongly heated together, they fuse and react to form cement clinker.
  • This clinker is mixed with 2-3% by weight of gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O) to form cement.
  • The important ingredients present in Portland cement are dicalcium silicate (Ca2SiO4) 26%, tricalcium silicate (Ca3SiO5) 51% and tricalcium aluminate (Ca3Al2O6) 11%.

docs.title: Setting of Cement
docs.text:
• When mixed with water, cement sets to give a hard mass. This is due to the hydration of the molecules of the constituents and their rearrangement.
  • Gypsum is added only to slow down the process of setting of cement so that it gets sufficiently hardened.

docs.title: Uses of Cement
docs.text:
• Cement is a commodity of national necessity for any country, next to iron and steel.
  • It is used in concrete and reinforced concrete, in plastering and in the construction of bridges, dams and buildings.

docs.title: Biological Importance of Magnesium and Calcium
docs.text: • An adult body contains about 25 g of Mg and 1200 g of Ca, compared with only 5 g of iron and 0.06 g of copper. The daily requirement in the human body is estimated to be 200-300 mg.

docs.title: Magnesium
docs.text:
• All enzymes that utilise ATP in phosphate transfer require magnesium as the cofactor.
  • Chlorophyll, the main pigment for the absorption of light in plants, contains magnesium.

docs.title: Calcium
docs.text:
• About 99% of body calcium is present in bones and teeth.
  • It plays important roles in neuromuscular function, interneuronal transmission, cell membrane integrity and blood coagulation.
  • The calcium concentration in plasma is regulated at about 100 mg L-1. It is maintained by two hormones: calcitonin and parathyroid hormone.
  • Bone is not an inert and unchanging substance. It is continuously being solubilised and redeposited to the extent of about 400 mg per day in man, and all this calcium passes through the plasma.

docs.title: Alkaline Earth Metals | General Characteristics
docs.text: Group 2 elements are known as alkaline earth metals. These include Beryllium(Be), Magnesium(Mg), Calcium(Ca), Strontium(Sr), Barium(Ba) and Radium(Ra).

docs.title: Group 2 Elements
docs.text:
• Group 2 elements follow the alkali metals in the periodic table.
  • With the exception of beryllium, these elements are called alkaline earth metals because their oxides and hydroxides are alkaline in nature and these metal oxides are found in the earth's crust.
  • Calcium and magnesium are the fifth and sixth most abundant elements in the earth's crust. Strontium and barium are much less abundant.
  • Beryllium is rare and radium is the rarest of all, making up only about 10-10 per cent of igneous rocks.
  • The first element, beryllium, differs from the rest of the group and shows a diagonal relationship with aluminium.

docs.title: Electronic configuration of Alkaline Earth Metals
docs.text:
General electronic configuration is [noble gas]ns2

\[Be → 1s^2\ 2s^2\ or\ [He]2s^2\] \[Mg → 1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^2\ or\ [Ne]3s^2\] \[Ca → 1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^2\ 3p^6\ 4s^2\ or\ [Ar]4s^2\] \[Sr → [Kr]5s^2\] \[Ba → [Xe]6s^2\] \[Ra → [Rn]7s^2\]
  • These elements have two electrons in the s-orbital of the valence shell. They lose both of them to form dipositive M2+ ions.
  • Like alkali metals, the compounds of alkaline earth metals are also predominantly ionic.

docs.title: Atomic and Ionic radii of Alkaline Earth Metals
docs.text:
• The atomic and ionic radii of alkaline earth metals are smaller than those of the corresponding alkali metals in the same period. This is due to the increased nuclear charge in these elements, which pulls the electrons closer.
  • Within the group, atomic and ionic radii increase with increase in atomic number because a new shell is added at each step down the group.
Element Metallic radius / pm Ionic radius M2+ / pm Be 112 31 Mg 160 72 Ca 197 100 Sr 215 118 Ba 222 135 Ra - 148

docs.title: Ionization Enthalpy of Alkaline Earth Metals
docs.text:
• The alkaline earth metals have low ionization enthalpies due to the fairly large size of their atoms.
  • Ionization enthalpy decreases down the group because atomic size increases down the group.
  • The first ionization enthalpies of alkaline earth metals are higher than those of the corresponding group 1 metals. This is due to their smaller size; the electron is held more tightly by the nucleus. Also, removing an electron from a filled ns2 subshell requires more energy.
  • Interestingly, the second ionization enthalpies of alkaline earth metals are smaller than those of the corresponding alkali metals. For an alkali metal, the second electron has to be removed from a stable noble gas core, while for an alkaline earth metal the second electron still comes from the valence s-orbital.
Element ΔiH1 / kJ mol-1 ΔiH2 / kJ mol-1 Be 899 1757 Mg 737 1450 Ca 590 1145 Sr 549 1064 Ba 503 965 Ra 509 979

docs.title: Hydration Enthalpy of Alkaline Earth Metal Cations
docs.text:
• Like alkali metal ions, the hydration enthalpies of alkaline earth metal ions decrease with increase in ionic size down the group.
\[Be^{2+} > Mg^{2+} > Ca^{2+} > Sr^{2+} > Ba^{2+}\]
  • The hydration enthalpies of alkaline earth metal ions are larger than those of alkali metal ions because of their smaller size and higher (+2) charge.
  • Therefore, compounds of alkaline earth metals are more extensively hydrated than those of alkali metals.

Example

MgCl2 and CaCl2 exist as MgCl2.6H2O and CaCl2.6H2O, while NaCl and KCl do not form such hydrates.

Element Hydration enthalpy / kJ mol-1 Be -2494 Mg -1921 Ca -1577 Sr -1443 Ba -1305

docs.title: Alkaline Earth Metals | Physical Characteristics
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the physical properties of alkaline earth metals like appearance, density, melting and boiling points, electropositive character and characteristic flame test.

docs.title: Appearance and Hardness
docs.text:
• The alkaline earth metals are, in general, silvery white, lustrous and relatively soft.
  • However, they are harder than the alkali metals because they have two valence electrons, which gives stronger metallic bonding.
  • Beryllium and magnesium appear to be somewhat greyish.

docs.title: Density of Alkaline Earth Metals
docs.text:
• Alkaline earth metals are denser than the corresponding alkali metals because of their smaller size and greater atomic mass.
  • Density first decreases from Be to Ca and then increases up to Ra.
Element Density / g cm-3 Be 1.84 Mg 1.74 Ca 1.55 Sr 2.63 Ba 3.59 Ra (5.5)

docs.title: Melting and Boiling Points of Alkaline Earth Metals
docs.text:
• The melting and boiling points of alkaline earth metals are higher than those of the corresponding alkali metals. This is due to their smaller size and two valence electrons, which make metallic bonding stronger.
  • The trend down the group is, however, not systematic. Beryllium has the highest melting point and magnesium has the lowest.
Element m.p. / K b.p. / K Be 1560 2745 Mg 924 1363 Ca 1124 1767 Sr 1062 1655 Ba 1002 2078 Ra 973 (1973)

docs.title: Electropositive Character
docs.text:
• Because of their low ionization enthalpies, alkaline earth metals are strongly electropositive in nature.
  • Electropositive character increases down the group from Be to Ba as the ionization enthalpy decreases.
\[Be < Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba\]

docs.title: Characteristic flame test of Alkaline Earth Metals
docs.text:
• Calcium, strontium and barium impart characteristic colours to the flame.
  • In the flame, the valence electrons are excited to higher energy levels. When they drop back to the ground state, energy is emitted in the form of visible light.
Metal Characteristic Colour to flame Ca Brick red Sr Crimson Ba Apple green
  • The electrons in beryllium and magnesium are too strongly bound (because of their small size and high ionization enthalpy) to get excited by the energy of the flame. Hence, Be and Mg do not impart any colour to the flame.
  • The flame test for Ca, Sr and Ba is useful for their detection in qualitative analysis and for their estimation by flame photometry.

docs.title: Conductivity
docs.text: • Like alkali metals, the alkaline earth metals have high electrical and thermal conductivities, which are typical characteristics of metals.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Compare the alkali metals and alkaline earth metals with respect to (i) ionization enthalpy (ii) basicity of oxides and (iii) solubility of hydroxides.

  • Ionization enthalpy: The first ionization enthalpy of alkaline earth metals is higher than that of the corresponding alkali metals because of their smaller size and higher nuclear charge. However, their second ionization enthalpy is lower than that of alkali metals, since an alkali metal has to lose its second electron from a stable noble gas core.
  • Basicity of oxides: Alkali metal oxides are more basic than alkaline earth metal oxides. Alkali metals are more electropositive, so their oxides are more ionic. BeO is even amphoteric.
  • Solubility of hydroxides: Alkali metal hydroxides are highly soluble in water, while alkaline earth metal hydroxides are only sparingly soluble. The M2+ ions are smaller and doubly charged, so the lattice enthalpies of their hydroxides are much higher.

Explain why alkali and alkaline earth metals cannot be obtained by chemical reduction methods.

  • Alkali and alkaline earth metals are themselves among the strongest reducing agents (large negative E0 values).
  • Their oxides and halides are very stable, so no common chemical reducing agent is strong enough to reduce them to the metal.
  • Therefore, these metals are obtained by electrolysis of their fused chlorides.

Beryllium and magnesium do not give colour to flame whereas other alkaline earth metals do so. Why?

Be and Mg are small atoms with high ionization enthalpies. Their valence electrons are held so strongly that the energy of the flame is not enough to excite them to higher energy levels. Hence, no visible light is emitted and they do not colour the flame. In Ca, Sr and Ba, the electrons are excited easily and emit visible light (brick red, crimson and apple green respectively) when they return to the ground state.

Compare the solubility and thermal stability of the following compounds of the alkali metals with those of the alkaline earth metals: (a) Nitrates (b) Carbonates (c) Sulphates.

  • Nitrates: Nitrates of both groups are soluble in water. Alkali metal nitrates (except LiNO3) decompose on heating to give nitrites, while alkaline earth metal nitrates decompose to give oxides.
\[2NaNO_3 → 2NaNO_2 + O_2\] \[2M(NO_3)_2 → 2MO + 4NO_2 + O_2\]
  • Carbonates: Alkali metal carbonates are soluble in water and thermally stable (except Li2CO3). Alkaline earth metal carbonates are insoluble in water and decompose on heating to give the oxide and CO2. Their thermal stability increases down the group.
\[MCO_3 → MO + CO_2\]
  • Sulphates: Alkali metal sulphates are soluble in water and thermally stable. Among alkaline earth metal sulphates, BeSO4 and MgSO4 are soluble, but the solubility decreases from CaSO4 to BaSO4. They are also stable to heat.

What happens when (i) magnesium is burnt in air (ii) quick lime is heated with silica (iii) chlorine reacts with slaked lime (iv) calcium nitrate is heated?

  • (i) Magnesium burns with dazzling brilliance to form magnesium oxide and magnesium nitride.
\[2Mg + O_2 → 2MgO\] \[3Mg + N_2 → Mg_3N_2\]
  • (ii) Calcium silicate is formed.
\[CaO + SiO_2 → CaSiO_3\]
  • (iii) Bleaching powder is formed.
\[2Ca(OH)_2 + 2Cl_2 → CaCl_2 + Ca(OCl)_2 + 2H_2O\]
  • (iv) Calcium oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen are formed.
\[2Ca(NO_3)_2 → 2CaO + 4NO_2 + O_2\]

Draw the structure of (i) BeCl2 (vapour) (ii) BeCl2 (solid).

  • (i) In the vapour phase, BeCl2 exists as a chloro-bridged dimer, which dissociates at about 1200 K into a linear monomer:
\[Cl - Be - Cl\]
  • (ii) In the solid state, BeCl2 has a polymeric chain structure in which each Be is bonded to four Cl atoms through chlorine bridges:

The hydroxides and carbonates of sodium and potassium are easily soluble in water while the corresponding salts of magnesium and calcium are sparingly soluble in water. Explain.

  • A salt dissolves when its hydration enthalpy is greater than its lattice enthalpy.
  • Mg2+ and Ca2+ are smaller and carry a double charge compared with Na+ and K+. Hence the lattice enthalpies of their hydroxides and carbonates are much higher.
  • For Mg and Ca salts, the high lattice enthalpy is not overcome by hydration enthalpy, so they are sparingly soluble. For Na and K salts, the lattice enthalpy is lower and hydration enthalpy wins, so they dissolve easily.

Describe the importance of the following: (i) limestone (ii) cement (iii) plaster of paris.

  • (i) Limestone (CaCO3): It is used as a building material (marble), in the manufacture of quick lime and cement, as a flux in the extraction of iron, and (when specially precipitated) in paper making, tooth paste, antacids and cosmetics.
  • (ii) Cement: It is a commodity of national necessity next to iron and steel. It is used in concrete and reinforced concrete, in plastering and in the construction of bridges, dams and buildings.
  • (iii) Plaster of Paris: It sets into a hard mass with water. It is used in the building industry and in plasters, for immobilizing fractured bones, in dentistry, in ornamental work and for making casts of statues and busts.

Explain the significance of magnesium and calcium in biological fluids.

  • Magnesium: All enzymes that use ATP in phosphate transfer require Mg2+ as a cofactor. Chlorophyll in plants contains magnesium.
  • Calcium: About 99% of body calcium is in bones and teeth. Ca2+ plays important roles in neuromuscular function, interneuronal transmission, cell membrane integrity and blood coagulation. Its plasma concentration (about 100 mg L-1) is maintained by calcitonin and parathyroid hormone.

Comment on the observation: E0 for M2+(aq) + 2e- → M(s) (where M = Ca, Sr or Ba) is nearly constant.

  • The electrode potential depends on the sublimation enthalpy, ionization enthalpy and hydration enthalpy of the metal.
  • From Ca to Ba, the sublimation and ionization enthalpies decrease, which favours oxidation. At the same time, the hydration enthalpy of M2+ also decreases, which opposes it.
  • These effects nearly cancel each other, so E0 values for Ca, Sr and Ba are nearly constant (-2.84 V, -2.89 V and -2.92 V).

How would you explain the following observations?(i) BeO is almost insoluble but BeSO4 is soluble in water.(ii) BaO is soluble but BaSO4 is insoluble in water.

  • (i) Be2+ and O2- are both small, so BeO has a very high lattice enthalpy (and is largely covalent). Its hydration enthalpy cannot overcome this, so BeO is almost insoluble. In BeSO4, the large SO42- ion lowers the lattice enthalpy, while the very high hydration enthalpy of the small Be2+ ion is enough to overcome it. Hence BeSO4 is soluble.
  • (ii) In BaO, the large Ba2+ and small O2- give a relatively low lattice enthalpy, which is overcome by hydration; BaO also reacts with water to form soluble Ba(OH)2. In BaSO4, the large SO42- ion keeps the lattice enthalpy almost constant, but the hydration enthalpy of the large Ba2+ ion is too small to overcome it. Hence BaSO4 is insoluble.

docs.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Ethers
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the preparation, physical properties and chemical reactions of ethers (R–O–R', Ar–O–R).

docs.title: 1. By Dehydration of Alcohols
docs.text:
• Alcohols are dehydrated by protic acids (H2SO4, H3PO4). Whether an alkene or an ether is formed depends on the conditions.
  • For example, ethanol gives ethene with H2SO4 at 443 K, but at 413 K ethoxyethane is the main product.
\[CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4,\ 443\ K} CH_2=CH_2\] \[CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4,\ 413\ K} C_2H_5OC_2H_5\]

Mechanism: Formation of ether is a nucleophilic bimolecular reaction (SN2), in which an alcohol molecule attacks a protonated alcohol.

\[(i)\ CH_3-CH_2-\ddot{O}-H + H^+ → CH_3-CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2\] \[(ii)\ CH_3CH_2-\ddot{O}H + CH_3-CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2 → CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}(H)-CH_2CH_3 + H_2O\] \[(iii)\ CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}(H)-CH_2CH_3 → CH_3CH_2-O-CH_2CH_3 + H^+\]
  • Acidic dehydration of alcohols to alkenes is always accompanied by this substitution reaction giving an ether.
  • This method is suitable only for ethers with primary alkyl groups. The alkyl group should be unhindered and the temperature kept low; otherwise alkene formation is favoured.
  • With secondary and tertiary alcohols, the reaction follows an SN1 pathway, and elimination competes over substitution. So alkenes are formed easily and the method fails for such ethers.
  • The method is also not suitable for unsymmetrical ethers such as ethyl methyl ether. A mixture of two different alcohols would give a mixture of three ethers (dimethyl, diethyl and ethyl methyl ether).

docs.title: 2. Williamson Synthesis
docs.text:
• This is an important laboratory method for preparing both symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers.
  • An alkyl halide is allowed to react with a sodium alkoxide.
\[R-X + R'-\ddot{O}Na → R-\ddot{O}-R' + NaX\]
  • Ethers containing secondary or tertiary alkyl groups can also be made. The reaction involves SN2 attack of an alkoxide ion on a primary alkyl halide.
\[(CH_3)_3C-O^-Na^+ + CH_3-Br → CH_3-O-C(CH_3)_3 + NaBr\]
  • Best results are obtained with primary alkyl halides. With secondary and tertiary alkyl halides, elimination competes over substitution.
  • With a tertiary alkyl halide, an alkene is the only product. For example, CH3ONa with (CH3)3C–Br gives only 2-methylpropene:
\[(CH_3)_3C-Br + Na^+\ ^-O-CH_3 → CH_3-C(CH_3)=CH_2 + NaBr + CH_3OH\]
  • This happens because alkoxides are not only nucleophiles but also strong bases, and they bring about elimination with hindered alkyl halides.

Conclusion

In Williamson synthesis, the bulky (secondary/tertiary) group should come from the alkoxide, and the alkyl halide should be primary (or methyl).

  • Phenols are also converted to ethers by this method, using the phenoxide ion as the nucleophile.
\[C_6H_5OH + NaOH → C_6H_5O^-Na^+ + H_2O\] \[C_6H_5O^-Na^+ + R-X → C_6H_5-O-R + NaX\]
  • An aryl halide cannot be used as the halide component, because aryl halides do not undergo SN2 reactions easily.

docs.title: Physical Properties of Ethers
docs.text:
• The C–O bonds in ethers are polar, so ethers have a net dipole moment. However, this weak polarity hardly affects their boiling points.
  • Boiling points of ethers are comparable to those of alkanes of similar molecular mass, and much lower than those of alcohols:
Compound Formula b.p./K n-Pentane CH3(CH2)3CH3 309.1 Ethoxyethane C2H5–O–C2H5 307.6 Butan-1-ol CH3(CH2)3–OH 390
  • The large difference between alcohols and ethers is due to hydrogen bonding in alcohols, which is absent between ether molecules.
  • Solubility: Miscibility of ethers with water is similar to that of alcohols of the same molecular mass. Ethoxyethane and butan-1-ol dissolve to almost the same extent (7.5 g and 9 g per 100 mL of water respectively), while pentane is essentially immiscible.
  • This is because the oxygen of an ether can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules (R2O···H–O–H), just as alcohols do.

Note

Diethyl ether was widely used as an inhalation anaesthetic. Due to its slow effect and unpleasant recovery period, it has been replaced by other compounds.

docs.title: 1. Cleavage of C–O Bond in Ethers
docs.text:
• Ethers are the least reactive of these functional groups. Their C–O bond is cleaved only under drastic conditions, with excess hydrogen halide.
  • A dialkyl ether gives two molecules of alkyl halide:
\[R-O-R + HX → RX + R-OH\] \[R-OH + HX → R-X + H_2O\]
  • Ethers with two different alkyl groups are cleaved in the same manner:
\[R-O-R' + HX → R-X + R'-OH\]
  • Order of reactivity of hydrogen halides: HI > HBr > HCl. Cleavage is carried out with concentrated HI or HBr at high temperature.

docs.title: Mechanism (reaction of an ether with concentrated HI)
docs.text:
• Step 1: The ether is protonated. HBr and HI are acidic enough for this.
\[CH_3-\ddot{O}-CH_2CH_3 + H-I ⇌ CH_3-\overset{+}{O}(H)-CH_2CH_3 + I^-\]
  • Step 2: Iodide is a good nucleophile. It attacks the least substituted carbon of the oxonium ion and displaces an alcohol molecule by SN2 mechanism.
\[I^- + CH_3-\overset{+}{O}(H)-CH_2CH_3 → [I\cdots CH_3\cdots \overset{+}{O}(H)CH_2CH_3]^{-} → CH_3-I + CH_3CH_2-OH\]
  • Step 3: With excess HI at high temperature, the ethanol formed reacts with another HI molecule to give ethyl iodide.
\[CH_3CH_2-OH + H-I ⇌ CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2 + I^-\] \[I^- + CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2 → CH_3CH_2I + H_2O\]
  • So in mixed ethers with primary or secondary alkyl groups, it is the smaller alkyl group that forms the alkyl iodide (SN2).

docs.title: When one group is tertiary
docs.text:
• If one alkyl group is tertiary, the halide formed is a tertiary halide.
\[(CH_3)_3C-O-CH_3 + HI → CH_3OH + (CH_3)_3C-I\]
  • Here, in step 2, the leaving group (HO–CH3) departs to give a stable tertiary carbocation, (CH3)3C+, so the reaction follows an SN1 mechanism.
\[(CH_3)_3C-\overset{+}{O}(H)-CH_3 \xrightarrow{slow} (CH_3)_3C^+ + CH_3OH\] \[(CH_3)_3C^+ + I^- \xrightarrow{fast} (CH_3)_3C-I\]

docs.title: Alkyl aryl ethers
docs.text:
• Alkyl aryl ethers are cleaved at the alkyl–oxygen bond, giving a phenol and an alkyl halide.
\[C_6H_5-O-R + H-X → C_6H_5OH + R-X\]
  • In anisole, protonation gives the methylphenyl oxonium ion, C6H5–O+(H)–CH3. The O–C6H5 bond is stronger than the O–CH3 bond, because the phenyl carbon is sp2 hybridised and the bond has partial double bond character. So I- breaks the O–CH3 bond to form CH3I.
  • The phenol formed does not react further to give an aryl halide, because the sp2 carbon of phenol cannot undergo the nucleophilic substitution needed.

docs.title: 2. Electrophilic Substitution in Aromatic Ethers
docs.text: • The alkoxy group (–OR) activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and is ortho, para directing, in the same way as the –OH group in phenol. Resonance increases the electron density at ortho and para positions:

docs.title: (i) Halogenation
docs.text:
• Anisole undergoes bromination with bromine in ethanoic acid even without an iron(III) bromide catalyst, because the methoxy group strongly activates the ring. The para isomer is obtained in 90% yield.
\[C_6H_5OCH_3 \xrightarrow{Br_2\ in\ ethanoic\ acid} p-BrC_6H_4OCH_3\ (major) + o-BrC_6H_4OCH_3\ (minor)\]

docs.title: (ii) Friedel-Crafts reaction
docs.text:
• Alkyl and acyl groups are introduced at ortho and para positions by reaction with an alkyl halide or acyl halide, in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3 (a Lewis acid) as catalyst.
\[C_6H_5OCH_3 + CH_3Cl \xrightarrow{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3,\ CS_2} p-CH_3C_6H_4OCH_3\ (major) + o-CH_3C_6H_4OCH_3\ (minor)\] \[(4-Methoxytoluene\ and\ 2-methoxytoluene)\] \[C_6H_5OCH_3 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} p-CH_3COC_6H_4OCH_3\ (major) + o-CH_3COC_6H_4OCH_3\ (minor)\] \[(4-Methoxyacetophenone\ and\ 2-methoxyacetophenone)\]

docs.title: (iii) Nitration
docs.text:
• Anisole reacts with a mixture of concentrated H2SO4 and HNO3 to give a mixture of ortho- and para-nitroanisole.
\[C_6H_5OCH_3 \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4,\ HNO_3} p-O_2NC_6H_4OCH_3\ (major) + o-O_2NC_6H_4OCH_3\ (minor)\] \[(4-Nitroanisole\ and\ 2-nitroanisole)\]

docs.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Introduction and Nomenclature
Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Introduction and Nomenclature
Introduction
docs.text:
• When a hydrogen atom of a hydrocarbon is replaced by an –OH group, we get an alcohol (if the hydrocarbon is aliphatic) or a phenol (if the hydrocarbon is aromatic).
  • An alcohol contains one or more hydroxyl (–OH) groups directly attached to carbon atom(s) of an aliphatic system. Example: CH3OH.
  • A phenol contains –OH group(s) directly attached to carbon atom(s) of an aromatic ring. Example: C6H5OH.
  • When a hydrogen atom of a hydrocarbon is replaced by an alkoxy or aryloxy group (R–O– or Ar–O–), we get an ether. Example: CH3OCH3 (dimethyl ether).
  • An ether can also be pictured as an alcohol or phenol in which the hydrogen of the –OH group has been replaced by an alkyl or aryl group.
  • These compounds are everywhere: ethanol is the main component of spirit used for polishing furniture, and sugar, cotton and paper are all made of compounds containing –OH groups. Alcohols, phenols and ethers are also the basic compounds used for making detergents, antiseptics and fragrances respectively.

docs.title: 1. Mono, Di, Tri or Polyhydric Compounds
docs.text:
Alcohols and phenols are classified as mono-, di-, tri- or polyhydric depending on whether they contain one, two, three or many –OH groups.

Type Alcohol example Phenol example Monohydric C2H5OH Phenol, C6H5OH Dihydric HOCH2–CH2OH (ethane-1,2-diol) Benzene-1,2-diol (catechol) Trihydric HOCH2–CH(OH)–CH2OH (glycerol) Benzene-1,2,4-triol

docs.title: 2. Classification based on hybridisation of carbon bearing –OH
docs.text: Monohydric alcohols are further classified according to the hybridisation of the carbon atom to which the –OH group is attached.

docs.title: (i) Compounds containing C<sub>sp<sup>3</sup></sub>–OH bond
docs.text:
The –OH group is attached to an sp3 hybridised carbon of an alkyl group. These are of the following types:

  • Primary (1°), secondary (2°) and tertiary (3°) alcohols: The –OH group is attached to a primary, secondary or tertiary carbon atom respectively.
\[Primary\ (1^0):\ RCH_2-OH\] \[Secondary\ (2^0):\ R_2CH-OH\] \[Tertiary\ (3^0):\ R_3C-OH\]
  • Allylic alcohols: The –OH group is attached to an sp3 carbon next to a C=C double bond, i.e. to an allylic carbon. Example: CH2=CH–CH2–OH (a primary allylic alcohol).
  • Benzylic alcohols: The –OH group is attached to an sp3 carbon next to an aromatic ring. Example: C6H5CH2OH (a primary benzylic alcohol).
  • Allylic and benzylic alcohols can themselves be primary, secondary or tertiary, depending on how many carbons are attached to the carbinol carbon (the carbon carrying –OH).

docs.title: (ii) Compounds containing C<sub>sp<sup>2</sup></sub>–OH bond
docs.text:
• Here the –OH group is attached to a carbon of a C=C double bond (a vinylic carbon) or to an aryl carbon. These are known as vinylic alcohols.
  • Vinylic alcohol: CH2=CH–OH
  • Phenols: C6H5OH, o-CH3C6H4OH (o-cresol), etc.

docs.title: Classification of Ethers
docs.text:
• Simple or symmetrical ethers: Both groups attached to oxygen are the same. Example: diethyl ether, C2H5OC2H5.
  • Mixed or unsymmetrical ethers: The two groups attached to oxygen are different. Examples: C2H5OCH3 and C2H5OC6H5.

docs.title: Nomenclature of Alcohols
docs.text:
• Common name: Name of the alkyl group followed by the word "alcohol". Example: CH3OH is methyl alcohol.
  • IUPAC name: Replace the ending 'e' of the parent alkane with the suffix 'ol'.
  • The longest carbon chain containing the –OH group is the parent chain. It is numbered from the end nearest to the –OH group, and positions of –OH and other substituents are shown by locants.
  • For polyhydric alcohols, the 'e' of the alkane is retained and a multiplicative prefix (di, tri, ...) is added before 'ol'. Example: HO–CH2–CH2–OH is ethane-1,2-diol.
  • Cyclic alcohols use the prefix cyclo, and the carbon carrying –OH is taken as C-1. Examples: cyclohexanol, 2-methylcyclopentanol.
Compound Common name IUPAC name CH3–OH Methyl alcohol Methanol CH3–CH2–CH2–OH n-Propyl alcohol Propan-1-ol CH3–CH(OH)–CH3 Isopropyl alcohol Propan-2-ol CH3–CH2–CH2–CH2–OH n-Butyl alcohol Butan-1-ol CH3–CH(OH)–CH2–CH3 sec-Butyl alcohol Butan-2-ol (CH3)2CH–CH2–OH Isobutyl alcohol 2-Methylpropan-1-ol (CH3)3C–OH tert-Butyl alcohol 2-Methylpropan-2-ol HOCH2–CH(OH)–CH2OH Glycerol Propane-1,2,3-triol

docs.title: Nomenclature of Phenols
docs.text:
• The simplest hydroxy derivative of benzene is phenol. "Phenol" is both its common name and an accepted IUPAC name.
  • In common names of substituted phenols, the terms ortho (1,2-), meta (1,3-) and para (1,4-) are used.
Compound Common name IUPAC name C6H5OH Phenol Phenol o-CH3C6H4OH o-Cresol 2-Methylphenol m-CH3C6H4OH m-Cresol 3-Methylphenol p-CH3C6H4OH p-Cresol 4-Methylphenol o-C6H4(OH)2 Catechol Benzene-1,2-diol m-C6H4(OH)2 Resorcinol Benzene-1,3-diol p-C6H4(OH)2 Hydroquinone or quinol Benzene-1,4-diol

docs.title: Nomenclature of Ethers
docs.text:
• Common name: Names of the two alkyl/aryl groups are written as separate words in alphabetical order, followed by the word "ether". Example: CH3OC2H5 is ethylmethyl ether. If both groups are the same, the prefix 'di' is used, e.g. diethyl ether.
  • IUPAC name: An ether is treated as a hydrocarbon in which one hydrogen is replaced by an –OR or –OAr group (alkoxy or aryloxy). The larger group is chosen as the parent hydrocarbon, and the smaller one is named as the alkoxy substituent.
Compound Common name IUPAC name CH3OCH3 Dimethyl ether Methoxymethane C2H5OC2H5 Diethyl ether Ethoxyethane CH3OCH2CH2CH3 Methyl n-propyl ether 1-Methoxypropane C6H5OCH3 Methylphenyl ether (Anisole) Methoxybenzene (Anisole) C6H5OCH2CH3 Ethylphenyl ether (Phenetole) Ethoxybenzene C6H5O(CH2)6–CH3 Heptylphenyl ether 1-Phenoxyheptane CH3O–CH(CH3)–CH3 Methyl isopropyl ether 2-Methoxypropane C6H5–O–CH2–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH3 Phenylisopentyl ether 3-Methylbutoxybenzene CH3–O–CH2–CH2–OCH3 – 1,2-Dimethoxyethane

docs.title: 1. Alcohols
docs.text:
• The oxygen of the –OH group is bonded to carbon by a sigma bond formed by overlap of an sp3 hybrid orbital of carbon with an sp3 hybrid orbital of oxygen.
  • The C–O–H bond angle (108.9° in methanol) is slightly less than the tetrahedral angle (109°28'). This is because the two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bond pairs and squeeze the angle.
  • In methanol, C–O bond length = 142 pm and O–H bond length = 96 pm.

docs.title: 2. Phenols
docs.text:
• The –OH group is attached to an sp2 hybridised carbon of the aromatic ring.
  • The C–O bond length in phenol (136 pm) is slightly less than in methanol. This is due to:
    • partial double bond character, because the lone pair of oxygen is in conjugation with the aromatic ring, and
    • the sp2 hybridised state of the carbon to which oxygen is attached.

docs.title: 3. Ethers
docs.text:
• The four electron pairs on oxygen (two bond pairs and two lone pairs) are arranged approximately tetrahedrally.
  • The C–O–C bond angle (111.7° in methoxymethane) is slightly greater than the tetrahedral angle, because of repulsion between the two bulky –R groups.
  • The C–O bond length (141 pm) is almost the same as in alcohols.

docs.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Physical Properties and Acidity
Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Physical Properties and Acidity
docs.text: Alcohols and phenols consist of two parts: an alkyl/aryl group and a hydroxyl group. Their properties are chiefly due to the –OH group; the alkyl or aryl group only modifies these properties.

docs.title: Physical Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
1. Boiling Points
docs.text:
• Boiling points increase with increase in the number of carbon atoms, because van der Waals forces increase.
  • In alcohols, boiling points decrease with increase in branching. Branching reduces the surface area and hence the van der Waals forces.
  • The –OH group of alcohols and phenols takes part in intermolecular hydrogen bonding:
  • Because of this hydrogen bonding, alcohols and phenols boil at much higher temperatures than hydrocarbons, ethers, haloalkanes and haloarenes of comparable molecular masses.
Compound Formula Molecular mass Boiling point Ethanol CH3CH2OH 46 351 K Methoxymethane CH3OCH3 46 248 K Propane CH3CH2CH3 44 231 K
  • Ethanol and propane have similar molecular masses but very different boiling points. Methoxymethane (polar, but with no O–H hydrogen) lies in between.

docs.title: 2. Solubility
docs.text:
• Alcohols and phenols are soluble in water because they can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
  • Solubility decreases as the size of the alkyl/aryl (hydrophobic) group increases.
  • Several lower alcohols are miscible with water in all proportions.

docs.title: Chemical Reactions: An Overview
docs.text:
Alcohols are versatile: they can react both as nucleophiles and as electrophiles.

  • As nucleophiles, the O–H bond breaks. The lone pair on oxygen attacks an electrophilic carbon and a proton is then lost.
\[R-\ddot{O}-H + \overset{+}{C}< → R-\overset{+}{O}(H)-C< → R-O-C< + H^+\]
  • As electrophiles, the C–O bond breaks. Protonated alcohols react in this manner, since –OH2+ leaves easily as water.
\[R-CH_2-OH + H^+ → R-CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2\] \[Br^- + R-CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2 → Br-CH_2-R + H_2O\]

So the reactions of alcohols and phenols can be divided into two groups: (a) those involving cleavage of the O–H bond and (b) those involving cleavage of the C–O bond. This page covers group (a).

docs.title: Reactions Involving Cleavage of O–H Bond
(i) Reaction with metals
docs.text:
• Alcohols and phenols react with active metals such as sodium, potassium and aluminium to give alkoxides/phenoxides and hydrogen gas.
\[2R-O-H + 2Na → 2R-O-Na + H_2\ \ (sodium\ alkoxide)\] \[6(CH_3)_3C-OH + 2Al → 2[(CH_3)_3C-O]_3Al + 3H_2\] \[(aluminium\ tert-butoxide)\] \[2C_6H_5OH + 2Na → 2C_6H_5ONa + H_2\ \ (sodium\ phenoxide)\]
  • In addition, phenols (but not alcohols) react with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form sodium phenoxide:
\[C_6H_5OH + NaOH → C_6H_5ONa + H_2O\]
  • These reactions show that alcohols and phenols are Brönsted acids, i.e. they can donate a proton to a stronger base (B:-).
\[B:^- + H-O-R → B-H + R-O:^-\] \[(Base)\ \ (Acid)\ \ \ \ (Conjugate\ acid)\ \ (Conjugate\ base)\]

docs.title: (ii) Acidity of alcohols
docs.text:
• The acidic character of alcohols is due to the polar nature of the O–H bond.
  • Electron-releasing alkyl groups (–CH3, –C2H5) increase the electron density on oxygen. This decreases the polarity of the O–H bond and hence the acid strength.
  • More alkyl groups on the carbinol carbon means weaker acid. So the order of acid strength is:
\[RCH_2OH\ (1^0) > R_2CHOH\ (2^0) \gg R_3COH\ (3^0)\]
  • Alcohols are weaker acids than water. This is shown by the reaction of an alkoxide with water:
\[R-O^- + H-O-H → R-O-H + OH^-\]
  • Here water acts as the proton donor (acid) and alkoxide as the proton acceptor (base). Thus water is a stronger acid than an alcohol, and an alkoxide ion is a stronger base than hydroxide ion. For example, sodium ethoxide is a stronger base than sodium hydroxide.
  • Alcohols can also act as Brönsted bases, because the lone pairs on oxygen can accept a proton.

docs.title: (iii) Acidity of phenols
docs.text:
• The reactions of phenol with metals and with aqueous NaOH show that phenols are stronger acids than alcohols and water.
  • In phenol, the –OH group is attached to an sp2 hybridised carbon of the benzene ring, which acts as an electron withdrawing group. Resonance pushes the lone pair of oxygen into the ring, making the oxygen partially positive:
  • The ionisation of an alcohol and a phenol can be written as:
\[R-O-H ⇌ R-O^- + H^+\] \[C_6H_5-OH ⇌ C_6H_5-O^- + H^+\]

Phenol is more acidic than an alcohol for two reasons:

  • Polarity of O–H bond: The sp2 carbon attached to –OH in phenol is more electronegative than the sp3 carbon in alcohols. Electron density on oxygen decreases, the O–H bond becomes more polar, and ionisation is easier.
  • Stability of the anion: In an alkoxide ion, the negative charge is localised on oxygen. In a phenoxide ion, the negative charge is delocalised over the ring (structures I–V), which makes phenoxide more stable and favours ionisation of phenol.

  • Phenol itself also shows resonance, but its resonance structures involve charge separation, so phenol is less stabilised than phenoxide ion.

docs.title: (iv) Effect of substituents on acidity of phenols
docs.text:
• Electron withdrawing groups such as –NO2 increase the acid strength of phenol. The effect is stronger when the group is at the ortho or para position, because the negative charge of the phenoxide ion can then be delocalised onto the nitro group.
  • Electron releasing groups such as alkyl groups do not favour formation of the phenoxide ion, so they decrease the acid strength. For example, cresols are less acidic than phenol.
  • Remember: the greater the pKa value, the weaker the acid.
Compound Formula pKa o-Nitrophenol o-O2N–C6H4–OH 7.2 m-Nitrophenol m-O2N–C6H4–OH 8.3 p-Nitrophenol p-O2N–C6H4–OH 7.1 Phenol C6H5–OH 10.0 o-Cresol o-CH3–C6H4–OH 10.2 m-Cresol m-CH3–C6H4–OH 10.1 p-Cresol p-CH3–C6H4–OH 10.2 Ethanol C2H5OH 15.9

Conclusion

  • The pKa of phenol (10.0) is about 6 units lower than that of ethanol (15.9), so phenol is about a million times more acidic than ethanol.

  • 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (picric acid) is a strong acid, because its three electron withdrawing –NO2 groups make release of H+ very easy.

  • Order of acidity: alkanol < water < cresols < phenol < m-nitrophenol < o-/p-nitrophenol.

docs.title: 2. Esterification
docs.text:
• Alcohols and phenols react with carboxylic acids, acid chlorides and acid anhydrides to form esters.
\[Ar/RO-H + R'-COOH \overset{H^+}{⇌} Ar/ROCOR' + H_2O\] \[Ar/R-OH + (R'CO)_2O \overset{H^+}{⇌} Ar/ROCOR' + R'COOH\] \[R/ArOH + R'COCl \xrightarrow{Pyridine} R/ArOCOR' + HCl\]
  • With carboxylic acids and anhydrides, a small amount of concentrated H2SO4 is used as catalyst. The reaction is reversible, so water is removed as soon as it forms.
  • With acid chlorides, a base (pyridine) is added to neutralise the HCl formed. This shifts the equilibrium to the right.
  • Introduction of an acetyl (CH3CO–) group into an alcohol or phenol is called acetylation. Acetylation of salicylic acid gives aspirin, which has analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic properties.
\[o-HOC_6H_4COOH + (CH_3CO)_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} o-CH_3COOC_6H_4COOH + CH_3COOH\] \[(Salicylic\ acid)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (Acetylsalicylic\ acid\ or\ aspirin)\]

docs.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Preparation of Alcohols and Phenols
Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Preparation of Alcohols and Phenols
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the important methods for preparing alcohols and phenols.

docs.title: (i) Acid catalysed hydration
docs.text:
• Alkenes react with water in the presence of an acid catalyst to form alcohols.
  • For unsymmetrical alkenes, the addition follows Markovnikov's rule: H goes to the double-bonded carbon that already has more hydrogens, and –OH goes to the other carbon.
\[>C=C< + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} >C(H)-C(OH)<\] \[CH_3CH=CH_2 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3\]

Mechanism: The reaction takes place in three steps.

  • Step 1: Protonation of alkene to form a carbocation by electrophilic attack of H3O+.
\[H_2O + H^+ → H_3O^+\] \[>C=C< + H_3O^+ ⇌ >CH-\overset{+}{C}< + H_2O\]
  • Step 2: Nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation to form a protonated alcohol (oxonium ion).
\[>CH-\overset{+}{C}< + H_2O ⇌ >CH-C(\overset{+}{O}H_2)<\]
  • Step 3: Deprotonation to form the alcohol.
\[>CH-C(\overset{+}{O}H_2)< + H_2O → >CH-C(OH)< + H_3O^+\]
  • Since the more stable carbocation is formed in step 1, the –OH finally ends up on the more substituted carbon. This is why the reaction obeys Markovnikov's rule.

docs.title: (ii) Hydroboration–oxidation
docs.text:
• Diborane, (BH3)2, adds to alkenes to give trialkylboranes. These are oxidised to alcohols by hydrogen peroxide in the presence of aqueous sodium hydroxide.
\[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + (H-BH_2)_2 → CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-BH_2\] \[CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-BH_2 \xrightarrow{CH_3-CH=CH_2} (CH_3-CH_2-CH_2)_2BH \xrightarrow{CH_3-CH=CH_2} (CH_3-CH_2-CH_2)_3B\] \[(CH_3-CH_2-CH_2)_3B \xrightarrow{H_2O,\ 3H_2O_2,\ \overset{-}{O}H} 3CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-OH + B(OH)_3\] \[(Propan-1-ol)\]
  • Boron gets attached to the sp2 carbon carrying the greater number of hydrogen atoms.
  • As a result, the alcohol formed looks as if water has been added to the alkene opposite to Markovnikov's rule (anti-Markovnikov product).
  • The yield of alcohol is excellent.

Note

Compare the two methods for propene: acid catalysed hydration gives propan-2-ol, while hydroboration–oxidation gives propan-1-ol. Hydroboration–oxidation was first reported by H.C. Brown in 1959.

docs.title: (i) Reduction of aldehydes and ketones
docs.text:
• Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols by adding hydrogen in the presence of a finely divided metal catalyst such as Pt, Pd or Ni (catalytic hydrogenation).
  • They can also be reduced by sodium borohydride (NaBH4) or lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4).
  • Aldehydes give primary alcohols, while ketones give secondary alcohols.
\[RCHO + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd} RCH_2OH\] \[RCOR' \xrightarrow{NaBH_4} R-CH(OH)-R'\]

docs.title: (ii) Reduction of carboxylic acids and esters
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols in excellent yields by LiAlH4, a strong reducing agent.
\[RCOOH \xrightarrow{(i)\ LiAlH_4,\ (ii)\ H_2O} RCH_2OH\]

The numbering (i), (ii) means the second reagent is added only after the reaction with the first is complete.

  • LiAlH4 is expensive, so it is used only for special chemicals. Commercially, acids are first converted to esters, which are then reduced by hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst.
\[RCOOH \xrightarrow{R'OH,\ H^+} RCOOR' \xrightarrow{H_2,\ catalyst} RCH_2OH + R'OH\]

docs.title: 3. From Grignard Reagents
docs.text:
• Grignard reagents (RMgX) react with aldehydes and ketones to give alcohols.
  • Step 1: Nucleophilic addition of the Grignard reagent to the carbonyl group forms an adduct. The alkyl group (Rδ-) attacks the carbonyl carbon and the MgX part bonds to oxygen.
  • Step 2: Hydrolysis of the adduct gives the alcohol.
\[>C=O + R-MgX → >C(R)-OMgX\ \ (adduct)\] \[>C(R)-OMgX \xrightarrow{H_2O} >C(R)-OH + Mg(OH)X\]

The overall reactions with different carbonyl compounds are:

\[HCHO + RMgX → RCH_2OMgX \xrightarrow{H_2O} RCH_2OH + Mg(OH)X\] \[RCHO + R'MgX → RCH(R')OMgX \xrightarrow{H_2O} RCH(R')OH + Mg(OH)X\] \[RCOR + R'MgX → R_2C(R')OMgX \xrightarrow{H_2O} R_2C(R')OH + Mg(OH)X\]

Conclusion

  • Methanal (HCHO) gives a primary alcohol.

  • Other aldehydes give secondary alcohols.

  • Ketones give tertiary alcohols.

docs.title: Preparation of Phenols
docs.text:
• Phenol, also called carbolic acid, was first isolated from coal tar in the early nineteenth century. Today it is made synthetically.
  • In the laboratory, phenols are prepared from benzene derivatives by the following methods.

docs.title: 1. From Haloarenes
docs.text:
• Chlorobenzene is fused with NaOH at 623 K and 320 atm pressure to form sodium phenoxide. Acidification of sodium phenoxide gives phenol.
\[C_6H_5Cl + NaOH \xrightarrow{623\ K,\ 320\ atm} C_6H_5ONa \xrightarrow{HCl} C_6H_5OH\]

docs.title: 2. From Benzenesulphonic Acid
docs.text:
• Benzene is sulphonated with oleum to give benzenesulphonic acid.
  • Benzenesulphonic acid is converted to sodium phenoxide by heating with molten NaOH. Acidification then gives phenol.
\[C_6H_6 \xrightarrow{Oleum} C_6H_5SO_3H \xrightarrow{(i)\ NaOH,\ (ii)\ H^+} C_6H_5OH\]

docs.title: 3. From Diazonium Salts
docs.text:
• An aromatic primary amine is treated with nitrous acid (NaNO2 + HCl) at 273–278 K to form a diazonium salt. Aniline, for example, gives benzene diazonium chloride.
  • Diazonium salts are hydrolysed to phenols by warming with water or by treating with dilute acids.
\[C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2 + HCl,\ 273-278\ K} C_6H_5\overset{+}{N_2}\overset{-}{Cl}\] \[C_6H_5\overset{+}{N_2}\overset{-}{Cl} + H_2O \xrightarrow{Warm} C_6H_5OH + N_2 + HCl\]

docs.title: 4. From Cumene
docs.text:
• Most of the world's phenol is manufactured from cumene (isopropylbenzene).
  • Cumene is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which is converted to phenol and acetone on treatment with dilute acid.
  • Acetone, the by-product, is also obtained in large quantities by this method.
\[C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2 \xrightarrow{O_2} C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H\] \[C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H \xrightarrow{H^+,\ H_2O} C_6H_5OH + CH_3COCH_3\]

docs.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Questions
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some questions based on nomenclature, preparation, properties and reactions of alcohols, phenols and ethers.

docs.title: Classification and Nomenclature
docs.text:
Classify the following as primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, and identify the allylic alcohols: (i) (CH3)3C–CH2OH (ii) H2C=CH–CH2OH (iii) CH3–CH2–CH2–OH (iv) C6H5–CH(OH)–CH3 (v) C6H5–CH2–CH(OH)–CH3 (vi) C6H5–CH=CH–C(CH3)2–OH

  • Primary alcohols: (i), (ii), (iii) — the carbinol carbon is bonded to only one carbon.

  • Secondary alcohols: (iv) and (v) — the carbinol carbon is bonded to two carbons.

  • Tertiary alcohol: (vi) — the carbinol carbon is bonded to three carbons.

  • Allylic alcohols: (ii) and (vi), since in both the –OH is on an sp3 carbon next to a C=C double bond.

Give IUPAC names of the following compounds: (i) CH3–CH(Cl)–CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–CH2OH (ii) CH3–CH(CH3)–O–CH2CH3 (iii) Phenol with –CH3 groups at both ortho positions (iv) Cyclohexane with –OC2H5 and –NO2 on adjacent carbons

  • (i) The chain is numbered from the –CH2OH end: 4-Chloro-2,3-dimethylpentan-1-ol

  • (ii) The larger group (propane) is the parent; ethoxy is the substituent: 2-Ethoxypropane

  • (iii) 2,6-Dimethylphenol

  • (iv) Substituents are numbered in alphabetical order (ethoxy before nitro): 1-Ethoxy-2-nitrocyclohexane

Name the following according to the IUPAC system: (i) CH3–CH2–CH(CH2Cl)–CH(CH2OH)–CH(CH3)–CH3 (ii) (CH3)2CH–CH2–CH(OH)–CH(CH3)–CH2OH (iii) Cyclohexanol with Br at C-3 (iv) H2C=CH–CH(OH)–CH2–CH2–CH3 (v) CH3–C(CH3)=C(Br)–CH2OH

  • (i) The longest chain containing the –CH2OH carbon is numbered from that carbon: 3-Chloromethyl-2-isopropylpentan-1-ol

  • (ii) Both –OH groups lie on the main chain: 2,5-Dimethylhexane-1,3-diol

  • (iii) 3-Bromocyclohexanol

  • (iv) Hex-1-en-3-ol

  • (v) 2-Bromo-3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol

Give the structures and IUPAC names of monohydric phenols of molecular formula C7H8O.

C7H8O as a monohydric phenol means C6H4(CH3)OH. The –CH3 can be ortho, meta or para to –OH:

  • o-CH3C6H4OH: 2-Methylphenol (o-cresol)

  • m-CH3C6H4OH: 3-Methylphenol (m-cresol)

  • p-CH3C6H4OH: 4-Methylphenol (p-cresol)

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
Give the structures and IUPAC names of the products expected from: (a) Catalytic reduction of butanal. (b) Hydration of propene in the presence of dilute sulphuric acid. (c) Reaction of propanone with methylmagnesium bromide followed by hydrolysis.

\[(a)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2CHO + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd} CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-OH\ \ (Butan-1-ol)\] \[(b)\ CH_3CH=CH_2 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3\ \ (Propan-2-ol)\]

Markovnikov addition places –OH on the middle carbon.

\[(c)\ CH_3COCH_3 + CH_3MgBr → (CH_3)_3C-OMgBr \xrightarrow{H_2O} (CH_3)_3C-OH\]

The product is 2-methylpropan-2-ol (a ketone gives a tertiary alcohol).

Show how the following alcohols are prepared by the reaction of a suitable Grignard reagent on methanal: (i) (CH3)2CH–CH2OH (ii) Cyclohexylmethanol, C6H11CH2OH

Methanal adds one –CH2OH carbon to the R group of RMgX, so R must be the rest of the molecule.

\[(i)\ (CH_3)_2CH-MgBr + HCHO → (CH_3)_2CH-CH_2-OMgBr \xrightarrow{H_2O} (CH_3)_2CH-CH_2OH + Mg(OH)Br\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_{11}MgBr + HCHO → C_6H_{11}CH_2OMgBr \xrightarrow{H_2O} C_6H_{11}CH_2OH + Mg(OH)Br\]

Write the products of the following reactions: (i) CH3–CH=CH2 with H2O/H+ (ii) Methyl 2-(2-oxocyclohexyl)ethanoate (cyclohexanone carrying a –CH2COOCH3 group on C-2) with NaBH4 (iii) CH3–CH2–CH(CH3)–CHO with NaBH4

  • (i) CH3–CH(OH)–CH3 (Markovnikov addition)

  • (ii) NaBH4 reduces the ketone C=O to –CH(OH)– but does not reduce the ester group. The product is the cyclohexanol carrying the unchanged –CH2COOCH3 group on the adjacent carbon.

  • (iii) The aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol: CH3–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2OH

How are the following conversions carried out? (i) Propene to propan-2-ol (ii) Benzyl chloride to benzyl alcohol (iii) Ethylmagnesium chloride to propan-1-ol (iv) Methylmagnesium bromide to 2-methylpropan-2-ol

\[(i)\ CH_3CH=CH_2 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3CH(OH)CH_3\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5CH_2Cl + aq\ NaOH → C_6H_5CH_2OH + NaCl\] \[(iii)\ C_2H_5MgCl + HCHO → CH_3CH_2CH_2OMgCl \xrightarrow{H_2O} CH_3CH_2CH_2OH\] \[(iv)\ CH_3MgBr + CH_3COCH_3 → (CH_3)_3COMgBr \xrightarrow{H_2O} (CH_3)_3COH\]

docs.title: Physical Properties and Acidity
docs.text:
Arrange the following in increasing order of boiling points: (a) Pentan-1-ol, butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, methanol. (b) Pentan-1-ol, n-butane, pentanal, ethoxyethane.

  • (a) Boiling point increases with molar mass; among isomers, the branched one (butan-2-ol) boils lower:
\[Methanol < Ethanol < Propan-1-ol < Butan-2-ol < Butan-1-ol < Pentan-1-ol\]
  • (b) n-Butane is non-polar; ethoxyethane is weakly polar; pentanal has a stronger C=O dipole; pentan-1-ol has hydrogen bonding:
\[n-Butane < Ethoxyethane < Pentanal < Pentan-1-ol\]

Why does ethanol have a higher boiling point than methoxymethane, although both have molecular mass 46?

Ethanol has an O–H group, so its molecules are associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Methoxymethane has no hydrogen attached to oxygen and cannot form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules. More energy is needed to separate ethanol molecules, so ethanol boils at 351 K while methoxymethane boils at 248 K.

Arrange the following in increasing order of acid strength: Propan-1-ol, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, 3-nitrophenol, 3,5-dinitrophenol, phenol, 4-methylphenol.

  • An alcohol is the weakest acid. Electron releasing –CH3 makes 4-methylphenol weaker than phenol.

  • Electron withdrawing –NO2 groups increase acidity; the more nitro groups, and the more of them at ortho/para positions, the stronger the acid.

\[Propan-1-ol < 4-Methylphenol < Phenol < 3-Nitrophenol < 3,5-Dinitrophenol < 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol\]

Explain why ortho-nitrophenol is more acidic than ortho-methoxyphenol.

  • –NO2 is an electron withdrawing group. It pulls electron density away from oxygen and delocalises the negative charge of the phenoxide ion onto itself, stabilising the ion. So o-nitrophenol ionises more easily.

  • –OCH3 is an electron releasing group (by resonance). It increases the electron density on the ring and on the phenoxide oxygen, destabilising the phenoxide ion. So o-methoxyphenol is less acidic.

While separating a mixture of ortho and para nitrophenols by steam distillation, which isomer will be steam volatile? Give reason.

o-Nitrophenol is steam volatile. It has intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the –OH and the neighbouring –NO2 group, so its molecules do not associate with each other. p-Nitrophenol has intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which associates its molecules and lowers its volatility.

docs.title: Reactions of Alcohols and Phenols
docs.text:
Give the products when (i) butan-1-ol and (ii) 2-methylbutan-2-ol react with (a) HCl–ZnCl2 (b) HBr and (c) SOCl2.

In each case, –OH is replaced by a halogen.

Reagent Butan-1-ol 2-Methylbutan-2-ol HCl–ZnCl2 CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl (slow; no turbidity at room temperature) CH3CH2C(CH3)2Cl (immediate turbidity) HBr CH3CH2CH2CH2Br CH3CH2C(CH3)2Br SOCl2 CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl CH3CH2C(CH3)2Cl

Predict the major product of acid catalysed dehydration of (i) 1-methylcyclohexanol and (ii) butan-1-ol.

  • (i) The tertiary carbocation loses a proton from the ring carbon to give the more substituted alkene: 1-Methylcyclohexene.

  • (ii) Loss of water and a proton from C-2 gives but-1-ene.

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2 + H_2O\]

Write the mechanism of acid dehydration of ethanol to yield ethene.

\[Step\ 1\ (fast):\ CH_3CH_2OH + H^+ ⇌ CH_3CH_2\overset{+}{O}H_2\] \[Step\ 2\ (slow):\ CH_3CH_2\overset{+}{O}H_2 ⇌ CH_3\overset{+}{C}H_2 + H_2O\] \[Step\ 3:\ CH_3\overset{+}{C}H_2 ⇌ CH_2=CH_2 + H^+\]

Step 2 is the rate determining step. Ethene is removed as it forms to drive the equilibrium forward.

Name the reagents used for: (i) Oxidation of a primary alcohol to carboxylic acid (ii) Oxidation of a primary alcohol to aldehyde (iii) Bromination of phenol to 2,4,6-tribromophenol (iv) Benzyl alcohol to benzoic acid (v) Dehydration of propan-2-ol to propene (vi) Butan-2-one to butan-2-ol

  • (i) Acidified potassium permanganate (KMnO4/H+)

  • (ii) Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC), or CrO3 in anhydrous medium

  • (iii) Bromine water

  • (iv) Acidified KMnO4

  • (v) 85% H3PO4 at 440 K (or conc. H2SO4)

  • (vi) NaBH4 or LiAlH4 (or H2 with Pt/Pd/Ni)

Write the structures of the major products expected from: (a) Mononitration of 3-methylphenol (b) Dinitration of 3-methylphenol

Both –OH and –CH3 are ortho, para directing; –OH is the stronger director. The nitro group enters positions that are ortho/para to –OH and not too crowded.

  • (a) A mixture of 3-methyl-4-nitrophenol (–NO2 para to –OH) and 5-methyl-2-nitrophenol (–NO2 ortho to –OH, on the side away from –CH3).

  • (b) 5-Methyl-2,4-dinitrophenol (nitro groups at one ortho and the para position of –OH).

Ortho and para nitrophenols are more acidic than phenol. Explain using the resonance structures of the corresponding phenoxide ions.

  • In o- and p-nitrophenoxide ions, the negative charge on oxygen is delocalised into the ring and onto the ortho and para carbons, just as in phenoxide ion.

  • Since the –NO2 group sits on one of these carbons, the charge can move further onto the nitro group, giving an extra resonance structure in which the negative charge is on the oxygen of –NO2 (–N+(O-)O-).

  • This extra delocalisation stabilises the o- and p-nitrophenoxide ions more than phenoxide ion, so o- and p-nitrophenols ionise more readily. In m-nitrophenoxide, the charge never reaches the carbon bearing –NO2, so only the weaker inductive effect operates, which is why m-nitrophenol (pKa 8.3) is less acidic than the o- and p-isomers.

When 3-methylbutan-2-ol is treated with HBr, 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is formed. Give a mechanism for this reaction.

\[Step\ 1:\ (CH_3)_2CH-CH(OH)-CH_3 + H^+ → (CH_3)_2CH-CH(\overset{+}{O}H_2)-CH_3\] \[Step\ 2:\ (CH_3)_2CH-CH(\overset{+}{O}H_2)-CH_3 → (CH_3)_2CH-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3 + H_2O\]

A secondary carbocation is formed. A hydride ion shifts from the neighbouring (3rd) carbon to give a more stable tertiary carbocation:

\[Step\ 3:\ (CH_3)_2CH-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3 → (CH_3)_2\overset{+}{C}-CH_2-CH_3\] \[Step\ 4:\ (CH_3)_2\overset{+}{C}-CH_2-CH_3 + Br^- → (CH_3)_2C(Br)-CH_2-CH_3\]

docs.title: Ethers
docs.text:
The reaction C2H5ONa + (CH3)3C–Cl is not appropriate for preparing t-butyl ethyl ether. (i) What would be the major product? (ii) Write a suitable reaction for the preparation of t-butyl ethyl ether.

  • (i) The major product is 2-methylprop-1-ene, (CH3)2C=CH2. Sodium ethoxide is a strong base as well as a nucleophile, and with a tertiary halide elimination predominates over substitution.

  • (ii) Take the tertiary group from the alkoxide and use a primary halide:

\[(CH_3)_3C-O^-Na^+ + CH_3CH_2Cl → (CH_3)_3C-OC_2H_5 + NaCl\]

Write the reactions of Williamson synthesis of 2-ethoxy-3-methylpentane starting from ethanol and 3-methylpentan-2-ol.

The secondary group comes from the alkoxide; ethanol is converted into the primary halide.

\[CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH(OH)CH_3 + Na → CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH(ONa)CH_3 + {1 \over 2}H_2\] \[C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{HBr} C_2H_5Br\] \[CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH(ONa)CH_3 + C_2H_5Br → CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH(OC_2H_5)CH_3 + NaBr\]

Which of the following is an appropriate set of reactants for the preparation of 1-methoxy-4-nitrobenzene, and why? (i) p-BrC6H4NO2 + CH3ONa (ii) p-NaOC6H4NO2 + CH3Br

Set (ii) is appropriate. Williamson synthesis needs SN2 attack on an alkyl halide. In (ii), the phenoxide ion attacks CH3Br easily. In (i), the halogen is on an aryl (sp2) carbon, and aryl halides do not undergo SN2 substitution under these conditions because the C–Br bond has partial double bond character.

\[p-O_2NC_6H_4ONa + CH_3Br → p-O_2NC_6H_4OCH_3 + NaBr\]

Why is acid dehydration of secondary or tertiary alcohols not a suitable method for preparing ethers?

With secondary and tertiary alcohols, the reaction goes through a carbocation (SN1). Such carbocations readily lose a proton, so elimination competes strongly with substitution and alkenes are formed instead of ethers.

Give the major products formed by heating each of the following ethers with HI: (i) CH3–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2–O–CH2–CH3 (ii) CH3–CH2–CH2–O–C(CH3)2–CH2CH3 (iii) C6H5–CH2–O–C6H5

  • (i) Both groups are primary; I- attacks the less hindered ethyl group (SN2):
\[CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH_2OH + CH_3CH_2I\]
  • (ii) One group is tertiary, so the reaction is SN1 and the tertiary iodide forms:
\[CH_3CH_2CH_2OH + CH_3CH_2C(CH_3)_2I\]
  • (iii) The aryl–O bond is not broken; the benzyl–O bond breaks:
\[C_6H_5CH_2I + C_6H_5OH\]

Predict the products of the following reactions: (i) CH3–CH2–CH2–O–CH3 + HBr (ii) C6H5OC2H5 + HBr (iii) C6H5OC2H5 with conc. H2SO4 / conc. HNO3 (iv) (CH3)3C–OC2H5 + HI

\[(i)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2OH + CH_3Br\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5OH + C_2H_5Br\] \[(iii)\ o-O_2NC_6H_4OC_2H_5 + p-O_2NC_6H_4OC_2H_5\] \[(iv)\ (CH_3)_3C-I + C_2H_5OH\]

In (i), Br- attacks the smaller methyl group (SN2); in (iv), the tertiary carbocation forms (SN1).

docs.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Reactions of Alcohols
Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Reactions of Alcohols
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the reactions of alcohols that involve cleavage of the carbon–oxygen (C–O) bond, oxidation of alcohols, and two commercially important alcohols: methanol and ethanol.

docs.title: Reactions Involving Cleavage of C–O Bond
docs.text:
• Reactions involving cleavage of the C–O bond take place only in alcohols.
  • Phenols show this type of reaction only with zinc (phenol is reduced to benzene on heating with zinc dust). The C–O bond in phenol is too strong because of its partial double bond character.

docs.title: 1. Reaction with Hydrogen Halides
docs.text:
• Alcohols react with hydrogen halides to form alkyl halides.
\[ROH + HX → R-X + H_2O\]

docs.title: Lucas Test
docs.text:
• The three classes of alcohols react with HCl at very different rates. This difference is used to distinguish them (Lucas test).
  • Lucas reagent is a mixture of concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl2.
  • Alcohols are soluble in Lucas reagent, but the alkyl chlorides formed are immiscible and make the solution turbid.
Alcohol type Observation with Lucas reagent at room temperature Tertiary (3°) Turbidity appears immediately (halide forms easily) Secondary (2°) Turbidity appears after some time Primary (1°) No turbidity at room temperature

docs.title: 2. Reaction with Phosphorus Trihalides
docs.text:
• Alcohols are converted to alkyl bromides by reaction with phosphorus tribromide.
\[3ROH + PBr_3 → 3R-Br + H_3PO_3\]

docs.title: 3. Dehydration
docs.text:
• Alcohols lose a molecule of water to form alkenes when treated with a protic acid such as concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4, or with catalysts such as anhydrous ZnCl2 or alumina.
\[>CH-C(OH)< \xrightarrow{H^+,\ Heat} >C=C< + H_2O\]
  • Ethanol is dehydrated by heating with concentrated H2SO4 at 443 K.
\[C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4,\ 443\ K} CH_2=CH_2 + H_2O\]
  • Secondary and tertiary alcohols are dehydrated under milder conditions:
\[CH_3CH(OH)CH_3 \xrightarrow{85\%\ H_3PO_4,\ 440\ K} CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H_2O\] \[(CH_3)_3C-OH \xrightarrow{20\%\ H_3PO_4,\ 358\ K} CH_3-C(CH_3)=CH_2 + H_2O\]
  • The relative ease of dehydration is:
\[Tertiary > Secondary > Primary\]
  • This is because tertiary carbocations are more stable, and hence easier to form, than secondary and primary carbocations.

docs.title: Mechanism of dehydration of ethanol
docs.text:
• Step 1: Formation of protonated alcohol (ethyl oxonium ion). This step is fast.
\[CH_3-CH_2-\ddot{O}-H + H^+ \overset{Fast}{⇌} CH_3-CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2\]
  • Step 2: Formation of carbocation. Water leaves from the protonated alcohol. This is the slowest step and hence the rate determining step.
\[CH_3-CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2 \overset{Slow}{⇌} CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H_2 + H_2O\]
  • Step 3: Formation of ethene by elimination of a proton from the carbon next to the positive carbon.
\[H-CH_2-\overset{+}{C}H_2 ⇌ CH_2=CH_2 + H^+\]
  • The acid used in step 1 is released again in step 3. To drive the equilibrium to the right, ethene is removed as soon as it is formed.

docs.title: 4. Oxidation
docs.text:
• Oxidation of alcohols involves formation of a C=O double bond with cleavage of an O–H bond and a C–H bond (on the carbinol carbon).
  • Since a molecule of dihydrogen is effectively lost, these reactions are also called dehydrogenation reactions.
\[>C(H)-O-H → >C=O\ \ (C-H\ and\ O-H\ bonds\ break)\]

docs.title: (i) Primary alcohols
docs.text:
• A primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde, which is further oxidised to a carboxylic acid.
\[RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{Oxidation} RCHO \xrightarrow{Oxidation} RCOOH\]
  • Strong oxidising agents such as acidified potassium permanganate give carboxylic acids directly.
  • CrO3 in an anhydrous medium is used to stop the oxidation at the aldehyde stage.
\[RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{CrO_3} RCHO\]
  • A better reagent for getting aldehydes in good yield is pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC), a complex of CrO3 with pyridine and HCl.
\[CH_3-CH=CH-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{PCC} CH_3-CH=CH-CHO\]

docs.title: (ii) Secondary alcohols
docs.text:
• Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones by chromic anhydride (CrO3).
\[R-CH(OH)-R' \xrightarrow{CrO_3} R-CO-R'\]

docs.title: (iii) Tertiary alcohols
docs.text:
• Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation under normal conditions, as there is no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon.
  • Under strong conditions (strong oxidising agents like KMnO4 and high temperature), various C–C bonds break and a mixture of carboxylic acids with fewer carbon atoms is formed.

docs.title: (iv) Dehydrogenation over heated copper
docs.text:
• When vapours of a primary or secondary alcohol are passed over heated copper at 573 K, dehydrogenation gives an aldehyde or a ketone. Tertiary alcohols undergo dehydration instead.
\[RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{Cu,\ 573\ K} RCHO\] \[R-CH(OH)-R' \xrightarrow{Cu,\ 573\ K} R-CO-R'\] \[(CH_3)_3C-OH \xrightarrow{Cu,\ 573\ K} CH_3-C(CH_3)=CH_2\]

Biological oxidation of methanol

In the body, methanol and ethanol are oxidised first to the corresponding aldehyde and then to the acid. Methanol is oxidised to methanal and then to methanoic acid, which can cause blindness and death. Methanol is sometimes present in denatured alcohol, which may be drunk by mistake. A methanol-poisoned patient is treated with intravenous infusions of diluted ethanol: the enzyme that oxidises the aldehyde (HCHO) to acid gets busy with ethanol, giving the kidneys time to excrete methanol.

docs.title: 1. Methanol
docs.text:
• Methanol, CH3OH, is also called wood spirit because it was earlier produced by destructive distillation of wood.
  • Today, most methanol is produced by catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide at high pressure and temperature using a ZnO–Cr2O3 catalyst.
\[CO + 2H_2 \xrightarrow{ZnO-Cr_2O_3,\ 200-300\ atm,\ 573-673\ K} CH_3OH\]
  • Methanol is a colourless liquid with boiling point 337 K.
  • It is highly poisonous. Even small quantities can cause blindness, and large quantities can cause death.
  • It is used as a solvent in paints and varnishes, and chiefly for making formaldehyde.

docs.title: 2. Ethanol
docs.text:
• Ethanol, C2H5OH, is obtained commercially by fermentation of sugars, the oldest method.
  • The sugar in molasses, sugarcane or fruits such as grapes is converted into glucose and fructose (both C6H12O6) by the enzyme invertase.
  • Glucose and fructose are then fermented to ethanol by the enzyme zymase, found in yeast.
\[C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} + H_2O \xrightarrow{Invertase} C_6H_{12}O_6\ (glucose) + C_6H_{12}O_6\ (fructose)\] \[C_6H_{12}O_6 \xrightarrow{Zymase} 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2\]
  • In wine making, grapes provide both the sugar and the yeast (which grows on the outer skin of ripening grapes). When grapes are crushed, sugar and enzyme come in contact and fermentation starts.
  • Fermentation takes place in anaerobic conditions (absence of air), and CO2 is released.
  • Zymase stops working once the alcohol content exceeds about 14 percent.
  • If air enters the fermentation mixture, oxygen oxidises ethanol to ethanoic acid, which spoils the taste of alcoholic drinks.
  • Ethanol is a colourless liquid with boiling point 351 K. It is used as a solvent in the paint industry and for preparing many carbon compounds.
  • Denaturation of alcohol: Commercial alcohol is made unfit for drinking by adding some copper sulphate (to give it colour) and pyridine (a foul smelling liquid).
  • Nowadays, large quantities of ethanol are also obtained by the acid catalysed hydration of ethene.
  • Ethanol acts on the central nervous system. Moderate amounts affect judgement and lower inhibitions, higher concentrations cause nausea and loss of consciousness, and still higher amounts interfere with breathing and can be fatal.

docs.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Reactions of Phenols
Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers | Reactions of Phenols
docs.text: Apart from the O–H cleavage reactions (acidity and esterification) common to alcohols and phenols, phenols show some reactions of their own, mostly on the aromatic ring.

docs.title: 1. Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
docs.text:
• The –OH group attached to the benzene ring activates it towards electrophilic substitution.
  • It also directs the incoming group to the ortho and para positions. The resonance structures of phenol show that these positions become electron rich, because the lone pair of oxygen is delocalised into the ring.

docs.title: (i) Nitration
docs.text:
• With dilute nitric acid at low temperature (298 K), phenol gives a mixture of ortho- and para-nitrophenols.
\[C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{Dilute\ HNO_3} o-O_2NC_6H_4OH + p-O_2NC_6H_4OH\]
  • The two isomers are separated by steam distillation:
    • o-Nitrophenol is steam volatile because of intramolecular hydrogen bonding (the –OH and –NO2 groups of the same molecule are hydrogen bonded), so its molecules do not associate.
    • p-Nitrophenol is less volatile because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which causes association of molecules.
  • With concentrated nitric acid, phenol is converted to 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid), but the yield is poor.
\[C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{Conc.\ HNO_3} 2,4,6-(NO_2)_3C_6H_2OH\]
  • Nowadays, picric acid is prepared by first treating phenol with concentrated H2SO4, which gives phenol-2,4-disulphonic acid, and then with concentrated HNO3.
\[C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{Conc.\ H_2SO_4} 2,4-(HO_3S)_2C_6H_3OH\] \[2,4-(HO_3S)_2C_6H_3OH + 3HNO_3 → 2,4,6-(NO_2)_3C_6H_2OH + 2H_2SO_4 + H_2O\]

docs.title: (ii) Halogenation
docs.text:
The product of bromination depends on the conditions.

  • (a) In a solvent of low polarity (CHCl3 or CS2) at low temperature (273 K), monobromophenols are formed. p-Bromophenol is the major product and o-bromophenol the minor product.
\[C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{Br_2\ in\ CS_2,\ 273\ K} p-BrC_6H_4OH\ (major) + o-BrC_6H_4OH\ (minor)\]

  • Normally, halogenation of benzene needs a Lewis acid such as FeBr3 to polarise the halogen molecule. In phenol, the bromine molecule is polarised even without a Lewis acid, because the –OH group strongly activates the ring.

  • (b) With bromine water, 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed as a white precipitate.

\[C_6H_5OH + 3Br_2 \xrightarrow{H_2O} 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2OH\ ↓ + 3HBr\]
  • In water (a polar solvent), phenol partly ionises to phenoxide ion, which is even more strongly activating. So all three ortho and para positions get substituted.

docs.title: 2. Kolbe's Reaction
docs.text:
• Phenoxide ion, obtained by treating phenol with NaOH, is even more reactive than phenol towards electrophilic substitution.
  • So it reacts even with carbon dioxide, a weak electrophile. Ortho-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid) is the main product.
\[C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{NaOH} C_6H_5ONa \xrightarrow{(i)\ CO_2,\ (ii)\ H^+} o-HOC_6H_4COOH\]

The product is 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid).

docs.title: 3. Reimer-Tiemann Reaction
docs.text:
• When phenol is treated with chloroform in the presence of sodium hydroxide, a –CHO group is introduced at the ortho position of the ring.
  • The intermediate (a substituted benzal chloride, –CHCl2) is hydrolysed by the alkali, and acidification finally gives salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde).
