\[C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{(i)\ CHCl_3 + aq\ NaOH,\ (ii)\ H^+} o-HOC_6H_4CHO\]

docs.title: 4. Reaction with Zinc Dust
docs.text:
• Phenol is converted to benzene on heating with zinc dust. This is the only reaction in which phenol shows cleavage of the C–O bond.
\[C_6H_5OH + Zn → C_6H_6 + ZnO\]

docs.title: 5. Oxidation
docs.text:
• Oxidation of phenol with chromic acid (Na2Cr2O7 / H2SO4) gives a conjugated diketone called benzoquinone (p-benzoquinone, O=C6H4=O).
\[C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{Na_2Cr_2O_7,\ H_2SO_4} C_6H_4O_2\ (benzoquinone)\]
  • In the presence of air, phenols are slowly oxidised to dark coloured mixtures containing quinones. This is why old samples of phenol turn pink or brown.

HNO<sub>3</sub> 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (picric acid) Bromination Br<sub>2</sub> in CS<sub>2</sub>, 273 K p-Bromophenol (major) + o-bromophenol Bromination Bromine water 2,4,6-Tribromophenol (white ppt) Kolbe's reaction NaOH, then CO<sub>2</sub>, H<sup>+</sup> Salicylic acid Reimer-Tiemann CHCl<sub>3</sub> + aq NaOH, then H<sup>+</sup> Salicylaldehyde Zinc dust Zn, heat Benzene Oxidation Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> Benzoquinone

docs.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Acidity and Reactions of Carboxylic Acids
Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Acidity and Reactions of Carboxylic Acids
docs.text: The reactions of carboxylic acids can be grouped into four types: reactions involving cleavage of the O–H bond, reactions involving cleavage of the C–OH bond, reactions of the –COOH group as a whole, and substitution in the hydrocarbon part.

docs.title: Reactions Involving Cleavage of O–H Bond (Acidity)
1. Reactions with metals and alkalies
docs.text:
• Like alcohols, carboxylic acids evolve hydrogen with electropositive metals. Like phenols, they form salts with alkalies.
  • Unlike phenols, they also react with weaker bases such as carbonates and hydrogencarbonates and evolve CO2. This brisk effervescence with NaHCO3 is used to detect the carboxyl group.
\[2RCOOH + 2Na → 2RCOO^-Na^+ + H_2\] \[RCOOH + NaOH → RCOO^-Na^+ + H_2O\] \[RCOOH + NaHCO_3 → RCOO^-Na^+ + H_2O + CO_2 ↑\]

docs.title: 2. Dissociation in water
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids dissociate in water to give a resonance stabilised carboxylate anion and the hydronium ion.
  • In the carboxylate ion, the negative charge is shared equally between the two oxygen atoms, so both C–O bonds are identical.
\[RCOOH + H_2O ⇌ H_3O^+ + RCOO^-\] \[R-C(=O)-O^- \longleftrightarrow R-C(-O^-)=O\] \[K_{eq} = {[H_3O^+][RCOO^-] \over [H_2O][RCOOH]}\] \[K_a = K_{eq}[H_2O] = {[H_3O^+][RCOO^-] \over [RCOOH]}\] \[pK_a = -\log K_a\]
  • Ka is the acid dissociation constant. Acid strength is usually expressed by pKa. Smaller the pKa, stronger the acid.
Acid strength pKa range Strong acids < 1 Moderately strong acids 1 to 5 Weak acids 5 to 15 Extremely weak acids > 15 Acid pKa Hydrochloric acid –7.0 Trifluoroacetic acid (strongest organic acid) 0.23 Benzoic acid 4.19 Acetic acid 4.76 Phenol 10 Ethanol ~16

docs.title: 3. Why carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids are weaker than mineral acids but stronger than alcohols and most simple phenols.
  • The carboxylate ion is stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures, with the negative charge on the more electronegative oxygen atom in each.
  • The phenoxide ion has non-equivalent resonance structures, several of which put the negative charge on the less electronegative carbon atoms of the ring. These contribute less.
  • In the carboxylate ion the negative charge is spread over two electronegative oxygens, while in phenoxide it is spread less effectively over one oxygen and some carbons.

Conclusion

The carboxylate ion is more stable than the phenoxide ion, so carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols, even though phenoxide has more resonance structures.

docs.title: 4. Effect of substituents on acidity
docs.text:
• Any substituent that stabilises the carboxylate ion (conjugate base) increases acidity, and any that destabilises it decreases acidity.
  • Electron withdrawing groups (EWG) disperse the negative charge by inductive and/or resonance effects, stabilise the anion and increase acidity.
  • Electron donating groups (EDG) intensify the negative charge, destabilise the anion and decrease acidity.
  • The effect of common groups in order of increasing acidity is:
\[Ph < I < Br < Cl < F < CN < NO_2 < CF_3\]
  • So, the following acids are in order of decreasing acidity (based on pKa):
\[CF_3COOH > CCl_3COOH > CHCl_2COOH > NO_2CH_2COOH > NC-CH_2COOH >\] \[FCH_2COOH > ClCH_2COOH > BrCH_2COOH > HCOOH > ClCH_2CH_2COOH >\] \[C_6H_5COOH > C_6H_5CH_2COOH > CH_3COOH > CH_3CH_2COOH\]

From this order we can see that:

  • More halogen atoms means greater acidity (CCl3COOH > CHCl2COOH > ClCH2COOH).
  • More electronegative halogens give greater acidity (F > Cl > Br).
  • The inductive effect weakens with distance, so ClCH2CH2COOH is weaker than ClCH2COOH.
  • Alkyl groups are electron donating, so CH3COOH is weaker than HCOOH and CH3CH2COOH is weaker still.

docs.title: 5. Effect of phenyl and vinyl groups
docs.text:
• Directly attaching a phenyl or vinyl group to –COOH increases acidity, even though resonance would be expected to decrease it.
  • This is because the carboxyl carbon is attached to an sp2 hybridised carbon, which is more electronegative than an sp3 carbon. So benzoic acid (pKa 4.19) is stronger than acetic acid (pKa 4.76).
  • In aromatic acids, electron withdrawing groups on the ring increase acidity, while electron donating groups decrease it:
Acid pKa 4-Methoxybenzoic acid 4.46 Benzoic acid 4.19 4-Nitrobenzoic acid 3.41

docs.title: Reactions Involving Cleavage of C–OH Bond
1. Formation of anhydride
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids give anhydrides on heating with mineral acids such as H2SO4, or with P2O5.
\[2CH_3COOH \xrightarrow{H^+,\ Δ\ or\ P_2O_5,\ Δ} (CH_3CO)_2O + H_2O\] \[Ethanoic\ acid \qquad \qquad Ethanoic\ anhydride\]

docs.title: 2. Esterification
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids react with alcohols or phenols in the presence of a mineral acid catalyst (conc. H2SO4 or HCl gas) to form esters.
\[RCOOH + R'OH \overset{H^+}{⇌} RCOOR' + H_2O\]

docs.title: Mechanism of esterification
docs.text:
• Esterification is a nucleophilic acyl substitution.
  • Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen activates the carbonyl group towards nucleophilic addition of the alcohol.
  • A proton transfer in the tetrahedral intermediate converts an –OH group into an –OH2+ group, which is a better leaving group and is lost as a neutral water molecule.
  • The protonated ester finally loses a proton to give the ester.

docs.title: 3. Reactions with PCl<sub>5</sub>, PCl<sub>3</sub> and SOCl<sub>2</sub>
docs.text:
• The –OH group of carboxylic acids is replaced by a chlorine atom, just as in alcohols, giving acyl chlorides.
  • Thionyl chloride is preferred because the other two products (SO2 and HCl) are gases that escape, which makes purification of the acyl chloride easier.
\[RCOOH + PCl_5 → RCOCl + POCl_3 + HCl\] \[3RCOOH + PCl_3 → 3RCOCl + H_3PO_3\] \[RCOOH + SOCl_2 → RCOCl + SO_2 ↑ + HCl ↑\]

docs.title: 4. Reaction with ammonia
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids react with ammonia to form ammonium salts, which on further heating at high temperature lose water to give amides.
\[CH_3COOH + NH_3 ⇌ CH_3COONH_4 \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{Δ} CH_3CONH_2\] \[Ammonium\ acetate \qquad Acetamide\] \[C_6H_5COOH + NH_3 ⇌ C_6H_5COONH_4 \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{Δ} C_6H_5CONH_2\] \[Ammonium\ benzoate \qquad Benzamide\]
  • Phthalic acid gives ammonium phthalate, which on heating gives phthalamide. Strong heating of phthalamide removes NH3 to give the cyclic imide, phthalimide.
\[C_6H_4(COOH)_2 + 2NH_3 ⇌ C_6H_4(COONH_4)_2 \xrightarrow[-2H_2O]{Δ} C_6H_4(CONH_2)_2 \xrightarrow[-NH_3]{strong\ heating} C_6H_4(CO)_2NH\]

docs.title: 1. Reduction
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols by lithium aluminium hydride, or better by diborane (B2H6).
  • Diborane does not easily reduce groups like ester, nitro and halo groups.
  • Sodium borohydride does not reduce the carboxyl group.
\[R-COOH \xrightarrow{(i)\ LiAlH_4/ether\ or\ B_2H_6\ \ (ii)\ H_3O^+} R-CH_2OH\]

docs.title: 2. Decarboxylation
docs.text:
• Sodium salts of carboxylic acids lose CO2 to form hydrocarbons when heated with sodalime (NaOH and CaO in the ratio 3 : 1). This is called decarboxylation.
\[R-COONa \xrightarrow[Heat]{NaOH\ \&\ CaO} R-H + Na_2CO_3\]
  • Alkali metal salts of carboxylic acids also undergo decarboxylation when their aqueous solutions are electrolysed. The hydrocarbon formed has twice the number of carbon atoms present in the alkyl group of the acid. This is Kolbe electrolysis.
\[2CH_3COONa + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{electrolysis} CH_3-CH_3 + 2CO_2 + 2NaOH + H_2\]

docs.title: Substitution Reactions in the Hydrocarbon Part
1. Halogenation: Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids having an α-hydrogen are halogenated at the α-position when treated with chlorine or bromine in the presence of a small amount of red phosphorus, giving α-halocarboxylic acids.
\[R-CH_2-COOH \xrightarrow{(i)\ X_2/Red\ phosphorus\ \ (ii)\ H_2O} R-CH(X)-COOH \qquad (X = Cl,\ Br)\]

docs.title: 2. Ring substitution
docs.text:
• Aromatic carboxylic acids undergo electrophilic substitution. The –COOH group is deactivating and meta-directing.
\[C_6H_5COOH \xrightarrow{conc.\ HNO_3 + conc.\ H_2SO_4} m-NO_2C_6H_4COOH \qquad (m-Nitrobenzoic\ acid)\] \[C_6H_5COOH \xrightarrow{Br_2/FeBr_3} m-BrC_6H_4COOH \qquad (m-Bromobenzoic\ acid)\]
  • Aromatic acids do not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction, because the carboxyl group is deactivating and the Lewis acid catalyst AlCl3 gets bonded to the carboxyl group.

docs.title: Uses of Carboxylic Acids
docs.text:
• Methanoic acid: used in the rubber, textile, dyeing, leather and electroplating industries.
  • Ethanoic acid: used as a solvent and as vinegar in the food industry.
  • Hexanedioic acid (adipic acid): used in the manufacture of nylon-6,6.
  • Esters of benzoic acid: used in perfumery.
  • Sodium benzoate: used as a food preservative.
  • Higher fatty acids: used for making soaps and detergents.

docs.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Carboxylic Acids - Nomenclature and Preparation
Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Carboxylic Acids - Nomenclature and Preparation
Carboxylic Acids
docs.text:
Carboxylic acids are carbon compounds containing the carboxyl functional group, –COOH, which is a carbonyl group attached to a hydroxyl group (hence the name carboxyl).

  • They may be aliphatic (RCOOH) or aromatic (ArCOOH), depending on whether an alkyl or aryl group is attached to the carboxylic carbon.
  • Many carboxylic acids occur in nature. Higher aliphatic acids (C12 – C18), called fatty acids, occur in natural fats as esters of glycerol.
  • Carboxylic acids are starting materials for anhydrides, esters, acid chlorides, amides, etc.

docs.title: 1. Common names
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids were among the earliest organic compounds isolated from nature, so many are known by common names ending in –ic acid, taken from the Latin or Greek names of their natural sources.
  • Formic acid (HCOOH) was first obtained from red ants (Latin formica = ant), acetic acid (CH3COOH) from vinegar (Latin acetum = vinegar), and butyric acid (CH3CH2CH2COOH) from rancid butter (Latin butyrum = butter).

docs.title: 2. IUPAC names
docs.text:
• The ending –e of the corresponding alkane is replaced by –oic acid.
  • The carboxylic carbon is numbered 1.
  • For compounds with more than one –COOH group, the ending –e of the alkane is retained and the number of carboxyl groups is shown by di, tri, etc. before oic (e.g. ethanedioic acid). Positions of the –COOH groups are shown by numbers before the multiplying prefix.
Structure Common name IUPAC name HCOOH Formic acid Methanoic acid CH3COOH Acetic acid Ethanoic acid CH3CH2COOH Propionic acid Propanoic acid CH3CH2CH2COOH Butyric acid Butanoic acid (CH3)2CHCOOH Isobutyric acid 2-Methylpropanoic acid HOOC–COOH Oxalic acid Ethanedioic acid HOOC–CH2–COOH Malonic acid Propanedioic acid HOOC–(CH2)2–COOH Succinic acid Butanedioic acid HOOC–(CH2)3–COOH Glutaric acid Pentanedioic acid HOOC–(CH2)4–COOH Adipic acid Hexanedioic acid HOOC–CH2–CH(COOH)–CH2–COOH – Propane-1,2,3-tricarboxylic acid C6H5COOH Benzoic acid Benzenecarboxylic acid (Benzoic acid) C6H5CH2COOH Phenylacetic acid 2-Phenylethanoic acid o-C6H4(COOH)2 Phthalic acid Benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid

docs.title: Structure of the Carboxyl Group
docs.text:
• The bonds to the carboxyl carbon lie in one plane and are separated by about 120°.
  • The carboxylic carbon is less electrophilic than the carbonyl carbon of aldehydes and ketones. This is because the lone pair on the –OH oxygen is delocalised into the C=O group by resonance:
\[-C(=O)-\ddot{O}H \longleftrightarrow -\overset{+}{C}(O^-)-\ddot{O}H \longleftrightarrow -C(O^-)=\overset{+}{O}H\]

docs.title: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
1. From primary alcohols and aldehydes
docs.text:
• Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by KMnO4 (in neutral, acidic or alkaline medium), or by K2Cr2O7 or CrO3 in acidic medium.
\[RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{1.\ alkaline\ KMnO_4\ \ 2.\ H_3O^+} RCOOH\] \[CH_3(CH_2)_8CH_2OH \xrightarrow{CrO_3-H_2SO_4} CH_3(CH_2)_8COOH\] \[1-Decanol \qquad \qquad Decanoic\ acid\]
  • Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids even by mild oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent.

docs.title: 2. From alkylbenzenes
docs.text:
• Vigorous oxidation of alkylbenzenes with chromic acid or acidic/alkaline KMnO4 gives aromatic carboxylic acids.
  • The entire side chain is oxidised to –COOH, whatever its length.
  • Primary and secondary alkyl groups are oxidised in this way, but a tertiary alkyl group is not affected.
  • Suitably substituted alkenes are also oxidised to carboxylic acids by these reagents.
\[C_6H_5CH_3 \xrightarrow[heat]{KMnO_4-KOH} C_6H_5COOK \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_6H_5COOH\] \[C_6H_5CH_2CH_2CH_3 \xrightarrow[Δ]{KMnO_4-KOH} C_6H_5COOK \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_6H_5COOH\]

docs.title: 3. From nitriles and amides
docs.text:
• Nitriles are hydrolysed first to amides and then to acids in the presence of H+ or OH- as catalyst.
  • Mild conditions stop the reaction at the amide stage.
\[R-CN \xrightarrow[H_2O]{H^+\ or\ OH^-} R-CONH_2 \xrightarrow[Δ]{H^+\ or\ OH^-} RCOOH\] \[CH_3CONH_2 \xrightarrow[Δ]{H_3O^+} CH_3COOH + NH_3\] \[C_6H_5CONH_2 \xrightarrow[Δ]{H_3O^+} C_6H_5COOH + NH_3\]

docs.title: 4. From Grignard reagents
docs.text:
• Grignard reagents react with carbon dioxide (dry ice) to form salts of carboxylic acids, which on acidification with mineral acid give the carboxylic acids.
\[R-MgX + O=C=O \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} R-COO^-MgX^+ \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} RCOOH\]

Note

Grignard reagents and nitriles are both made from alkyl halides. So methods 3 and 4 convert an alkyl halide into a carboxylic acid with one carbon atom more than the alkyl halide (ascending the series).

docs.title: 5. From acyl halides and anhydrides
docs.text:
• Acid chlorides are hydrolysed by water to carboxylic acids. They are hydrolysed more readily by aqueous base to carboxylate ions, which on acidification give the acids.
  • Anhydrides are hydrolysed by water to the corresponding acid(s).
\[RCOCl \xrightarrow{H_2O} RCOOH + Cl^-\] \[RCOCl \xrightarrow{OH^-/H_2O} RCOO^- + Cl^- \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} RCOOH\] \[(C_6H_5CO)_2O \xrightarrow{H_2O} 2C_6H_5COOH\] \[C_6H_5COOCOCH_3 \xrightarrow{H_2O} C_6H_5COOH + CH_3COOH\]

docs.title: 6. From esters
docs.text:
• Acidic hydrolysis of esters gives carboxylic acids directly.
  • Basic hydrolysis gives carboxylates, which on acidification give the carboxylic acids.
\[C_6H_5COOC_2H_5 \overset{H_3O^+}{⇌} C_6H_5COOH + C_2H_5OH\] \[CH_3CH_2CH_2COOC_2H_5 \xrightarrow{NaOH} CH_3CH_2CH_2COONa + C_2H_5OH\] \[CH_3CH_2CH_2COONa \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} CH_3CH_2CH_2COOH\]

docs.title: 1. Physical state and odour
docs.text:
• Aliphatic carboxylic acids with up to nine carbon atoms are colourless liquids with unpleasant odours at room temperature.
  • Higher acids are wax-like solids and are almost odourless because of their low volatility.

docs.title: 2. Boiling points
docs.text:
• Carboxylic acids boil at higher temperatures than aldehydes, ketones and even alcohols of comparable molecular mass.
  • This is due to more extensive association of the molecules through intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
  • These hydrogen bonds are not broken completely even in the vapour phase. Most carboxylic acids exist as dimers in the vapour phase or in aprotic solvents.

docs.title: 3. Solubility
docs.text:
• Simple aliphatic acids with up to four carbon atoms are miscible with water, because they form hydrogen bonds with water.
  • Solubility decreases as the number of carbon atoms increases, because the hydrophobic hydrocarbon part becomes larger. Higher acids are practically insoluble in water.
  • Benzoic acid, the simplest aromatic acid, is nearly insoluble in cold water.
  • Carboxylic acids dissolve in less polar organic solvents such as benzene, ether, alcohol and chloroform.

docs.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Introduction and Nomenclature
Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Introduction and Nomenclature
Introduction
docs.text:
Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are organic compounds containing the carbon-oxygen double bond (>C=O), called the carbonyl group. It is one of the most important functional groups in organic chemistry.

  • In aldehydes, the carbonyl group is bonded to one carbon and one hydrogen.
  • In ketones, the carbonyl group is bonded to two carbon atoms.
  • In carboxylic acids, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to an –OH group. Their derivatives such as esters and anhydrides also have the carbonyl carbon bonded to oxygen.
  • When the carbonyl carbon is bonded to nitrogen, the compound is an amide; when it is bonded to a halogen, it is an acyl halide.
Class General formula Example Aldehyde R–CHO CH3CHO Ketone R–CO–R' CH3COCH3 Carboxylic acid R–COOH CH3COOH Acyl halide R–COX (X = halogen) CH3COCl Acid anhydride R–CO–O–CO–R' (CH3CO)2O Ester R–COOR' CH3COOC2H5 Amide R–CONH2 CH3CONH2
  • These compounds are widespread in plants and animals and play an important role in biochemical processes.
  • Many have pleasant fragrances: vanillin (from vanilla beans), salicylaldehyde (from meadow sweet) and cinnamaldehyde (from cinnamon, C6H5CH=CHCHO).
  • They are used in food products and pharmaceuticals as flavours, as solvents (e.g. acetone), and for making adhesives, paints, resins, perfumes, plastics and fabrics.

docs.title: Nomenclature of Aldehydes and Ketones
docs.text: There are two systems of naming aldehydes and ketones: common names and IUPAC names.

docs.title: 1. Common names
docs.text:
• The common name of an aldehyde is derived from the common name of the corresponding carboxylic acid by replacing the ending –ic acid with aldehyde. For example, formic acid → formaldehyde, acetic acid → acetaldehyde.
  • The position of a substituent is indicated by Greek letters \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\), \(\delta\), etc. The \(\alpha\)-carbon is the one directly linked to the aldehyde group, the \(\beta\)-carbon is the next one, and so on.

Example

\[\overset{\gamma}{C}H_3-\overset{\beta}{C}H(Br)-\overset{\alpha}{C}H_2-CHO\]

This compound is called \(\beta\)-bromobutyraldehyde.

  • The common name of a ketone is derived by naming the two alkyl or aryl groups attached to the carbonyl group, followed by the word ketone (e.g. methyl n-propyl ketone).
  • In ketones, positions are indicated as \(\alpha\), \(\alpha'\), \(\beta\), \(\beta'\), and so on, starting from the carbons on either side of the carbonyl group.
  • Some ketones have historical names. The simplest one, dimethyl ketone, is called acetone.
  • Alkyl phenyl ketones are named by adding the acyl group as a prefix to phenone:

Examples

  • C6H5COCH3 : Acetophenone
  • C6H5COCH2CH3 : Propiophenone
  • C6H5COC6H5 : Benzophenone

docs.title: 2. IUPAC names
docs.text:
• The IUPAC names of open chain aliphatic aldehydes and ketones are derived from the name of the parent alkane by replacing the ending –e with –al (aldehydes) and –one (ketones).
  • For aldehydes, the longest chain is numbered starting from the carbon of the –CHO group.
  • For ketones, numbering starts from the end nearer to the carbonyl group.
  • Substituents are written as prefixes in alphabetical order with numbers showing their positions.
  • In cyclic ketones, the carbonyl carbon is numbered 1.
  • When the –CHO group is attached to a ring, the suffix carbaldehyde is added after the full name of the ring (e.g. cyclohexanecarbaldehyde). Numbering of the ring starts from the carbon carrying the –CHO group.
  • The simplest aromatic aldehyde, C6H5CHO, is benzenecarbaldehyde, but its common name benzaldehyde is also accepted by IUPAC. Other aromatic aldehydes are named as substituted benzaldehydes.

Examples

  • CH3CH2CH2CH(Br)CH(CH3)CH2CHO : 4-Bromo-3-methylheptanal
  • CH3CH2CH=CHCHO : Pent-2-enal
  • CH3CH2COCH2CHO : 3-Oxopentanal
  • C6H5COCH2CH3 : 1-Phenylpropan-1-one
  • Cyclopentanone with a CH3 group on C-3 : 3-Methylcyclopentanone
  • p-NO2C6H4CHO : 4-Nitrobenzenecarbaldehyde or 4-Nitrobenzaldehyde
  • OHC–CH2–CH(CHO)–CH2–CHO : Propane-1,2,3-tricarbaldehyde

Note

In propane-1,2,3-tricarbaldehyde, all three –CHO groups are treated identically by naming them as carbaldehyde substituents on a propane chain, rather than including two of them in the main chain.

docs.title: Structure of the Carbonyl Group
docs.text:
• The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised and forms three sigma (\(\sigma\)) bonds.
  • Its fourth valence electron stays in an unhybridised p-orbital, which overlaps sideways with a p-orbital of oxygen to form a \(\pi\)-bond.
  • The oxygen atom also carries two non-bonding (lone) pairs of electrons.
  • So the carbonyl carbon and the three atoms attached to it lie in one plane, and the \(\pi\)-electron cloud lies above and below this plane.
  • The bond angles are about 120°, as expected for a trigonal planar arrangement.

docs.title: Polarity of the carbonyl group
docs.text:
• Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polarised. The carbonyl carbon is an electrophilic centre (Lewis acid) and the carbonyl oxygen is a nucleophilic centre (Lewis base).
  • Carbonyl compounds therefore have large dipole moments and are more polar than ethers.
  • This high polarity is explained by resonance between a neutral structure (A) and a dipolar structure (B):
\[\underset{(A)}{>C=O} \longleftrightarrow \underset{(B)}{>\overset{+}{C}-\overset{-}{O}}\]

Conclusion

The electron-poor carbonyl carbon is the site attacked by nucleophiles. This explains why the typical reactions of aldehydes and ketones are nucleophilic addition reactions.

docs.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Physical Properties and Nucleophilic Addition
Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Physical Properties and Nucleophilic Addition
Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
1. Physical state
docs.text:
• Methanal is a gas at room temperature and ethanal is a volatile liquid.
  • Other aldehydes and ketones are liquids or solids at room temperature.

docs.title: 2. Boiling points
docs.text:
• Boiling points of aldehydes and ketones are higher than those of hydrocarbons and ethers of comparable molecular mass. This is because the polar carbonyl groups attract each other through dipole-dipole interactions, giving weak molecular association.
  • Their boiling points are lower than those of alcohols of similar molecular mass, because aldehydes and ketones cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with each other.
Compound Molecular mass b.p. (K) n-Butane 58 273 Methoxyethane 60 281 Propanal 58 322 Acetone 58 329 Propan-1-ol 60 370

docs.title: 3. Solubility
docs.text:
• Methanal, ethanal and propanone are miscible with water in all proportions because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
  • Solubility in water falls rapidly as the alkyl chain gets longer.
  • All aldehydes and ketones are fairly soluble in organic solvents such as benzene, ether, methanol and chloroform.

docs.title: 4. Odour
docs.text:
• Lower aldehydes have sharp, pungent odours. As molecular size increases, the odour becomes less pungent and more fragrant.
  • Many naturally occurring aldehydes and ketones are used in perfumes and flavouring agents.

docs.title: Chemical Reactions: Nucleophilic Addition
docs.text: Since aldehydes and ketones both contain the carbonyl group, they show similar chemical reactions. Unlike alkenes, which undergo electrophilic addition, aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition reactions.

docs.title: 1. Mechanism of nucleophilic addition
docs.text:
• A nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon from a direction roughly perpendicular to the plane of its sp2 hybrid orbitals.
  • During this attack, the hybridisation of carbon changes from sp2 to sp3 and a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is formed. This is the slow step.
  • The intermediate then picks up a proton from the reaction medium (fast step) to give the neutral addition product.
  • The overall result is the addition of Nu- and H+ across the C=O double bond.

docs.title: 2. Reactivity
docs.text:
Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition for two reasons:

  • Steric reason: a ketone has two relatively large groups on the carbonyl carbon, which hinder the approach of the nucleophile more than the single group in an aldehyde.
  • Electronic reason: alkyl groups are electron releasing. Two alkyl groups in a ketone reduce the electrophilicity (positive character) of the carbonyl carbon more than one alkyl group in an aldehyde.

Example

Benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal in nucleophilic addition. The benzene ring donates electrons to the carbonyl group by resonance, which reduces the polarity of the carbonyl group and makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic.

\[C_6H_5-CH=O \longleftrightarrow \overset{+}{C_6H_5}=CH-\overset{-}{O}\]

docs.title: 1. Addition of hydrogen cyanide (HCN)
docs.text:
• Aldehydes and ketones react with HCN to form cyanohydrins.
  • With pure HCN the reaction is very slow, so it is catalysed by a base. The base generates the cyanide ion (CN-), a much stronger nucleophile, which adds readily to the carbonyl group.
  • Cyanohydrins are useful synthetic intermediates.
\[HCN + OH^- ⇌ CN^- + H_2O\] \[>C=O + CN^- ⇌ >C(O^-)CN \xrightarrow{H^+} >C(OH)CN\] \[CH_3CHO + HCN → CH_3CH(OH)CN\]

docs.title: 2. Addition of sodium hydrogensulphite (NaHSO<sub>3</sub>)
docs.text:
• Sodium hydrogensulphite adds to aldehydes and ketones to form crystalline bisulphite addition compounds.
\[>C=O + NaHSO_3 ⇌ >C(ONa)OSO_2H ⇌ >C(OH)SO_3Na\]
  • The equilibrium lies largely to the right for most aldehydes and to the left for most ketones, for steric reasons.
  • The addition compound is water soluble and gives back the original carbonyl compound when treated with dilute mineral acid or alkali. So this reaction is used for separation and purification of aldehydes.

docs.title: 3. Addition of Grignard reagents
docs.text:
• Grignard reagents (RMgX) add to the carbonyl group, and hydrolysis of the adduct gives alcohols. Methanal gives primary alcohols, other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give tertiary alcohols.
\[>C=O + RMgX → >C(R)OMgX \xrightarrow{H_2O} >C(R)OH + Mg(OH)X\]

docs.title: 4. Addition of alcohols
docs.text:
• An aldehyde reacts with one equivalent of a monohydric alcohol in the presence of dry HCl to give an alkoxyalcohol called a hemiacetal.
  • The hemiacetal reacts with one more molecule of alcohol to give a gem-dialkoxy compound called an acetal.
\[RCHO \underset{HCl\ gas}{\overset{R'OH}{⇌}} RCH(OH)OR' \underset{H^+}{\overset{R'OH}{⇌}} RCH(OR')_2 + H_2O\] \[\qquad \qquad Hemiacetal \qquad \qquad Acetal\]
  • Ketones react with ethylene glycol under similar conditions to give cyclic products called ethylene glycol ketals.
\[R_2C=O + HOCH_2CH_2OH \underset{dil.\ HCl}{\overset{HCl\ gas}{⇌}} R_2C(OCH_2)_2 + H_2O\]
  • Dry HCl protonates the carbonyl oxygen, increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon and making the attack by the alcohol easier.
  • Acetals and ketals are hydrolysed by aqueous mineral acids back to the aldehydes and ketones.

docs.title: 5. Addition of ammonia and its derivatives
docs.text:
• Ammonia and its derivatives, H2N–Z, add to the carbonyl group. The reaction is reversible and acid catalysed.
  • The equilibrium favours the product because the intermediate rapidly loses water to form >C=N–Z. This is an addition-elimination reaction.
\[>C=O + H_2N-Z ⇌ >C(OH)NHZ → >C=N-Z + H_2O\] \[Z = alkyl,\ aryl,\ OH,\ NH_2,\ C_6H_5NH,\ NHCONH_2,\ etc.\] Z Reagent Carbonyl derivative Product name –H Ammonia >C=NH Imine –R Amine >C=NR Substituted imine (Schiff's base) –OH Hydroxylamine >C=N–OH Oxime –NH2 Hydrazine >C=N–NH2 Hydrazone –NHC6H5 Phenylhydrazine >C=N–NHC6H5 Phenylhydrazone –NHC6H3(NO2)2 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) >C=N–NHC6H3(NO2)2 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazone –NHCONH2 Semicarbazide >C=N–NHCONH2 Semicarbazone

Note

2,4-DNP derivatives are yellow, orange or red solids. They are used to identify (characterise) aldehydes and ketones.

Example

\[CH_3CHO + NH_2OH \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3CH=N-OH + H_2O\] \[Ethanal \qquad \qquad Acetaldoxime\]

docs.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
docs.text: Aldehydes and ketones are prepared by oxidation or dehydrogenation of alcohols, from hydrocarbons, and by several named reactions. Some methods give both classes, while others are specific to aldehydes or to ketones.

docs.title: Methods for both Aldehydes and Ketones
1. By oxidation of alcohols
docs.text:
• Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes and secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.
  • To stop a primary alcohol at the aldehyde stage, a mild oxidising agent such as pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC, C5H5NH+CrO3Cl-) is used. Secondary alcohols can be oxidised with K2Cr2O7 in acidic medium.
\[RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{[O]} RCHO\] \[R_2CHOH \xrightarrow{[O]} R_2C=O\]

docs.title: 2. By dehydrogenation of alcohols
docs.text:
• Vapours of the alcohol are passed over a heavy metal catalyst (Ag or Cu).
  • Primary alcohols give aldehydes and secondary alcohols give ketones.
  • This method suits volatile alcohols and is used industrially.
\[RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{Cu,\ 573\ K} RCHO + H_2\] \[R_2CHOH \xrightarrow{Cu,\ 573\ K} R_2CO + H_2\]

docs.title: (i) Ozonolysis of alkenes
docs.text:
• Alkenes react with ozone to form ozonides, which on treatment with zinc dust and water give aldehydes, ketones or a mixture of both, depending on how the alkene is substituted.
\[CH_3CH=CHCH_3 \xrightarrow{1.\ O_3\ \ 2.\ Zn/H_2O} 2CH_3CHO\]

docs.title: (ii) Hydration of alkynes
docs.text:
• Water adds to alkynes in the presence of H2SO4 and HgSO4.
  • Ethyne gives acetaldehyde; all other alkynes give ketones.
\[HC \equiv CH + H_2O \xrightarrow{HgSO_4,\ H_2SO_4} CH_3CHO\] \[CH_3C \equiv CH + H_2O \xrightarrow{Hg^{2+},\ H_2SO_4} CH_3COCH_3\]

docs.title: 1. From acyl chlorides: Rosenmund reduction
docs.text:
• An acyl chloride (acid chloride) is hydrogenated over palladium supported on barium sulphate. The BaSO4 poisons the catalyst so that the aldehyde is not reduced further to an alcohol.
\[C_6H_5COCl + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd-BaSO_4} C_6H_5CHO + HCl\] \[Benzoyl\ chloride \qquad \qquad Benzaldehyde\]

docs.title: (i) Stephen reaction
docs.text:
• Nitriles are reduced by stannous chloride and hydrochloric acid to an imine, which on hydrolysis gives the aldehyde.
\[RCN + SnCl_2 + HCl → RCH=NH \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} RCHO\]

docs.title: (ii) Reduction with DIBAL-H
docs.text:
• Diisobutylaluminium hydride, AlH(i-Bu)2 (DIBAL-H), selectively reduces nitriles to imines, which are hydrolysed to aldehydes.
  • It does not affect a C=C double bond present in the molecule.
  • Esters are also reduced to aldehydes by DIBAL-H.
\[RCN \xrightarrow{1.\ AlH(i-Bu)_2\ \ 2.\ H_2O} RCHO\] \[CH_3-CH=CH-CH_2CH_2-CN \xrightarrow{1.\ AlH(i-Bu)_2\ \ 2.\ H_2O} CH_3-CH=CH-CH_2CH_2-CHO\] \[CH_3(CH_2)_9COOC_2H_5 \xrightarrow{1.\ DIBAL-H\ \ 2.\ H_2O} CH_3(CH_2)_9CHO\]

docs.title: 3. From hydrocarbons (aromatic aldehydes)
docs.text: Strong oxidising agents oxidise toluene all the way to benzoic acid. To stop at benzaldehyde, reagents are used that convert the –CH3 group into an intermediate that resists further oxidation.

docs.title: (i) Etard reaction
docs.text:
• Chromyl chloride (CrO2Cl2) in CS2 oxidises the methyl group of toluene to a chromium complex, which on hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde.
\[C_6H_5CH_3 + CrO_2Cl_2 \xrightarrow{CS_2} C_6H_5CH(OCrOHCl_2)_2 \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_6H_5CHO\] \[Toluene \qquad \qquad Chromium\ complex \qquad \qquad Benzaldehyde\]

docs.title: (ii) Using chromic oxide
docs.text:
• Toluene (or a substituted toluene) with chromic oxide (CrO3) in acetic anhydride at 273–283 K gives benzylidene diacetate, which is hydrolysed by aqueous acid to benzaldehyde.
\[C_6H_5CH_3 + CrO_3 + (CH_3CO)_2O \xrightarrow{273-283\ K} C_6H_5CH(OCOCH_3)_2 \xrightarrow[Δ]{H_3O^+} C_6H_5CHO\]

docs.title: (iii) Side chain chlorination followed by hydrolysis
docs.text:
• Side chain chlorination of toluene gives benzal chloride, which on hydrolysis at 373 K gives benzaldehyde. This is a commercial method for making benzaldehyde.
\[C_6H_5CH_3 \xrightarrow{Cl_2/h\nu} C_6H_5CHCl_2 \xrightarrow{H_2O,\ 373\ K} C_6H_5CHO\] \[Toluene \qquad \qquad Benzal\ chloride \qquad \qquad Benzaldehyde\]

docs.title: (iv) Gatterman-Koch reaction
docs.text:
• Benzene or its derivative, when treated with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3 or CuCl, gives benzaldehyde or a substituted benzaldehyde.
\[C_6H_6 \xrightarrow{CO,\ HCl,\ anhyd.\ AlCl_3/CuCl} C_6H_5CHO\]

docs.title: 1. From acyl chlorides
docs.text:
• A dialkylcadmium is first prepared by reacting cadmium chloride with a Grignard reagent.
  • Treating an acyl chloride with the dialkylcadmium gives a ketone.
\[2R-Mg-X + CdCl_2 → R_2Cd + 2Mg(X)Cl\] \[2R'-COCl + R_2Cd → 2R'-CO-R + CdCl_2\]

docs.title: 2. From nitriles
docs.text:
• A nitrile reacts with a Grignard reagent to give an imine salt, which on hydrolysis yields a ketone.
\[CH_3CH_2C \equiv N + C_6H_5MgBr \xrightarrow{ether} CH_3CH_2C(=NMgBr)C_6H_5 \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_2H_5COC_6H_5\] \[Propiophenone\ (1-Phenylpropanone)\]

docs.title: 3. From benzene or substituted benzenes: Friedel-Crafts acylation
docs.text:
• Benzene or a substituted benzene reacts with an acid chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3 to give the corresponding aryl ketone.
\[C_6H_6 + Ar/R-COCl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5-CO-Ar/R\]

Conclusion

Reaction Reagent Product Rosenmund reduction H2, Pd-BaSO4 RCOCl → RCHO Stephen reaction SnCl2/HCl, then H3O+ RCN → RCHO DIBAL-H reduction AlH(i-Bu)2, then H2O RCN or RCOOR' → RCHO Etard reaction CrO2Cl2/CS2, then H3O+ C6H5CH3 → C6H5CHO Gatterman-Koch reaction CO, HCl, anhyd. AlCl3/CuCl C6H6 → C6H5CHO Friedel-Crafts acylation RCOCl, anhyd. AlCl3 C6H6 → C6H5COR

docs.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Questions
Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Questions
Nomenclature and Preparation
docs.text:
Give the IUPAC names of:(i) PhCH2CH2COOH(ii) (CH3)2C=CHCOOH(iii) CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH2CHO(iv) CH3COCH2COCH3(v) (CH3)3CCH2COOH

  • (i) The –COOH carbon is C-1 and the phenyl group is on C-3: 3-Phenylpropanoic acid.

  • (ii) Numbering from –COOH, the double bond is at C-2 and a methyl group is on C-3: 3-Methylbut-2-enoic acid.

  • (iii) Numbering from –CHO, the methyl group is on C-4: 4-Methylpentanal.

  • (iv) A five carbon chain with C=O groups at C-2 and C-4: Pentane-2,4-dione.

  • (v) Numbering from –COOH, three methyl groups are on C-3: 3,3-Dimethylbutanoic acid.

Name the reagents used to bring about the following transformations:(i) Hexan-1-ol to hexanal(ii) Cyclohexanol to cyclohexanone(iii) p-Fluorotoluene to p-fluorobenzaldehyde(iv) Ethanenitrile to ethanal(v) Allyl alcohol to propenal(vi) But-2-ene to ethanal

  • (i) Pyridinium chlorochromate, C5H5NH+CrO3Cl- (PCC), which stops the oxidation at the aldehyde stage.

  • (ii) K2Cr2O7 in acidic medium.

  • (iii) CrO3 in acetic anhydride followed by hydrolysis, or 1. CrO2Cl2 2. H2O (Etard reaction).

  • (iv) Diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL-H) followed by hydrolysis.

  • (v) PCC (it does not attack the C=C bond).

  • (vi) O3 followed by H2O/Zn dust (ozonolysis).

\[CH_3CH=CHCH_3 \xrightarrow{1.\ O_3\ \ 2.\ Zn/H_2O} 2CH_3CHO\]

Write the products of the following reactions:(i) Benzene + C2H5COCl in presence of anhyd. AlCl3/CS2(ii) (C6H5CH2)2Cd + 2CH3COCl(iii) CH3C≡CH with Hg2+, H2SO4(iv) p-Nitrotoluene with 1. CrO2Cl2 2. H3O+

  • (i) Friedel-Crafts acylation gives propiophenone:
\[C_6H_6 + C_2H_5COCl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5COC_2H_5 + HCl\]
  • (ii) The dialkylcadmium gives a ketone, 1-phenylpropan-2-one:
\[(C_6H_5CH_2)_2Cd + 2CH_3COCl → 2C_6H_5CH_2COCH_3 + CdCl_2\]
  • (iii) Hydration of propyne gives acetone:
\[CH_3C \equiv CH + H_2O \xrightarrow{Hg^{2+},\ H_2SO_4} CH_3COCH_3\]
  • (iv) The Etard reaction gives 4-nitrobenzaldehyde, p-NO2C6H4CHO.

Write chemical reactions to bring about the following transformations:(i) Butan-1-ol to butanoic acid(ii) Benzyl alcohol to phenylethanoic acid(iii) 3-Nitrobromobenzene to 3-nitrobenzoic acid(iv) 4-Methylacetophenone to benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid(v) Cyclohexene to hexane-1,6-dioic acid(vi) Butanal to butanoic acid

\[(i)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH \xrightarrow{CrO_3-H_2SO_4\ (Jones\ reagent)} CH_3CH_2CH_2COOH\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HBr} C_6H_5CH_2Br \xrightarrow{KCN} C_6H_5CH_2CN \xrightarrow[Δ]{H_3O^+} C_6H_5CH_2COOH\] \[(iii)\ m-O_2NC_6H_4Br \xrightarrow{Mg,\ ether} m-O_2NC_6H_4MgBr \xrightarrow{CO_2\ (dry\ ice)} m-O_2NC_6H_4COOMgBr \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} m-O_2NC_6H_4COOH\] \[(iv)\ p-CH_3C_6H_4COCH_3 \xrightarrow{KMnO_4/KOH} p-KOOCC_6H_4COOK \xrightarrow{dil.\ H_2SO_4} p-HOOCC_6H_4COOH\]

The product in (iv) is terephthalic acid. Both side chains are oxidised completely to –COOH.

\[(v)\ Cyclohexene \xrightarrow[Heat]{KMnO_4-H_2SO_4} HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH\ (Adipic\ acid)\] \[(vi)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2CHO \xrightarrow{Tollens'\ reagent} CH_3CH_2CH_2COOH\]

Show how each of the following compounds can be converted to benzoic acid:(i) Ethylbenzene (ii) Acetophenone (iii) Bromobenzene (iv) Phenylethene (Styrene)

\[(i)\ C_6H_5CH_2CH_3 \xrightarrow{KMnO_4-KOH} C_6H_5COOK \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_6H_5COOH\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5COCH_3 \xrightarrow{KMnO_4-KOH} C_6H_5COOK \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_6H_5COOH\] \[(iii)\ C_6H_5Br \xrightarrow{Mg,\ ether} C_6H_5MgBr \xrightarrow{CO_2} C_6H_5COOMgBr \xrightarrow{H_2O} C_6H_5COOH\] \[(iv)\ C_6H_5CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{KMnO_4-KOH} C_6H_5COOK + HCOOK \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_6H_5COOH\]

docs.title: Physical Properties and Reactivity
docs.text:
Arrange the following in increasing order of boiling points:CH3CH2CH2CHO, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH, H5C2–O–C2H5, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3

  • All four compounds have molecular masses in the range 72 to 74.

  • n-Pentane has only weak van der Waals forces, so it boils lowest.

  • Butanal is more polar than ethoxyethane, so dipole-dipole attraction is stronger in butanal.

  • Only butan-1-ol has extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding, so it boils highest.

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3 < H_5C_2-O-C_2H_5 < CH_3CH_2CH_2CHO < CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH\]

Arrange in increasing order of boiling points: CH3CHO, CH3CH2OH, CH3OCH3, CH3CH2CH3

Propane is non-polar, dimethyl ether is weakly polar, ethanal has a strongly polar C=O group, and ethanol forms hydrogen bonds.

\[CH_3CH_2CH_3 < CH_3OCH_3 < CH_3CHO < CH_3CH_2OH\]

Arrange in increasing order of reactivity in nucleophilic addition reactions:(i) Ethanal, Propanal, Propanone, Butanone(ii) Benzaldehyde, p-Tolualdehyde, p-Nitrobenzaldehyde, Acetophenone

  • (i) Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes. Among the ketones, the larger ethyl group in butanone gives more steric hindrance and more electron release. Among the aldehydes, ethanal has the smaller alkyl group.
\[Butanone < Propanone < Propanal < Ethanal\]
  • (ii) Acetophenone is a ketone, so it is least reactive. The –CH3 group in p-tolualdehyde is electron releasing and reduces the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon, while the –NO2 group in p-nitrobenzaldehyde is electron withdrawing and increases it.
\[Acetophenone < p-Tolualdehyde < Benzaldehyde < p-Nitrobenzaldehyde\]

Arrange in increasing order of reactivity towards HCN: Acetaldehyde, Acetone, Di-tert-butyl ketone, Methyl tert-butyl ketone

Reactivity falls as the groups on the carbonyl carbon become bulkier and more electron releasing.

\[Di-tert-butyl\ ketone < Methyl\ tert-butyl\ ketone < Acetone < Acetaldehyde\]

Predict the products:(i) Cyclopentanone + HO–NH2 (H+)(ii) Cyclohexanone + 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine(iii) R–CH=CH–CHO + NH2CONHNH2 (H+)(iv) C6H5COCH3 + CH3CH2NH2 (H+)

In each case the –NH2 group adds to C=O and water is eliminated to form >C=N–.

  • (i) Cyclopentanone oxime: (CH2)4C=N–OH

  • (ii) Cyclohexanone 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone: (CH2)5C=N–NH–C6H3(NO2)2

  • (iii) Semicarbazone: R–CH=CH–CH=N–NH–CO–NH2

  • (iv) Schiff's base: C6H5C(CH3)=N–CH2CH3

There are two –NH2 groups in semicarbazide. However, only one is involved in the formation of semicarbazones. Why?

In semicarbazide, H2N–CO–NH–NH2, the lone pair of the –NH2 group attached to C=O is delocalised into the carbonyl group by resonance:

\[H_2N-C(=O)-NH-NH_2 \longleftrightarrow H_2\overset{+}{N}=C(-O^-)-NH-NH_2\]

So this –NH2 group is not nucleophilic. Only the terminal –NH2 group (attached to NH) has a free lone pair and attacks the carbonyl carbon.

Cyclohexanone forms cyanohydrin in good yield but 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexanone does not. Why?

In 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexanone, the three methyl groups on the carbons next to C=O cause strong steric hindrance. The CN- ion cannot easily approach the carbonyl carbon, so the cyanohydrin is formed in poor yield. Cyclohexanone has no such hindrance.

During the preparation of esters from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst, the water or the ester should be removed as soon as it is formed. Why?

Esterification is reversible:

\[RCOOH + R'OH \overset{H^+}{⇌} RCOOR' + H_2O\]

By Le Chatelier's principle, removing a product (water or ester) shifts the equilibrium forward, increasing the yield of the ester and preventing its hydrolysis back to acid and alcohol.

docs.title: Aldol and Cannizzaro Reactions
docs.text:
Which of the following would undergo aldol condensation, which the Cannizzaro reaction and which neither?(i) Methanal (ii) 2-Methylpentanal (iii) Benzaldehyde (iv) Benzophenone (v) Cyclohexanone (vi) 1-Phenylpropanone (vii) Phenylacetaldehyde (viii) Butan-1-ol (ix) 2,2-Dimethylbutanal

  • Aldol condensation (have α-hydrogen): 2-methylpentanal, cyclohexanone, 1-phenylpropanone, phenylacetaldehyde.

  • Cannizzaro reaction (aldehydes with no α-hydrogen): methanal, benzaldehyde, 2,2-dimethylbutanal.

  • Neither: benzophenone (a ketone with no α-hydrogen) and butan-1-ol (not a carbonyl compound).

\[2HCHO \xrightarrow{conc.\ NaOH} CH_3OH + HCOONa\] \[2CH_3CH_2C(CH_3)_2CHO \xrightarrow{conc.\ NaOH} CH_3CH_2C(CH_3)_2CH_2OH + CH_3CH_2C(CH_3)_2COONa\] \[2C_6H_5CH_2CHO \xrightarrow{dil.\ NaOH} C_6H_5CH_2CH(OH)CH(C_6H_5)CHO \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{Δ} C_6H_5CH_2CH=C(C_6H_5)CHO\]

How will you convert ethanal into (i) Butane-1,3-diol (ii) But-2-enal (iii) But-2-enoic acid?

All three start with the aldol reaction of ethanal:

\[2CH_3CHO \xrightarrow{dil.\ NaOH} CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO\] \[(i)\ CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO \xrightarrow{NaBH_4} CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_2OH\] \[(ii)\ CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{Δ} CH_3CH=CHCHO\] \[(iii)\ CH_3CH=CHCHO \xrightarrow{Tollens'\ reagent} CH_3CH=CHCOOH\]

Tollens' reagent is used in (iii) because it oxidises the –CHO group without attacking the C=C bond.

docs.title: Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
docs.text:
Which acid of each pair would you expect to be stronger?(i) CH3CO2H or CH2FCO2H(ii) CH2FCO2H or CH2ClCO2H(iii) CH2FCH2CH2CO2H or CH3CHFCH2CO2H(iv) F3C–C6H4–COOH or H3C–C6H4–COOH (para)

  • (i) CH2FCO2H: the electron withdrawing F stabilises the carboxylate ion.

  • (ii) CH2FCO2H: F is more electronegative than Cl, so its –I effect is stronger.

  • (iii) CH3CHFCH2CO2H: F is closer to the –COOH group, and the –I effect decreases with distance.

  • (iv) F3C–C6H4–COOH: –CF3 is strongly electron withdrawing, while –CH3 is electron donating.

Arrange in increasing order of acid strength:(i) CH3CH2CH(Br)COOH, CH3CH(Br)CH2COOH, (CH3)2CHCOOH, CH3CH2CH2COOH(ii) Benzoic acid, 4-Nitrobenzoic acid, 3,4-Dinitrobenzoic acid, 4-Methoxybenzoic acid

  • (i) The isopropyl group releases more electrons than the n-propyl group. Br is electron withdrawing, and its effect is stronger when it is closer to –COOH.
\[(CH_3)_2CHCOOH < CH_3CH_2CH_2COOH < CH_3CH(Br)CH_2COOH < CH_3CH_2CH(Br)COOH\]
  • (ii) –OCH3 is electron donating and decreases acidity, while –NO2 groups are electron withdrawing and increase it. Two –NO2 groups increase it more than one.
\[4-Methoxybenzoic < Benzoic < 4-Nitrobenzoic < 3,4-Dinitrobenzoic\]

Although the phenoxide ion has more resonating structures than the carboxylate ion, carboxylic acid is a stronger acid than phenol. Why?

  • The two resonance structures of the carboxylate ion are equivalent, and in both the negative charge is on an electronegative oxygen atom.

  • In the phenoxide ion, the structures are non-equivalent, and in most of them the negative charge is on a less electronegative carbon atom. These contribute little to stability.

  • So the negative charge is delocalised more effectively over two oxygens in the carboxylate ion than over one oxygen and ring carbons in phenoxide. The carboxylate ion is more stable, and hence carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols.

docs.title: Identification Problems
docs.text:
An organic compound (A), C8H8O, forms an orange-red precipitate with 2,4-DNP reagent and gives a yellow precipitate on heating with iodine and sodium hydroxide. It neither reduces Tollens' or Fehling's reagent, nor decolourises bromine water or Baeyer's reagent. On drastic oxidation with chromic acid, it gives a carboxylic acid (B), C7H6O2. Identify (A) and (B).

  • (A) forms a 2,4-DNP derivative, so it is an aldehyde or a ketone. It does not reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent, so it is a ketone.

  • (A) gives the iodoform test, so it is a methyl ketone.

  • C8H8O is highly unsaturated, but (A) does not decolourise bromine water or Baeyer's reagent, so the unsaturation is due to an aromatic ring.

  • (B), C7H6O2, is benzoic acid. So (A) is a monosubstituted aromatic methyl ketone: acetophenone, C6H5COCH3.

\[C_6H_5COCH_3 + H_2NNHC_6H_3(NO_2)_2 \xrightarrow{-H_2O} C_6H_5C(CH_3)=NNHC_6H_3(NO_2)_2\ (2,4-DNP\ derivative)\] \[C_6H_5COCH_3 \xrightarrow{NaOH/I_2} C_6H_5COONa + CHI_3 ↓\] \[C_6H_5COCH_3 \xrightarrow{H_2CrO_4} C_6H_5COOH\ (B)\]

An organic compound C9H10O forms a 2,4-DNP derivative, reduces Tollens' reagent and undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction. On vigorous oxidation, it gives 1,2-benzenedicarboxylic acid. Identify the compound.

  • It forms a 2,4-DNP derivative and reduces Tollens' reagent, so it is an aldehyde.

  • It undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction, so the –CHO group has no α-hydrogen. The –CHO group must be directly attached to the benzene ring.

  • Vigorous oxidation gives phthalic acid, so the ring has two substituents in ortho positions.

  • C9H10O minus C6H4 and –CHO leaves C2H5. So the compound is 2-ethylbenzaldehyde, o-C2H5C6H4CHO.

\[o-C_2H_5C_6H_4CHO \xrightarrow{KMnO_4,\ vigorous} o-C_6H_4(COOH)_2\]

An organic compound (A), C8H16O2, was hydrolysed with dilute sulphuric acid to give a carboxylic acid (B) and an alcohol (C). Oxidation of (C) with chromic acid produced (B). (C) on dehydration gives but-1-ene. Write the reactions involved.

  • (C) dehydrates to but-1-ene, so (C) is butan-1-ol.

  • Oxidation of (C) gives (B), so (B) is butanoic acid, with the same carbon skeleton.

  • (A) is the ester of these two: butyl butanoate, CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH2CH2CH3 (C8H16O2).

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2COOC_4H_9 + H_2O \xrightarrow{dil.\ H_2SO_4} CH_3CH_2CH_2COOH + CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH\] \[CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH \xrightarrow{H_2CrO_4} CH_3CH_2CH_2COOH\] \[CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{conc.\ H_2SO_4,\ Δ} CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2\]

An organic compound contains 69.77% carbon, 11.63% hydrogen and the rest oxygen. Its molecular mass is 86. It does not reduce Tollens' reagent but forms an addition compound with sodium hydrogensulphite and gives a positive iodoform test. On vigorous oxidation it gives ethanoic and propanoic acid. Write its possible structure.

\[\%\ O = 100 - 69.77 - 11.63 = 18.60\] \[C : H : O = {69.77 \over 12} : {11.63 \over 1} : {18.60 \over 16} = 5.81 : 11.63 : 1.16 = 5 : 10 : 1\] \[Empirical\ formula = C_5H_{10}O,\ mass = 86\] \[∴ Molecular\ formula = C_5H_{10}O\]

  • It does not reduce Tollens' reagent, so it is a ketone. It forms a bisulphite compound and gives the iodoform test, so it is a methyl ketone.

  • The possible methyl ketones are pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one. Only pentan-2-one gives ethanoic acid and propanoic acid on oxidation:

\[CH_3COCH_2CH_2CH_3 \xrightarrow{[O]} CH_3COOH + CH_3CH_2COOH\]

So the compound is pentan-2-one.

docs.title: Distinguishing Tests
docs.text:
Give simple chemical tests to distinguish between:(i) Propanal and Propanone(ii) Acetophenone and Benzophenone(iii) Phenol and Benzoic acid(iv) Benzoic acid and Ethyl benzoate(v) Pentan-2-one and Pentan-3-one(vi) Benzaldehyde and Acetophenone(vii) Ethanal and Propanal

  • (i) Tollens' test: propanal gives a silver mirror; propanone does not.

  • (ii) Iodoform test: acetophenone (C6H5COCH3) gives a yellow precipitate of CHI3; benzophenone does not.

  • (iii) NaHCO3 test: benzoic acid gives brisk effervescence of CO2; phenol does not. (Phenol gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl3.)

  • (iv) NaHCO3 test: benzoic acid gives effervescence; ethyl benzoate does not.

  • (v) Iodoform test: pentan-2-one (a methyl ketone) gives a yellow precipitate; pentan-3-one does not.

  • (vi) Tollens' test: benzaldehyde gives a silver mirror; acetophenone does not. Alternatively, acetophenone gives the iodoform test while benzaldehyde does not.

  • (vii) Iodoform test: ethanal (CH3CHO) gives a yellow precipitate; propanal does not.

docs.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Reduction, Oxidation and Other Reactions
Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids | Reduction, Oxidation and Other Reactions
1. Reduction to alcohols
docs.text:
• Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols by sodium borohydride (NaBH4), lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4) or catalytic hydrogenation.
\[RCHO \xrightarrow{NaBH_4\ or\ LiAlH_4} RCH_2OH\] \[R_2CO \xrightarrow{NaBH_4\ or\ LiAlH_4} R_2CHOH\]

docs.title: 2. Reduction to hydrocarbons
docs.text:
The carbonyl group can be reduced completely to a –CH2– group in two ways:

  • Clemmensen reduction: heating with zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid.
  • Wolff-Kishner reduction: reaction with hydrazine to form a hydrazone, then heating with KOH or NaOH in a high boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol.
\[>C=O \xrightarrow{Zn-Hg,\ HCl} >CH_2 + H_2O \qquad (Clemmensen\ reduction)\] \[>C=O \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{NH_2NH_2} >C=NNH_2 \xrightarrow[heat]{KOH/ethylene\ glycol} >CH_2 + N_2 \qquad (Wolff-Kishner\ reduction)\]

docs.title: Oxidation
docs.text:
• Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids by common oxidising agents such as HNO3, KMnO4 and K2Cr2O7. Even mild oxidising agents like Tollens' reagent and Fehling's reagent oxidise them.
\[RCHO \xrightarrow{[O]} RCOOH\]
  • Ketones are oxidised only under vigorous conditions (strong oxidising agents and high temperature). The C–C bond next to the carbonyl group breaks, giving a mixture of carboxylic acids each having fewer carbon atoms than the ketone.
\[R-\overset{1}{C}H_2-\overset{2}{C}O-\overset{3}{C}H_2-R' \xrightarrow{[O]} RCOOH + R'CH_2COOH\ \ (C_1-C_2\ cleavage)\] \[\qquad \qquad \qquad + \ RCH_2COOH + R'COOH\ \ (C_2-C_3\ cleavage)\]

The following mild oxidising agents are used to distinguish aldehydes from ketones.

docs.title: 1. Tollens' test
docs.text:
• On warming an aldehyde with freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate solution (Tollens' reagent), a bright silver mirror is formed due to deposition of silver metal.
  • The aldehyde is oxidised to the carboxylate anion. The reaction occurs in alkaline medium.
\[RCHO + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+ + 3OH^- → RCOO^- + 2Ag ↓ + 2H_2O + 4NH_3\]

docs.title: 2. Fehling's test
docs.text:
• Fehling's reagent is made by mixing equal amounts of Fehling solution A (aqueous copper sulphate) and Fehling solution B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate, called Rochelle salt) just before the test.
  • On heating an aldehyde with Fehling's reagent, a reddish brown precipitate of Cu2O is formed.
  • Aromatic aldehydes do not respond to this test.
\[RCHO + 2Cu^{2+} + 5OH^- → RCOO^- + Cu_2O ↓ + 3H_2O\]

docs.title: 3. Haloform reaction
docs.text:
• Aldehydes and ketones having at least one methyl group attached to the carbonyl carbon (CH3CO– group, i.e. methyl ketones) are oxidised by sodium hypohalite (NaOX) to the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid having one carbon atom less. The methyl group is converted into a haloform (CHX3).
  • A C=C double bond present in the molecule is not affected.
\[RCOCH_3 \xrightarrow{NaOX} RCOONa + CHX_3 \qquad (X = Cl,\ Br,\ I)\] \[CH_3CH=C(CH_3)COCH_3 \xrightarrow{NaOCl} CH_3CH=C(CH_3)COONa + CHCl_3\]
  • With sodium hypoiodite (I2 + NaOH), yellow iodoform (CHI3) is formed. The iodoform test detects the CH3CO– group, and also the CH3CH(OH)– group, which is oxidised to CH3CO– under the test conditions.

docs.title: Reactions due to α-Hydrogen
docs.text:
• A hydrogen on the carbon next to the carbonyl group (the α-carbon) is acidic.
  • This acidity is due to the strong electron withdrawing effect of the carbonyl group and the resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base (enolate ion) formed when a base removes the α-hydrogen.
\[-CO-CH< \ \xrightarrow{:B} \ [-CO-\overset{-}{C}< \ \longleftrightarrow \ -C(O^-)=C<]\]

docs.title: 1. Aldol condensation
docs.text:
• Aldehydes and ketones having at least one α-hydrogen react in the presence of dilute alkali to form β-hydroxy aldehydes (aldol) or β-hydroxy ketones (ketol). This is the aldol reaction. The name aldol comes from the two functional groups in the product: aldehyde and alcohol.
  • The aldol or ketol readily loses water on heating to form an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound. This overall reaction is called aldol condensation.
  • Ketones give ketols, but the reaction is still called aldol condensation because of its similarity to the aldehyde reaction.
\[2CH_3CHO \overset{dil.\ NaOH}{⇌} CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{Δ} CH_3CH=CHCHO\] \[Ethanal \qquad 3-Hydroxybutanal\ (aldol) \qquad But-2-enal\] \[2CH_3COCH_3 \overset{Ba(OH)_2}{⇌} (CH_3)_2C(OH)CH_2COCH_3 \xrightarrow[-H_2O]{Δ} (CH_3)_2C=CHCOCH_3\] \[Propanone \qquad 4-Hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one\ (ketol) \qquad 4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one\]

docs.title: 2. Cross aldol condensation
docs.text:
• Aldol condensation between two different aldehydes and/or ketones is called cross aldol condensation.
  • If both of them have α-hydrogens, a mixture of four products is formed. For example, a mixture of ethanal and propanal (1. NaOH, 2. heat) gives:
Product Formed from CH3CH=CHCHO (But-2-enal) Two molecules of ethanal (self aldol) CH3CH2CH=C(CH3)CHO (2-Methylpent-2-enal) Two molecules of propanal (self aldol) CH3CH=C(CH3)CHO (2-Methylbut-2-enal) Ethanal + propanal (cross aldol) CH3CH2CH=CHCHO (Pent-2-enal) Ethanal + propanal (cross aldol)
  • Ketones can also be one component in a cross aldol reaction. Benzaldehyde (no α-hydrogen) and acetophenone give benzalacetophenone as the major product:
\[C_6H_5CHO + CH_3COC_6H_5 \xrightarrow{OH^-,\ 293\ K} C_6H_5CH=CHCOC_6H_5\] \[1,3-Diphenylprop-2-en-1-one\ (Benzalacetophenone)\]

docs.title: 1. Cannizzaro reaction
docs.text:
• Aldehydes which have no α-hydrogen undergo self oxidation and reduction (disproportionation) when treated with concentrated alkali.
  • One molecule of the aldehyde is reduced to an alcohol while another is oxidised to the salt of a carboxylic acid.
\[2HCHO + conc.\ KOH → CH_3OH + HCOOK\] \[Formaldehyde \qquad Methanol \qquad Potassium\ formate\] \[2C_6H_5CHO + conc.\ NaOH → C_6H_5CH_2OH + C_6H_5COONa\] \[Benzaldehyde \qquad Benzyl\ alcohol \qquad Sodium\ benzoate\]

Conclusion

  • Aldehydes/ketones with α-hydrogen + dilute alkali → aldol condensation.

  • Aldehydes without α-hydrogen (HCHO, C6H5CHO, (CH3)3CCHO) + concentrated alkali → Cannizzaro reaction.

docs.title: 2. Electrophilic substitution
docs.text:
• Aromatic aldehydes and ketones undergo electrophilic substitution on the ring. The carbonyl group is deactivating and meta-directing.
\[C_6H_5CHO \xrightarrow{HNO_3/H_2SO_4,\ 273-283\ K} m-NO_2C_6H_4CHO\] \[Benzaldehyde \qquad \qquad m-Nitrobenzaldehyde\]

docs.title: Uses of Aldehydes and Ketones
docs.text:
• Aldehydes and ketones are used in the chemical industry as solvents, starting materials and reagents.
  • Formaldehyde: its 40% solution, formalin, is used to preserve biological specimens. It is also used to make bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde resin), urea-formaldehyde glues and other polymers.
  • Acetaldehyde: mainly a starting material for making acetic acid, ethyl acetate, vinyl acetate, polymers and drugs.
  • Benzaldehyde: used in perfumery and in the dye industry.
  • Acetone and ethyl methyl ketone: common industrial solvents.
  • Butyraldehyde, vanillin, acetophenone and camphor are well known for their odours and flavours.

docs.title: Alkyl Halides | Elimination and Reaction with Metals
Alkyl Halides | Elimination and Reaction with Metals
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the elimination reactions of haloalkanes (dehydrohalogenation), the competition between elimination and substitution, and the reactions of haloalkanes with metals.

docs.title: Elimination Reactions
docs.text:
• When a haloalkane having a β-hydrogen atom is heated with alcoholic KOH, a hydrogen atom is removed from the β-carbon and the halogen atom from the α-carbon.
  • The α-carbon is the one carrying the halogen; the carbon next to it is the β-carbon.
  • As a result, an alkene is formed. Since a β-hydrogen is involved, the reaction is called β-elimination (or dehydrohalogenation).
\[B^- + H-\overset{\beta}{C}-\overset{\alpha}{C}-X → >C=C< + B-H + X^-\] \[B = Base;\ \ X = Leaving\ group\]

Example

\[CH_3CH_2Br + KOH_{(alc)} \xrightarrow{Δ} CH_2=CH_2 + KBr + H_2O\]

docs.title: Saytzeff (Zaitsev) Rule
docs.text:
• If the halide has more than one type of β-hydrogen, more than one alkene can form. Usually, one of them is the major product.
  • In 1875, the Russian chemist Alexander Zaitsev (also written Saytzeff) gave a rule:

Saytzeff Rule

In dehydrohalogenation reactions, the preferred product is that alkene which has the greater number of alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbon atoms.

  • In simple words, the more substituted (and more stable) alkene is the major product.

Example: Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromopentane

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2CH(Br)CH_3 \xrightarrow{alc.\ KOH} \underset{Pent-2-ene\ (81\%)}{CH_3CH_2CH=CHCH_3} + \underset{Pent-1-ene\ (19\%)}{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH=CH_2}\]

Pent-2-ene has two alkyl groups on the double bond carbons while pent-1-ene has only one. So pent-2-ene is the major product.

docs.title: Elimination versus Substitution
docs.text:
• An alkyl halide with β-hydrogens, when treated with a base or nucleophile, has two competing routes: substitution (SN1 or SN2) and elimination.
  • A reaction is like a race: the route that is easiest (fastest) wins. Which route is taken depends on the nature of the alkyl halide, the strength and size of the base/nucleophile, and the reaction conditions.
  • A bulky nucleophile (e.g. (CH3)3CO-) finds it hard to approach the crowded tetravalent carbon. So it prefers to act as a base and pull off a proton, giving elimination. A small nucleophile (e.g. CH3CH2O-) more easily gives substitution.
Type of alkyl halide Preferred route Primary SN2 Secondary SN2 or elimination, depending on the strength of the base/nucleophile Tertiary SN1 or elimination, depending on the stability of the carbocation or of the more substituted alkene

Note

Aqueous KOH gives mainly alcohols, since OH- in water is a good nucleophile (substitution). Alcoholic KOH contains the alkoxide ion RO-, a stronger base, which favours elimination and gives alkenes.

docs.title: Reaction with Metals
docs.text: • Most organic chlorides, bromides and iodides react with certain metals to give compounds containing carbon-metal bonds. These are called organometallic compounds.

docs.title: 1. Grignard Reagents
docs.text:
• Alkyl magnesium halides, RMgX, were discovered by Victor Grignard in 1900. They are called Grignard reagents.
  • They are prepared by reacting a haloalkane with magnesium metal in dry ether.
\[CH_3CH_2Br + Mg \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} CH_3CH_2MgBr\] \[(Ethylmagnesium\ bromide,\ a\ Grignard\ reagent)\]
  • In RMgX, the C-Mg bond is covalent but highly polar: carbon pulls electrons from the electropositive magnesium. The Mg-X bond is essentially ionic.
\[\overset{\delta-}{R}-\overset{\delta+}{Mg}-\overset{\delta-}{X}\]
  • Grignard reagents are highly reactive. They react with any source of proton to give hydrocarbons. Even water, alcohols and amines are acidic enough to destroy them.
\[RMgX + H_2O → RH + Mg(OH)X\]
  • So, even traces of moisture must be avoided while preparing a Grignard reagent (anhydrous conditions). On the other hand, this reaction is also a method of converting halides into hydrocarbons.
  • Grignard was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1912, shared with Paul Sabatier.

docs.title: 2. Wurtz Reaction
docs.text:
• Alkyl halides react with sodium in dry ether to give hydrocarbons containing double the number of carbon atoms present in the halide.
\[2RX + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} R-R + 2NaX\]

Example

\[2CH_3Br + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} CH_3-CH_3 + 2NaBr\] \[2CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} CH_3(CH_2)_6CH_3 + 2NaCl\]

1-Chlorobutane gives n-octane.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Alkyl halides are halogen substituted alkanes. A monohaloalkane is written as R-X, where X is any halogen atom (F, Cl. Br and l).

The general formula of monohaloalkanes is CnH2n+1X while that of a dihaloalkane is CnH2nX2.

Alkyl halides of a particular kind, in which halogen atom is attached to a saturated carbon, which in turn is linked to unsaturated carbon, are called allyl halides. And when halogen atom is attached to an unsaturated (sp2) carbon, they are called vinyl halides.

Examples

Alkyl halides are classified as primary (10), secondary (20) or tertiary (30), depending upon the type of carbon to which X is bonded. When X is bonded to a carbon which is bonded to one more carbon, it is called 10 halide and their general representation is RCH2X. When X is linked to a carbon which is bonded to two carbons, it is called 20 halides and is denoted by R2CHX. When X is bonded to a carbon, which is attached to 3 carbons is called 30 halides and is designated as R3CX. CH3X is unique (not classified as 10 , 20 or 30) as carbon is bonded to only hydrogens and is simply called methyl halide. Dihaloalkanes with both halogens on same carbon are called gemdihalides and with halogen on adjacent carbons are called vicinal dihalides.

docs.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alkyl halides
docs.text:
IUPAC nomenclature of alkyl halides with one halogen is haloalkanes and with tvvo similar halogens is dihaloalkanes. If the halogens present are different, they are prefixed in alphabetical order.

Examples

docs.title: Alkyl Halides | Nature of C-X Bond and Methods of Preparation
Alkyl Halides | Nature of C-X Bond and Methods of Preparation
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the nature of the carbon-halogen bond and the important methods used to prepare haloalkanes and haloarenes.

docs.title: Nature of C-X Bond
docs.text:
• Halogen atoms are more electronegative than carbon. So, the C-X bond in an alkyl halide is polarised: carbon carries a partial positive charge (δ+) and halogen carries a partial negative charge (δ-).
\[\overset{\delta+}{C} - \overset{\delta-}{X}\]
  • The size of the halogen atom increases down the group (F is smallest, I is largest). Hence, the C-X bond length increases from C-F to C-I, while the bond enthalpy decreases.
Bond Bond length (pm) C-X Bond enthalpy (kJ mol-1) Dipole moment (Debye) CH3-F 139 452 1.847 CH3-Cl 178 351 1.860 CH3-Br 193 293 1.830 CH3-I 214 234 1.636

Note

A longer, weaker C-X bond breaks more easily. This is why the reactivity of alkyl halides follows the order R-I > R-Br > R-Cl > R-F.

docs.title: 1. From Alcohols
docs.text:
• Alcohols are easily available, so they are the best starting material for alkyl halides.
  • The -OH group of an alcohol is replaced by a halogen using concentrated halogen acids (HX), phosphorus halides (PX3, PCl5) or thionyl chloride (SOCl2).
\[R-OH + HX \xrightarrow{ZnCl_2} R-X + H_2O\] \[R-OH + NaBr + H_2SO_4 → R-Br + NaHSO_4 + H_2O\] \[3R-OH + PX_3 → 3R-X + H_3PO_3\ \ (X = Cl,\ Br)\] \[R-OH + PCl_5 → R-Cl + POCl_3 + HCl\] \[R-OH \xrightarrow{red\ P/X_2\ (X_2 = Br_2,\ I_2)} R-X\] \[R-OH + SOCl_2 → R-Cl + SO_2 ↑ + HCl ↑\]
  • Thionyl chloride is preferred, because both by-products (SO2 and HCl) are gases that escape, leaving pure alkyl chloride behind.
  • PBr3 and PI3 are usually generated in situ (inside the reaction mixture) by reacting red phosphorus with bromine or iodine.
  • Alkyl chlorides are made either by passing dry HCl gas through the alcohol, or by heating the alcohol with concentrated aqueous HCl.
  • Primary and secondary alcohols need anhydrous ZnCl2 as catalyst with HX. Tertiary alcohols react simply on shaking with concentrated HCl at room temperature.
  • Alkyl bromides are prepared by constant boiling with HBr (48%). Good yields of alkyl iodides are obtained by heating the alcohol with NaI or KI in 95% phosphoric acid.
  • Order of reactivity of alcohols with a given haloacid:
\[3^0 > 2^0 > 1^0\]

Note

This method cannot be used to make aryl halides from phenols. The C-O bond in phenol has partial double bond character (due to resonance), so it is stronger than a single bond and difficult to break.

docs.title: (a) Free radical halogenation
docs.text:
• Chlorination or bromination of alkanes in UV light or heat gives a complex mixture of isomeric mono- and polyhaloalkanes.
  • These are difficult to separate, so the yield of any single product is low.
\[CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3 \xrightarrow[or\ heat]{Cl_2/UV\ light} CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl + CH_3CH_2CHClCH_3\]

docs.title: (b) Electrophilic substitution (for haloarenes)
docs.text:
• Aryl chlorides and bromides are prepared by treating arenes with Cl2 or Br2 in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as iron or FeCl3, in the dark.
\[C_6H_5CH_3 + X_2 \xrightarrow[dark]{Fe} o-XC_6H_4CH_3 + p-XC_6H_4CH_3\] \[(o-Halotoluene\ and\ p-Halotoluene)\]
  • The ortho and para isomers are easily separated because of the large difference in their melting points.
  • Iodination is reversible. An oxidising agent (HNO3 or HIO4) is needed to oxidise the HI formed, so that the reaction moves forward.
  • Fluoroarenes are not made this way because fluorine is too reactive.

docs.title: (c) Sandmeyer's reaction (for haloarenes)
docs.text:
• A primary aromatic amine in cold aqueous mineral acid is treated with sodium nitrite (NaNO2) at 273-278 K to form a diazonium salt.
  • The freshly prepared diazonium salt is mixed with cuprous chloride or cuprous bromide. The diazonium group is replaced by -Cl or -Br.
\[C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow[273-278\ K]{NaNO_2\ +\ HX} C_6H_5N_2^+X^-\] \[C_6H_5N_2^+X^- \xrightarrow{Cu_2X_2} C_6H_5X + N_2 ↑\ \ (X = Cl,\ Br)\]
  • For iodobenzene, cuprous halide is not needed. The diazonium salt is simply shaken with potassium iodide.
\[C_6H_5N_2^+X^- + KI → C_6H_5I + N_2 ↑ + KX\]

docs.title: (d) From alkenes
docs.text:
(i) Addition of hydrogen halides: An alkene adds HCl, HBr or HI to form an alkyl halide.

\[>C=C< + HX → >CH-CX<\]
  • Unsymmetrical alkenes like propene can give two products, but the major one is decided by Markovnikov's rule (the halogen goes to the carbon having fewer hydrogens).
\[CH_3CH=CH_2 + HI → \underset{minor}{CH_3CH_2CH_2I} + \underset{major}{CH_3CHICH_3}\]
  • In the presence of peroxide, HBr adds in the anti-Markovnikov manner.

(ii) Addition of halogens: Bromine in CCl4 adds across a double bond to form a colourless vic-dibromide. The disappearance of the reddish-brown colour of bromine is a laboratory test for unsaturation.

\[CH_2=CH_2 + Br_2 \xrightarrow{CCl_4} BrCH_2-CH_2Br\] \[(vic-Dibromide)\]

docs.title: (a) Finkelstein reaction
docs.text:
• Alkyl iodides are prepared by heating alkyl chlorides or bromides with NaI in dry acetone.
\[R-X + NaI \xrightarrow{dry\ acetone} R-I + NaX\ \ (X = Cl,\ Br)\]
  • NaCl or NaBr formed is insoluble in dry acetone and precipitates out. Removal of a product pushes the equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier's principle).

docs.title: (b) Swarts reaction
docs.text:
• Alkyl fluorides are best prepared by heating an alkyl chloride or bromide with a metallic fluoride such as AgF, Hg2F2, CoF2 or SbF3.
\[H_3C-Br + AgF → H_3C-F + AgBr\]

Conclusion

Fluorides and iodides are difficult to make by direct halogenation, so they are best prepared by halogen exchange: Swarts reaction for fluorides and Finkelstein reaction for iodides.

docs.title: Alkyl Halides | Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions
docs.text:
The reactions of haloalkanes can be divided into three categories:

  • Nucleophilic substitution
  • Elimination reactions
  • Reaction with metals

In this article, we will discuss nucleophilic substitution and its two mechanisms, SN2 and SN1.

docs.title: Nucleophilic Substitution
docs.text:
• In a haloalkane, the carbon bonded to the halogen carries a partial positive charge.
  • A nucleophile (an electron-rich species, Nu-) attacks this carbon. The halogen departs as a halide ion, called the leaving group.
  • Since the reaction is started by a nucleophile, it is called a nucleophilic substitution reaction.
\[Nu^- + R-X → R-Nu + X^-\]
  • This is one of the most useful reactions of alkyl halides, in which halogen is bonded to an sp3 hybridised carbon.
Reagent Nucleophile (Nu-) Product (R-Nu) Class of main product NaOH (KOH) HO- ROH Alcohol H2O H2O ROH Alcohol NaOR' R'O- ROR' Ether NaI I- R-I Alkyl iodide NH3 NH3 RNH2 Primary amine R'NH2 R'NH2 RNHR' Secondary amine R'R''NH R'R''NH RNR'R'' Tertiary amine KCN C≡N- RCN Nitrile (cyanide) AgCN Ag-CN: RNC Isonitrile (isocyanide) KNO2 O=N-O- R-O-N=O Alkyl nitrite AgNO2 Ag-O-N=O R-NO2 Nitroalkane R'COOAg R'COO- R'COOR Ester LiAlH4 H- RH Hydrocarbon R'-M+ R'- RR' Alkane

docs.title: Ambident Nucleophiles
docs.text:
• Nucleophiles that have two nucleophilic centres (two atoms that can donate an electron pair) are called ambident nucleophiles. Examples: cyanide and nitrite ions.
  • The cyanide ion is a resonance hybrid of two structures, so it can attack through carbon (giving alkyl cyanides) or through nitrogen (giving isocyanides).
\[^-:C≡N: \ \ ↔ \ \ :C=\ddot{N}:^-\]
  • The nitrite ion can attack through oxygen (giving alkyl nitrites, R-O-N=O) or through nitrogen (giving nitroalkanes, R-NO2).

Why does KCN give alkyl cyanides but AgCN gives isocyanides?

  • KCN is predominantly ionic and provides free cyanide ions in solution. Although both C and N can donate an electron pair, attack occurs mainly through carbon, because a C-C bond is more stable than a C-N bond. So, alkyl cyanide (RCN) is the main product.
  • AgCN is mainly covalent. The carbon is bonded to silver, so only the nitrogen is free to donate its electron pair. So, isocyanide (RNC) is the main product.
\[R-X + KCN → R-CN + KX\] \[R-X + AgCN → R-NC + AgX\]

docs.title: Mechanism of Nucleophilic Substitution
docs.text: Nucleophilic substitution proceeds by two different mechanisms: SN2 and SN1.

docs.title: 1. Substitution Nucleophilic Bimolecular (S<sub>N</sub>2)
docs.text:
• The reaction between CH3Cl and hydroxide ion to give methanol follows second order kinetics: the rate depends on the concentration of both reactants.
\[Rate = k[CH_3Cl][OH^-]\]
  • The nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite to the halogen (backside attack). The C-OH bond forms and the C-Cl bond breaks simultaneously, in a single step. No intermediate is formed.

Mechanism

  • In the transition state, the carbon is partially bonded to five atoms (the incoming OH and the outgoing Cl). Such a structure is unstable and cannot be isolated.
  • As the reaction proceeds, the three other groups on carbon flip over, like an umbrella turning inside out in strong wind. This is called inversion of configuration.
  • The SN2 mechanism was proposed by Edward Davies Hughes and Sir Christopher Ingold in 1937.

docs.title: Reactivity order in S<sub>N</sub>2
docs.text:
• The nucleophile must approach the carbon carrying the halogen. Bulky groups on or near this carbon block the approach (steric hindrance) and slow down the reaction.
  • Methyl halides react fastest because there are only three small H atoms around the carbon. Tertiary halides are the least reactive.

Steric effects in SN2 (relative rates in brackets)

\[CH_3X > 1^0\ halide > 2^0\ halide > 3^0\ halide\]

docs.title: 2. Substitution Nucleophilic Unimolecular (S<sub>N</sub>1)
docs.text:
• SN1 reactions are generally carried out in polar protic solvents like water, alcohol or acetic acid.
  • The reaction of tert-butyl bromide with hydroxide ion follows first order kinetics: the rate depends only on the concentration of tert-butyl bromide.
\[(CH_3)_3CBr + OH^- → (CH_3)_3COH + Br^-\] \[(2-Bromo-2-methylpropane) \ \ \ \ (2-Methylpropan-2-ol)\] \[Rate = k[(CH_3)_3CBr]\]
  • It occurs in two steps:
\[Step\ I\ (slow):\ (CH_3)_3C-Br ⇌ (CH_3)_3C^+ + Br^-\] \[Step\ II\ (fast):\ (CH_3)_3C^+ + OH^- → (CH_3)_3COH\]
  • Step I is the slowest and reversible step. The polarised C-Br bond breaks to form a carbocation and a bromide ion. The energy for breaking the bond comes from solvation of the halide ion by the protic solvent.
  • Step II: the carbocation is quickly attacked by the nucleophile.
  • The rate depends only on the slowest step, so it depends only on [alkyl halide] and not on [OH-].

docs.title: Reactivity order in S<sub>N</sub>1
docs.text:
• The more stable the carbocation, the more easily it forms and the faster the reaction.
  • 30 carbocations are the most stable, so 30 alkyl halides undergo SN1 reaction very fast.
\[3^0\ halide > 2^0\ halide > 1^0\ halide > CH_3X\]
  • For the same reason, allylic and benzylic halides are highly reactive towards SN1. The carbocation they form is stabilised by resonance:

Resonance in allyl and benzyl carbocations

docs.title: Comparison of S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2
docs.text:
Feature SN2 SN1 Kinetics Second order: rate = k[RX][Nu-] First order: rate = k[RX] Number of steps One step, no intermediate Two steps, via carbocation Controlling factor Steric hindrance Stability of carbocation Reactivity order CH3X > 10 > 20 > 30 30 > 20 > 10 > CH3X Stereochemistry Complete inversion Racemisation
  • For a given alkyl group, the reactivity of the halide follows the same order in both mechanisms, because the weakest C-X bond breaks most easily (iodide is the best leaving group):
\[R-I > R-Br > R-Cl >> R-F\]

Example

  • C6H11CH2Cl (a primary halide) undergoes SN2 faster than C6H11Cl (a secondary halide, chlorocyclohexane), because there is less steric hindrance.
  • CH3CH2CH2CH2I undergoes SN2 faster than CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl, because iodide, being large, is the better leaving group.

docs.title: Alkyl Halides | Physical Properties
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the physical properties of haloalkanes and haloarenes like colour, boiling point, melting point, density and solubility.

docs.title: 1. Physical State, Colour and Smell
docs.text:
• Alkyl halides are colourless when pure. However, bromides and iodides develop colour on exposure to light (they slowly decompose to give free halogen).
  • Many volatile halogen compounds have a sweet smell.
  • Methyl chloride, methyl bromide, ethyl chloride and some chlorofluoromethanes are gases at room temperature. Higher members are liquids or solids.

docs.title: (a) Comparison with hydrocarbons
docs.text:
• Organic halogen compounds are polar. They also have a higher molecular mass than the parent hydrocarbon.
  • Because of this, the intermolecular forces (dipole-dipole and van der Waals forces) are stronger in haloalkanes.
  • Hence, chlorides, bromides and iodides boil at considerably higher temperatures than hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass.

docs.title: (b) Effect of the halogen
docs.text:
• For the same alkyl group, the boiling point increases as the halogen gets bigger. A larger halogen has more electrons and greater mass, so the van der Waals forces are stronger.
\[RI > RBr > RCl > RF\]
  • The boiling point also rises as the size of the alkyl group increases. For example, CH3CH2CH2X > CH3CH2X > CH3X for the same halogen.

docs.title: (c) Effect of branching
docs.text:
• Boiling points of isomeric haloalkanes decrease with increase in branching. A branched molecule is more compact (nearly spherical), so it has a smaller surface area for intermolecular contact.
Compound Structure Boiling point (K) 1-Bromobutane CH3CH2CH2CH2Br 375 2-Bromobutane CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3 364 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane (CH3)3CBr 346
  • 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane, the most branched isomer, has the lowest boiling point.

docs.title: 3. Melting Points of Dihalobenzenes
docs.text:
• The boiling points of isomeric dihalobenzenes (ortho, meta and para) are very nearly the same.
  • However, the para-isomer has a much higher melting point than the ortho- and meta-isomers.
  • This is because the para-isomer is symmetrical and fits better into the crystal lattice. More energy is then needed to break the lattice.

docs.title: 4. Density
docs.text:
• Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives of hydrocarbons are heavier than water.
  • Density increases with increase in the number of carbon atoms, the number of halogen atoms and the atomic mass of the halogen.
Compound Density (g/mL) Compound Density (g/mL) n-C3H7Cl 0.89 CH2Cl2 1.336 n-C3H7Br 1.335 CHCl3 1.489 n-C3H7I 1.747 CCl4 1.595

docs.title: 5. Solubility
docs.text:
• Haloalkanes are only very slightly soluble in water, even though they are polar.
  • To dissolve a haloalkane in water, energy is needed to overcome the attractions between haloalkane molecules and to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
  • The new attractions formed between haloalkane and water molecules are weaker than the original hydrogen bonds in water. So less energy is released than is absorbed, and solubility remains low.
  • Haloalkanes dissolve readily in organic solvents, because the new attractions between haloalkane and solvent molecules are of about the same strength as the ones being broken.

Conclusion

Haloalkanes cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so they are immiscible with water but completely soluble in organic solvents.
