docs.title: Alkyl Halides | Polyhalogen Compounds
docs.text: Carbon compounds containing more than one halogen atom are called polyhalogen compounds. Many of them are useful in industry and agriculture, but several are toxic or harmful to the environment. In this article, we will discuss some important polyhalogen compounds.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Solvent, for example as a paint remover.
  • Propellant in aerosols.
  • Process solvent in the manufacture of drugs.
  • Metal cleaning and finishing solvent.

docs.title: Harmful effects
docs.text:
• It harms the human central nervous system.
  • Low levels in air can slightly impair hearing and vision. Higher levels cause dizziness, nausea, and tingling and numbness in the fingers and toes.
  • Direct skin contact causes intense burning and mild redness. Direct contact with the eyes can burn the cornea.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Solvent for fats, alkaloids, iodine and other substances.
  • Its major use today is in the production of the freon refrigerant R-22.
  • It was once used as a general anaesthetic in surgery, but has been replaced by safer anaesthetics such as ether.

docs.title: Harmful effects
docs.text:
• Inhaling chloroform vapours depresses the central nervous system. Breathing about 900 ppm of chloroform in air for a short time can cause dizziness, fatigue and headache.
  • Chronic exposure may damage the liver (where chloroform is metabolised to phosgene) and the kidneys. Some people develop sores when skin is immersed in chloroform.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• Chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in the presence of light to an extremely poisonous gas, carbonyl chloride (phosgene).
\[2CHCl_3 + O_2 \xrightarrow{light} 2COCl_2 + 2HCl\] \[(Phosgene)\]
  • So, chloroform is stored in closed, dark coloured bottles filled completely, so that air and light are kept out.

docs.title: 3. Triiodomethane (Iodoform), CHI<sub>3</sub>
docs.text:
• It was used earlier as an antiseptic. However, the antiseptic property is due to the free iodine it liberates, not due to iodoform itself.
  • Because of its objectionable smell, it has been replaced by other formulations containing iodine.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
• Manufacture of refrigerants and propellants for aerosol cans.
  • Feedstock in the synthesis of chlorofluorocarbons and other chemicals.
  • Pharmaceutical manufacturing and general solvent use.
  • Until the mid 1960s, it was widely used as a cleaning fluid, as a degreasing agent in industry, as a spot remover at home and in fire extinguishers.

docs.title: Harmful effects
docs.text:
• There is some evidence that exposure causes liver cancer in humans.
  • Common effects are dizziness, light-headedness, nausea and vomiting, which can permanently damage nerve cells. Severe cases can lead to stupor, coma, unconsciousness or death.
  • It can make the heart beat irregularly or stop, and may irritate the eyes.
  • When released into air, it rises to the atmosphere and depletes the ozone layer. Ozone depletion increases exposure to UV rays, leading to skin cancer, eye diseases and possible disruption of the immune system.

docs.title: 5. Freons
docs.text:
• The chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) compounds of methane and ethane are collectively called freons.
  • They are extremely stable, unreactive, non-toxic, non-corrosive and easily liquefiable gases.
  • Freon 12 (CCl2F2) is one of the most common freons in industrial use. It is manufactured from tetrachloromethane by the Swarts reaction.
\[CCl_4 \xrightarrow{SbF_3} CCl_2F_2\]

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: • Aerosol propellants, refrigeration and air conditioning.

docs.title: Environmental effect
docs.text:
• By 1974, world freon production was about 2 billion pounds a year.
  • Most freon, even that used in refrigeration, eventually escapes into the atmosphere and diffuses unchanged into the stratosphere.
  • In the stratosphere, freon initiates radical chain reactions that upset the natural ozone balance (ozone depletion).

docs.title: 6. p,p'-Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT)
docs.text:
• DDT was the first chlorinated organic insecticide. It was first prepared in 1873, but its effectiveness as an insecticide was discovered only in 1939 by Paul Muller (Geigy Pharmaceuticals, Switzerland). He received the Nobel Prize in Medicine and Physiology in 1948 for this discovery.

Structure of DDT

\[(p-ClC_6H_4)_2CH-CCl_3\]

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: • After World War II, its use increased enormously, mainly against the mosquito that spreads malaria and lice that carry typhus.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
• Many species of insects developed resistance to DDT.
  • It is highly toxic towards fish.
  • DDT is chemically stable and fat soluble. It is not metabolised quickly by animals; instead, it is deposited and stored in fatty tissues. With steady intake, it builds up in the animal over time.
  • Its use was banned in the United States in 1973, although it is still used in some other parts of the world.

Conclusion

Many polyhalogen compounds are very useful, but because they do not decompose easily, some of them accumulate in living organisms or deplete the ozone layer and are proving to be environmental hazards.

docs.title: Alkyl Halides | Questions
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some questions based on preparation, properties and reactions of haloalkanes and haloarenes.

docs.title: Preparation and Physical Properties
docs.text:
Identify all the possible monochloro structural isomers expected to be formed on free radical monochlorination of (CH3)2CHCH2CH3.

  • The molecule has four different types of hydrogen atoms: the two equivalent CH3 groups on C-2, the single H on C-2, the CH2 hydrogens, and the terminal CH3 hydrogens.
  • Replacing each type gives a different product:
\[(CH_3)_2CHCH_2CH_2Cl\] \[(CH_3)_2CHCH(Cl)CH_3\] \[(CH_3)_2C(Cl)CH_2CH_3\] \[CH_3CH(CH_2Cl)CH_2CH_3\]

Why is sulphuric acid not used during the reaction of alcohols with KI?

  • H2SO4 converts KI into HI, but being an oxidising agent, it then oxidises HI to I2. So no alkyl iodide is formed.
\[2KI + H_2SO_4 → 2HI + K_2SO_4\] \[2HI + H_2SO_4 → I_2 + SO_2 + 2H_2O\]
  • A non-oxidising acid such as H3PO4 is used instead.

Among the isomeric alkanes of molecular formula C5H12, identify the one that on photochemical chlorination yields: (i) A single monochloride (ii) Three isomeric monochlorides (iii) Four isomeric monochlorides

  • (i) Neopentane, C(CH3)4: all 12 hydrogens are equivalent, so only one monochloride is formed.
  • (ii) n-Pentane, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3: it has three types of equivalent hydrogens (C-1/C-5, C-2/C-4 and C-3), so three monochlorides are formed.
  • (iii) Isopentane, (CH3)2CHCH2CH3: it has four types of hydrogens, so four monochlorides are formed.

Write the major monohalo product in each of the following: (i) Cyclohexanol + SOCl2 (ii) p-O2NC6H4CH2CH3 + Br2, heat or UV light (iii) p-HOC6H4CH2OH + HCl, heat (iv) 1-Methylcyclohexene + HI (v) CH3CH2Br + NaI (vi) Cyclohexene + Br2, heat or UV light

  • (i) Chlorocyclohexane, C6H11Cl.
  • (ii) p-O2NC6H4CH(Br)CH3. Free radical bromination occurs at the benzylic carbon, as the benzylic radical is most stable.
  • (iii) p-HOC6H4CH2Cl. Only the alcoholic -OH is replaced; the phenolic -OH is not, because its C-O bond has partial double bond character.
  • (iv) 1-Iodo-1-methylcyclohexane (Markovnikov addition: I goes to the more substituted carbon).
  • (v) CH3CH2I (Finkelstein reaction).
  • (vi) 3-Bromocyclohexene. Under heat or light, substitution occurs at the allylic position.

Arrange each set of compounds in order of increasing boiling points: (i) Bromomethane, Bromoform, Chloromethane, Dibromomethane (ii) 1-Chloropropane, Isopropyl chloride, 1-Chlorobutane

  • (i) Chloromethane < Bromomethane < Dibromomethane < Bromoform. Boiling point increases with increase in molecular mass (stronger van der Waals forces).
  • (ii) Isopropyl chloride < 1-Chloropropane < 1-Chlorobutane. Isopropyl chloride is branched, so it has a lower boiling point than 1-chloropropane. 1-Chlorobutane has the largest molecular mass.

Which one of the following has the highest dipole moment? (i) CH2Cl2 (ii) CHCl3 (iii) CCl4

  • CCl4 is perfectly symmetrical (tetrahedral), so the four C-Cl bond dipoles cancel out and its dipole moment is zero.
  • In CHCl3, the C-Cl dipoles partly cancel each other.
  • In CH2Cl2, the two C-Cl dipoles reinforce each other the most.
  • So, CH2Cl2 has the highest dipole moment.

A hydrocarbon C5H10 does not react with chlorine in dark but gives a single monochloro compound C5H9Cl in bright sunlight. Identify the hydrocarbon.

  • C5H10 fits CnH2n, so it is either an alkene or a cycloalkane.
  • It does not react with Cl2 in the dark, so there is no double bond. It must be a cycloalkane.
  • It gives only one monochloro product in sunlight, so all hydrogens are equivalent.
  • The hydrocarbon is cyclopentane, C5H10.
\[C_5H_{10} + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} C_5H_9Cl + HCl\]

Write the equations for the preparation of 1-iodobutane from: (i) 1-Butanol (ii) 1-Chlorobutane (iii) But-1-ene

\[(i)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH + KI \xrightarrow{95\%\ H_3PO_4,\ Δ} CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2I\] \[(ii)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl + NaI \xrightarrow{dry\ acetone} CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2I + NaCl\] \[(iii)\ CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2 + HBr \xrightarrow{peroxide} CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br \xrightarrow{NaI,\ dry\ acetone} CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2I\]

In (iii), anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr in presence of peroxide puts Br on the terminal carbon, which is then exchanged for I by the Finkelstein reaction.

docs.title: Substitution and Elimination
docs.text:
Which compound in each of the following pairs will react faster in SN2 reaction with OH-? (i) CH3Br or CH3I (ii) (CH3)3CCl or CH3Cl

  • (i) CH3I, because I- is a better leaving group than Br- (C-I bond is weaker).
  • (ii) CH3Cl, because there is very little steric hindrance around the carbon, while in (CH3)3CCl three bulky methyl groups block the backside attack.

Predict the order of reactivity of the four isomeric bromobutanes in SN1 and SN2 reactions.

\[S_N1:\ CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br < (CH_3)_2CHCH_2Br < CH_3CH_2CH(Br)CH_3 < (CH_3)_3CBr\] \[S_N2:\ CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br > (CH_3)_2CHCH_2Br > CH_3CH_2CH(Br)CH_3 > (CH_3)_3CBr\]
  • Of the two primary bromides, the carbocation from (CH3)2CHCH2Br is more stable due to the greater electron donating inductive effect of the (CH3)2CH- group. So it is more reactive in SN1.
  • CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3 is secondary and (CH3)3CBr is tertiary, so they follow the order of carbocation stability in SN1.
  • SN2 follows the reverse order, because steric hindrance around the carbon increases in the same sequence.

Predict the order of reactivity of C6H5CH2Br, C6H5CH(C6H5)Br, C6H5CH(CH3)Br and C6H5C(CH3)(C6H5)Br in SN1 and SN2 reactions.

\[S_N1:\ C_6H_5C(CH_3)(C_6H_5)Br > C_6H_5CH(C_6H_5)Br > C_6H_5CH(CH_3)Br > C_6H_5CH_2Br\] \[S_N2:\ C_6H_5C(CH_3)(C_6H_5)Br < C_6H_5CH(C_6H_5)Br < C_6H_5CH(CH_3)Br < C_6H_5CH_2Br\]
  • Of the two secondary bromides, the carbocation from C6H5CH(C6H5)Br is stabilised by resonance with two phenyl groups, so it is more reactive in SN1.
  • A phenyl group is bulkier than a methyl group, so C6H5CH(C6H5)Br is less reactive than C6H5CH(CH3)Br in SN2.

Which alkyl halide from the following pairs would react more rapidly by SN2 mechanism? (i) CH3CH2CH2CH2Br or CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3 (ii) CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3 or (CH3)3CBr (iii) (CH3)2CHCH2CH2Br or CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2Br

  • (i) CH3CH2CH2CH2Br. Being a primary halide, it has the least steric hindrance.
  • (ii) CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3. A secondary halide reacts faster than a tertiary halide.
  • (iii) (CH3)2CHCH2CH2Br. In the other compound, the methyl branch is closer to the carbon carrying Br, which increases steric hindrance and lowers the rate.

Which compound in each pair undergoes faster SN1 reaction? (i) 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane or 3-Chloropentane (ii) 2-Chloroheptane or 1-Chlorohexane

  • (i) 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CCl. A tertiary halide reacts faster than a secondary one, because the 30 carbocation is more stable.
  • (ii) 2-Chloroheptane. It forms a secondary carbocation, which is more stable than the primary carbocation from 1-chlorohexane.

Arrange the compounds of each set in order of reactivity towards SN2 displacement: (i) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromopentane, 2-Bromopentane (ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane (iii) 1-Bromobutane, 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane

SN2 reactivity decreases as steric hindrance near the carbon carrying Br increases.

  • (i) 1-Bromopentane (10) > 2-Bromopentane (20) > 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane (30)
  • (ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane (10) > 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane (20) > 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane (30)
  • (iii) 1-Bromobutane > 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane > 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane > 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane. All are primary; the closer and bulkier the branching to the C-Br carbon, the slower the reaction.

Out of C6H5CH2Cl and C6H5CHClC6H5, which is more easily hydrolysed by aqueous KOH?

  • Hydrolysis of these benzylic halides by aqueous KOH proceeds mainly through the SN1 mechanism.
  • C6H5CHClC6H5 forms the carbocation (C6H5)2CH+, which is stabilised by resonance with two phenyl rings. C6H5CH2Cl forms C6H5CH2+, stabilised by only one ring.
  • So C6H5CHClC6H5 is hydrolysed more easily.

Predict all the alkenes that would be formed by dehydrohalogenation of the following halides with sodium ethoxide in ethanol and identify the major alkene: (i) 1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane (ii) 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane (iii) 2,2,3-Trimethyl-3-bromopentane

  • (i) Two alkenes can form: 1-methylcyclohexene (from a ring β-hydrogen) and methylenecyclohexane (from the CH3 β-hydrogen). 1-Methylcyclohexene is more substituted, so it is the major product (Saytzeff rule).
  • (ii) (CH3)2C(Cl)CH2CH3 gives:
\[\underset{2-Methylbut-2-ene\ (major)}{(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_3} + \underset{2-Methylbut-1-ene\ (minor)}{CH_2=C(CH_3)CH_2CH_3}\]
  • (iii) The halide is (CH3)3C-C(Br)(CH3)-CH2CH3. The C-2 carbon has no hydrogen, so β-hydrogens are available only from the C-3 methyl group and from C-4:
\[\underset{3,4,4-Trimethylpent-2-ene\ (major)}{(CH_3)_3C-C(CH_3)=CHCH_3} + \underset{2-Ethyl-3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene\ (minor)}{(CH_3)_3C-C(=CH_2)CH_2CH_3}\]

The major product has three alkyl groups on the double bond, the minor one only two.

The treatment of alkyl chlorides with aqueous KOH leads to the formation of alcohols but in the presence of alcoholic KOH, alkenes are major products. Explain.

  • In aqueous solution, KOH gives OH- ions which are highly hydrated. Hydrated OH- acts mainly as a nucleophile, so substitution occurs and alcohols are formed.
  • In alcoholic solution, KOH forms alkoxide ions (RO-), which are stronger bases than OH-. They preferentially abstract a β-hydrogen, so elimination (dehydrohalogenation) occurs and alkenes are formed.
\[R-CH_2CH_2Cl + KOH_{(aq)} → R-CH_2CH_2OH + KCl\] \[R-CH_2CH_2Cl + KOH_{(alc)} → R-CH=CH_2 + KCl + H_2O\]

docs.title: Reactions with Metals and Haloarenes
docs.text:
Identify A, B, C, D, E, R and R1 in the following: Bromocyclohexane + Mg (dry ether) → A; A + H2O → B R-Br + Mg (dry ether) → C; C + D2O → CH3CH(D)CH3 R1-X + Na/ether → (CH3)3C-C(CH3)3; R1-X + Mg → D; D + H2O → E

  • A = C6H11MgBr (cyclohexylmagnesium bromide); B = C6H12 (cyclohexane).
  • D2O places D on the carbon that carried MgBr. Since the product is CH3CH(D)CH3, R = (CH3)2CH- (isopropyl) and C = (CH3)2CHMgBr.
  • Wurtz reaction joins two R1 groups. Since the product is (CH3)3C-C(CH3)3, R1 = (CH3)3C- (tert-butyl).
  • D = (CH3)3CMgX and E = (CH3)3CH (2-methylpropane).

Primary alkyl halide C4H9Br (a) reacted with alcoholic KOH to give compound (b). Compound (b) is reacted with HBr to give (c) which is an isomer of (a). When (a) is reacted with sodium metal it gives compound (d), C8H18, which is different from the compound formed when n-butyl bromide is reacted with sodium. Give the structural formula of (a) and write the equations for all the reactions.

  • (a) is a primary C4H9Br, but it is not n-butyl bromide (its Wurtz product is different). So (a) is 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (isobutyl bromide), (CH3)2CHCH2Br.
\[(CH_3)_2CHCH_2Br\ (a) + KOH_{(alc)} → (CH_3)_2C=CH_2\ (b) + KBr + H_2O\] \[(CH_3)_2C=CH_2\ (b) + HBr → (CH_3)_3CBr\ (c)\] \[2(CH_3)_2CHCH_2Br\ (a) + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} (CH_3)_2CHCH_2CH_2CH(CH_3)_2\ (d) + 2NaBr\]
  • (b) is 2-methylpropene, (c) is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (Markovnikov addition), and (d) is 2,5-dimethylhexane. n-Butyl bromide would instead give n-octane.

Explain why: (i) the dipole moment of chlorobenzene is lower than that of cyclohexyl chloride (ii) alkyl halides, though polar, are immiscible with water (iii) Grignard reagents should be prepared under anhydrous conditions

  • (i) In chlorobenzene, the C-Cl carbon is sp2 hybridised and more electronegative than the sp3 carbon of cyclohexyl chloride, so the C-Cl bond is less polar. Also, resonance pushes the lone pair of Cl towards the ring, which opposes the C-Cl bond dipole. Hence the dipole moment of chlorobenzene is lower.
  • (ii) Alkyl halides cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. The energy released by the new haloalkane-water attractions is less than the energy needed to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. So they do not dissolve.
  • (iii) Grignard reagents react with even traces of water to form hydrocarbons, so they would be destroyed:
\[RMgX + H_2O → RH + Mg(OH)X\]

p-Dichlorobenzene has a higher melting point than the o- and m-isomers. Discuss.

  • p-Dichlorobenzene is a symmetrical molecule. It fits more closely and neatly into the crystal lattice than the ortho- and meta-isomers.
  • So stronger intermolecular forces hold the crystal together, and more energy is needed to melt it. Hence its melting point is higher.

What happens when: (i) n-butyl chloride is treated with alcoholic KOH (ii) bromobenzene is treated with Mg in the presence of dry ether (iii) chlorobenzene is subjected to hydrolysis (iv) ethyl chloride is treated with aqueous KOH (v) methyl bromide is treated with sodium in the presence of dry ether (vi) methyl chloride is treated with KCN

\[(i)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl + KOH_{(alc)} → CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2 + KCl + H_2O\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5Br + Mg \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} C_6H_5MgBr\] \[(iii)\ C_6H_5Cl \xrightarrow[(ii)\ H^+]{(i)\ NaOH,\ 623\ K,\ 300\ atm} C_6H_5OH\] \[(iv)\ C_2H_5Cl + KOH_{(aq)} → C_2H_5OH + KCl\] \[(v)\ 2CH_3Br + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} CH_3CH_3 + 2NaBr\] \[(vi)\ CH_3Cl + KCN → CH_3CN + KCl\]

The products are but-1-ene, phenylmagnesium bromide, phenol, ethanol, ethane and ethanenitrile (methyl cyanide) respectively.

Write the structure of the major organic product in each of the following reactions: (i) CH3CH2CH2Cl + NaI (acetone, heat) (ii) (CH3)3CBr + KOH (ethanol, heat) (iii) CH3CH(Br)CH2CH3 + NaOH (water) (iv) CH3CH2Br + KCN (aq. ethanol) (v) C6H5ONa + C2H5Cl (vi) CH3CH2CH2OH + SOCl2 (vii) CH3CH2CH=CH2 + HBr (peroxide) (viii) CH3CH=C(CH3)2 + HBr

  • (i) CH3CH2CH2I (Finkelstein reaction)
  • (ii) (CH3)2C=CH2 (elimination by alcoholic KOH)
  • (iii) CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 (substitution by aqueous NaOH)
  • (iv) CH3CH2CN (propanenitrile)
  • (v) C6H5OC2H5 (ethoxybenzene)
  • (vi) CH3CH2CH2Cl
  • (vii) CH3CH2CH2CH2Br (anti-Markovnikov addition)
  • (viii) CH3CH2C(Br)(CH3)2 (Markovnikov addition)

docs.title: Conversions
docs.text:
How will you bring about the following conversions? (i) Ethanol to ethyl fluoride (ii) Propene to propan-1-ol (iii) 1-Bromopropane to 2-bromopropane (iv) Ethyl chloride to propanoic acid (v) 2-Chlorobutane to 3,4-dimethylhexane (vi) Aniline to chlorobenzene (vii) Chlorobenzene to p-nitrophenol (viii) Benzene to biphenyl

\[(i)\ C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{SOCl_2} C_2H_5Cl \xrightarrow{AgF} C_2H_5F\] \[(ii)\ CH_3CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{HBr,\ peroxide} CH_3CH_2CH_2Br \xrightarrow{aq.\ KOH} CH_3CH_2CH_2OH\] \[(iii)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2Br \xrightarrow{alc.\ KOH} CH_3CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{HBr} CH_3CHBrCH_3\] \[(iv)\ C_2H_5Cl \xrightarrow{KCN} C_2H_5CN \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_2H_5COOH\] \[(v)\ 2CH_3CH_2CH(Cl)CH_3 + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)-CH(CH_3)CH_2CH_3 + 2NaCl\] \[(vi)\ C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow[273-278\ K]{NaNO_2\ +\ HCl} C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{Cu_2Cl_2} C_6H_5Cl + N_2\] \[(vii)\ C_6H_5Cl \xrightarrow[conc.\ H_2SO_4]{conc.\ HNO_3} p-ClC_6H_4NO_2 \xrightarrow[(ii)\ H^+]{(i)\ NaOH,\ 443\ K} p-HOC_6H_4NO_2\] \[(viii)\ C_6H_6 \xrightarrow[FeCl_3]{Br_2} C_6H_5Br \xrightarrow{Na,\ dry\ ether} C_6H_5-C_6H_5\]
  • (v) is a Wurtz reaction, (vi) is Sandmeyer's reaction and the last step of (viii) is the Fittig reaction. In (vii), the p-nitro group (the major nitration product) activates the C-Cl bond towards hydrolysis.

docs.title: Haloarenes | Chemical Reactions
docs.text: Haloarenes (aryl halides) have the halogen attached to an sp2 hybridised carbon of a benzene ring. In this article, we will discuss their three main types of reactions: nucleophilic substitution, electrophilic substitution and reaction with metals.

docs.title: 1. Nucleophilic Substitution
docs.text: Aryl halides are extremely less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution than alkyl halides. The reasons are:

docs.title: (i) Resonance effect
docs.text:
• The lone pairs on the halogen are in conjugation with the π-electrons of the ring. The following resonating structures are possible:

Resonance in chlorobenzene

  • Due to resonance, the C-Cl bond acquires partial double bond character. It is therefore harder to break than the C-Cl bond of a haloalkane.

docs.title: (ii) Difference in hybridisation of carbon in C-X bond
docs.text:
• In a haloalkane, the carbon attached to halogen is sp3 hybridised. In a haloarene, it is sp2 hybridised.
  • An sp2 carbon has greater s-character (33%) than an sp3 carbon (25%). So it is more electronegative and holds the electron pair of the C-X bond more tightly.
  • As a result, the C-X bond in haloarenes is shorter and stronger:
Compound C-Cl bond length Haloalkane 177 pm Haloarene 169 pm
  • A shorter bond is more difficult to break, so haloarenes are less reactive.

docs.title: (iii) Instability of phenyl cation
docs.text: • If a haloarene ionised on its own, it would form a phenyl cation (C6H5+). This cation is not stabilised by resonance. So the SN1 mechanism is ruled out.

docs.title: (iv) Repulsion between nucleophile and ring
docs.text: • The electron-rich nucleophile is repelled by the electron-rich benzene ring, so it is less likely to approach it.

docs.title: Replacement by hydroxyl group
docs.text:
• Chlorobenzene can be converted to phenol only under drastic conditions: heating with aqueous NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm, followed by acidification.
\[C_6H_5Cl \xrightarrow[(ii)\ H^+]{(i)\ NaOH,\ 623\ K,\ 300\ atm} C_6H_5OH\]

docs.title: Effect of -NO<sub>2</sub> group (activation)
docs.text:
• The presence of an electron withdrawing group like -NO2 at the ortho and para positions increases the reactivity of haloarenes. The more such groups, the milder the conditions needed:
\[Chlorobenzene \xrightarrow[(ii)\ H^+]{(i)\ NaOH,\ 623\ K,\ 300\ atm} Phenol\] \[4-Nitrochlorobenzene \xrightarrow[(ii)\ H^+]{(i)\ NaOH,\ 443\ K} 4-Nitrophenol\] \[2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene \xrightarrow[(ii)\ H^+]{(i)\ NaOH,\ 368\ K} 2,4-Dinitrophenol\] \[2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene \xrightarrow[H_2O]{warm} 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol\]
  • An -NO2 group at the meta position has no such effect on reactivity.

docs.title: Mechanism
docs.text:
• The OH- attacks the carbon carrying Cl in a slow step, forming a negatively charged intermediate (a carbanion) stabilised by resonance.
  • In a fast step, Cl- is lost and the aromatic ring is restored.

Para-nitrochlorobenzene

Meta-nitrochlorobenzene

Why does the NO2 group show its effect only at ortho- and para-positions and not at meta-position?

  • The -NO2 group at ortho and para positions withdraws electron density from the ring, which makes the attack of the nucleophile easier.
  • In the carbanion intermediate, the negative charge appears at the ortho and para positions with respect to the halogen. When -NO2 is at one of these positions, one resonating structure puts the negative charge directly on the carbon bearing -NO2, and the charge can then be spread onto the nitro group. This strongly stabilises the intermediate.
  • In meta-nitrochlorobenzene, none of the resonating structures has the negative charge on the carbon bearing -NO2. So the nitro group cannot stabilise the charge, and there is no effect on reactivity.

docs.title: 2. Electrophilic Substitution
docs.text:
• Haloarenes undergo the usual electrophilic substitution reactions of benzene: halogenation, nitration, sulphonation and Friedel-Crafts reactions.
  • The halogen is slightly deactivating but ortho, para-directing. So further substitution occurs at the ortho and para positions with respect to the halogen.

docs.title: Why is halogen o, p-directing yet deactivating?
docs.text:
• Resonance (+R effect): The resonating structures of halobenzene (same as shown above) place a negative charge (higher electron density) at the ortho and para positions. So the electrophile attacks there.
  • Inductive (-I effect): Being electronegative, the halogen withdraws electrons from the ring. This deactivates the ring compared to benzene, so reactions are slower and need more drastic conditions.
  • The inductive effect is stronger than resonance, so there is net deactivation. But the resonance effect stabilises the intermediate carbocation for ortho and para attack, so the deactivation is less at those positions.

Conclusion

Reactivity is controlled by the stronger inductive effect, and orientation is controlled by the resonance effect.

docs.title: (i) Halogenation
docs.text: \[C_6H_5Cl + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{Anhyd.\ FeCl_3} \underset{(Major)}{1,4-Dichlorobenzene} + \underset{(Minor)}{1,2-Dichlorobenzene}\]

docs.title: (ii) Nitration
docs.text: \[C_6H_5Cl \xrightarrow[conc.\ H_2SO_4]{HNO_3} \underset{(Major)}{1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene} + \underset{(Minor)}{1-Chloro-2-nitrobenzene}\]

docs.title: (iii) Sulphonation
docs.text: \[C_6H_5Cl \xrightarrow[&Delta;]{conc.\ H_2SO_4} \underset{(Major)}{4-Chlorobenzenesulphonic\ acid} + \underset{(Minor)}{2-Chlorobenzenesulphonic\ acid}\]

docs.title: (iv) Friedel-Crafts reaction
docs.text:
\[C_6H_5Cl + CH_3Cl \xrightarrow{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} \underset{(Major)}{1-Chloro-4-methylbenzene} + \underset{(Minor)}{1-Chloro-2-methylbenzene}\] \[C_6H_5Cl + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} \underset{(Major)}{4-Chloroacetophenone} + \underset{(Minor)}{2-Chloroacetophenone}\]
  • In each case the para product is major. The ortho position is more crowded because it is next to the halogen.

docs.title: (i) Wurtz-Fittig reaction
docs.text:
• A mixture of an alkyl halide and an aryl halide gives an alkylarene when treated with sodium in dry ether.
\[C_6H_5X + 2Na + RX \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} C_6H_5-R + 2NaX\]

docs.title: (ii) Fittig reaction
docs.text:
• Aryl halides alone, when treated with sodium in dry ether, give compounds in which two aryl groups are joined together.
\[2C_6H_5X + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} C_6H_5-C_6H_5 + 2NaX\] \[(Biphenyl)\]

docs.title: Alkyl Halides | Stereochemistry of Nucleophilic Substitution
Alkyl Halides | Stereochemistry of Nucleophilic Substitution
docs.text: An SN2 reaction proceeds with complete stereochemical inversion while an SN1 reaction proceeds with racemisation. To understand why, we first need some basic ideas of stereochemistry: optical activity, chirality, retention, inversion and racemisation.

docs.title: 1. Plane Polarised Light and Optical Activity
docs.text:
• Ordinary light vibrates in all planes. When it is passed through a Nicol prism, light vibrating in only one plane comes out. This is called plane polarised light.
  • Certain compounds rotate the plane of polarised light when it passes through their solutions. These are called optically active compounds.
  • The angle of rotation is measured with an instrument called a polarimeter.
Type Direction of rotation Representation Dextrorotatory (d-form) To the right (clockwise) (+) sign before degree of rotation Laevorotatory (l-form) To the left (anticlockwise) (-) sign before degree of rotation
  • Such (+) and (-) isomers of a compound are called optical isomers, and the phenomenon is called optical isomerism.

docs.title: 2. Molecular Asymmetry and Chirality
docs.text:
• Louis Pasteur (1848) observed that crystals of certain compounds exist as mirror images. Solutions of the two kinds of crystals rotated plane polarised light by equal amounts but in opposite directions. He linked this to the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms (configuration).
  • In 1874, van't Hoff and Le Bel independently proposed that the four groups around a carbon are arranged tetrahedrally.
  • If all four groups attached to a carbon are different, that carbon is called an asymmetric carbon or stereocentre. A molecule containing it lacks symmetry and is called an asymmetric molecule. This asymmetry is responsible for optical activity.

docs.title: Chiral and achiral objects
docs.text:
• An object which is non-superimposable on its mirror image is called chiral, and the property is called chirality. Example: left and right hands.
  • An object which is superimposable on its mirror image is called achiral. Examples: a sphere, a cube, a cone.
  • A simple test for a chiral molecule is the presence of a single asymmetric carbon atom.

Propan-2-ol and butan-2-ol

  • Propan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH3: the central carbon carries two identical CH3 groups. It has no asymmetric carbon, and it is superimposable on its mirror image. So it is achiral.
  • Butan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3: the central carbon carries four different groups (H, OH, CH3, C2H5). Even after rotation, it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image. So it is chiral.

  • Other examples of chiral molecules: 2-chlorobutane, 2,3-dihydroxypropanal (OHC-CHOH-CH2OH), bromochloroiodomethane (BrClCHI), 2-bromopropanoic acid (H3C-CHBr-COOH).

docs.title: 3. Enantiomers and Racemic Mixture
docs.text:
• Stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other are called enantiomers.
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties (melting point, boiling point, solubility, refractive index, etc.). They differ only in the direction in which they rotate plane polarised light: if one is dextrorotatory, the other is laevorotatory.

Note

The sign of optical rotation, (+) or (-), is not necessarily related to the absolute configuration (actual 3D arrangement) of the molecule.

  • A mixture containing two enantiomers in equal proportions has zero optical rotation, because the rotation of one cancels the other. It is called a racemic mixture or racemic modification.
  • A racemic mixture is shown by prefixing dl or (±) before the name, e.g. (±)-butan-2-ol.
  • The conversion of an enantiomer into a racemic mixture is called racemisation.

docs.title: 4. Retention, Inversion and Racemisation
docs.text:
Consider a reaction at an asymmetric carbon in which a group X is replaced by Y. There are three possible outcomes:

Outcome Product obtained Meaning Retention Only A Y takes the same position that X occupied; relative configuration is preserved Inversion Only B Y comes in from the side opposite to X; configuration is turned inside out Racemisation 50:50 mixture of A and B Product is optically inactive

docs.title: Retention of configuration
docs.text:
• Retention is the preservation of the spatial arrangement of bonds around an asymmetric centre during a reaction. XCabc is converted into YCabc with the same relative configuration.
  • In general, if no bond to the stereocentre is broken during a reaction, the product keeps the same configuration as the reactant.

Example

When (-)-2-methylbutan-1-ol is heated with concentrated HCl, the bond that breaks is the CH2-OH bond, not a bond to the stereocentre. So the product, (+)-1-chloro-2-methylbutane, has the same configuration.

\[\underset{(-)-2-Methylbutan-1-ol}{CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH_2OH} + HCl \xrightarrow{heat} \underset{(+)-1-Chloro-2-methylbutane}{CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH_2Cl} + H_2O\]

Note that the sign of rotation changes from (-) to (+), even though the configuration is retained.

docs.title: 5. Stereochemistry of S<sub>N</sub>2 Reactions: Inversion
docs.text:
• In SN2, the nucleophile attaches itself on the side opposite to the halogen. So, the product from an optically active alkyl halide has the inverted configuration.
  • Example: (-)-2-bromooctane reacts with sodium hydroxide to form (+)-octan-2-ol, with -OH occupying the position opposite to where Br was.

Conclusion

SN2 reactions of optically active halides are accompanied by inversion of configuration.

docs.title: 6. Stereochemistry of S<sub>N</sub>1 Reactions: Racemisation
docs.text:
• In SN1, the carbocation formed in the slow step is sp2 hybridised and therefore planar (achiral).
  • The nucleophile can attack this flat carbocation from either face:
    • Attack from the same side as the departed halide gives the product with the same configuration (retention).
    • Attack from the opposite side gives the product with the opposite configuration (inversion).
  • Both happen equally, so a racemic mixture is formed.
  • Example: hydrolysis of optically active 2-bromobutane gives (±)-butan-2-ol.

Conclusion

SN1 reactions of optically active halides are accompanied by racemisation.

docs.title: Amines | Chemical Reactions of Amines
docs.text: The reactions of amines are governed by the lone pair of electrons on nitrogen and by the number of hydrogen atoms attached to it. That is why primary (-NH2), secondary (>N-H) and tertiary (>N-) amines behave differently in many reactions. The basic character of amines is discussed on the previous page; here we look at their other reactions.

docs.title: 1. Alkylation
docs.text:
• Amines are nucleophiles, so they react with alkyl halides. Each step replaces one H on nitrogen by an alkyl group, finally giving a quaternary ammonium salt.
\[RNH_2 \xrightarrow{R'X} RNHR' \xrightarrow{R'X} RNR'_2 \xrightarrow{R'X} R\overset{+}{N}R'_3\overset{-}{X}\]

Example

With excess methyl iodide (in Na2CO3 solution, which neutralises the HI formed), aniline is fully methylated:

\[C_6H_5NH_2 + 3CH_3I \xrightarrow{Na_2CO_3} C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}(CH_3)_3\overset{-}{I}\]

The product is N,N,N-trimethylanilinium iodide, a quaternary ammonium salt.

docs.title: 2. Acylation
docs.text:
• Primary and secondary amines (aliphatic and aromatic) react with acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters by nucleophilic substitution. The H on nitrogen is replaced by an acyl group (RCO-) and an amide is formed.
  • The reaction is carried out in the presence of a base stronger than the amine, like pyridine. It removes the HCl formed and shifts the equilibrium to the right.
  • Tertiary amines have no H on nitrogen, so they do not undergo acylation.
\[C_2H_5NH_2 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{Base} C_2H_5NHCOCH_3 + HCl\] \[(C_2H_5)_2NH + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{Base} (C_2H_5)_2NCOCH_3 + HCl\] \[C_6H_5NH_2 + (CH_3CO)_2O → C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 + CH_3COOH\]

  • The products are N-ethylethanamide (from ethanamine), N,N-diethylethanamide (from N-ethylethanamine) and N-phenylethanamide or acetanilide (from aniline and ethanoic anhydride).

  • The reaction with benzoyl chloride (C6H5COCl) is called benzoylation:

\[CH_3NH_2 + C_6H_5COCl → CH_3NHCOC_6H_5\ (N-methylbenzamide) + HCl\]
  • With carboxylic acids, amines simply form salts at room temperature.

docs.title: 3. Carbylamine Reaction (Isocyanide Test)
docs.text:
• Aliphatic and aromatic primary amines on heating with chloroform and ethanolic KOH form isocyanides (carbylamines), which have a very foul smell.
\[R-NH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \xrightarrow{Heat} R-NC + 3KCl + 3H_2O\] \[C_6H_5NH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \xrightarrow{Heat} C_6H_5NC\ (phenyl\ isocyanide) + 3KCl + 3H_2O\]
  • Secondary and tertiary amines do not give this reaction. So it is used as a test for primary amines.

docs.title: 4. Reaction with Nitrous Acid
docs.text: Nitrous acid (HNO2) is unstable, so it is prepared in situ from sodium nitrite and a mineral acid. The three classes of amines react differently with it.

docs.title: (a) Primary aliphatic amines
docs.text:
• They form aliphatic diazonium salts, which are very unstable. These decompose at once, liberating nitrogen gas quantitatively and forming alcohols.
  • The measured volume of N2 is used in the estimation of amino acids and proteins.
\[R-NH_2 + HNO_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2 + HCl} [R-\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl}] \xrightarrow{H_2O} ROH + N_2 ↑ + HCl\]

docs.title: (b) Primary aromatic amines
docs.text:
• At low temperature (273-278 K) they form arenediazonium salts, which are very useful in synthesis (see the next page). This process is called diazotisation.
\[C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2 + 2HCl,\ 273-278\ K} C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl} + NaCl + 2H_2O\]

docs.title: (c) Secondary and tertiary amines
docs.text: • These react with nitrous acid in a different way and do not give diazonium salts or nitrogen gas.

docs.title: 5. Reaction with Arylsulphonyl Chloride (Hinsberg Test)
docs.text: Benzenesulphonyl chloride (C6H5SO2Cl), also called Hinsberg's reagent, reacts with primary and secondary amines to form sulphonamides.

docs.title: (a) Primary amine
docs.text:
\[C_6H_5SO_2Cl + H-NH-C_2H_5 → C_6H_5SO_2-NH-C_2H_5 + HCl\] \[(N-Ethylbenzenesulphonamide,\ soluble\ in\ alkali)\]
  • The H left on nitrogen in the sulphonamide is strongly acidic, because the sulphonyl group is strongly electron withdrawing. So the product dissolves in alkali (KOH/NaOH).

docs.title: (b) Secondary amine
docs.text:
\[C_6H_5SO_2Cl + H-N(C_2H_5)_2 → C_6H_5SO_2-N(C_2H_5)_2 + HCl\] \[(N,N-Diethylbenzenesulphonamide,\ insoluble\ in\ alkali)\]
  • This sulphonamide has no H on nitrogen, so it is not acidic and is insoluble in alkali.

docs.title: (c) Tertiary amine
docs.text:
• Tertiary amines have no H on nitrogen and do not react with benzenesulphonyl chloride.

Conclusion

Amine Reaction with Hinsberg's reagent Product in alkali Primary (RNH2) Forms sulphonamide Soluble (clear solution) Secondary (R2NH) Forms sulphonamide Insoluble (precipitate) Tertiary (R3N) No reaction Amine remains unreacted

This difference is used to distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° amines and also to separate a mixture of them. Nowadays p-toluenesulphonyl chloride is used in place of benzenesulphonyl chloride.

docs.title: 6. Electrophilic Substitution in Aniline
docs.text:
• From the resonance structures of aniline, the ortho and para positions carry high electron density.
  • So the -NH2 group is ortho and para directing and a powerful activating group.

docs.title: (a) Bromination
docs.text:
• Aniline reacts with bromine water at room temperature to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. Substitution occurs at all three o- and p-positions.
\[C_6H_5NH_2 + 3Br_2 \xrightarrow{H_2O} 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2NH_2 ↓ + 3HBr\]

docs.title: Controlling the reactivity: protection of -NH<sub>2</sub>
docs.text:
• Because aniline is so reactive, it is hard to stop at monosubstitution. To make a monosubstituted product, the -NH2 group is first protected by acetylation with acetic anhydride. The substitution is then carried out, and finally the amide is hydrolysed back to the amine.
\[C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{(CH_3CO)_2O,\ pyridine} C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 \xrightarrow{Br_2,\ CH_3COOH} p-BrC_6H_4NHCOCH_3 \xrightarrow{OH^-\ or\ H^+} p-BrC_6H_4NH_2\] \[(Aniline → Acetanilide → 4-Bromoacetanilide\ (major) → 4-Bromoaniline)\]
  • Why does this work? In acetanilide the lone pair on nitrogen is also in resonance with the C=O group:
\[>\ddot{N}-C(=O)-CH_3\ \ ↔\ \ >\overset{+}{N}=C(-\overset{-}{O})-CH_3\]
  • So the lone pair is less available for donation to the ring, and -NHCOCH3 is a weaker activator than -NH2.

docs.title: (b) Nitration
docs.text:
• Direct nitration of aniline gives tarry oxidation products along with nitro derivatives.
  • In the strongly acidic nitrating mixture, aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion (C6H5NH3+), which is meta directing. So a large amount of the meta product is also formed.
\[C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{HNO_3,\ H_2SO_4,\ 288\ K} p-nitroaniline\ (51\%) + m-nitroaniline\ (47\%) + o-nitroaniline\ (2\%)\]
  • By protecting -NH2 through acetylation, nitration can be controlled and p-nitroaniline is obtained as the major product:
\[C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{(CH_3CO)_2O,\ pyridine} C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 \xrightarrow{HNO_3,\ H_2SO_4,\ 288\ K} p-O_2NC_6H_4NHCOCH_3 \xrightarrow{OH^-\ or\ H^+} p-O_2NC_6H_4NH_2\]

docs.title: (c) Sulphonation
docs.text:
• Aniline reacts with concentrated H2SO4 to form anilinium hydrogensulphate. On heating with H2SO4 at 453-473 K, this gives p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid, commonly called sulphanilic acid, as the major product.
  • Sulphanilic acid exists mainly as a zwitter ion (p-H3N+-C6H4-SO3-).
\[C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}H_3\ HSO_4^- \xrightarrow{453-473\ K} p-H_2NC_6H_4SO_3H ⇌ p-H_3\overset{+}{N}C_6H_4SO_3^-\]

docs.title: (d) Friedel-Crafts reaction
docs.text: • Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation or acylation. Aniline (a Lewis base) forms a salt with the catalyst AlCl3 (a Lewis acid). The nitrogen then carries a positive charge and acts as a strong deactivating group for further reaction.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Diazonium salts have the general formula R\(\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{X}\), where R is an aryl group and X- is an anion such as Cl-, Br-, HSO4- or BF4-. The -N2+ group is called the diazonium group.

  • They are named by adding "diazonium" to the name of the parent hydrocarbon, followed by the name of the anion.

Examples

  • C6H5N2+Cl- : benzenediazonium chloride
  • C6H5N2+HSO4- : benzenediazonium hydrogensulphate

docs.title: Stability of Arenediazonium Salts
docs.text:
• Primary aliphatic amines form alkyldiazonium salts that are highly unstable and decompose at once.
  • Primary aromatic amines form arenediazonium salts, which are stable for a short time in solution at low temperature (273-278 K).
  • The extra stability of the arenediazonium ion is due to resonance: the positive charge is delocalised over the benzene ring.

docs.title: Preparation of Diazonium Salts
docs.text:
• Benzenediazonium chloride is prepared by reacting aniline with nitrous acid at 273-278 K. Nitrous acid is generated in the reaction mixture from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid.
  • The conversion of a primary aromatic amine into a diazonium salt is called diazotisation.
\[NaNO_2 + HCl → HNO_2 + NaCl\] \[C_6H_5NH_2 + NaNO_2 + 2HCl \xrightarrow{273-278\ K} C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl} + NaCl + 2H_2O\]
  • Because it is unstable, the diazonium salt is usually not stored. It is used immediately after preparation.

docs.title: Physical Properties
docs.text:
• Benzenediazonium chloride is a colourless crystalline solid.
  • It is readily soluble in water and is stable in the cold, but reacts with water when warmed.
  • It decomposes easily in the dry state.
  • Benzenediazonium fluoroborate (C6H5N2+BF4-) is insoluble in water and stable at room temperature.

docs.title: Chemical Reactions
docs.text: The reactions of diazonium salts fall into two groups: (A) reactions in which nitrogen is displaced, and (B) reactions in which the diazo group is retained.

docs.title: A. Reactions Involving Displacement of Nitrogen
docs.text: The diazonium group is a very good leaving group. It is replaced by groups like Cl-, Br-, I-, CN- and OH-, and the nitrogen escapes from the reaction mixture as a gas.

docs.title: 1. Replacement by halide or cyanide ion
(a) Sandmeyer reaction
docs.text:
• Cl-, Br- and CN- can be introduced into the ring in the presence of Cu(I) ions.
\[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{X} \xrightarrow{CuCl/HCl} ArCl + N_2\] \[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{X} \xrightarrow{CuBr/HBr} ArBr + N_2\] \[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{X} \xrightarrow{CuCN/KCN} ArCN + N_2\]

docs.title: (b) Gattermann reaction
docs.text:
• Chlorine or bromine can also be introduced by treating the diazonium salt with the corresponding halogen acid in the presence of copper powder.
\[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{X} \xrightarrow{Cu/HCl} ArCl + N_2 + CuX\] \[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{X} \xrightarrow{Cu/HBr} ArBr + N_2 + CuX\]

Note

The yield in the Sandmeyer reaction is better than in the Gattermann reaction.

docs.title: 2. Replacement by iodide ion
docs.text:
• Iodine cannot easily be introduced into the ring directly. But when a diazonium salt solution is warmed with potassium iodide, iodobenzene is formed.
\[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl} + KI → ArI + KCl + N_2\]

docs.title: 3. Replacement by fluoride ion (Balz-Schiemann reaction)
docs.text:
• When an arenediazonium chloride is treated with fluoroboric acid (HBF4), arenediazonium fluoroborate precipitates. On heating, it decomposes to give the aryl fluoride.
\[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl} + HBF_4 → Ar-\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{B}F_4 \xrightarrow{Δ} Ar-F + BF_3 + N_2\]

docs.title: 4. Replacement by H
docs.text:
• Mild reducing agents like hypophosphorous acid (phosphinic acid, H3PO2) or ethanol reduce diazonium salts to arenes. They themselves are oxidised to phosphorous acid and ethanal respectively.
\[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl} + H_3PO_2 + H_2O → ArH + N_2 + H_3PO_3 + HCl\] \[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl} + CH_3CH_2OH → ArH + N_2 + CH_3CHO + HCl\]
  • This reaction is useful for removing an -NH2 group from a ring after it has been used to direct other substituents.

docs.title: 5. Replacement by hydroxyl group
docs.text:
• If the temperature of the diazonium salt solution is allowed to rise up to 283 K, the salt is hydrolysed to phenol.
\[Ar\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl} + H_2O → ArOH + N_2 + HCl\]

docs.title: 6. Replacement by -NO<sub>2</sub> group
docs.text:
• When diazonium fluoroborate is heated with aqueous sodium nitrite in the presence of copper, the diazonium group is replaced by -NO2.
\[C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{Cl} + HBF_4 → C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}_2\overset{-}{B}F_4 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2,\ Cu,\ Δ} C_6H_5NO_2 + N_2 + NaBF_4\]

docs.title: B. Reactions Involving Retention of Diazo Group: Coupling Reactions
docs.text:
• Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with phenol: the phenol molecule is attacked at its para position by the diazonium ion to form p-hydroxyazobenzene (an orange dye). This is called a coupling reaction.
  • Similarly, with aniline it gives p-aminoazobenzene (a yellow dye).
  • The diazonium ion acts as an electrophile, so coupling is an example of electrophilic substitution.
  • The products contain two aromatic rings joined through an -N=N- (azo) bond. This extended conjugated system makes them coloured, so azo compounds are used as dyes.

docs.title: Importance of Diazonium Salts in Synthesis
docs.text:
• Diazonium salts are excellent intermediates for introducing -F, -Cl, -Br, -I, -CN, -OH and -NO2 groups into an aromatic ring.
  • Aryl fluorides and iodides cannot be made by direct halogenation, but are easily made from diazonium salts.
  • The cyano group cannot be introduced by nucleophilic substitution of chlorine in chlorobenzene, but cyanobenzene is easily made from a diazonium salt.
  • So, by replacing the diazo group, we can prepare substituted aromatic compounds that cannot be prepared by direct substitution in benzene or substituted benzene.

Example: Convert 4-nitrotoluene into 2-bromobenzoic acid.

  • Bromine is introduced ortho to CH3. The -NO2 group is then reduced to -NH2, diazotised, and removed with H3PO2. Finally CH3 is oxidised to COOH.
\[4-CH_3C_6H_4NO_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2} 2-Br-4-nitrotoluene \xrightarrow{Sn/HCl} 2-Br-4-aminotoluene\] \[\xrightarrow{NaNO_2/HCl,\ 273-278\ K} 2-Br-4-(N_2^+Cl^-)toluene \xrightarrow{H_3PO_2,\ H_2O} 2-bromotoluene\] \[\xrightarrow{KMnO_4/\overset{-}{O}H} 2-bromobenzoic\ acid\]

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Amines are derivatives of ammonia obtained by replacing one, two or all three hydrogen atoms of NH3 by alkyl and/or aryl groups.

Examples

CH3-NH2, C6H5-NH2, CH3-NH-CH3, (CH3)3N

  • Amines occur widely in nature in proteins, vitamins, alkaloids and hormones. Synthetic amines are found in polymers, dyestuffs and drugs.
  • Adrenaline and ephedrine (both secondary amines) are used to raise blood pressure. Novocain, a synthetic amine, is used as an anaesthetic in dentistry, and the antihistamine Benadryl contains a tertiary amino group.
  • Quaternary ammonium salts are used as surfactants, and diazonium salts are key intermediates in making dyes and many other aromatic compounds.

docs.title: Structure of Amines
docs.text:
• Like ammonia, the nitrogen atom in an amine is trivalent and carries one unshared (lone) pair of electrons.
  • Nitrogen is sp3 hybridised. Three sp3 orbitals overlap with orbitals of hydrogen or carbon, and the fourth sp3 orbital holds the lone pair.
  • So the geometry of amines is pyramidal.
  • The lone pair repels the bond pairs more strongly than they repel each other, so the C-N-E angle (E = C or H) is less than the tetrahedral angle of 109.5°. In trimethylamine it is 108°.

docs.title: Classification of Amines
docs.text: Amines are classified as primary (1°), secondary (2°) or tertiary (3°) depending on how many hydrogen atoms of ammonia have been replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.

docs.title: 1. Primary amine (1°)
docs.text: One hydrogen of NH3 is replaced by R or Ar. General formula: RNH2 or ArNH2.

docs.title: 2. Secondary amine (2°)
docs.text: Two hydrogens of NH3 are replaced. General formula: R-NH-R'.

docs.title: 3. Tertiary amine (3°)
docs.text:
All three hydrogens are replaced. General formula: R3N or RR'NR''.

\[NH_3 → RNH_2\ (1^0) → R_2NH\ (2^0) → R_3N\ (3^0)\]
  • Secondary and tertiary amines are called simple amines when all the alkyl/aryl groups are the same, e.g. (CH3)3N, and mixed amines when they are different, e.g. CH3-NH-C2H5.
  • Note that the classification of amines depends on the number of groups on nitrogen, not on the type of carbon (unlike alcohols and alkyl halides). For example, (CH3)3C-NH2 is a primary amine.

docs.title: 1. Common system
docs.text:
• An aliphatic amine is named by writing the name of the alkyl group followed by "amine" as one word, i.e. alkylamine. Example: CH3NH2 is methylamine.
  • In secondary and tertiary amines, if two or more groups are the same, the prefix di or tri is added before the alkyl group. Example: (CH3)2NH is dimethylamine.

docs.title: 2. IUPAC system
docs.text:
• Amines are named as alkanamines: the final 'e' of the alkane is replaced by 'amine'. Example: CH3NH2 is methanamine.
  • In secondary and tertiary amines, the longest alkyl chain is taken as the parent; the other groups on nitrogen are written as prefixes with the locant N. Example: CH3-NH-C2H5 is N-methylethanamine.
  • When more than one -NH2 group is present, their positions are given by numbers and prefixes like di, tri are used. Here the 'e' of the hydrocarbon is retained. Example: H2N-CH2-CH2-NH2 is ethane-1,2-diamine.

docs.title: 3. Arylamines
docs.text:
• In arylamines, the -NH2 group is directly attached to the benzene ring. The simplest arylamine is C6H5NH2, commonly called aniline (also an accepted IUPAC name).
  • In the IUPAC system, the 'e' of the arene is replaced by 'amine'. So C6H5NH2 is benzenamine.

docs.title: Common and IUPAC names of some amines
docs.text: Amine Common name IUPAC name CH<sub>3</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub> Ethylamine Ethanamine CH<sub>3</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub> n-Propylamine Propan-1-amine CH<sub>3</sub>-CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)-CH<sub>3</sub> Isopropylamine Propan-2-amine CH<sub>3</sub>-NH-CH<sub>2</sub>-CH<sub>3</sub> Ethylmethylamine N-Methylethanamine (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N Trimethylamine N,N-Dimethylmethanamine (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>N-CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> N,N-Diethylbutylamine N,N-Diethylbutan-1-amine NH<sub>2</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>-CH=CH<sub>2</sub> Allylamine Prop-2-en-1-amine NH<sub>2</sub>-(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub> Hexamethylenediamine Hexane-1,6-diamine C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub> Aniline Aniline or Benzenamine o-CH<sub>3</sub>-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub> o-Toluidine 2-Aminotoluene p-Br-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub> p-Bromoaniline 4-Bromobenzenamine or 4-Bromoaniline C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>-N(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> N,N-Dimethylaniline N,N-Dimethylbenzenamine

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Classify the following amines as primary, secondary or tertiary:(i) 1-Naphthylamine (NH2 on a naphthalene ring) (ii) N,N-Dimethyl-1-naphthylamine (iii) (C2H5)2CHNH2 (iv) (C2H5)2NH

  • (i) Only one aryl group on nitrogen (-NH2): primary amine.
  • (ii) -N(CH3)2: nitrogen carries three carbon groups, so it is a tertiary amine.
  • (iii) Nitrogen is attached to only one carbon group (-NH2): primary amine.
  • (iv) Nitrogen carries two ethyl groups and one H: secondary amine.

Write structures and IUPAC names of the isomeric amines with molecular formula C4H11N. What type of isomerism do they show?

Primary amines:

  • CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2 - Butan-1-amine
  • CH3CH2CH(NH2)CH3 - Butan-2-amine
  • (CH3)2CHCH2NH2 - 2-Methylpropan-1-amine
  • (CH3)3CNH2 - 2-Methylpropan-2-amine

Secondary amines:

  • CH3CH2CH2NHCH3 - N-Methylpropan-1-amine
  • (CH3)2CHNHCH3 - N-Methylpropan-2-amine
  • CH3CH2NHCH2CH3 - N-Ethylethanamine

Tertiary amine:

  • (CH3)2NCH2CH3 - N,N-Dimethylethanamine

Isomerism:

  • Butan-1-amine and butan-2-amine (or the two N-methylpropanamines) differ in the position of the amino group: position isomerism.
  • Butan-1-amine and 2-methylpropan-1-amine differ in the carbon skeleton: chain isomerism.
  • N-Ethylethanamine and N-methylpropan-1-amine have different alkyl groups on either side of the same functional group: metamerism.
  • A primary, a secondary and a tertiary amine of the same formula (e.g. butan-1-amine, N-ethylethanamine and N,N-dimethylethanamine) have different types of amino groups: functional isomerism.

docs.title: Amines | Physical Properties and Basic Character
Amines | Physical Properties and Basic Character
1. Physical state and colour
docs.text:
• Lower aliphatic amines are gases with a fishy odour.
  • Primary amines with three or more carbon atoms are liquids, and higher ones are solids.
  • Aniline and other arylamines are usually colourless when pure, but they become coloured on storage due to atmospheric oxidation.

docs.title: 2. Solubility
docs.text:
• Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
  • Solubility decreases as molar mass increases, because the hydrophobic alkyl part becomes larger. Higher amines are practically insoluble in water.
  • Amines are soluble in organic solvents like alcohol, ether and benzene.
  • Nitrogen (electronegativity 3.0) is less electronegative than oxygen (3.5). So alcohols are more polar than amines and form stronger hydrogen bonds. For example, butan-1-ol is more soluble in water than butan-1-amine.

docs.title: 3. Boiling point
docs.text:
• Primary and secondary amines show intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the N of one molecule and the H of another.
  • A primary amine has two H atoms on nitrogen, so its association is greater than that of a secondary amine (one H). A tertiary amine has no H on nitrogen and so shows no intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
  • Therefore, for isomeric amines, the order of boiling points is:
\[Primary\ >\ Secondary\ >\ Tertiary\]
  • Amines boil higher than alkanes of similar molar mass (no H-bonding in alkanes) but lower than alcohols (O-H...O bonds are stronger than N-H...N bonds).
Compound Molar mass b.p. (K) n-C4H9NH2 (1° amine) 73 350.8 (C2H5)2NH (2° amine) 73 329.3 C2H5N(CH3)2 (3° amine) 73 310.5 C2H5CH(CH3)2 (alkane) 72 300.8 n-C4H9OH (alcohol) 74 390.3

docs.title: Basic Character of Amines
docs.text:
• The difference in electronegativity between N and H and the lone pair on nitrogen make amines reactive. Because of the lone pair, amines act as Lewis bases and as nucleophiles.
  • Amines react with acids to form salts:
\[R-\ddot{N}H_2 + HX ⇌ R-\overset{+}{N}H_3\overset{-}{X}\ (salt)\] \[C_6H_5NH_2 + HCl ⇌ C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}H_3\overset{-}{Cl}\ (anilinium\ chloride)\]
  • A base like NaOH regenerates the parent amine from its salt:
\[R\overset{+}{N}H_3\overset{-}{X} + \overset{-}{O}H → R\ddot{N}H_2 + H_2O + \overset{-}{X}\]
  • Amine salts are soluble in water but insoluble in organic solvents like ether. This is used to separate amines from non-basic organic compounds that are insoluble in water.

docs.title: K<sub>b</sub> and pK<sub>b</sub> of amines
docs.text:
• In water, an amine accepts a proton from water:
\[R-NH_2 + H_2O ⇌ R-\overset{+}{N}H_3 + \overset{-}{O}H\] \[K = {[R-\overset{+}{N}H_3][\overset{-}{O}H] \over [R-NH_2][H_2O]}\] \[K[H_2O] = K_b = {[R-\overset{+}{N}H_3][\overset{-}{O}H] \over [R-NH_2]}\] \[pK_b = -log\ K_b\]
  • Larger the Kb (or smaller the pKb), stronger is the base.
  • pKb of ammonia is 4.75. Aliphatic amines (pKb 3 to 4.22) are stronger bases than ammonia, while aromatic amines are much weaker.
Name of amine Formula pKb Methanamine CH3NH2 3.38 N-Methylmethanamine (CH3)2NH 3.27 N,N-Dimethylmethanamine (CH3)3N 4.22 Ethanamine C2H5NH2 3.29 N-Ethylethanamine (C2H5)2NH 3.00 N,N-Diethylethanamine (C2H5)3N 3.25 Benzenamine C6H5NH2 9.38 Phenylmethanamine C6H5CH2NH2 4.70 N-Methylaniline C6H5NHCH3 9.30 N,N-Dimethylaniline C6H5N(CH3)2 8.92

docs.title: Structure-Basicity Relationship
docs.text: The basic strength of an amine depends on how easily it accepts a proton to form a cation. The more stable the cation relative to the amine, the more basic the amine.

docs.title: 1. Alkanamines versus ammonia
docs.text:
\[R-\ddot{N}H_2 + H^+ ⇌ R-\overset{+}{N}H_3\] \[H-\ddot{N}H_2 + H^+ ⇌ H-\overset{+}{N}H_3\]
  • The alkyl group is electron releasing (+I effect). It pushes electron density towards nitrogen, making the lone pair more available for the proton.
  • The +I effect also disperses the positive charge of the substituted ammonium ion and stabilises it.
  • Hence alkylamines are stronger bases than ammonia.

docs.title: (a) Gas phase
docs.text:
• Only the inductive effect operates, so basicity increases with the number of alkyl groups:
\[3^0\ amine\ >\ 2^0\ amine\ >\ 1^0\ amine\ >\ NH_3\]

docs.title: (b) Aqueous phase
docs.text:
In water the order is not regular (see the pKb table). Three factors act together:

  • Inductive effect: favours 3° > 2° > 1°.
  • Solvation effect: the ammonium cation is stabilised by hydrogen bonding with water. A 1° cation (RNH3+) has three H atoms for H-bonding, a 2° cation has two and a 3° cation only one. Also, the larger the ion, the less it is solvated. So stability by solvation is 1° > 2° > 3°, which is opposite to the inductive order.
  • Steric hindrance: small groups like -CH3 hardly hinder H-bonding, but bigger groups like -C2H5 do. So changing the alkyl group changes the order.

The balance of these effects gives the following orders in aqueous solution:

\[(C_2H_5)_2NH\ >\ (C_2H_5)_3N\ >\ C_2H_5NH_2\ >\ NH_3\] \[(CH_3)_2NH\ >\ CH_3NH_2\ >\ (CH_3)_3N\ >\ NH_3\]

docs.title: 2. Arylamines versus ammonia
docs.text:
• pKb of aniline (9.38) is much higher than that of ammonia (4.75), so aniline is a much weaker base.
  • In aniline the -NH2 group is attached directly to the benzene ring. The lone pair on nitrogen is in conjugation with the ring, so it is less available for protonation.
  • Aniline is a resonance hybrid of five structures:
  • The anilinium ion (C6H5NH3+) has no lone pair on nitrogen to delocalise, so it has only two (Kekule) resonance structures.
  • More resonance structures means more stability. So aniline is stabilised more than the anilinium ion, and it has little tendency to accept a proton. Hence aniline is a weaker base than ammonia.

Effect of substituents on the ring

  • Electron releasing groups like -OCH3 and -CH3 increase the basic strength of aniline.
  • Electron withdrawing groups like -NO2, -SO3H, -COOH and -X decrease it.

Note

In benzylamine (C6H5CH2NH2), the -NH2 is attached to a CH2 group, not to the ring. Its lone pair is not delocalised, so it behaves like an aliphatic amine (pKb 4.70) and is much more basic than aniline.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Arrange in decreasing order of basic strength: C6H5NH2, C2H5NH2, (C2H5)2NH, NH3

Aliphatic amines are stronger than NH3 (+I effect), and in the ethyl series the 2° amine is the strongest in water. Aniline is the weakest because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring.

\[(C_2H_5)_2NH\ >\ C_2H_5NH_2\ >\ NH_3\ >\ C_6H_5NH_2\]

Arrange in increasing order of basic strength:(i) C2H5NH2, C6H5NH2, NH3, C6H5CH2NH2, (C2H5)2NH(ii) C2H5NH2, (C2H5)2NH, (C2H5)3N, C6H5NH2(iii) CH3NH2, (CH3)2NH, (CH3)3N, C6H5NH2, C6H5CH2NH2

Using pKb values (lower pKb = stronger base):

\[(i)\ C_6H_5NH_2 < NH_3 < C_6H_5CH_2NH_2 < C_2H_5NH_2 < (C_2H_5)_2NH\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5NH_2 < C_2H_5NH_2 < (C_2H_5)_3N < (C_2H_5)_2NH\] \[(iii)\ C_6H_5NH_2 < C_6H_5CH_2NH_2 < (CH_3)_3N < CH_3NH_2 < (CH_3)_2NH\]

Complete the following acid-base reactions and name the products:(i) CH3CH2CH2NH2 + HCl → (ii) (C2H5)3N + HCl →

\[(i)\ CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2 + HCl → CH_3CH_2CH_2\overset{+}{N}H_3\overset{-}{Cl}\]

Product: propan-1-aminium chloride (n-propylammonium chloride).

\[(ii)\ (C_2H_5)_3N + HCl → (C_2H_5)_3\overset{+}{N}H\overset{-}{Cl}\]

Product: N,N-diethylethanaminium chloride (triethylammonium chloride).

Why do primary amines have higher boiling points than tertiary amines?

Primary amines have two H atoms on nitrogen and form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Tertiary amines have no H on nitrogen and cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. More energy is needed to separate the associated molecules of a primary amine, so its boiling point is higher.

Why are amines less acidic than alcohols of comparable molecular masses?

Loss of a proton from an amine gives RNH-, and from an alcohol gives RO-. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so it holds the negative charge better and RO- is more stable than RNH-. Therefore alcohols lose a proton more easily and are more acidic than amines.

docs.title: Amines | Preparation of Amines
docs.text: Amines can be prepared by reduction of nitro compounds, nitriles and amides, by ammonolysis of alkyl halides, by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis and by Hoffmann bromamide degradation. Let us look at each method.

docs.title: 1. Reduction of Nitro Compounds
docs.text:
• Nitro compounds are reduced to amines either by passing hydrogen gas in the presence of finely divided Ni, Pd or Pt (catalytic hydrogenation), or by metals in acidic medium (Sn + HCl or Fe + HCl).
  • Nitroalkanes are reduced in the same way to the corresponding alkanamines.
\[C_6H_5NO_2 + 3H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd,\ ethanol} C_6H_5NH_2 + 2H_2O\] \[C_6H_5NO_2 \xrightarrow{Sn + HCl\ or\ Fe + HCl} C_6H_5NH_2\] \[R-NO_2 + 6[H] → R-NH_2 + 2H_2O\]
  • Reduction with iron scrap and HCl is preferred industrially. The FeCl2 formed gets hydrolysed and releases HCl during the reaction, so only a small amount of HCl is needed to start the reaction.

docs.title: 2. Ammonolysis of Alkyl Halides
docs.text:
• The C-X bond in alkyl or benzyl halides is easily broken by a nucleophile. When an alkyl or benzyl halide is heated with an ethanolic solution of ammonia, the halogen is replaced by -NH2 by nucleophilic substitution.
  • This cleavage of the C-X bond by ammonia is called ammonolysis. It is carried out in a sealed tube at 373 K.
\[\ddot{N}H_3 + R-X → R-\overset{+}{N}H_3\overset{-}{X}\ (substituted\ ammonium\ salt)\]
  • The primary amine formed is itself a nucleophile. It reacts with more alkyl halide to give secondary and tertiary amines and finally a quaternary ammonium salt:
\[RNH_2\ (1^0) \xrightarrow{RX} R_2NH\ (2^0) \xrightarrow{RX} R_3N\ (3^0) \xrightarrow{RX} R_4\overset{+}{N}\overset{-}{X}\ (quaternary\ salt)\]
  • The free amine is liberated from its ammonium salt by a strong base:
\[R-\overset{+}{N}H_3\overset{-}{X} + NaOH → R-NH_2 + H_2O + NaX\]

Note

  • The main drawback of ammonolysis is that it gives a mixture of 1°, 2° and 3° amines along with the quaternary salt.
  • The primary amine can be made the major product by using a large excess of ammonia.
  • Order of reactivity of halides: RI > RBr > RCl.

docs.title: 3. Reduction of Nitriles
docs.text:
• Nitriles are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4, by catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Ni) or by sodium amalgam in ethanol.
\[R-C \equiv N \xrightarrow{H_2/Ni\ or\ Na(Hg)/C_2H_5OH} R-CH_2-NH_2\]
  • Since a nitrile is made from an alkyl halide (R-X + CN-), this route adds one carbon. It is used for the ascent of the amine series, i.e. to make an amine with one carbon atom more than the starting compound.

docs.title: 4. Reduction of Amides
docs.text:
• Amides are reduced to amines by lithium aluminium hydride. The carbonyl group becomes CH2, so the number of carbon atoms stays the same.
\[R-CO-NH_2 \xrightarrow{(i)\ LiAlH_4,\ (ii)\ H_2O} R-CH_2-NH_2\]

docs.title: 5. Gabriel Phthalimide Synthesis
docs.text:
• Gabriel synthesis is used to prepare pure primary amines (free from 2° and 3° amines).
  • Steps:
    1. Phthalimide is treated with ethanolic KOH. The acidic N-H proton is removed and potassium phthalimide is formed.
    2. Potassium phthalimide is heated with an alkyl halide. The phthalimide anion acts as a nucleophile and gives N-alkylphthalimide.
    3. N-alkylphthalimide is hydrolysed with aqueous NaOH, giving the primary amine and sodium phthalate.
  • Since nitrogen is attached to only one alkyl group in N-alkylphthalimide, no further alkylation is possible. That is why only the primary amine is obtained.

Note

Aromatic primary amines (like aniline) cannot be prepared by this method, because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.

docs.title: 6. Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation Reaction
docs.text:
• A primary amide is heated with bromine in an aqueous or ethanolic solution of sodium hydroxide to give a primary amine.
  • During the reaction, the alkyl or aryl group migrates from the carbonyl carbon to the nitrogen atom, and the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate.
  • Hence the amine formed contains one carbon atom less than the amide. This reaction is used for the descent of series.
\[R-CO-NH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH → R-NH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O\]

Example

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2CONH_2\ (butanamide) \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2\ (propan-1-amine)\] \[C_6H_5CONH_2\ (benzamide) \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} C_6H_5NH_2\ (aniline)\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Write chemical equations for: (i) Reaction of ethanolic NH3 with C2H5Cl. (ii) Ammonolysis of benzyl chloride and reaction of the amine so formed with two moles of CH3Cl.

(i) Ammonia gives ethanamine, which reacts further with chloroethane:

\[C_2H_5Cl \xrightarrow{NH_3} C_2H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{C_2H_5Cl} (C_2H_5)_2NH \xrightarrow{C_2H_5Cl} (C_2H_5)_3N\]

Chloroethane → Ethanamine → N-Ethylethanamine → N,N-Diethylethanamine

(ii)

\[C_6H_5CH_2Cl \xrightarrow{NH_3} C_6H_5CH_2NH_2 \xrightarrow{2CH_3Cl} C_6H_5CH_2N(CH_3)_2\]

Benzyl chloride → Benzylamine → N,N-Dimethylphenylmethanamine

Write chemical equations for the following conversions:(i) CH3-CH2-Cl into CH3-CH2-CH2-NH2(ii) C6H5-CH2-Cl into C6H5-CH2-CH2-NH2

One carbon has to be added in each case, so we go through the nitrile and then reduce it.

\[(i)\ CH_3CH_2Cl \xrightarrow{ethanolic\ NaCN} CH_3CH_2C \equiv N \xrightarrow{reduction} CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2\]

Chloroethane → Propanenitrile → Propan-1-amine

\[(ii)\ C_6H_5CH_2Cl \xrightarrow{ethanolic\ NaCN} C_6H_5CH_2C \equiv N \xrightarrow{H_2/Ni} C_6H_5CH_2CH_2NH_2\]

Benzyl chloride → Phenylethanenitrile (benzyl cyanide) → 2-Phenylethanamine

Write structures and IUPAC names of (i) the amide which gives propanamine by Hoffmann bromamide reaction, (ii) the amine produced by Hoffmann degradation of benzamide.

(i) Propanamine has three carbons. Hoffmann degradation removes one carbon, so the amide must have four carbons: CH3CH2CH2CONH2, butanamide.

(ii) Benzamide (C6H5CONH2) has seven carbons, so the amine has six carbons: C6H5NH2, aniline (benzenamine).

How will you convert (i) Benzene into aniline (ii) Benzene into N,N-dimethylaniline (iii) Cl-(CH2)4-Cl into hexane-1,6-diamine?

\[(i)\ C_6H_6 \xrightarrow{conc.\ HNO_3 + conc.\ H_2SO_4} C_6H_5NO_2 \xrightarrow{Sn/HCl} C_6H_5NH_2\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_6 → C_6H_5NO_2 → C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{2CH_3Cl} C_6H_5N(CH_3)_2\] \[(iii)\ Cl-(CH_2)_4-Cl \xrightarrow{ethanolic\ NaCN} NC-(CH_2)_4-CN \xrightarrow{H_2/Ni} H_2N-(CH_2)_6-NH_2\]

In (iii), each -CN adds one carbon, so the four-carbon dichloride gives a six-carbon diamine.

Why cannot aromatic primary amines be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?

The key step of Gabriel synthesis is nucleophilic substitution of the halide by the phthalimide anion. Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution easily because the C-X bond has partial double bond character (resonance with the ring) and the sp2 carbon holds the halogen strongly. So aryl halides do not react with potassium phthalimide, and aromatic primary amines cannot be made this way.

docs.title: Amines | Questions
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some important questions on amines and diazonium salts, including distinction tests, basicity orders, conversions and reaction sequences.

docs.title: Distinction and Identification
docs.text:
Give one chemical test to distinguish between the following pairs:(i) Methylamine and dimethylamine (ii) Secondary and tertiary amines (iii) Ethylamine and aniline (iv) Aniline and benzylamine (v) Aniline and N-methylaniline

  • (i) Carbylamine test: heat with CHCl3 and ethanolic KOH. Methylamine (1°) gives the foul smell of methyl isocyanide; dimethylamine (2°) does not.
\[CH_3NH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH → CH_3NC + 3KCl + 3H_2O\]
  • (ii) Hinsberg test: with benzenesulphonyl chloride, a secondary amine gives N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, insoluble in alkali. A tertiary amine does not react.
  • (iii) Azo dye test: treat with NaNO2 + HCl at 273-278 K, then add alkaline phenol. Aniline forms a diazonium salt that couples to give an orange dye (p-hydroxyazobenzene). Ethylamine gives brisk evolution of N2 and no dye.
  • (iv) Nitrous acid test: benzylamine (NH2 not on the ring) behaves like an aliphatic amine, giving N2 gas and benzyl alcohol. Aniline gives a diazonium salt at 273-278 K which forms an orange dye with alkaline phenol.
  • (v) Carbylamine test: aniline (1°) gives a foul-smelling phenyl isocyanide; N-methylaniline (2°) does not.

Describe a method for the identification of primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Write the equations involved.

Use Hinsberg's reagent (benzenesulphonyl chloride, C6H5SO2Cl) followed by alkali.

\[Primary:\ C_6H_5SO_2Cl + RNH_2 → C_6H_5SO_2NHR + HCl\]

The N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide has an acidic H on N, so it dissolves in KOH.

\[Secondary:\ C_6H_5SO_2Cl + R_2NH → C_6H_5SO_2NR_2 + HCl\]

The N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide has no H on N, so it is insoluble in KOH.

\[Tertiary:\ R_3N + C_6H_5SO_2Cl → No\ reaction\]

The primary amine can be confirmed further by the carbylamine test.

docs.title: Account for the Following
docs.text:
(i) pKb of aniline is more than that of methylamine.(ii) Ethylamine is soluble in water whereas aniline is not.

(i) In aniline, the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance and is less available for a proton. In methylamine, the +I effect of CH3 increases electron density on N. So methylamine is the stronger base (smaller pKb, 3.38) and aniline is weaker (larger pKb, 9.38).

(ii) Ethylamine forms hydrogen bonds with water and its alkyl part is small. In aniline the large hydrophobic phenyl group outweighs the hydrogen bonding of -NH2, so it is only slightly soluble.

Methylamine in water reacts with ferric chloride to precipitate hydrated ferric oxide.

Methylamine is a stronger base than ammonia and produces OH- ions in water. These precipitate Fe3+ as hydrated ferric oxide:

\[CH_3NH_2 + H_2O ⇌ CH_3\overset{+}{N}H_3 + \overset{-}{O}H\] \[FeCl_3 + 3\overset{-}{O}H → Fe(OH)_3 ↓ + 3Cl^-\]

Although the amino group is o- and p-directing, aniline on nitration gives a substantial amount of m-nitroaniline.

Nitration is done in a strongly acidic medium. Here aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion, C6H5NH3+. The -NH3+ group is electron withdrawing and meta directing. So along with o- and p-products (2% and 51%), about 47% of m-nitroaniline is formed.

(i) Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.(ii) Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are more stable than those of aliphatic amines.(iii) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is preferred for synthesising primary amines.

(i) Aniline (a Lewis base) forms a salt with AlCl3 (a Lewis acid). Nitrogen then carries a positive charge and strongly deactivates the ring, so the reaction does not occur.

(ii) In arenediazonium ions the positive charge is delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance. Alkyldiazonium ions have no such stabilisation and lose N2 immediately.

(iii) It gives only the primary amine, free from secondary and tertiary amines, because the nitrogen of N-alkylphthalimide cannot be alkylated further. Ammonolysis, by contrast, gives a mixture.

Why are aliphatic amines stronger bases than aromatic amines?

In aliphatic amines, the +I effect of alkyl groups increases electron density on nitrogen and stabilises the ammonium ion. In aromatic amines, the lone pair is delocalised into the ring (aniline has five resonance structures but the anilinium ion only two), so it is less available for protonation. Hence aliphatic amines are stronger bases.

docs.title: Arranging in Order
docs.text:
Arrange:(i) In decreasing order of pKb: C2H5NH2, C6H5NHCH3, (C2H5)2NH, C6H5NH2(ii) In increasing order of basic strength: C6H5NH2, C6H5N(CH3)2, (C2H5)2NH, CH3NH2

\[(i)\ C_6H_5NH_2\ (9.38) > C_6H_5NHCH_3\ (9.30) > C_2H_5NH_2\ (3.29) > (C_2H_5)_2NH\ (3.00)\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5NH_2 < C_6H_5N(CH_3)_2 < CH_3NH_2 < (C_2H_5)_2NH\]

Arrange in increasing order of basic strength:(a) Aniline, p-nitroaniline and p-toluidine(b) C6H5NH2, C6H5NHCH3, C6H5CH2NH2

(a) -NO2 withdraws electrons and lowers basicity; -CH3 releases electrons and raises it.

\[p-nitroaniline < aniline < p-toluidine\]

(b) In benzylamine the lone pair is not delocalised, so it is the strongest.

\[C_6H_5NH_2 < C_6H_5NHCH_3 < C_6H_5CH_2NH_2\]

Arrange:(i) In decreasing order of basic strength in gas phase: C2H5NH2, (C2H5)2NH, (C2H5)3N, NH3(ii) In increasing order of boiling point: C2H5OH, (CH3)2NH, C2H5NH2(iii) In increasing order of solubility in water: C6H5NH2, (C2H5)2NH, C2H5NH2

(i) In the gas phase only the +I effect matters:

\[(C_2H_5)_3N > (C_2H_5)_2NH > C_2H_5NH_2 > NH_3\]

(ii) O-H...O hydrogen bonds are strongest; a 1° amine has two N-H bonds, a 2° amine only one:

\[(CH_3)_2NH < C_2H_5NH_2 < C_2H_5OH\]

(iii) Solubility falls as the hydrophobic part grows and as H-bonding decreases:

\[C_6H_5NH_2 < (C_2H_5)_2NH < C_2H_5NH_2\]

docs.title: Conversions
docs.text:
How will you convert:(i) Ethanoic acid into methanamine (ii) Hexanenitrile into 1-aminopentane (iii) Methanol to ethanoic acid (iv) Ethanamine into methanamine

\[(i)\ CH_3COOH \xrightarrow{NH_3,\ Δ} CH_3CONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} CH_3NH_2\] \[(ii)\ CH_3(CH_2)_4CN \xrightarrow{partial\ hydrolysis\ (OH^-)} CH_3(CH_2)_4CONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} CH_3(CH_2)_4NH_2\] \[(iii)\ CH_3OH \xrightarrow{PCl_5} CH_3Cl \xrightarrow{KCN} CH_3CN \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} CH_3COOH\] \[(iv)\ C_2H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{HNO_2} C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{KMnO_4/H^+} CH_3COOH \xrightarrow{NH_3,\ Δ} CH_3CONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} CH_3NH_2\]

How will you convert:(i) Ethanoic acid into propanoic acid (ii) Methanamine into ethanamine (iii) Nitromethane into dimethylamine (iv) Propanoic acid into ethanoic acid

\[(i)\ CH_3COOH \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{PCl_5} CH_3CH_2Cl \xrightarrow{KCN} CH_3CH_2CN \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} CH_3CH_2COOH\] \[(ii)\ CH_3NH_2 \xrightarrow{HNO_2} CH_3OH \xrightarrow{PCl_5} CH_3Cl \xrightarrow{KCN} CH_3CN \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} CH_3CH_2NH_2\] \[(iii)\ CH_3NO_2 \xrightarrow{Sn/HCl} CH_3NH_2 \xrightarrow{CHCl_3/KOH} CH_3NC \xrightarrow{H_2/Pt} CH_3NHCH_3\]

In (iii), reduction of an isocyanide gives a secondary amine.

\[(iv)\ CH_3CH_2COOH \xrightarrow{NH_3,\ Δ} CH_3CH_2CONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} CH_3CH_2NH_2 \xrightarrow{HNO_2} CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{KMnO_4/H^+} CH_3COOH\]

Accomplish the following conversions:(i) Nitrobenzene to benzoic acid (ii) Benzene to m-bromophenol (iii) Benzoic acid to aniline (iv) Aniline to 2,4,6-tribromofluorobenzene

\[(i)\ C_6H_5NO_2 \xrightarrow{Sn/HCl} C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2/HCl,\ 273\ K} C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{CuCN/KCN} C_6H_5CN \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} C_6H_5COOH\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_6 \xrightarrow{HNO_3/H_2SO_4} C_6H_5NO_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/FeBr_3} m-BrC_6H_4NO_2 \xrightarrow{Sn/HCl} m-BrC_6H_4NH_2\] \[\xrightarrow{NaNO_2/HCl,\ 273\ K} m-BrC_6H_4N_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{H_2O,\ warm} m-BrC_6H_4OH\]

(-NO2 is meta directing, so Br enters the meta position.)

\[(iii)\ C_6H_5COOH \xrightarrow{NH_3,\ Δ} C_6H_5CONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} C_6H_5NH_2\] \[(iv)\ C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/H_2O} 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2NH_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2/HCl,\ 273\ K} 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2N_2^+Cl^-\] \[\xrightarrow{HBF_4} 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2N_2^+BF_4^- \xrightarrow{Δ} 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2F\]

Accomplish the following conversions:(i) Chlorobenzene to p-chloroaniline (ii) Aniline to p-bromoaniline (iii) Benzamide to toluene (iv) Aniline to benzyl alcohol

\[(i)\ C_6H_5Cl \xrightarrow{HNO_3/H_2SO_4} p-ClC_6H_4NO_2\ (major) \xrightarrow{Sn/HCl} p-ClC_6H_4NH_2\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{(CH_3CO)_2O} C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 \xrightarrow{Br_2/CH_3COOH} p-BrC_6H_4NHCOCH_3 \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} p-BrC_6H_4NH_2\] \[(iii)\ C_6H_5CONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2/HCl,\ 273\ K} C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{H_3PO_2} C_6H_6 \xrightarrow{CH_3Cl/AlCl_3} C_6H_5CH_3\] \[(iv)\ C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2/HCl,\ 273\ K} C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{CuCN/KCN} C_6H_5CN \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} C_6H_5CH_2NH_2 \xrightarrow{HNO_2} C_6H_5CH_2OH\]

Convert (i) 3-Methylaniline into 3-nitrotoluene (ii) Aniline into 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.

\[(i)\ 3-CH_3C_6H_4NH_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2/HCl,\ 273\ K} 3-CH_3C_6H_4N_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{HBF_4} 3-CH_3C_6H_4N_2^+BF_4^- \xrightarrow{NaNO_2,\ Cu,\ Δ} 3-CH_3C_6H_4NO_2\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/H_2O} 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2NH_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2/HCl,\ 273\ K} 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2N_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{H_3PO_2} 1,3,5-C_6H_3Br_3\]

In (ii), -NH2 places three Br atoms meta to each other and is then removed.

docs.title: Reaction Sequences
docs.text:
Give the structures of A, B and C:(i) CH3CH2I + NaCN → A; A + OH- (partial hydrolysis) → B; B + NaOH/Br2 → C(ii) C6H5N2Cl + CuCN → A; A + H2O/H+ → B; B + NH3, Δ → C(iii) CH3CH2Br + KCN → A; A + LiAlH4 → B; B + HNO2 (0°C) → C

  • (i) A = CH3CH2CN, B = CH3CH2CONH2, C = CH3CH2NH2
  • (ii) A = C6H5CN, B = C6H5COOH, C = C6H5CONH2
  • (iii) A = CH3CH2CN, B = CH3CH2CH2NH2, C = CH3CH2CH2OH

Give the structures of A, B and C:(i) C6H5NO2 + Fe/HCl → A; A + NaNO2/HCl (273 K) → B; B + H2O/H+, Δ → C(ii) CH3COOH + NH3, Δ → A; A + NaOBr → B; B + NaNO2/HCl → C(iii) C6H5NO2 + Fe/HCl → A; A + HNO2 (273 K) → B; B + C6H5OH → C

  • (i) A = C6H5NH2, B = C6H5N2+Cl-, C = C6H5OH
  • (ii) A = CH3CONH2, B = CH3NH2, C = CH3OH
  • (iii) A = C6H5NH2, B = C6H5N2+Cl-, C = p-HO-C6H4-N=N-C6H5 (p-hydroxyazobenzene)
