An aromatic compound 'A' on treatment with aqueous ammonia and heating forms compound 'B', which on heating with Br2 and KOH forms compound 'C' of molecular formula C6H7N. Write the structures and IUPAC names of A, B and C.

  • C6H7N formed by Hoffmann bromamide reaction is C6H5NH2. So B is the amide with one more carbon, and A is the corresponding acid.
  • A = C6H5COOH (benzoic acid or benzenecarboxylic acid)
  • B = C6H5CONH2 (benzamide or benzenecarboxamide)
  • C = C6H5NH2 (aniline or benzenamine)
\[C_6H_5COOH \xrightarrow{NH_3,\ Δ} C_6H_5CONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/KOH} C_6H_5NH_2\]

Complete the following reactions:(i) C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + alc. KOH → (ii) C6H5N2Cl + H3PO2 + H2O → (iii) C6H5NH2 + H2SO4 (conc.) → (iv) C6H5N2Cl + C2H5OH →(v) C6H5NH2 + Br2(aq) → (vi) C6H5NH2 + (CH3CO)2O → (vii) C6H5N2Cl + (i) HBF4 (ii) NaNO2/Cu, Δ →

\[(i)\ C_6H_5NH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH → C_6H_5NC + 3KCl + 3H_2O\] \[(ii)\ C_6H_5N_2Cl + H_3PO_2 + H_2O → C_6H_6 + N_2 + H_3PO_3 + HCl\] \[(iii)\ C_6H_5NH_2 + H_2SO_4 → C_6H_5NH_3^+HSO_4^-\ \xrightarrow{453-473\ K} p-H_2NC_6H_4SO_3H\] \[(iv)\ C_6H_5N_2Cl + C_2H_5OH → C_6H_6 + N_2 + CH_3CHO + HCl\] \[(v)\ C_6H_5NH_2 + 3Br_2 → 2,4,6-Br_3C_6H_2NH_2 ↓ + 3HBr\] \[(vi)\ C_6H_5NH_2 + (CH_3CO)_2O → C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 + CH_3COOH\] \[(vii)\ C_6H_5N_2Cl \xrightarrow{HBF_4} C_6H_5N_2^+BF_4^- \xrightarrow{NaNO_2/Cu,\ Δ} C_6H_5NO_2 + N_2 + NaBF_4\]

docs.title: Miscellaneous
docs.text:
Write the reaction of aniline with benzoyl chloride and name the product.

\[C_6H_5NH_2 + C_6H_5COCl → C_6H_5NHCOC_6H_5 + HCl\]

The product is N-phenylbenzamide (benzanilide).

Write structures of the isomers of C3H9N. Name the isomers which liberate nitrogen gas with nitrous acid.

  • CH3CH2CH2NH2 - Propan-1-amine (1°)
  • CH3CH(NH2)CH3 - Propan-2-amine (1°)
  • CH3NHCH2CH3 - N-Methylethanamine (2°)
  • (CH3)3N - N,N-Dimethylmethanamine (3°)

Only primary aliphatic amines liberate N2 with nitrous acid, i.e. propan-1-amine and propan-2-amine.

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2 + HNO_2 → CH_3CH_2CH_2OH + N_2 + H_2O\]

Write the reactions of (i) aromatic and (ii) aliphatic primary amines with nitrous acid.

\[(i)\ C_6H_5NH_2 + NaNO_2 + 2HCl \xrightarrow{273-278\ K} C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + NaCl + 2H_2O\] \[(ii)\ RNH_2 + HNO_2 \xrightarrow{NaNO_2 + HCl} [RN_2^+Cl^-] \xrightarrow{H_2O} ROH + N_2 + HCl\]

Aromatic amines give a diazonium salt that is stable in the cold, while aliphatic amines give an unstable diazonium salt that decomposes to an alcohol with evolution of nitrogen.

docs.title: Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Classification and Isomerism
Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Classification and Isomerism
docs.text: Organic compounds are broadly classified on the basis of their structure into acyclic (open chain) and cyclic (closed chain or ring) compounds, and on the basis of functional groups into homologous series.

docs.title: Classification of Organic Compounds
docs.text:
The classification of organic compounds on the basis of structure can be summarised as:

  • Organic compounds
    • I. Acyclic or open chain compounds (aliphatic)
    • II. Cyclic or closed chain or ring compounds
      • Homocyclic or carbocyclic compounds
        • Alicyclic compounds
        • Aromatic compounds
          • Benzenoid compounds
          • Non-benzenoid compounds
      • Heterocyclic compounds

docs.title: I. Acyclic or open chain compounds
docs.text:
• These are also called aliphatic compounds. They contain straight or branched chains of carbon atoms.

Examples

  • Ethane: CH3CH3
  • Isobutane: CH3CH(CH3)CH3
  • Acetaldehyde: CH3CHO
  • Acetic acid: CH3COOH

docs.title: II. Alicyclic or closed chain compounds
docs.text:
• Alicyclic (aliphatic cyclic) compounds have carbon atoms joined in the form of a ring (homocyclic).
  • Sometimes atoms other than carbon are also present in the ring (heterocyclic), e.g. tetrahydrofuran.
  • They show some properties similar to those of aliphatic compounds.

Examples

docs.title: III. Aromatic compounds
docs.text:
• Aromatic compounds are special ring compounds. They include benzene and related ring compounds (benzenoid).
  • Aromatic compounds without a benzene ring are called non-benzenoid aromatic compounds, e.g. tropolone.
  • Like alicyclic compounds, aromatic compounds may also contain a heteroatom in the ring. These are called heterocyclic aromatic compounds.

Benzenoid and non-benzenoid aromatic compounds

Heterocyclic aromatic compounds

docs.title: Functional Group
docs.text:
• A functional group is an atom or group of atoms joined in a specific manner which is responsible for the characteristic chemical properties of an organic compound.
  • Examples: hydroxyl group (-OH), aldehyde group (-CHO) and carboxylic acid group (-COOH).
  • Compounds having the same functional group undergo similar reactions. For example, CH3OH, CH3CH2OH and (CH3)2CHOH all contain -OH and all liberate hydrogen with sodium metal.

docs.title: Homologous Series
docs.text:
• A group or series of organic compounds containing the same functional group is called a homologous series, and its members are called homologues.
  • Members of a homologous series:
    • can be represented by a general molecular formula,
    • differ from each other in molecular formula by a -CH2 unit,
    • show similar chemical properties and a gradation in physical properties.
  • Examples of homologous series: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, haloalkanes, alkanols, alkanals, alkanones, alkanoic acids, amines etc.

Example: Alkanol series

CH3OH, CH3CH2OH, CH3CH2CH2OH, ... (general formula CnH2n+1OH)

docs.title: Isomerism
docs.text:
• The phenomenon of existence of two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different properties is called isomerism. Such compounds are called isomers.
  • Isomerism is of two main types:
    • Structural isomerism: chain, position, functional group isomerism and metamerism.
    • Stereoisomerism: geometrical and optical isomerism.

docs.title: Structural Isomerism
docs.text: Compounds having the same molecular formula but different structures (i.e. different ways in which the atoms are linked) are called structural isomers.

docs.title: 1. Chain isomerism
docs.text:
When two or more compounds have the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons, they are called chain isomers.

Example: C5H12

  • Pentane: CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3
  • Isopentane (2-Methylbutane): CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3
  • Neopentane (2,2-Dimethylpropane): C(CH3)4

docs.title: 2. Position isomerism
docs.text:
When two or more compounds differ in the position of a substituent atom or functional group on the same carbon skeleton, they are called position isomers.

Example: C3H8O

  • Propan-1-ol: CH3CH2CH2OH
  • Propan-2-ol: CH3CH(OH)CH3

docs.title: 3. Functional group isomerism
docs.text:
Two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different functional groups are called functional isomers.

Example: C3H6O

  • Propanone (a ketone): CH3COCH3
  • Propanal (an aldehyde): CH3CH2CHO

docs.title: 4. Metamerism
docs.text:
Metamerism arises due to different alkyl chains on either side of the functional group in the molecule.

Example: C4H10O

  • Methoxypropane: CH3OC3H7
  • Ethoxyethane: C2H5OC2H5

docs.title: Stereoisomerism
docs.text:
• Compounds that have the same constitution and sequence of covalent bonds but differ in the relative positions of their atoms or groups in space are called stereoisomers.
  • This type of isomerism is called stereoisomerism. It is classified as geometrical isomerism and optical isomerism.
  • Geometrical isomerism arises due to restricted rotation about a C=C bond, e.g. cis- and trans-but-2-ene.

docs.title: Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Electronic Effects
Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Electronic Effects
docs.text:
Electron displacement in an organic molecule may take place in the ground state under the influence of an atom or substituent group, or in the presence of an attacking reagent.

  • Displacements caused by an atom or group present in the molecule cause permanent polarisation of bonds. Examples: inductive effect, resonance effect and hyperconjugation.
  • Displacements seen only when a reagent approaches to attack are temporary. This is called the electromeric effect or polarisability effect.

docs.title: 1. Inductive Effect
docs.text:
• When a covalent bond is formed between atoms of different electronegativity, the electron density shifts towards the more electronegative atom. The bond becomes a polar covalent bond.
  • Consider chloroethane (CH3CH2Cl). The C-Cl bond is polarised so that carbon-1 gets a partial positive charge (δ+) and chlorine a partial negative charge (δ-). The shift is shown by an arrow pointing from the δ+ end to the δ- end.
\[\underset{2}{\overset{\delta\delta+}{C}H_3} \rightarrow \underset{1}{\overset{\delta+}{C}H_2} \rightarrow \overset{\delta-}{Cl}\]
  • Carbon-1, now having δ+ charge, pulls some electron density from the adjacent C-C bond. So, a smaller positive charge (δδ+) develops on carbon-2 also.
  • Thus, the polar C-Cl bond induces polarity in the adjacent bonds. The polarisation of a σ bond caused by the polarisation of an adjacent σ bond is called the inductive effect.
  • The effect is passed on to further bonds, but it decreases rapidly as the number of intervening bonds increases, and becomes vanishingly small after three bonds.

docs.title: Electron-withdrawing and electron-donating groups
docs.text:
Based on their ability to withdraw or donate electron density relative to hydrogen, substituents are classified as:

  • Electron-withdrawing groups (-I effect): halogens, nitro (-NO2), cyano (-CN), carboxy (-COOH), ester (-COOR), aryloxy (-OAr, e.g. -OC6H5) etc.
  • Electron-donating groups (+I effect): alkyl groups like methyl (-CH3) and ethyl (-CH2CH3).

Application

An electron-withdrawing group stabilises a negative charge. For example, O2NCH2CH2O- is more stable than CH3CH2O-, because the -NO2 group (-I) disperses the negative charge, while the -CH3 group (+I) intensifies it.

docs.title: 2. Resonance Structures
docs.text:
• Many molecules cannot be represented by a single Lewis structure. Benzene is an example.
  • A benzene ring with alternating C-C single and C=C double bonds should have two different bond lengths. But experimentally, all C-C bonds in benzene are of equal length, 139 pm, which is between the C-C single bond (154 pm) and the C=C double bond (134 pm).
  • Benzene is represented equally well by two energetically identical structures I and II (the two Kekule structures, in which the positions of the double bonds are interchanged).
\[Structure\ I \longleftrightarrow Structure\ II\]
  • According to resonance theory, the actual structure of benzene is a resonance hybrid of I and II. These are called resonance structures (canonical or contributing structures).
  • The resonance structures are hypothetical and individually do not represent any real molecule. They contribute to the actual structure in proportion to their stability.

Example: Nitromethane (CH3NO2)

Nitromethane can be written as two Lewis structures, each with one N=O and one N-O bond:

\[\underset{I}{CH_3-\overset{+}{N}(=O)-O^-} \longleftrightarrow \underset{II}{CH_3-\overset{+}{N}(-O^-)=O}\]

The two structures differ only in which oxygen is double bonded to nitrogen. Experimentally, both N-O bonds are of the same length (intermediate between N-O and N=O), so the actual structure is a resonance hybrid of I and II.

docs.title: Resonance energy
docs.text:
• The energy of the actual structure (resonance hybrid) is lower than that of any canonical structure.
  • The difference in energy between the actual structure and the lowest energy resonance structure is called the resonance stabilisation energy or resonance energy.
  • More the number of important contributing structures, more is the resonance energy. Resonance is especially important when the contributing structures are equivalent in energy.

docs.title: Rules for writing resonance structures
docs.text:
1. Resonance structures must have the same positions of nuclei.
  2. They must have the same number of unpaired electrons.

A resonance structure is more stable (contributes more) if it has:

  • more number of covalent bonds,
  • all atoms with an octet of electrons (except hydrogen, which has a duplet),
  • less separation of opposite charges,
  • a negative charge, if any, on the more electronegative atom and a positive charge, if any, on the more electropositive atom,
  • more dispersal of charge.

Example: Acrolein (CH2=CH-CHO)

\[\underset{I}{CH_2=CH-CH=O} \longleftrightarrow \underset{II}{\overset{+}{C}H_2-CH=CH-O^-} \longleftrightarrow \underset{III}{\overset{-}{C}H_2-CH=CH-\overset{+}{O}}\] \[Stability:\ I > II > III\]
  • I is most stable: more covalent bonds, every C and O has an octet and there is no charge separation.
  • II has a negative charge on the more electronegative atom (O) and a positive charge on the more electropositive atom (C).
  • III does not contribute, as O carries a positive charge and C a negative charge.

docs.title: 3. Resonance Effect (Mesomeric Effect)
docs.text:
• The resonance effect is defined as the polarity produced in the molecule by the interaction of two π bonds, or between a π bond and a lone pair of electrons present on an adjacent atom.
  • The effect is transmitted through the chain. It is designated as the R or M effect.

docs.title: (i) Positive resonance effect (+R effect)
docs.text:
• Electrons are transferred away from the atom or group attached to the conjugated system. This makes certain positions of the molecule electron rich.
  • In aniline, the lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring. Besides the normal structure (I), three more contributing structures (II, III and IV) can be written. In each of them, N forms a double bond with the ring carbon and carries a positive charge (=N+H2), while a negative charge appears on one of the two ortho carbons (II and IV) or on the para carbon (III).
  • Thus, the ortho and para positions of aniline become electron rich.

docs.title: (ii) Negative resonance effect (-R effect)
docs.text:
• Electrons are transferred towards the atom or group attached to the conjugated system.
  • In nitrobenzene, π electrons of the ring move towards the -NO2 group, In the contributing structures, a ring carbon forms a double bond with N, both oxygens carry a negative charge, and a positive charge develops on an ortho or para carbon of the ring.
  • Thus, the ortho and para positions of nitrobenzene become electron deficient.

Groups showing +R and -R effects:

Effect Groups +R effect -halogen, -OH, -OR, -OCOR, -NH2, -NHR, -NR2, -NHCOR -R effect -COOH, -CHO, >C=O, -CN, -NO2
  • The presence of alternate single and double bonds in an open chain or cyclic system is called a conjugated system, e.g. 1,3-butadiene, aniline and nitrobenzene. In such systems the π electrons are delocalised and the system develops polarity.

docs.title: 4. Electromeric Effect (E effect)
docs.text:
• It is a temporary effect shown by compounds having a multiple bond (double or triple bond), only in the presence of an attacking reagent.
  • It is defined as the complete transfer of a shared pair of π electrons to one of the atoms joined by a multiple bond on the demand of an attacking reagent.
  • The effect disappears as soon as the attacking reagent is removed. It is shown by a curved arrow from the π bond to the atom receiving the electrons.

docs.title: (i) Positive electromeric effect (+E effect)
docs.text:
The π electrons are transferred to the atom to which the reagent gets attached.

\[>C=C< + H^+ → >\overset{+}{C}-C(H)<\]

docs.title: (ii) Negative electromeric effect (-E effect)
docs.text:
The π electrons are transferred to the atom to which the reagent does not get attached.

\[>C=O + CN^- → >C(CN)-O^-\]

Note

When inductive and electromeric effects act in opposite directions, the electromeric effect predominates.

docs.title: 5. Hyperconjugation
docs.text:
• Hyperconjugation is a general stabilising interaction. It involves delocalisation of σ electrons of a C-H bond of an alkyl group directly attached to an atom of an unsaturated system or to an atom with an unshared (empty) p orbital.
  • It is a permanent effect.

docs.title: Hyperconjugation in carbocations
docs.text:
• In the ethyl cation (CH3CH2+), the positively charged carbon has an empty p orbital.
  • One of the C-H bonds of the methyl group can align in the plane of this empty p orbital, and its electrons get delocalised into the empty p orbital.
  • This electron density from the adjacent σ bond helps in dispersing the positive charge, which stabilises the carbocation.
\[H-CH_2-\overset{+}{C}H_2 \longleftrightarrow H^+\ CH_2=CH_2\]
  • Greater the number of alkyl groups attached to the positive carbon, greater is the number of C-H bonds available for hyperconjugation, and greater is the stability:
\[(CH_3)_3\overset{+}{C} > (CH_3)_2\overset{+}{C}H > CH_3\overset{+}{C}H_2 > \overset{+}{C}H_3\]

docs.title: Hyperconjugation in alkenes
docs.text:
• Hyperconjugation is also possible in alkenes and alkylarenes. In propene, the C-H σ electrons of the methyl group are delocalised into the π system:
\[H-CH_2-CH=CH_2 \longleftrightarrow H^+\ CH_2=CH-\overset{-}{C}H_2\]
  • One way of looking at hyperconjugation is to regard the C-H bond as having partial ionic character due to resonance. Since one contributing structure has no bond between C and H, hyperconjugation is also called no bond resonance.

docs.title: Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Fundamentals of Reaction Mechanism
Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Fundamentals of Reaction Mechanism
docs.text: A sequential account of each step of an organic reaction, describing the details of electron movement, energetics during bond cleavage and bond formation, and the rates of transformation of reactants into products (kinetics), is called the reaction mechanism.

docs.title: Substrate and Reagent
docs.text:
• In an organic reaction, the organic molecule (substrate) reacts with an attacking reagent to form one or more intermediates and finally the product(s) and by-products.
\[Substrate \xrightarrow{Attacking\ reagent} [Intermediate] → Product(s) + By\text{-}products\]
  • The substrate is the reactant which supplies carbon to the new bond. The other reactant is the reagent.
  • If both reactants supply carbon to the new bond, the choice is arbitrary, and the molecule on which attention is focused is called the substrate.
  • In a reaction, a covalent bond between two carbons, or between carbon and another atom, is broken and a new bond is formed. Knowing the mechanism helps us understand reactivity and plan syntheses.

docs.title: Fission of a Covalent Bond
docs.text: A covalent bond can be broken in two ways: (i) heterolytic cleavage and (ii) homolytic cleavage.

docs.title: 1. Heterolytic cleavage
docs.text:
• In heterolytic cleavage, the bond breaks in such a way that the shared pair of electrons stays with one of the fragments.
  • After heterolysis, one atom has a sextet of electrons and a positive charge, and the other has an octet with at least one lone pair and a negative charge.
\[H_3C-Br → H_3\overset{+}{C} + Br^-\]
  • Reactions which proceed through heterolytic cleavage are called ionic, heteropolar or simply polar reactions.

docs.title: Carbocations
docs.text:
• A species having a carbon atom with a sextet of electrons and a positive charge is called a carbocation (earlier called carbonium ion). \(CH_3^+\) is the methyl cation.
  • Carbocations are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary depending on whether one, two or three carbons are directly attached to the positively charged carbon.

Examples

  • CH3CH2+ (ethyl cation): primary carbocation
  • (CH3)2CH+ (isopropyl cation): secondary carbocation
  • (CH3)3C+ (tert-butyl cation): tertiary carbocation
  • Carbocations are highly unstable and reactive. Alkyl groups attached to the positive carbon stabilise it by inductive and hyperconjugation effects. The observed order of stability is:
\[\overset{+}{C}H_3 < CH_3\overset{+}{C}H_2 < (CH_3)_2\overset{+}{C}H < (CH_3)_3\overset{+}{C}\]
  • Shape: The positively charged carbon is sp2 hybridised, so carbocations are trigonal planar. In \(CH_3^+\), the three sp2 orbitals of carbon overlap with the 1s orbitals of three hydrogens to form three C(sp2)-H(1s) sigma bonds. The remaining unhybridised p orbital is perpendicular to the molecular plane and is empty.

docs.title: Carbanions
docs.text:
• Heterolytic cleavage can also give a species in which carbon keeps the shared pair of electrons. When a group Z leaves without the electron pair, the methyl anion is formed.
\[CH_3-Z → H_3C:^- + Z^+\]
  • A carbon species carrying a negative charge on the carbon atom is called a carbanion. Carbanions are also unstable and reactive.

docs.title: 2. Homolytic cleavage
docs.text:
• In homolytic cleavage, one electron of the shared pair goes with each of the bonded atoms.
  • The movement of a single electron is shown by a half-headed ('fish hook') curved arrow.
  • Homolysis gives neutral species containing an unpaired electron, called free radicals. Like carbocations and carbanions, free radicals are very reactive.
\[R-X \xrightarrow{Heat\ or\ Light} \underset{Alkyl\ free\ radical}{\dot{R}} + \dot{X}\]
  • Alkyl radicals are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary. Their stability increases from primary to tertiary:
\[\underset{Methyl}{\dot{C}H_3} < \underset{Ethyl}{\dot{C}H_2CH_3} < \underset{Isopropyl}{\dot{C}H(CH_3)_2} < \underset{tert\text{-}Butyl}{\dot{C}(CH_3)_3}\]
  • Reactions which proceed by homolytic fission are called free radical, homopolar or nonpolar reactions.

docs.title: Nucleophile
docs.text:
• A reagent that brings an electron pair is called a nucleophile (Nu:), i.e. nucleus seeking. The reaction is then called nucleophilic.
  • Examples:
    • Negatively charged ions with lone pairs: hydroxide (HO-), cyanide (NC-) and carbanions (R3C:-).
    • Neutral molecules with lone pairs: H2O:, R3N:, R2NH: etc. (lone pairs on O and N).

docs.title: Electrophile
docs.text:
• A reagent that takes away an electron pair is called an electrophile (E+), i.e. electron seeking. The reaction is called electrophilic.

  • Examples:

    • Carbocations (\(CH_3^+\)): the carbon has only a sextet, so it is electron deficient and can accept an electron pair.
    • Neutral molecules having polar functional groups like carbonyl (>C=O) or alkyl halides (R3C-X). Due to the polarity of the C-X bond, the carbon gets a partial positive charge and becomes an electrophilic centre.

  • During a polar reaction, a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic centre (electron deficient site) of the substrate. Similarly, an electrophile attacks the nucleophilic centre (electron rich site) of the substrate.

  • The electrophile receives an electron pair from the nucleophile when the two bond together.

Note

Electrophiles may be neutral, like BF3 and AlCl3, which have an incomplete octet on the central atom. Nucleophiles may also be neutral, like NH3 and H2O, which have lone pairs.

docs.title: Electron Movement in Organic Reactions
docs.text:
• The movement of electrons in a reaction is shown by curved-arrow notation.
  • A curved arrow starts from the point from where an electron pair is shifted and ends at the location to which the pair moves.
  • A full-headed curved arrow shows the movement of an electron pair. A single-barbed 'fish hook' (half-headed) arrow shows the movement of a single electron.
  • An electron pair can shift:
    1. from a π bond to an adjacent bond position,
    2. from a π bond to an adjacent atom,
    3. from an atom (lone pair) to an adjacent bond position.

Example

In the reaction of hydroxide ion with chloromethane to give methanol, one curved arrow is drawn from a lone pair on O of HO- to the carbon, and a second arrow from the C-Cl bond to Cl, showing Cl leaving as Cl-.

\[HO^- + CH_3-Cl → HO-CH_3 + Cl^-\]

docs.title: Types of Organic Reactions
docs.text: Organic reactions can be classified into the following categories:

docs.title: 1. Substitution reactions
docs.text:
An atom or group in the substrate is replaced by another atom or group.

\[CH_3CH_2Br + HS^- → CH_3CH_2SH + Br^-\]

docs.title: 2. Addition reactions
docs.text:
Two molecules combine to give a single product; this usually happens at a multiple bond.

\[(CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + HCl → (CH_3)_2CClCH_3\]

docs.title: 3. Elimination reactions
docs.text:
Atoms or groups are removed from adjacent carbons of the substrate to form a multiple bond.

\[CH_3CH_2Br + HO^- → CH_2=CH_2 + H_2O + Br^-\]

docs.title: 4. Rearrangement reactions
docs.text:
The carbon skeleton or the position of atoms/groups in the molecule changes to give an isomeric structure.

\[(CH_3)_3C-CH_2OH + HBr → (CH_3)_2CBrCH_2CH_3 + H_2O\]

docs.title: Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Introduction and Structural Representation
Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Introduction and Structural Representation
docs.text: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry which deals with the study of compounds of carbon formed by covalent bonding with other carbon atoms and with elements like hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• Carbon has a unique property called catenation, i.e. the ability to form covalent bonds with other carbon atoms to give long chains and rings. This is the reason for the huge number of organic compounds.
  • Organic compounds are essential for life. DNA (which carries genetic information) and proteins (found in blood, muscles and skin) are organic compounds.
  • Clothing, fuels, polymers, dyes and medicines are also made up of organic compounds.

docs.title: Vital force theory and its rejection
docs.text:
• Around 1780, chemists started distinguishing between organic compounds (obtained from plants and animals) and inorganic compounds (obtained from minerals).
  • Berzelius, a Swedish chemist, proposed that a 'vital force' present in living organisms was necessary to make organic compounds.
  • This idea was rejected in 1828 when F. Wohler prepared urea, an organic compound, by heating ammonium cyanate, an inorganic compound.
\[\underset{Ammonium\ cyanate}{NH_4CNO} \xrightarrow{Heat} \underset{Urea}{NH_2CONH_2}\]
  • Later, the synthesis of acetic acid by Kolbe (1845) and of methane by Berthelot (1856) proved that organic compounds can be made in the laboratory from inorganic sources.

docs.title: Tetravalence of Carbon and Shapes of Organic Compounds
docs.text:
• Carbon has the electronic configuration 1s2 2s2 2p2. In its compounds it shows a valency of four (tetravalence), which is explained by hybridisation of its s and p orbitals.
  • The shapes of methane (CH4), ethene (C2H4) and ethyne (C2H2) are explained by sp3, sp2 and sp hybridisation of carbon respectively.
Hybridisation of carbon s character Shape Bond angle Example sp3 25% Tetrahedral 109.5° CH4, C2H6 sp2 33.3% Trigonal planar 120° C2H4, HCHO sp 50% Linear 180° C2H2, HCN

docs.title: Effect of hybridisation on bond length, bond strength and electronegativity
docs.text:
• An sp hybrid orbital has more s character, so it is held closer to the nucleus. Hence, it forms shorter and stronger bonds than an sp3 orbital.
  • An sp2 orbital is intermediate in s character, so the length and strength of its bonds are also intermediate between those of sp and sp3.
  • Greater the s character of a hybrid orbital, greater is the electronegativity of the carbon atom. So, an sp hybridised carbon (50% s character) is more electronegative than an sp2 or sp3 hybridised carbon.
\[Electronegativity\ of\ carbon:\ sp > sp^2 > sp^3\] \[Bond\ length:\ C(sp)-H < C(sp^2)-H < C(sp^3)-H\]

docs.title: Some characteristic features of π bonds
docs.text:
• A π (pi) bond is formed by the sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals on adjacent atoms.
  • For proper sideways overlap, the p orbitals must be parallel. Therefore, in H2C=CH2, all six atoms lie in the same plane and both p orbitals are perpendicular to this plane.
  • Rotation of one CH2 group with respect to the other would destroy the overlap of p orbitals. Hence, rotation about a C=C double bond is restricted.
  • The electron cloud of a π bond lies above and below the plane of the bonded atoms. These electrons are easily available to attacking reagents, so π bonds are the most reactive centres in molecules containing multiple bonds.

docs.title: Structural Representations of Organic Compounds
docs.text: Organic compounds can be represented in several ways: Lewis (dot) structures, dash structures, condensed structures and bond-line structures.

docs.title: 1. Complete structural formula
docs.text:
• In a complete structural formula, every covalent bond is shown by a dash (-). A single dash means a single bond, a double dash (=) a double bond and a triple dash (≡) a triple bond.
  • Lone pairs on heteroatoms (O, N, S, halogens) may or may not be shown.

Examples

  • Ethane: H3C-CH3 written with all six C-H bonds and the C-C bond drawn as dashes.
  • Ethene: H2C=CH2 with each carbon bonded to two H atoms by dashes.
  • Ethyne: H-C≡C-H
  • Methanol: H3C-O-H, with the three C-H bonds and the O-H bond drawn as dashes.

docs.title: 2. Condensed structural formula
docs.text:
• Here, some or all of the dashes are omitted, and the number of identical groups attached to an atom is shown by a subscript.

Examples

  • Ethane: CH3CH3
  • Ethene: H2C=CH2
  • Ethyne: HC≡CH
  • Methanol: CH3OH
  • CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3 can be further condensed to CH3(CH2)6CH3.

docs.title: 3. Bond-line structural formula
docs.text:
• In a bond-line formula, carbon and hydrogen atoms are not written. Carbon-carbon bonds are drawn as lines in a zig-zag fashion.
  • Only heteroatoms like oxygen, chlorine and nitrogen are written specifically.
  • The terminals (line ends) represent methyl (-CH3) groups, unless a functional group is shown there.
  • Every line junction represents a carbon atom carrying enough hydrogens to complete its valency of four.

Example: 3-Methyloctane

  • Condensed formula: CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3
  • Bond-line formula:

Example: 2-Bromobutane

  • Condensed formula: CH3CHBrCH2CH3
  • In the bond-line formula, a four-carbon zig-zag is drawn and Br is written on the line going down from the second carbon.
  • In cyclic compounds, the ring is drawn as a polygon. Each corner is a carbon atom.

Bond-line formulas of cyclic compounds

docs.title: Three-Dimensional Representation of Organic Molecules
docs.text:
• The 3-D structure of a molecule can be shown on paper using the wedge-and-dash formula.
  • A solid wedge shows a bond projecting out of the plane of the paper, towards the observer.
  • A dashed wedge shows a bond projecting behind the plane of the paper, away from the observer.
  • Bonds lying in the plane of the paper are shown by normal lines. The broad end of a wedge is towards the observer.
  • For example, in methane, two C-H bonds are drawn in the plane of the paper, one as a solid wedge and one as a dashed wedge, giving the tetrahedral shape.

docs.title: Molecular models
docs.text:
Molecular models are physical devices made of wood, plastic or metal that help to visualise the 3-D shapes of molecules. Three common types are:

  1. Framework model: Only the bonds are shown, not the atoms. It shows the pattern of bonds and ignores the size of atoms.
  2. Ball-and-stick model: Balls represent atoms and sticks represent bonds. Molecules containing C=C (e.g. ethene) are better shown using springs in place of sticks (ball-and-spring model).
  3. Space-filling model: It shows the relative size of each atom based on its van der Waals radius. Bonds are not shown. It conveys the volume occupied by each atom.

Computer graphics are also used today for molecular modelling.

docs.title: Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | IUPAC Nomenclature
Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | IUPAC Nomenclature
docs.text: The IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) system of nomenclature is a systematic method of naming organic compounds in which the name is correlated with the structure, so that the structure can be deduced from the name.

docs.title: Common or Trivial Names
docs.text:
• Before the IUPAC system, compounds were named after their origin or properties. For example, citric acid is found in citrus fruits and formic acid in red ants (Latin formica = ant).
  • Such names are called trivial or common names. Many are still used, e.g. Buckminsterfullerene for the C60 cluster.
Compound Common name CH4 Methane H3CCH2CH2CH3 n-Butane (H3C)2CHCH3 Isobutane (H3C)4C Neopentane H3CCH2CH2OH n-Propyl alcohol HCHO Formaldehyde (H3C)2CO Acetone CHCl3 Chloroform CH3COOH Acetic acid C6H6 Benzene C6H5OCH3 Anisole C6H5NH2 Aniline C6H5COCH3 Acetophenone CH3OCH2CH3 Ethyl methyl ether

docs.title: The IUPAC System
docs.text:
• An IUPAC name is built by identifying the parent hydrocarbon (parent chain) and the functional group(s) attached to it, and then adding suitable prefixes and suffixes.
  • Compounds of carbon and hydrogen only are called hydrocarbons. A hydrocarbon containing only C-C single bonds is saturated (alkane, earlier called paraffin, Latin: little affinity). One with at least one C=C or C≡C bond is unsaturated.

docs.title: Straight chain alkanes
docs.text:
• The name has a prefix showing the number of carbon atoms and the suffix -ane. (The names from CH4 to C4H10 come from trivial names.)
  • Successive members differ by a -CH2 group; they are homologues.
Name Molecular formula Name Molecular formula Methane CH4 Heptane C7H16 Ethane C2H6 Octane C8H18 Propane C3H8 Nonane C9H20 Butane C4H10 Decane C10H22 Pentane C5H12 Icosane C20H42 Hexane C6H14 Triacontane C30H62

docs.title: Alkyl groups
docs.text:
• An alkyl group is obtained by removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane. It is named by replacing '-ane' with '-yl'. Thus, CH4 becomes -CH3 (methyl).
Alkane Alkyl group Name Abbreviation CH4 (Methane) -CH3 Methyl Me C2H6 (Ethane) -CH2CH3 Ethyl Et C3H8 (Propane) -CH2CH2CH3 Propyl Pr C4H10 (Butane) -CH2CH2CH2CH3 Butyl Bu C10H22 (Decane) -CH2(CH2)8CH3 Decyl -
  • Branched alkyl groups have common names:
Branched alkyl group Structure Isopropyl (CH3)2CH- sec-Butyl CH3CH2CH(CH3)- Isobutyl (CH3)2CHCH2- tert-Butyl (CH3)3C- Neopentyl (CH3)3CCH2-

docs.title: Rules for naming branched chain alkanes
1. Select the longest chain
docs.text:
• The longest carbon chain in the molecule is identified as the parent (root) chain, even if it is not written in a straight line.
  • If two chains of equal length are possible, the chain with more side chains is selected.

docs.title: 2. Number the chain (lowest locant rule)
docs.text:
• The chain is numbered from the end which gives the lowest possible numbers to the branched carbon atoms.
  • For example, branches at carbons 2 and 6 (numbering from left) is preferred over 4 and 8 (numbering from right).

docs.title: 3. Name and position the substituents
docs.text:
• Names of alkyl groups are prefixed to the parent alkane with their position numbers. Different alkyl groups are written in alphabetical order.
  • Numbers are separated from words by hyphens, and there is no gap between the substituent name and the parent name, e.g. 6-ethyl-2-methylnonane.

docs.title: 4. Identical substituents
docs.text:
• If two or more identical groups are present, their positions are separated by commas and the prefixes di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa etc. are used.
  • These multiplying prefixes are not considered in alphabetical order.

Examples

  • (CH3)2CHCH2CH(CH3)2: 2,4-Dimethylpentane
  • (CH3)3CCH2CH(CH3)2: 2,2,4-Trimethylpentane
  • CH3CH2CH(C2H5)C(CH3)2CH2CH2CH3: 3-Ethyl-4,4-dimethylheptane

docs.title: 5. Substituents at equivalent positions
docs.text:
• If two substituents are at equivalent positions, the lower number is given to the one coming first in alphabetical order.
  • Thus, CH3CH2CH(C2H5)CH2CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 3-ethyl-6-methyloctane and not 6-ethyl-3-methyloctane.

docs.title: 6. Branched (complex) substituents
docs.text:
• A branched substituent is numbered starting from the carbon that is attached to the parent chain (this carbon gets number 1). For example, -CH(CH3)CH2CH(CH3)CH3 is 1,3-dimethylbutyl.
  • Its name is written in parentheses.
  • In alphabetical ordering, the prefixes iso- and neo- are part of the alkyl group name, but sec- and tert- are not.

Examples

  • 5-(2-Ethylbutyl)-3,3-dimethyldecane [not 5-(2,2-dimethylbutyl)-3-ethyldecane]
  • 5-sec-Butyl-4-isopropyldecane
  • 5-(2,2-Dimethylpropyl)nonane

docs.title: Cyclic compounds
docs.text:
• A saturated monocyclic compound is named by adding the prefix cyclo to the name of the straight chain alkane with the same number of carbons.
  • Side chains are named using the above rules. When there is a choice, the substituent first in alphabetical order, or the more branched carbon, gets the lower number.

Examples

docs.title: Nomenclature of Compounds Having Functional Groups
docs.text:
• First, the functional group is identified. It decides the suffix of the name.
  • The longest chain containing the functional group is numbered so that the functional group gets the lowest possible number.
Class of compounds Functional group IUPAC prefix IUPAC suffix Example Alkanes - - -ane Butane, CH3(CH2)2CH3 Alkenes >C=C< - -ene But-1-ene, CH2=CHCH2CH3 Alkynes -C≡C- - -yne But-1-yne, CH≡CCH2CH3 Arenes - - - Benzene, C6H6 Halides -X (X = F, Cl, Br, I) halo- - 1-Bromobutane, CH3(CH2)2CH2Br Alcohols -OH hydroxy- -ol Butan-2-ol, CH3CH2CHOHCH3 Aldehydes -CHO formyl or oxo -al Butanal, CH3(CH2)2CHO Ketones >C=O oxo- -one Butan-2-one, CH3CH2COCH3 Nitriles -C≡N cyano nitrile Pentanenitrile, CH3CH2CH2CH2CN Ethers -R-O-R- alkoxy- - Ethoxyethane, CH3CH2OCH2CH3 Carboxylic acids -COOH carboxy -oic acid Butanoic acid, CH3(CH2)2CO2H Carboxylate ions -COO- - -oate Sodium butanoate, CH3(CH2)2CO2-Na+ Esters -COOR alkoxycarbonyl -oate Methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3 Acyl halides -COX (X = F, Cl, Br, I) halocarbonyl -oyl halide Butanoyl chloride, CH3(CH2)2COCl Amines -NH2, >NH, >N- amino- -amine Butan-2-amine, CH3CHNH2CH2CH3 Amides -CONH2, -CONHR, -CONR2 carbamoyl -amide Butanamide, CH3(CH2)2CONH2 Nitro compounds -NO2 nitro - 1-Nitrobutane, CH3(CH2)3NO2

docs.title: Polyfunctional compounds
docs.text:
• When more than one functional group is present, one is chosen as the principal functional group and decides the suffix. The others are named as substituents using prefixes.
  • The principal group is chosen by the following order of decreasing priority:
\[-COOH > -SO_3H > -COOR > -COCl > -CONH_2 > -CN > -CHO > >C=O > -OH > -NH_2 > >C=C< > -C≡C-\]
  • The groups -R, C6H5-, halogens (F, Cl, Br, I), -NO2 and alkoxy (-OR) are always written as prefixes.

Examples

  • HOCH2(CH2)3CH2COCH3 is 7-hydroxyheptan-2-one (not 2-oxoheptan-7-ol), since a keto group has higher priority than -OH.
  • BrCH2CH=CH2 is 3-bromoprop-1-ene (not 1-bromoprop-2-ene).

docs.title: More than one functional group of the same type
docs.text:
• Their number is shown by di, tri etc. before the class suffix. The full name of the parent alkane is kept before the suffix, e.g. CH2(OH)CH2(OH) is ethane-1,2-diol.
  • However, the ending '-ne' of the parent alkane is dropped for compounds having more than one double or triple bond, e.g. CH2=CH-CH=CH2 is buta-1,3-diene.

docs.title: Nomenclature of Substituted Benzene Compounds
docs.text:
• For monosubstituted benzene, the substituent is written as a prefix to the word benzene. Common names (in brackets) are also widely used.

Examples

docs.title: Disubstituted benzene
docs.text:
• The ring carbons are numbered so that the substituents get the lowest possible numbers. So, compound (b) below is 1,3-dibromobenzene and not 1,5-dibromobenzene.
  • In the trivial system, ortho (o-), meta (m-) and para (p-) are used for the 1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4- positions respectively.

Examples

  • 1,2-Dibromobenzene = o-dibromobenzene
  • 1,3-Dibromobenzene = m-dibromobenzene
  • 1,4-Dibromobenzene = p-dibromobenzene

docs.title: Tri- or higher substituted benzene
docs.text:
• The o-, m-, p- prefixes cannot be used. The compound is named by the lowest locant rule.
  • Sometimes the common name of a benzene derivative (anisole, aniline, phenol, toluene) is used as the base compound. Its substituent gets number 1, and numbering is done in the direction which gives the next substituent the lowest number.
  • Substituents appear in alphabetical order.

Examples

docs.title: Phenyl group
docs.text: • When a benzene ring is attached to an alkane chain carrying a functional group, the benzene ring is treated as a substituent. Benzene as a substituent is called phenyl (C6H5-, abbreviated as Ph). For example, C6H5CH2CHBrCHBrCH2CH3 is 2,3-dibromo-1-phenylpentane.

docs.title: Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Methods of Purification
Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Methods of Purification
docs.text:
Once an organic compound is extracted from a natural source or synthesised in the laboratory, it must be purified. The method chosen depends on the nature of the compound and the impurity present in it.

The common techniques used for purification are:

  1. Sublimation
  2. Crystallisation
  3. Distillation
  4. Differential extraction
  5. Chromatography
  • The purity of a compound is checked by finding its melting point or boiling point. Most pure compounds have sharp melting and boiling points.
  • Modern methods of checking purity are based on different chromatographic and spectroscopic techniques.

docs.title: 1. Sublimation
docs.text:
• Some solids change directly into vapour on heating, without passing through the liquid state. This is called sublimation.
  • This principle is used to separate sublimable compounds from non-sublimable impurities. For example, camphor can be separated from calcium sulphate by sublimation.

docs.title: 2. Crystallisation
docs.text:
• This is one of the most commonly used techniques for purifying solid organic compounds.
  • It is based on the difference in solubilities of the compound and the impurities in a suitable solvent.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
• The impure compound is dissolved in a solvent in which it is sparingly soluble at room temperature but appreciably soluble at higher temperature.
  • The solution is concentrated to get a nearly saturated solution.
  • On cooling, the pure compound crystallises out and is removed by filtration.
  • The filtrate (mother liquor) contains the impurities and a small quantity of the compound.

docs.title: Points to remember
docs.text:
• If the compound is highly soluble in one solvent and very little soluble in another, crystallisation can be done in a mixture of these solvents.
  • Impurities which impart colour to the solution are removed by adsorbing them over activated charcoal.
  • Repeated crystallisation is needed when the impurities have solubilities comparable to the compound.

docs.title: 3. Distillation
docs.text: Distillation is used to separate (i) volatile liquids from non-volatile impurities and (ii) liquids having a sufficient difference in their boiling points.

docs.title: (a) Simple distillation
docs.text:
• Liquids having different boiling points vaporise at different temperatures. The vapours are cooled and the liquids so formed are collected separately.
  • The mixture is taken in a round bottom flask and heated carefully. Vapours of the lower boiling component form first; they are condensed in a condenser and collected in a receiver. The higher boiling component vaporises later and is collected separately.
  • Example: Chloroform (b.p. 334 K) and aniline (b.p. 457 K) are easily separated by simple distillation.

docs.title: (b) Fractional distillation
docs.text:
• If the difference in boiling points of two liquids is small, simple distillation cannot separate them, as both vaporise in the same temperature range.
  • In fractional distillation, the vapours are passed through a fractionating column fitted over the mouth of the round bottom flask, before condensation.
  • Vapours of the higher boiling liquid condense before those of the lower boiling liquid. So, the vapours rising up the column become richer in the more volatile component.
  • The column provides many surfaces for heat exchange between the rising vapours and the descending condensed liquid. Some of the condensing liquid takes heat from the rising vapours and revaporises.
  • At the top, the vapours are pure in the low boiling component; they pass into the condenser and are collected. After successive distillations, the liquid left in the flask is enriched in the high boiling component.
  • Each successive condensation and vaporisation unit in the column is called a theoretical plate. Commercial columns have hundreds of plates.
  • Application: separating different fractions of crude oil in the petroleum industry.

docs.title: (c) Distillation under reduced pressure (vacuum distillation)
docs.text:
• Used to purify liquids having very high boiling points and those which decompose at or below their boiling points.
  • A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. By reducing the pressure on its surface with a water pump or vacuum pump, the liquid boils at a temperature lower than its normal boiling point.
  • Application: glycerol is separated from spent-lye in the soap industry.

docs.title: (d) Steam distillation
docs.text:
• Used to separate substances which are steam volatile and immiscible with water.
  • Steam from a steam generator is passed through a heated flask containing the liquid. The mixture of steam and the volatile organic compound is condensed and collected. The compound is then separated from water using a separating funnel.
  • The liquid boils when the sum of the vapour pressures of the organic liquid (p1) and of water (p2) becomes equal to the atmospheric pressure (p):
\[p = p_1 + p_2\]
  • Since p1 is lower than p, the organic liquid vaporises at a temperature lower than its boiling point. A mixture of water and a water-insoluble substance boils close to, but below, 373 K.
  • Example: aniline is separated from an aniline-water mixture by steam distillation.

docs.title: 4. Differential Extraction
docs.text:
• When an organic compound is present in an aqueous medium, it is separated by shaking it with an organic solvent in which it is more soluble than in water.
  • The organic solvent and water must be immiscible, so that they form two distinct layers which can be separated using a separatory funnel.
  • The organic solvent is then removed by distillation or evaporation to get back the compound.
  • If the compound is only slightly soluble in the organic solvent, a very large quantity of solvent would be needed. In such cases, continuous extraction is used, in which the same solvent is used repeatedly.

docs.title: 5. Chromatography
docs.text:
• Chromatography (Greek chroma = colour, as it was first used for separating coloured plant substances) is used to separate mixtures into their components, purify compounds and test their purity.
  • The mixture is applied onto a stationary phase (a solid or a liquid). A pure solvent, a mixture of solvents, or a gas (the mobile phase) is allowed to move slowly over it. The components get gradually separated from one another.
  • Based on the principle involved, chromatography is classified as:
    • Adsorption chromatography
    • Partition chromatography

docs.title: (a) Adsorption chromatography
docs.text:
• It is based on the fact that different compounds are adsorbed on an adsorbent to different degrees. Commonly used adsorbents are silica gel and alumina.
  • As the mobile phase moves over the stationary phase (adsorbent), the components of the mixture move by different distances.
  • Two main types are column chromatography and thin layer chromatography.

docs.title: Column chromatography
docs.text:
• The mixture is separated over a column of adsorbent (stationary phase) packed in a glass tube fitted with a stopcock at its lower end.
  • The mixture adsorbed on the adsorbent is placed on top of the column, and a suitable eluant (a liquid or a mixture of liquids) is allowed to flow down slowly.
  • The most readily adsorbed substances are retained near the top, and the others come down to various distances in the column, giving complete separation.

docs.title: Thin layer chromatography (TLC)
docs.text:
• A thin layer (about 0.2 mm thick) of adsorbent (silica gel or alumina) is spread over a glass plate. This is called a TLC plate or chromaplate.
  • The mixture is applied as a small spot about 2 cm above one end of the plate. The plate is placed in a closed jar containing the eluant.
  • As the eluant rises up the plate, the components move up to different distances depending on their degree of adsorption.
  • The relative adsorption of each component is expressed by its retardation factor (Rf value):
\[R_f = {Distance\ moved\ by\ the\ substance\ from\ base\ line\ (x) \over Distance\ moved\ by\ the\ solvent\ from\ base\ line\ (y)}\]
  • Detecting spots:
    • Coloured compounds are visible due to their own colour.
    • Colourless compounds which fluoresce are seen under ultraviolet light.
    • The plate may be placed in a covered jar containing a few crystals of iodine; compounds which adsorb iodine show up as brown spots.
    • A suitable reagent may be sprayed on the plate. For example, amino acids are detected by spraying ninhydrin solution.

docs.title: (b) Partition chromatography
docs.text:
• It is based on continuous differential partitioning of the components of a mixture between the stationary and mobile phases.
  • Paper chromatography is a type of partition chromatography. A special chromatography paper is used, which contains water trapped in it; this water acts as the stationary phase.
  • A strip of the paper, spotted at the base with the mixture, is suspended in a suitable solvent or mixture of solvents (the mobile phase).
  • The solvent rises up the paper by capillary action and flows over the spot. The paper selectively retains different components according to their differing partition between the two phases.
  • The developed paper strip is called a chromatogram. Coloured components are seen as spots at different heights; colourless ones are detected under UV light or with a spray reagent, as in TLC.

Conclusion

  • Sublimation: sublimable solid + non-sublimable impurity.
  • Crystallisation: solids, based on difference in solubility.
  • Simple distillation: liquids with large difference in boiling points.
  • Fractional distillation: liquids with small difference in boiling points.
  • Vacuum distillation: high boiling liquids or liquids that decompose at their boiling point.
  • Steam distillation: steam volatile liquids immiscible with water.
  • Chromatography: the best and latest technique for isolation, purification and separation of organic compounds.

docs.title: Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Qualitative and Quantitative Analysis
Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Qualitative and Quantitative Analysis
docs.text: The elements present in organic compounds are carbon and hydrogen, and they may also contain oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, halogens and phosphorus. Qualitative analysis detects these elements, while quantitative analysis finds their percentage composition.

docs.title: Detection of Carbon and Hydrogen
docs.text:
• The compound is heated with copper(II) oxide. Carbon is oxidised to CO2 and hydrogen to H2O.
  • CO2 turns lime water milky (turbid), and H2O turns white anhydrous copper sulphate blue.
\[C + 2CuO \xrightarrow{Δ} 2Cu + CO_2\] \[2H + CuO \xrightarrow{Δ} Cu + H_2O\] \[CO_2 + Ca(OH)_2 → CaCO_3 ↓ + H_2O\] \[\underset{White}{CuSO_4} + 5H_2O → \underset{Blue}{CuSO_4.5H_2O}\]

docs.title: Lassaigne's Test (Detection of N, S and Halogens)
docs.text:
• Nitrogen, sulphur and halogens are detected by Lassaigne's test. The organic compound is fused with sodium metal, which converts these elements from covalent form into ionic form (NaCN, Na2S, NaX).
\[Na + C + N \xrightarrow{Δ} NaCN\] \[2Na + S \xrightarrow{Δ} Na_2S\] \[Na + X \xrightarrow{Δ} NaX\ \ (X = Cl,\ Br\ or\ I)\]
  • C, N, S and X come from the organic compound.
  • The fused mass is boiled with distilled water to extract the sodium cyanide, sulphide and halide. This is called the sodium fusion extract.

docs.title: (A) Test for nitrogen
docs.text:
• The sodium fusion extract is boiled with iron(II) sulphate and then acidified with concentrated sulphuric acid. A Prussian blue colour confirms nitrogen.
  • Sodium cyanide first reacts with iron(II) sulphate to form sodium hexacyanoferrate(II). On heating with conc. H2SO4, some Fe2+ ions are oxidised to Fe3+, which react with hexacyanoferrate(II) to give iron(III) hexacyanoferrate(II) (ferriferrocyanide), which is Prussian blue.
\[6CN^- + Fe^{2+} → [Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}\] \[3[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} + 4Fe^{3+} \xrightarrow{xH_2O} \underset{Prussian\ blue}{Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3.xH_2O}\]

docs.title: (B) Test for sulphur
docs.text:
• (a) The extract is acidified with acetic acid and lead acetate is added. A black precipitate of lead sulphide shows sulphur.
\[S^{2-} + Pb^{2+} → \underset{Black}{PbS}\]
  • (b) On treating the extract with sodium nitroprusside, a violet colour shows sulphur.
\[S^{2-} + [Fe(CN)_5NO]^{2-} → \underset{Violet}{[Fe(CN)_5NOS]^{4-}}\]

docs.title: When both N and S are present
docs.text:
• Sodium thiocyanate is formed. It gives a blood red colour with Fe3+ and no Prussian blue, since there are no free cyanide ions.
\[Na + C + N + S → NaSCN\] \[Fe^{3+} + SCN^- → \underset{Blood\ red}{[Fe(SCN)]^{2+}}\]
  • If fusion is done with excess sodium, the thiocyanate decomposes into cyanide and sulphide, which then give their usual tests.
\[NaSCN + 2Na → NaCN + Na_2S\]

docs.title: (C) Test for halogens
docs.text:
• The extract is acidified with nitric acid and then treated with silver nitrate.
\[X^- + Ag^+ → AgX\] Precipitate Solubility in ammonium hydroxide Halogen White Soluble Chlorine Yellowish Sparingly soluble Bromine Yellow Insoluble Iodine

Note

If nitrogen or sulphur is also present, the extract is first boiled with concentrated nitric acid to decompose the NaCN or Na2S. Otherwise, CN- and S2- ions would react with silver nitrate and interfere with the test for halogens.

docs.title: (D) Test for phosphorus
docs.text:
• The compound is heated with an oxidising agent (sodium peroxide), which oxidises phosphorus to phosphate.
  • The solution is boiled with nitric acid and treated with ammonium molybdate. A yellow colour or precipitate shows phosphorus.
\[Na_3PO_4 + 3HNO_3 → H_3PO_4 + 3NaNO_3\] \[H_3PO_4 + 12(NH_4)_2MoO_4 + 21HNO_3 → \underset{Ammonium\ phosphomolybdate}{(NH_4)_3PO_4.12MoO_3} + 21NH_4NO_3 + 12H_2O\]

docs.title: Quantitative Analysis
docs.text: In all the formulas below, m is the mass (in g) of the organic compound taken.

docs.title: 1. Carbon and hydrogen (Liebig's method)
docs.text:
• A known mass of the compound is burnt in excess oxygen and copper(II) oxide. Carbon and hydrogen are oxidised to CO2 and H2O.
\[C_xH_y + (x + {y \over 4})O_2 → xCO_2 + {y \over 2}H_2O\]
  • The gases are passed through two weighed U-tubes connected in series: the first contains anhydrous calcium chloride (absorbs water) and the second contains concentrated KOH solution (absorbs CO2).
  • The increase in mass of the U-tubes gives the mass of water (m1) and carbon dioxide (m2).
\[Percentage\ of\ carbon = {12 \times m_2 \times 100 \over 44 \times m}\] \[Percentage\ of\ hydrogen = {2 \times m_1 \times 100 \over 18 \times m}\]

docs.title: (i) Dumas method
docs.text:
• The compound is heated with copper oxide in an atmosphere of CO2. It gives free nitrogen along with CO2 and water.
\[C_xH_yN_z + (2x + {y \over 2})CuO → xCO_2 + {y \over 2}H_2O + {z \over 2}N_2 + (2x + {y \over 2})Cu\]
  • Traces of nitrogen oxides formed are reduced to N2 by passing the gases over a heated copper gauze.
  • The gases are collected over aqueous KOH, which absorbs CO2. Nitrogen collects in the upper part of a graduated tube (nitrometer).
  • Let the volume of N2 collected be V1 mL at room temperature T1 K and pressure p1 mm. Here, p1 is obtained by subtracting the aqueous tension from the atmospheric pressure, since nitrogen is collected over water.
\[p_1 = Atmospheric\ pressure - Aqueous\ tension\] \[Volume\ of\ N_2\ at\ STP,\ V = {p_1V_1 \times 273 \over 760 \times T_1}\ mL\] \[22400\ mL\ of\ N_2\ at\ STP\ weighs\ 28\ g\] \[Percentage\ of\ nitrogen = {28 \times V \times 100 \over 22400 \times m}\]

docs.title: (ii) Kjeldahl's method
docs.text:
• The compound is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid, which converts its nitrogen into ammonium sulphate.
  • The mixture is then heated with excess NaOH. The liberated ammonia is absorbed in an excess of standard H2SO4.
  • The unreacted acid is estimated by titrating with standard alkali. The difference between the acid taken and the acid left gives the acid that reacted with ammonia.
\[Organic\ compound + H_2SO_4 → (NH_4)_2SO_4 \xrightarrow{2NaOH} Na_2SO_4 + 2NH_3 + 2H_2O\] \[2NH_3 + H_2SO_4 → (NH_4)_2SO_4\]
  • Let V mL of H2SO4 of molarity M be taken, and let the excess acid need V1 mL of NaOH of molarity M.
\[V_1\ mL\ of\ NaOH\ (M) = {V_1 \over 2}\ mL\ of\ H_2SO_4\ (M)\] \[H_2SO_4\ used\ by\ NH_3 = (V - {V_1 \over 2})\ mL\] \[(V - {V_1 \over 2})\ mL\ of\ H_2SO_4\ (M) = 2(V - {V_1 \over 2})\ mL\ of\ NH_3\ (M)\] \[1000\ mL\ of\ 1\ M\ NH_3\ contains\ 14\ g\ N\] \[Percentage\ of\ N = {14 \times M \times 2(V - V_1/2) \over 1000} \times {100 \over m} = {1.4 \times M \times 2(V - V_1/2) \over m}\]

Note

Kjeldahl's method is not applicable to compounds containing nitrogen in nitro and azo groups and nitrogen present in a ring (e.g. pyridine), because their nitrogen does not change into ammonium sulphate under these conditions.

docs.title: 3. Halogens (Carius method)
docs.text:
• A known mass of the compound is heated with fuming nitric acid in the presence of silver nitrate in a hard glass tube called a Carius tube, in a furnace.
  • C and H are oxidised to CO2 and H2O. The halogen forms silver halide (AgX), which is filtered, washed, dried and weighed. Let its mass be m1 g.
\[Percentage\ of\ halogen = {Atomic\ mass\ of\ X \times m_1 \times 100 \over Molecular\ mass\ of\ AgX \times m}\]

docs.title: 4. Sulphur
docs.text:
• A known mass of the compound is heated in a Carius tube with sodium peroxide or fuming nitric acid. Sulphur is oxidised to sulphuric acid.
  • It is precipitated as barium sulphate by adding excess BaCl2 solution. The precipitate (m1 g) is filtered, washed, dried and weighed.
\[1\ mol\ BaSO_4 = 233\ g\ BaSO_4 \equiv 32\ g\ S\] \[Percentage\ of\ sulphur = {32 \times m_1 \times 100 \over 233 \times m}\]

docs.title: 5. Phosphorus
docs.text:
• The compound is heated with fuming nitric acid, which oxidises phosphorus to phosphoric acid.
  • It is precipitated as ammonium phosphomolybdate, (NH4)3PO4.12MoO3, by adding ammonia and ammonium molybdate. Alternatively, it is precipitated as MgNH4PO4 using magnesia mixture, which on ignition gives Mg2P2O7.
\[Percentage\ of\ P\ (as\ ammonium\ phosphomolybdate,\ M = 1877\ g) = {31 \times m_1 \times 100 \over 1877 \times m}\] \[Percentage\ of\ P\ (as\ Mg_2P_2O_7,\ M = 222\ u) = {62 \times m_1 \times 100 \over 222 \times m}\]

Where m1 is the mass of the precipitate, and 62 is the mass of two P atoms in Mg2P2O7.

docs.title: 6. Oxygen
docs.text:
• Usually, the percentage of oxygen is found by difference: 100 minus the sum of the percentages of all other elements.
  • It can also be estimated directly. The compound is heated in a stream of nitrogen. The gaseous products containing oxygen are passed over red-hot coke, converting all oxygen into CO. The mixture is then passed through warm iodine pentoxide (I2O5), which oxidises CO to CO2, liberating iodine.
\[Compound \xrightarrow{heat} O_2 + other\ gaseous\ products\] \[2C + O_2 \xrightarrow{1373\ K} 2CO\] \[I_2O_5 + 5CO → I_2 + 5CO_2\] \[Percentage\ of\ oxygen = {32 \times m_1 \times 100 \over 44 \times m}\]

Where m1 is the mass of CO2 produced.

  • Today, C, H and N are estimated using an automatic CHN elemental analyser, which needs only 1-3 mg of the substance and displays the result quickly.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
On complete combustion, 0.246 g of an organic compound gave 0.198 g of carbon dioxide and 0.1014 g of water. Determine the percentage composition of carbon and hydrogen in the compound.

\[Percentage\ of\ carbon = {12 \times 0.198 \times 100 \over 44 \times 0.246} = 21.95\ \%\] \[Percentage\ of\ hydrogen = {2 \times 0.1014 \times 100 \over 18 \times 0.246} = 4.58\ \%\]

In Dumas' method for estimation of nitrogen, 0.3 g of an organic compound gave 50 mL of nitrogen collected at 300 K temperature and 715 mm pressure. Calculate the percentage composition of nitrogen in the compound. (Aqueous tension at 300 K = 15 mm)

\[Actual\ pressure = 715 - 15 = 700\ mm\] \[Volume\ of\ N_2\ at\ STP = {273 \times 700 \times 50 \over 300 \times 760} = 41.9\ mL\] \[41.9\ mL\ of\ N_2\ weighs = {28 \times 41.9 \over 22400}\ g\] \[Percentage\ of\ nitrogen = {28 \times 41.9 \times 100 \over 22400 \times 0.3} = 17.46\ \%\]

During estimation of nitrogen present in an organic compound by Kjeldahl's method, the ammonia evolved from 0.5 g of the compound neutralized 10 mL of 1 M H2SO4. Find out the percentage of nitrogen in the compound.

\[10\ mL\ of\ 1\ M\ H_2SO_4 \equiv 20\ mL\ of\ 1\ M\ NH_3\] \[1000\ mL\ of\ 1\ M\ NH_3\ contains\ 14\ g\ N\] \[20\ mL\ of\ 1\ M\ NH_3\ contains\ {14 \times 20 \over 1000}\ g\ N\] \[Percentage\ of\ nitrogen = {14 \times 20 \times 100 \over 1000 \times 0.5} = 56.0\ \%\]

A sample of 0.50 g of an organic compound was treated according to Kjeldahl's method. The ammonia evolved was absorbed in 50 mL of 0.5 M H2SO4. The residual acid required 60 mL of 0.5 M solution of NaOH for neutralisation. Find the percentage composition of nitrogen in the compound.

\[Here,\ M = 0.5,\ V = 50\ mL,\ V_1 = 60\ mL,\ m = 0.50\ g\] \[H_2SO_4\ used\ by\ NH_3 = V - {V_1 \over 2} = 50 - 30 = 20\ mL\] \[Percentage\ of\ N = {1.4 \times M \times 2(V - V_1/2) \over m} = {1.4 \times 0.5 \times 2 \times 20 \over 0.50} = 56\ \%\]

In Carius method of estimation of halogen, 0.15 g of an organic compound gave 0.12 g of AgBr. Find out the percentage of bromine in the compound.

\[Molar\ mass\ of\ AgBr = 108 + 80 = 188\ g\ mol^{-1}\] \[188\ g\ AgBr\ contains\ 80\ g\ Br\] \[Percentage\ of\ bromine = {80 \times 0.12 \times 100 \over 188 \times 0.15} = 34.04\ \%\]

0.3780 g of an organic chloro compound gave 0.5740 g of silver chloride in Carius estimation. Calculate the percentage of chlorine present in the compound.

\[Molar\ mass\ of\ AgCl = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5\ g\ mol^{-1}\] \[Percentage\ of\ chlorine = {35.5 \times 0.5740 \times 100 \over 143.5 \times 0.3780} = 37.57\ \%\]

In sulphur estimation, 0.157 g of an organic compound gave 0.4813 g of barium sulphate. What is the percentage of sulphur in the compound?

\[Molar\ mass\ of\ BaSO_4 = 137 + 32 + 64 = 233\ g\] \[Percentage\ of\ sulphur = {32 \times 0.4813 \times 100 \over 233 \times 0.157} = 42.10\ \%\]

In the estimation of sulphur by Carius method, 0.468 g of an organic sulphur compound afforded 0.668 g of barium sulphate. Find out the percentage of sulphur in the given compound.

\[Percentage\ of\ sulphur = {32 \times 0.668 \times 100 \over 233 \times 0.468} = 19.60\ \%\]

An organic compound contains 69% carbon and 4.8% hydrogen, the remainder being oxygen. Calculate the masses of carbon dioxide and water produced when 0.20 g of this substance is subjected to complete combustion.

\[Mass\ of\ C = {69 \times 0.20 \over 100} = 0.138\ g\] \[12\ g\ C\ gives\ 44\ g\ CO_2:\ Mass\ of\ CO_2 = {44 \times 0.138 \over 12} = 0.506\ g\] \[Mass\ of\ H = {4.8 \times 0.20 \over 100} = 0.0096\ g\] \[2\ g\ H\ gives\ 18\ g\ H_2O:\ Mass\ of\ H_2O = {18 \times 0.0096 \over 2} = 0.0864\ g\]

docs.title: Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Questions
Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry | Questions
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some questions related to hybridisation, structural formulas, IUPAC nomenclature, reaction intermediates, electronic effects and purification of organic compounds.

docs.title: Hybridisation and Bonding
docs.text:
How many σ and π bonds are present in each of the following molecules? (a) HC≡CCH=CHCH3 (b) CH2=C=CHCH3

  • (a) σC-C: 4; σC-H: 6; πC=C: 1; πC≡C: 2
  • (b) σC-C: 3; σC-H: 6; πC=C: 2

What is the type of hybridisation of each carbon in the following compounds? (a) CH3Cl (b) (CH3)2CO (c) CH3CN (d) HCONH2 (e) CH3CH=CHCN

  • (a) sp3
  • (b) sp3 (CH3), sp2 (C=O)
  • (c) sp3 (CH3), sp (C≡N)
  • (d) sp2
  • (e) sp3, sp2, sp2, sp

Write the state of hybridisation of carbon in the following compounds and shapes of each of the molecules. (a) H2C=O (b) CH3F (c) HC≡N

  • (a) sp2 hybridised carbon, trigonal planar
  • (b) sp3 hybridised carbon, tetrahedral
  • (c) sp hybridised carbon, linear

What are the hybridisation states of each carbon atom in the following compounds? CH2=C=O, CH3CH=CH2, (CH3)2CO, CH2=CHCN, C6H6

  • CH2=C=O: sp2, sp
  • CH3CH=CH2: sp3, sp2, sp2
  • (CH3)2CO: sp3 (both CH3), sp2 (C=O)
  • CH2=CHCN: sp2, sp2, sp
  • C6H6: all six carbons are sp2

Indicate the σ and π bonds in the following molecules: C6H6, C6H12, CH2Cl2, CH2=C=CH2, CH3NO2, HCONHCH3

Molecule σ bonds π bonds C6H6 12 3 C6H12 (cyclohexane) 18 0 CH2Cl2 4 0 CH2=C=CH2 6 2 CH3NO2 6 1 HCONHCH3 8 1

In the organic compound CH2=CH-CH2-CH2-C≡CH, the pair of hybridised orbitals involved in the formation of the C2-C3 bond is: (a) sp-sp2 (b) sp-sp3 (c) sp2-sp3 (d) sp3-sp3

  • C2 is a doubly bonded carbon (sp2) and C3 is a CH2 carbon (sp3).
  • Answer: (c) sp2-sp3

docs.title: Structural Formulas and Nomenclature
docs.text:
Write a condensed formula for: (a) HOCH2CH2CH2CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH3 (b) N≡C-CH(OH)-C≡N

  • (a) HO(CH2)3CH(CH3)CH(CH3)2
  • (b) HOCH(CN)2

Explain why the following names are incorrect: (a) CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH2CH3: 2,5,6-Trimethyloctane [and not 3,4,7-Trimethyloctane] (b) CH3CH2CH(C2H5)CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3: 3-Ethyl-5-methylheptane [and not 5-Ethyl-3-methylheptane]

  • (a) Lowest locant rule: the set 2,5,6 is lower than 3,4,7.
  • (b) The substituents are in equivalent positions, so the lower number is given to the one that comes first in alphabetical order (ethyl).

Write the IUPAC names of the following compounds: (i) CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3 (ii) CH3CH2COCH2COCH3 (iii) CH3COCH2CH2CH2COOH (iv) CH≡C-CH=CH-CH=CH2

  • (i) The functional group is -OH (suffix '-ol'). The longest chain containing it has 8 carbons (octane). -OH is on C-3 and a methyl group on C-6. Name: 6-Methyloctan-3-ol.
  • (ii) Two keto groups (suffix '-dione') on C-2 and C-4 of a six-carbon chain. Name: Hexane-2,4-dione.
  • (iii) Carboxylic acid is the principal group (suffix '-oic acid'); numbering starts from -COOH. The keto group at C-5 is shown as 'oxo'. Name: 5-Oxohexanoic acid.
  • (iv) Two C=C at carbons 1 and 3 and one C≡C at carbon 5 of a six-carbon chain. Name: Hexa-1,3-dien-5-yne.

Derive the structures of: (i) 2-Chlorohexane (ii) Pent-4-en-2-ol (iii) 3-Nitrocyclohexene (iv) Cyclohex-2-en-1-ol (v) 6-Hydroxyheptanal

  • (i) CH3CH2CH2CH2CH(Cl)CH3
  • (ii) CH2=CHCH2CH(OH)CH3
  • (iii) A cyclohexene ring numbered so that the double bond is between C-1 and C-2; -NO2 is on C-3. The double bond is a suffixed group, so it gets preference over the prefixed -NO2.
  • (iv) -OH on C-1 of the ring and the double bond between C-2 and C-3. -OH (suffix) gets preference over C=C.
  • (v) CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2CH2CH2CHO (the -CHO carbon is C-1).

Give the IUPAC names of: (a) C6H5CH2CH2CH3 (b) CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CN (c) CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3 (d) CH3CH2C(Cl)(Br)CH2CH2CH2CH3 (e) ClCH2CH2CHO (f) Cl2CHCH2OH

  • (a) Propylbenzene
  • (b) 3-Methylpentanenitrile
  • (c) 2,5-Dimethylheptane
  • (d) 3-Bromo-3-chloroheptane
  • (e) 3-Chloropropanal
  • (f) 2,2-Dichloroethanol

Which of the following represents the correct IUPAC name? (a) 2,2-Dimethylpentane or 2-Dimethylpentane (b) 2,4,7-Trimethyloctane or 2,5,7-Trimethyloctane (c) 2-Chloro-4-methylpentane or 4-Chloro-2-methylpentane (d) But-3-yn-1-ol or But-4-ol-1-yne

  • (a) 2,2-Dimethylpentane: each methyl group needs its own locant.
  • (b) 2,4,7-Trimethyloctane: the locant set 2,4,7 is lower than 2,5,7.
  • (c) 2-Chloro-4-methylpentane: both sets are 2,4; the lower number goes to chloro, which comes first alphabetically.
  • (d) But-3-yn-1-ol: -OH is the principal group and gets the lowest number.

Give condensed formulas and identify the functional groups present in: (a) 2,2,4-Trimethylpentane (b) 2-Hydroxy-1,2,3-propanetricarboxylic acid (c) Hexanedial

  • (a) (CH3)3CCH2CH(CH3)2: no functional group (alkane).
  • (b) HOOCCH2C(OH)(COOH)CH2COOH: hydroxyl (-OH) and carboxylic acid (-COOH) groups.
  • (c) OHC(CH2)4CHO: two aldehyde (-CHO) groups.

docs.title: Reaction Intermediates and Reagents
docs.text:
Show the formation of reactive intermediates when the following covalent bonds undergo heterolytic cleavage: (a) CH3-SCH3 (b) CH3-CN (c) CH3-Cu

\[(a)\ CH_3-SCH_3 → \overset{+}{C}H_3 + \overset{-}{S}CH_3\] \[(b)\ CH_3-CN → \overset{+}{C}H_3 + \overset{-}{C}N\] \[(c)\ CH_3-Cu → \overset{-}{C}H_3 + \overset{+}{C}u\]

In (a) and (b) the more electronegative group takes the electron pair, giving a carbocation. In (c), carbon is more electronegative than Cu, so it keeps the pair and a carbanion forms.

Categorise the following as nucleophile or electrophile: HS-, BF3, C2H5O-, (CH3)3N:, Cl+, CH3-C+=O, H2N:-, NO2+

  • Nucleophiles: HS-, C2H5O-, (CH3)3N:, H2N:-. They have unshared pairs of electrons which can be donated to an electrophile.
  • Electrophiles: BF3, Cl+, CH3-C+=O, NO2+. Their reactive sites have only six valence electrons and can accept an electron pair.

Identify the electrophilic centre in: CH3CH=O, CH3CN, CH3I.

  • The carbonyl carbon in CH3HC=O, the cyano carbon in H3C-C≡N and the CH3 carbon in H3C-I are electrophilic centres, as they carry a partial positive charge due to bond polarity.

Identify the reagents in bold as nucleophiles or electrophiles: (a) CH3COOH + HO- → CH3COO- + H2O (b) CH3COCH3 + -CN → (CH3)2C(CN)(OH) (c) C6H6 + CH3C+O → C6H5COCH3

  • (a) HO-: nucleophile (b) -CN: nucleophile (c) CH3C+O: electrophile

Classify the following reactions: (a) CH3CH2Br + HS- → CH3CH2SH (b) (CH3)2C=CH2 + HCl → (CH3)2ClC-CH3 (c) CH3CH2Br + HO- → CH2=CH2 + H2O (d) (CH3)3C-CH2OH + HBr → (CH3)2CBrCH2CH3

  • (a) Substitution (nucleophilic) (b) Addition (electrophilic) (c) Elimination (d) Rearrangement (along with substitution)

Classify each bond cleavage as homolysis or heterolysis and identify the intermediate: (a) CH3O-OCH3 → 2CH3O· (b) Removal of an α-H+ from a ketone by -OH (c) (CH3)3C-Br → (CH3)3C+ + Br- (d) Benzene + E+ → arenium ion

  • (a) Homolysis; free radicals (CH3O·).
  • (b) Heterolysis; carbanion.
  • (c) Heterolysis; carbocation.
  • (d) Heterolysis; carbocation (the positive charge is on the ring).

Which of the following carbocations is most stable? (a) (CH3)3C-C+H2 (b) (CH3)3C+ (c) CH3CH2C+H2 (d) CH3C+HCH2CH3

  • Answer: (b) (CH3)3C+. It is tertiary and is stabilised by hyperconjugation with nine C-H bonds and by the +I effect of three methyl groups.

docs.title: Electronic Effects
docs.text:
Which bond is more polar in the following pairs? (a) H3C-H, H3C-Br (b) H3C-NH2, H3C-OH (c) H3C-OH, H3C-SH

  • (a) C-Br, since Br is more electronegative than H.
  • (b) C-O (c) C-O

In which C-C bond of CH3CH2CH2Br is the inductive effect expected to be the least?

  • The magnitude of the inductive effect decreases as the number of intervening bonds increases. Hence, it is least in the bond between carbon-3 and hydrogen (the bonds farthest from Br).

Write resonance structures of CH3COO-.

\[CH_3-C(=O)-O^- \longleftrightarrow CH_3-C(-O^-)=O\]
  • A lone pair on the negative oxygen moves to form a C=O bond, while the π electrons of the original C=O move onto the other oxygen. The two structures are equivalent.

Explain why the following two structures, I and II, cannot be the major contributors to the real structure of CH3COOCH3: I: CH3-C+(O-)-OCH3 II: CH3-C(O-)=O+-CH3

  • Both structures involve separation of charge, so they are less important contributors.
  • Additionally, in structure I, the carbon atom has an incomplete octet.

Explain why (CH3)3C+ is more stable than CH3CH2+, and CH3+ is the least stable cation.

  • Hyperconjugation in (CH3)3C+ is greater than in CH3CH2+, as (CH3)3C+ has nine C-H bonds (CH3CH2+ has only three).
  • In CH3+, the vacant p orbital is perpendicular to the plane in which the C-H bonds lie, so they cannot overlap with it. Thus, CH3+ has no hyperconjugative stability.

Which of the two, O2NCH2CH2O- or CH3CH2O-, is expected to be more stable and why?

  • O2NCH2CH2O- is more stable. The -NO2 group is electron withdrawing (-I effect) and disperses the negative charge on oxygen.
  • In CH3CH2O-, the ethyl group is electron donating (+I effect) and intensifies the negative charge, making it less stable.

Explain why alkyl groups act as electron donors when attached to a π system.

  • Due to hyperconjugation. The σ electrons of the C-H bonds of the alkyl group are delocalised into the adjacent π system, increasing its electron density. More C-H bonds give a greater effect.

Which electron displacement effect explains the following orders of acidity? (a) Cl3CCOOH > Cl2CHCOOH > ClCH2COOH (b) CH3CH2COOH > (CH3)2CHCOOH > (CH3)3CCOOH

  • (a) -I effect of chlorine. More Cl atoms withdraw more electron density, stabilising the carboxylate ion and increasing acidity.
  • (b) +I effect of alkyl groups. More alkyl groups push more electron density towards -COO-, destabilising it and decreasing acidity.

docs.title: Purification and Analysis
docs.text:
Name a suitable technique to separate the components of a mixture of calcium sulphate and camphor.

  • Sublimation. Camphor sublimes on heating, while calcium sulphate does not.

Explain why an organic liquid vaporises at a temperature below its boiling point in steam distillation.

  • The liquid boils when the sum of its vapour pressure (p1) and that of water (p2) equals atmospheric pressure, i.e. p = p1 + p2. Since p1 needs to be only a part of p, the organic liquid vaporises at a temperature lower than its boiling point.

Why is nitric acid added to sodium extract before adding silver nitrate for testing halogens?

  • To decompose NaCN and Na2S (if N or S is present). Otherwise, CN- and S2- would react with Ag+ and interfere with the test.

Explain the reason for the fusion of an organic compound with metallic sodium for testing nitrogen, sulphur and halogens.

  • In organic compounds these elements are covalently bonded and cannot be detected directly. Fusion with sodium converts them into ionic compounds (NaCN, Na2S, NaX), which dissolve in water and give the usual ionic tests.

Will CCl4 give a white precipitate of AgCl on heating it with silver nitrate? Give reason.

  • No. CCl4 is a covalent compound and does not ionise to give Cl- ions, so no AgCl is formed.

Why is a solution of potassium hydroxide used to absorb carbon dioxide evolved during the estimation of carbon?

  • CO2 is acidic and is completely absorbed by KOH. The increase in mass of the KOH tube gives the mass of CO2.
\[2KOH + CO_2 → K_2CO_3 + H_2O\]

Why is acetic acid and not sulphuric acid used for acidification of sodium extract for testing sulphur by the lead acetate test?

  • Sulphuric acid would react with lead acetate to form a white precipitate of lead sulphate, which interferes with the detection of black PbS. Acetic acid does not cause this.

In Lassaigne's test for nitrogen, the Prussian blue colour is due to the formation of: (a) Na4[Fe(CN)6] (b) Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 (c) Fe2[Fe(CN)6] (d) Fe3[Fe(CN)6]4

  • Answer: (b) Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3, iron(III) hexacyanoferrate(II).

The reaction CH3CH2I + KOH(aq) → CH3CH2OH + KI is classified as: (a) electrophilic substitution (b) nucleophilic substitution (c) elimination (d) addition

  • Answer: (b) nucleophilic substitution. The nucleophile OH- replaces I-.

docs.title: Biomolecules
docs.text:
• A living system grows, sustains and reproduces itself, yet it is built entirely from non-living atoms and molecules.
  • The study of the chemistry that goes on inside living systems is called biochemistry.
  • Living systems are made up of complex biomolecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids. Simpler molecules like vitamins and mineral salts also play important roles.
  • Proteins and carbohydrates are essential constituents of our food.

docs.title: Carbohydrates
docs.text:
• Carbohydrates are produced mainly by plants and form a very large group of naturally occurring organic compounds. Common examples are cane sugar, glucose and starch.
  • Most of them have the general formula Cx(H2O)y, so they were once thought to be "hydrates of carbon". This is where the name carbohydrate comes from.

Example

Glucose, C6H12O6, can be written as C6(H2O)6.

  • However, this general formula is not a reliable definition:
    • Acetic acid, CH3COOH, fits the formula as C2(H2O)2, but it is not a carbohydrate.
    • Rhamnose, C6H12O5, is a carbohydrate but does not fit the formula.
  • Their reactions show that carbohydrates contain specific functional groups. So chemically, carbohydrates are defined as:

Definition

Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or the compounds which produce such units on hydrolysis.

  • Carbohydrates which are sweet in taste are called sugars. The sugar used at home is sucrose, and the sugar present in milk is lactose.
  • Carbohydrates are also called saccharides (Greek sakcharon = sugar).

docs.title: Classification of Carbohydrates
docs.text: Carbohydrates are classified on the basis of their behaviour on hydrolysis into three groups.

docs.title: 1. Monosaccharides
docs.text:
• A carbohydrate that cannot be hydrolysed further to give a simpler polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone is called a monosaccharide.
  • About 20 monosaccharides occur in nature. Examples: glucose, fructose, ribose.

docs.title: 2. Oligosaccharides
docs.text:
• Carbohydrates that give two to ten monosaccharide units on hydrolysis are called oligosaccharides.
  • They are further named disaccharides, trisaccharides, tetrasaccharides, etc., depending on the number of monosaccharide units they give. Disaccharides are the most common.
  • The two units from a disaccharide may be the same or different:
    • Sucrose gives one molecule each of glucose and fructose.
    • Maltose gives two molecules of glucose only.

docs.title: 3. Polysaccharides
docs.text:
• Carbohydrates which give a large number of monosaccharide units on hydrolysis are called polysaccharides. Examples: starch, cellulose, glycogen, gums.
  • Polysaccharides are not sweet in taste, so they are also called non-sugars.

docs.title: Reducing and Non-reducing Sugars
docs.text:
• Carbohydrates which reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent are called reducing sugars.
  • All monosaccharides, whether aldoses or ketoses, are reducing sugars.
  • In a disaccharide:
    • If the reducing groups (aldehydic or ketonic groups) of both monosaccharide units are used up in bonding, the sugar is non-reducing. Example: sucrose.
    • If one of these groups is still free, the sugar is reducing. Examples: maltose and lactose.

docs.title: Classification of Monosaccharides
docs.text:
