• Monosaccharides are further classified by the functional group and the number of carbon atoms they contain.
  • A monosaccharide with an aldehyde group is called an aldose; one with a keto group is called a ketose.
  • The number of carbon atoms is also included in the name.
Carbon atoms General term Aldehyde Ketone 3 Triose Aldotriose Ketotriose 4 Tetrose Aldotetrose Ketotetrose 5 Pentose Aldopentose Ketopentose 6 Hexose Aldohexose Ketohexose 7 Heptose Aldoheptose Ketoheptose

Examples

Glucose is an aldohexose (6 carbons, aldehyde group). Fructose is a ketohexose (6 carbons, keto group). Ribose is an aldopentose.

docs.title: Glucose
docs.text:
• Glucose occurs freely in nature as well as in combined form. It is present in sweet fruits and honey; ripe grapes contain glucose in large amounts.
  • Glucose is an aldohexose and is also known as dextrose.
  • It is the monomer of many larger carbohydrates such as starch and cellulose, and is probably the most abundant organic compound on earth.

docs.title: 1. From sucrose (cane sugar)
docs.text:
• When sucrose is boiled with dilute HCl or H2SO4 in alcoholic solution, glucose and fructose are obtained in equal amounts.
\[\underset{Sucrose}{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} \underset{Glucose}{C_6H_{12}O_6} + \underset{Fructose}{C_6H_{12}O_6}\]

docs.title: 2. From starch
docs.text:
• Commercially, glucose is obtained by hydrolysis of starch by boiling it with dilute H2SO4 at 393 K under pressure (2-3 atm).
\[\underset{Starch\ or\ cellulose}{(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n} + nH_2O \xrightarrow[393\ K;\ 2-3\ atm]{H^+} \underset{Glucose}{nC_6H_{12}O_6}\]

docs.title: Glycosidic Linkage
docs.text:
• Disaccharides, on hydrolysis with dilute acids or enzymes, give two molecules of the same or different monosaccharides.
  • The two monosaccharide units are joined by an oxide linkage formed by the loss of a water molecule.
  • Such a linkage between two monosaccharide units through an oxygen atom is called a glycosidic linkage.

docs.title: 1. Sucrose
docs.text:
• Sucrose (cane sugar) on hydrolysis gives an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose.
\[\underset{Sucrose}{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + H_2O → \underset{D-(+)-Glucose}{C_6H_{12}O_6} + \underset{D-(-)-Fructose}{C_6H_{12}O_6}\]
  • The two units are held together by a glycosidic linkage between C-1 of α-glucose and C-2 of β-fructose.
  • Since the reducing groups of both glucose (C-1) and fructose (C-2) are used up in the glycosidic bond, sucrose is a non-reducing sugar.

docs.title: Invert sugar
docs.text:
• Sucrose is dextrorotatory. After hydrolysis it gives dextrorotatory glucose (+52.5°) and laevorotatory fructose (-92.4°).
  • Since the laevorotation of fructose is greater than the dextrorotation of glucose, the mixture is laevorotatory.
  • So hydrolysis of sucrose changes the sign of rotation from dextro (+) to laevo (-). The product is called invert sugar.

docs.title: 2. Maltose
docs.text:
• Maltose is made up of two α-D-glucose units, in which C-1 of one glucose (I) is linked to C-4 of the other glucose (II).
  • A free aldehyde group can be produced at C-1 of the second glucose unit in solution, so maltose shows reducing properties. It is a reducing sugar.

docs.title: 3. Lactose
docs.text:
• Lactose is commonly called milk sugar because it is found in milk.
  • It is composed of β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose. The linkage is between C-1 of galactose and C-4 of glucose.
  • C-1 of the glucose unit is free, so lactose is also a reducing sugar.

docs.title: Comparison of disaccharides
docs.text: Disaccharide Monosaccharide units Glycosidic linkage Reducing? Sucrose α-D-glucose + β-D-fructose C-1 (glucose) - C-2 (fructose) No Maltose α-D-glucose + α-D-glucose C-1 - C-4 Yes Lactose β-D-galactose + β-D-glucose C-1 (galactose) - C-4 (glucose) Yes

docs.title: Polysaccharides
docs.text:
• Polysaccharides contain a large number of monosaccharide units joined together by glycosidic linkages.
  • They are the most commonly found carbohydrates in nature and mainly act as food storage or structural materials.

docs.title: 1. Starch
docs.text:
• Starch is the main storage polysaccharide of plants and the most important dietary source for human beings.
  • Cereals, roots, tubers and some vegetables have a high starch content.
  • It is a polymer of α-glucose and consists of two components: amylose and amylopectin.

docs.title: Amylose
docs.text:
• Water-soluble component; about 15-20% of starch.
  • A long unbranched chain of 200-1000 α-D-(+)-glucose units held by C1-C4 glycosidic linkages.

docs.title: Amylopectin
docs.text:
• Water-insoluble component; about 80-85% of starch.
  • A branched chain polymer of α-D-glucose units. The chain is formed by C1-C4 glycosidic linkages, while branching occurs through C1-C6 glycosidic linkages.

docs.title: 2. Cellulose
docs.text:
• Cellulose occurs exclusively in plants and is the most abundant organic substance in the plant kingdom. It is the main constituent of the cell wall of plant cells.
  • It is a straight chain polysaccharide made up only of β-D-glucose units joined by glycosidic linkages between C-1 of one unit and C-4 of the next.

Note

Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose. The key structural difference is that starch is made of α-D-glucose units (with branching in amylopectin), while cellulose is an unbranched chain of β-D-glucose units.

docs.title: 3. Glycogen
docs.text:
• Carbohydrates are stored in the animal body as glycogen.
  • It is called animal starch because its structure is similar to amylopectin, but it is even more highly branched.
  • It is present in the liver, muscles and brain. When the body needs glucose, enzymes break glycogen down to glucose.
  • Glycogen is also found in yeast and fungi.

docs.title: Importance of Carbohydrates
docs.text:
• Carbohydrates are essential for life in both plants and animals and form a major portion of our food.
  • Honey has long been used as an instant source of energy by 'Vaids' in the ayurvedic system of medicine.
  • They act as storage molecules: starch in plants and glycogen in animals.
  • The cell walls of bacteria and plants are made up of cellulose. We build furniture from cellulose in the form of wood and clothe ourselves with cellulose in the form of cotton fibre.
  • They provide raw materials for industries like textiles, paper, lacquers and breweries.
  • Two aldopentoses, D-ribose and 2-deoxy-D-ribose, are present in nucleic acids.
  • Carbohydrates are found in biosystems in combination with many proteins and lipids.

docs.title: Enzymes
docs.text:
• Life depends on the coordination of many chemical reactions in living organisms, for example digestion of food, absorption of molecules and production of energy.
  • These reactions occur in the body under very mild conditions. This is possible because of biocatalysts called enzymes.
  • Almost all enzymes are globular proteins.

docs.title: Characteristics of enzymes
docs.text:
• Enzymes are very specific, both for a particular reaction and for a particular substrate.
  • They are needed only in small quantities for a reaction to proceed.
  • Like chemical catalysts, they lower the activation energy of a reaction.

Example

The activation energy for acid hydrolysis of sucrose is 6.22 kJ mol-1, while for hydrolysis by the enzyme sucrase it is only 2.15 kJ mol-1.

docs.title: Naming of enzymes
docs.text:
• Enzymes are generally named after the compound (or class of compounds) on which they act. The name ends in -ase.
  • For example, the enzyme that hydrolyses maltose into glucose is called maltase:
\[\underset{Maltose}{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + H_2O \xrightarrow{Maltase} \underset{Glucose}{2C_6H_{12}O_6}\]
  • Sometimes enzymes are named after the reaction they catalyse. Enzymes that catalyse the oxidation of one substrate with simultaneous reduction of another are called oxidoreductases.

docs.title: Vitamins
docs.text:
• Certain organic compounds are needed in small amounts in our diet, and their deficiency causes specific diseases. These compounds are called vitamins.
  • Most vitamins cannot be synthesised in our body, but plants can synthesise almost all of them, so they are considered essential food factors. Bacteria of the gut can produce some of the vitamins we need.
  • Vitamins belong to many different chemical classes, so it is hard to define them by structure. They are regarded as:

Definition

Vitamins are organic compounds required in the diet in small amounts to perform specific biological functions for normal maintenance of optimum growth and health of the organism.

  • Vitamins are designated by letters A, B, C, D, etc. Some are divided into sub-groups, e.g. B1, B2, B6, B12.
  • Excess of vitamins is also harmful, so vitamin pills should not be taken without a doctor's advice.

Note

The term "vitamine" was coined from vital + amine, because the first compounds identified contained amino groups. Later it was found that most of them do not contain amino groups, so the final 'e' was dropped.

docs.title: Classification of Vitamins
docs.text: Vitamins are classified into two groups depending on their solubility in water or fat.

docs.title: 1. Fat soluble vitamins
docs.text:
• Soluble in fats and oils but insoluble in water.
  • These are vitamins A, D, E and K.
  • They are stored in the liver and adipose (fat-storing) tissues.

docs.title: 2. Water soluble vitamins
docs.text:
• B group vitamins and vitamin C are soluble in water.
  • They must be supplied regularly in the diet because they are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored in the body (except vitamin B12).

docs.title: Important Vitamins, Sources and Deficiency Diseases
docs.text:
No. Vitamin Sources Deficiency diseases 1 Vitamin A Fish liver oil, carrots, butter and milk Xerophthalmia (hardening of cornea of eye), night blindness 2 Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) Yeast, milk, green vegetables and cereals Beri beri (loss of appetite, retarded growth) 3 Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) Milk, egg white, liver, kidney Cheilosis (fissuring at corners of mouth and lips), digestive disorders and burning sensation of the skin 4 Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) Yeast, milk, egg yolk, cereals and grams Convulsions 5 Vitamin B12 Meat, fish, egg and curd Pernicious anaemia (RBC deficient in haemoglobin) 6 Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid) Citrus fruits, amla and green leafy vegetables Scurvy (bleeding gums) 7 Vitamin D Exposure to sunlight, fish and egg yolk Rickets (bone deformities in children) and osteomalacia (soft bones and joint pain in adults) 8 Vitamin E Vegetable oils like wheat germ oil, sunflower oil Increased fragility of RBCs and muscular weakness 9 Vitamin K Green leafy vegetables Increased blood clotting time

Remember

  • Vitamin K is the vitamin responsible for coagulation (clotting) of blood.
  • Vitamin B12 is the only water soluble vitamin that can be stored in the body.

docs.title: Nucleic Acids
docs.text:
• Every generation of a species resembles its ancestors. The transmission of inherent characters from one generation to the next is called heredity, and the nucleus of a living cell is responsible for it.
  • The particles in the nucleus responsible for heredity are called chromosomes. They are made up of proteins and another type of biomolecule called nucleic acids.
  • Nucleic acids are of two main types: deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA).
  • Nucleic acids are long chain polymers of nucleotides, so they are also called polynucleotides.

docs.title: Chemical Composition of Nucleic Acids
docs.text: Complete hydrolysis of DNA or RNA gives three components:

docs.title: 1. A pentose sugar
docs.text:
• In DNA, the sugar is β-D-2-deoxyribose.
  • In RNA, the sugar is β-D-ribose.
  • 2-deoxyribose differs from ribose in having -H in place of -OH at C-2.

docs.title: 3. Nitrogenous bases
docs.text:
• These are nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds.
  • DNA contains adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).
  • RNA contains adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and uracil (U). So the fourth base in RNA is uracil instead of thymine.
  • Adenine and guanine are purines (two fused rings); cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines (single ring).

docs.title: Nucleoside
docs.text:
• A unit formed by attachment of a base to the 1' position of the sugar is called a nucleoside.
  • In nucleosides, the sugar carbons are numbered 1', 2', 3', etc. to distinguish them from the atoms of the base.
\[Nucleoside = Base + Sugar\]

docs.title: Nucleotide
docs.text:
• When a nucleoside is linked to phosphoric acid at the 5' position of the sugar, a nucleotide is formed.
\[Nucleotide = Base + Sugar + Phosphate\]

docs.title: Phosphodiester linkage
docs.text:
• Nucleotides are joined together by phosphodiester linkages between the 5' and 3' carbon atoms of the pentose sugars.
  • The formation of a dinucleotide is shown below. The chain has a free 5' end and a free 3' end.
  • A simplified version of a nucleic acid chain is:
\[\begin{array}{c} Base \\ | \\ -Sugar- \end{array} Phosphate \left[ \begin{array}{c} Base \\ | \\ -Sugar- \end{array} Phosphate \right]_n \begin{array}{c} Base \\ | \\ -Sugar- \end{array}\]

docs.title: Primary structure
docs.text: • The sequence of nucleotides in the chain of a nucleic acid is called its primary structure.

docs.title: Secondary structure of DNA
docs.text:
• James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double strand helix structure of DNA.
  • Two nucleic acid chains are wound about each other and held together by hydrogen bonds between pairs of bases.
  • The two strands are complementary (not identical) because hydrogen bonds form only between specific pairs of bases:
    • Adenine pairs with thymine (A = T).
    • Cytosine pairs with guanine (C ≡ G).
  • So the sequence of bases on one strand fixes the sequence on the other.

Note

Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine for the double helix model. It resembles a gently twisted ladder: the rails are alternating phosphate and deoxyribose units, and the rungs are pairs of purine/pyrimidine bases. Complementary base pairing explains how identical copies of parental DNA pass to two daughter cells.

docs.title: Secondary structure of RNA
docs.text:
• In RNA, the helices are only single stranded. Sometimes they fold back on themselves to form a double helix structure.
  • RNA molecules are of three types, each with a different function:
    • Messenger RNA (m-RNA)
    • Ribosomal RNA (r-RNA)
    • Transfer RNA (t-RNA)

docs.title: DNA vs RNA
docs.text: Feature DNA RNA Sugar β-D-2-deoxyribose β-D-ribose Bases A, G, C, T A, G, C, U Structure Double stranded helix Single stranded Base pairing Complementary strands (A-T, C-G) No fixed ratio between bases Function Chemical basis of heredity; carries the coded message for protein synthesis Actually carries out protein synthesis Types - m-RNA, r-RNA, t-RNA

docs.title: Biological Functions of Nucleic Acids
docs.text:
• DNA is the chemical basis of heredity and is regarded as the reserve of genetic information.
  • DNA is responsible for maintaining the identity of different species over millions of years.
  • A DNA molecule can self-duplicate during cell division, so identical DNA strands are passed on to daughter cells.
  • Nucleic acids carry out protein synthesis in the cell. Proteins are actually synthesised by the various RNA molecules, but the message for synthesis of a particular protein is present in DNA.

Note

Har Gobind Khorana shared the 1968 Nobel Prize for Medicine and Physiology with Marshall Nirenberg and Robert Holley for cracking the genetic code.

docs.title: DNA Fingerprinting
docs.text:
• Fingerprints at the tips of fingers are unique to each person and have long been used for identification, but they can be altered by surgery.
  • The sequence of bases on DNA is also unique for every person. Information about this sequence is called DNA fingerprinting.
  • It is the same for every cell of a person and cannot be altered by any known treatment.
  • DNA fingerprinting is used:
    • in forensic laboratories to identify criminals,
    • to determine the paternity of an individual,
    • to identify dead bodies in accidents by comparing the DNA of parents or children,
    • to identify racial groups and rewrite biological evolution.

docs.title: Proteins
docs.text:
• Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the living system. Chief sources are milk, cheese, pulses, peanuts, fish and meat.
  • They occur in every part of the body, form the basis of its structure and functions, and are needed for growth and maintenance of the body.
  • The word protein comes from the Greek proteios, meaning "primary" or "of prime importance".
  • All proteins are polymers of α-amino acids.

docs.title: Amino Acids
docs.text:
• Amino acids contain an amino (-NH2) group and a carboxyl (-COOH) group.
  • Depending on the position of the amino group relative to the carboxyl group, amino acids are classified as α, β, γ, δ and so on.
  • Only α-amino acids (-NH2 on the carbon next to -COOH) are obtained on hydrolysis of proteins. They may contain other functional groups too.

General structure of an α-amino acid

\[R-CH(NH_2)-COOH\]

Here R is the side chain, which is different for each amino acid.

  • All α-amino acids have trivial names that usually reflect a property or source. Glycine is named for its sweet taste (Greek glykos = sweet) and tyrosine was first obtained from cheese (Greek tyros = cheese).
  • Amino acids are represented by a three-letter symbol, and sometimes by a one-letter code.

docs.title: Natural amino acids
docs.text:
No. Amino acid Side chain, R Three-letter symbol One-letter code 1 Glycine -H Gly G 2 Alanine -CH3 Ala A 3 Valine* (CH3)2CH- Val V 4 Leucine* (CH3)2CH-CH2- Leu L 5 Isoleucine* CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)- Ile I 6 Arginine* HN=C(NH2)-NH-(CH2)3- Arg R 7 Lysine* H2N-(CH2)4- Lys K 8 Glutamic acid HOOC-CH2-CH2- Glu E 9 Aspartic acid HOOC-CH2- Asp D 10 Glutamine H2N-CO-CH2-CH2- Gln Q 11 Asparagine H2N-CO-CH2- Asn N 12 Threonine* CH3-CH(OH)- Thr T 13 Serine HO-CH2- Ser S 14 Cysteine HS-CH2- Cys C 15 Methionine* CH3-S-CH2-CH2- Met M 16 Phenylalanine* C6H5-CH2- Phe F 17 Tyrosine (p)HO-C6H4-CH2- Tyr Y 18 Tryptophan* Indol-3-yl-CH2- (indole ring) Trp W 19 Histidine* Imidazol-4-yl-CH2- (imidazole ring) His H 20 Proline Cyclic: the side chain -(CH2)3- joins back to the α-N (pyrrolidine ring) Pro P

* Essential amino acid.

docs.title: On the basis of acidic/basic character
docs.text:
• Neutral amino acids: equal number of amino and carboxyl groups. Example: glycine, alanine.
  • Basic amino acids: more amino groups than carboxyl groups. Example: lysine, arginine.
  • Acidic amino acids: more carboxyl groups than amino groups. Example: glutamic acid, aspartic acid.

docs.title: On the basis of synthesis in the body
docs.text:
• Non-essential amino acids can be synthesised in the body. Examples: glycine, alanine.
  • Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised in the body and must be obtained through the diet. Examples: valine, leucine (marked * in the table). Ten amino acids are essential.

docs.title: Properties of Amino Acids
docs.text:
• Amino acids are usually colourless, crystalline, water-soluble, high-melting solids.
  • They behave like salts rather than like simple amines or carboxylic acids. This is because both an acidic (-COOH) and a basic (-NH2) group are present in the same molecule.

docs.title: Zwitter ion
docs.text:
• In aqueous solution, the carboxyl group loses a proton and the amino group accepts a proton. This gives a dipolar ion called a zwitter ion.
  • It is neutral overall but contains both positive and negative charges.
\[R-CH(NH_2)-COOH\ ⇌\ \underset{Zwitter\ ion}{R-CH(\overset{+}{N}H_3)-COO^-}\]
  • In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour: they react with both acids and bases.
    • With acid, -COO- accepts a proton and the amino acid becomes a cation.
    • With base, -N+H3 loses a proton and the amino acid becomes an anion.

docs.title: Optical activity
docs.text:
• Except glycine (where R = H), all naturally occurring α-amino acids are optically active, because the α-carbon is asymmetric.
  • They exist in both D and L forms. Most naturally occurring amino acids have L-configuration. L-amino acids are drawn with the -NH2 group on the left in the Fischer projection.

docs.title: Peptide Bond
docs.text:
• Proteins are polymers of α-amino acids connected by peptide bonds (peptide linkages).
  • Chemically, a peptide linkage is an amide (-CO-NH-) formed between the -COOH group of one amino acid and the -NH2 group of another, with elimination of a water molecule.
  • The product of two amino acids is a dipeptide. For example, the carboxyl group of glycine combines with the amino group of alanine to give glycylalanine (Gly-Ala):
\[\underset{Glycine}{H_2N-CH_2-COOH} + \underset{Alanine}{H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COOH} \xrightarrow{-H_2O} \underset{Glycylalanine\ (Gly-Ala)}{H_2N-CH_2-\boxed{CO-NH}-CH(CH_3)-COOH}\]
  • Three amino acids joined by two peptide linkages give a tripeptide. Similarly, four, five or six amino acids give a tetrapeptide, pentapeptide or hexapeptide.
  • When more than ten amino acids are joined, the product is a polypeptide.
  • A polypeptide with more than a hundred amino acid residues and molecular mass above 10,000 u is called a protein.
  • The distinction is not sharp: a smaller polypeptide with a well-defined protein-like conformation is also called a protein. Example: insulin, which contains 51 amino acids.

docs.title: 1. Fibrous proteins
docs.text:
• The polypeptide chains run parallel and are held together by hydrogen and disulphide bonds, giving a fibre-like structure.
  • They are generally insoluble in water.
  • Examples: keratin (hair, wool, silk) and myosin (muscles).

docs.title: 2. Globular proteins
docs.text:
• The polypeptide chains coil around to give a spherical shape.
  • They are usually soluble in water.
  • Examples: insulin and albumins.

docs.title: Structure of Proteins
docs.text: The structure and shape of proteins is studied at four levels, each more complex than the previous one.

docs.title: 1. Primary structure
docs.text:
• A protein may have one or more polypeptide chains. In each chain, the amino acids are linked in a specific sequence. This sequence is the primary structure of the protein.
  • Any change in the sequence of amino acids creates a different protein.

docs.title: 2. Secondary structure
docs.text:
• It refers to the shape in which a long polypeptide chain can exist.
  • It arises from regular folding of the polypeptide backbone due to hydrogen bonding between the >C=O and -NH- groups of the peptide bonds.
  • There are two types:

docs.title: (a) α-Helix
docs.text:
• The polypeptide chain forms all possible hydrogen bonds by twisting into a right-handed screw (helix).
  • The -NH group of each amino acid residue is hydrogen-bonded to the >C=O of an adjacent turn of the helix (intramolecular hydrogen bonding).

docs.title: (b) β-Pleated sheet
docs.text:
• All the peptide chains are stretched out to nearly maximum extension and laid side by side.
  • They are held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
  • The structure resembles the pleated folds of drapery, hence the name.

docs.title: 3. Tertiary structure
docs.text:
• It represents the overall folding of the polypeptide chains, i.e. further folding of the secondary structure.
  • It gives rise to the two major molecular shapes: fibrous and globular.
  • The main forces that stabilise the 2° and 3° structures are hydrogen bonds, disulphide linkages, van der Waals forces and electrostatic forces of attraction.

docs.title: 4. Quaternary structure
docs.text:
• Some proteins are made of two or more polypeptide chains called sub-units.
  • The spatial arrangement of these sub-units with respect to each other is the quaternary structure. Example: haemoglobin.

docs.title: Denaturation of Proteins
docs.text:
• A protein in a biological system with a unique three-dimensional structure and biological activity is called a native protein.
  • When a native protein is subjected to a physical change (like change in temperature) or a chemical change (like change in pH), its hydrogen bonds are disturbed.
  • As a result, the globules unfold, the helices uncoil and the protein loses its biological activity. This is called denaturation.
  • During denaturation, the 2° and 3° structures are destroyed but the 1° structure remains intact.

Examples

  • Coagulation of egg white on boiling.
  • Curdling of milk, caused by lactic acid formed by bacteria present in milk.

docs.title: Biomolecules | Questions on Biomolecules
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some questions related to carbohydrates, proteins, enzymes, vitamins and nucleic acids.

docs.title: Carbohydrates
docs.text:
Glucose or sucrose are soluble in water but cyclohexane or benzene (simple six membered ring compounds) are insoluble in water. Explain.

  • Glucose has five -OH groups and sucrose has eight -OH groups.
  • These -OH groups form extensive hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so glucose and sucrose dissolve readily in water.
  • Cyclohexane and benzene are non-polar hydrocarbons with no -OH groups. They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so they are insoluble.

What are the expected products of hydrolysis of lactose?

  • Lactose is made of β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose joined by a C1-C4 glycosidic linkage. Hydrolysis breaks this linkage:
\[\underset{Lactose}{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+\ or\ lactase} \underset{β-D-Galactose}{C_6H_{12}O_6} + \underset{β-D-Glucose}{C_6H_{12}O_6}\]

How do you explain the absence of aldehyde group in the pentaacetate of D-glucose?

  • In the cyclic structure of glucose, the -OH at C-1 (anomeric carbon) is part of a hemiacetal. In glucose itself, this ring can open to give a free -CHO group in solution.
  • In the pentaacetate, the C-1 -OH is also acetylated. The ring can no longer open to form the open chain with a free -CHO group.
  • So glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine, showing the absence of a free aldehyde group.

What are monosaccharides? What are reducing sugars?

  • Monosaccharides are carbohydrates that cannot be hydrolysed further to give simpler polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Examples: glucose, fructose, ribose.
  • Reducing sugars are carbohydrates that reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent. All monosaccharides, and disaccharides with a free aldehydic or ketonic group (e.g. maltose, lactose), are reducing sugars.

Write two main functions of carbohydrates in plants.

  • Storage: plants store food as starch.
  • Structure: cellulose forms the cell wall of plant cells.

Classify the following into monosaccharides and disaccharides:Ribose, 2-deoxyribose, maltose, galactose, fructose and lactose.

  • Monosaccharides: ribose, 2-deoxyribose, galactose, fructose.
  • Disaccharides: maltose, lactose.

What is glycogen? How is it different from starch?

  • Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals, also called animal starch. It is found in liver, muscles and brain, and also in yeast and fungi.
  • Starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants and is a mixture of amylose (unbranched, 15-20%) and amylopectin (branched, 80-85%).
  • Glycogen is similar in structure to amylopectin but is more highly branched.

What are the hydrolysis products of (i) sucrose and (ii) lactose?

\[(i)\ Sucrose + H_2O → D-(+)-Glucose + D-(-)-Fructose\] \[(ii)\ Lactose + H_2O → β-D-Galactose + β-D-Glucose\]

What is the basic structural difference between starch and cellulose?

  • Starch is a polymer of α-D-glucose. Its amylose part is an unbranched C1-C4 chain and its amylopectin part is branched through C1-C6 linkages.
  • Cellulose is a straight chain polymer of β-D-glucose units joined by C1-C4 glycosidic linkages.

What happens when D-glucose is treated with the following reagents?(i) HI (ii) Bromine water (iii) HNO3

  • (i) On prolonged heating with HI, n-hexane is formed:
\[CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HI,\ \Delta} CH_3-(CH_2)_4-CH_3\]
  • (ii) Bromine water oxidises the -CHO group to give gluconic acid:
\[CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{Br_2\ water} COOH-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH\]
  • (iii) Nitric acid oxidises both the -CHO and the -CH2OH groups to give saccharic acid:
\[CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HNO_3} COOH-(CHOH)_4-COOH\]

Enumerate the reactions of D-glucose which cannot be explained by its open chain structure.

  • Glucose does not give the 2,4-DNP test or Schiff's test, even though it has an aldehyde group.
  • Glucose does not form a hydrogensulphite addition product with NaHSO3.
  • Glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine, showing no free -CHO group.
  • Glucose exists in two crystalline forms, α (m.p. 419 K) and β (m.p. 423 K).

These are explained by the cyclic hemiacetal structure formed by reaction of the C-5 -OH with the -CHO group.

docs.title: Proteins and Enzymes
docs.text:
The melting points and solubility in water of amino acids are generally higher than that of the corresponding halo acids. Explain.

  • Amino acids exist as zwitter ions (H3N+-CHR-COO-). The strong electrostatic attraction between these dipolar ions gives them a salt-like character, so their melting points are high.
  • Being ionic, they are also strongly solvated by water, so they are highly soluble.
  • Halo acids do not form zwitter ions; they have only weaker dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding interactions. So their melting points and solubility are lower.

Where does the water present in the egg go after boiling the egg?

  • On boiling, the egg white protein is denatured and coagulates.
  • The water present in the egg gets trapped in (absorbed by) the coagulated protein network, mainly through hydrogen bonding. So no free water is seen.

What are essential and non-essential amino acids? Give two examples of each type.

  • Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised in the body and must be taken through the diet. Examples: valine, leucine.
  • Non-essential amino acids can be synthesised in the body. Examples: glycine, alanine.

Define the following as related to proteins: (i) Peptide linkage (ii) Primary structure (iii) Denaturation.

  • (i) Peptide linkage: the amide bond (-CO-NH-) formed between the -COOH group of one amino acid and the -NH2 group of another, with loss of a water molecule.
  • (ii) Primary structure: the specific sequence in which amino acids are linked in a polypeptide chain.
  • (iii) Denaturation: the loss of biological activity of a native protein when the hydrogen bonds are disturbed by a change in temperature or pH. The 2° and 3° structures are destroyed but the 1° structure remains intact.

What are the common types of secondary structure of proteins? What type of bonding helps in stabilising the α-helix structure?

  • The two common types are the α-helix and the β-pleated sheet.
  • The α-helix is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between the -NH group of each amino acid residue and the >C=O group of an adjacent turn of the helix.

Differentiate between globular and fibrous proteins.

Fibrous proteins Globular proteins Polypeptide chains run parallel, held by hydrogen and disulphide bonds Polypeptide chains coil around to give a spherical shape Fibre-like structure Spherical structure Generally insoluble in water Usually soluble in water Examples: keratin, myosin Examples: insulin, albumins

How do you explain the amphoteric behaviour of amino acids?

  • In aqueous solution, amino acids exist as zwitter ions, which contain both an acidic group (-N+H3) and a basic group (-COO-).
  • With an acid, the -COO- group accepts a proton; with a base, the -N+H3 group gives up a proton:
\[H_3\overset{+}{N}-CHR-COOH \xleftarrow{H^+} H_3\overset{+}{N}-CHR-COO^- \xrightarrow{OH^-} H_2N-CHR-COO^-\]
  • Since they react with both acids and bases, amino acids are amphoteric.

What are enzymes? What is the effect of denaturation on the structure of proteins?

  • Enzymes are biocatalysts, almost all of which are globular proteins. They are highly specific and speed up reactions in living systems under mild conditions by lowering the activation energy.
  • On denaturation, the globules unfold and helices uncoil: the secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed, while the primary structure (amino acid sequence) remains intact. The protein loses its biological activity.

docs.title: Vitamins and Nucleic Acids
docs.text:
Why cannot vitamin C be stored in our body?

  • Vitamin C is water soluble. It is readily excreted in urine and therefore cannot be stored in the body. It must be supplied regularly through the diet.

How are vitamins classified? Name the vitamin responsible for the coagulation of blood.

  • Vitamins are classified as fat soluble (A, D, E and K) and water soluble (B group and C).
  • Vitamin K is responsible for coagulation of blood. Its deficiency increases blood clotting time.

Why are vitamin A and vitamin C essential to us? Give their important sources.

  • Deficiency of vitamin A causes xerophthalmia (hardening of the cornea) and night blindness. Sources: fish liver oil, carrots, butter and milk.
  • Deficiency of vitamin C causes scurvy (bleeding gums). Sources: citrus fruits, amla and green leafy vegetables.

What products would be formed when a nucleotide from DNA containing thymine is hydrolysed?

  • A DNA nucleotide consists of a base, the sugar and a phosphate group. On hydrolysis it gives:
\[Thymine + β-D-2-Deoxyribose + Phosphoric\ acid\]

When RNA is hydrolysed, there is no relationship among the quantities of different bases obtained. What does this fact suggest about the structure of RNA?

  • In DNA, A always pairs with T and C with G, so the amounts of these pairs are equal. This is a consequence of its double strand structure.
  • In RNA, no such relationship exists between the bases. This suggests that RNA has a single strand structure with no complementary base pairing between two strands.

What are nucleic acids? Mention their two important functions.

  • Nucleic acids are long chain polymers of nucleotides (polynucleotides) present in the nucleus. They are of two types, DNA and RNA.
  • Functions:
    • DNA is the chemical basis of heredity and transfers characters from parents to offspring through self duplication.
    • Nucleic acids carry out protein synthesis in the cell (the message is in DNA; RNA actually synthesises the protein).

What is the difference between a nucleoside and a nucleotide?

\[Nucleoside = Base + Sugar\] \[Nucleotide = Base + Sugar + Phosphate\]
  • A nucleoside is formed when a base is attached at the 1' position of the sugar.
  • A nucleotide is formed when a nucleoside is linked to phosphoric acid at the 5' position of the sugar.

The two strands in DNA are not identical but are complementary. Explain.

  • The two strands of DNA are held together by hydrogen bonds between specific pairs of bases: adenine pairs only with thymine and cytosine pairs only with guanine.
  • So wherever one strand has A, the other has T; wherever one has C, the other has G. The sequence of one strand decides the sequence of the other, but the two sequences are not the same. Hence the strands are complementary, not identical.

Write the important structural and functional differences between DNA and RNA. What are the different types of RNA found in the cell?

  • Structural differences:
    • The sugar in DNA is β-D-2-deoxyribose; in RNA it is β-D-ribose.
    • DNA contains thymine (T); RNA contains uracil (U) instead. Both contain A, G and C.
    • DNA has a double strand helix structure; RNA is single stranded.
  • Functional differences:
    • DNA is the chemical basis of heredity and carries the coded message for protein synthesis.
    • RNA actually carries out protein synthesis in the cell.
  • Types of RNA: messenger RNA (m-RNA), ribosomal RNA (r-RNA) and transfer RNA (t-RNA).

docs.title: Biomolecules | Structure of Glucose and Fructose
Biomolecules | Structure of Glucose and Fructose
Open Chain Structure of Glucose
docs.text: Glucose was assigned the open chain structure CHO-(CHOH)4-CH2OH on the basis of the following evidences.

docs.title: 1. Molecular formula
docs.text: • The molecular formula of glucose was found to be C6H12O6.

docs.title: 2. Straight chain of six carbons
docs.text:
• On prolonged heating with HI, glucose forms n-hexane. This shows that all six carbon atoms are linked in a straight chain.
\[CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HI,\ \Delta} \underset{n-Hexane}{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\]

docs.title: 3. Presence of a carbonyl group
docs.text:
• Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine to form an oxime and adds a molecule of HCN to give a cyanohydrin. These reactions confirm the presence of a carbonyl group (>C=O).
\[CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{NH_2OH} \underset{Oxime}{CH(=N-OH)-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\] \[CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HCN} \underset{Cyanohydrin}{CH(OH)(CN)-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\]

docs.title: 4. Carbonyl group is an aldehyde
docs.text:
• A mild oxidising agent like bromine water oxidises glucose to a six-carbon carboxylic acid, gluconic acid. This shows the carbonyl group is an aldehydic group (ketones are not oxidised so easily).
\[CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{Br_2\ water} \underset{Gluconic\ acid}{COOH-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\]

docs.title: 5. Five -OH groups
docs.text:
• Acetylation of glucose with acetic anhydride gives glucose pentaacetate, which confirms the presence of five -OH groups.
  • Since the pentaacetate is a stable compound, the five -OH groups must be attached to different carbon atoms (two -OH groups on one carbon are unstable).
\[CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{Acetic\ anhydride} CHO-(CH-OCOCH_3)_4-CH_2-OCOCH_3\]

docs.title: 6. Primary alcoholic group
docs.text:
• On oxidation with nitric acid, both glucose and gluconic acid give the same dicarboxylic acid, saccharic acid. This shows the presence of a primary alcoholic (-CH2OH) group in glucose.
\[\underset{Glucose}{CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{HNO_3} \underset{Saccharic\ acid}{COOH-(CHOH)_4-COOH}\] \[\underset{Gluconic\ acid}{COOH-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{HNO_3} \underset{Saccharic\ acid}{COOH-(CHOH)_4-COOH}\]

docs.title: Fischer projection of glucose
docs.text:
• The exact spatial arrangement of the -OH groups was worked out by Fischer. Glucose (I), gluconic acid (II) and saccharic acid (III) are represented as:
\[\underset{(I)\ Glucose}{\begin{array}{c} CHO \\ H-C-OH \\ HO-C-H \\ H-C-OH \\ H-C-OH \\ CH_2OH \end{array}} \qquad \underset{(II)\ Gluconic\ acid}{\begin{array}{c} COOH \\ H-C-OH \\ HO-C-H \\ H-C-OH \\ H-C-OH \\ CH_2OH \end{array}} \qquad \underset{(III)\ Saccharic\ acid}{\begin{array}{c} COOH \\ H-C-OH \\ HO-C-H \\ H-C-OH \\ H-C-OH \\ COOH \end{array}}\]

docs.title: D and L Configuration
docs.text:
• Glucose is correctly named D-(+)-glucose. 'D' represents its configuration and '(+)' represents its dextrorotatory nature.
  • 'D' and 'L' have no relation with the optical activity (sign of rotation) of the compound.
  • The letters D or L tell the relative configuration of a stereoisomer by comparing it with glyceraldehyde. Glyceraldehyde has one asymmetric carbon and exists as two enantiomers:
\[\underset{(+)-Glyceraldehyde}{\begin{array}{c} CHO \\ H-C-OH \\ CH_2OH \end{array}} \qquad \underset{(-)-Glyceraldehyde}{\begin{array}{c} CHO \\ HO-C-H \\ CH_2OH \end{array}}\]
  • Compounds that can be chemically correlated to (+)-glyceraldehyde have D-configuration; those correlated to (-)-glyceraldehyde have L-configuration.
  • For monosaccharides, the structure is written with the most oxidised carbon (CHO) at the top, and the lowest asymmetric carbon (C-5 in glucose) is compared.
  • In (+)-glucose, the -OH on the lowest asymmetric carbon is on the right, just like in (+)-glyceraldehyde. So it is assigned D-configuration.

docs.title: Cyclic Structure of Glucose
docs.text:
The open chain structure (I) explained most properties of glucose, but the following facts could not be explained by it:

  1. Despite having an aldehyde group, glucose does not give the 2,4-DNP test or Schiff's test, and does not form a hydrogensulphite addition product with NaHSO3.
  2. Glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine, showing the absence of a free -CHO group.
  3. Glucose exists in two crystalline forms, α and β:
    • α-form (m.p. 419 K) is obtained by crystallisation from a concentrated solution of glucose at 303 K.
    • β-form (m.p. 423 K) is obtained by crystallisation from a hot, saturated aqueous solution at 371 K.
  • To explain these facts, it was proposed that one of the -OH groups adds to the -CHO group to form a cyclic hemiacetal.
  • Glucose forms a six-membered ring in which the -OH at C-5 is involved in ring formation. This explains the absence of a free -CHO group and the existence of two forms.
  • The two cyclic forms exist in equilibrium with the open chain structure:

docs.title: Anomers
docs.text:
• The two cyclic forms differ only in the configuration of the -OH group at C-1. This carbon (the aldehyde carbon before cyclisation) is called the anomeric carbon.
  • Such isomers, i.e. the α-form and β-form, are called anomers.
    • In α-D-glucose, the -OH at C-1 is on the right (same side as the ring oxygen in the Fischer form).
    • In β-D-glucose, the -OH at C-1 is on the left.

docs.title: Pyranose structure and Haworth projection
docs.text:
• The six-membered ring of glucose (five carbons + one oxygen) is called the pyranose structure, by analogy with pyran, a cyclic compound with one oxygen and five carbon atoms in the ring.
  • The cyclic structure is more correctly represented by the Haworth structure:

Note

In the Haworth structure, groups that are on the right in the Fischer projection are drawn below the ring, and groups on the left are drawn above it. In α-D-glucopyranose the C-1 -OH is below the ring; in β-D-glucopyranose it is above the ring.

docs.title: Structure of Fructose
docs.text:
• Fructose is an important ketohexose. It is obtained along with glucose by hydrolysis of sucrose.
  • It also has the molecular formula C6H12O6. Its reactions show a ketonic group at C-2 and six carbons in a straight chain, as in glucose.
  • It belongs to the D-series and is laevorotatory, so it is written as D-(-)-fructose.

Open chain structure of D-(-)-fructose

\[\begin{array}{c} CH_2OH \\ C=O \\ HO-C-H \\ H-C-OH \\ H-C-OH \\ CH_2OH \end{array}\]
  • Fructose also exists in two cyclic forms, obtained by addition of the -OH at C-5 to the >C=O group (at C-2).
  • The ring formed is five-membered and is called furanose, by analogy with furan, a five-membered cyclic compound with one oxygen and four carbon atoms.
  • C-2 is the anomeric carbon in fructose. The Haworth structures of the two anomers are:

docs.title: Glucose vs Fructose
docs.text: Property Glucose Fructose Type Aldohexose Ketohexose Carbonyl group -CHO at C-1 >C=O at C-2 Optical rotation Dextrorotatory, D-(+) Laevorotatory, D-(-) Ring formed by -OH at C-5 C-5 Ring size Six-membered (pyranose) Five-membered (furanose) Anomeric carbon C-1 C-2

docs.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life | Chemicals in Food
Chemistry in Everyday Life | Chemicals in Food
docs.text: Chemicals are added to food for three reasons: (i) its preservation, (ii) enhancing its appeal, and (iii) adding nutritive value to it.

docs.title: Food Additives
docs.text:
The main categories of food additives are:

  1. Food colours
  2. Flavours and sweeteners
  3. Fat emulsifiers and stabilising agents
  4. Flour improvers - antistaling agents and bleaches
  5. Antioxidants
  6. Preservatives
  7. Nutritional supplements such as minerals, vitamins and amino acids
  • Except for nutritional supplements (category 7), none of these additives has any nutritive value.
  • They are added either to increase the shelf life of stored food or for cosmetic purposes (colour, taste, appearance).

docs.title: Artificial Sweetening Agents
docs.text:
• Natural sweeteners such as sucrose add to calorie intake. So many people, especially diabetic persons and those who need to control calorie intake, prefer artificial sweeteners.
  • Artificial sweeteners give a sweet taste without adding (significant) calories.

docs.title: 1. Saccharin
docs.text:
• Ortho-sulphobenzimide, called saccharin, was the first popular artificial sweetener. It has been used since its discovery in 1879.
  • It is about 550 times as sweet as cane sugar.
  • It is excreted from the body in urine unchanged, and appears to be entirely inert and harmless.
  • It is of great value to diabetic persons and people who need to control their calorie intake.

docs.title: 2. Aspartame
docs.text:
• Aspartame is the most successful and widely used artificial sweetener. It is roughly 100 times as sweet as cane sugar.
  • It is the methyl ester of a dipeptide formed from aspartic acid and phenylalanine.
  • It is unstable at cooking temperature, so its use is limited to cold foods and soft drinks.

docs.title: 3. Alitame
docs.text:
• Alitame is a high-potency sweetener, about 2000 times as sweet as cane sugar.
  • It is more stable than aspartame, but it is difficult to control the sweetness of food when using it.

docs.title: 4. Sucrolose
docs.text:
• Sucrolose (sucralose) is a trichloro derivative of sucrose. It is about 600 times as sweet as cane sugar.
  • Its appearance and taste are like sugar.
  • It is stable at cooking temperature and does not provide calories.

docs.title: Summary of Artificial Sweeteners
docs.text:
Artificial sweetener Sweetness relative to cane sugar Key point Aspartame 100 Methyl ester of aspartyl-phenylalanine; unstable on cooking Saccharin 550 First popular sweetener; excreted unchanged in urine Sucrolose 600 Trichloro derivative of sucrose; stable on cooking; no calories Alitame 2000 High potency; sweetness hard to control

Structures of artificial sweeteners

docs.title: Food Preservatives
docs.text:
• Food preservatives prevent spoilage of food due to microbial growth.
  • The most commonly used preservatives are table salt, sugar, vegetable oils and sodium benzoate (C6H5COONa).
  • Sodium benzoate is used in limited quantities and is metabolised in the body.
  • Salts of sorbic acid and propanoic acid are also used as preservatives.

docs.title: Antioxidants
docs.text:
• Antioxidants are additives that slow down the oxidation of food, especially of fats and oils. Oxidation of fats causes rancidity (bad smell and taste).
  • They act by reacting with oxygen (or with the free radicals formed during oxidation) more readily than the food does, so the food itself is protected.
  • Common examples are BHT (butylated hydroxytoluene) and BHA (butylated hydroxyanisole). Sulphur dioxide and sulphites are used as antioxidants in wines, beers, sugar syrups and dried fruits.

Note

Preservatives fight microbes, while antioxidants fight oxidation. Both increase the shelf life of food but by different mechanisms.

docs.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life | Cleansing Agents
Chemistry in Everyday Life | Cleansing Agents
docs.text: Two types of detergents are used as cleansing agents: soaps and synthetic detergents. Both improve the cleansing properties of water and help remove the fats which bind other materials (dirt) to the fabric or skin.

docs.title: Soaps
docs.text:
• Soaps are the detergents used since ancient times.
  • Soaps used for cleaning are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids, such as stearic, oleic and palmitic acids.

docs.title: Saponification
docs.text:
• Sodium soaps are made by heating a fat (a glyceryl ester of fatty acids) with aqueous sodium hydroxide. This reaction is called saponification.
\[\underset{Glyceryl\ stearate\ (fat)}{(C_{17}H_{35}COO)_3C_3H_5} + 3NaOH → \underset{Sodium\ stearate\ (soap)}{3C_{17}H_{35}COONa} + \underset{Glycerol}{C_3H_5(OH)_3}\]
  • In this reaction the esters of fatty acids are hydrolysed. The soap formed remains in colloidal form.
  • The soap is precipitated by adding sodium chloride (salting out).
  • The remaining solution contains glycerol, which is recovered by fractional distillation.
  • Only sodium and potassium soaps are soluble in water and are used for cleaning.
  • Potassium soaps are softer to the skin than sodium soaps. They are made using KOH solution instead of NaOH.

docs.title: Cleansing action of soap
docs.text:
• A soap anion, such as C17H35COO-, has two parts: a long hydrophobic (water-repelling, oil-loving) hydrocarbon tail and a hydrophilic (water-loving) ionic head, -COO-.
  • In water, soap anions cluster into micelles: the tails point inwards and dissolve in the oily dirt, while the ionic heads face the water.
  • The oil droplet is thus surrounded by negative charges and gets emulsified in water. The dirt is then washed away with the water.

docs.title: Types of soaps
docs.text:
All soaps are made by boiling fats or oils with a suitable soluble hydroxide. Different raw materials and additives give different types:

Type of soap How it is made / what it contains Toilet soaps Better grades of fats and oils; excess alkali removed; colour and perfume added Floating soaps Tiny air bubbles are beaten in before the soap hardens Transparent soaps Soap is dissolved in ethanol and the excess solvent is evaporated Medicated soaps Substances of medicinal value added (some soaps also contain deodorants) Shaving soaps Contain glycerol to prevent rapid drying; rosin gum added, which forms sodium rosinate that lathers well Laundry soaps Contain fillers like sodium rosinate, sodium silicate, borax and sodium carbonate Soap chips A thin sheet of melted soap is run onto a cool cylinder and scraped off in small pieces Soap granules Dried miniature soap bubbles Soap powders and scouring soaps Some soap, an abrasive (powdered pumice or fine sand) and builders like sodium carbonate and trisodium phosphate
  • Builders make soaps act more rapidly.

docs.title: Why Soaps Do Not Work in Hard Water
docs.text:
• Hard water contains calcium and magnesium ions. These react with sodium or potassium soaps to form insoluble calcium and magnesium soaps.
\[\underset{Soap}{2C_{17}H_{35}COONa} + CaCl_2 → 2NaCl + \underset{Insoluble\ calcium\ stearate}{(C_{17}H_{35}COO)_2Ca} ↓\]
  • These insoluble soaps separate as scum and are useless as cleansing agents.
  • They actually hinder washing: the precipitate sticks to the fibres of cloth as a gummy mass.
  • Hair washed with hard water looks dull because of this sticky precipitate.
  • Dyes do not absorb evenly on cloth washed with soap in hard water.

docs.title: Synthetic Detergents
docs.text:
• Synthetic detergents are cleansing agents which have all the properties of soaps but do not contain any soap.
  • They can be used in both soft and hard water, as they foam even in hard water. Some give foam even in ice-cold water.
  • They are classified into three categories: anionic, cationic and non-ionic detergents.

docs.title: 1. Anionic Detergents
docs.text:
• Anionic detergents are sodium salts of sulphonated long-chain alcohols or hydrocarbons.
  • Alkyl hydrogensulphates, formed by treating long-chain alcohols with concentrated sulphuric acid, are neutralised with alkali to give anionic detergents.
\[\underset{Lauryl\ alcohol}{CH_3(CH_2)_{10}CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} \underset{Lauryl\ hydrogensulphate}{CH_3(CH_2)_{10}CH_2OSO_3H} \xrightarrow{NaOH(aq)} \underset{Sodium\ laurylsulphate}{CH_3(CH_2)_{10}CH_2OSO_3^-Na^+}\]
  • Similarly, alkylbenzenesulphonates are obtained by neutralising alkylbenzenesulphonic acids with alkali.
\[\underset{Dodecylbenzene}{CH_3(CH_2)_{11}C_6H_5} \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} \underset{Dodecylbenzenesulphonic\ acid}{CH_3(CH_2)_{11}C_6H_4SO_3H} \xrightarrow{NaOH(aq)} \underset{Sodium\ dodecylbenzenesulphonate}{CH_3(CH_2)_{11}C_6H_4SO_3^-Na^+}\] \[(The\ -SO_3H\ group\ enters\ para\ to\ the\ alkyl\ chain)\]
  • The anionic part of the molecule is involved in the cleansing action.
  • Sodium alkylbenzenesulphonates are an important class of anionic detergents.
  • Uses: mostly for household work; also used in toothpastes.

docs.title: 2. Cationic Detergents
docs.text:
• Cationic detergents are quaternary ammonium salts of amines with acetates, chlorides or bromides as anions.
  • The cationic part has a long hydrocarbon chain and a positive charge on the nitrogen atom, hence the name.
  • Example: cetyltrimethylammonium bromide, a popular cationic detergent used in hair conditioners.
\[[CH_3(CH_2)_{15}N^+(CH_3)_3]Br^-\] \[Cetyltrimethylammonium\ bromide\]
  • Cationic detergents have germicidal properties, but they are expensive, so they are of limited use.

docs.title: 3. Non-ionic Detergents
docs.text:
• Non-ionic detergents do not contain any ion in their constitution.
  • One such detergent is formed when stearic acid reacts with polyethyleneglycol (an esterification):
\[\underset{Stearic\ acid}{CH_3(CH_2)_{16}COOH} + \underset{Polyethyleneglycol}{HO(CH_2CH_2O)_nCH_2CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{-H_2O} CH_3(CH_2)_{16}COO(CH_2CH_2O)_nCH_2CH_2OH\]
  • Liquid dishwashing detergents are of the non-ionic type.
  • Their cleansing mechanism is the same as that of soaps: they remove grease and oil by micelle formation.

docs.title: Comparison of Detergents
docs.text: Type Nature of active part Example Use Anionic Large anion (sulphate / sulphonate) Sodium laurylsulphate, sodium dodecylbenzenesulphonate Household cleaning, toothpastes Cationic Large cation (quaternary ammonium) Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide Hair conditioners; germicidal Non-ionic No ions; polar ester/ether chain Ester of stearic acid and polyethyleneglycol Liquid dishwashing detergents

docs.title: Biodegradability of Detergents
docs.text:
• The main problem with detergents arises when their hydrocarbon chain is highly branched: bacteria cannot degrade such chains easily.
  • Such detergents are non-biodegradable. They accumulate, reach rivers and ponds through effluents, persist even after sewage treatment, cause foaming and pollute the water.
  • Detergents with unbranched (straight) hydrocarbon chains are degraded easily by bacteria and are called biodegradable detergents.
  • Today, branching of the hydrocarbon chain is controlled and kept to a minimum to prevent pollution.

Example

  • Biodegradable: sodium laurylsulphate, CH3(CH2)10CH2OSO3-Na+ (straight chain).
  • Non-biodegradable: sodium 4-(1,3,5,7-tetramethyloctyl)benzenesulphonate (highly branched chain).

Conclusion

Synthetic detergents are preferred over soaps because they work even in hard water. Among detergents, straight-chain ones are preferred over branched-chain ones because the latter are non-biodegradable and cause pollution.

docs.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life | Drugs and Drug-Target Interaction
Chemistry in Everyday Life | Drugs and Drug-Target Interaction
docs.text: Chemistry touches almost every part of daily life: soaps and detergents for cleanliness, dyes and synthetic fibres in clothes, additives in food and, of course, medicines. In this chapter we look at three such areas: medicines, food chemicals and cleansing agents.

docs.title: Drugs
docs.text:
• Drugs are chemicals of low molecular mass (about 100 - 500 u) which interact with macromolecular targets in the body and produce a biological response.
  • When this biological response is therapeutic and useful, the chemicals are called medicines. Medicines are used in the diagnosis, prevention and treatment of diseases.
  • Most drugs used as medicines become potential poisons if taken in doses higher than those recommended. This is why medicines should never be taken without consulting a doctor.
  • The use of chemicals for therapeutic effect is called chemotherapy.

docs.title: Classification of Drugs
docs.text: Drugs can be classified in four main ways. Each classification is useful to a different group of people.

docs.title: 1. On the basis of pharmacological effect
docs.text:
• Drugs are grouped by the effect they produce in the body.
  • This is useful for doctors, because it gives them the whole range of drugs available for treating a particular problem.
  • Example: analgesics have a pain-killing effect; antiseptics kill or arrest the growth of microorganisms.

docs.title: 2. On the basis of drug action
docs.text:
• Drugs are grouped by their action on a particular biochemical process.
  • Example: all antihistamines inhibit the action of histamine, the compound which causes inflammation in the body. (Histamine action can be blocked in different ways, as discussed under antihistamines.)

docs.title: 3. On the basis of chemical structure
docs.text:
• Drugs which share common structural features are grouped together. Such drugs often have similar pharmacological activity.
  • Example: all sulphonamides contain the common structural unit H2N-C6H4-SO2-NHR, i.e., a benzene ring carrying an -NH2 group and, para to it, a sulphonamide group -SO2NHR.

docs.title: 4. On the basis of molecular targets
docs.text:
• Drugs usually interact with biomolecules such as carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. These are called target molecules or drug targets.
  • Drugs with common structural features may have the same mechanism of action on their targets.
  • This classification is the most useful for medicinal chemists.

Note

The same drug can be described in more than one way. For example, "ranitidine is an antacid" is a classification based on pharmacological effect, since any drug that counteracts excess stomach acid is called an antacid.

docs.title: Drug-Target Interaction
docs.text:
Macromolecules of biological origin perform different functions in the body:

  • Enzymes: proteins that act as biological catalysts.
  • Receptors: proteins that are crucial to the body's communication system.
  • Carrier proteins: carry polar molecules across the cell membrane.
  • Nucleic acids: carry the coded genetic information of the cell.
  • Lipids and carbohydrates: structural parts of the cell membrane.

We will understand drug-target interaction using two examples: enzymes and receptors.

docs.title: 1. Catalytic action of enzymes
docs.text:
An enzyme performs two major functions during catalysis:

  • It holds the substrate: The active site of the enzyme holds the substrate molecule in a suitable position so that the reagent can attack it effectively. Substrates bind to the active site through ionic bonding, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals interaction or dipole-dipole interaction.
  • It provides functional groups that attack the substrate and carry out the chemical reaction.

docs.title: 2. Drug-enzyme interaction
docs.text:
• Drugs can block either of the above functions. They can block the binding site and prevent the substrate from binding, or they can inhibit the catalytic activity of the enzyme. Such drugs are called enzyme inhibitors.
  • Drugs prevent the attachment of the substrate to the active site in two ways:

docs.title: (a) Competitive inhibitors
docs.text:
• The drug competes with the natural substrate for the active site of the enzyme.
  • When the drug occupies the active site, the substrate cannot bind and the reaction is blocked.

docs.title: (b) Inhibitors binding at the allosteric site (non-competitive inhibitors)
docs.text:
• Some drugs do not bind to the active site at all. They bind to a different site on the enzyme, called the allosteric site.
  • This binding changes the shape of the active site so that the substrate can no longer recognise it.

Note

If the bond formed between the enzyme and the inhibitor is a strong covalent bond that cannot be broken easily, the enzyme is blocked permanently. The body then degrades the enzyme-inhibitor complex and synthesises fresh enzyme.

docs.title: Receptors as Drug Targets
docs.text:
• Receptors are proteins crucial to the body's communication process. Most of them are embedded in cell membranes, with the small part carrying the active site projecting out of the membrane towards the outside of the cell.
  • Messages between two neurons, and between neurons and muscles, are carried by chemicals called chemical messengers (neurotransmitters and hormones).
  • A chemical messenger binds at the binding site of the receptor. To accommodate it, the shape of the receptor site changes (induced fit). This change transfers the message into the cell.
  • Thus, the chemical messenger passes its message to the cell without entering the cell. When the messenger leaves, the receptor regains its original shape.
  • There are many different receptors in the body. Each receptor is selective for a particular messenger because binding sites differ in shape, structure and amino acid composition.

docs.title: Antagonists and Agonists
docs.text:
Drugs can act on receptors in two opposite ways:

Type of drug What it does When it is useful Antagonist Binds to the receptor site and inhibits its natural function When the message needs to be blocked Agonist Mimics the natural messenger and switches on the receptor When there is a lack of natural messenger

Conclusion

Drugs are designed to interact with specific targets so that they have the least chance of affecting other targets. This minimises side effects and localises the action of the drug.

docs.title: Drugs and Drug-Target Interaction
docs.text:
Why do we need to classify drugs in different ways?

Different classifications serve different users:

  • Classification by pharmacological effect helps doctors, as it gives the whole range of drugs available for a particular problem.
  • Classification by drug action groups drugs that act on the same biochemical process.
  • Classification by chemical structure groups drugs with common structural features, which often have similar activity.
  • Classification by molecular targets is most useful to medicinal chemists for designing drugs.

Explain the term target molecules or drug targets as used in medicinal chemistry. Name the macromolecules that are chosen as drug targets.

Drugs interact with biological macromolecules in the body to produce their effect. These macromolecules are called target molecules or drug targets.

The macromolecules chosen as drug targets are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins (such as enzymes and receptors) and nucleic acids.

Define the term chemotherapy.

The use of chemicals for therapeutic effect, i.e., for the diagnosis, prevention and treatment of diseases, is called chemotherapy.

Why should medicines not be taken without consulting doctors? (Also: why are sleeping pills not to be taken without a doctor's advice?)

Most drugs act as poisons if taken in doses higher than recommended, and a drug may have side effects or act on unintended targets. Only a doctor can decide the correct drug and safe dose. Sleeping pills, for example, are tranquilizers; an overdose can be harmful or even fatal. Hence a doctor should always be consulted before taking medicine.

Which forces are involved in holding the drugs to the active site of enzymes?

Drugs (and substrates) are held at the active site of enzymes by ionic bonding, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals interactions and dipole-dipole interactions.

With reference to which classification has the statement, 'ranitidine is an antacid' been given?

It refers to classification based on pharmacological effect, because any drug used to counteract the effect of excess acid in the stomach is called an antacid.

docs.title: Therapeutic Action of Drugs
docs.text:
While antacids and antiallergic drugs interfere with the function of histamines, why do these not interfere with the function of each other?

Antacids (like cimetidine and ranitidine) and antiallergic drugs (antihistamines like brompheniramine) work on different receptors. Since each receptor is selective for its binding partner, a drug that blocks one type of histamine receptor does not affect the other.

Low level of noradrenaline is the cause of depression. What type of drugs are needed to cure this problem? Name two drugs.

Antidepressant drugs are needed. They inhibit the enzymes that degrade noradrenaline, so noradrenaline is metabolised slowly and activates its receptor for longer.

Examples: iproniazid and phenelzine.

Why are cimetidine and ranitidine better antacids than sodium hydrogencarbonate or magnesium or aluminium hydroxide?

  • NaHCO3 and metal hydroxides only neutralise the acid already present; they control the symptoms, not the cause. Excess NaHCO3 can even make the stomach alkaline and trigger more acid production.
  • Cimetidine and ranitidine prevent the interaction of histamine with the receptors in the stomach wall. Since histamine stimulates acid secretion, less acid is released. They therefore act on the cause of hyperacidity.

What is meant by the term 'broad spectrum antibiotics'? Explain.

Antibiotics which kill or inhibit a wide range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria are called broad spectrum antibiotics.

Examples: ampicillin, amoxycillin, chloramphenicol, vancomycin and ofloxacin. In contrast, penicillin G is a narrow spectrum antibiotic.

How do antiseptics differ from disinfectants? Give one example of each.

  • Antiseptics are applied to living tissues such as wounds, cuts, ulcers and diseased skin. Example: dettol (or tincture of iodine).
  • Disinfectants are applied to inanimate objects such as floors, drains and instruments. Example: 1% phenol solution (or chlorine at 0.2 - 0.4 ppm).

Name a substance which can be used as an antiseptic as well as disinfectant.

Phenol: a 0.2% solution is an antiseptic, while a 1% solution is a disinfectant.

What are the main constituents of dettol?

Dettol is a mixture of chloroxylenol and terpineol.

What is tincture of iodine? What is its use?

A 2-3% solution of iodine in an alcohol-water mixture is called tincture of iodine. It is a powerful antiseptic and is applied on wounds.

docs.title: Chemicals in Food
docs.text:
What are food preservatives?

Food preservatives are chemicals that prevent the spoilage of food due to microbial growth. Examples: table salt, sugar, vegetable oils, sodium benzoate (C6H5COONa), and salts of sorbic acid and propanoic acid.

Why do we require artificial sweetening agents?

Natural sweeteners like sucrose add to the calorie intake and are harmful for diabetic patients. Artificial sweeteners give a sweet taste while adding little or no calories. They are useful for diabetic persons and for people who need to control calorie intake.

What are artificial sweetening agents? Give two examples.

Artificial sweetening agents are chemical substances that taste sweet but add little or no calories to the body. Examples: saccharin and aspartame (others: sucrolose, alitame).

Why is use of aspartame limited to cold foods and drinks?

Aspartame is unstable at cooking temperature; it decomposes on heating. Hence it is used only in cold foods and soft drinks.

Name the sweetening agent used in the preparation of sweets for a diabetic patient.

Sucrolose is suitable, as it is stable at cooking temperature and provides no calories. (Saccharin and alitame can also be used.)

What problem arises in using alitame as artificial sweetener?

Alitame is a high-potency sweetener (about 2000 times as sweet as cane sugar), so it is difficult to control the sweetness of food while using it.

docs.title: Cleansing Agents
docs.text:
Write the chemical equation for preparing sodium soap from glyceryl oleate and glyceryl palmitate.(i) (C15H31COO)3C3H5 - Glyceryl palmitate(ii) (C17H32COO)3C3H5 - Glyceryl oleate

Heating each fat with aqueous NaOH (saponification) gives the sodium soap and glycerol:

\[\underset{Glyceryl\ palmitate}{(C_{15}H_{31}COO)_3C_3H_5} + 3NaOH → \underset{Sodium\ palmitate}{3C_{15}H_{31}COONa} + \underset{Glycerol}{C_3H_5(OH)_3}\] \[\underset{Glyceryl\ oleate}{(C_{17}H_{32}COO)_3C_3H_5} + 3NaOH → \underset{Sodium\ oleate}{3C_{17}H_{32}COONa} + \underset{Glycerol}{C_3H_5(OH)_3}\]

Why do soaps not work in hard water?

Hard water contains Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions. These form insoluble calcium and magnesium soaps with sodium or potassium soaps:

\[2C_{17}H_{35}COONa + CaCl_2 → 2NaCl + (C_{17}H_{35}COO)_2Ca ↓\]

The insoluble soap separates as scum, which is useless for cleaning and sticks to cloth as a gummy mass. So soap is wasted and does not lather.

How are synthetic detergents better than soaps?

  • Synthetic detergents can be used in both soft and hard water, because their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble. Soaps form scum in hard water.
  • Some detergents give foam even in ice-cold water.
  • They do not leave a gummy precipitate on clothes.

Explain the following terms with suitable examples: (i) cationic detergents (ii) anionic detergents and (iii) non-ionic detergents.

(i) Cationic detergents: Quaternary ammonium salts of amines with acetate, chloride or bromide anions. The cationic part has a long hydrocarbon chain and a positive charge on nitrogen. Example: cetyltrimethylammonium bromide, [CH3(CH2)15N(CH3)3]+Br-, used in hair conditioners.

(ii) Anionic detergents: Sodium salts of sulphonated long-chain alcohols or hydrocarbons; the anionic part does the cleansing. Examples: sodium laurylsulphate, CH3(CH2)10CH2OSO3-Na+, and sodium dodecylbenzenesulphonate.

(iii) Non-ionic detergents: Contain no ions. Example: the ester formed from stearic acid and polyethyleneglycol, CH3(CH2)16COO(CH2CH2O)nCH2CH2OH, used in liquid dishwashing detergents.

What are biodegradable and non-biodegradable detergents? Give one example of each.

  • Biodegradable detergents have straight (unbranched) hydrocarbon chains and are easily degraded by bacteria. Example: sodium laurylsulphate.
  • Non-biodegradable detergents have highly branched hydrocarbon chains which bacteria cannot degrade easily, so they accumulate and pollute water bodies. Example: sodium 4-(1,3,5,7-tetramethyloctyl)benzenesulphonate.

Can you use soaps and synthetic detergents to check the hardness of water?

Soaps can be used: in hard water they form a curdy precipitate (scum) and lather poorly, while in soft water they lather easily.

Synthetic detergents cannot be used, because they lather well in both hard and soft water.

If water contains dissolved calcium hydrogencarbonate, out of soaps and synthetic detergents which one will you use for cleaning clothes?

Water containing Ca(HCO3)2 is hard. Soap would form insoluble calcium soap (scum) with Ca2+ ions. Hence synthetic detergents should be used, as they work well even in hard water.

Explain the cleansing action of soaps.

  • A soap anion (e.g., C17H35COO-) has a long non-polar hydrophobic tail and a polar hydrophilic head (-COO-).
  • In water, the anions form micelles: the hydrophobic tails dissolve in the oily dirt, while the ionic heads stay in water, pointing outwards.
  • The oil drop is thus surrounded by negatively charged heads. These charged droplets repel each other and stay emulsified in water instead of coalescing.
  • On rinsing, the emulsified oil along with the dirt is washed away.

Label the hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts in the following compounds:(i) CH3(CH2)10CH2OSO3-Na+(ii) CH3(CH2)15N+(CH3)3Br-(iii) CH3(CH2)16COO(CH2CH2O)nCH2CH2OH

Compound Hydrophobic part (tail) Hydrophilic part (head) (i) CH3(CH2)10CH2- -OSO3-Na+ (ii) CH3(CH2)15- -N+(CH3)3Br- (iii) CH3(CH2)16- -COO(CH2CH2O)nCH2CH2OH

The non-ionic detergent C9H19-C6H4-O(CH2CH2O)xCH2CH2OH (x = 5 to 10, para-substituted benzene ring) is present in liquid detergents, emulsifying agents and wetting agents. Label the hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts in the molecule. Identify the functional group(s) present.

  • Hydrophobic (non-polar) part: the C9H19-C6H4- portion (alkyl chain plus benzene ring).
  • Hydrophilic (polar) part: the -O(CH2CH2O)xCH2CH2OH chain.
  • Functional groups: ether linkages (-O-) and a primary alcohol group (-OH).

docs.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life | Therapeutic Action of Drugs
Chemistry in Everyday Life | Therapeutic Action of Drugs
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss how some important classes of drugs act on the body: antacids, antihistamines, neurologically active drugs, antimicrobials and antifertility drugs.

docs.title: 1. Antacids
docs.text:
• Overproduction of acid in the stomach causes irritation and pain. In severe cases, ulcers develop in the stomach.
  • Until 1970, the only treatment was an antacid such as sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO3) or a mixture of aluminium and magnesium hydroxide.
\[NaHCO_3 + HCl → NaCl + H_2O + CO_2\] \[Mg(OH)_2 + 2HCl → MgCl_2 + 2H_2O\]
  • Drawback of NaHCO3: an excess can make the stomach alkaline, which triggers the production of even more acid.
  • Metal hydroxides are better: being insoluble, they do not raise the pH above neutrality.
  • However, both treatments only control the symptoms, not the cause. In advanced stages ulcers become life-threatening, and the only remedy used to be removal of the affected part of the stomach.

docs.title: Cimetidine and Ranitidine
docs.text:
• A major breakthrough came with the discovery that histamine stimulates the secretion of pepsin and hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
  • The drug cimetidine (Tagamet) was designed to prevent the interaction of histamine with the receptors in the stomach wall, so less acid is released. It remained the world's largest-selling drug until ranitidine (Zantac) was discovered.
  • These drugs act on the cause (histamine-triggered acid release), which is why they are better antacids than NaHCO3 or metal hydroxides.

docs.title: 2. Antihistamines
docs.text:
• Histamine is a potent vasodilator. It contracts the smooth muscles in the bronchi and gut, and relaxes other muscles such as those in the walls of fine blood vessels.
  • Histamine is also responsible for the nasal congestion of a common cold and for the allergic response to pollen.
  • Synthetic drugs brompheniramine (Dimetapp) and terfenadine (Seldane) act as antihistamines. They compete with histamine for the binding sites of the receptors where histamine exerts its effect.

Why don't antihistamines affect the secretion of acid in the stomach?

Antiallergic drugs (antihistamines) and antacid drugs (like cimetidine) work on different receptors. Hence, an antihistamine that blocks the allergy receptor does not block the receptor in the stomach wall, and vice versa.

docs.title: 3. Neurologically Active Drugs
docs.text: Tranquilizers and analgesics are neurologically active drugs. They affect the message transfer mechanism from nerve to receptor.

docs.title: (a) Tranquilizers
docs.text:
• Tranquilizers are used for the treatment of stress and of mild or even severe mental diseases.
  • They relieve anxiety, stress, irritability or excitement by inducing a sense of well-being. They are an essential component of sleeping pills.
  • Different tranquilizers work by different mechanisms:

docs.title: Antidepressants
docs.text:
• Noradrenaline is a neurotransmitter that plays a role in mood changes. If its level is low, signal-sending activity falls and the person suffers from depression.
  • Antidepressant drugs inhibit the enzymes which catalyse the degradation of noradrenaline. The neurotransmitter is then metabolised slowly and can activate its receptor for longer periods, counteracting depression.
  • Examples: iproniazid and phenelzine.

docs.title: Mild tranquilizers
docs.text:
• Chlordiazepoxide and meprobamate are relatively mild tranquilizers used for relieving tension.
  • Equanil is used to control depression and hypertension.

docs.title: Barbiturates
docs.text:
• Derivatives of barbituric acid, such as veronal, amytal, nembutal, luminal and seconal, are called barbiturates. They are an important class of tranquilizers.
  • Barbiturates are hypnotic, i.e., sleep-producing agents.
  • Other substances used as tranquilizers are valium and serotonin.

docs.title: (b) Analgesics
docs.text: Analgesics reduce or abolish pain without causing impairment of consciousness, mental confusion, incoordination, paralysis or other disturbances of the nervous system. They are of two types:

docs.title: (i) Non-narcotic (non-addictive) analgesics
docs.text:
• Examples: aspirin and paracetamol.
  • Aspirin inhibits the synthesis of prostaglandins, chemicals which stimulate inflammation in tissue and cause pain.
  • These drugs are effective in relieving skeletal pain such as that due to arthritis.
  • They also reduce fever (antipyretic action) and prevent platelet coagulation. Because of its anti-blood-clotting action, aspirin is used to prevent heart attacks.

docs.title: (ii) Narcotic analgesics
docs.text:
• Morphine and many of its homologues (such as heroin and codeine) relieve pain and produce sleep when given in medicinal doses.
  • In poisonous doses they produce stupor, coma, convulsions and ultimately death.
  • Morphine narcotics are also called opiates, since they are obtained from the opium poppy.
  • They are mainly used for the relief of postoperative pain, cardiac pain, pains of terminal cancer, and in childbirth.

docs.title: 4. Antimicrobials
docs.text:
• Diseases may be caused by microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and other pathogens.
  • An antimicrobial selectively destroys, prevents the development of, or inhibits the pathogenic action of microbes. Depending on the target they are antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral or antiparasitic drugs.
  • Antibiotics, antiseptics and disinfectants are antimicrobial drugs.

docs.title: (a) Antibiotics
docs.text:
• Antibiotics are used to treat infections because of their low toxicity to humans and animals.
  • Originally, antibiotics meant chemicals produced by microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, moulds) that inhibit the growth of, or destroy, other microorganisms.
  • Since many are now made synthetically, the definition has been modified: an antibiotic is a substance produced wholly or partly by chemical synthesis which, in low concentrations, inhibits the growth of or destroys microorganisms by intervening in their metabolic processes.

docs.title: History of antibacterial drugs
docs.text:
• Paul Ehrlich investigated arsenic-based compounds to treat syphilis and developed arsphenamine, known as salvarsan (Nobel Prize in Medicine, 1908). It was the first effective treatment for syphilis. Salvarsan is toxic to humans, but far more toxic to the spirochete bacteria that cause syphilis.
  • Ehrlich noted that the -As=As- linkage of salvarsan resembles the -N=N- linkage of azo dyes. He searched for azo-dye-like compounds that bind selectively to bacteria, and in 1932 the first effective antibacterial agent, prontosil, was prepared.
  • In the body, prontosil is converted to sulphanilamide, which is the real active compound. This led to the sulpha drugs; one of the most effective is sulphapyridine.
  • The real revolution came with Alexander Fleming's discovery (1929) of the antibacterial properties of a Penicillium fungus. Isolating and purifying enough penicillin for clinical trials took 13 years. Fleming and H.W. Florey shared the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1945.

docs.title: Bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics
docs.text:
Antibiotics have either a cidal (killing) effect or a static (inhibitory) effect on microbes.

Bactericidal (kill microbes) Bacteriostatic (inhibit growth) Penicillin Erythromycin Aminoglycosides Tetracycline Ofloxacin Chloramphenicol

docs.title: Spectrum of action
docs.text:
The range of microorganisms affected by an antibiotic is called its spectrum of action.
