Type Effective against Examples Broad spectrum antibiotics A wide range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria Ampicillin, amoxycillin, chloramphenicol, vancomycin, ofloxacin Narrow spectrum antibiotics Mainly Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria Penicillin G Limited spectrum antibiotics A single organism or disease -
  • Ampicillin and amoxycillin are synthetic modifications of penicillin with a broad spectrum.
  • Patients must be tested for sensitivity (allergy) to penicillin before it is given. In India, penicillin is manufactured at Hindustan Antibiotics, Pimpri, and in the private sector.
  • Chloramphenicol (isolated in 1947) is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, so it can be given orally for typhoid, dysentery, acute fever, some urinary infections, meningitis and pneumonia.
  • The antibiotic dysidazirine is believed to be toxic towards certain strains of cancer cells.

docs.title: (b) Antiseptics and Disinfectants
docs.text:
Both kill or prevent the growth of microorganisms. The difference lies in where they are applied.

Antiseptics Disinfectants Applied to living tissues such as wounds, cuts, ulcers and diseased skin Applied to inanimate objects such as floors, drains and instruments Safe for living tissue Harmful to living tissue Examples: furacine, soframicine, dettol, tincture of iodine, iodoform, boric acid Examples: 1% phenol, chlorine (0.2 - 0.4 ppm), SO2 in low concentration

docs.title: Common antiseptics
docs.text:
• Dettol is a mixture of chloroxylenol and terpineol.
  • Bithionol (also called bithional) is added to soaps to give them antiseptic properties.
  • Iodine is a powerful antiseptic. A 2-3% solution of iodine in alcohol-water mixture is called tincture of iodine and is applied on wounds.
  • Iodoform (CHI3) is also used as an antiseptic for wounds.
  • Boric acid in dilute aqueous solution is a weak antiseptic for eyes.
  • Antiseptics are not ingested like antibiotics.

Same substance as antiseptic and disinfectant

The same substance can act as an antiseptic or a disinfectant depending on its concentration. A 0.2% solution of phenol is an antiseptic, while a 1% solution is a disinfectant.

docs.title: 5. Antifertility Drugs
docs.text:
• Antibiotics have nearly doubled life expectancy. The resulting population growth has created problems of food, environment and employment, which led to the concept of family planning. Antifertility drugs help in this direction.
  • Birth control pills contain a mixture of synthetic estrogen and progesterone derivatives. Both are hormones.
  • Progesterone suppresses ovulation. Synthetic progesterone derivatives are more potent than progesterone itself.
  • Norethindrone is the most widely used synthetic progesterone derivative in antifertility drugs.
  • The estrogen derivative used in combination with it is ethynylestradiol (novestrol).

docs.title: Hydrocarbons | Chemical Properties and Conformations of Alkanes
Hydrocarbons | Chemical Properties and Conformations of Alkanes
docs.text: Alkanes are generally inert towards acids, bases, oxidising and reducing agents. However, under certain conditions they undergo the following reactions.

docs.title: 1. Substitution Reactions
docs.text:
• One or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane can be replaced by halogens, nitro group or sulphonic acid group. Such reactions are called substitution reactions.
  • Lower alkanes do not undergo nitration and sulphonation.

docs.title: Halogenation
docs.text:
Halogenation takes place either at high temperature (573–773 K) or in the presence of diffused sunlight or ultraviolet light. Chlorination of methane continues step by step until all four hydrogens are replaced:

\[CH_4 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h u} CH_3Cl + HCl\ \ \ (Chloromethane)\] \[CH_3Cl + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h u} CH_2Cl_2 + HCl\ \ \ (Dichloromethane)\] \[CH_2Cl_2 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h u} CHCl_3 + HCl\ \ \ (Trichloromethane)\] \[CHCl_3 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h u} CCl_4 + HCl\ \ \ (Tetrachloromethane)\] \[CH_3-CH_3 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h u} CH_3-CH_2Cl + HCl\ \ \ (Chloroethane)\]
  • Rate of reaction of alkanes with halogens:
\[F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2\]
  • Rate of replacement of hydrogens of alkanes:
\[3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ\]
  • Fluorination is too violent to be controlled. Iodination is very slow and reversible. It is carried out in the presence of oxidising agents like HIO3 or HNO3, which destroy the HI formed:
\[CH_4 + I_2 ⇌ CH_3I + HI\] \[HIO_3 + 5HI → 3I_2 + 3H_2O\]

docs.title: Mechanism of Halogenation (Free Radical Chain Mechanism)
docs.text: Halogenation proceeds through a free radical chain mechanism in three steps.

docs.title: (i) Initiation
docs.text:
The reaction starts with homolysis of the chlorine molecule by light or heat. The Cl–Cl bond is weaker than the C–C and C–H bonds, so it breaks most easily.

\[Cl-Cl \xrightarrow[homolysis]{h\nu} \dot{C}l + \dot{C}l\]

docs.title: (ii) Propagation
docs.text:
The chlorine free radical attacks methane, breaking a C–H bond to give a methyl free radical and HCl. The methyl radical then attacks another Cl2 molecule to give CH3Cl and a new chlorine radical.

\[(a)\ CH_4 + \dot{C}l \xrightarrow{h\nu} \dot{C}H_3 + HCl\] \[(b)\ \dot{C}H_3 + Cl-Cl \xrightarrow{h\nu} CH_3-Cl + \dot{C}l\]
  • Steps (a) and (b) repeat, setting up a chain. Other propagation steps explain how more highly halogenated products are formed:
\[CH_3Cl + \dot{C}l → \dot{C}H_2Cl + HCl\] \[\dot{C}H_2Cl + Cl-Cl → CH_2Cl_2 + \dot{C}l\]

docs.title: (iii) Termination
docs.text:
The reaction stops when reactants are used up or when free radicals combine with each other:

\[(a)\ \dot{C}l + \dot{C}l → Cl-Cl\] \[(b)\ H_3\dot{C} + \dot{C}H_3 → H_3C-CH_3\] \[(c)\ H_3\dot{C} + \dot{C}l → H_3C-Cl\]

Conclusion

In step (c), CH3Cl is formed but the radicals are consumed, so the chain ends. Step (b) explains why ethane is formed as a by-product during chlorination of methane.

docs.title: 2. Combustion
docs.text:
Alkanes burn in air or dioxygen and are completely oxidised to CO2 and water, with the evolution of a large amount of heat. That is why alkanes are used as fuels.

\[CH_{4(g)} + 2O_{2(g)} → CO_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)};\ \ \Delta_cH^\circ = -890\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\] \[C_4H_{10(g)} + {13 \over 2}O_{2(g)} → 4CO_{2(g)} + 5H_2O_{(l)};\ \ \Delta_cH^\circ = -2875.84\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • General combustion equation for any alkane:
\[C_nH_{2n+2} + \left({3n+1 \over 2}\right)O_2 → nCO_2 + (n+1)H_2O\]
  • With an insufficient supply of air, incomplete combustion gives carbon black, which is used in making ink, printer ink, black pigments and as filters.
\[CH_{4(g)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Incomplete\ combustion} C_{(s)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}\]

docs.title: 3. Controlled Oxidation
docs.text:
Heating alkanes with a regulated supply of air or O2 at high pressure, in the presence of suitable catalysts, gives a variety of oxidation products:

\[2CH_4 + O_2 \xrightarrow{Cu/523\ K/100\ atm} 2CH_3OH\ \ \ (Methanol)\] \[CH_4 + O_2 \xrightarrow[Δ]{Mo_2O_3} HCHO + H_2O\ \ \ (Methanal)\] \[2CH_3CH_3 + 3O_2 \xrightarrow[Δ]{(CH_3COO)_2Mn} 2CH_3COOH + 2H_2O\ \ \ (Ethanoic\ acid)\]
  • Ordinarily alkanes resist oxidation, but alkanes having a tertiary H atom are oxidised to the corresponding alcohols by KMnO4:
\[(CH_3)_3CH \xrightarrow[Oxidation]{KMnO_4} (CH_3)_3COH\] \[2\text{-}Methylpropane → 2\text{-}Methylpropan\text{-}2\text{-}ol\]

docs.title: 4. Isomerisation
docs.text:
n-Alkanes, on heating with anhydrous AlCl3 and HCl gas, isomerise to branched chain alkanes:

\[CH_3(CH_2)_4CH_3 \xrightarrow{Anhy.\ AlCl_3/HCl} CH_3CH(CH_3)(CH_2)_2CH_3 + CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH_2CH_3\] \[n\text{-}Hexane → 2\text{-}Methylpentane + 3\text{-}Methylpentane\]

docs.title: 5. Aromatisation (Reforming)
docs.text:
n-Alkanes with six or more carbon atoms, on heating to 773 K at 10–20 atm in the presence of oxides of vanadium, molybdenum or chromium supported on alumina, are dehydrogenated and cyclised to benzene and its homologues.

\[CH_3(CH_2)_4CH_3 \xrightarrow[773\ K,\ 10-20\ atm]{Cr_2O_3\ or\ V_2O_5\ or\ Mo_2O_3} C_6H_6 + 4H_2\] \[n\text{-}Hexane → Benzene\]
  • Toluene (C6H5CH3) can similarly be prepared from n-heptane.

docs.title: 6. Reaction with Steam
docs.text:
Methane reacts with steam at 1273 K in the presence of nickel to give CO and H2. This is used for the industrial preparation of dihydrogen.

\[CH_4 + H_2O \xrightarrow[Δ]{Ni} CO + 3H_2\]

docs.title: 7. Pyrolysis (Cracking)
docs.text:
• Higher alkanes, on heating to high temperature, decompose into lower alkanes, alkenes, etc. This decomposition by heat is called pyrolysis or cracking. It is believed to be a free radical reaction.
\[C_6H_{14} \xrightarrow{773\ K} C_6H_{12} + H_2\] \[C_6H_{14} \xrightarrow{773\ K} C_4H_8 + C_2H_6\] \[C_6H_{14} \xrightarrow{773\ K} C_3H_6 + C_2H_4 + CH_4\]
  • Oil gas or petrol gas is prepared from kerosene or petrol on this principle. For example, dodecane (from kerosene) at 973 K with Pt, Pd or Ni gives heptane and pentene:
\[C_{12}H_{26} \xrightarrow[973\ K]{Pt/Pd/Ni} C_7H_{16} + C_5H_{10} + other\ products\]

docs.title: Conformations of Alkanes
docs.text:
• The electron distribution of a C–C σ bond is symmetrical about the internuclear axis and is not disturbed by rotation. This permits free rotation about C–C single bonds.
  • Spatial arrangements of atoms which can be converted into one another by rotation around a C–C single bond are called conformations, conformers or rotamers.
  • The rotation is not completely free. It is hindered by a small energy barrier of 1–20 kJ mol-1 due to weak repulsion between adjacent bonds. This repulsion is called torsional strain.

docs.title: Conformations of Ethane
docs.text:
If one carbon of ethane is kept fixed and the other is rotated about the C–C axis, an infinite number of conformations result. Two of them are extreme cases:

  • Eclipsed conformation: the hydrogen atoms on the two carbons are as close together as possible.
  • Staggered conformation: the hydrogen atoms are as far apart as possible.
  • Any intermediate conformation is called a skew conformation.
  • Bond angles and bond lengths remain the same in all conformations.

docs.title: 1. Sawhorse Projection
docs.text:
• The molecule is viewed along the C–C axis and drawn with the C–C bond as a longer slanted line.
  • The front carbon is at the lower end and the rear carbon at the upper end. Each carbon has three lines (C–H bonds) at 120° to each other.

docs.title: 2. Newman Projection
docs.text:
• The molecule is viewed along the C–C bond head on.
  • The front carbon is shown as a point with three C–H bonds at 120°. The rear carbon is shown as a circle, with its three C–H bonds as shorter lines coming out of the circle.
  • The angle between C–H bonds on the front and rear carbons is the dihedral angle (torsional angle or angle of rotation).

docs.title: Relative Stability of Conformations
docs.text:
• In the staggered form, C–H bond electron clouds are as far apart as possible. So repulsion is minimum, energy is minimum and stability is maximum.
  • In the eclipsed form, the electron clouds come closer, repulsion increases, and the molecule has higher energy and lower stability.
  • Magnitude of torsional strain depends on the dihedral angle.

Conclusion

The staggered form has the least torsional strain and the eclipsed form has the maximum. The energy difference between them is only about 12.5 kJ mol-1. Even at ordinary temperatures, molecules gain enough energy from collisions to cross this barrier, so rotation about the C–C bond in ethane is almost free and its conformers cannot be separated.

docs.title: Hydrocarbons | Alkenes
docs.text:
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.

  • With one double bond, an alkene has two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane. So the general formula is:
\[C_nH_{2n}\]
  • Alkenes are also called olefins (oil forming), because the first member, ethylene (C2H4), forms an oily liquid with chlorine.

docs.title: Structure of the Double Bond
docs.text:
• A C=C double bond consists of one strong σ bond (bond enthalpy about 397 kJ mol-1), formed by head-on overlap of sp2 hybrid orbitals, and one weak π bond (about 284 kJ mol-1), formed by sideways overlap of the two unhybridised 2p orbitals.
  • The C=C bond length (134 pm) is shorter than the C–C single bond (154 pm).
  • In ethene, each carbon is sp2 hybridised. The H–C–C angle is 121.7°, the H–C–H angle is 116.6° and the C–H bond length is 110 pm. The π electron cloud lies above and below the plane of the molecule.
  • The C=C bond enthalpy (681 kJ mol-1) is greater than that of the C–C single bond in ethane (348 kJ mol-1).

Conclusion

The π bond is weak and its electrons are loosely held. So alkenes act as a source of mobile electrons and are easily attacked by electrophilic reagents (electron seeking species). This makes alkenes less stable than alkanes, and they readily add reagents to become single-bonded compounds.

docs.title: Nomenclature
docs.text:
• The longest chain containing the double bond is selected.
  • Numbering starts from the end nearer to the double bond.
  • The suffix '-ane' of the alkane is replaced by '-ene'.
  • The first member, CH2 (methene), has a very short life. The first stable member is C2H4, ethylene (common) or ethene (IUPAC).
Structure IUPAC Name CH3–CH=CH2 Propene CH3–CH2–CH=CH2 But-1-ene CH3–CH=CH–CH3 But-2-ene CH2=CH–CH=CH2 Buta-1,3-diene CH2=C(CH3)–CH3 2-Methylprop-1-ene CH2=CH–CH(CH3)–CH3 3-Methylbut-1-ene

docs.title: Isomerism in Alkenes
docs.text: Alkenes show both structural isomerism and geometrical isomerism.

docs.title: 1. Structural Isomerism
docs.text:
Ethene and propene have only one structure each. C4H8 can be written in three ways:

Isomers of C4H8

\[I.\ CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (But\text{-}1\text{-}ene)\] \[II.\ CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3\ \ \ (But\text{-}2\text{-}ene)\] \[III.\ CH_2=C(CH_3)-CH_3\ \ \ (2\text{-}Methylprop\text{-}1\text{-}ene)\]
  • I and III, and II and III, are chain isomers.
  • I and II are position isomers (they differ in the position of the double bond).

docs.title: 2. Geometrical Isomerism
docs.text:
• Rotation about a C=C bond is restricted, because rotating would break the π bond.
  • If each doubly bonded carbon carries two different atoms or groups (type YXC=CXY), two different spatial arrangements are possible. Such stereoisomers are called geometrical isomers.
  • Cis isomer: identical atoms or groups lie on the same side of the double bond.
  • Trans isomer: identical atoms or groups lie on opposite sides of the double bond.
  • Cis and trans isomers have the same structure but different configuration, so they differ in m.p., b.p., dipole moment, solubility, etc.

Example: But-2-ene

  • cis-But-2-ene: both CH3 groups on the same side; b.p. 277 K; dipole moment 0.33 D.
  • trans-But-2-ene: CH3 groups on opposite sides; b.p. 274 K; dipole moment almost zero.
  • The cis form is more polar. In the trans form, the two C–CH3 bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel each other, making it non-polar.
  • Among solids, the trans isomer has a higher melting point than the cis form (it packs better).
  • Geometrical isomerism is also shown by alkenes of the types XYC=CXZ and XYC=CZW.

Note

If either doubly bonded carbon carries two identical groups (for example (CH3)2C=CH–C2H5 or CH2=CBr2), cis-trans isomerism is not possible.

docs.title: 1. From Alkynes (Partial Reduction)
docs.text:
• Alkynes are partially reduced with a calculated amount of H2 in the presence of palladised charcoal partially deactivated with poisons like sulphur compounds or quinoline. This catalyst is called Lindlar's catalyst. The alkene formed has cis geometry.
  • Reduction with sodium in liquid ammonia gives trans alkenes.
\[RC \equiv CR' + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd/C} cis\text{-}RCH=CHR'\] \[RC \equiv CR' + H_2 \xrightarrow{Na/liquid\ NH_3} trans\text{-}RCH=CHR'\] \[CH \equiv CH + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd/C} CH_2=CH_2\] \[CH_3-C \equiv CH + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd/C} CH_3-CH=CH_2\]
  • Propene obtained this way does not show geometrical isomerism, because one of its doubly bonded carbons (=CH2) has two identical H atoms.

docs.title: 2. From Alkyl Halides (Dehydrohalogenation)
docs.text:
• Alkyl halides, on heating with alcoholic KOH, eliminate one molecule of halogen acid to form alkenes. This is called dehydrohalogenation.
  • It is a β-elimination reaction, because the H atom is removed from the β-carbon (the carbon next to the one carrying the halogen).
\[CH_3-CH_2X \xrightarrow[Δ]{alc.\ KOH} CH_2=CH_2 + HX\ \ \ (X = Cl,\ Br,\ I)\]
  • Rate depends on the halogen and the alkyl group:
\[Halogen:\ I > Br > Cl\] \[Alkyl\ group:\ tert > sec > primary\]

docs.title: 3. From Vicinal Dihalides (Dehalogenation)
docs.text:
Dihalides with the two halogens on adjacent carbons are called vicinal dihalides. On treatment with zinc metal they lose ZnX2 to form alkenes. This is called dehalogenation.

\[CH_2Br-CH_2Br + Zn → CH_2=CH_2 + ZnBr_2\] \[CH_3CHBr-CH_2Br + Zn → CH_3CH=CH_2 + ZnBr_2\]

docs.title: 4. From Alcohols (Acidic Dehydration)
docs.text:
Alcohols, on heating with concentrated sulphuric acid, lose a water molecule to form alkenes. This is also a β-elimination, since the –OH group takes out one H atom from the β-carbon.

\[CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow[Δ]{Conc.\ H_2SO_4} CH_2=CH_2 + H_2O\]

docs.title: Physical Properties of Alkenes
docs.text:
• Alkenes resemble alkanes in physical properties, except in the types of isomerism and polar nature.
  • The first three members are gases, the next fourteen are liquids and the higher ones are solids.
  • Ethene is a colourless gas with a faint sweet smell. Other alkenes are colourless and odourless.
  • They are insoluble in water but fairly soluble in non-polar solvents like benzene and petroleum ether.
  • Boiling point rises regularly with size: every –CH2 group added increases b.p. by 20–30 K. Straight chain alkenes boil higher than their branched isomers.

docs.title: Hydrocarbons | Alkynes
docs.text:
Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one triple bond between two carbon atoms. They have even fewer hydrogen atoms than alkenes or alkanes.

\[General\ formula:\ C_nH_{2n-2}\]
  • The first stable member is ethyne, popularly known as acetylene. It is used for arc welding in the form of the oxyacetylene flame (acetylene mixed with oxygen).
  • Alkynes are starting materials for a large number of organic compounds.

docs.title: Nomenclature and Isomerism
docs.text:
• In the common system, alkynes are named as derivatives of acetylene.
  • In the IUPAC system, the suffix '-ane' of the corresponding alkane is replaced by '-yne'. The position of the triple bond is indicated by the first triply bonded carbon.
Value of n Formula Structure Common name IUPAC name 2 C2H2 H–C≡C–H Acetylene Ethyne 3 C3H4 CH3–C≡CH Methylacetylene Propyne 4 C4H6 CH3CH2–C≡CH Ethylacetylene But-1-yne 4 C4H6 CH3–C≡C–CH3 Dimethylacetylene But-2-yne
  • Ethyne and propyne have only one structure each. But-1-yne and but-2-yne differ in the position of the triple bond, so they are position isomers.
  • For C5H8, three structures are possible:

Isomers of C5H8

\[I.\ HC \equiv C-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (Pent\text{-}1\text{-}yne)\] \[II.\ H_3C-C \equiv C-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (Pent\text{-}2\text{-}yne)\] \[III.\ H_3C-CH(CH_3)-C \equiv CH\ \ \ (3\text{-}Methylbut\text{-}1\text{-}yne)\]

I and II are position isomers. I and III, or II and III, are chain isomers.

docs.title: Structure of the Triple Bond
docs.text:
• Each carbon atom of ethyne has two sp hybrid orbitals.
  • A C–C σ bond is formed by head-on overlap of one sp orbital from each carbon. The other sp orbital of each carbon overlaps with the 1s orbital of a hydrogen atom to form two C–H σ bonds. The H–C–C bond angle is 180°.
  • Each carbon still has two unhybridised p orbitals, perpendicular to each other and to the C–C axis. These overlap sideways with those of the other carbon to form two π bonds.
  • So ethyne has one C–C σ bond, two C–H σ bonds and two C–C π bonds.
  • The electron cloud between the two carbons is cylindrically symmetrical about the internuclear axis. Thus, ethyne is a linear molecule.
Bond Bond enthalpy (kJ mol-1) Bond length (pm) C≡C 823 120 C=C 681 133 C–C 348 154

docs.title: 1. From Calcium Carbide
docs.text:
On industrial scale, ethyne is prepared by treating calcium carbide with water. Calcium carbide is made by heating quick lime with coke, and quick lime is obtained by heating limestone.

\[CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{Δ} CaO + CO_2\] \[CaO + 3C → CaC_2 + CO\] \[CaC_2 + 2H_2O → Ca(OH)_2 + C_2H_2\]

docs.title: 2. From Vicinal Dihalides
docs.text:
Vicinal dihalides undergo dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH. One molecule of HX is eliminated to give an alkenyl halide, which on treatment with sodamide (NaNH2) gives the alkyne.

\[CH_2Br-CH_2Br + KOH \xrightarrow{alcohol} CH_2=CHBr + KBr + H_2O\] \[CH_2=CHBr + NaNH_2 → CH \equiv CH + NaBr + NH_3\]

docs.title: Physical Properties
docs.text:
• Physical properties follow the same trend as alkenes and alkanes.
  • The first three members are gases, the next eight are liquids and the higher ones are solids.
  • All alkynes are colourless. Ethyne has a characteristic odour; other members are odourless.
  • Alkynes are weakly polar, lighter than water and immiscible with it, but soluble in organic solvents like ethers, CCl4 and benzene.
  • Melting point, boiling point and density increase with molar mass.

docs.title: A. Acidic Character of Alkynes
docs.text:
Sodium metal and sodamide (NaNH2) are strong bases. They react with ethyne to form sodium acetylide with the liberation of H2. Ethene and ethane do not show such reactions.

\[HC \equiv CH + Na → HC \equiv C^-Na^+ + {1 \over 2}H_2\ \ \ (Monosodium\ ethynide)\] \[HC \equiv C^-Na^+ + Na → Na^+\ ^-C \equiv C^-Na^+ + {1 \over 2}H_2\ \ \ (Disodium\ ethynide)\] \[CH_3-C \equiv C-H + Na^+NH_2^- → CH_3-C \equiv C^-Na^+ + NH_3\ \ \ (Sodium\ propynide)\]

docs.title: Reason for acidity
docs.text:
• In ethyne, the hydrogen atoms are attached to sp hybridised carbon. In ethene they are attached to sp2 and in ethane to sp3 carbon.
  • The sp orbital has the maximum s character (50%), so the sp carbon is the most electronegative. It pulls the shared electron pair of the C–H bond towards itself more strongly than sp2 or sp3 carbon.
  • Hence the H atom of ethyne is released as a proton more easily.
  • Only hydrogens attached to the triply bonded carbon are acidic, not all the hydrogens of an alkyne. So but-1-yne reacts with Na or NaNH2, but but-2-yne does not.

Order of acidic character

\[HC \equiv CH > H_2C=CH_2 > CH_3-CH_3\] \[HC \equiv CH > CH_3-C \equiv CH >> CH_3-C \equiv C-CH_3\]

These reactions are used to distinguish alkynes (with terminal H) from alkenes and alkanes.

docs.title: B. Addition Reactions
docs.text:
Alkynes have a triple bond, so they can add two molecules of H2, halogen, hydrogen halide, etc. Most additions are electrophilic and proceed through a vinylic cation:

\[-C \equiv C- + H-Z \xrightarrow{H^+} -CH=\overset{+}{C}- + Z^- → -CH=CZ-\]

The product depends on the stability of the vinylic cation. In unsymmetrical alkynes, addition follows the Markovnikov rule.

docs.title: (i) Addition of Dihydrogen
docs.text: \[HC \equiv CH + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pt/Pd/Ni} [H_2C=CH_2] \xrightarrow{H_2} CH_3-CH_3\] \[CH_3-C \equiv CH + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pt/Pd/Ni} [CH_3-CH=CH_2] \xrightarrow{H_2} CH_3-CH_2-CH_3\]

docs.title: (ii) Addition of Halogens
docs.text:
\[CH_3-C \equiv CH + Br-Br → [CH_3CBr=CHBr] \xrightarrow{Br_2} CH_3CBr_2-CHBr_2\] \[1,2\text{-}Dibromopropene → 1,1,2,2\text{-}Tetrabromopropane\]
  • The reddish orange colour of Br2 in CCl4 is decolourised. This is a test for unsaturation.

docs.title: (iii) Addition of Hydrogen Halides
docs.text:
Two molecules of HCl, HBr or HI add to give gem dihalides (both halogens on the same carbon).

\[H-C \equiv C-H + H-Br → [CH_2=CH-Br] → CH_3CHBr_2\ \ \ (1,1\text{-}Dibromoethane)\] \[CH_3-C \equiv CH + H-Br → [CH_3-CBr=CH_2] → CH_3-CBr_2-CH_3\ \ \ (2,2\text{-}Dibromopropane)\]

docs.title: (iv) Addition of Water
docs.text:
Alkynes do not react with water normally. However, on warming with mercuric sulphate and dilute sulphuric acid at 333 K, one molecule of water adds to give an enol, which isomerises to a carbonyl compound.

\[HC \equiv CH + H-OH \xrightarrow[333\ K]{Hg^{2+}/H^+} [CH_2=CH-OH] \xrightarrow{Isomerisation} CH_3CHO\ \ \ (Ethanal)\] \[CH_3-C \equiv CH + H-OH \xrightarrow[333\ K]{Hg^{2+}/H^+} [CH_3-C(OH)=CH_2] \xrightarrow{Isomerisation} CH_3COCH_3\ \ \ (Propanone)\]

docs.title: (v) Polymerisation
docs.text:
(a) Linear polymerisation: Under suitable conditions, ethyne polymerises to polyacetylene (polyethyne), a high molecular weight polyene with repeating units –(CH=CH–CH=CH)n–. Under special conditions this polymer conducts electricity. Thin films of polyacetylene are used as electrodes in batteries; they are good conductors, lighter and cheaper than metal conductors.

(b) Cyclic polymerisation: When ethyne is passed through a red hot iron tube at 873 K, three molecules combine to form benzene. This is the best route from aliphatic to aromatic compounds.

\[3HC \equiv CH \xrightarrow[873\ K]{Red\ hot\ iron\ tube} C_6H_6\]

docs.title: Hydrocarbons | Aromatic Hydrocarbons and Structure of Benzene
Hydrocarbons | Aromatic Hydrocarbons and Structure of Benzene
docs.text:
Aromatic hydrocarbons, also known as arenes, are compounds which mostly contain a benzene ring. Since most of them have a pleasant odour (Greek: aroma = pleasant smelling), they were named aromatic compounds.

  • The benzene ring is highly unsaturated, but in most reactions of aromatic compounds this unsaturation is retained.
  • Aromatic compounds containing a benzene ring are called benzenoids. Those that are aromatic without a benzene ring (containing another highly unsaturated ring) are called non-benzenoids.
  • Examples of arenes: benzene (C6H6), toluene (C6H5CH3), naphthalene (C10H8) and biphenyl (C6H5–C6H5).

docs.title: Nomenclature and Isomerism
docs.text:
• All six hydrogen atoms of benzene are equivalent. So benzene forms one and only one monosubstituted product, for example methylbenzene (toluene).
  • When two H atoms are replaced by two similar or different groups, three position isomers are possible:
Positions Prefix Example 1,2 (or 1,6) ortho (o-) 1,2-Dimethylbenzene (o-xylene) 1,3 (or 1,5) meta (m-) 1,3-Dimethylbenzene (m-xylene) 1,4 para (p-) 1,4-Dimethylbenzene (p-xylene)

docs.title: Structure of Benzene
docs.text:
• Benzene was isolated by Michael Faraday in 1825. Its molecular formula C6H6 indicates a high degree of unsaturation, yet it is a very stable molecule.
  • Benzene forms a triozonide, which indicates the presence of three double bonds.
  • It forms only one monosubstituted derivative, which shows that all six carbon and six hydrogen atoms are identical.

docs.title: Kekulé Structure
docs.text:
• In 1865, August Kekulé proposed a cyclic arrangement of six carbon atoms with alternate single and double bonds, and one hydrogen atom on each carbon.
  • This structure predicts two isomeric 1,2-dibromobenzenes: one with the Br atoms on a doubly bonded pair of carbons, the other with Br atoms on a singly bonded pair. But benzene actually forms only one ortho disubstituted product.
  • Kekulé overcame this by suggesting that the double bonds in benzene oscillate between the two possible positions.
  • Even this modification could not explain the unusual stability of benzene and its preference for substitution over addition reactions. These were later explained by resonance.

docs.title: Resonance and Stability of Benzene
docs.text:
• According to valence bond theory, benzene is a resonance hybrid of various resonating structures. The two Kekulé structures (A) and (B) are the main contributors.
  • The hybrid is shown by drawing a circle (or dotted circle) inside the hexagon, as in (C). The circle represents the six electrons delocalised over the six carbon atoms.

docs.title: Orbital Picture of Benzene
docs.text:
• All six carbon atoms of benzene are sp2 hybridised.
  • Two sp2 orbitals of each carbon overlap with those of adjacent carbons to form six C–C σ bonds lying in the hexagonal plane. The third sp2 orbital of each carbon overlaps with the s orbital of hydrogen to form six C–H σ bonds.
  • Each carbon is left with one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the ring.
  • These p orbitals could form three π bonds in two equally likely ways: C1–C2, C3–C4, C5–C6 or C2–C3, C4–C5, C6–C1. These correspond to the two Kekulé structures with localised π bonds.
  • X-ray diffraction shows that all C–C internuclear distances are the same, so the p orbital of each carbon overlaps equally with the p orbitals of both neighbours. This forms two doughnut-shaped rings of electron cloud, one above and one below the plane of the ring.
  • The six π electrons are delocalised and can move freely around the six carbon nuclei. The delocalised cloud is attracted more strongly by the nuclei than a cloud localised between two carbons. So benzene is more stable than the hypothetical cyclohexatriene.
  • X-ray data shows benzene is planar and all six C–C bond lengths are 139 pm, which is in between the C–C single bond (154 pm) and the C=C double bond (133 pm).

Conclusion

Benzene has no pure double bonds. This explains its reluctance to undergo addition reactions under normal conditions and its unusual stability.

docs.title: Aromaticity (Hückel Rule)
docs.text:
Benzene was considered the parent 'aromatic' compound. Now the term is applied to all ring systems, with or without a benzene ring, that have the following characteristics:

  1. Planarity.
  2. Complete delocalisation of the π electrons in the ring.
  3. Presence of (4n + 2) π electrons in the ring, where n is an integer (n = 0, 1, 2, ...).

This is often called the Hückel rule.

Aromatic compound Number of π electrons n Benzene 6 1 Cyclopentadienyl anion 6 1 Cycloheptatrienyl cation 6 1 Naphthalene 10 2 Anthracene 14 3 Phenanthrene 14 3

Note

The cyclopentadienyl anion and the cycloheptatrienyl (tropylium) cation have no benzene ring, yet they are aromatic because they are planar, fully conjugated rings with 6 π electrons. They are examples of non-benzenoid aromatic species.

docs.title: Preparation of Benzene
docs.text: Benzene is commercially isolated from coal tar. In the laboratory it can be prepared by the following methods.

docs.title: 1. Cyclic Polymerisation of Ethyne
docs.text: \[3HC \equiv CH \xrightarrow[873\ K]{Red\ hot\ iron\ tube} C_6H_6\]

docs.title: 2. Decarboxylation of Aromatic Acids
docs.text:
Sodium benzoate on heating with soda lime gives benzene.

\[C_6H_5COONa + NaOH \xrightarrow[Δ]{CaO} C_6H_6 + Na_2CO_3\]

docs.title: 3. Reduction of Phenol
docs.text:
Phenol is reduced to benzene by passing its vapours over heated zinc dust.

\[C_6H_5OH + Zn \xrightarrow{Δ} C_6H_6 + ZnO\]

docs.title: Physical Properties of Aromatic Hydrocarbons
docs.text:
• Aromatic hydrocarbons are non-polar molecules and are usually colourless liquids or solids with a characteristic aroma.
  • Naphthalene balls are used in toilets and to preserve clothes because of their smell and moth repellent property.
  • They are immiscible with water but readily miscible with organic solvents.
  • They burn with a sooty flame.

docs.title: Hydrocarbons | Chemical Properties of Alkenes
docs.text:
Alkenes are a rich source of loosely held π electrons, so they mainly undergo addition reactions in which electrophiles add on to the carbon-carbon double bond.

  • Some reagents add by a free radical mechanism.
  • Oxidation and ozonolysis are also important reactions of alkenes.

docs.title: 1. Addition of Dihydrogen
docs.text:
Alkenes add one molecule of H2 in the presence of finely divided Ni, Pd or Pt to form alkanes.

\[CH_2=CH_2 + H_2 \xrightarrow{Ni/Pd/Pt} CH_3-CH_3\]

docs.title: 2. Addition of Halogens
docs.text:
• Bromine or chlorine adds to alkenes to give vicinal dihalides. Iodine does not add under normal conditions.
  • The reddish orange colour of bromine in CCl4 disappears when bromine adds to an unsaturated site. This is used as a test for unsaturation.
  • It is an electrophilic addition reaction that proceeds through a cyclic halonium ion.
\[CH_2=CH_2 + Br-Br \xrightarrow{CCl_4} BrCH_2-CH_2Br\ \ \ (1,2\text{-}Dibromoethane)\] \[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + Cl-Cl → CH_3-CHCl-CH_2Cl\ \ \ (1,2\text{-}Dichloropropane)\]

docs.title: 3. Addition of Hydrogen Halides
docs.text:
• HCl, HBr and HI add to alkenes to form alkyl halides by electrophilic addition.
  • Order of reactivity:
\[HI > HBr > HCl\]

docs.title: Addition to Symmetrical Alkenes
docs.text:
When the same groups are attached to both doubly bonded carbons, only one product is possible:

\[CH_2=CH_2 + H-Br → CH_3-CH_2-Br\] \[CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3 + HBr → CH_3-CH_2-CHBr-CH_3\]

docs.title: Addition to Unsymmetrical Alkenes (Markovnikov Rule)
docs.text:
HBr can add to propene in two ways:

\[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H-Br → CH_3-CHBr-CH_3\ \ \ (I:\ 2\text{-}Bromopropane)\] \[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H-Br → CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br\ \ \ (II:\ 1\text{-}Bromopropane)\]

Markovnikov Rule

The negative part of the addendum (adding molecule) gets attached to that carbon atom which possesses the lesser number of hydrogen atoms.

According to this rule (framed by the Russian chemist Markovnikov in 1869), product I, 2-bromopropane, is expected, and it is indeed the principal product.

docs.title: Mechanism
docs.text:
HBr provides the electrophile H+, which attacks the double bond to form a carbocation. Two carbocations are possible:

\[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H^+ → CH_3-CH_2-\overset{+}{C}H_2\ \ \ (a:\ less\ stable\ 1^\circ\ carbocation)\] \[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H^+ → CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3\ \ \ (b:\ more\ stable\ 2^\circ\ carbocation)\]
  • The secondary carbocation (b) is more stable than the primary carbocation (a), so it is formed faster and predominates.
  • Br- then attacks carbocation (b):
\[CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3 + Br^- → CH_3-CHBr-CH_3\ \ \ (2\text{-}Bromopropane,\ major)\]

docs.title: Anti-Markovnikov Addition (Peroxide Effect or Kharash Effect)
docs.text:
• In the presence of a peroxide, HBr adds to unsymmetrical alkenes like propene contrary to the Markovnikov rule.
  • This was observed by M.S. Kharash and F.R. Mayo in 1933 at the University of Chicago. It is called the peroxide effect or Kharash effect.
  • It happens only with HBr, not with HCl or HI.
\[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + HBr \xrightarrow{(C_6H_5CO)_2O_2} CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br\ \ \ (1\text{-}Bromopropane)\]

docs.title: Mechanism (Free Radical Chain)
docs.text:
\[(i)\ C_6H_5COO-OOCC_6H_5 \xrightarrow{Homolysis} 2C_6H_5CO\dot{O} → 2\dot{C}_6H_5 + 2CO_2\] \[(ii)\ \dot{C}_6H_5 + H-Br \xrightarrow{Homolysis} C_6H_6 + \dot{B}r\] \[(iii)\ CH_3-CH=CH_2 + \dot{B}r → CH_3-\dot{C}H-CH_2Br\ \ \ (b:\ more\ stable\ 2^\circ\ radical)\] \[\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ CH_3-CH=CH_2 + \dot{B}r → CH_3-CHBr-\dot{C}H_2\ \ \ (a:\ less\ stable\ 1^\circ\ radical)\] \[(iv)\ CH_3-\dot{C}H-CH_2Br + H-Br → CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br + \dot{B}r\ \ \ (major)\] \[(v)\ CH_3-CHBr-\dot{C}H_2 + H-Br → CH_3-CHBr-CH_3 + \dot{B}r\ \ \ (minor)\]
  • The bromine radical adds to the terminal carbon so that the more stable secondary free radical is formed. This explains why 1-bromopropane is the major product.

Why no peroxide effect with HCl and HI?

  • The H–Cl bond (430.5 kJ mol-1) is stronger than the H–Br bond (363.7 kJ mol-1), so it is not cleaved by the free radical.
  • The H–I bond (296.8 kJ mol-1) is weaker, but iodine free radicals combine with each other to form I2 instead of adding to the double bond.

docs.title: 4. Addition of Sulphuric Acid
docs.text:
Cold concentrated H2SO4 adds to alkenes according to the Markovnikov rule, forming alkyl hydrogen sulphates by electrophilic addition.

\[CH_2=CH_2 + H-OSO_2OH → CH_3-CH_2-OSO_2OH\ \ \ (Ethyl\ hydrogen\ sulphate)\] \[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + HOSO_2OH → CH_3-CH(OSO_2OH)-CH_3\ \ \ (Propyl\ hydrogen\ sulphate)\]

docs.title: 5. Addition of Water (Hydration)
docs.text:
In the presence of a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid, alkenes react with water to form alcohols, following the Markovnikov rule.

\[(CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} (CH_3)_3C-OH\] \[2\text{-}Methylpropene → 2\text{-}Methylpropan\text{-}2\text{-}ol\]

docs.title: (a) With cold dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> (Baeyer's reagent)
docs.text:
Alkenes react with cold, dilute aqueous KMnO4 to give vicinal glycols. Decolourisation of the purple KMnO4 solution is used as a test for unsaturation.

\[CH_2=CH_2 + H_2O + O \xrightarrow[273\ K]{dil.\ KMnO_4} HOCH_2-CH_2OH\ \ \ (Ethane\text{-}1,2\text{-}diol\ or\ glycol)\] \[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H_2O + O \xrightarrow[273\ K]{dil.\ KMnO_4} CH_3CH(OH)CH_2OH\ \ \ (Propane\text{-}1,2\text{-}diol)\]

docs.title: (b) With acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> or acidic K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
docs.text:
These oxidise alkenes to ketones and/or acids, depending on the alkene and the conditions. The double bond is cleaved.

\[(CH_3)_2C=CH_2 \xrightarrow{KMnO_4/H^+} (CH_3)_2C=O + CO_2 + H_2O\] \[CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3 \xrightarrow{KMnO_4/H^+} 2CH_3COOH\]

docs.title: 7. Ozonolysis
docs.text:
• Ozone adds to the alkene to form an ozonide, which is then cleaved by Zn–H2O into smaller molecules (aldehydes and/or ketones).
  • Each doubly bonded carbon becomes a C=O group. So by identifying the products, the position of the double bond can be located.
\[CH_3CH=CH_2 + O_3 → Propene\ ozonide \xrightarrow{Zn + H_2O} CH_3CHO + HCHO\] \[(CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + O_3 → Ozonide \xrightarrow{Zn + H_2O} (CH_3)_2C=O + HCHO\]

Example

Propene gives ethanal and methanal, while 2-methylpropene gives propan-2-one (acetone) and methanal.

docs.title: 8. Polymerisation
docs.text:
• A large number of ethene molecules combine at high temperature, high pressure and in the presence of a catalyst to give polythene. The large molecules formed are called polymers, the simple starting molecules are monomers, and the reaction is called polymerisation.
\[n(CH_2=CH_2) \xrightarrow[Catalyst]{High\ temp./pressure} -(CH_2-CH_2)_n-\ \ \ (Polythene)\] \[n(CH_3-CH=CH_2) \xrightarrow[Catalyst]{High\ temp./pressure} -(CH(CH_3)-CH_2)_n-\ \ \ (Polypropene)\]
  • Polythene is used for plastic bags, squeeze bottles, refrigerator dishes, toys, pipes, radio and T.V. cabinets.
  • Polypropene is used for milk crates, plastic buckets and other moulded articles.
  • Excessive use of polythene and polypropylene is a matter of great environmental concern.

docs.title: Hydrocarbons | Chemical Properties of Benzene
docs.text: Arenes are characterised by electrophilic substitution reactions. Under special conditions they can also undergo addition and oxidation reactions.

docs.title: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions
docs.text: The common electrophilic substitution reactions of arenes are nitration, halogenation, sulphonation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation. In each, the attacking reagent is an electrophile (E+).

docs.title: 1. Nitration
docs.text:
A nitro group is introduced into the benzene ring when benzene is heated with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulphuric acid (nitrating mixture).

\[C_6H_6 + Conc.\ HNO_3 \xrightarrow[323-333\ K]{Conc.\ H_2SO_4} C_6H_5NO_2 + H_2O\ \ \ (Nitrobenzene)\]

docs.title: 2. Halogenation
docs.text:
Arenes react with halogens in the presence of a Lewis acid like anhydrous FeCl3, FeBr3 or AlCl3 to give haloarenes.

\[C_6H_6 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5Cl + HCl\ \ \ (Chlorobenzene)\]

docs.title: 3. Sulphonation
docs.text:
Replacement of a ring hydrogen by a sulphonic acid group is called sulphonation. It is carried out by heating benzene with fuming sulphuric acid (oleum).

\[C_6H_6 + H_2SO_4(SO_3) \xrightarrow{Δ} C_6H_5SO_3H + H_2O\ \ \ (Benzenesulphonic\ acid)\]

docs.title: 4. Friedel-Crafts Alkylation
docs.text:
When benzene is treated with an alkyl halide in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3, an alkylbenzene is formed.

\[C_6H_6 + CH_3Cl \xrightarrow{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5CH_3 + HCl\ \ \ (Toluene)\] \[C_6H_6 + C_2H_5Cl \xrightarrow{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5C_2H_5 + HCl\ \ \ (Ethylbenzene)\]

Note

Benzene with 1-chloropropane gives isopropylbenzene rather than n-propylbenzene. The primary carbocation CH3CH2CH2+ first formed rearranges (by a hydride shift) to the more stable secondary carbocation (CH3)2CH+, which then attacks the ring.

docs.title: 5. Friedel-Crafts Acylation
docs.text:
Benzene reacts with an acyl halide or acid anhydride in the presence of a Lewis acid (AlCl3) to give an acyl benzene.

\[C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow[Δ]{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl\ \ \ (Acetophenone)\] \[C_6H_6 + (CH_3CO)_2O \xrightarrow[Δ]{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3 + CH_3COOH\]

docs.title: Further Substitution
docs.text:
With excess electrophilic reagent, the other ring hydrogens can be replaced one after another. For example, benzene with excess chlorine and anhydrous AlCl3 in the dark gives hexachlorobenzene:

\[C_6H_6 + 6Cl_2 \xrightarrow[dark,\ cold]{Anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6Cl_6 + 6HCl\]

docs.title: Mechanism of Electrophilic Substitution
docs.text:
Electrophilic substitution (SE; S = substitution, E = electrophilic) reactions are believed to proceed in three steps:

  1. Generation of the electrophile
  2. Formation of a carbocation intermediate
  3. Removal of a proton from the carbocation intermediate

docs.title: Step 1: Generation of the Electrophile (E<sup>+</sup>)
docs.text:
In chlorination, alkylation and acylation, anhydrous AlCl3 (a Lewis acid) combines with the attacking reagent to generate Cl+, R+ or RC+O (acylium ion) respectively:

\[Cl-Cl + AlCl_3 → Cl^+ + [AlCl_4]^-\ \ \ (Chloronium\ ion)\] \[CH_3-Cl + AlCl_3 → CH_3^+ + [AlCl_4]^-\] \[CH_3COCl + AlCl_3 → CH_3\overset{+}{C}O + [AlCl_4]^-\ \ \ (Acylium\ ion)\]

In nitration, the electrophile is the nitronium ion, NO2+. It forms by transfer of a proton from sulphuric acid to nitric acid:

\[Step\ I:\ HOSO_2O-H + H-O-NO_2 ⇌ H-\overset{+}{O}H-NO_2 + HSO_4^-\] \[Step\ II:\ H_2\overset{+}{O}-NO_2 ⇌ H_2O + NO_2^+\]
  • Here sulphuric acid acts as an acid and nitric acid as a base. So it is a simple acid-base equilibrium.

docs.title: Step 2: Formation of the Carbocation (Arenium Ion)
docs.text:
The electrophile attacks the ring to form a σ-complex or arenium ion, in which one carbon becomes sp3 hybridised.

The arenium ion is stabilised by resonance:

  • The arenium ion loses its aromatic character, because delocalisation of electrons stops at the sp3 carbon.

docs.title: Step 3: Removal of a Proton
docs.text:
To restore aromaticity, the σ-complex releases a proton from the sp3 carbon on attack by [AlCl4]- (in halogenation, alkylation and acylation) or [HSO4]- (in nitration).

\[C_6H_6E^+ + [AlCl_4]^- → C_6H_5E + HCl + AlCl_3\] \[C_6H_6E^+ + [HSO_4]^- → C_6H_5E + H_2SO_4\]

docs.title: Addition Reactions
docs.text:
• Under vigorous conditions (high temperature and/or pressure, Ni catalyst), benzene is hydrogenated to cyclohexane:
\[C_6H_6 + 3H_2 \xrightarrow[Δ]{Ni} C_6H_{12}\ \ \ (Cyclohexane)\]
  • Under ultraviolet light, three chlorine molecules add to benzene to give benzene hexachloride (BHC), C6H6Cl6, also called gammaxane:
\[C_6H_6 + 3Cl_2 \xrightarrow[500\ K]{UV} C_6H_6Cl_6\]

docs.title: Combustion
docs.text:
Benzene burns in air with a sooty flame, producing CO2 and H2O:

\[C_6H_6 + {15 \over 2}O_2 → 6CO_2 + 3H_2O\]

General combustion equation for any hydrocarbon:

\[C_xH_y + \left(x + {y \over 4}\right)O_2 → xCO_2 + {y \over 2}H_2O\]

docs.title: Directive Influence of a Functional Group in Monosubstituted Benzene
docs.text:
• When a monosubstituted benzene undergoes further substitution, the three possible disubstituted products are not formed in equal amounts. Either ortho and para products, or the meta product, are formed predominantly.
  • This depends on the nature of the substituent already present in the ring, not on the incoming group. This is called the directive influence of substituents.

docs.title: 1. Ortho and Para Directing Groups
docs.text:
Groups that direct the incoming group to ortho and para positions. Take the –OH group of phenol as an example. Phenol is a resonance hybrid of the following structures:

  • The resonance structures show that electron density is higher at the o- and p-positions. So substitution takes place mainly at these positions.
  • The –I effect of –OH slightly reduces the electron density at ortho and para positions, but the overall electron density at these positions still increases due to resonance.
  • So –OH activates the benzene ring for attack by an electrophile.
  • Other activating (o, p directing) groups: –NH2, –NHR, –NHCOCH3, –OCH3, –CH3, –C2H5, etc.

Halogens

In aryl halides, halogens are moderately deactivating: their strong –I effect lowers the overall electron density of the ring, making further substitution difficult. But due to resonance, the electron density at o- and p-positions is greater than at the m-position. So halogens are deactivating yet o- and p-directing.

docs.title: 2. Meta Directing Groups
docs.text:
Groups that direct the incoming group to the meta position. Examples: –NO2, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –SO3H, etc.

Take the nitro group as an example. It reduces the electron density of the ring by its strong –I effect. Nitrobenzene is a resonance hybrid of the following structures:

  • The overall electron density of the ring decreases, making further substitution difficult. So these groups are also called deactivating groups.
  • The positive charge appears at o- and p-positions, so their electron density is lower than at the meta position. The electrophile therefore attacks the comparatively electron rich meta position.
Group type Examples Effect on ring o, p directing (activating) –OH, –NH2, –NHR, –NHCOCH3, –OCH3, –CH3, –C2H5 Increases electron density o, p directing (deactivating) –Cl, –Br, –I Decreases electron density m directing (deactivating) –NO2, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –SO3H Decreases electron density

docs.title: Carcinogenicity and Toxicity
docs.text:
• Benzene and polynuclear hydrocarbons containing more than two fused benzene rings are toxic and are said to have cancer producing (carcinogenic) property.
  • Such polynuclear hydrocarbons are formed by incomplete combustion of organic materials like tobacco, coal and petroleum.
  • They enter the human body, undergo various biochemical reactions and finally damage DNA and cause cancer.

Some carcinogenic hydrocarbons

docs.title: Hydrocarbons | Introduction and Alkanes
docs.text:
Hydrocarbons are compounds made up of carbon and hydrogen only. They are the main sources of energy in our daily life.

  • LPG (liquified petroleum gas), CNG (compressed natural gas) and LNG (liquified natural gas) are all hydrocarbon fuels.
  • Petrol, diesel and kerosene are obtained by fractional distillation of petroleum. Coal gas is obtained by destructive distillation of coal.
  • Hydrocarbons are also used to make polymers like polythene, polypropene and polystyrene. Higher hydrocarbons are used as solvents for paints and as starting materials for dyes and drugs.

docs.title: Classification of Hydrocarbons
docs.text: Depending upon the type of carbon-carbon bonds present, hydrocarbons are classified into three main categories:

docs.title: 1. Saturated Hydrocarbons
docs.text:
• They contain only carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen single bonds.
  • Open chain saturated hydrocarbons are called alkanes. Example: CH3CH3 (ethane).
  • When the carbon atoms form a closed chain or ring, they are called cycloalkanes. Example: cyclohexane.

docs.title: 2. Unsaturated Hydrocarbons
docs.text:
• They contain carbon-carbon multiple bonds: double bonds, triple bonds or both.
  • Examples: alkenes (CH2=CH2) and alkynes (HC≡CH).

docs.title: 3. Aromatic Hydrocarbons
docs.text: • These are a special type of cyclic compounds, such as benzene (C6H6) and its derivatives.

docs.title: Alkanes
docs.text:
Alkanes are saturated open chain hydrocarbons containing carbon-carbon single bonds only.

  • Methane (CH4) is the first member. It is found in coal mines and marshy places.
  • If one H atom of methane is replaced by a –CH3 group, we get ethane (C2H6). Repeating this gives C3H8, C4H10 and so on.
  • Alkanes are quite inert under normal conditions and do not react with acids, bases and other reagents. Hence, they were earlier called paraffins (Latin: parum = little, affinis = affinity).
  • The general formula of the alkane family (homologous series) is:
\[C_nH_{2n+2}\]

Where n is the number of carbon atoms.

docs.title: Structure of Alkanes
docs.text:
• In methane, carbon is sp3 hybridised. The molecule is tetrahedral, with carbon at the centre and four H atoms at the corners of a regular tetrahedron. All H–C–H bond angles are 109.5°.
  • In higher alkanes, such tetrahedra are joined together. C–C and C–H bond lengths are 154 pm and 112 pm respectively.
  • C–C and C–H σ bonds are formed by head-on overlapping of sp3 hybrid orbitals of carbon and 1s orbitals of hydrogen.

docs.title: Nomenclature and Isomerism
docs.text:
• Methane, ethane and propane have only one possible structure. Higher alkanes can have more than one structure.
  • For C4H10, the four carbon atoms can be joined in a continuous chain or as a branched chain:

Isomers of C4H10

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3\ \ \ (Butane\ or\ n\text{-}butane,\ b.p.\ 273\ K)\] \[(CH_3)_2CHCH_3\ \ \ (2\text{-}Methylpropane\ or\ isobutane,\ b.p.\ 261\ K)\]

Isomers of C5H12

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3\ \ \ (Pentane\ or\ n\text{-}pentane,\ b.p.\ 309\ K)\] \[(CH_3)_2CHCH_2CH_3\ \ \ (2\text{-}Methylbutane\ or\ isopentane,\ b.p.\ 301\ K)\] \[C(CH_3)_4\ \ \ (2,2\text{-}Dimethylpropane\ or\ neopentane,\ b.p.\ 282.5\ K)\]
  • Compounds having the same molecular formula but different structures (and hence different properties) are called structural isomers.
  • Structural isomers which differ only in the chain of carbon atoms (straight or branched) are called chain isomers. C4H10 has two and C5H12 has three chain isomers.
  • The number of isomers grows quickly with chain length: C6H14 has 5 isomers, C7H16 has 9, and C10H22 has as many as 75.

docs.title: Types of Carbon Atoms
docs.text:
Based on the number of carbon atoms attached to a given carbon atom:

Type of carbon Attached to Example Primary (1°) One carbon atom (or none, as in methane) Terminal carbons, both carbons of ethane Secondary (2°) Two carbon atoms Middle carbons of n-butane Tertiary (3°) Three carbon atoms C-2 of isobutane Quaternary (4°) Four carbon atoms C-2 of neopentane

docs.title: Alkyl Groups
docs.text: • Groups like –CH3, –C2H5, –C3H7 are derived from alkanes by removal of one hydrogen atom. They are called alkyl groups, with general formula CnH2n+1.

docs.title: IUPAC Rules: Some Worked Names
docs.text:
The longest carbon chain is chosen as the parent, numbered to give substituents the lowest set of locants, and substituents are written in alphabetical order.

Structure IUPAC Name Remark CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH(C2H5)CH2CH3 4-Ethyl-2-methylhexane Lowest sum and alphabetical arrangement CH3CH2CH(C2H5)CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3 3-Ethyl-5-methylheptane Alphabetical priority order Decane with CH(CH3)2 at C-4 and CH(CH3)CH2CH3 at C-5 5-sec-Butyl-4-isopropyldecane sec is ignored in alphabetising; isopropyl is taken as one word Nonane with –CH2C(CH3)3 at C-5 5-(2,2-Dimethylpropyl)nonane The side chain is numbered separately

docs.title: Writing a Structure from its IUPAC Name
docs.text:
To write the structure of 3-ethyl-2,2-dimethylpentane:

  1. Draw the parent chain of five carbon atoms: C–C–C–C–C
  2. Number it: C1–C2–C3–C4–C5
  3. Attach an ethyl group at C-3 and two methyl groups at C-2.
  4. Satisfy the valency of each carbon with hydrogen atoms:
\[CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH(C_2H_5)-CH_2-CH_3\]

docs.title: Preparation of Alkanes
docs.text: Petroleum and natural gas are the main sources of alkanes. In the laboratory, they can be prepared by the following methods.

docs.title: 1. From Unsaturated Hydrocarbons (Hydrogenation)
docs.text:
• Dihydrogen adds to alkenes and alkynes in the presence of finely divided Pt, Pd or Ni to form alkanes. This is called hydrogenation.
  • These metals adsorb H2 on their surface and activate the H–H bond. Pt and Pd work at room temperature, while Ni needs relatively higher temperature and pressure.
\[CH_2=CH_2 + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pt/Pd/Ni} CH_3-CH_3\] \[CH_3-CH=CH_2 + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pt/Pd/Ni} CH_3-CH_2-CH_3\] \[CH_3-C \equiv CH + 2H_2 \xrightarrow{Pt/Pd/Ni} CH_3-CH_2-CH_3\]

docs.title: (a) Reduction with zinc and dilute HCl
docs.text:
Alkyl halides (except fluorides) are reduced to alkanes by zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid.

\[CH_3Cl + H_2 \xrightarrow{Zn,\ H^+} CH_4 + HCl\] \[C_2H_5Cl + H_2 \xrightarrow{Zn,\ H^+} C_2H_6 + HCl\] \[CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl + H_2 \xrightarrow{Zn,\ H^+} CH_3CH_2CH_3 + HCl\]

docs.title: (b) Wurtz Reaction
docs.text:
• Alkyl halides react with sodium metal in dry ether (free from moisture) to give higher alkanes with double the number of carbon atoms.
  • It is used to prepare higher alkanes containing an even number of carbon atoms.
\[CH_3Br + 2Na + BrCH_3 \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} CH_3-CH_3 + 2NaBr\] \[C_2H_5Br + 2Na + BrC_2H_5 \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} C_2H_5-C_2H_5 + 2NaBr\]

Note

If two different alkyl halides are used, a mixture of three alkanes is obtained, which is difficult to separate. That is why the Wurtz reaction is not suitable for alkanes with an odd number of carbon atoms.

docs.title: (a) Decarboxylation
docs.text:
• Sodium salts of carboxylic acids, on heating with soda lime (NaOH + CaO), give alkanes containing one carbon atom less than the carboxylic acid.
  • This elimination of CO2 from a carboxylic acid is called decarboxylation.
\[CH_3COO^-Na^+ + NaOH \xrightarrow[Δ]{CaO} CH_4 + Na_2CO_3\]

docs.title: (b) Kolbe's Electrolytic Method
docs.text:
An aqueous solution of the sodium or potassium salt of a carboxylic acid, on electrolysis, gives an alkane with an even number of carbon atoms at the anode.

\[2CH_3COO^-Na^+ + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{Electrolysis} CH_3-CH_3 + 2CO_2 + H_2 + 2NaOH\]

The reaction follows a free radical path:

Mechanism

\[(i)\ 2CH_3COO^-Na^+ ⇌ 2CH_3COO^- + 2Na^+\] \[(ii)\ At\ anode:\ 2CH_3COO^- \xrightarrow{-2e^-} 2CH_3CO\dot{O} → 2\dot{C}H_3 + 2CO_2 ↑\] \[(iii)\ \dot{C}H_3 + \dot{C}H_3 → CH_3-CH_3 ↑\] \[(iv)\ At\ cathode:\ H_2O + e^- → OH^- + \dot{H}\ ;\ \ 2\dot{H} → H_2 ↑\]
  • Methane cannot be prepared by this method because two alkyl radicals always join, so the product has at least two carbon atoms.

docs.title: Physical Properties of Alkanes
docs.text:
• Alkanes are almost non-polar because of the covalent C–C and C–H bonds and the very small electronegativity difference between C and H. They have only weak van der Waals forces.
  • C1 to C4 are gases, C5 to C17 are liquids and C18 onwards are solids at 298 K. They are colourless and odourless.
  • Being non-polar, alkanes are insoluble in water (hydrophobic) but soluble in non-polar solvents (like dissolves like). Petrol is used for dry cleaning because grease (a mixture of higher alkanes) is non-polar.

docs.title: Boiling Point
docs.text:
• Boiling point increases steadily with molecular mass, because van der Waals forces increase with molecular size or surface area.
  • Among isomers, branching lowers the boiling point. With more branching, the molecule becomes nearly spherical, so the area of contact and hence intermolecular forces are smaller.
Molecular formula Name Molecular mass (u) b.p. (K) m.p. (K) CH4 Methane 16 111.0 90.5 C2H6 Ethane 30 184.4 101.0 C3H8 Propane 44 230.9 85.3 C4H10 Butane 58 272.4 134.6 C4H10 2-Methylpropane 58 261.0 114.7 C5H12 Pentane 72 309.1 143.3 C5H12 2-Methylbutane 72 300.9 113.1 C5H12 2,2-Dimethylpropane 72 282.5 256.4 C6H14 Hexane 86 341.9 178.5 C7H16 Heptane 100 371.4 182.4 C8H18 Octane 114 398.7 216.2 C9H20 Nonane 128 423.8 222.0 C10H22 Decane 142 447.1 243.3 C20H42 Eicosane 282 615.0 236.2

Conclusion

Among the isomeric pentanes, n-pentane (continuous chain) has the highest boiling point (309.1 K), while the most branched 2,2-dimethylpropane has the lowest (282.5 K).

docs.title: Hydrocarbons | Questions
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some questions based on alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and aromatic hydrocarbons.

docs.title: Questions on Alkanes
docs.text:
Write structures of different chain isomers of alkanes corresponding to the molecular formula C6H14. Also write their IUPAC names.

\[(i)\ CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (n\text{-}Hexane)\] \[(ii)\ CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (2\text{-}Methylpentane)\] \[(iii)\ CH_3-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (3\text{-}Methylpentane)\] \[(iv)\ CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH(CH_3)-CH_3\ \ \ (2,3\text{-}Dimethylbutane)\] \[(v)\ CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (2,2\text{-}Dimethylbutane)\]

Write IUPAC names of the following compounds: (i) (CH3)3CCH2C(CH3)3 (ii) (CH3)2C(C2H5)2 (iii) tetra-tert-butylmethane

  • (i) 2,2,4,4-Tetramethylpentane
  • (ii) 3,3-Dimethylpentane
  • (iii) 3,3-Di-tert-butyl-2,2,4,4-tetramethylpentane

Write structures for the following compounds. Why are the given names incorrect? Write correct IUPAC names. (i) 2-Ethylpentane (ii) 5-Ethyl-3-methylheptane

  • (i) The structure is:
\[CH_3-CH(C_2H_5)-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3\]

The longest chain has six carbon atoms, not five. Hence, the correct name is 3-methylhexane.

  • (ii) The structure is:
\[CH_3-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH(C_2H_5)-CH_2-CH_3\]

Numbering must start from the end that gives the lower number to the ethyl group (alphabetical priority, since both sets of locants are 3,5). Hence, the correct name is 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane.

Sodium salt of which acid will be needed for the preparation of propane? Write the chemical equation for the reaction.

Decarboxylation removes one carbon atom, so a four carbon acid is needed: butanoic acid.

\[CH_3CH_2CH_2COO^-Na^+ + NaOH \xrightarrow{CaO} CH_3CH_2CH_3 + Na_2CO_3\]

How do you account for the formation of ethane during chlorination of methane?

Chlorination of methane is a free radical chain reaction. During propagation, methyl free radicals (\(\dot{C}H_3\)) are produced:

\[CH_4 + \dot{C}l → \dot{C}H_3 + HCl\]

In the termination step, two methyl radicals can combine with each other:

\[\dot{C}H_3 + \dot{C}H_3 → CH_3-CH_3\]

Hence, ethane is obtained as a by-product.

Why is Wurtz reaction not preferred for the preparation of alkanes containing an odd number of carbon atoms? Illustrate your answer by taking one example.

To get an odd-carbon alkane, two different alkyl halides must be used. For propane, CH3Br and C2H5Br would be needed. But each halide can also couple with itself, so three alkanes form:

\[CH_3Br + C_2H_5Br + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} CH_3-C_2H_5\ (propane) + 2NaBr\] \[CH_3Br + CH_3Br + 2Na → CH_3-CH_3\ (ethane) + 2NaBr\] \[C_2H_5Br + C_2H_5Br + 2Na → C_2H_5-C_2H_5\ (butane) + 2NaBr\]

The mixture of ethane, propane and butane is difficult to separate. Hence, Wurtz reaction is not preferred for odd-carbon alkanes.

docs.title: Questions on Alkenes
docs.text:
Write structures and IUPAC names of different structural isomers of alkenes corresponding to C5H10.

\[(a)\ CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (Pent\text{-}1\text{-}ene)\] \[(b)\ CH_3-CH=CH-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (Pent\text{-}2\text{-}ene)\] \[(c)\ CH_3-C(CH_3)=CH-CH_3\ \ \ (2\text{-}Methylbut\text{-}2\text{-}ene)\] \[(d)\ CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH=CH_2\ \ \ (3\text{-}Methylbut\text{-}1\text{-}ene)\] \[(e)\ CH_2=C(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3\ \ \ (2\text{-}Methylbut\text{-}1\text{-}ene)\]

Which of the following compounds will show cis-trans isomerism? (i) (CH3)2C=CH–C2H5 (ii) CH2=CBr2 (iii) C6H5CH=CH–CH3 (iv) CH3CH=CClCH3

Compounds (iii) and (iv) show cis-trans isomerism. In (i) and (ii), one of the doubly bonded carbons carries two identical groups (two CH3 in (i), two H and two Br in (ii)), so cis and trans forms are not possible.

Draw the cis and trans structures of hex-2-ene. Which isomer will have higher b.p. and why?

  • cis-Hex-2-ene: the CH3 and C3H7 groups are on the same side of the double bond.
  • trans-Hex-2-ene: the CH3 and C3H7 groups are on opposite sides of the double bond.

The cis isomer has the higher boiling point. In the cis form, the bond dipoles do not cancel, so it has a net dipole moment and stronger dipole-dipole attractions. In the trans form, the dipoles nearly cancel, so it is almost non-polar.

Write IUPAC names of the products obtained by addition reactions of HBr to hex-1-ene (i) in the absence of peroxide and (ii) in the presence of peroxide.

  • (i) Without peroxide, addition follows the Markovnikov rule:
\[CH_2=CH-(CH_2)_3-CH_3 + HBr → CH_3-CHBr-(CH_2)_3-CH_3\ \ \ (2\text{-}Bromohexane)\]
  • (ii) With peroxide, anti-Markovnikov addition takes place:
\[CH_2=CH-(CH_2)_3-CH_3 + HBr \xrightarrow{Peroxide} BrCH_2-CH_2-(CH_2)_3-CH_3\ \ \ (1\text{-}Bromohexane)\]

An alkene 'A' on ozonolysis gives a mixture of ethanal and pentan-3-one. Write structure and IUPAC name of 'A'.

Join the two carbonyl carbons by a double bond (removing the oxygens):

\[CH_3CHO + O=C(C_2H_5)_2 ⇒ CH_3-CH=C(C_2H_5)-CH_2-CH_3\]

'A' is 3-ethylpent-2-ene.

An alkene 'A' contains three C–C, eight C–H σ bonds and one C–C π bond. 'A' on ozonolysis gives two moles of an aldehyde of molar mass 44 u. Write IUPAC name of 'A'.

  • An aldehyde of molar mass 44 u is ethanal, CH3CHO (24 + 4 + 16 = 44).
  • Two moles of ethanal come from a symmetrical alkene: joining two CH3CH= units gives CH3–CH=CH–CH3.
  • Check: it has three C–C σ bonds (including the σ part of C=C), eight C–H σ bonds and one π bond.

'A' is but-2-ene.

Propanal and pentan-3-one are the ozonolysis products of an alkene. What is the structural formula of the alkene?

\[CH_3CH_2CHO + O=C(C_2H_5)_2 ⇒ CH_3CH_2-CH=C(CH_2CH_3)-CH_2CH_3\]

The alkene is 3-ethylhex-3-ene.

docs.title: Questions on Alkynes
docs.text:
How will you convert ethanoic acid into benzene?

\[CH_3COOH \xrightarrow{NaOH(aq)} CH_3COONa \xrightarrow[Δ]{Soda\ lime} CH_4\] \[CH_4 \xrightarrow[h\nu]{Cl_2} CH_3Cl \xrightarrow[Wurtz\ reaction]{Na/dry\ ether} C_2H_6 \xrightarrow[h\nu]{Cl_2} C_2H_5Cl\] \[C_2H_5Cl \xrightarrow{alc.\ KOH} CH_2=CH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2} BrCH_2-CH_2Br\] \[BrCH_2-CH_2Br \xrightarrow{alc.\ KOH} CH_2=CHBr \xrightarrow{NaNH_2} CH \equiv CH\] \[3CH \equiv CH \xrightarrow[873\ K]{Red\ hot\ iron\ tube} C_6H_6\]

Arrange benzene, n-hexane and ethyne in decreasing order of acidic behaviour. Also give reason for this behaviour.

\[Ethyne > Benzene > n\text{-}Hexane\]

The C–H carbon is sp hybridised in ethyne (50% s character), sp2 in benzene (33% s character) and sp3 in n-hexane (25% s character). Greater s character means greater electronegativity of carbon, so the C–H electron pair is held more tightly by carbon and the H is released as a proton more easily.

docs.title: Questions on Aromatic Hydrocarbons
docs.text:
Why is benzene extraordinarily stable though it contains three double bonds?

Benzene is a resonance hybrid of two Kekulé structures. Its six π electrons are delocalised over all six carbon atoms, forming electron clouds above and below the ring. The delocalised cloud is held more strongly by the nuclei than localised π bonds, which lowers the energy of the molecule. All C–C bonds are equal (139 pm), so there are no true double bonds, and benzene resists addition reactions.

Explain why the following systems are not aromatic: (i) cyclohexadiene with an exocyclic =CH2 group (methylenecyclohexadiene) (ii) cyclopentadiene (iii) cyclooctatetraene

  • (i) One ring carbon is sp3 hybridised, so the π electrons are not completely delocalised around the ring.
  • (ii) The CH2 carbon of the ring is sp3 hybridised, so there is no complete delocalisation. Also, it has only 4 π electrons, which does not fit (4n + 2).
  • (iii) It has 8 π electrons, which is not a (4n + 2) number. It is also non-planar (tub shaped), so complete delocalisation is not possible.

How will you convert benzene into (i) p-nitrobromobenzene (ii) m-nitrochlorobenzene (iii) p-nitrotoluene (iv) acetophenone?

  • (i) Brominate first, because –Br is o, p directing. Then nitrate and separate the para isomer:
\[C_6H_6 \xrightarrow{Br_2/FeBr_3} C_6H_5Br \xrightarrow{Conc.\ HNO_3/H_2SO_4} p\text{-}BrC_6H_4NO_2\ (+\ ortho\ isomer)\]
  • (ii) Nitrate first, because –NO2 is meta directing. Then chlorinate:
\[C_6H_6 \xrightarrow{Conc.\ HNO_3/H_2SO_4} C_6H_5NO_2 \xrightarrow{Cl_2/anhyd.\ AlCl_3} m\text{-}ClC_6H_4NO_2\]
  • (iii) Methylate first by Friedel-Crafts alkylation (–CH3 is o, p directing), then nitrate and separate the para isomer:
\[C_6H_6 \xrightarrow{CH_3Cl/anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5CH_3 \xrightarrow{Conc.\ HNO_3/H_2SO_4} p\text{-}CH_3C_6H_4NO_2\ (+\ ortho\ isomer)\]
  • (iv) Friedel-Crafts acylation:
\[C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl\]

Write down the products of ozonolysis of 1,2-dimethylbenzene (o-xylene). How does the result support Kekulé structure for benzene?

o-Xylene can be written as two Kekulé structures. Ozonolysis of each gives a different set of products:

\[Structure\ I → 2\ CH_3COCHO\ (methylglyoxal) + OHC-CHO\ (glyoxal)\] \[Structure\ II → CH_3COCOCH_3\ (dimethylglyoxal) + 2\ OHC-CHO\ (glyoxal)\]

In practice, all three products (glyoxal, methylglyoxal and dimethylglyoxal) are obtained. This can only happen if o-xylene (and hence benzene) is a resonance hybrid of both Kekulé structures.

Arrange the following in decreasing order of reactivity with an electrophile, E+: (a) Chlorobenzene, 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene, p-nitrochlorobenzene (b) Toluene, p-H3C–C6H4–NO2, p-O2N–C6H4–NO2

Electron withdrawing –NO2 groups deactivate the ring, while the electron donating –CH3 group activates it.

\[(a)\ Chlorobenzene > p\text{-}Nitrochlorobenzene > 2,4\text{-}Dinitrochlorobenzene\] \[(b)\ Toluene > p\text{-}CH_3C_6H_4NO_2 > p\text{-}O_2NC_6H_4NO_2\]

Out of benzene, m-dinitrobenzene and toluene, which will undergo nitration most easily and why?

Toluene undergoes nitration most easily. The –CH3 group is electron donating and activates the ring, increasing its electron density. Two –NO2 groups in m-dinitrobenzene strongly deactivate the ring. So the order is: toluene > benzene > m-dinitrobenzene.

Suggest the name of a Lewis acid other than anhydrous aluminium chloride which can be used during ethylation of benzene.

Anhydrous ferric chloride, FeCl3.

Why does benzene undergo electrophilic substitution reactions easily and nucleophilic substitutions with difficulty?

Benzene has a cloud of six delocalised π electrons above and below the ring, which makes it electron rich. It therefore attracts electrophiles (electron seeking species) easily. Nucleophiles are electron rich themselves and are repelled by the π electron cloud, so nucleophilic substitution is difficult.

docs.title: Types of Polymerisation Reactions
docs.text:
There are two broad types of polymerisation reactions:

  1. Addition or chain growth polymerisation
  2. Condensation or step growth polymerisation

docs.title: Addition or Chain Growth Polymerisation
docs.text:
In addition or chain growth polymerisation, molecules of the same or different unsaturated monomers add together on a large scale to form a polymer, without the loss of any small molecule.

  • The monomers are unsaturated compounds such as alkenes, alkadienes and their derivatives.
  • The chain length increases (chain growth) through reactive intermediates, either free radicals or ionic species.
  • Free radical addition polymerisation is the most common mode.

docs.title: Free Radical Mechanism
docs.text:
• Alkenes, dienes and their derivatives polymerise in the presence of a free radical generating initiator (catalyst) such as benzoyl peroxide, acetyl peroxide or tert-butyl peroxide.
  • For example, polythene is made by heating (or exposing to light) ethene with a small amount of benzoyl peroxide.
  • The mechanism has three steps: chain initiation, chain propagation and chain termination.

docs.title: 1. Chain initiation steps
docs.text:
• The weak O-O bond of benzoyl peroxide breaks homolytically to give benzoyloxy radicals, which lose CO2 to form phenyl radicals.
  • The phenyl radical adds to the C=C double bond of ethene, generating a new, larger free radical.
\[C_6H_5-\overset{O}{\overset{||}{C}}-O-O-\overset{O}{\overset{||}{C}}-C_6H_5 → 2C_6H_5-\overset{O}{\overset{||}{C}}-\dot{O} → 2\dot{C}_6H_5 + 2CO_2\] \[Benzoyl\ peroxide\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ Phenyl\ radical\] \[\dot{C}_6H_5 + CH_2=CH_2 → C_6H_5-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2\]

docs.title: 2. Chain propagating step
docs.text:
• The new radical attacks another ethene molecule, forming a still bigger radical.
  • Repetition of this step with bigger and bigger radicals carries the chain forward.
\[C_6H_5-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2 + CH_2=CH_2 → C_6H_5-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2\] \[↓\] \[C_6H_5-(CH_2-CH_2)_n-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2\]

docs.title: 3. Chain terminating step
docs.text:
• Finally, the growing radical meets another radical and the two combine, ending the chain. Radicals can terminate in different ways; one mode is combination of two chain radicals:
\[2\ C_6H_5-(CH_2-CH_2)_n-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2 → C_6H_5-(CH_2-CH_2)_n-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-(CH_2-CH_2)_n-C_6H_5\] \[Polythene\]

Note

Only a small amount of initiator is needed, because one initiating radical starts a chain that adds thousands of monomer units before it terminates.

docs.title: Preparation of Some Important Addition Polymers
1. Polythene
docs.text: There are two types of polythene, made under very different conditions.

docs.title: (a) Low density polythene (LDP)
docs.text:
• Made by polymerising ethene at a high pressure of 1000 to 2000 atm and a temperature of 350 K to 570 K, in the presence of traces of dioxygen or a peroxide initiator.
  • It forms by free radical addition along with H-atom abstraction, which gives a highly branched structure. The branches prevent close packing, so the density is low.
  • Properties: chemically inert, tough but flexible, and a poor conductor of electricity.
  • Uses: insulation of electric wires, squeeze bottles, toys and flexible pipes.

docs.title: (b) High density polythene (HDP)
docs.text:
• Made by polymerising ethene in a hydrocarbon solvent with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst (triethylaluminium and titanium tetrachloride) at 333 K to 343 K and a pressure of 6-7 atm.
  • It consists of linear molecules which pack closely, giving a high density.
  • Properties: chemically inert, tougher and harder than LDP.
  • Uses: buckets, dustbins, bottles and pipes.

Note

G. Natta (Italy) and Karl Ziegler (Germany) were awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry in 1963 for developing the Ziegler-Natta catalyst.

Property LDP HDP Conditions 1000-2000 atm, 350-570 K, O2 or peroxide 6-7 atm, 333-343 K, Ziegler-Natta catalyst Structure Highly branched Linear Packing Loose (low density) Close (high density) Nature Tough, flexible Tougher, harder Uses Wire insulation, squeeze bottles, toys Buckets, dustbins, bottles, pipes

docs.title: 2. Polytetrafluoroethene (Teflon)
docs.text:
• Made by heating tetrafluoroethene with a free radical or persulphate catalyst at high pressure.
\[n\ CF_2=CF_2 \xrightarrow[High\ pressure]{Catalyst} -(CF_2-CF_2)_n-\] \[Tetrafluoroethene\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ Teflon\]
  • It is chemically inert and resists attack by corrosive reagents.
  • Uses: oil seals, gaskets and non-stick coatings on utensils.
  • Teflon coatings decompose at temperatures above 300 °C.

docs.title: 3. Polyacrylonitrile (PAN)
docs.text:
• Formed by addition polymerisation of acrylonitrile in the presence of a peroxide catalyst.
\[n\ CH_2=CHCN \xrightarrow[Peroxide\ catalyst]{Polymerisation} -(CH_2-CH(CN))_n-\] \[Acrylonitrile\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ Polyacrylonitrile\]
  • Used as a substitute for wool in commercial fibres such as orlon or acrilan.
  • Acrylic fibres resist stains, chemicals, insects and fungi well.

docs.title: Polymers | Molecular Mass, Biodegradable and Commercial Polymers
Polymers | Molecular Mass, Biodegradable and Commercial Polymers
Molecular Mass of Polymers
docs.text:
A polymer sample contains chains of varying lengths, so its molecular mass is always expressed as an average value.

  • The properties of a polymer are closely related to its molecular mass, size and structure.
  • During synthesis, how long a chain grows depends on how much monomer is available to it in the reaction mixture. So different chains in the same sample end up with different lengths.
  • The average molecular mass of a polymer can be determined by chemical and physical methods.

docs.title: Biodegradable Polymers
docs.text:
• Many polymers strongly resist environmental degradation. Their solid waste accumulates and stays undegraded for a long time, causing serious environmental problems.
  • To tackle this, new biodegradable synthetic polymers have been developed. They contain functional groups similar to those present in biopolymers, so microorganisms can break them down.
  • Aliphatic polyesters are an important class of biodegradable polymers.

docs.title: 1. PHBV (Poly-β-hydroxybutyrate-co-β-hydroxyvalerate)
docs.text:
• Obtained by copolymerisation of 3-hydroxybutanoic acid and 3-hydroxypentanoic acid. The -OH of one unit forms an ester with the -COOH of the next.
\[CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-COOH + CH_3-CH_2-CH(OH)-CH_2-COOH → -[O-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CO-O-CH(CH_2CH_3)-CH_2-CO]_n-\] \[3-Hydroxybutanoic\ acid\ +\ 3-Hydroxypentanoic\ acid\ →\ PHBV\]
  • PHBV undergoes bacterial degradation in the environment.
  • Uses: speciality packaging, orthopaedic devices and controlled release of drugs.

docs.title: 2. Nylon-2-nylon-6
docs.text:
• An alternating polyamide copolymer of glycine (H2N-CH2-COOH) and amino caproic acid (H2N-(CH2)5-COOH).
  • Glycine contributes a 2-carbon unit and amino caproic acid a 6-carbon unit, hence the name. It is biodegradable.
\[n\ H_2N-CH_2-COOH + n\ H_2N-(CH_2)_5-COOH → -[NH-CH_2-CO-NH-(CH_2)_5-CO]_n- + (2n-1)H_2O\]

docs.title: Polymers of Commercial Importance
docs.text:
Besides the polymers already discussed, some other commercially important polymers are listed below.

Name of polymer Monomer(s) Structure (repeating unit) Uses Polypropene Propene -(CH2-CH(CH3))n- Ropes, toys, pipes, fibres Polystyrene Styrene -(CH2-CH(C6H5))n- Insulator, wrapping material, toys, radio and television cabinets Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) Vinyl chloride -(CH2-CH(Cl))n- Raincoats, hand bags, vinyl flooring, water pipes Urea-formaldehyde resin (a) Urea (b) Formaldehyde -(NH-CO-NH-CH2)n- Unbreakable cups, laminated sheets Glyptal (a) Ethylene glycol (b) Phthalic acid -(OCH2-CH2OOC-C6H4-CO)n- Paints and lacquers Bakelite (a) Phenol (b) Formaldehyde Phenol rings linked by -CH2- bridges (cross linked) Combs, electrical switches, handles of utensils, computer discs

In glyptal, phthalic acid is benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid, so the two -CO- groups are ortho to each other on the ring.

docs.title: Summary of polymers and their monomers
docs.text: Polymer Monomer(s) Type Polythene Ethene Addition, homopolymer Teflon Tetrafluoroethene Addition, homopolymer Polyacrylonitrile Acrylonitrile Addition, homopolymer PVC Vinyl chloride Addition, homopolymer Natural rubber Isoprene Addition, homopolymer Neoprene Chloroprene Addition, homopolymer Buna-S 1,3-Butadiene + Styrene Addition, copolymer Buna-N 1,3-Butadiene + Acrylonitrile Addition, copolymer Nylon 6,6 Hexamethylenediamine + Adipic acid Condensation (polyamide) Nylon 6 Caprolactam Condensation (polyamide) Terylene (Dacron) Ethylene glycol + Terephthalic acid Condensation (polyester) Glyptal Ethylene glycol + Phthalic acid Condensation (polyester) Bakelite Phenol + Formaldehyde Condensation, cross linked Melamine polymer Melamine + Formaldehyde Condensation, cross linked PHBV 3-Hydroxybutanoic acid + 3-Hydroxypentanoic acid Condensation copolymer, biodegradable Nylon-2-nylon-6 Glycine + Amino caproic acid Condensation copolymer, biodegradable

docs.title: Condensation or Step Growth Polymerisation
docs.text:
Condensation or step growth polymerisation involves repeated condensation between two bi-functional monomers, usually with the loss of simple molecules such as water or alcohol, to form high molecular mass polymers.

  • The product of each condensation step is again a bi-functional species, so it can condense further and the chain keeps growing.
  • Each step produces a distinct functionalised species and is independent of the others. That is why it is called step growth polymerisation.
  • Condensation polymers are named after their linking unit: polyamides (-CO-NH-), polyesters (-CO-O-), and so on.
Addition polymerisation Condensation polymerisation Monomers are unsaturated (C=C, C≡C) Monomers are bi- or tri-functional (-OH, -COOH, -NH2) No small molecule is lost Small molecules (H2O, CH3OH, HCl) are lost Chain grows by adding to a reactive chain end Chain grows by independent condensation steps Chain growth polymers, e.g. polythene, PVC, Teflon Step growth polymers, e.g. nylon 6,6, terylene, bakelite

docs.title: 1. Polyamides (Nylons)
docs.text:
• Polymers containing amide linkages (-CO-NH-). They are important synthetic fibres, called nylons.
  • Made by condensation of diamines with dicarboxylic acids, or from amino acids and their lactams.

docs.title: (a) Nylon 6,6
docs.text:
• Prepared by condensation polymerisation of hexamethylenediamine with adipic acid at high pressure and high temperature (553 K).
  • The name 6,6 means that each monomer contributes six carbon atoms.
\[n\ HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH + n\ H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 \xrightarrow[High\ pressure]{553\ K} -[NH-(CH_2)_6-NH-CO-(CH_2)_4-CO]_n- + (2n-1)H_2O\] \[Adipic\ acid\ +\ Hexamethylenediamine\ →\ Nylon\ 6,6\]
  • When n molecules of each monomer combine into one chain, (2n-1) molecules of water are eliminated. For a long chain this is often written loosely as n or 2n H2O.
  • Uses: sheets, bristles for brushes and in the textile industry.

docs.title: (b) Nylon 6
docs.text:
• Obtained by heating caprolactam with water at a high temperature (533-543 K). The ring opens and the units join through amide links.
  • Its repeating unit, -CO-(CH2)5-NH-, has six carbon atoms and comes from a single monomer, hence nylon 6.
  • Uses: tyre cords, fabrics and ropes.

docs.title: 2. Polyesters
docs.text:
• Polycondensation products of dicarboxylic acids and diols, joined by ester linkages.
  • The best known example is terylene (dacron).
  • It is made by heating a mixture of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) at 420 to 460 K in the presence of a zinc acetate-antimony trioxide catalyst. Water is eliminated.
\[n\ HOCH_2CH_2OH + n\ HOOC-C_6H_4-COOH → -[OCH_2CH_2O-CO-C_6H_4-CO]_n- + (2n-1)H_2O\]
  • Dacron fibre is crease resistant. It is blended with cotton and wool fibres and also used as glass reinforcing material in safety helmets.

docs.title: 3. Phenol-Formaldehyde Polymers (Bakelite and Related Polymers)
docs.text:
• These are the oldest synthetic polymers.
  • Formed by condensation of phenol with formaldehyde in the presence of an acid or a base catalyst.
  • The reaction first gives o- and/or p-hydroxymethylphenol derivatives. These react further with phenol, so that the rings get joined to each other through -CH2- groups.
  • The initial product is a linear polymer called Novolac, which is used in paints.
  • When Novolac is heated with more formaldehyde, the chains become cross linked through -CH2- bridges at the remaining ortho/para positions, giving an infusible solid mass called bakelite.
  • Bakelite is a thermosetting polymer.
  • Uses: combs, phonograph records, electrical switches and handles of various utensils.

docs.title: 4. Melamine-Formaldehyde Polymer
docs.text:
