• Formed by condensation polymerisation of melamine (2,4,6-triamino-1,3,5-triazine) and formaldehyde.
  • Formaldehyde first reacts with an -NH2 group to give a resin intermediate containing -NHCH2OH, which then polymerises.
  • Uses: manufacture of unbreakable crockery.

docs.title: Copolymerisation
docs.text:
Copolymerisation is a polymerisation reaction in which a mixture of more than one monomeric species is allowed to polymerise and form a copolymer containing multiple units of each monomer in the same chain.

  • A copolymer can be made by chain growth (addition) polymerisation as well as by step growth (condensation) polymerisation.
  • Copolymers have properties quite different from the homopolymers of the individual monomers.

docs.title: Buna-S (butadiene-styrene copolymer)
docs.text:
• A mixture of 1,3-butadiene and styrene copolymerises to give Buna-S.
\[n\ CH_2=CH-CH=CH_2 + n\ C_6H_5CH=CH_2 → -[CH_2-CH=CH-CH_2-CH(C_6H_5)-CH_2]_n-\] \[1,3-Butadiene\ +\ Styrene\ →\ Butadiene-styrene\ copolymer\ (Buna-S)\]
  • Note that butadiene adds 1,4: its two ends join the chain and a new double bond appears between C-2 and C-3.
  • Buna-S is quite tough and is a good substitute for natural rubber.
  • Uses: autotyres, floor tiles, footwear components and cable insulation.
  • The name comes from Butadiene + Na (sodium, once used as the catalyst) + Styrene.

docs.title: 1. Natural Rubber
docs.text:
• Rubber is a natural polymer with elastic properties, so it is also called an elastomer.
  • It is made from rubber latex, a colloidal dispersion of rubber in water, obtained from the bark of the rubber tree (grown in India, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Malaysia and South America).
  • Natural rubber is a linear polymer of isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) and is called cis-1,4-polyisoprene.
\[Isoprene:\ CH_2=\overset{\large CH_3}{\overset{|}{C}}-CH=CH_2\] \[n\ CH_2=C(CH_3)-CH=CH_2 → -[CH_2-C(CH_3)=CH-CH_2]_n-\ \ \ (cis)\]
  • Each repeating unit keeps one C=C double bond, with the chain continuing on the same side (cis). This causes the chains to bend and coil.
  • The chains are held together only by weak van der Waals forces. Due to the coiled structure, rubber can be stretched like a spring and shows elastic properties.

docs.title: Vulcanisation of Rubber
docs.text:
Natural rubber has several drawbacks:

  • It becomes soft at high temperature (> 335 K) and brittle at low temperature (< 283 K).
  • It has a high water absorption capacity.
  • It is soluble in non-polar solvents and is easily attacked by oxidising agents.

To improve these properties, rubber is vulcanised.

  • Vulcanisation is heating raw rubber with sulphur and a suitable additive at 373 K to 415 K.
  • Sulphur forms cross links between chains at the reactive sites, i.e. at the double bonds and the allylic positions next to them. The rubber becomes stiffer and stronger.
  • In the manufacture of tyre rubber, about 5% sulphur is used as the cross linking agent.
  • The probable structures of vulcanised rubber are:

Conclusion

The double bonds in natural rubber give it a cis, coiled structure (elasticity) and also provide reactive sites where sulphur can form cross links during vulcanisation. The cross links stop the chains from slipping past each other, so vulcanised rubber is less sticky, more elastic over a wider temperature range and more resistant to solvents and oxidation.

docs.title: 2. Synthetic Rubbers
docs.text:
• A synthetic rubber is any vulcanisable, rubber-like polymer which can be stretched to twice its length and returns to its original shape and size as soon as the stretching force is removed.
  • Synthetic rubbers are either homopolymers of 1,3-butadiene derivatives or copolymers of 1,3-butadiene (or its derivatives) with another unsaturated monomer.

docs.title: (a) Neoprene
docs.text:
• Neoprene (polychloroprene) is formed by free radical polymerisation of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene).
\[n\ CH_2=C(Cl)-CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{Polymerisation} -[CH_2-C(Cl)=CH-CH_2]_n-\] \[Chloroprene\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ Neoprene\]
  • It has superior resistance to vegetable and mineral oils.
  • Uses: conveyor belts, gaskets and hoses.

docs.title: (b) Buna-N
docs.text:
• Obtained by copolymerisation of 1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile in the presence of a peroxide catalyst.
\[n\ CH_2=CH-CH=CH_2 + n\ CH_2=CH(CN) \xrightarrow{Copolymerisation} -[CH_2-CH=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH(CN)]_n-\] \[1,3-Butadiene\ +\ Acrylonitrile\ →\ Buna-N\]
  • It is resistant to petrol, lubricating oil and organic solvents.
  • Uses: oil seals and tank linings.
Rubber Monomer(s) Type Special property / Uses Natural rubber Isoprene Homopolymer Elastic; cis-1,4-polyisoprene Neoprene Chloroprene Homopolymer Resists oils; conveyor belts, gaskets, hoses Buna-S 1,3-Butadiene + Styrene Copolymer Tough; autotyres, floor tiles, footwear Buna-N 1,3-Butadiene + Acrylonitrile Copolymer Resists petrol and solvents; oil seals, tank linings

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Polymers are very large molecules of high molecular mass (103-107 u), formed by joining a large number of repeating structural units. They are also called macromolecules.

  • The word polymer comes from two Greek words: poly (many) and mer (unit or part).
  • The repeating units are derived from simple, reactive molecules called monomers. Monomers in a polymer are joined to each other by covalent bonds.
  • The process of forming a polymer from its monomers is called polymerisation.
  • Polymers are the backbone of four major industries: plastics, elastomers (rubbers), fibres, and paints and varnishes. Buckets, toys, packaging bags, synthetic clothes, tyres, gears, seals and electrical insulation are all made of polymers.

Examples

Ethene polymerises to polythene. Hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid react to form nylon 6,6. These are two different types of polymerisation reactions, as we will see below.

\[n\ CH_2=CH_2 → -(CH_2-CH_2)_n-\] \[Ethene\ (monomer)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ Polythene\ (polymer)\]
  • Functionality of a monomer is the number of bonding sites (reactive functional groups) it has. Ethene has one double bond and can join to two other units, so it behaves as bi-functional. Ethylene glycol (two -OH groups) and adipic acid (two -COOH groups) are bi-functional; melamine is poly-functional.

docs.title: Classification of Polymers
docs.text: Polymers can be classified in several ways depending on what we look at: where they come from, their structure, how they are made, the forces between their chains, and how the chain grows.

docs.title: (a) Natural polymers
docs.text:
• Found in plants and animals.
  • Examples: proteins, cellulose, starch, resins and rubber.

docs.title: (b) Semi-synthetic polymers
docs.text:
• Obtained by chemically modifying natural polymers.
  • Examples: cellulose derivatives such as cellulose acetate (rayon) and cellulose nitrate.

docs.title: (c) Synthetic polymers
docs.text:
• Man-made polymers, widely used in daily life and industry.
  • Examples: plastics (polythene), synthetic fibres (nylon 6,6) and synthetic rubbers (Buna-S).

docs.title: (a) Linear polymers
docs.text:
• Consist of long, straight chains lying side by side.
  • Examples: high density polythene (HDP), polyvinyl chloride (PVC).

docs.title: (b) Branched chain polymers
docs.text:
• Linear chains carrying some side branches. The branches prevent close packing of chains.
  • Example: low density polythene (LDP).

docs.title: (c) Cross linked or network polymers
docs.text:
• Usually formed from bi-functional and tri-functional monomers.
  • Strong covalent bonds link the different linear chains together, giving a three-dimensional network.
  • Examples: bakelite, melamine-formaldehyde polymer.

docs.title: 3. Classification Based on Mode of Polymerisation
(a) Addition polymers
docs.text:
• Formed by repeated addition of monomer molecules that contain double or triple bonds. No molecule is lost in the process.
  • Examples: polythene from ethene, polypropene from propene.
  • An addition polymer made from a single kind of monomer is called a homopolymer, e.g. polythene.
  • An addition polymer made from two different monomers is called a copolymer, e.g. Buna-S, Buna-N.
\[n\ CH_2=CH_2 → -(CH_2-CH_2)_n-\ \ \ (Homopolymer)\] \[n\ CH_2=CH-CH=CH_2 + n\ C_6H_5CH=CH_2 → -(CH_2-CH=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH(C_6H_5))_n-\] \[1,3-Butadiene\ +\ Styrene\ →\ Butadiene-styrene\ copolymer\ (Buna-S)\]

docs.title: (b) Condensation polymers
docs.text:
• Formed by repeated condensation reactions between two different bi-functional or tri-functional monomers.
  • Each condensation step eliminates a small molecule such as water, alcohol or hydrogen chloride.
  • Examples: terylene (dacron), nylon 6,6, nylon 6.
\[n\ H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 + n\ HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH → -[NH(CH_2)_6NHCO(CH_2)_4CO]_n- + (2n-1)H_2O\] \[Hexamethylene\ diamine\ +\ Adipic\ acid\ →\ Nylon\ 6,6\]

Example

Is -(CH2-CH(C6H5))n- a homopolymer or a copolymer?

It is a homopolymer. Its only monomer is styrene, C6H5CH=CH2.

docs.title: 4. Classification Based on Molecular Forces
docs.text:
• Mechanical properties of a polymer, such as tensile strength, elasticity and toughness, depend on the intermolecular forces (van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonds) that hold the chains together.
  • On the basis of the strength of these forces, polymers fall into four groups.

docs.title: (a) Elastomers
docs.text:
• Rubber-like solids with elastic properties.
  • Chains are held by the weakest intermolecular forces, so the polymer can be stretched.
  • A few cross links between chains pull the polymer back to its original shape when the force is released, as in vulcanised rubber.
  • Examples: Buna-S, Buna-N, neoprene.

docs.title: (b) Fibres
docs.text:
• Thread-forming solids with high tensile strength and high modulus.
  • Chains are held by strong forces such as hydrogen bonding. These forces also pack the chains closely, giving a crystalline nature.
  • Examples: polyamides (nylon 6,6), polyesters (terylene).

docs.title: (c) Thermoplastic polymers
docs.text:
• Linear or slightly branched long-chain molecules.
  • They soften on heating and harden on cooling, repeatedly, so they can be remoulded.
  • Intermolecular forces are intermediate between those of elastomers and fibres.
  • Examples: polythene, polystyrene, polyvinyls.

docs.title: (d) Thermosetting polymers
docs.text:
• Cross linked or heavily branched molecules.
  • On heating in moulds they undergo extensive cross linking and become hard and infusible. They cannot be softened and reused.
  • Examples: bakelite, urea-formaldehyde resins.

Conclusion

Order of intermolecular forces: Elastomers < Thermoplastics < Fibres. Thermosetting polymers owe their rigidity to a permanent covalent cross-linked network.

docs.title: 5. Classification Based on Growth Polymerisation
docs.text:
• Addition polymers are also called chain growth polymers, because the chain grows by successive addition of monomer units to a reactive (free radical or ionic) chain end.
  • Condensation polymers are also called step growth polymers, because the chain grows through separate, independent condensation steps between functional groups.
Basis Types Examples Source Natural, Semi-synthetic, Synthetic Starch; Cellulose acetate; Nylon 6,6 Structure Linear, Branched, Cross linked HDP, PVC; LDP; Bakelite Mode of polymerisation Addition (homo/co), Condensation Polythene, Buna-S; Terylene Molecular forces Elastomers, Fibres, Thermoplastics, Thermosetting Neoprene; Nylon 6,6; Polystyrene; Bakelite Growth Chain growth, Step growth Polythene; Nylon 6,6

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Explain the terms polymer and monomer.

  • A polymer is a very large molecule of high molecular mass (103-107 u) made of a large number of repeating structural units joined by covalent bonds. Examples: polythene, bakelite, rubber, nylon 6,6.
  • A monomer is the simple, reactive molecule from which these repeating units are derived. Example: ethene is the monomer of polythene.

What are natural and synthetic polymers? Give two examples of each type.

  • Natural polymers are found in plants and animals. Examples: proteins, cellulose, starch, natural rubber.
  • Synthetic polymers are man-made. Examples: polythene, nylon 6,6, Buna-S, terylene.

Distinguish between the terms homopolymer and copolymer and give an example of each.

  • A homopolymer is formed from a single type of monomer. Example: polythene from ethene, -(CH2-CH2)n-.
  • A copolymer is formed from two or more different monomers, with units of each in the same chain. Example: Buna-S from 1,3-butadiene and styrene.

How do you explain the functionality of a monomer?

The functionality of a monomer is the number of bonding sites (reactive functional groups or reactive bonds) present in it.

  • Ethene, ethylene glycol (HOCH2CH2OH) and adipic acid are bi-functional.
  • Bi-functional monomers give linear polymers. Tri-functional monomers (for example phenol, with three reactive ortho/para positions, or melamine) can give cross linked polymers.

Is -(NH-CHR-CO)n- a homopolymer or copolymer?

It is a homopolymer, because it is formed from a single monomer, the amino acid H2N-CHR-COOH. (If R varies from unit to unit, as in a natural protein, the chain becomes a copolymer.)

How can you differentiate between addition and condensation polymerisation?

  • In addition polymerisation, unsaturated monomers (alkenes, dienes) add to each other repeatedly without losing any molecule. The chain grows by adding monomers to a reactive end (free radical or ion). Examples: polythene, PVC, Teflon.
  • In condensation polymerisation, bi- or tri-functional monomers condense step by step with loss of small molecules such as H2O, CH3OH or HCl. Examples: nylon 6,6, terylene, bakelite.

Write the free radical mechanism for the polymerisation of ethene.

Chain initiation: Benzoyl peroxide breaks into phenyl radicals, which add to ethene.

\[(C_6H_5COO)_2 → 2C_6H_5CO\dot{O} → 2\dot{C}_6H_5 + 2CO_2\] \[\dot{C}_6H_5 + CH_2=CH_2 → C_6H_5-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2\]

Chain propagation: The radical keeps adding ethene molecules.

\[C_6H_5-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2 + CH_2=CH_2 → C_6H_5-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2\] \[↓\] \[C_6H_5-(CH_2-CH_2)_n-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2\]

Chain termination: Two growing radicals combine.

\[2\ C_6H_5-(CH_2-CH_2)_n-CH_2-\dot{C}H_2 → C_6H_5-(CH_2-CH_2)_n-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-(CH_2-CH_2)_n-C_6H_5\]

Define thermoplastics and thermosetting polymers with two examples of each.

  • Thermoplastics are linear or slightly branched polymers that soften on heating and harden on cooling repeatedly. Examples: polythene, polystyrene, PVC.
  • Thermosetting polymers are cross linked or heavily branched polymers which, on heating in moulds, undergo extensive cross linking and become permanently hard and infusible. They cannot be reused. Examples: bakelite, urea-formaldehyde resin.

Write the monomers used for getting the following polymers: (i) Polyvinyl chloride (ii) Teflon (iii) Bakelite

(i) Vinyl chloride, CH2=CHCl

(ii) Tetrafluoroethene, CF2=CF2

(iii) Phenol, C6H5OH and formaldehyde, HCHO

Write the name and structure of one of the common initiators used in free radical addition polymerisation.

Benzoyl peroxide:

\[C_6H_5-\overset{O}{\overset{||}{C}}-O-O-\overset{O}{\overset{||}{C}}-C_6H_5\]

Write the names of monomers of the following polymers: (i) -[NH-(CH2)6-NH-CO-(CH2)4-CO]n- (ii) -[CO-(CH2)5-NH]n- (iii) -(CF2-CF2)n-

(i) Hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid (nylon 6,6)

(ii) Caprolactam (nylon 6)

(iii) Tetrafluoroethene (Teflon)

Classify the following as addition and condensation polymers: Terylene, Bakelite, Polyvinyl chloride, Polythene.

  • Addition polymers: polyvinyl chloride, polythene
  • Condensation polymers: terylene, bakelite

Explain the difference between Buna-N and Buna-S.

Both are synthetic rubbers made by addition copolymerisation of 1,3-butadiene.

  • Buna-N is a copolymer of 1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile. It resists petrol, lubricating oil and organic solvents.
  • Buna-S is a copolymer of 1,3-butadiene and styrene. It is tough and used as a substitute for natural rubber, e.g. in autotyres.

Arrange the following polymers in increasing order of their intermolecular forces. (i) Nylon 6,6, Buna-S, Polythene (ii) Nylon 6, Neoprene, Polyvinyl chloride

Elastomers have the weakest forces, thermoplastics intermediate, and fibres (hydrogen bonded) the strongest.

(i) Buna-S (elastomer) < Polythene (thermoplastic) < Nylon 6,6 (fibre)

(ii) Neoprene (elastomer) < Polyvinyl chloride (thermoplastic) < Nylon 6 (fibre)

How does the presence of double bonds in rubber molecules influence their structure and reactivity?

  • Natural rubber is cis-1,4-polyisoprene. The cis double bond in each unit bends the chain, so the chains cannot pack closely. They are held only by weak van der Waals forces and take up a coiled shape, which makes rubber elastic.
  • The double bonds (and the allylic positions next to them) are reactive sites. Sulphur forms cross links at these sites during vulcanisation, and oxidising agents also attack them.

Discuss the main purpose of vulcanisation of rubber.

Raw natural rubber becomes soft above 335 K and brittle below 283 K, absorbs a lot of water, dissolves in non-polar solvents and is easily oxidised. Heating it with sulphur (and an additive) at 373-415 K introduces sulphur cross links between chains. This makes rubber stiffer, stronger, more elastic over a wider temperature range and more resistant to solvents and oxidising agents.

What are the monomeric repeating units of Nylon-6 and Nylon-6,6?

  • Nylon 6: -[NH-(CH2)5-CO]- , derived from caprolactam.
  • Nylon 6,6: -[NH-(CH2)6-NH-CO-(CH2)4-CO]- , derived from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid.

Write the names and structures of the monomers of the following polymers: (i) Buna-S (ii) Buna-N (iii) Dacron (iv) Neoprene

(i) Buna-S: 1,3-butadiene, CH2=CH-CH=CH2 and styrene, C6H5CH=CH2

(ii) Buna-N: 1,3-butadiene, CH2=CH-CH=CH2 and acrylonitrile, CH2=CH-CN

(iii) Dacron: ethylene glycol, HOCH2CH2OH and terephthalic acid, HOOC-C6H4-COOH (para)

(iv) Neoprene: chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene), CH2=C(Cl)-CH=CH2

Identify the monomers in the following polymeric structures: (i) -[CO-(CH2)8-CO-NH-(CH2)6-NH]n- (ii) the melamine-formaldehyde polymer -[HN-C3N3(NH-)-NH-CH2]n-

(i) The -CO-(CH2)8-CO- part comes from decanedioic acid (sebacic acid), HOOC-(CH2)8-COOH, and the -NH-(CH2)6-NH- part from hexamethylenediamine, H2N-(CH2)6-NH2. (This polymer is nylon 6,10.)

(ii) Melamine (2,4,6-triamino-1,3,5-triazine) and formaldehyde, HCHO.

How is dacron obtained from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid?

A mixture of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid is heated at 420 to 460 K in the presence of a zinc acetate-antimony trioxide catalyst. The -OH groups and -COOH groups condense to form ester links, with loss of water.

\[n\ HOCH_2CH_2OH + n\ HOOC-C_6H_4-COOH → -[OCH_2CH_2O-CO-C_6H_4-CO]_n- + (2n-1)H_2O\]

What is a biodegradable polymer? Give an example of a biodegradable aliphatic polyester.

A biodegradable polymer is one that can be broken down by microorganisms (bacteria) in the environment. Such polymers contain functional groups similar to those in biopolymers.

Example of a biodegradable aliphatic polyester: PHBV (poly-β-hydroxybutyrate-co-β-hydroxyvalerate), a copolymer of 3-hydroxybutanoic acid and 3-hydroxypentanoic acid.

docs.title: Degree of dissociation (α)
docs.text:
• Fraction of reactants dissociated is known as degree of dissociation.
\[α = {{Moles\ of\ reactants\ dissociated \times 100} \over Initial\ moles\ of\ reactants}\]

Let us consider an example, in which moles of A given is 2.

\[ A ⇌ 2B + 3C\] \[At\ t=0,\ moles\ of\ A = 2,\ moles\ of\ B = 0,\ moles\ of\ C = 0\]

At equilibrium:

\[moles\ of\ A = 2-2α,\ moles\ of\ B = 2\times 2α,\ moles\ of\ C = 3\times 3α\]

If degree of dissociation of NH3 is 75%, then calculate the partial pressure of each gas at equilibrium. The total pressure at equilibrium is 1 atm. \(2NH_{3_{(g)}} ⇌ N_{2_{(g)}} + 3H_{2_{(g)}}\)

Let us consider that at t = 0, moles of NH3 = a, moles of N2 = 0 and moles of H2 = 0.

If α is the degree of dissociation, then at equilibrium, we can calculate:

\[moles\ of\ NH_3 = a - a\ α\] \[moles\ of\ N_2 = {{a α} \over 2}\] \[moles\ of\ H_2 = {{3a α} \over 2}\] \[Total\ moles\ at\ equilibrium = a - aα + {{a α} \over 2} + {{3a α} \over 2} = a(1+α)\] \[Partial\ pressure\ of\ NH_3 = {Χ_{NH_3} \times Total\ pressure} = {a(1-α) \over a(1+α)} \times 1 = {1-0.75 \over 1+0.75} = {1\over7} atm\] \[Similarly,\ partial\ pressure\ of\ N_2 = {3\over14} atm\] \[And,\ partial\ pressure\ of\ H_2 = {9\over14} atm\]

docs.title: 1. Reactions with Δn<sub>g</sub> = 0
docs.text:
Let us consider an example where Δng is zero (decomposition of HI)

\[2HI_{(g)} ⇌ H_{2_{(g)}} + I_{2_{(g)}}\] \[At\ t=0,\ let\ moles\ of\ HI = a\] \[At\ t=0,\ moles\ of\ H_2\ and\ I_2 = 0\]

If α is the rate of dissociation ,then at equilibrium:

\[moles\ of\ HI = a - aα\] \[moles\ of\ H_2 = {aα\over 2}\] \[moles\ of\ I_2 = {aα\over 2}\]

Also, let the volume of container be V. Then, the concentrations are:

\[Concentration\ of\ HI = {a(1-α)\over V}\] \[Concentration\ of\ H_2 = {aα\over 2V}\] \[Concentration\ of\ I_2 = {aα\over 2V}\]

Now we can calculate Kc as below:

\[K_c = {{[H_2][I_2]}\over{[HI]^2}}\] \[K_c = {{{aα\over 2V} \times {aα\over 2V}} \over ({{a(1-α)}\over V})^2}\] \[K_c = {α^2 \over 4(1 - α)^2}\]

Also, Kp is given by:

\[K_p = K_c\ (RT)^{Δn_g}\]

Here, Δng = 0, so we can write:

\[K_p = K_c = {α^2 \over 4(1 - α)^2}\]

Kp can also be calculated alternatively using the below method:

\[Total\ moles\ at\ equilibrium = a - aα + {aα\over 2} + {aα\over 2} = a\]

Let total pressure be P and we know that:

\[Partial\ pressure = mole\ fraction \times total\ pressure\]

Hence, we can find partial pressure of each gas as:

\[P_{H_2} = {aα\over 2a} \times P = {Pα \over 2}\] \[P_{I_2} = {aα\over 2a} \times P = {Pα \over 2}\] \[P_{HI} = {{a(1-α)\over a} \times P} = P(1-α)\] \[K_p = {{P_{H_2} \times P_{I_2}} \over (P_{HI})^2} = {α^2 \over {4(1-α)^2}}\]

docs.title: 2. Reactions with Δn<sub>g</sub> > 0
docs.text:
Let us consider an example where Δng > 0 (decomposition of PCl5)

\[PCl_{5_{(g)}} ⇌ PCl_{3_{(g)}} + Cl_{2_{(g)}}\] \[At\ t=0,\ let\ moles\ of\ PCl_5 = a\] \[At\ t=0,\ moles\ of\ PCl_3\ and\ PCl_5\ = 0\]

If α is the rate of dissociation, then at equilibrium:

\[moles\ of\ PCl_5 = a-aα\] \[moles\ of\ PCl_3 = aα\] \[moles\ of\ Cl_2 = aα\]

If volume of container is V, then the concentrations at equilibrium:

\[Concentration of PCl_5 = {a-aα \over V}\] \[Concentration of PCl_3 = {aα \over V}\] \[Concentration of Cl_2 = {aα \over V}\] \[K_c = {[PCl_3][Cl_2]\over [PCl_5]}\] \[K_c = {{aα\over V}\times{aα\over V}\over{a(1-α)\over V}} = {aα^2 \over (1-α)V}\]

Now, let us calculate Kp in terms of pressure. Let the total pressure be P.

\[Total\ moles\ at\ equilibrium = a-aα+aα+aα = a(1+α)\]

We know that partial pressure = mole fraction * Total Pressure. Hence:

\[P_{PCl_3} = {{aα\over a(1+α)} \times P} = {Pα\over(1+α)}\] \[P_{Cl_2} = {{aα\over a(1+α)} \times P} = {Pα\over(1+α)}\] \[P_{PCl_5} = {{a(1-α)\over a(1+α)}\times P} = {P(1-α)\over (1+α)}\]

We can calculate Kp as:

\[K_p = {{P_{PCl_3} \times P_{Cl_2}} \over P_{PCl_5}}\] \[K_p = {{Pα\over (1+α)} \times {Pα\over (1+α)} \over {P(1-α)\over(1+α)}}\] \[K_p = {Pα^2 \over (1-α^2)}\]

docs.title: 3. Reactions with Δn<sub>g</sub> < 0
docs.text:
Let us consider a reaction in which Δng is less than 0.

\[N_{2_{(g)}} + 3H_{2_{(g)}} ⇌ 2NH_{3_{(g)}}\]

At time t = 0, let the moles of N2 and H2 be a and moles of NH3 be 0.

Now, if α is the degree of dissociation, then at equilibrium:

\[moles\ of\ N_2 = a - {1 \over 3}aα\] \[moles\ of\ H_2 = a - aα\] \[moles\ of\ NH_3 = {2\over 3} aα\]

Let the volume of container be V. Now, we can calculate Kc as shown below:

\[K_c = {[NH_3]^2 \over [N_2] [H_2]^3}\] \[K_c = {({2aα\over 3V})^2 \over ({a-{aα\over 3} \over V}) \times ({a-aα\over V})^3 }\] \[K_c = {4α^2V \over 3a(3-α)(1-α)^2}\]

Can you calculate Kp for this reaction in terms of total pressure P?

docs.title: Equilibrium Constant (K<sub>c</sub>)
docs.text:
• The ratio of rate constants of forward and backward reaction is known as equilibrium constant.
\[Reactants ⇌ Products\] \[K_c = {K_f \over K_b}\]

Here, Kf = Rate of forward reaction and Kb = Rate of backward reaction

Example

\[n_1A + n_2B ⇌ n_3C + n_4D\]

From law of mass action, we can write:

\[r_f = K_f\ [A]^{n_1}\ [B]^{n_2}\] \[r_b = K_b\ [C]^{n_3}\ [D]^{n_4}\]

where, rf = Rate of forward reaction and rb = Rate of backward reaction

At equilibrium, rate of forward reaction = rate of backward reaction.

\[K_f\ [A]^{n_1}\ [B]^{n_2} = K_b\ [C]^{n_3}\ [D]^{n_4}\] \[ {K_f \over K_b} = {{[C]^{n_3}\ [D]^{n_4}} \over {[A]^{n_1}\ [B]^{n_2}}}\] \[ K_c = {{[C]^{n_3}\ [D]^{n_4}} \over {[A]^{n_1}\ [B]^{n_2}}}\]

docs.title: Equilibrium Constant (K<sub>p</sub>)
docs.text:
• There is another equilibrium constant, Kp defined for gaseous phase reactions.

Example

\[n_1A_{(g)} + n_2B_{(g)} ⇌ n_3C_{(g)} + n_4D_{(g)}\] \[ K_p = {{{p_C}^{n_3} \times {p_D}^{n_4}} \over {{p_A}^{n_1} \times {p_B}^{n_2}}}\]

Here, pC = Partial pressure of C

pD = Partial pressure of D

pA = Partial pressure of A

pB = Partial pressure of B

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example 1

The reaction given below can be considered as a gaseous phase reaction because CO2 is a gas and other substances are pure solids.

\[CaCO_{3_{(s)}} ⇌ CaO_{(s)} + CO_{2_{(g)}}\]

So, we can define both Kc and Kp for this reaction.

\[K_p = p_{CO_2}\] \[K_c = [CO_2]\]

Example 2

\[N_{2_{(g)}} + 3H_{2_{(g)}} ⇌ 2NH_{3_{(g)}}\]

This is a gaseous phase reaction. So, we can define both Kc and Kp for this reaction.

\[K_c = {{[NH_3]^2} \over {[N_2]\ [H_2]^3}}\] \[K_p = {{p^2_{(NH_3)}} \over {p_{N_2}\ p^3_{H_2}}}\]

Example 3

The reaction given below is a homogeneous liquid phase reaction.

CH3COOC2H5(l) + H2O(l) ⇌ CH3COOH(l) + C2H5OH(l)

In this case, we can define only Kc.

\[K_c = {{[CH_3COOH]\ [C_2H_5OH]} \over {[CH_3COOC_2H_5]\ [H_2O]}}\]

docs.title: Relation between K<sub>p</sub> and K<sub>c</sub>
docs.text:
• Let us consider a gaseous phase reaction:
\[n_1A_{(g)} + n_2B_{(g)} ⇌ n_3C_{(g)} + n_4D_{(g)}\] \[K_p = {{p^{n_3}_C \times p^{n_4}_D} \over {p^{n_1}_A \times p^{n_2}_B}}\]
  • According to ideal gas equation, we can write:
\[PV = nRT\] \[P = {n \over V}RT\] \[P = CRT\]
  • By applying P = CRT in the above expression of Kp, we can write that:
\[K_p = {{(C_CRT)^{n_3} (C_DRT)^{n_4}} \over {(C_ART)^{n_1} (C_BRT)^{n_2}}}\] \[K_p = {{(C_C)^{n_3} (C_D)^{n_4}} \over {(C_A)^{n_1} (C_B)^{n_2}}} \times {RT}^{(n_3+n_4)-(n_1+n_2)}\] \[K_p = K_c \times (RT)^{Δn_g}\]
  • Here, Δng = Total no. of gaseous moles of products - Total no. of gaseous moles of reactants.

Example

\[N_{2_{(g)}} + 3H_{2_{(g)}} ⇌ 2NH_{3_{(g)}}\] \[Δn_g = 2 - (3+1) = -2\] \[K_p = K_c \times (RT)^{-2}\]
  • The units of Kp and Kc depend on Δng. The unit of Kp is (atm)Δng and that of Kc is (mol/L)Δng

docs.title: Characteristics of Equilibrium Constant
docs.text:
• When an equilibrium reaction is reversed, its equilibrium constant (Kp or Kc) gets inverted.
  • When two reactions are added or subtracted, their equilibrium constants will get multiplied or divided respectively.
  • When an equilibrium reaction with equilibrium constant K is multiplied by any number x, then equilibrium constant becomes Kx.

docs.title: Equilibrium State
docs.text:
• Equilibrium is defined as the state of a system in which the measurable properties of a system like colour, concentration, pressure etc become constant.
  • There are two types of equilibrium: (a) Physical equilibrium (b) Chemical equilibrium.
  • Equilibrium involving physical processes is called physical equilibrium.

Examples of physical equilibrium

(i) Melting of solids (solid ⇌ liquid).

(ii) Vaporization of liquids (Liquid ⇌ Gas).

  • Equilibrium involving chemical processes is called chemical equilibrium.

Example of chemical equilibrium

N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3

docs.title: Characteristics of chemical equilibrium
docs.text:
• Chemical equilibrium can be achieved in reversible reactions only because reversible reactions can occur in both forward and backward directions while irreversible reactions occur only in one direction.
  • Equilibrium can only be achieved in a closed container, ie, products should not be allowed to escape.

Example

\[CaCO_{3(s)} ⇌ CaO_s + CO_{2(g)}\]

If the container is open in this reaction, then CO2 will escape and reaction will not move in backward direction. Thus, equilibrium will never be achieved.

  • Equilibrium can be achieved from both product and reactant sides.

Example

\[CaCO_{3(s)} ⇌ CaO_s + CO_{2(g)}\]

We can achieve equilibrium by decomposing CaCO3 or by starting reaction with CaO and CO2 in a closed container.

  • The concentration of reactants decreases and that of products increases and both become constant at equilibrium. It should be noted that the concentration of reactants and products may or may not be equal at equilibrium but they are always constant at equilibrium.

At point P, the concentration of both reactants and products are equal but equilibrium has not been achieved. At time = t, equilibrium is achieved.

  • The rate of forward reaction decreases and that of backward reaction increases and both become equal at equilibrium.

At point P, rate of forward reaction becomes equal to that of backward reaction and equilibrium has been achieved.

Key Point

At equilibrium, concentration of products and reactants are constant (but may or may not be equal) and rates of forward and backward reactions are equal.

  • Chemical equilibrium is dynamic in nature, ie, none of the forward and backward reactions stop. Both forward and backward reactions occur at the same rate.

docs.title: Chemical Equilibrium | Law of Mass Action
Chemical Equilibrium | Law of Mass Action
Law of Mass Action
docs.text:
• According to this law, the rate of a reactions is directly proportional to the product of active masses of reactants raised to the power of their stoichiometric coefficients.

Example

Let us consider a reaction:

\[n_1A + n_2B → Products\]

According to law of mass action, we can write:

\[rate ∝ [A]^{n_1}\ [B]^{n_2}\] \[rate = {k\ [A]^{n_1}\ [B]^{n_2}}\]

Here, k = rate constant and the above expression is called rate law or rate equation.

docs.title: Active Mass
docs.text:
• Active mass of a component A is denoted by [A].
  • Active mass can be defined in two phases: solution phase and gaseous phase.
  • When reaction occurs in solution phase, active mass is taken as molarity.
\[Active\ mass = molarity\]

When reaction occurs in gaseous phase, active mass can be taken as partial pressure.

\[Active\ mass = Partial\ pressure\]

Since, partial pressure = mole fraction x Total pressure

We can write:

\[Active\ mass = Mole\ fraction \times Total\ pressure\]
  • For gaseous reactants, both molarity and partial pressure can be used as active mass interchangeably.
  • Active mass of solid substance in a chemical reaction is always taken as 1.

Example

\[A_{(aq)} + B_{(s)} ⇌ C_{(aq)}\] \[[B] = 1\]
  • If any one of the substance in reactant or product is solid or aqueous, then the active mass of other liquids will be taken as 1.

Example

\[A_{(l)} + B{(aq)} ⇌ C_{(l)} + D_{(l)}\] \[[A] = 1, [C] = 1, [D] = 1\]
  • For a homogeneous liquid phase reaction, the active mass of pure liquid will not be taken as unity.

Example

\[A_{(l)} + B_{(l)} ⇌ C_{(l)} + D_{(l)}\] \[[A] ≠ 1, [B] ≠ 1, [C] ≠ 1, [D] ≠ 1\]

docs.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
docs.text: Le Chatelier's Principle states that if any change is imposed on equilibrium state, then equilibrium will shift itself in that direction in which the effect of that change is nullified.

docs.title: Effect of change in concentration of reactants and products
docs.text:
• Let us consider a reaction: A + B ⇌ C + D
  • If concentration of reactants is increased, then to achieve equilibrium again, the concentration of reactants needs to de decreased. For this to happen, the reaction will shift in forward direction.
  • If concentration of products is increased, then to achieve equilibrium again, the concentration of products needs to be decreased. For this to happen, reaction will shift in backward direction.
  • If concentration of reactants is decreased, then to achieve equilibrium again, the concentration of reactants needs to be increased. For this to happen, reaction will shift in backward direction.
  • If concentration of products is decreased, then to achieve equilibrium again, the concentration of products needs to be increased. For this to happen, reaction will shift in forward direction.

docs.title: Effect of change in temperature
docs.text:
• Exothermic reactions are favoured at low temperature and endothermic reactions are favoured at high temperature.
  • For exothermic reaction, if temperature is increased, then reaction will shift in backward direction and if temperature is decreased, then reaction will shift in forward direction.
  • For endothermic reaction, if temperature is increased, then reaction will shift in forward direction and if temperature is decreased, then reaction will shift in backward direction.

docs.title: Effect of change in pressure
docs.text:
• Let us consider a reaction: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)
\[K_p = {(p_{NH_3})^2 \over p_{N_2} \times (p_{H_2})^3}\]
  • Also, we know that partial pressure of a gas depends on total pressure and mole fraction of gas. Partial pressure = Mole fraction * Total pressure
\[K_p = {P^2 \times (Χ_{NH_3})^2 \over {P \times Χ_{N_2} \times P^3 \times (Χ_{H_2})^3}}\] \[K_p = {{1 \over P^2} \times {(Χ_{NH_3})^2 \over {Χ_{N_2} \times (Χ_{H_2})^3}}}\]

  • In this reaction, if total pressure P is increased, then to maintain equilibrium, the moles of NH3 should increase. Hence, reaction will move in forward direction.

  • Similarly, if total pressure P is decreased, then to maintain equilibrium, the moles of NH3 should decrease and that of reactants should increase. Hence, reaction will move in backward direction.

Conclusion

  • On increasing pressure, the reaction will move in that direction in which total number of gaseous moles is less and on decreasing pressure, the reaction will move in that direction in which total number of gaseous moles is more.

  • The reaction for which Δng = 0 has no effect of pressure.

docs.title: Effect of addition of inert gas
docs.text:
• If inert gas is added at constant volume, then there will be no effect on equilibrium state. This is because at constant volume if inert gas is added, then total pressure increases but mole fraction of individual gases decreases, so partial pressure of individual gases will remain same.
  • If inert gas is added at constant pressure, then mole fraction of individual gases will decrease. This decreases the individual partial pressure of each gas. However, the direction of reaction will depend on Δng.

Let us consider an example where Δng > 0:

\[A_{(g)} ⇌ B_{(g)} + C_{(g)}\] \[K_p = {p_B \times p_C \over p_A}\] \[K_p = {P \times Χ_B \times P \times Χ_C \over P \times Χ_A}\] \[K_p = {P {(n_B/N) \times (n_C/N) \over (n_A/N)}}\] \[K_p ∝ {1 \over N},\ where\ N = total\ moles\ of\ gases\]

Since no. of gaseous moles are increased and Qp will become less than Kp, the reaction will shift in forward direction to achieve equilibrium.

Conclusion

If inert gas is added at constant pressure:

  • Δng > 0 : Forward Shift

  • Δng < 0 : Backward Shift

  • Δng = 0 : No effect on equilibrium

docs.title: Effect of catalyst
docs.text:
• Catalyst is a substance which can alter the rate of a reaction.
  • Catalyst has no effect on equilibrium state but it changes the time taken to achieve equilibrium state.
  • Positive catalyst decreases the time taken to achieve equilibrium while negative catalyst increases the time taken to achieve equilibrium.

docs.title: Reaction Quotient (Q<sub>c</sub>)
docs.text:
• Reaction quotient helps in predicting the direction of reaction. It helps to decide whether the reaction is moving in forward direction or in backward direction.
  • Qc has a tendency to become equal to Kc.

Let us consider a chemical reaction:

\[n_1A + n_2B ⇌ n_3C + n_4D\]

At any time t, we can define reaction quotient as:

\[Q_c = {[C]^{n_3} [D]^{n4} \over [A]^{n_1} [B]^{n_2}}\]

Case 1: If Qc > Kc

Qc tends to become equal to Kc. For this, its value should decrease. Hence, the concentration of C and D will decrease and that of A and B will increase.

This indicates that reaction will shift in backward direction.

Case 2: If Qc < Kc

Qc tends to become equal to Kc. For this, its value should increase. Hence, the concentration of C and D will increase and that of A and B will decrease.

This indicates that reaction will shift in forward direction.

Case 3: If Qc = Kc

Reaction has already reached equilibrium.

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
At 1400 K, Kc = 2.5 x 10-3 for the reaction: CH4(g) + 2H2Sg ⇌ CS2(g) + 4H2(g)A 10 L reaction vessel at 1400 K contains 2 moles of CH4, 3 moles of CS2, 3 moles of H2 and 4 moles of H2S. Is the reaction mixture at equilibrium? If not, in which direction does the reaction proceed to reach equilibrium?

\[Q_c = {[CS_2][H_2]^4 \over [CH_4][H_2S]^2}\] \[Q_c = {({3 \over 10}) \times ({3 \over 10})^4 \over ({2\over 5})\times ({4\over 10})^2} = 7.5 \times 10^{-2}\]

Here Qc > Kc. Hence, the reaction will proceed in backward direction to achieve equilibrium.

docs.title: Chemical Kinetics | Half-Life and Pseudo First Order Reactions
Chemical Kinetics | Half-Life and Pseudo First Order Reactions
Half-Life of a Reaction
docs.text: The half-life of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of a reactant is reduced to one half of its initial concentration. It is represented as t1/2.

docs.title: 1. Half-life of a zero order reaction
docs.text:
\[k = {[R]_0 - [R] \over t}\] \[At\ t = t_{1/2},\ \ [R] = {1 \over 2}[R]_0\] \[k = {[R]_0 - {1 \over 2}[R]_0 \over t_{1/2}}\] \[t_{1/2} = {[R]_0 \over 2k}\]
  • For a zero order reaction, t1/2 is directly proportional to the initial concentration of reactant and inversely proportional to the rate constant.

docs.title: 2. Half-life of a first order reaction
docs.text:
\[k = {2.303 \over t} log{[R]_0 \over [R]}\] \[At\ t = t_{1/2},\ \ [R] = {[R]_0 \over 2}\] \[k = {2.303 \over t_{1/2}} log{[R]_0 \over [R]_0/2}\] \[t_{1/2} = {2.303 \over k} log\ 2 = {2.303 \over k} \times 0.301\] \[t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over k}\]
  • For a first order reaction, the half-life is constant, i.e. it does not depend on the initial concentration of the reactant.
  • So t1/2 can be found directly from k, and k from t1/2.
  • After n half-lives, the amount of reactant left is (1/2)n of the initial amount.

Conclusion

  • For a zero order reaction: t1/2 ∝ [R]0

  • For a first order reaction: t1/2 is independent of [R]0

docs.text: Order Reaction type Differential rate law Integrated rate law Straight line plot Half-life Units of k 0 R → P d[R]/dt = -k kt = [R]<sub>0</sub> - [R] [R] vs t [R]<sub>0</sub>/2k mol L<sup>-1</sup>s<sup>-1</sup> 1 R → P d[R]/dt = -k[R] [R] = [R]<sub>0</sub>e<sup>-kt</sup> or kt = ln([R]<sub>0</sub>/[R]) ln[R] vs t ln 2/k s<sup>-1</sup>

docs.title: Pseudo First Order Reaction
docs.text:
• The order of a reaction is sometimes changed by the conditions. This happens when one reactant is present in large excess.
  • Consider the acid hydrolysis of 0.01 mol of ethyl acetate with 10 mol of water:
\[CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3COOH + C_2H_5OH\] Time CH3COOC2H5 H2O CH3COOH C2H5OH t = 0 0.01 mol 10 mol 0 mol 0 mol t (completion) 0 mol 9.9 mol 0.01 mol 0.01 mol
  • The amount of water hardly changes during the reaction. So [H2O] can be taken as constant:
\[Rate = k'[CH_3COOC_2H_5][H_2O]\] \[Rate = k[CH_3COOC_2H_5],\ \ where\ k = k'[H_2O]\]
  • The reaction is actually second order but behaves as a first order reaction. Such reactions are called pseudo first order reactions.
  • Inversion of cane sugar is another pseudo first order reaction:
\[\underset{Cane\ sugar}{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} \underset{Glucose}{C_6H_{12}O_6} + \underset{Fructose}{C_6H_{12}O_6}\] \[Rate = k[C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}]\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
A first order reaction is found to have a rate constant, k = 5.5 × 10-14 s-1. Find the half-life of the reaction.

\[t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over k} = {0.693 \over 5.5 \times 10^{-14}\ s^{-1}}\] \[t_{1/2} = 1.26 \times 10^{13}\ s\]

Show that in a first order reaction, time required for completion of 99.9% is 10 times of half-life (t1/2) of the reaction.

  • When the reaction is 99.9% complete:
\[[R] = [R]_0 - 0.999[R]_0 = 0.001[R]_0\] \[t_{99.9\%} = {2.303 \over k} log{[R]_0 \over 0.001[R]_0} = {2.303 \over k} log\ 10^3\] \[t_{99.9\%} = {6.909 \over k}\] \[t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over k}\] \[{t_{99.9\%} \over t_{1/2}} = {6.909 \over k} \times {k \over 0.693} = 10\]

A first order reaction has a rate constant 1.15 × 10-3 s-1. How long will 5 g of this reactant take to reduce to 3 g?

\[t = {2.303 \over k} log{[R]_0 \over [R]}\] \[t = {2.303 \over 1.15 \times 10^{-3}} log{5 \over 3}\] \[t = {2.303 \over 1.15 \times 10^{-3}} \times 0.2219\] \[t = 444\ s\]

Time required to decompose SO2Cl2 to half of its initial amount is 60 minutes. If the decomposition is a first order reaction, calculate the rate constant of the reaction.

\[k = {0.693 \over t_{1/2}} = {0.693 \over 60\ min}\] \[k = 1.155 \times 10^{-2}\ min^{-1}\] \[k = {1.155 \times 10^{-2} \over 60} = 1.925 \times 10^{-4}\ s^{-1}\]

Hydrolysis of methyl acetate in aqueous solution has been studied by titrating the liberated acetic acid against sodium hydroxide. The concentration of the ester at different times is given below.t/min: 0, 30, 60, 90C/mol L-1: 0.8500, 0.8004, 0.7538, 0.7096Show that it follows a pseudo first order reaction, as the concentration of water remains nearly constant (55 mol L-1) during the course of the reaction. What is the value of k' in the equation Rate = k'[CH3COOCH3][H2O]?

  • For a pseudo first order reaction, the reaction should be first order with respect to the ester when [H2O] is constant.
\[k = {2.303 \over t} log{C_0 \over C},\ \ where\ k = k'[H_2O]\] \[At\ t = 30\ min:\ k = {2.303 \over 30} log{0.8500 \over 0.8004} = 2.004 \times 10^{-3}\ min^{-1}\] \[At\ t = 60\ min:\ k = {2.303 \over 60} log{0.8500 \over 0.7538} = 2.002 \times 10^{-3}\ min^{-1}\] \[At\ t = 90\ min:\ k = {2.303 \over 90} log{0.8500 \over 0.7096} = 2.005 \times 10^{-3}\ min^{-1}\]
  • Since k'[H2O] is constant (about 2.004 × 10-3 min-1), the reaction is pseudo first order.
\[k'[H_2O] = 2.004 \times 10^{-3}\ min^{-1}\] \[k' \times 55\ mol\ L^{-1} = 2.004 \times 10^{-3}\ min^{-1}\] \[k' = 3.64 \times 10^{-5}\ mol^{-1}L\ min^{-1}\]

docs.title: Chemical Kinetics | Integrated Rate Equations
docs.text: Integrated rate equations relate the concentration of reactants at different times directly to the rate constant, and are obtained by integrating the differential rate equation.

docs.title: Why Integrated Rate Equations?
docs.text:
• The differential rate equation needs the instantaneous rate, which is found from the slope of a tangent on a concentration vs time curve. This is difficult to measure accurately, so finding the rate law and order this way is not easy.
  • To avoid this, the differential rate equation is integrated. This gives a relation between quantities we can measure directly: concentrations at different times and the rate constant.
  • The integrated equations are different for reactions of different orders. Here we derive them for zero and first order reactions.

docs.title: Zero Order Reactions
docs.text:
In a zero order reaction, the rate is proportional to the zero power of the concentration of reactants, i.e. the rate does not depend on concentration.

\[R → P\] \[Rate = -{d[R] \over dt} = k[R]^0 = k\] \[d[R] = -k\ dt\]
  • Integrating both sides:
\[[R] = -kt + I\]

Where, I is the constant of integration.

  • At t = 0, [R] = [R]0 (initial concentration). So, [R]0 = -k × 0 + I, i.e. I = [R]0.
\[[R] = -kt + [R]_0\] \[k = {[R]_0 - [R] \over t}\]
  • Comparing with y = mx + c, a plot of [R] against t is a straight line with slope = -k and intercept = [R]0.

docs.title: Examples of Zero Order Reactions
docs.text:
• Zero order reactions are uncommon but occur under special conditions. Some enzyme catalysed reactions and reactions on metal surfaces are zero order.
  • Decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum surface at high pressure:
\[2NH_{3(g)} \xrightarrow[Pt\ catalyst]{1130\ K} N_{2(g)} + 3H_{2(g)}\] \[Rate = k[NH_3]^0 = k\]
  • At high pressure, the platinum surface is fully covered (saturated) with gas molecules. A further change in conditions cannot change the amount of ammonia on the surface. So the rate becomes independent of concentration.
  • Thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface is another zero order reaction.

docs.title: First Order Reactions
docs.text:
In a first order reaction, the rate is proportional to the first power of the concentration of reactant R.

\[R → P\] \[Rate = -{d[R] \over dt} = k[R]\] \[{d[R] \over [R]} = -k\ dt\]
  • Integrating both sides:
\[ln[R] = -kt + I\]
  • At t = 0, [R] = [R]0, so I = ln[R]0.
\[ln[R] = -kt + ln[R]_0\] \[ln{[R] \over [R]_0} = -kt\] \[k = {1 \over t} ln{[R]_0 \over [R]}\] \[k = {2.303 \over t} log{[R]_0 \over [R]}\]
  • Taking antilog, the concentration falls exponentially with time:
\[[R] = [R]_0\ e^{-kt}\]
  • If [R]1 and [R]2 are concentrations at times t1 and t2, subtracting the two equations gives:
\[ln[R]_1 - ln[R]_2 = -kt_1 - (-kt_2)\] \[k = {1 \over (t_2 - t_1)} ln{[R]_1 \over [R]_2} = {2.303 \over (t_2 - t_1)} log{[R]_1 \over [R]_2}\]

docs.title: Graphs for a First Order Reaction
docs.text:
• A plot of ln[R] against t is a straight line with slope = -k and intercept = ln[R]0.
  • A plot of log([R]0/[R]) against t is a straight line through the origin with slope = k/2.303.
\[log{[R]_0 \over [R]} = {kt \over 2.303}\]

docs.title: Examples of First Order Reactions
docs.text:
• Hydrogenation of ethene:
\[C_2H_{4(g)} + H_{2(g)} → C_2H_{6(g)}\] \[Rate = k[C_2H_4]\]
  • All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei:
\[^{226}_{88}Ra → ^4_2He + ^{222}_{86}Rn\] \[Rate = k[Ra]\]
  • Decomposition of N2O5 and N2O.

docs.title: First Order Gas Phase Reactions
docs.text:
• For gas phase reactions, it is easier to measure the total pressure than concentration. Consider:
\[A_{(g)} → B_{(g)} + C_{(g)}\]
  • Let pi be the initial pressure of A and pt the total pressure at time t. If the pressure of A decreases by x atm, the pressures of B and C each increase by x atm.
Time pA pB pC t = 0 pi 0 0 t pi - x x x \[p_t = (p_i - x) + x + x = p_i + x\] \[x = p_t - p_i\] \[p_A = p_i - x = p_i - (p_t - p_i) = 2p_i - p_t\] \[k = {2.303 \over t} log{p_i \over p_A} = {2.303 \over t} log{p_i \over (2p_i - p_t)}\]

Note

The relation pA = 2pi - pt holds only for this particular stoichiometry (1 mole gas → 2 moles gas). For any other reaction, write the pressure table again and find pA in terms of pt.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The initial concentration of N2O5 in the first order reaction N2O5(g) → 2NO2(g) + 1/2 O2(g) was 1.24 × 10-2 mol L-1 at 318 K. The concentration of N2O5 after 60 minutes was 0.20 × 10-2 mol L-1. Calculate the rate constant of the reaction at 318 K.

\[k = {2.303 \over (t_2 - t_1)} log{[R]_1 \over [R]_2}\] \[k = {2.303 \over (60 - 0)\ min} log{1.24 \times 10^{-2} \over 0.20 \times 10^{-2}}\] \[k = {2.303 \over 60} log\ 6.2\] \[k = 0.0304\ min^{-1}\]

The following data were obtained during the first order thermal decomposition of N2O5(g) at constant volume: 2N2O5(g) → 2N2O4(g) + O2(g)At t = 0 s, total pressure = 0.5 atm; at t = 100 s, total pressure = 0.512 atm. Calculate the rate constant.

  • Let the pressure of N2O5 decrease by 2x atm. Then N2O4 increases by 2x atm and O2 by x atm.
\[At\ t = 0:\ p_{N_2O_5} = 0.5,\ p_{N_2O_4} = 0,\ p_{O_2} = 0\] \[At\ time\ t:\ p_{N_2O_5} = 0.5 - 2x,\ p_{N_2O_4} = 2x,\ p_{O_2} = x\] \[p_t = (0.5 - 2x) + 2x + x = 0.5 + x\] \[x = p_t - 0.5\] \[p_{N_2O_5} = 0.5 - 2(p_t - 0.5) = 1.5 - 2p_t\] \[At\ t = 100\ s:\ p_{N_2O_5} = 1.5 - 2 \times 0.512 = 0.476\ atm\] \[k = {2.303 \over t} log{p_i \over p_A} = {2.303 \over 100\ s} log{0.5 \over 0.476}\] \[k = {2.303 \over 100} \times 0.0216 = 4.98 \times 10^{-4}\ s^{-1}\]

docs.title: Chemical Kinetics | Introduction
docs.text: Chemical kinetics is the branch of chemistry which deals with the study of rates of chemical reactions, the factors affecting them and the mechanism by which reactions occur. The word kinetics comes from the Greek word 'kinesis', which means movement.

docs.title: Why Study Kinetics?
docs.text:
For any chemical reaction, chemists try to find out three things:

  • Feasibility: Whether the reaction can take place at all. This is predicted by thermodynamics. A reaction with ΔG < 0 at constant temperature and pressure is feasible.
  • Extent: How far the reaction will proceed. This is found from chemical equilibrium.
  • Speed: How fast the reaction takes place, i.e. the time it takes to reach equilibrium. This is the subject of chemical kinetics.

Thermodynamics tells us only whether a reaction is feasible, whereas kinetics tells us how fast it goes.

Example

Thermodynamic data shows that diamond should convert into graphite. In reality, this conversion is so slow that it cannot be noticed at all. That is why we say "diamond is forever".

  • Kinetics helps us find the rate of a reaction and also the conditions (concentration, temperature, pressure, catalyst) by which the rate can be changed.
  • At the macroscopic level, we study the amounts of substances reacted or formed and how fast they are consumed or formed.
  • At the molecular level, we study the reaction mechanism, i.e. the orientation and energy of molecules undergoing collisions.

docs.title: Rate of a Chemical Reaction
docs.text:
Reactions take place at very different speeds:

  • Very fast reactions: Ionic reactions, e.g. precipitation of AgCl on mixing aqueous solutions of AgNO3 and NaCl occurs instantly.
  • Very slow reactions: Rusting of iron in the presence of air and moisture.
  • Moderate reactions: Inversion of cane sugar and hydrolysis of starch.

Just as the speed of a car is the distance covered per unit time, the rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or a product per unit time. It can be expressed as:

  • the rate of decrease in concentration of any one of the reactants, or
  • the rate of increase in concentration of any one of the products.

Consider a hypothetical reaction at constant volume, in which one mole of reactant R gives one mole of product P:

\[R → P\]
  • Let [R]1 and [P]1 be the molar concentrations of R and P at time t1, and [R]2 and [P]2 at time t2. Square brackets denote molar concentration.
\[Δt = t_2 - t_1\] \[Δ[R] = [R]_2 - [R]_1\] \[Δ[P] = [P]_2 - [P]_1\] \[Rate\ of\ disappearance\ of\ R = {Decrease\ in\ concentration\ of\ R \over Time\ taken} = -{Δ[R] \over Δt}\] \[Rate\ of\ appearance\ of\ P = {Increase\ in\ concentration\ of\ P \over Time\ taken} = +{Δ[P] \over Δt}\]
  • Since the concentration of reactant decreases, Δ[R] is negative. It is multiplied by -1 so that the rate comes out as a positive quantity.

docs.title: Average Rate of a Reaction
docs.text:
• The expressions above give the average rate (rav) of a reaction over the time interval Δt.
  • Average rate depends on the change in concentration and the time taken for that change.
  • As a reaction proceeds, the concentration of reactants falls and so the rate usually decreases with time. Hence, the average rate is different for different time intervals.

docs.title: Instantaneous Rate of a Reaction
docs.text:
• An average rate cannot tell us the rate at a particular moment because it is assumed to be constant over the whole interval.
  • The rate at a particular instant of time is called the instantaneous rate (rinst). It is the average rate over an infinitesimally small time interval dt, i.e. when Δt approaches zero.
\[r_{av} = {-Δ[R] \over Δt} = {Δ[P] \over Δt}\] \[As\ Δt → 0:\ \ r_{inst} = {-d[R] \over dt} = {d[P] \over dt}\]
  • Graphically, the instantaneous rate at time t is found by drawing a tangent to the concentration vs time curve at time t and finding its slope.
  • For a reactant curve, rinst = -slope. For a product curve, rinst = +slope.

Example

For the hydrolysis of butyl chloride, a tangent drawn on the [C4H9Cl] vs time curve at t = 600 s passes through 0.037 mol L-1 at 400 s and 0.0165 mol L-1 at 800 s.

\[r_{inst}\ at\ 600\ s = -{(0.0165 - 0.037) \over (800 - 400)}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\] \[r_{inst} = 5.12 \times 10^{-5}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\]

docs.title: Units of Rate of Reaction
docs.text:
• Rate has the units of concentration time-1.
  • If concentration is in mol L-1 and time is in seconds, the unit of rate is mol L-1s-1.
  • For gaseous reactions, concentration is often expressed as partial pressure. Then the unit of rate is atm s-1. This works because, at constant temperature, the concentration of a gas is directly proportional to its partial pressure.

docs.title: Rate in Terms of Stoichiometric Coefficients
docs.text:
• When the stoichiometric coefficients of all reactants and products are equal, the rate of disappearance of any reactant is equal to the rate of appearance of any product.
\[Hg_{(l)} + Cl_{2(g)} → HgCl_{2(s)}\] \[Rate = -{Δ[Hg] \over Δt} = -{Δ[Cl_2] \over Δt} = {Δ[HgCl_2] \over Δt}\]
  • When the coefficients are not equal, the rate of disappearance of each reactant or rate of appearance of each product is divided by its stoichiometric coefficient. This gives one single value for the rate of reaction.
  • For example, in the decomposition of HI, two moles of HI are used to form one mole each of H2 and I2. So HI is consumed twice as fast as H2 is formed, and Δ[HI] is divided by 2.
\[2HI_{(g)} → H_{2(g)} + I_{2(g)}\] \[Rate = -{1 \over 2}{Δ[HI] \over Δt} = {Δ[H_2] \over Δt} = {Δ[I_2] \over Δt}\] \[5Br^-_{(aq)} + BrO^-_{3(aq)} + 6H^+_{(aq)} → 3Br_{2(aq)} + 3H_2O_{(l)}\] \[Rate = -{1 \over 5}{Δ[Br^-] \over Δt} = -{Δ[BrO_3^-] \over Δt} = -{1 \over 6}{Δ[H^+] \over Δt} = {1 \over 3}{Δ[Br_2] \over Δt} = {1 \over 3}{Δ[H_2O] \over Δt}\]

Conclusion

For a general reaction aA + bB → cC + dD:

\[Rate = -{1 \over a}{d[A] \over dt} = -{1 \over b}{d[B] \over dt} = {1 \over c}{d[C] \over dt} = {1 \over d}{d[D] \over dt}\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
From the concentrations of C4H9Cl (butyl chloride) at different times given below, calculate the average rate of the reaction C4H9Cl + H2O → C4H9OH + HCl during different intervals of time.t/s: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 700, 800[C4H9Cl]/mol L-1: 0.100, 0.0905, 0.0820, 0.0741, 0.0671, 0.0549, 0.0439, 0.0210, 0.017

  • The average rate for each interval is found by dividing the decrease in concentration by the time interval.
\[r_{av} = -{[C_4H_9Cl]_{t_2} - [C_4H_9Cl]_{t_1} \over t_2 - t_1}\] \[For\ 0-50\ s:\ r_{av} = -{0.0905 - 0.100 \over 50} = 1.90 \times 10^{-4}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\]
  • Similarly, for the other intervals:
t1/s t2/s rav × 104 / mol L-1s-1 0 50 1.90 50 100 1.70 100 150 1.58 150 200 1.40 200 300 1.22 300 400 1.10 700 800 0.4
  • The average rate falls from 1.90 × 10-4 to 0.4 × 10-4 mol L-1s-1 as the reactant is used up.

The decomposition of N2O5 in CCl4 at 318 K has been studied by monitoring the concentration of N2O5. Initially the concentration of N2O5 is 2.33 mol L-1 and after 184 minutes, it is reduced to 2.08 mol L-1. The reaction is: 2N2O5(g) → 4NO2(g) + O2(g). Calculate the average rate of this reaction in terms of hours, minutes and seconds. What is the rate of production of NO2 during this period?

\[Average\ rate = {1 \over 2}\left\{-{Δ[N_2O_5] \over Δt}\right\} = -{1 \over 2}\left[{(2.08 - 2.33)\ mol\ L^{-1} \over 184\ min}\right]\] \[Average\ rate = 6.79 \times 10^{-4}\ mol\ L^{-1}min^{-1}\] \[In\ hours = 6.79 \times 10^{-4} \times 60 = 4.07 \times 10^{-2}\ mol\ L^{-1}h^{-1}\] \[In\ seconds = {6.79 \times 10^{-4} \over 60} = 1.13 \times 10^{-5}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\]
  • Rate of production of NO2:
\[Rate = {1 \over 4}{Δ[NO_2] \over Δt}\] \[{Δ[NO_2] \over Δt} = 4 \times 6.79 \times 10^{-4} = 2.72 \times 10^{-3}\ mol\ L^{-1}min^{-1}\]

For the reaction R → P, the concentration of a reactant changes from 0.03 M to 0.02 M in 25 minutes. Calculate the average rate of reaction using units of time both in minutes and seconds.

\[r_{av} = -{Δ[R] \over Δt} = -{(0.02 - 0.03)\ M \over 25\ min}\] \[r_{av} = 4 \times 10^{-4}\ M\ min^{-1}\] \[r_{av} = {4 \times 10^{-4} \over 60} = 6.67 \times 10^{-6}\ M\ s^{-1}\]

In a reaction, 2A → Products, the concentration of A decreases from 0.5 mol L-1 to 0.4 mol L-1 in 10 minutes. Calculate the rate during this interval.

\[Rate = -{1 \over 2}{Δ[A] \over Δt} = -{1 \over 2} \times {(0.4 - 0.5) \over 10}\] \[Rate = 0.005\ mol\ L^{-1}min^{-1}\]
  • Note that the rate of disappearance of A is twice this value, i.e. 0.01 mol L-1min-1.

docs.title: Chemical Kinetics | Questions Based on Arrhenius Equation
Chemical Kinetics | Questions Based on Arrhenius Equation
docs.text:
In this article, we will solve some questions related to the Arrhenius equation, activation energy and the effect of temperature on rate constant.

Formulas used

\[k = A\ e^{-E_a/RT}\] \[log\ k = log\ A - {E_a \over 2.303RT}\] \[log{k_2 \over k_1} = {E_a \over 2.303R}\left[{T_2 - T_1 \over T_1T_2}\right]\] \[R = 8.314\ J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The rate constant for the decomposition of N2O5 at various temperatures is given below: T/°C: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 105 × k/s-1: 0.0787, 1.70, 25.7, 178, 2140 Draw a graph between ln k and 1/T and calculate the values of A and Ea. Predict the rate constant at 30° and 50°C.

  • Converting the data:
T/K 273 293 313 333 353 103/T (K-1) 3.663 3.413 3.195 3.003 2.833 ln k -14.06 -10.98 -8.27 -6.33 -3.84
  • The plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line. Its slope (from the best fit line) is:
\[Slope = -{E_a \over R} = -1.21 \times 10^4\ K\] \[E_a = 1.21 \times 10^4 \times 8.314 = 1.006 \times 10^5\ J\ mol^{-1} ≈ 100.6\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • The intercept of the line gives ln A:
\[ln\ A = 30.29\] \[A = 1.43 \times 10^{13}\ s^{-1}\]
  • Rate constant at 30 °C (303 K):
\[ln\ k = 30.29 - {1.21 \times 10^4 \over 303} = -9.65\] \[k ≈ 6.4 \times 10^{-5}\ s^{-1}\]
  • Rate constant at 50 °C (323 K):
\[ln\ k = 30.29 - {1.21 \times 10^4 \over 323} = -7.18\] \[k ≈ 7.6 \times 10^{-4}\ s^{-1}\]

Values read from a hand-drawn graph may differ slightly.

The rate constant for the decomposition of hydrocarbons is 2.418 × 10-5 s-1 at 546 K. If the energy of activation is 179.9 kJ/mol, what will be the value of pre-exponential factor?

\[log\ A = log\ k + {E_a \over 2.303RT}\] \[log\ A = log(2.418 \times 10^{-5}) + {179900 \over 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 546}\] \[log\ A = -4.6166 + 17.2082 = 12.5916\] \[A = 3.9 \times 10^{12}\ s^{-1}\]

The decomposition of hydrocarbon follows the equation k = (4.5 × 1011 s-1) e-28000 K/T. Calculate Ea.

  • Comparing with the Arrhenius equation k = Ae-Ea/RT:
\[{E_a \over R} = 28000\ K\] \[E_a = 28000 \times 8.314 = 232792\ J\ mol^{-1}\] \[E_a = 232.8\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

The rate constant for the first order decomposition of H2O2 is given by the following equation: log k = 14.34 - 1.25 × 104 K/T. Calculate Ea for this reaction and at what temperature will its half-period be 256 minutes?

  • Comparing with log k = log A - Ea/(2.303RT):
\[{E_a \over 2.303R} = 1.25 \times 10^4\ K\] \[E_a = 1.25 \times 10^4 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 = 239339\ J\ mol^{-1}\] \[E_a = 239.3\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • When t1/2 = 256 min:
\[k = {0.693 \over 256 \times 60\ s} = 4.51 \times 10^{-5}\ s^{-1}\] \[log\ k = log(4.51 \times 10^{-5}) = -4.346\] \[-4.346 = 14.34 - {1.25 \times 10^4 \over T}\] \[T = {1.25 \times 10^4 \over 18.686} = 669\ K\]

The decomposition of A into product has value of k as 4.5 × 103 s-1 at 10°C and energy of activation 60 kJ mol-1. At what temperature would k be 1.5 × 104 s-1?

\[k_1 = 4.5 \times 10^3\ s^{-1},\ T_1 = 283\ K,\ k_2 = 1.5 \times 10^4\ s^{-1},\ E_a = 60000\ J\ mol^{-1}\] \[log{k_2 \over k_1} = {E_a \over 2.303R}\left[{1 \over T_1} - {1 \over T_2}\right]\] \[log{1.5 \times 10^4 \over 4.5 \times 10^3} = {60000 \over 2.303 \times 8.314}\left[{1 \over 283} - {1 \over T_2}\right]\] \[0.5229 = 3133.6\left[{1 \over 283} - {1 \over T_2}\right]\] \[{1 \over T_2} = 3.5336 \times 10^{-3} - 1.6686 \times 10^{-4} = 3.3667 \times 10^{-3}\] \[T_2 = 297\ K = 24\ °C\]

The time required for 10% completion of a first order reaction at 298 K is equal to that required for its 25% completion at 308 K. If the value of A is 4 × 1010 s-1, calculate k at 318 K and Ea.

  • For a first order reaction, t = (2.303/k) log([R]0/[R]).
\[At\ 298\ K:\ t = {2.303 \over k_{298}} log{100 \over 90}\] \[At\ 308\ K:\ t = {2.303 \over k_{308}} log{100 \over 75}\]
  • Since the times are equal:
\[{k_{308} \over k_{298}} = {log(100/75) \over log(100/90)} = {0.1249 \over 0.0458} = 2.73\]
  • Calculation of Ea:
\[log\ 2.73 = {E_a \over 2.303 \times 8.314}\left[{308 - 298 \over 298 \times 308}\right]\] \[E_a = {2.303 \times 8.314 \times 0.4362 \times 298 \times 308 \over 10}\] \[E_a = 76664\ J\ mol^{-1} ≈ 76.7\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
  • Calculation of k at 318 K:
\[log\ k = log\ A - {E_a \over 2.303RT} = log(4 \times 10^{10}) - {76664 \over 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 318}\] \[log\ k = 10.602 - 12.591 = -1.989\] \[k = 1.02 \times 10^{-2}\ s^{-1}\]

The rate of a reaction quadruples when the temperature changes from 293 K to 313 K. Calculate the energy of activation of the reaction assuming that it does not change with temperature.

\[{k_2 \over k_1} = 4,\ T_1 = 293\ K,\ T_2 = 313\ K\] \[log\ 4 = {E_a \over 2.303 \times 8.314}\left[{313 - 293 \over 293 \times 313}\right]\] \[0.6021 = {E_a \over 19.147} \times 2.181 \times 10^{-4}\] \[E_a = 52860\ J\ mol^{-1} = 52.86\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

docs.title: Chemical Kinetics | Questions Based on Integrated Rate Equations
Chemical Kinetics | Questions Based on Integrated Rate Equations
docs.text:
In this article, we will solve some questions related to integrated rate equations and half-life of zero and first order reactions.

Formulas used

\[First\ order:\ k = {2.303 \over t} log{[R]_0 \over [R]}\] \[First\ order:\ t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over k}\] \[Zero\ order:\ k = {[R]_0 - [R] \over t},\ \ t_{1/2} = {[R]_0 \over 2k}\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the half-life of a first order reaction from their rate constants given below: (i) 200 s-1 (ii) 2 min-1 (iii) 4 years-1

\[(i)\ t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over 200\ s^{-1}} = 3.47 \times 10^{-3}\ s\] \[(ii)\ t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over 2\ min^{-1}} = 0.35\ min\] \[(iii)\ t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over 4\ years^{-1}} = 0.173\ years\]

The half-life for radioactive decay of 14C is 5730 years. An archaeological artifact containing wood had only 80% of the 14C found in a living tree. Estimate the age of the sample.

  • Radioactive decay follows first order kinetics.
\[k = {0.693 \over t_{1/2}} = {0.693 \over 5730}\ years^{-1}\] \[t = {2.303 \over k} log{[R]_0 \over [R]} = {2.303 \times 5730 \over 0.693} log{100 \over 80}\] \[t = {2.303 \times 5730 \over 0.693} \times 0.0969\] \[t = 1845\ years\]

The experimental data for decomposition of N2O5 [2N2O5 → 4NO2 + O2] in gas phase at 318 K are given below: t/s: 0, 400, 800, 1200, 1600, 2000, 2400, 2800, 3200 102 × [N2O5]/mol L-1: 1.63, 1.36, 1.14, 0.93, 0.78, 0.64, 0.53, 0.43, 0.35 (i) Plot [N2O5] against t. (ii) Find the half-life period for the reaction. (iii) Draw a graph between log[N2O5] and t. (iv) What is the rate law? (v) Calculate the rate constant. (vi) Calculate the half-life period from k and compare it with (ii).

  • (i) The plot of [N2O5] against t is a curve that falls steeply at first and then more slowly (an exponential decay).

  • (ii) Initial concentration = 1.63 × 10-2 mol L-1. Half of it is 0.815 × 10-2 mol L-1. From the graph, this concentration is reached at about t1/2 ≈ 1440 s.

  • (iii) Values of log[N2O5]:

t/s 0 400 800 1200 1600 2000 2400 2800 3200 log[N2O5] -1.79 -1.87 -1.94 -2.03 -2.11 -2.19 -2.28 -2.37 -2.46

The plot of log[N2O5] against t is a straight line with a negative slope.

  • (iv) Since log[N2O5] vs t is a straight line, the reaction is first order:
\[Rate = k[N_2O_5]\]
  • (v) For a first order reaction, slope of log[R] vs t = -k/2.303:
\[Slope = {-2.46 - (-1.79) \over 3200 - 0} = -2.09 \times 10^{-4}\ s^{-1}\] \[-{k \over 2.303} = -2.09 \times 10^{-4}\] \[k = 4.81 \times 10^{-4}\ s^{-1}\]
  • (vi) Half-life from k:
\[t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over k} = {0.693 \over 4.81 \times 10^{-4}} = 1441\ s\]

This agrees closely with the value of about 1440 s read from the graph in (ii).

The rate constant for a first order reaction is 60 s-1. How much time will it take to reduce the initial concentration of the reactant to its 1/16th value?

\[t = {2.303 \over k} log{[R]_0 \over [R]} = {2.303 \over 60} log\ 16\] \[t = {2.303 \over 60} \times 1.2041\] \[t = 4.62 \times 10^{-2}\ s\]
  • Alternatively, 1/16 = (1/2)4, so the time needed is 4 half-lives: 4 × (0.693/60) = 4.62 × 10-2 s.

During nuclear explosion, one of the products is 90Sr with half-life of 28.1 years. If 1 μg of 90Sr was absorbed in the bones of a newly born baby instead of calcium, how much of it will remain after 10 years and 60 years if it is not lost metabolically?

\[k = {0.693 \over 28.1} = 2.466 \times 10^{-2}\ years^{-1}\]
  • After 10 years:
\[log{[R]_0 \over [R]} = {kt \over 2.303} = {2.466 \times 10^{-2} \times 10 \over 2.303} = 0.1071\] \[{[R]_0 \over [R]} = 1.280\] \[[R] = {1 \over 1.280} = 0.7814\ μg\]
  • After 60 years:
\[log{[R]_0 \over [R]} = {2.466 \times 10^{-2} \times 60 \over 2.303} = 0.6425\] \[{[R]_0 \over [R]} = 4.392\] \[[R] = {1 \over 4.392} = 0.2277\ μg\]

For a first order reaction, show that time required for 99% completion is twice the time required for the completion of 90% of reaction.

  • For 99% completion, [R] = 0.01[R]0:
\[t_{99\%} = {2.303 \over k} log{[R]_0 \over 0.01[R]_0} = {2.303 \over k} log\ 100 = {2 \times 2.303 \over k}\]
  • For 90% completion, [R] = 0.1[R]0:
\[t_{90\%} = {2.303 \over k} log{[R]_0 \over 0.1[R]_0} = {2.303 \over k} log\ 10 = {2.303 \over k}\] \[{t_{99\%} \over t_{90\%}} = 2\] \[∴\ t_{99\%} = 2 \times t_{90\%}\]

A first order reaction takes 40 min for 30% decomposition. Calculate t1/2.

  • After 30% decomposition, 70% of the reactant is left.
\[k = {2.303 \over 40} log{100 \over 70} = {2.303 \over 40} \times 0.1549\] \[k = 8.918 \times 10^{-3}\ min^{-1}\] \[t_{1/2} = {0.693 \over k} = {0.693 \over 8.918 \times 10^{-3}}\] \[t_{1/2} = 77.7\ min\]

For the decomposition of azoisopropane to hexane and nitrogen at 543 K, the following data are obtained: t (sec): 0, 360, 720 P (mm of Hg): 35.0, 54.0, 63.0 Calculate the rate constant.

  • The reaction is:
\[(CH_3)_2CHN=NCH(CH_3)_2 → C_6H_{14} + N_2\]
  • Let the pressure of azoisopropane decrease by x. Then hexane and nitrogen each increase by x.
\[At\ t = 0:\ p_i,\ 0,\ 0\] \[At\ time\ t:\ p_i - x,\ x,\ x\] \[p_t = p_i + x,\ \ p_A = p_i - x = 2p_i - p_t\]
  • At t = 360 s:
\[p_A = 2 \times 35.0 - 54.0 = 16.0\ mm\ Hg\] \[k = {2.303 \over 360} log{35.0 \over 16.0} = 2.175 \times 10^{-3}\ s^{-1}\]
  • At t = 720 s:
\[p_A = 2 \times 35.0 - 63.0 = 7.0\ mm\ Hg\] \[k = {2.303 \over 720} log{35.0 \over 7.0} = 2.235 \times 10^{-3}\ s^{-1}\] \[Average\ k = {(2.175 + 2.235) \times 10^{-3} \over 2} = 2.20 \times 10^{-3}\ s^{-1}\]

The following data were obtained during the first order thermal decomposition of SO2Cl2 at a constant volume: SO2Cl2(g) → SO2(g) + Cl2(g) At t = 0 s, total pressure = 0.5 atm; at t = 100 s, total pressure = 0.6 atm. Calculate the rate of the reaction when total pressure is 0.65 atm.

  • The reaction is of the type A → B + C, so:
\[p_{SO_2Cl_2} = 2p_i - p_t\]
  • At t = 100 s:
\[p_{SO_2Cl_2} = 2 \times 0.5 - 0.6 = 0.4\ atm\] \[k = {2.303 \over 100} log{0.5 \over 0.4} = {2.303 \over 100} \times 0.0969\] \[k = 2.23 \times 10^{-3}\ s^{-1}\]
  • When total pressure is 0.65 atm:
\[p_{SO_2Cl_2} = 2 \times 0.5 - 0.65 = 0.35\ atm\] \[Rate = k \times p_{SO_2Cl_2} = 2.23 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.35\] \[Rate = 7.8 \times 10^{-4}\ atm\ s^{-1}\]

Consider a certain reaction A → Products with k = 2.0 × 10-2 s-1. Calculate the concentration of A remaining after 100 s if the initial concentration of A is 1.0 mol L-1.

  • The unit of k is s-1, so this is a first order reaction.
\[log{[A]_0 \over [A]} = {kt \over 2.303} = {2.0 \times 10^{-2} \times 100 \over 2.303} = 0.8684\] \[{[A]_0 \over [A]} = 7.389\] \[[A] = {1.0 \over 7.389} = 0.135\ mol\ L^{-1}\]

Sucrose decomposes in acid solution into glucose and fructose according to the first order rate law, with t1/2 = 3.00 hours. What fraction of sample of sucrose remains after 8 hours?

\[k = {0.693 \over t_{1/2}} = {0.693 \over 3.00} = 0.231\ h^{-1}\] \[log{[R]_0 \over [R]} = {kt \over 2.303} = {0.231 \times 8 \over 2.303} = 0.8024\] \[{[R]_0 \over [R]} = 6.345\] \[{[R] \over [R]_0} = {1 \over 6.345} = 0.158\]
  • So, about 0.158 (15.8%) of the sucrose remains after 8 hours.

docs.title: Chemical Kinetics | Questions Based on Rate Law
Chemical Kinetics | Questions Based on Rate Law
docs.text: In this article, we will solve some questions related to rate of reaction, rate law, order of reaction and units of rate constant.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
From the rate expression for the following reactions, determine their order of reaction and the dimensions of the rate constants. (i) 3NO(g) → N2O(g); Rate = k[NO]2 (ii) H2O2(aq) + 3I-(aq) + 2H+ → 2H2O(l) + I3-; Rate = k[H2O2][I-] (iii) CH3CHO(g) → CH4(g) + CO(g); Rate = k[CH3CHO]3/2 (iv) C2H5Cl(g) → C2H4(g) + HCl(g); Rate = k[C2H5Cl]

  • Units of k for order n:
\[Units\ of\ k = (mol\ L^{-1})^{1-n}\ s^{-1}\] Reaction Order Units of k (i) 2 mol-1L s-1 (ii) 1 + 1 = 2 mol-1L s-1 (iii) 3/2 mol-1/2L1/2s-1 (iv) 1 s-1

For the reaction: 2A + B → A2B, the rate = k[A][B]2 with k = 2.0 × 10-6 mol-2L2s-1. Calculate the initial rate of the reaction when [A] = 0.1 mol L-1, [B] = 0.2 mol L-1. Calculate the rate of reaction after [A] is reduced to 0.06 mol L-1.

  • Initial rate:
\[Rate = k[A][B]^2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.1 \times (0.2)^2\] \[Rate = 8.0 \times 10^{-9}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\]
  • When [A] falls to 0.06 mol L-1, A consumed = 0.1 - 0.06 = 0.04 mol L-1.
  • From the equation, 2 mol A reacts with 1 mol B. So B consumed = 0.04/2 = 0.02 mol L-1.
\[[B] = 0.2 - 0.02 = 0.18\ mol\ L^{-1}\] \[Rate = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.06 \times (0.18)^2\] \[Rate = 3.89 \times 10^{-9}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\]

The decomposition of NH3 on platinum surface is zero order reaction. What are the rates of production of N2 and H2 if k = 2.5 × 10-4 mol L-1s-1?

\[2NH_3 → N_2 + 3H_2\] \[Rate = -{1 \over 2}{d[NH_3] \over dt} = {d[N_2] \over dt} = {1 \over 3}{d[H_2] \over dt}\]
  • For a zero order reaction, rate = k = 2.5 × 10-4 mol L-1s-1.
\[Rate\ of\ production\ of\ N_2 = {d[N_2] \over dt} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\] \[Rate\ of\ production\ of\ H_2 = {d[H_2] \over dt} = 3 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-4} = 7.5 \times 10^{-4}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\]

The decomposition of dimethyl ether leads to the formation of CH4, H2 and CO and the reaction rate is given by Rate = k[CH3OCH3]3/2. The rate of reaction is followed by increase in pressure in a closed vessel, so the rate can also be expressed in terms of the partial pressure of dimethyl ether, i.e., Rate = k(pCH3OCH3)3/2. If the pressure is measured in bar and time in minutes, then what are the units of rate and rate constants?

  • Rate is the change in pressure per unit time:
\[Units\ of\ rate = bar\ min^{-1}\] \[k = {Rate \over (p_{CH_3OCH_3})^{3/2}} = {bar\ min^{-1} \over bar^{3/2}}\] \[Units\ of\ k = bar^{-1/2}\ min^{-1}\]

Mention the factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction.

  • Concentration of reactants: Rate generally increases with increase in concentration (pressure for gases).
  • Temperature: Rate increases with temperature. A 10° rise nearly doubles the rate constant.
  • Catalyst: A catalyst lowers the activation energy and increases the rate.
  • Nature of reactants and surface area: Ionic reactions are faster than covalent ones, and finely divided solids react faster.
  • Radiation: Some reactions, such as photochemical reactions, speed up in the presence of light.

A reaction is second order with respect to a reactant. How is the rate of reaction affected if the concentration of the reactant is (i) doubled (ii) reduced to half?

\[Rate = k[A]^2\]
  • (i) When [A] is doubled:
\[Rate' = k(2[A])^2 = 4k[A]^2 = 4 \times Rate\]

The rate becomes 4 times.

  • (ii) When [A] is halved:
\[Rate' = k\left({[A] \over 2}\right)^2 = {1 \over 4}k[A]^2\]

The rate becomes one-fourth.

What is the effect of temperature on the rate constant of a reaction? How can this temperature effect on rate constant be represented quantitatively?

  • The rate constant increases with temperature. For a 10° rise in temperature, the rate constant nearly doubles.
  • This effect is represented quantitatively by the Arrhenius equation:
\[k = A\ e^{-E_a/RT}\]

Where A is the Arrhenius (frequency) factor, Ea is the activation energy, R is the gas constant and T is the absolute temperature.

In a pseudo first order hydrolysis of ester in water, the following results were obtained: t/s: 0, 30, 60, 90 [Ester]/mol L-1: 0.55, 0.31, 0.17, 0.085 (i) Calculate the average rate of reaction between the time interval 30 to 60 seconds. (ii) Calculate the pseudo first order rate constant for the hydrolysis of ester.

  • (i) Average rate between 30 s and 60 s:
\[r_{av} = -{Δ[Ester] \over Δt} = -{(0.17 - 0.31) \over (60 - 30)}\] \[r_{av} = 4.67 \times 10^{-3}\ mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}\]
  • (ii) Using the first order equation:
\[k = {2.303 \over t} log{[R]_0 \over [R]}\] \[At\ t = 30\ s:\ k = {2.303 \over 30} log{0.55 \over 0.31} = 1.911 \times 10^{-2}\ s^{-1}\] \[At\ t = 60\ s:\ k = {2.303 \over 60} log{0.55 \over 0.17} = 1.957 \times 10^{-2}\ s^{-1}\] \[At\ t = 90\ s:\ k = {2.303 \over 90} log{0.55 \over 0.085} = 2.075 \times 10^{-2}\ s^{-1}\] \[Average\ k = {(1.911 + 1.957 + 2.075) \times 10^{-2} \over 3} = 1.98 \times 10^{-2}\ s^{-1}\]

A reaction is first order in A and second order in B. (i) Write the differential rate equation. (ii) How is the rate affected on increasing the concentration of B three times? (iii) How is the rate affected when the concentrations of both A and B are doubled?

  • (i) Differential rate equation:
\[-{d[R] \over dt} = k[A][B]^2\]
  • (ii) When [B] is made three times:
\[Rate' = k[A](3[B])^2 = 9k[A][B]^2\]

The rate increases 9 times.

  • (iii) When both [A] and [B] are doubled:
\[Rate' = k(2[A])(2[B])^2 = 8k[A][B]^2\]

The rate increases 8 times.

In a reaction between A and B, the initial rate of reaction (r0) was measured for different initial concentrations of A and B as given below: [A]/mol L-1: 0.20, 0.20, 0.40 [B]/mol L-1: 0.30, 0.10, 0.05 r0/mol L-1s-1: 5.07 × 10-5, 5.07 × 10-5, 1.43 × 10-4 What is the order of the reaction with respect to A and B?

  • Let rate = k[A]x[B]y.
\[(1):\ 5.07 \times 10^{-5} = k(0.20)^x(0.30)^y\] \[(2):\ 5.07 \times 10^{-5} = k(0.20)^x(0.10)^y\] \[(3):\ 1.43 \times 10^{-4} = k(0.40)^x(0.05)^y\]
  • Dividing (1) by (2):
\[1 = \left({0.30 \over 0.10}\right)^y = 3^y\] \[y = 0\]
  • Dividing (3) by (2), with y = 0:
\[{1.43 \times 10^{-4} \over 5.07 \times 10^{-5}} = \left({0.40 \over 0.20}\right)^x\] \[2.82 = 2^x\] \[x = {log\ 2.82 \over log\ 2} = {0.4503 \over 0.3010} = 1.5\]
  • Hence, the order with respect to A is 1.5 and with respect to B is zero.

The following results have been obtained during the kinetic studies of the reaction: 2A + B → C + D Experiment I: [A] = 0.1, [B] = 0.1, initial rate of formation of D = 6.0 × 10-3 mol L-1min-1 Experiment II: [A] = 0.3, [B] = 0.2, rate = 7.2 × 10-2 Experiment III: [A] = 0.3, [B] = 0.4, rate = 2.88 × 10-1 Experiment IV: [A] = 0.4, [B] = 0.1, rate = 2.40 × 10-2 Determine the rate law and the rate constant for the reaction.

  • Let rate = k[A]x[B]y.
  • Experiments I and IV ([B] constant):
\[{2.40 \times 10^{-2} \over 6.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \left({0.4 \over 0.1}\right)^x\] \[4 = 4^x,\ \ x = 1\]
  • Experiments II and III ([A] constant):
\[{2.88 \times 10^{-1} \over 7.2 \times 10^{-2}} = \left({0.4 \over 0.2}\right)^y\] \[4 = 2^y,\ \ y = 2\] \[Rate = k[A][B]^2\]
  • Rate constant from Experiment I:
\[k = {Rate \over [A][B]^2} = {6.0 \times 10^{-3} \over 0.1 \times (0.1)^2}\] \[k = 6.0\ mol^{-2}L^2min^{-1}\]

The reaction between A and B is first order with respect to A and zero order with respect to B. Fill in the blanks in the following table: Experiment I: [A] = 0.1, [B] = 0.1, initial rate = 2.0 × 10-2 mol L-1min-1 Experiment II: [A] = ?, [B] = 0.2, rate = 4.0 × 10-2 Experiment III: [A] = 0.4, [B] = 0.4, rate = ? Experiment IV: [A] = ?, [B] = 0.2, rate = 2.0 × 10-2

\[Rate = k[A]^1[B]^0 = k[A]\]
  • From Experiment I:
\[k = {2.0 \times 10^{-2} \over 0.1} = 0.2\ min^{-1}\] \[Experiment\ II:\ [A] = {4.0 \times 10^{-2} \over 0.2} = 0.2\ mol\ L^{-1}\] \[Experiment\ III:\ Rate = 0.2 \times 0.4 = 8.0 \times 10^{-2}\ mol\ L^{-1}min^{-1}\] \[Experiment\ IV:\ [A] = {2.0 \times 10^{-2} \over 0.2} = 0.1\ mol\ L^{-1}\]

docs.title: Chemical Kinetics | Rate Law, Order and Molecularity
Chemical Kinetics | Rate Law, Order and Molecularity
Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
docs.text:
The rate of a reaction depends on the experimental conditions such as:

  • Concentration of reactants (pressure in case of gases)
  • Temperature
  • Catalyst

docs.title: Rate Law and Rate Constant
docs.text:
• The rate of a reaction decreases with time as the concentration of reactants decreases. Conversely, rates generally increase when reactant concentrations increase. So, rate depends on the concentration of reactants.
  • The representation of rate of reaction in terms of concentration of reactants is called the rate law. It is also called the rate equation or rate expression.
  • Consider a general reaction:
\[aA + bB → cC + dD\] \[Rate ∝ [A]^x [B]^y\] \[Rate = k[A]^x [B]^y\] \[-{d[R] \over dt} = k[A]^x [B]^y\]
  • The last form is called the differential rate equation.
  • Here, k is a proportionality constant called the rate constant. The exponents x and y may or may not be equal to the stoichiometric coefficients a and b.
  • When [A] = [B] = 1 mol L-1, rate = k. So the rate constant is the rate of reaction when the concentration of each reactant is unity. It is also called the specific reaction rate.

Rate Law

Rate law is the expression in which reaction rate is given in terms of molar concentration of reactants with each term raised to some power, which may or may not be the same as the stoichiometric coefficient of the reacting species in a balanced chemical equation.

docs.title: Determining a Rate Law from Experiment
docs.text:
• Consider the reaction:
\[2NO_{(g)} + O_{2(g)} → 2NO_{2(g)}\]
  • The initial rate is measured by changing the concentration of one reactant while keeping the other constant:
Experiment Initial [NO] / mol L-1 Initial [O2] / mol L-1 Initial rate of formation of NO2 / mol L-1s-1 1 0.30 0.30 0.096 2 0.60 0.30 0.384 3 0.30 0.60 0.192 4 0.60 0.60 0.768
  • Experiments 1 and 2: [NO] is doubled, [O2] is constant. Rate increases four times (0.096 to 0.384). So rate depends on [NO]2.
  • Experiments 1 and 3: [O2] is doubled, [NO] is constant. Rate doubles. So rate depends on [O2]1.
\[Rate = k[NO]^2[O_2]\] \[-{d[R] \over dt} = k[NO]^2[O_2]\]
  • Here the exponents happen to equal the stoichiometric coefficients. This is not always so:
