Reaction Experimental rate expression CHCl3 + Cl2 → CCl4 + HCl Rate = k[CHCl3][Cl2]1/2 CH3COOC2H5 + H2O → CH3COOH + C2H5OH Rate = k[CH3COOC2H5]1[H2O]0

Note

The rate law for any reaction cannot be predicted just by looking at the balanced chemical equation. It must be determined experimentally.

docs.title: Order of a Reaction
docs.text:
• In the rate law Rate = k[A]x[B]y, x and y show how sensitive the rate is to a change in concentration of A and B.
  • x is the order with respect to A and y is the order with respect to B.
  • The sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the rate law expression is called the order of that chemical reaction.
\[Overall\ order = x + y\]
  • Order can be 0, 1, 2, 3 and even a fraction or negative.
  • A zero order reaction means that the rate is independent of the concentration of reactants.

Example

\[Rate = k[A]^{1/2}[B]^{3/2}:\ \ Order = {1 \over 2} + {3 \over 2} = 2\ (second\ order)\] \[Rate = k[A]^{3/2}[B]^{-1}:\ \ Order = {3 \over 2} + (-1) = {1 \over 2}\ (half\ order)\]

docs.title: Elementary and Complex Reactions
docs.text:
• A balanced chemical equation rarely shows how a reaction actually takes place, since very few reactions are completed in one step.
  • Reactions taking place in one step are called elementary reactions.
  • When a sequence of elementary reactions (called the mechanism) gives the products, the reaction is called a complex reaction.
  • Complex reactions may be:
    • Consecutive reactions, e.g. oxidation of ethane to CO2 and H2O passes through alcohol, aldehyde and acid as intermediates.
    • Reverse reactions.
    • Side reactions, e.g. nitration of phenol gives both o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol.

docs.title: Units of Rate Constant
docs.text:
For a reaction of order n, Rate = k[A]x[B]y with x + y = n:

\[k = {Rate \over [A]^x[B]^y} = {concentration \over time} \times {1 \over (concentration)^n}\] \[Units\ of\ k = (mol\ L^{-1})^{1-n}\ s^{-1}\] Reaction Order Units of rate constant Zero order 0 mol L-1s-1 First order 1 s-1 Second order 2 mol-1L s-1 Third order 3 mol-2L2s-1
  • So the order of a reaction can be identified just from the units of its rate constant.

Example

  • k = 2.3 × 10-5 L mol-1s-1 represents a second order reaction.
  • k = 3 × 10-4 s-1 represents a first order reaction.

docs.title: Molecularity of a Reaction
docs.text: The number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) taking part in an elementary reaction, which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction, is called the molecularity of the reaction.

docs.title: 1. Unimolecular reaction
docs.text:
One reacting species is involved. Example, decomposition of ammonium nitrite:

\[NH_4NO_2 → N_2 + 2H_2O\]

docs.title: 2. Bimolecular reaction
docs.text:
Two species collide simultaneously. Example, dissociation of hydrogen iodide:

\[2HI → H_2 + I_2\]

docs.title: 3. Trimolecular (termolecular) reaction
docs.text:
Three species collide simultaneously. Example:

\[2NO + O_2 → 2NO_2\]
  • The chance of more than three molecules colliding at the same moment is very small. So molecularity greater than three is not observed.
  • Hence, a reaction whose balanced equation has more than three molecules on the reactant side must take place in more than one step.

Example

\[KClO_3 + 6FeSO_4 + 3H_2SO_4 → KCl + 3Fe_2(SO_4)_3 + 3H_2O\]

This reaction looks like it should be of tenth order, but it is actually a second order reaction. This shows that it takes place in several steps.

docs.title: Rate Determining Step
docs.text:
• In a relay race, the chance of a team winning depends on its slowest runner. Similarly, the overall rate of a complex reaction is controlled by its slowest step, called the rate determining step.
  • Consider the decomposition of H2O2 catalysed by iodide ion in alkaline medium:
\[2H_2O_2 \xrightarrow[Alkaline\ medium]{I^-} 2H_2O + O_2\] \[Rate = -{d[H_2O_2] \over dt} = k[H_2O_2][I^-]\]
  • The reaction is first order with respect to both H2O2 and I-. It takes place in two steps:
\[Step\ 1\ (slow):\ H_2O_2 + I^- → H_2O + IO^-\] \[Step\ 2\ (fast):\ H_2O_2 + IO^- → H_2O + I^- + O_2\]
  • Both steps are bimolecular elementary reactions.
  • IO- is called an intermediate because it is formed during the reaction but does not appear in the overall balanced equation.
  • The first step is slow, so it is the rate determining step. The rate of formation of the intermediate decides the rate of the overall reaction.

docs.title: Order vs Molecularity
docs.text: Order Molecularity It is the sum of powers of concentration terms in the rate law. It is the number of species colliding simultaneously in an elementary step. It is an experimental quantity. It is a theoretical concept. It can be zero, a fraction or even negative. It is always a whole number (1, 2 or 3). It cannot be zero or a fraction. It applies to both elementary and complex reactions. It applies only to elementary reactions. For complex reactions it has no meaning. For a complex reaction, it is given by the slowest step. Generally, molecularity of the slowest step equals the order of the overall reaction.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
For a reaction, A + B → Product, the rate law is given by r = k[A]1/2[B]2. What is the order of the reaction?

\[Order = {1 \over 2} + 2 = {5 \over 2} = 2.5\]

The conversion of molecules X to Y follows second order kinetics. If concentration of X is increased to three times, how will it affect the rate of formation of Y?

\[Rate_1 = k[X]^2\] \[Rate_2 = k(3[X])^2 = 9k[X]^2\] \[Rate_2 = 9 \times Rate_1\]

So, the rate of formation of Y will increase 9 times.

Identify the reaction order from each of the following rate constants: (i) k = 2.3 × 10-5 L mol-1s-1 (ii) k = 3 × 10-4 s-1

  • (i) The unit of a second order rate constant is L mol-1s-1. Hence, it is a second order reaction.
  • (ii) The unit of a first order rate constant is s-1. Hence, it is a first order reaction.

docs.title: Chemical Kinetics | Temperature Dependence, Catalysis and Collision Theory
Chemical Kinetics | Temperature Dependence, Catalysis and Collision Theory
docs.text: Most chemical reactions are accelerated by an increase in temperature, and the temperature dependence of the rate constant is explained by the Arrhenius equation.

docs.title: Effect of Temperature on Rate
docs.text:
Examples

  • In the decomposition of N2O5, the time taken for half of the original amount to decompose is 12 min at 50 °C, 5 h at 25 °C and 10 days at 0 °C.

  • In a mixture of KMnO4 and oxalic acid (H2C2O4), the permanganate is decolourised faster at a higher temperature.

  • For a chemical reaction, a rise in temperature by 10° nearly doubles the rate constant.
  • The ratio of rate constants at two temperatures differing by 10° is called the temperature coefficient. Its value is usually between 2 and 3.
\[Temperature\ coefficient = {k_{T + 10} \over k_T} ≈ 2\]

docs.title: Arrhenius Equation
docs.text:
The temperature dependence of the rate of a chemical reaction is accurately explained by the Arrhenius equation. It was first proposed by the Dutch chemist J.H. van't Hoff, but the Swedish chemist Arrhenius gave its physical justification and interpretation.

\[k = A\ e^{-E_a/RT}\]
  • A is the Arrhenius factor or frequency factor. It is also called the pre-exponential factor. It is a constant specific to a particular reaction.
  • R is the gas constant (8.314 J K-1mol-1).
  • Ea is the activation energy, measured in J mol-1.

docs.title: Activation Energy and Activated Complex
docs.text:
• Consider the reaction:
\[H_{2(g)} + I_{2(g)} → 2HI_{(g)}\]
  • According to Arrhenius, this reaction takes place only when a molecule of H2 and a molecule of I2 collide to form an unstable intermediate. This intermediate exists for a very short time and then breaks up into two molecules of HI.
\[H_2 + I_2 → [H \cdots I \cdots H \cdots I]\ (intermediate) → 2HI\]
  • This intermediate is called the activated complex (C).
  • The energy required to form the activated complex is called the activation energy (Ea).
  • A plot of potential energy against reaction coordinate shows this energy barrier. The reaction coordinate shows the energy profile as reactants change into products.
  • Some energy is released when the activated complex decomposes to form products. So, the final heat of reaction (ΔH) depends on the nature of reactants and products.

docs.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution of Energies
docs.text:
• Not all molecules in a reacting mixture have the same kinetic energy. Ludwig Boltzmann and James Clerk Maxwell used statistics to describe the behaviour of a large number of molecules.
  • The distribution is shown by plotting the fraction of molecules (NE/NT) with a given kinetic energy E against the kinetic energy. NE is the number of molecules with energy E and NT is the total number of molecules.
  • The peak of the curve corresponds to the most probable kinetic energy, i.e. the kinetic energy of the largest fraction of molecules. Fewer molecules have energies higher or lower than this value.
  • When the temperature is raised, the peak shifts to a higher energy value and the curve broadens out, i.e. spreads to the right. So a greater fraction of molecules has much higher energies.
  • The total area under the curve stays constant, because the total probability is always one.
  • Increasing the temperature increases the fraction of molecules which collide with energy greater than Ea.
  • At (t + 10), the area showing the fraction of molecules with energy equal to or greater than Ea roughly doubles. This doubles the rate of reaction.
  • In the Arrhenius equation, the factor e-Ea/RT is the fraction of molecules having kinetic energy greater than Ea.

docs.title: Calculating E<sub>a</sub> and A
docs.text:
• Taking natural log of both sides of the Arrhenius equation:
\[ln\ k = -{E_a \over RT} + ln\ A\] \[log\ k = -{E_a \over 2.303RT} + log\ A\]
  • A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope = -Ea/R and intercept = ln A. So Ea and A can be found from this graph.
  • Hence, increasing the temperature or decreasing the activation energy increases the rate of reaction, and the rate constant increases exponentially.

docs.title: Rate constants at two temperatures
docs.text:
• Let k1 and k2 be the rate constants at temperatures T1 and T2. Since A is constant for a given reaction:
\[ln\ k_1 = -{E_a \over RT_1} + ln\ A\] \[ln\ k_2 = -{E_a \over RT_2} + ln\ A\] \[ln\ k_2 - ln\ k_1 = {E_a \over RT_1} - {E_a \over RT_2}\] \[ln{k_2 \over k_1} = {E_a \over R}\left[{1 \over T_1} - {1 \over T_2}\right]\] \[log{k_2 \over k_1} = {E_a \over 2.303R}\left[{T_2 - T_1 \over T_1T_2}\right]\]

docs.title: Effect of Catalyst
docs.text:
A catalyst is a substance which alters the rate of a reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change.

Example

MnO2 greatly increases the rate of decomposition of potassium chlorate:

\[2KClO_3 \xrightarrow{MnO_2} 2KCl + 3O_2\]
  • The action of a catalyst is explained by the intermediate complex theory. The catalyst takes part in the reaction by forming temporary bonds with the reactants, giving an intermediate complex. This complex exists only for a short time and then decomposes to give the products and the catalyst back.
  • A catalyst provides an alternate pathway (reaction mechanism) with a lower activation energy between reactants and products. This lowers the potential energy barrier.

  • From the Arrhenius equation, the lower the activation energy, the faster the reaction.

docs.title: Important points about a catalyst
docs.text:
• A small amount of catalyst can catalyse a large amount of reactants.
  • A catalyst does not change the Gibbs energy (ΔG) of a reaction. It catalyses spontaneous reactions but cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction happen.
  • A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant of a reaction. It speeds up the forward and backward reactions to the same extent, so equilibrium is reached faster but the equilibrium state stays the same.

docs.title: Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions
docs.text:
• Collision theory was developed by Max Trautz and William Lewis in 1916-18. It gives a deeper insight into the energy and mechanism of reactions, and is based on the kinetic theory of gases.
  • Reactant molecules are assumed to be hard spheres, and a reaction occurs when molecules collide with each other.
  • The number of collisions per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture is called the collision frequency (Z).
  • For a bimolecular elementary reaction A + B → Products:
\[Rate = Z_{AB}\ e^{-E_a/RT}\]
  • ZAB is the collision frequency of A and B, and e-Ea/RT is the fraction of molecules with energy equal to or greater than Ea.
  • Comparing with the Arrhenius equation, the factor A is related to the collision frequency.

docs.title: Effective Collisions
docs.text:
• The above equation works well for atoms and simple molecules, but shows large deviations for complex molecules. This is because not all collisions form products.
  • Collisions in which molecules collide with sufficient kinetic energy (called threshold energy) and proper orientation, so that old bonds break and new bonds form, are called effective collisions.
\[Threshold\ energy = Activation\ energy + Energy\ possessed\ by\ reacting\ species\]

Example

In the formation of methanol from bromomethane, CH3Br + OH- → CH3OH + Br-, the OH- must approach the carbon atom from the side opposite to Br. Proper orientation leads to bond formation, while improper orientation makes the molecules simply bounce back and no products are formed.

  • To account for orientation, a probability factor or steric factor (P) is introduced:
\[Rate = P\ Z_{AB}\ e^{-E_a/RT}\]

Conclusion

In collision theory, activation energy and proper orientation of molecules together decide whether a collision is effective, and hence the rate of a chemical reaction.

  • Drawback: Collision theory treats atoms and molecules as hard spheres and ignores their structural aspects.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The rate constants of a reaction at 500 K and 700 K are 0.02 s-1 and 0.07 s-1 respectively. Calculate the values of Ea and A.

\[log{k_2 \over k_1} = {E_a \over 2.303R}\left[{T_2 - T_1 \over T_1T_2}\right]\] \[log{0.07 \over 0.02} = {E_a \over 2.303 \times 8.314}\left[{700 - 500 \over 700 \times 500}\right]\] \[0.544 = {E_a \times 5.714 \times 10^{-4} \over 19.15}\] \[E_a = {0.544 \times 19.15 \over 5.714 \times 10^{-4}} = 18230.8\ J\ mol^{-1}\]
  • Calculation of A:
\[k = A\ e^{-E_a/RT}\] \[0.02 = A\ e^{-18230.8/(8.314 \times 500)} = A \times 0.012\] \[A = {0.02 \over 0.012} = 1.61\ s^{-1}\]

The first order rate constant for the decomposition of ethyl iodide by the reaction C2H5I(g) → C2H4(g) + HI(g) at 600 K is 1.60 × 10-5 s-1. Its energy of activation is 209 kJ/mol. Calculate the rate constant of the reaction at 700 K.

\[log\ k_2 = log\ k_1 + {E_a \over 2.303R}\left[{1 \over T_1} - {1 \over T_2}\right]\] \[log\ k_2 = log(1.60 \times 10^{-5}) + {209000 \over 2.303 \times 8.314}\left[{1 \over 600} - {1 \over 700}\right]\] \[log\ k_2 = -4.796 + 2.599 = -2.197\] \[k_2 = 6.36 \times 10^{-3}\ s^{-1}\]

What will be the effect of temperature on rate constant?

  • The rate constant increases with increase in temperature. For a 10° rise in temperature, the rate constant nearly doubles.
  • This is because more molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy at higher temperature. The dependence is given by the Arrhenius equation, k = Ae-Ea/RT.

The rate of the chemical reaction doubles for an increase of 10 K in absolute temperature from 298 K. Calculate Ea.

\[T_1 = 298\ K,\ T_2 = 308\ K,\ {k_2 \over k_1} = 2\] \[log\ 2 = {E_a \over 2.303 \times 8.314}\left[{308 - 298 \over 298 \times 308}\right]\] \[E_a = {2.303 \times 8.314 \times 0.3010 \times 298 \times 308 \over 10}\] \[E_a = 52903\ J\ mol^{-1} = 52.9\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

The activation energy for the reaction 2HI(g) → H2 + I2(g) is 209.5 kJ mol-1 at 581 K. Calculate the fraction of molecules of reactants having energy equal to or greater than activation energy.

  • The fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea is x = e-Ea/RT.
\[log\ x = -{E_a \over 2.303RT} = -{209500 \over 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 581}\] \[log\ x = -18.83\] \[x = 1.47 \times 10^{-19}\]

docs.title: Battery
docs.text:
Any battery or cell that we use as a source of electrical energy is basically a galvanic cell where the chemical energy is converted into electrical energy.

There are two types of batteries:

  • Primary batteries
  • Secondary batteries

docs.title: Primary Batteries
docs.text:
In primary batteries, the reaction occurs only once and after use over a period of time, battery becomes dead and cannot be used again.

Examples of primary batteries are:

  • Dry cell or Leclanche cell
  • Mercury cell

docs.title: Dry cell or Leclanche cell
docs.text:
• It consists of zinc container that also acts as anode and the cathode is a carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by powdered manganese dioxide and carbon.

  • The space between the electrodes is filled by a moist paste of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) and zinc chloride (ZnCl2). The electrode reactions are complex but they can be written approximately as:

\[Anode:\ Zn_{(s)} → Zn^{2+} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ MnO_2 + NH_4^+ + e^- → MnO(OH) + NH_3\]

  • In the reaction at cathode, manganese is reduced from +4 oxidation state to +3 oxidation state.

  • Ammonia produced in the reaction forms a complex with Zn2+ to give [Zn(NH3)4]4+.

  • The cell has a potential of nearly 1.5 V.

docs.title: Mercury Cell
docs.text:
• Mercury cell, suitable for low current devices like hearing aids, watches etc consists of zinc in mercury amalgam as anode and a paste of HgO and carbon as cathode.

  • The electrolyte is a paste of KOH and ZnO. The electrode reactions for the cell are given below:

\[Anode:\ Zn(Hg) + 2OH^- → ZnO + H_2O + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ HgO + H_2O + 2e^- → Hg_{(l)} + 2OH^-\]
  • The overall reaction is represented by:
\[Zn(Hg) + HgO_{(s)} → ZnO_{(s)} + Hg_{(l)}\]
  • The cell potential is approximately 1.35 V and remains constant during its life as the overall reaction does not involve any ion in solution whose concentration can change during its lifetime.

docs.title: Secondary Batteries
docs.text:
A secondary cell after use can be recharged by passing current through it in the opposite direction so that it can be used again.

Examples of secondary batteries are:

  • Lead storage battery
  • Nickel-Cadmium cell

docs.title: Lead storage battery
docs.text:
• It consists of a lead anode and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide (PbO2) as cathode.

  • A 38% solution of sulphuric acid is used as an electrolyte.

  • The cell reactions are given as:

\[Anode:\ Pb_{(s)} + {SO_4^{2-}}_{(aq)} → PbSO_{4(s)} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ PbO_{2(s)} + {SO_4^{2-}}_{(aq)} + 4H^+_{(aq)} + 2e^- → PbSO_{4(s)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • The overall cell reaction is given by:
\[Pb_{(s)} + PbO_{2(s)} + 2H_2SO_{4(aq)} → 2PbSO_4{(s)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • On charging the battery, the reaction is reversed and PbSO4 on anode and cathode is converted into Pb and PbO2 respectively.

docs.title: Nickel-Cadmium cell
docs.text:
• It has longer life than the lead storage battery but it is more expensive to manufacture.

  • The overall reaction during discharge is:

\[Cd_{(s)} + 2Ni(OH)_{3(s)} → CdO_{(s)} + 2Ni(OH)_{2(s)} + H_2O_{(l)}\]

docs.title: Fuel Cells
docs.text: Galvanic cells that are designed to convert the energy of combustion of fuels like hydrogen, methane, methanol etc directly into electrical energy are called fuel cells.

docs.title: Fuel cell using H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> produces electricity
docs.text:
• In this cell, hydrogen and oxygen are bubbled through porous carbon electrodes into concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide solution.

  • Catalysts like finely divided platinum or palladium metal are incorporated into the electrodes for increasing the rate of electrode reactions.

  • The cathode and anode reactions are given below:

\[Cathode:\ O_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} + 4e^- → 4OH^-_{(aq)}\] \[Anode:\ 2H_2O_{(g)} + 4OH^{-}_{(aq)} → 4H_2O_{(l)} + 4e^-\]
  • The overall reaction is given by:
\[2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} → 2H_2O_{(l)}\]

docs.title: Advantages of fuel cells
docs.text:
• Fuel cells produce electricity with an efficiency of about 60% compared to thermal plants whose efficiency is about 40%.
  • Fuel cells are pollution free.

Suggest two materials other than hydrogen that can be used as fuels in fuel cells.

Methane (CH4) and methanol (CH3OH) are the two materials other than hydrogen that can be used as fuels in fuel cells.

docs.title: Corrosion
docs.text:
• Corrosion slowly coats the surfaces of metallic objects with oxides or other salts of the metal.
  • The rusting of iron, tarnishing of silver, development of green coating on copper and bronze are some of the examples of corrosion.
  • It causes enormous damage to buildings, bridges, ships and to all objects made of metal especially that of iron.
  • In corrosion, a metal is oxidized by loss of electron to oxygen and formation of oxides.
  • Corrosion of iron (rusting) occurs in the presence of water and air.

docs.title: Corrosion is an electrochemical phenomenon
docs.text:
• At a particular spot of an object made of iron, oxidation takes place and that spot behaves as anode.
\[Anode:\ 2Fe_{(s)} → 2Fe^+_{(aq)} + 4e^-,\ E^0_{(Fe^{2+}/Fe)} = -0.44V\]
  • Electrons released at anodic spot move through the metal and go to another spot on the metal and reduce oxygen in the presence of H+. This spot behaves as cathode with the reaction:
\[Cathode:\ O_2{(g)} + 4H^+_{(aq)} + 4e^- → 2H_2O_{(l)},\ E^0_{H^+/O_2/H_2O} = 1.23V\]
  • The overall reaction is:
\[2Fe_{(s)} + O_{2((g)} + 4H^+_{(aq)} → 2Fe^+_{(aq)} + 2H_2O,\ E^0_{cell} = 1.67V\]
  • The ferrous ions are further oxidized by atmospheric oxygen to ferric ions which come out as rust in the form of hydrated ferric oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O) and with further production of hydrogen ions.

docs.title: Prevention of Corrosion
docs.text:
• By painting and greasing.
  • By coating the surface by some inert metals (Sn, Zn etc).
  • By alloying.

docs.title: Resistance
docs.text:
• The electrical resistance is directly proportional to the length of conductor, l and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, A.
\[R ∝ l\] \[R ∝ {1 \over A}\] \[ ∴ R ∝ {l \over A}\] \[ ∴ R = {ρ l\over A}\]

docs.title: Resistivity
docs.text:
• Resistivity of a substance is its resistance when it is one metre long and its area of cross-section is one sq. metre.
  • It is also known as specific resistance.
  • Its S.I. unit is ohm-metre (Ωm).

docs.title: Conductance
docs.text:
• The inverse of resistance, R is known as conductance, G. Its S.I. unit is ohm-1 (Ω-1) or mho or siemens (S).
\[G = {1 \over R}\] \[G = {1 \over ρ} {A \over l}\] \[ ∴ G = Κ {A \over l}\]
  • Here, Κ (Kappa) = Conductivity or specific conductance.

docs.title: Conductivity
docs.text:
• Conductivity of a material is its conductance when it is one metre long and its area of cross-section is one sq. metre.
  • Its S.I. unit is Siemens per metre (Sm-1).

docs.title: Factors affecting conductivity and resistivity
docs.text:
Conductivity and resistivity depend on following factors:

  • Nature of the material
  • Temperature and pressure at which the measurements are made.

docs.title: Classification of materials
docs.text:
• Conductors: The materials having very large conductivity are called conductors. Metals and their alloys are the examples of conductors. Certain non-metals like graphite, carbon-black and some organic polymers aee also electronically conducting.

  • Insulators: The materials having very low conductivity are called insulators. Examples: glass, ceramics etc.

  • Semi-conductors: The materials having conductivity between conductors and insulators are called semi-conductors. Examples: silicon, doped silicon, gallium arsenide etc.

  • Superconductors: By definition, superconductors are the materials having zero resistivity or infinite conductivity. Earlier only metals and their alloys at very low temperature (0 to 15 K) were known to behave as superconductors but nowadays, a number of ceramic materials and mixed oxides are also known to show superconductivity at 150 K.

docs.title: Metallic or Electronic Conductance
docs.text:
• Electrical conductance through metals is called metallic or electronic conductance and is due to the movement of electrons.
  • The electronic conductance depends on following factors:
    1. the conductance and structure of the metal.
    2. the number of valence electrons per atom.
    3. temperature (it decreases with increase in temperature).

docs.title: Electrolytic or Ionic Conductance
docs.text:
• The conductance of electricity by ions present in the solutions is called electrolytic or ionic conductance.
  • The conductivity of electrolytic (ionic) solutions depends on following factors:
    1. the nature of electrolyte added.
    2. size of the ions produced and their solvation.
    3. the nature of the solvent and its viscosity.
    4. concentration of the electrolyte.
    5. temperature (it increases with increase in temperature).

docs.title: Measurement of the conductivity of ionic solutions
docs.text:
• Resistance, R is given by:
\[R = ρ {l \over A}\] \[ {R \over ρ} = {l \over A}\] \[G^* = {l \over A}\]
  • Here, G* is known as cell constant.
\[G^* = {R \over ρ}\] \[G^* = R Κ\] \[ Κ = {G^* \over R}\]

docs.title: How to measure conductivity?
docs.text:
• The bridge is balanced when:
\[RR_3 = R_1R_4\] \[ ∴ R = {R_1R_4 \over R_3}\]
  • The conductivity of the solution is given by:
\[ Κ = {G^* \over R}\] \[ Κ = {G^*R_3 \over R_1R_4}\]
  • The conductivity of solutions of different electrolytes in the same solvent and at a given temperature differs due to charge and size of the ions in which they dissociate, the concentration of ions or ease with which the ions move under a potential gradient.

docs.title: Molar Conductivity (λ<sub>m</sub>)
docs.text:
• Molar conductivity is defined as the conductivity of solution per unit its concentration.
\[ λ_m = {Κ \over C} = {Κ \over Molarity}\]

  • Its S.I. unit is Sm2mol-1.

  • 1 S m2mol-1 = 104 S cm2mol-1

docs.title: Electrochemical Cells
docs.text:
• Devices which can convert electrical energy into chemical energy or chemical energy into electrical energy are called electrochemical cells.
  • There are two types of electrochemical cells: (a) Electrolytic cell (b) Galvanic cell.

docs.title: Electrolytic Cell
docs.text:
• An electrolytic cell converts electrical energy into chemical energy.
  • In an electrolytic cell, the reaction is non-spontaneous. So, \(ΔG > 0\). The reaction is made spontaneous by supplying current.
  • Anode is positively charged and cathode is negatively charged.

docs.title: Galvanic Cell
docs.text:
• It is also known as Daniell Cell.

  • A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.

  • Current is flown by a spontaneous process. So, \(ΔG < 0\).

  • Anode is negative and cathode is positive in a galvanic cell.

  • Oxidation Half Cell Reaction (At anode):

\[Zn_{(s)} → Zn^{+2}_{(aq)} + 2e^-\]
  • Reduction Half Cell Reaction (At cathode):
\[Cu^{+2}_{(aq)} + 2e^- → Cu_{(s)}\]
  • Current flows from cathode to anode in an external circuit.

docs.title: Salt Bridge
docs.text: • It is a U-Shaped tube which is filled with a mixture of agar-agar and an inert electrolyte like KNO3, NaNO3, KCl etc and both the ends of this tube are sealed with cotton wool.

docs.title: Functions of Salt Bridge:
docs.text:
• It completes the inner circuit.
  • It prevents the diffusion of electrolytic solution in the two half cells.
  • It maintains electrical neutrality in the two cells. If excess electrons get accumulated, then salt bridge releases cations like Na+ to maintain electrical neutrality. If excess electrons are consumed, then salt bridge releases anions like Cl- and NO3- to maintain electrical neutrality.

docs.title: Characteristics of Inert Electrolyte:
docs.text:
• Both of its ions should not participate in the cell reactions.
  • Velocities of both ions of the electrolyte should be same. In the above figure, velocity of Na+ is approximately equal to velocity of NO3-.

docs.title: Electrode Potential
docs.text:
• The potential difference between electrode and electrolytic solution is known as electrode potential.
  • The natural tendency of an electrode to gain or lose electron is measured in terms of volts, called electrode potential.
  • It is of two types: (a) Oxidation Potential (b) Reduction Potential
  • Oxidation potential is represented as Eox or EM/Mn+ and reduction potential is represented as Ered or EMn+/M.
\[E_{ox} = -E_{red}\]

docs.title: Standard Electrode Potential(E<sup>0</sup>)
docs.text:
• The potential difference between the electrode and electrolytic solution at 25oC and 1 bar pressure when concentration of electrolytic solution is 1 molar is known as standard electrode potential.
  • It is of two types: (a) Standard Oxidation Potential(E0ox) (b) Standard Reduction Potential(E0red)
  • The element having more positive value of reduction potential will easily undergo reduction. It will also act as a good oxidizing agent.
  • The element having more positive value of oxidation potential will easily undergo oxidation. It will also act as a good reducing agent.

The E0red of I2, Br2, Cl2 and F2 are 0.35 V, 0.45 V, 1.3 V and 2.7 V. Arrange them in decreasing order of strength of oxidizing agent.

The element having more positive value of reduction potential will easily undergo reduction. It will also act as a good oxidizing agent. So, the order will be: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2

docs.title: Determination of Electrode Potential
docs.text:
• Electrode Potential of a single electrode cannot be calculated. So, we need a standard electrode as a reference for measuring electrode potential.
  • This standard electrode is known as standard hydrogen electrode.
  • The electrode potential of Standard Hydrogen Electrode is taken as zero.

Example

If voltmeter shows 1.2 V, then:

\[V - V_o = 1.2\]

Vo will be zero because it is standard hydrogen electrode.

\[V - 0 = 1.2\] \[V = 1.2\ V\]

docs.title: Standard Hydrogen Electrode(SHE)
docs.text:
• Standard Hydrogen Electrode is taken as a standard for measuring electrode potentials.

  • It is a half cell and can be both as a cathode and an anode.

  • If it acts as a cathode:

\[H^+_{(aq)} + e^- → {1\over 2}H_2{(g)},\ E^o_{red} = 0\]
  • If it acts as an anode:
\[ {1\over 2}H_2{(g)} → H^+_{(aq)} + e^-,\ E^o_{ox} = 0\]

docs.title: Electrochemical Series
docs.text:
• When different elements are arranged in order of their Standard Reduction Potential or Standard Oxidation Potential, a series is obtained which is known as electrochemical series.

  • On the basis of decreasing standard oxidation potential, the series is:

Li > K > Ba > Sr > Ca > Na > Mg > Al > Mn > Zn > Cr > Fe > Cd > Co > Ni > Sn > Pb > H2 > Cu > I2 > Ag > Hg > Br2 > Pt > O2 > Cl2 > Au > F2.

  • The elements written before H2 like Li, K, Ca have positive standard oxidation potentials while the elements written after H2 like Cu, Pt, Hg have negative standard oxidation potentials.

docs.title: EMF of a Cell
docs.text:
• EMF stands for Electromotive Force.

  • EMF is the potential difference between the electrodes when the cell is not in use.

  • When the switch is OFF in the circuit:

\[EMF = V_{cathode} - V_{anode}\]

  • It is also defined as the maximum voltage which a cell can supply.

  • EMF is the voltage which is responsible for the motion of electrons in the external circuit.

docs.title: Calculation of EMF of a cell (E<sub>cell</sub>)
docs.text:
• EMF of a cell is given by:
\[E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode}\]

Use Reduction Potential values in this formula.

  • We can also calculate Ecell as:
\[E_{cell} = E_{ox} + E_{red}\]
  • Standard EMF of a cell is given by:
\[E^0_{cell} = E^0_{cathode} - E^0_{anode}\]

Use Standard Reduction Potential values in this formula.

  • We can also calculate E0cell as:
\[E^0_{cell} = E^0_{ox} + E^0_{red}\]

docs.title: Relation between Gibbs Free Energy and E<sub>cell</sub>
docs.text:
• The relation between Gibbs Free Energy and Ecell can be expressed using the below expression:
\[ΔG = -nFE_{cell}\]

Case 1. If the cell reaction is spontaneous

\[ΔG < 0\] \[-nFE_{cell} < 0\] \[E_{cell} > 0\]

Thus, for a cell reaction to be spontaneous, Ecell should be positive.

Case 2. If the cell reaction is non-spontaneous

\[ΔG > 0\] \[-nFE_{cell} > 0\] \[E_{cell} < 0\]

Thus, for a cell reaction to be non-spontaneous, Ecell should be negative.

Case 3. If the cell reaction is in equilibrium

\[ΔG = 0\] \[-nFE_{cell} = 0\] \[E_{cell} = 0\]

docs.title: Rules to represent a galvanic cell
docs.text:
• Left half of the cell should represent anode, where oxidation takes place.
  • Right half of the cell should represent cathode, where reduction takes place.
  • Left half and right half should be separated by the symbol of salt bridge (||).
  • If an inert electrode is used, it should be written in left side before anode separated by comma.

Represent a Daniell Cell with the following half cell reactions and Pt is used as an inert electrode

\[ Anode:\ Zn_{(s)} → Zn^{(2+)}_{(aq)} + 2e^- \] \[ Cathode:\ Cu^{(2+)}_{(aq)} + 2e^- → Cu_{(s)} \]

This cell can be represented by applying the above rules:

\[Pt_{(s)},\ Zn_{(s)}/{Zn^{2+}_{(C_1 M)}}\ || Cu^{2+}_{(C_2 M)}/Cu_{(s)}\]

Pt is the inert electrode, left part represent anode and right part represent cathode. "||" represents salt bridge which separates anode and cathode.

docs.title: Electrochemistry | Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis
docs.text: Electrolysis can be defined as a process to drive a non-spontaneous reaction by using a direct current. It can be used to decompose ionic compounds into their ions. Electrolysis is also used to separate elements from their ores.

docs.title: Faraday's First Law
docs.text:
• Faraday's First law of electrolysis states that the mass of chemical deposited due to flow of current through an electrolyte is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity or charge (Q) passed through it.
  • If m is the mass deposited and Q is the charge passed, then we can write:
\[m ∝ Q\] \[m = ZQ\] \[Or,\ m = Zit\]
  • Here, Z is known as Electrochemical Equivalence. It is defined as the mass deposited due to one coulomb charge.
  • Let us calculate the value of Z for a chemical reaction:
\[X^{n+} + ne^- → X\]

In this reaction, if 1 Farad charge (96500 C) is passed, then \({1 \over n}\) moles X is deposited.

In other words, we can say that if 96500 C charge is passed, then \({M \over n}\) grams X is deposited, where M = Molar mass of X.

If 1 C charge is passed, the \({M \over 96500n}\) grams mass is deposited. Thus, \(Z = {M \over 96500n}\)

\[Z = {M \over 96500n}\]

Putting this value of Z in m = Zit:

\[m = {Mit \over 96500n}\] \[Or,\ m = {Eit \over 96500}\]

Here, E = M/n is known as Equivalent mass.

docs.title: Faraday's Second Law
docs.text:
• Faraday's Second law of electrolysis states that when the same quantity of electricity is passed through several electrolytes, the mass of the substances deposited are proportional to their respective chemical equivalent or equivalent mass.
  • We have already derived the following equation:
\[m = {Eit \over 96500}\] \[m ∝ E\]
  • For two electrolytes 1 and 2, we can write:
\[ {m_1 \over m_2} = {E_1 \over E_2}\]

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
In an experiment of two cells in series, current was passed for five hours. The amount of gold deposited was 9.85 grams. Calculate the amount of copper deposited and magnitude of current. (Au = 197 u and Cu = 63.5 u)

Reactions of the process are given below:

\[Au^{+3} + 3e^- → Au\] \[Cu^{+2} + 2e^- → Cu\] \[Equivalent\ mass\ of\ Au\ (E_1) = {M \over n} = {197 \over 3}\] \[Equivalent\ mass\ of\ Cu\ (E_2) = {M \over n} = {63.5 \over 2}\] \[Mass\ of\ Au\ deposited\ (m_1) = 9.85\ g\] \[Let\ Mass\ of\ Au\ deposited\ = m_2\] \[ {m_1 \over m_2} = {E_1 \over E_2}\] \[m_2 = {m_1E_2 \over E_1}\] \[m_2 = {9.85 \times {63.5 \over 2} \over {197 \over 3}}\] \[m_2 = 4.7625\ g\]

Let us calculate the current used in the process:

\[m_1 = {E_1 it \over 96500}\] \[i = {m_1\times 96500 \over E_1t}\] \[i = {9.85 \times 96500 \over {197 \over 3} \times {5\times 60 \times 60}} = 0.804\ Ampere\]

docs.title: Electrochemistry | Introduction
docs.text: Electrochemistry can be defined as the branch of chemistry which deals with the study of relationships between electrical energy and chemical energy and interconversion of one form of energy into another.

docs.title: Charge
docs.text:
• A charged object can be either electron deficient (positively charged) or electron surplus (negatively charged).
  • If 'i' amount of current flows per second in a wire, then after time 't', the charge, Q can be calculated as:
\[Q = it\]
  • Standard unit of charge is coulomb, denoted by C.
  • Other commonly used unit of charge in electrochemistry is Faraday or Farad denoted by F.

docs.title: Definition of Faraday
docs.text:
• 1 Faraday can be defined as the charge on 1 mole of electrons.
  • Let us derive relation between Faraday(F) and Coulomb(C):
\[Charge\ on\ 1\ electron = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} C\] \[Charge\ on\ 1\ mole\ electrons = 6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} C\] \[∴\ 1\ F = 96500\ C\]

Example

4 F charge means charge on 4 moles of electrons. Similarly, 0.982 F means charge on 0.982 moles of electrons.

  • Number of Faradays can be calculated as:
\[Number\ of\ Faradays = {Charge\ in\ C \over 96500}\] \[Number\ of\ Faradays = {it \over 96500}\]

Where, 'i' is in Ampere and 't' in seconds.

Examples

In the given examples, let us consider 1 F of charge is used or 1 mole of electrons is used.

\[Ag_{(aq)}^+ + e^- → Ag_{(s)} ↓ (1\ mole\ Ag\ is\ deposited)\] \[Cu_{(aq)}^{2+} + 2e^- → Cu_{(s)} ↓ ({1\over 2}\ moles\ Cu\ is\ deposited)\] \[Al_{(aq)}^{3+} + 3e^- → Al_{(s)} ↓ ({1\over 3}\ moles\ Al\ is\ deposited)\]

Similarly:

\[M_{(aq)}^{n+} + ne^- → M_{(s)} ↓ ({1\over n}\ moles\ M\ is\ deposited)\]

Thus, if 1 Farad of charge supplied to 1 mole of Mn+, $ {1\over n} $ moles of metal, M is deposited.

  • If x Farad charge is supplied to 1 mole of Mn+, \({x\over n}\) moles of metal, M is deposited.
  • We can also say that: If x Farad charge is supplied to 1 mole of Mn+, then mass of metal deposited = \({xM \over n}\), where M = molar mass of metal.

docs.title: 1. Electrolyte
docs.text: An electrolyte is a substance which can make water conductive when mixed wih it. Example: Pure water is non-conductive but when salt(NaCl) is added to it, it becomes conductive. Hence, NaCl is an electrolyte.

docs.title: 2. Non-Electrolyte
docs.text: A non-electrolyte is a substance which cannot make water conductive when mixed wih it. Example: A sugar solution is non-conductive. Hence, sugar is a non-electrolyte.

docs.title: 3. Electrolytic Solution
docs.text: An electrolytic solution is a solution which is capable of conducting current. When an electrolyte is added to water, it becomes an electrolytic solution. Example, NaCl solution is an electrolytic solution.

docs.title: 4. Electrode
docs.text: It is a rod which is immersed in an electrolytic solution and conducts electricity. There are two types of electrodes: (a) Cathode (b) Anode.

docs.title: 5. Anode
docs.text: Anode is an electrode where oxidation takes place.

docs.title: 6. Cathode
docs.text: Cathode is an electrode where reduction takes place.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
In an electrolytic solution, 10 gm of Ag needs to be deposited on Cu surface. Calculate the time taken in this process if current passed is 2 x 10-3 A.

\[Ag^+ + e^- → Ag ↓\] \[Mass\ of\ Ag\ formed = 10\ g\] \[Moles\ of\ Ag\ formed = {10 \over 108}\] \[Moles\ of\ electrons\ required = {10 \over 108}\] \[∴ Charge\ required(Q) = {10 \over 108} F\] \[Q = {10 \over 108} \times 96500\ C\] \[it = {10 \over 108} \times 96500\] \[ {2 \times 10^{-3}} t = {10 \over 108} \times 96500\] \[t = {10 \times 96500 \times 1000 \over 108 \times 2}\] \[t = 4467592.593\ s = 1241\ hours\]

Hence, the time taken for deposition of 10 g Ag is 1241 hours.

In an electrolytic solution Cu gets deposited if 2 A current is passed for 3 hours. Calculate the mass of Cu deposited.

\[Cu^{2+} + 2e^- → Cu ↓\] \[Charge\ passed,\ Q = it\] \[Q = 2 \times 3\times 60\times 60 = 21600\ C\] \[Q = {21600 \over 96500} F \] \[Moles\ of\ electrons\ used = {21600 \over 96500}\]

If 2 moles electrons are used, 1 mole Cu is deposited.

If \({21600 \over 96500}\) moles electrons are used, \({21600 \over 96500 \times 2}\) moles Cu is deposited.

\[Mass\ of\ Cu\ deposited = {21600 \over 96500 \times 2} \times 63.5\ g\] \[Mass\ of\ Cu\ deposited = 7.107\ g\]

docs.title: Nernst Equation
docs.text:
• Nernst Equation is used to calculate EMF of a cell.

Nernst Equation derivation

At temperature T, change in Gibbs Free Energy is given by:

\[ ΔG = ΔG^0 + RTlnQ \]

where, Q = Reaction quotient, R = Universal Gas Constant

We know that:

\[ΔG^0 = -nFE^0_{cell}\] \[ΔG = -nFE_{cell}\]

Putting these two values in above equation:

\[ -nFE_{cell} = -nFE^0_{cell} + RTlnQ \] \[ E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {RT \over {nF}}lnQ \] \[ E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {2.303RT \over {nF}}logQ \]

This equation is known as Nernst Equation.

If T = 298 K and putting the values of F and R in the given equation:

\[ E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {0.0591 \over n}logQ \]

Here, n = Number of electrons exchanged during cell reaction

docs.title: How to apply Nernst Equation?
docs.text:
• Calculate E0cell = E0cathode - E0anode
  • Write oxidation half and reduction half reactions.
  • Add oxidation half and reduction half reactions to obtain net cell reaction.
  • Find number of electrons exchanged, n.
  • Calculate reaction quotient of the net cell reaction.
  • Use Nernst Equation to find Ecell:
\[ E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {0.0591 \over n}logQ \]

docs.title: Nernst Equation during Equilibrium
docs.text:
• At equilibrium, we know that change in Gibbs Free Energy is zero.
\[ΔG = 0\] \[-nFE_{cell} = 0\] \[E_{cell} = 0\]

  • Also, at equilibrium: \(Q = K_c\)

  • Therefore, at equilibrium, Nernst equation can be written as:

\[ E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {0.0591 \over n}logQ \] \[ 0 = E^0_{cell} - {0.0591 \over n}logK_c \] \[ E^0_{cell} = {0.0591 \over n}logK_c \]

docs.title: Nernst Equation For Half Cell Reactions
docs.text:
• Nernst Equation is applicable for half cell as well as complete cell.

  • For oxidation half cell, we can write:

\[ E_{ox} = E^0_{ox} - {0.0591 \over n}logQ_1 \]
  • For reduction half cell, we can write:
\[ E_{red} = E^0_{red} - {0.0591 \over n}logQ_2 \]
  • Adding oxidation and reduction half cell reaction, we get net cell reaction and Nernst equation of cell can be written as:
\[ E_{ox} + E_{red} = E^0_{ox} + E^0_{red} - {0.0591 \over n}log(Q_1Q_2) \]

We know that: \(E_{ox} + E_{red} = E_{cell}\)

\[E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {0.0591 \over n}log(Q)\]

docs.title: Electrochemical cell and Gibbs Energy of a Reaction
docs.text:
• Change in Gibbs Free Energy is given by:
\[ΔG = -nFE_{cell}\]
  • Standard Change in Gibbs Free Energy is given by:
\[ΔG^0 = -nFE^0_{cell}\]

Also,

\[ΔG^0 = -RTlnK_c\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Resistance of a conductivity cell filled with 0.1 molL-1 KCl solution is 100 Ω. If the resistance of the same cell filled with 0.02 molL-1 KCl solution is 520 Ω, calculate the conductivity and molar conductivity of 0.02 molL-1 KCl solution. The conductivity of 0.1 molL-1 KCL solution is 1.29 S/m.

  • Cell constant of 0.1 molL-1 KCl solution:
\[G^* = Κ \times R\] \[G^* = 1.29 S/m \times 100 Ω\] \[G^* = 129 m^{-1}\]
  • Conductivity of 0.02 molL-1 KCl solution:
\[Κ = {G^* \over R}\] \[Κ = {129 \over 520} = 0.248 Sm^{-1}\]
  • Concentration, C:
\[C = 0.02\ mol\ L^{-1} = 20\ mol\ m^{-3}\]
  • Molar conductivity of 0.02 molL-1 KCl solution:
\[λ_m = {Κ \over C}\] \[λ_m = {0.248 \over 20}\] \[λ_m = 124 \times 10^{-4}\ Sm^2mol^{-1}\]

The electrical resistance of a column of 0.05 molL-1 NaOH solution of diameter 1 cm and length 50 cm is 5.55 x 103 ohm. Calculate its resistivity, conductivity and molar conductivity.

  • Resistivity, ρ is given by:
\[ρ = {RA \over l}\] \[ρ = {5.55 \times 10^3 \times π \times (10^{-2})^2 \times 25 \over 50 \times 10^{-2} \times 100}\] \[ρ = 0.87135\ Ωm = 87.135\ Ωcm\]
  • Conductivity, Κ is given by:
\[Κ = {1 \over ρ}\] \[Κ = {1 \over 87.135}\ Scm^{-1} = 0.01148\ Scm^{-1}\]
  • Molar conductivity, λm is given by:
\[λ_m = {Κ \over C}\] \[λ_m = {0.01148 \times 1000 \over 0.05}\] \[λ_m = 229.6\ Scm^{2}mol^{-1}\]

Calculate λ0m for CaCl2 and MgSO4 if: \(λ^0_{(Ca^+)} = 119.0\ Scm^2mol^{-1}\) \(λ^0_{(Cl^-)} = 76.3\ Scm^2mol^{-1}\) \(λ^0_{(Mg^{2+})} = 106.0\ Scm^2mol^{-1}\) \(λ^0_{({SO_4}^{2-})} = 160.0\ Scm^2mol^{-1}\)

λ0m for CaCl2 and MgSO4 can be calculated from Kohlraush law:

\[(a)\ CaCl_2 → Ca^{2+} + 2Cl^-\] \[ λ^0_{m(CaCl_2)} = λ^0_{m(Ca^{2+})} + 2 \times λ^0_{m(Cl^-)}\] \[ λ^0_{m(CaCl_2)} = 119.0 + 2 \times 76.3\] \[ λ^0_{m(CaCl_2)} = 271.6\ Scm^2mol^{-1}\] \[(b)\ MgSO_4 → Mg^{2+} + SO_4^{2-}\] \[ λ^0_{m(MgSO_4)} = λ^0_{m(Mg^{2+})} + λ^0_{m(SO_4^{2-})}\] \[ λ^0_{m(MgSO_4)} = 106 + 160\] \[ λ^0_{m(MgSO_4)} = 266\ Scm^2mol^{-1}\]

λ0m for NaCl, HCl and NaAc are 126.4, 425.9 and 91.0 Scm2mol-1 respectively. Calculate λ0m for HAc.

\[ λ^0_{m(HAc)} = λ^0_{m(H^{+})} + λ^0_{m(Ac^-)}\] \[ λ^0_{m(HAc)} = λ^0_{m(H^{+})} + λ^0_{m(Cl^{-})} + λ^0_{m(Ac^-)} + λ^0_{m(Na^+)} - λ^0_{m(Cl^-)} - λ^0_{m(Na^+)}\] \[ λ^0_{m(HAc)} = λ^0_{m(HCl)} + λ^0_{m(NaAc)} - λ^0_{m(NaCl)}\] \[ λ^0_{m(HAc)} = (425.9 + 91.0 - 126.4) Scm^2mol^{-1}\] \[ λ^0_{m(HAc)} = 390.5\ Scm^2mol^{-1}\]

The conductivity of 0.001028 molL-1 acetic acid is 4.95 x 10-5 Scm-1. Calculate its dissociation constant if λ0m for acetic acid is 390.5 Scm2mol-1.

\[ λ_m = {Κ \over C} \] \[ λ_m = {4.95 \times 10^{-5} \over 0.001028} \] \[ λ_m = 48.15\ Scm^2mol^{-1} \]

Degree of dissociation, α:

\[ α = {λ_m \over λ^0_m} \] \[ α = {48.15 \over 390.5} = 0.1233 \] \[ Κ = {Cα^2 \over (1-α)} \] \[ Κ = {0.001028 \times (0.1233)^2 \over (1-0.1233)} \] \[ Κ = 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\ molL^{-1}\]

The molar conductivity of 0.025 molL-1 methanoic acid is 46.1 Scm2mol-1. Calculate its degree of dissociation and dissociation constant. Given λ0m(H+) = 349.6 Scm2mol-1 and λ0m(HCOO-1) = 54.6 Scm2mol-1.

\[ λ_{m(HCOOH)} = (349.6 + 54.6)\ Scm^2mol^{-1} \] \[ λ_{m(HCOOH)} = 404.2\ Scm^2mol^{-1} \]

Degree of dissociation:

\[ α = {λ_m \over λ^0_m}\] \[ α = {46.1 \over 404.2} = 0.114\]

Dissociation constant:

\[ K_a = {Cα^2 \over (1-α)}\] \[ K_a = {0.025 \times (0.114)^2 \over (1-0.114)}\] \[ K_a = 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\ molL^{-1}\]

Suggest a way to determine the λ0m value of water.

Molar conductivity of water can be calculated using the below method:

\[ H_2O ⇋ H^+ + OH^- \] \[ λ_{m(H_2O)} = λ_{m(H^+)} + λ_{m(OH^-)} \] \[ λ_{m(H_2O)} = λ_{m(H^+)} + λ_{m(Cl^-)} + λ_{m(Na^+)} + λ_{m(OH^-)} - (λ_{m(Na^+)} + λ_{m(Cl^-)}) \] \[ λ_{m(H_2O)} = λ_{m(HCl)} + λ_{m(NaOH)} - λ_{m(NaCl)} \]

Why does the conductivity of a solution decrease with dilution?

The conductivity of a solution is related with the number of ions present per unit volume of the solution. When the solution is diluted, the number of ions per unit volume of solution decreases. Hence, conductivity of the solution also decreases.

docs.title: Electrochemistry | Questions Based on Nernst Equation
Electrochemistry | Questions Based on Nernst Equation
Questions
docs.text:
Represent the cell in which the following reaction takes place: Mg(s) + 2Ag+(0.0001 M) → Mg2+(0.130 M) + 2Ag(s) Calculate its Ecell if E0cell = 3.17 V.

  • The half cell reactions can be written as:
\[Anode:\ Mg_{(s)} → Mg^{2+}_{(0.130M)} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ 2Ag_{(0.0001\ M)}^+ + 2e^- → 2Ag_{(s)}\]
  • The cell can be represented as:
\[Mg_{(s)}/Mg^{2+}_{(0.130\ M)} || Ag^+_{(0.0001\ M)}/Ag_{(s)}\]
  • Calculation of Ecell:
\[Number\ of\ electrons\ exchanged,\ n = 2\] \[Reaction\ Quotient,\ Q = {[Mg^{2+}] \over [Ag^+]^2}\] \[Q = {0.130 \over (1 \times 10^{-4})^2} = 1.3 \times 10^7\] \[E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {0.0591 \over n} logQ\] \[E_{cell} = 3.17 - {0.0591 \over 2}log(1.3 \times 10^7) = 2.96\ V\]

Calculate the emf of cell in which the following reaction takes place: Ni(s) + 2Ag+(0.002 M) → Ni2+(0.160 M) + 2Ag(s) Given that: E0cell = 1.05 V.

  • The half cell reactions can be written as:
\[Anode:\ Ni_{(s)} → Ni^{2+}_{(0.160M)} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ 2Ag^+_{(0.002\ M)} + 2e^- → 2Ag_{(s)}\]
  • The cell can be represented as:
\[Ni_{(s)}/Ni^{2+}_{(0.130\ M)} || Ag^+_{(0.002\ M)}/Ag_{(s)}\]
  • Calculation of Ecell:
\[Number\ of\ electrons\ exchanged,\ n = 2\] \[Reaction\ Quotient,\ Q = {[Ni^{2+}] \over [Ag^+]^2}\] \[Q = {0.160 \over (0.002)^2} = 4 \times 10^4\] \[E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {0.0591 \over n} logQ\] \[E_{cell} = 1.05 - {0.0591 \over 2}log(4 \times 10^4) = 0.91\ V\]

Calculate the equilibrium constant of the reaction: Cu(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Cu2+(aq) + 2Ag(s) Given that: E0cell = 0.46 V.

  • The half cell reactions can be written as:
\[Anode:\ Cu_{(s)} → Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ 2Ag^+_{(aq)} + 2e^- → 2Ag_{(s)}\] \[Number\ of\ electrons\ exchanged,\ n = 2\]
  • At Equilibrium:
\[E^0_{cell} = {0.0591 \over n}logK_c\] \[0.46 = {0.0591 \over 2}logK_c\] \[K_c = 3.92 \times 10^{15}\]

The cell in which the following reaction occurs: 2Fe3+(aq) + 2I-(aq) → 2Fe+(aq) + I2(aq) has E0cell = 0.236 V$ at 298 K. Calculate the standard Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant of the reaction.

  • The half cell reactions can be written as:
\[Anode:\ 2I^-_{(aq)} → I_{2(s)} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ 2Fe^{3+}_{(aq)} + 2e^- → 2Fe^{2+}_{(aq)}\] \[Number\ of\ electrons\ exchanged,\ n = 2\]
  • Calculation of Standard Gibbs energy:
\[ΔG^0 = -nFE^0_{cell}\] \[ΔG^0 = -2 \times 96500 \times 0.236\] \[K_c = -45548\ J\]
  • Calculation of equilibrium constant:
\[E^0_{cell} = {0.0591 \over n}logK_c\] \[0.236 = {0.0591 \over 2}logK_c\] \[logK_c = {2 \times 0.236 \times 10 \over 0.0591}\] \[K_c = 9.6 \times 10^7\]

The standard electrode potential for Daniell cell is 1.1 V. Calculate the standard Gibbs Energy for the reaction: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)

Number of electrons exchanged, n = 2

Standard Gibbs Energy of the reaction:

\[ΔG^0 = -nFE^0_{cell}\] \[ΔG^0 = -2 \times 96500 \times 1.1\] \[ΔG^0 = -212300\ J = 212.3\ KJ\]

Calculate the potential of hydrogen electrode in contact with a solution whose pH is 10.

  • We know that pH can be calculated as:
\[pH = -log[H^+]\] \[10 = -log[H^+]\] \[[H^+] = 10^{-10} M\]
  • For hydrogen electrode:
\[H^+ + e^- → {1 \over 2} H_2\] \[Q = {1 \over [H^+]} = {1 \over 10^{-10}} = 10^{10}\]

  • Number of electrons exchanges, n = 1

  • Applying Nernst Equation:

\[E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - {0.0591 \over n}logQ\] \[E_{cell} = 0 - {0.0591 \over 1}log(10^{10}) = -0.591\ V\]

docs.title: Electrochemistry | Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration
Electrochemistry | Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration
Conductivity
docs.text:
• The conductivity of a solution at any given concentration is the conductance of one unit volume of solution kept between platinum electrodes with unit area of cross-section and at a distance of unit length.
\[G = { ΚA \over l} = Κ\]
  • Conductivity always decreases with decrease in concentration both for weak and strong electrolyte because the number of ions per unit volume that carry the current in a solution decreases on dilution.

docs.title: Molar Conductivity
docs.text:
• Molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is the conductance of the volume V of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with area of cross section A and distance of unit length.

  • Molar conductivity is also defined as the conductivity of solution per unit its concentration.

\[ λ_m = {Κ \over C}\] \[ λ_m = {Κ \over {n \over V}}\] \[ ∴ λ_m = {Κ V \over n} \]

  • Molar conductivity increases with decrease in concentration because \(λ_m ∝ {1 \over C}\).

  • It has been found that decrease in conductivity on dilution of a solution is more than compensated by increase in its volume. Physically, it means that at a given concentration, λm can be defined as the conductance of the electrolytic solution kept between the electrodes of a conductivity cell at a unit distance but having area of cross-section large enough to accommodate sufficient volume of solution that contains one mole of the electrolyte.

  • Limiting Molar Conductivity: When the concentration approaches zero, the molar conductivity is known as limiting molar conductivity and is represented by \(λ^0_m\).

  • The variation of molar conductivity, λm with concentration is different for strong and weak electrolytes.

docs.title: Variation of Molar Conductivity with Concentration in Strong Electrolytes
docs.text:
• For strong electrolytes, λm increases slowly with dilution and can be represented by the equation:
\[ λ_m = λ^0_m - AC^{1/2} \]

Here, intercept = \(λ^0_m\) and slope = A

  • The value of 'A' for a given solvent and temperature depends on the type of electrolyte, ie, charges on the cation and anion produced on the dissociation of the electrolyte in the solution.

  • NaCl, CaCl2, MgSO4 are 1-1, 2-1 and 2-2 electrolytes respectively. All electrolytes of particular type have the same value for 'A'.

docs.title: Kohlrausch Law of independent migration of ions
docs.text:
• It states that limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte can be represented as the sum of the individual contributions of the anion and cation of the electrolyte.

  • In general, if an electrolyte on dissociation gives $ ν+ $ cations and $ ν- $ anions, then its limiting molar conductivity is given by:

\[ λ^0_m = ν_+ λ^0_+ + ν_- λ^0_- \]
  • Here, \(λ^0_+\) = Limiting molar conductivity of cation and \(λ^0_-\) = Limiting molar conductivity of anion

docs.title: Variation of Molar Conductivity with Concentration in Weak Electrolytes
docs.text:
• For weak electrolytes, molar conductivity (λm) increases steeply on dilution, especially near lower concentrations. Therefore, limiting molar conductivity (λ0m) cannot be obtained by extrapolation of λm to zero concentration.

  • At infinite dilution (i.e, concentration → 0), electrolyte dissociates completely (α=1) but at such low concentration, the conductivity of the solution cannot be measured accurately.

  • Therefore, λ0m for weak electrolytes is obtained by using Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions.

  • At any concentration C, if α is the degree of dissociation, then it can be approximated to the ratio of molar conductivity λm at the concentration C to limiting molar conductivity λ0m.

\[ α = {λ_m \over λ^0_m} \]
  • For weak electrolytes like acetic acid:
\[CH_3COOH ⇌ CH_3COO^- + H^+\]

At time t = 0, let concentration of CH3COOH = c and concentration of CH3COO- and H+ = 0.

If α is the degree of dissociation, at time t = t, concentration of CH3COOH = c-cα and concentration of CH3COO- and H+ = cα

Dissociation constant, Ka is given by:

\[K_a = {[CH_3COO^-] [H^+] \over [CH_3COOH]}\] \[K_a = {cα \times cα \over c-cα}\] \[K_a = {cα^2 \over (1-α)}\] \[where, α = {λ_m \over λ^0_m}\]

docs.title: Boyle's Law
docs.text:
• At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume.
\[P ∝ {1 \over V}\] \[PV = constant\]

docs.title: Charle's Law
docs.text:
• At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature.
\[V ∝ T\] \[ {V \over T} = constant\]

where, T = Absolute Temperature (Kelvin scale)

\[Slope, m = tan Θ = {V_0 \over 273.15} ≈ {V_0 \over 273}\] \[∴ V = {V_0 \over 273}T + V_0\]

where, T is in celsius.

  • A new temperature scale was introduced known as Kelvin scale.

docs.title: Gay Lussac's Law
docs.text:
• At constant volume, for a fixed mass of a gas, pressure is directly proportional to its temperature.
\[P ∝ T\] \[ {T \over P} = constant \]

where, T = Absolute Temperature (Kelvin scale)

Note

Mean free path, \(λ ∝ {T \over P}\). If Gay Lussac's Law is valid or applicable, then mean free path is constant. We will discuss mean free path in detail later.

docs.title: Avogadro's Hypothesis
docs.text:
• At constant temperature and pressure, volume occupied by a gas, V is directly proportional to its number of moles, n.

  • More accurately, if \({T \over P} = constant\), then:

\[V ∝ n\]

docs.title: Ideal Gas Equation
docs.text:
• By Boyle's Law, we know that for a given mass of a gas, pressure is inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature.
\[P ∝ {1 \over V}\]
  • By Charle's Law, we know that for a given mass of a gas, volume occupied by the gas is directly proportional to temperature at constant pressure.
\[V ∝ T\]
  • By Gay Lussac's Law, we know that for a given mass of a gas, pressure is directly proportional to temperature at constant volume.
\[P ∝ T\]
  • By Avogadro's Law, we know that volume occupied by a gas is directly proportional to its moles at constant temperature and pressure.
\[V ∝ n\]
  • Combining all above four equations, we obtain the ideal gas equation:
\[PV ∝ nT\] \[PV = nRT\]

Here, R = Universal Gas Constant

Values of R in different units

\[R = 0.0821\ atm\ L\ mol^{-1}\] \[R = 8.314\ J\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}\] \[R = 1.98 ≈ 2\ calorie\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}\]
  • Note that \(1\ calorie = 4.184\ J\)

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
An ideal gas at 300 K is kept in an open container of volume 5 L. When temperature is raised to 500 K keeping pressure constant, calculate the percentage of moles of gas molecules escaped.

\[PV = nRT\]

Here, PV = constant because P and V both are constants.

\[Constant = nRT\] \[n ∝ {1 \over T}\]

Let initial and final moles be ni and nf respectively and let initial and final temperatures be Ti and Tf.

\[ {n_i \over n_f} = {T_f \over T_i} \] \[ {n_i \over n_f} = {500 \over 300} \] \[ {n_i \over n_f} = {5 \over 3} \] \[ {n_f \over n_i} = {3 \over 5} \]

Percentage of moles of gas escaped:

\[Percentage\ of\ moles\ of\ gas\ escaped = {n_i - n_f \over n_i} \times 100\] \[Percentage\ of\ moles\ of\ gas\ escaped = {1 - {n_f \over n_i}} \times 100\] \[Percentage\ of\ moles\ of\ gas\ escaped = {1 - {3 \over 5}} \times 100 = 40\]

A water bubble on the surface has volume = 4V. When it reaches at a depth of 'h', its volume becomes V. If 10 m water = 1 atm, calculate the value of 'h'.

Let initial pressure be \(P_1\), final pressure be \(P_2\), initial volume be \(V_1\) and final volume be \(V_2\).

\[ {P_1 \over P_2} = {V_2 \over V_1}\] \[ {1\ atm + h \over 1\ atm} = {4V \over V}\] \[ {10 + h \over 10} = 4\] \[ h = 30\ m\]

Find the common pressure when the stop cork is removed. The scenario is shown below:

Let the common pressure attained when the stop cork is removed be P.

\[Initial\ moles = Final\ moles\] \[ {P_A V \over RT} + {P_B V \over RT} = {P(V + V) \over RT} \] \[ P_A + P_B = 2P \] \[ 3 + 6 = 2P \] \[ P = 4.5\ atm \]

docs.title: Gaseous State | Introduction
docs.text: In the chapter of gaseous state, we will mainly focus on three things: (a) Ideal Gas Equation (b) Kinetic Theory of Gases and (c) Real Gases.

docs.title: Volume of a container
docs.text:
• The maximum amount of quantity contained by the container is known as its volume.

  • There are two types of containers - open container and closed container.

  • Open containers allow exchange of both matter and energy while closed containers do not allow exchange of matter but can allow exchange of energy through walls.

  • While calculating volume of the open container, we consider an imaginary boundary at the open end.

  • There are several units of volume: cubic centimetre(cm3), cubic metre(m3), millilitres(mL), litres(L). The standard unit of volume is litre(L).
\[1\ cm^3 = 1\ mL\] \[1000\ cm^3 = 1\ L\] \[1000\ mL = 1\ L\]

docs.title: Pressure
docs.text:
• Force (F) applied per unit area (A) is known as pressure (P). Mathematically, it can be stated as:
\[P = {F \over A}\]

  • The SI unit of pressure is Newton per square metre (N/m2) or Pascal (Pa).

  • There are other units of pressure such as atm, bar, torr etc.

Remember

\[1\ bar = 10^5\ Pa = 10^5\ N/m^2\] \[1\ atm = 101325\ Pa ≈ 10^5\ Pa\] \[1\ atm ≈ 1\ bar\] \[760\ mm\ of\ Hg = 1\ atm\] \[1\ atm = 760\ torr\]
  • At the open end of a container under normal conditions, pressure is always 1 atm.

  • Pressure at a depth 'h' of a liquid:

Let the density of a liquid be ρ, mass be M and volume be V.

\[ρ = {M \over V}\] \[M = ρV\] \[M = ρhA\]

Now, we know that pressure can be calculated as:

\[P = {F \over A}\] \[P = {Mg \over A}\] \[P = {ρhAg \over A}\] \[P = ρgh\]
  • Pressure is same at the same horizontal level.

\[P_1 = P_2 = P_3\]
  • For an open container, at depth 'h' of a fluid, net pressure is:

\[P = (1 atm) + ρgh\]
  • Pressure is same at all faces of a container. In other words, there exists a same external pressure for a container.

docs.title: Measurement of Pressure
docs.text:
• Let us consider a container filled with liquid mercury at 1 atm external pressure and let a test tube be placed inverted above the surface of the liquid.
\[P_A = P_B\] \[1\ atm = ρgh\] \[10^5\ Pa = (13.6\ g/mL) \times 9.8 \times h\] \[10^5\ Pa = (13.6 \times 1000 kg/m^3) \times h\] \[h = 0.76\ m\ of\ Hg\] \[h = 76\ cm\ of\ Hg\] \[h = 760\ mm\ of\ Hg\]

Note

Water cannot be used for measuring pressure because the height of water will be very large, so it will be difficult to get such a ling test tube.

If water is used, height of test tube, hw is calculated as:

\[ρ_wgh_w = ρ_{Hg}gh_{Hg}\] \[1 \times h_w = 13.6 \times 0.76\] \[h_w = 10.336\ m\]

docs.title: Gaseous State | Kinetic Theory of Gases
Gaseous State | Kinetic Theory of Gases
Postulates of Kinetic Theory of Gases
docs.text:
1. A gas consists of a large number of very small tiny particles, which are identified as molecules. The molecules of a given gas are completely identical in size, shape and mass.
  2. The volume occupied by the molecules is negligible in comparison to the volume of the gas.
  3. The molecules are in rapid motion, which is completely random. During their motion, they collide with the sides of the vessel. The collisions are perfectly elastic in nature.
  4. The laws of classical mechanics are applicable to the molecules in motion.
  5. There is no force of attraction or repulsion amongst the molecules, i.e., they are moving independent of each other.
  6. At any given instant, a molecule can have energy ranging from a small value to a large value, but the average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature of the gas.
\[(K.E.)_{avg.} ∝ T\]

This also means that at fixed temperature, average kinetic energy of gas molecule is fixed.

Note

  • Kinetic Theory of gases is applicable only for ideal gases.

  • All the gas laws can be derived from Kinetic Theory of gases.

docs.title: Buffer Solutions
docs.text:
The solutions which resist change in pH on dilution or with the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali are called buffer solutions.

  • Many body fluids like blood and urine have a definite pH, and any deviation indicates malfunctioning of the body. Control of pH is also important in many chemical and biochemical processes, and in medical and cosmetic formulations.
  • A buffer of known pH can be prepared from the pKa of an acid (or pKb of a base) by controlling the ratio of salt and acid (or salt and base).

docs.title: 1. Acidic buffer
docs.text:
• A mixture of a weak acid and its salt with a strong base.
  • Example: Acetic acid and sodium acetate (CH3COOH + CH3COONa) acts as a buffer around pH 4.75.

docs.title: 2. Basic buffer
docs.text:
• A mixture of a weak base and its salt with a strong acid.
  • Example: Ammonium hydroxide and ammonium chloride (NH4OH + NH4Cl) acts as a buffer around pH 9.25.

docs.title: Buffer Action
docs.text:
• A buffer contains a large reserve of both an acid (to consume added OH-) and a base (to consume added H+). The common ion effect keeps the weak electrolyte almost unionized.

Acidic buffer: CH3COOH + CH3COONa

\[CH_3COONa → CH_3COO^- + Na^+\ (complete)\] \[CH_3COOH ⇌ CH_3COO^- + H^+\ (suppressed\ by\ common\ ion)\]
  • On adding a small amount of acid, the added H+ combine with the large reserve of acetate ions:
\[CH_3COO^- + H^+ → CH_3COOH\]
  • On adding a small amount of base, the added OH- are neutralized by acetic acid:
\[CH_3COOH + OH^- → CH_3COO^- + H_2O\]

Basic buffer: NH4OH + NH4Cl

  • Added H+ are consumed by NH4OH:
\[NH_4OH + H^+ → NH_4^+ + H_2O\]
  • Added OH- are consumed by NH4+:
\[NH_4^+ + OH^- → NH_4OH\]
  • In each case, only the ratio [salt]/[acid] changes slightly, so the pH changes very little.

docs.title: 1. For an acidic buffer
docs.text:
• For a weak acid HA in presence of its salt:
\[HA ⇌ H^+ + A^-,\ \ K_a = {[H^+][A^-] \over [HA]}\] \[[H^+] = K_a {[HA] \over [A^-]}\]

Taking negative log on both sides:

\[-log[H^+] = -log\ K_a - log{[HA] \over [A^-]}\] \[pH = pK_a + log{[A^-] \over [HA]}\]
  • Since the acid is weakly ionized (and further suppressed by the common ion), [HA] ≈ initial concentration of acid, and [A-] ≈ concentration of salt.
\[pH = pK_a + log{[Salt] \over [Acid]}\]

docs.title: 2. For a basic buffer
docs.text:
\[BOH ⇌ B^+ + OH^-,\ \ K_b = {[B^+][OH^-] \over [BOH]}\] \[pOH = pK_b + log{[Salt] \over [Base]}\] \[pH = 14 - pOH = 14 - pK_b - log{[Salt] \over [Base]}\]

Conclusion

  • The pH of a buffer depends on the ratio [salt]/[acid] (or [salt]/[base]), not on the actual amounts. Since dilution does not change this ratio, the pH of a buffer does not change on dilution.

  • When [salt] = [acid], pH = pKa. When [salt] = [base], pOH = pKb. The buffer resists change best (maximum buffer capacity) at this point.

  • A buffer works effectively in the range pH = pKa ± 1 (i.e., [salt]/[acid] between 1/10 and 10). So, to prepare a buffer of a desired pH, choose a weak acid whose pKa is close to that pH.

  • Since the Henderson equation uses concentrations in a ratio, moles (or millimoles) can be used directly when acid and salt are in the same solution.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the pH of solution formed on mixing 0.2 M NH4Cl and 0.1 M NH3. The pOH of ammonia solution is 4.75.

The pOH value given here is used as pKb of ammonia:

\[K_b = antilog(-pK_b) = 10^{-4.75} = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\] \[NH_3 + H_2O ⇌ NH_4^+ + OH^-\] \[Equilibrium\ (M):\ \ 0.10 - x\ \ \ \ \ \ 0.20 + x\ \ \ \ \ \ x\] \[K_b = {(0.20 + x)(x) \over 0.10 - x} = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\]

As Kb is small, x can be neglected compared to 0.1 M and 0.2 M:

\[[OH^-] = x = 1.77 \times 10^{-5} \times {0.10 \over 0.20} = 0.88 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[[H^+] = {10^{-14} \over 0.88 \times 10^{-5}} = 1.12 \times 10^{-9}\ M\] \[pH = -log(1.12 \times 10^{-9}) = 8.95\]

Using the Henderson equation directly:

\[pOH = 4.75 + log{0.2 \over 0.1} = 4.75 + 0.30 = 5.05,\ \ pH = 8.95\]

Calculate the pH of a buffer containing 0.1 M acetic acid and 0.2 M sodium acetate. (pKa of acetic acid = 4.74)

\[pH = pK_a + log{[Salt] \over [Acid]}\] \[pH = 4.74 + log{0.2 \over 0.1} = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04\]

In what ratio should sodium acetate and acetic acid be mixed to obtain a buffer of pH 5.74? (pKa of acetic acid = 4.74)

\[5.74 = 4.74 + log{[Salt] \over [Acid]}\] \[log{[Salt] \over [Acid]} = 1\] \[{[Salt] \over [Acid]} = 10\]

So sodium acetate and acetic acid must be mixed in a 10 : 1 molar ratio.

1 litre of a buffer contains 0.1 mol acetic acid and 0.1 mol sodium acetate (pKa = 4.74). Calculate the change in pH on adding (a) 0.01 mol HCl (b) 0.01 mol NaOH. Compare with the change when 0.01 mol HCl is added to 1 litre of pure water.

Initial pH:

\[pH = 4.74 + log{0.1 \over 0.1} = 4.74\]

(a) Added H+ converts acetate into acetic acid:

\[CH_3COO^- + H^+ → CH_3COOH\] \[Acetate = 0.1 - 0.01 = 0.09\ mol,\ \ Acid = 0.1 + 0.01 = 0.11\ mol\] \[pH = 4.74 + log{0.09 \over 0.11} = 4.74 - 0.09 = 4.65\]

(b) Added OH- converts acetic acid into acetate:

\[Acetate = 0.11\ mol,\ \ Acid = 0.09\ mol\] \[pH = 4.74 + log{0.11 \over 0.09} = 4.74 + 0.09 = 4.83\]

The pH changes by only about 0.09 unit. In pure water, 0.01 mol HCl in 1 litre gives [H+] = 0.01 M, so the pH falls from 7 to 2, a change of 5 units.

50 mL of 0.2 M acetic acid is mixed with 50 mL of 0.1 M NaOH. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution. (pKa = 4.74)

\[mmol\ CH_3COOH = 0.2 \times 50 = 10,\ \ mmol\ NaOH = 0.1 \times 50 = 5\] \[CH_3COOH + NaOH → CH_3COONa + H_2O\] \[After\ reaction:\ \ CH_3COOH = 5\ mmol,\ \ CH_3COONa = 5\ mmol\]

The solution is a buffer with equal amounts of acid and salt:

\[pH = 4.74 + log{5 \over 5} = 4.74\]

This is why the pH at half-neutralization of a weak acid equals its pKa.

How many grams of NH4Cl must be added to 500 mL of 0.1 M NH3 solution to obtain a buffer of pH 9.0? (pKb of NH3 = 4.75, assume no change in volume)

\[pOH = 14 - 9.0 = 5.0\] \[5.0 = 4.75 + log{[NH_4Cl] \over [NH_3]}\] \[{[NH_4Cl] \over [NH_3]} = 10^{0.25} = 1.78\] \[[NH_4Cl] = 1.78 \times 0.1 = 0.178\ M\] \[Moles\ of\ NH_4Cl = 0.178 \times 0.5 = 0.089\ mol\] \[Mass\ of\ NH_4Cl = 0.089 \times 53.5 = 4.76\ g\]

docs.title: Common Ion Effect
docs.text:
Common ion effect can be defined as the shift in equilibrium on adding a substance that provides more of an ionic species already present in the dissociation equilibrium. It is an application of Le Chatelier's principle.

  • Consider the dissociation of acetic acid:
\[CH_3COOH_{(aq)} ⇌ H^+_{(aq)} + CH_3COO^-_{(aq)}\] \[or\ \ HAc_{(aq)} ⇌ H^+_{(aq)} + Ac^-_{(aq)}\] \[K_a = {[H^+][Ac^-] \over [HAc]}\]
  • If acetate ions are added (for example, as sodium acetate, CH3COONa), the concentration of Ac- increases. To keep Ka constant, the equilibrium shifts backward, and [H+] decreases.
  • Similarly, if H+ ions are added from an external source (such as HCl), the equilibrium moves towards undissociated acetic acid, reducing the ionization of the acid.

Conclusion

  • Addition of a common ion suppresses the ionization of a weak electrolyte.

  • The degree of ionization of a weak acid decreases in presence of a strong acid or its own salt. The degree of ionization of a weak base decreases in presence of a strong base or its own salt.

docs.title: pH of 0.05 M acetic acid containing 0.05 M acetate ion
docs.text:
Example

\[HAc_{(aq)} ⇌ H^+_{(aq)} + Ac^-_{(aq)}\] \[Initial\ (M):\ \ 0.05\ \ \ \ 0\ \ \ \ 0.05\]

Let x be the extent of ionization of acetic acid.

\[Change\ (M):\ \ -x\ \ \ \ +x\ \ \ \ +x\] \[Equilibrium\ (M):\ \ 0.05 - x\ \ \ \ x\ \ \ \ 0.05 + x\] \[K_a = {[H^+][Ac^-] \over [HAc]} = {(0.05 + x)(x) \over 0.05 - x}\]

As Ka is small for a very weak acid, x << 0.05. Hence, (0.05 + x) ≈ (0.05 - x) ≈ 0.05.

\[1.8 \times 10^{-5} = {x(0.05) \over 0.05}\] \[x = [H^+] = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[pH = -log(1.8 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.74\]
  • Without the added acetate, the same 0.05 M acetic acid has [H+] = √(Kac) ≈ 9.5 × 10-4 M and pH ≈ 3.0. The common ion has reduced [H+] about 50 times.

docs.title: General result
docs.text:
• For a weak acid HA (concentration c) in presence of a strong acid giving [H+] = C', or its salt giving [A-] = C':
\[Weak\ acid + strong\ acid:\ \ α = {K_a \over C'}\] \[Weak\ acid + its\ salt:\ \ [H^+] = {K_a \times [HA] \over [A^-]}\]
  • Similarly, for a weak base in presence of a strong base giving [OH-] = C':
\[α = {K_b \over C'}\]
  • A mixture of a weak acid and its salt (or a weak base and its salt) resists change in pH. Such mixtures are buffer solutions, discussed in a later page.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the pH of a 0.10 M ammonia solution. Calculate the pH after 50.0 mL of this solution is treated with 25.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl. The dissociation constant of ammonia, Kb = 1.77 × 10-5.

Before neutralization

\[NH_3 + H_2O ⇌ NH_4^+ + OH^-\] \[K_b = {[NH_4^+][OH^-] \over [NH_3]} = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\]

Let [NH4+] = [OH-] = x, then [NH3] = 0.10 - x ≈ 0.10.

\[{x^2 \over 0.10} = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\] \[x = 1.33 \times 10^{-3}\ M = [OH^-]\] \[[H^+] = {K_w \over [OH^-]} = {10^{-14} \over 1.33 \times 10^{-3}} = 7.51 \times 10^{-12}\ M\] \[pH = -log(7.51 \times 10^{-12}) = 11.12\]

After adding HCl

25 mL of 0.1 M HCl = 2.5 mmol HCl. 50 mL of 0.1 M NH3 = 5 mmol NH3. So 2.5 mmol NH3 is neutralized.

\[NH_3 + HCl → NH_4^+ + Cl^-\] \[Before:\ \ 5\ \ \ \ 2.5\ \ \ \ 0\ \ \ \ 0\ \ (mmol)\] \[After:\ \ 2.5\ \ \ \ 0\ \ \ \ 2.5\ \ \ \ 2.5\ \ (mmol)\]

The resulting 75 mL contains 2.5 mmol NH4+ (0.033 M) and 2.5 mmol unneutralized NH3 (0.033 M). This NH3 ionizes in presence of the common ion NH4+:

\[NH_4OH ⇌ NH_4^+ + OH^-\] \[Equilibrium:\ \ 0.033 - y\ \ \ \ 0.033 + y\ \ \ \ y\]

As y is small, [NH4OH] ≈ 0.033 M and [NH4+] ≈ 0.033 M.

\[K_b = {[NH_4^+][OH^-] \over [NH_4OH]} = {y(0.033) \over 0.033} = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\] \[y = [OH^-] = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[[H^+] = {10^{-14} \over 1.77 \times 10^{-5}} = 0.56 \times 10^{-9}\ M\] \[pH = 9.24\]

The ionization constant of phenol is 1.0 × 10-10. What is the concentration of phenolate ion in 0.05 M solution of phenol? What will be its degree of ionization if the solution is also 0.01 M in sodium phenolate?

\[C_6H_5OH ⇌ H^+ + C_6H_5O^-\]

In 0.05 M phenol alone

\[[C_6H_5O^-] = \sqrt{K_a\ c} = \sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{-10} \times 0.05} = 2.24 \times 10^{-6}\ M\] \[α = {2.24 \times 10^{-6} \over 0.05} = 4.47 \times 10^{-5}\]

In presence of 0.01 M sodium phenolate

Sodium phenolate is fully ionized, so [C6H5O-] ≈ 0.01 M (the phenol's own contribution is negligible).

\[[H^+] = {K_a[C_6H_5OH] \over [C_6H_5O^-]} = {1.0 \times 10^{-10} \times 0.05 \over 0.01} = 5.0 \times 10^{-10}\ M\] \[α = {[H^+] \over c} = {5.0 \times 10^{-10} \over 0.05} = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\]

The degree of ionization drops from 4.47 × 10-5 to 1.0 × 10-8 because of the common ion.

Calculate the degree of ionization of 0.05 M acetic acid if its pKa value is 4.74. How is the degree of dissociation affected when its solution also contains (a) 0.01 M (b) 0.1 M in HCl?

\[K_a = 10^{-4.74} = 1.82 \times 10^{-5}\]

Without HCl

\[α = \sqrt{K_a \over c} = \sqrt{1.82 \times 10^{-5} \over 0.05} = 0.019\]

With HCl, [H+] ≈ [HCl], and α = Ka/[H+]:

\[(a)\ α = {1.82 \times 10^{-5} \over 0.01} = 1.82 \times 10^{-3}\] \[(b)\ α = {1.82 \times 10^{-5} \over 0.1} = 1.82 \times 10^{-4}\]

The degree of dissociation decreases as more HCl (common ion H+) is added.

The ionization constant of dimethylamine is 5.4 × 10-4. Calculate its degree of ionization in its 0.02 M solution. What percentage of dimethylamine is ionized if the solution is also 0.1 M in NaOH?

\[(CH_3)_2NH + H_2O ⇌ (CH_3)_2NH_2^+ + OH^-\]

In 0.02 M solution

\[α = \sqrt{K_b \over c} = \sqrt{5.4 \times 10^{-4} \over 0.02} = 0.164\]

Since α is more than 5%, solving the full quadratic, 0.02α2 + 5.4 × 10-4α - 5.4 × 10-4 = 0, gives the more exact value α = 0.151.

In presence of 0.1 M NaOH

[OH-] ≈ 0.1 M from NaOH, so:

\[α = {K_b \over [OH^-]} = {5.4 \times 10^{-4} \over 0.1} = 5.4 \times 10^{-3}\]

So only 0.54% of dimethylamine is ionized.

The ionization constant of propanoic acid is 1.32 × 10-5. Calculate the degree of ionization of the acid in its 0.05 M solution and also its pH. What will be its degree of ionization if the solution is 0.01 M in HCl also?

\[α = \sqrt{K_a \over c} = \sqrt{1.32 \times 10^{-5} \over 0.05} = 1.63 \times 10^{-2}\] \[[H^+] = cα = 0.05 \times 1.63 \times 10^{-2} = 8.12 \times 10^{-4}\ M\] \[pH = -log(8.12 \times 10^{-4}) = 3.09\]

In presence of 0.01 M HCl:

\[α = {K_a \over [H^+]} = {1.32 \times 10^{-5} \over 0.01} = 1.32 \times 10^{-3}\]

docs.title: Salt Hydrolysis
docs.text:
Salt hydrolysis is the process of interaction between water and the cations, anions or both of a salt, which changes the pH of the solution.

  • Salts are formed by the reaction of acids and bases in definite proportions. In water, salts ionize completely.
  • The ions formed either simply get hydrated, or react with water to re-form the corresponding acid or base. The second process is hydrolysis.
  • Cations of strong bases (Na+, K+, Ca2+, Ba2+ etc.) and anions of strong acids (Cl-, Br-, NO3-, ClO4- etc.) only get hydrated and do not hydrolyse.
  • So, solutions of salts of strong acids and strong bases (like NaCl, KNO3) are neutral, with pH = 7.
  • Ions coming from weak acids or weak bases do hydrolyse. We consider three types of such salts:
Type of salt Example Ion that hydrolyses Nature of solution Weak acid + strong base CH3COONa Anion (CH3COO-) Basic (pH > 7) Strong acid + weak base NH4Cl Cation (NH4+) Acidic (pH < 7) Weak acid + weak base CH3COONH4 Both ions Depends on pKa and pKb Strong acid + strong base NaCl None Neutral (pH = 7)

docs.title: 1. Salt of Weak Acid and Strong Base
docs.text:
• CH3COONa, a salt of the weak acid CH3COOH and the strong base NaOH, is completely ionized in water.
\[CH_3COONa_{(aq)} → CH_3COO^-_{(aq)} + Na^+_{(aq)}\]
  • The acetate ion undergoes hydrolysis to give acetic acid and OH- ions:
\[CH_3COO^-_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ CH_3COOH_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\]
  • Acetic acid is a weak acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10-5), so it remains mainly unionized. OH- ions build up and the solution becomes alkaline (pH > 7).

docs.title: Hydrolysis constant, degree of hydrolysis and pH
docs.text:
• Let c be the concentration of the salt and h the degree of hydrolysis (fraction of the salt hydrolysed).
\[CH_3COO^- + H_2O ⇌ CH_3COOH + OH^-\] \[Equilibrium:\ \ c(1-h)\ \ \ \ \ \ ch\ \ \ \ \ \ ch\] \[K_h = {[CH_3COOH][OH^-] \over [CH_3COO^-]}\]
  • Multiplying numerator and denominator by [H+]:
\[K_h = {[CH_3COOH] \over [CH_3COO^-][H^+]} \times [H^+][OH^-] = {K_w \over K_a}\] \[K_h = {ch^2 \over 1-h} ≈ ch^2\ \ \ (h \ll 1)\] \[h = \sqrt{K_h \over c} = \sqrt{K_w \over K_a\ c}\] \[[OH^-] = ch = \sqrt{K_w\ c \over K_a}\] \[pH = 7 + {1 \over 2}pK_a + {1 \over 2}log\ c\ \ \ (at\ 298\ K)\]

docs.title: 2. Salt of Strong Acid and Weak Base
docs.text:
• NH4Cl, formed from the weak base NH4OH and the strong acid HCl, dissociates completely in water.
\[NH_4Cl_{(aq)} → NH^+_{4(aq)} + Cl^-_{(aq)}\]
  • Ammonium ions undergo hydrolysis to form NH4OH and H+ ions:
\[NH^+_{4(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ NH_4OH_{(aq)} + H^+_{(aq)}\]
  • NH4OH is a weak base (Kb = 1.77 × 10-5) and remains almost unionized. H+ ion concentration increases, so the solution is acidic and its pH is less than 7.

docs.title: Hydrolysis constant, degree of hydrolysis and pH
docs.text: \[K_h = {[NH_4OH][H^+] \over [NH_4^+]} = {K_w \over K_b}\] \[h = \sqrt{K_w \over K_b\ c}\] \[[H^+] = ch = \sqrt{K_w\ c \over K_b}\] \[pH = 7 - {1 \over 2}pK_b - {1 \over 2}log\ c\ \ \ (at\ 298\ K)\]

docs.title: 3. Salt of Weak Acid and Weak Base
docs.text:
• In CH3COONH4, both ions undergo hydrolysis:
\[CH_3COO^- + NH_4^+ + H_2O ⇌ CH_3COOH + NH_4OH\]
  • CH3COOH and NH4OH also remain in partially dissociated form:
\[CH_3COOH ⇌ CH_3COO^- + H^+\] \[NH_4OH ⇌ NH_4^+ + OH^-\] \[H_2O ⇌ H^+ + OH^-\]

docs.title: Hydrolysis constant, degree of hydrolysis and pH
docs.text:
\[Equilibrium:\ \ c(1-h)\ \ \ \ c(1-h)\ \ \ \ \ \ ch\ \ \ \ ch\] \[K_h = {[CH_3COOH][NH_4OH] \over [CH_3COO^-][NH_4^+]} = {K_w \over K_a K_b}\] \[K_h = {h^2 \over (1-h)^2},\ \ \ {h \over 1-h} = \sqrt{K_h}\] \[[H^+] = K_a{[CH_3COOH] \over [CH_3COO^-]} = K_a{h \over 1-h} = \sqrt{K_w K_a \over K_b}\] \[pH = 7 + {1 \over 2}(pK_a - pK_b)\]

Conclusion

  • For a salt of a weak acid and a weak base, the degree of hydrolysis and the pH are independent of the concentration of the solution. The pH depends only on pKa and pKb.

  • pH > 7 if pKa > pKb (the base is relatively stronger), pH < 7 if pKa < pKb, and pH ≈ 7 if pKa = pKb.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
