The pKa of acetic acid and pKb of ammonium hydroxide are 4.76 and 4.75 respectively. Calculate the pH of ammonium acetate solution.

\[pH = 7 + {1 \over 2}[pK_a - pK_b]\] \[pH = 7 + {1 \over 2}[4.76 - 4.75]\] \[pH = 7 + {1 \over 2}[0.01] = 7 + 0.005 = 7.005\]

Calculate the pH of a 0.1 M sodium acetate solution and its degree of hydrolysis. (Ka of acetic acid = 1.8 × 10-5)

\[K_h = {K_w \over K_a} = {10^{-14} \over 1.8 \times 10^{-5}} = 5.56 \times 10^{-10}\] \[h = \sqrt{K_h \over c} = \sqrt{5.56 \times 10^{-10} \over 0.1} = 7.45 \times 10^{-5}\] \[[OH^-] = ch = 0.1 \times 7.45 \times 10^{-5} = 7.45 \times 10^{-6}\ M\] \[pOH = 5.13,\ \ pH = 14 - 5.13 = 8.87\]

Check with the formula: pH = 7 + ½(4.74) + ½log(0.1) = 7 + 2.37 - 0.5 = 8.87.

Calculate the pH of a 0.1 M ammonium chloride solution. (Kb of NH4OH = 1.77 × 10-5)

\[pK_b = -log(1.77 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.75\] \[pH = 7 - {1 \over 2}pK_b - {1 \over 2}log\ c\] \[pH = 7 - {1 \over 2}(4.75) - {1 \over 2}log(0.1) = 7 - 2.375 + 0.5 = 5.12\]

The ionization constant of nitrous acid is 4.5 × 10-4. Calculate the pH of 0.04 M sodium nitrite solution and also its degree of hydrolysis.

NaNO2 is a salt of a weak acid and strong base, so NO2- hydrolyses:

\[NO_2^- + H_2O ⇌ HNO_2 + OH^-\] \[K_h = {K_w \over K_a} = {10^{-14} \over 4.5 \times 10^{-4}} = 2.22 \times 10^{-11}\] \[h = \sqrt{K_h \over c} = \sqrt{2.22 \times 10^{-11} \over 0.04} = 2.36 \times 10^{-5}\] \[[OH^-] = ch = 0.04 \times 2.36 \times 10^{-5} = 9.43 \times 10^{-7}\ M\] \[pOH = 6.03,\ \ pH = 14 - 6.03 = 7.97\]

A 0.02 M solution of pyridinium hydrochloride has pH = 3.44. Calculate the ionization constant of pyridine.

Pyridinium hydrochloride (C5H5NH+Cl-) is a salt of a weak base and strong acid. The cation hydrolyses:

\[C_5H_5NH^+ + H_2O ⇌ C_5H_5N + H_3O^+\] \[[H^+] = 10^{-3.44} = 3.63 \times 10^{-4}\ M\] \[K_h = {[H^+]^2 \over c} = {(3.63 \times 10^{-4})^2 \over 0.02} = 6.6 \times 10^{-6}\] \[K_b = {K_w \over K_h} = {10^{-14} \over 6.6 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-9}\]

Predict if the solutions of the following salts are neutral, acidic or basic: NaCl, KBr, NaCN, NH4NO3, NaNO2 and KF.

Salt Formed from Nature NaCl Strong acid (HCl) + strong base (NaOH) Neutral KBr Strong acid (HBr) + strong base (KOH) Neutral NaCN Weak acid (HCN) + strong base (NaOH) Basic NH4NO3 Strong acid (HNO3) + weak base (NH4OH) Acidic NaNO2 Weak acid (HNO2) + strong base (NaOH) Basic KF Weak acid (HF) + strong base (KOH) Basic

The ionization constant of chloroacetic acid is 1.35 × 10-3. What will be the pH of 0.1 M acid and its 0.1 M sodium salt solution?

0.1 M chloroacetic acid

\[[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a\ c} = \sqrt{1.35 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.1} = 1.16 \times 10^{-2}\ M\] \[pH = -log(1.16 \times 10^{-2}) = 1.94\]

(Here α ≈ 0.12; solving the full quadratic gives [H+] = 1.10 × 10-2 M and pH = 1.96.)

0.1 M sodium chloroacetate

The anion hydrolyses, giving a basic solution:

\[K_h = {K_w \over K_a} = {10^{-14} \over 1.35 \times 10^{-3}} = 7.41 \times 10^{-12}\] \[[OH^-] = \sqrt{K_h\ c} = \sqrt{7.41 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.1} = 8.61 \times 10^{-7}\ M\] \[pOH = 6.07,\ \ pH = 14 - 6.07 = 7.93\]

docs.title: Ionic Equilibrium | Introduction
docs.text:
Ionic equilibrium is the equilibrium established between the ions and the unionized molecules of a weak electrolyte in aqueous solution. Acids, bases and salts are electrolytes, so the study of ionic equilibrium is largely the study of how acids, bases and salts behave in water.

  • A simple example of an equilibrium involving only ions is:
\[Fe^{3+}_{(aq)} + SCN^-_{(aq)} ⇌ [Fe(SCN)]^{2+}_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: Electrolytes and Non-Electrolytes
docs.text:
• An aqueous solution of sugar does not conduct electricity, but a solution of common salt (NaCl) does. Its conductance also increases as more salt is dissolved.
  • Michael Faraday classified substances into two categories on the basis of their ability to conduct electricity in aqueous solution.

docs.title: 1. Electrolytes
docs.text: • Substances which conduct electricity in their aqueous solutions are called electrolytes. Example: NaCl, HCl, CH3COOH, NaOH.

docs.title: 2. Non-Electrolytes
docs.text:
• Substances which do not conduct electricity in their aqueous solutions are called non-electrolytes. Example: sugar, urea.

Faraday further divided electrolytes into strong and weak electrolytes.

docs.title: 3. Strong Electrolytes
docs.text:
• Strong electrolytes ionize almost completely (nearly 100%) on dissolution in water.
  • Example: An aqueous solution of NaCl contains only Na+ and Cl- ions. HCl is also completely ionized in water.

docs.title: 4. Weak Electrolytes
docs.text:
• Weak electrolytes are only partially ionized in water.
  • Example: An aqueous solution of acetic acid mainly contains unionized CH3COOH molecules and only a few CH3COO- and H+ ions (less than 5% ionization).
  • In a weak electrolyte, an equilibrium is set up between the ions and the unionized molecules. This is the ionic equilibrium.
\[CH_3COOH_{(aq)} ⇌ CH_3COO^-_{(aq)} + H^+_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: Why do ionic compounds dissolve in water?
docs.text:
• Solid NaCl is a cluster of Na+ and Cl- ions held together by electrostatic forces.
  • The electrostatic force between two charges is inversely proportional to the dielectric constant of the medium. Water has a very high dielectric constant of 80.
  • So, when NaCl is dissolved in water, the attraction between the ions is reduced by a factor of 80. The ions move freely in the solution and are kept apart by hydration with polar water molecules.
  • Both HCl and CH3COOH are polar covalent molecules, yet HCl is completely ionized while acetic acid is only partially ionized. The extent of ionization depends on the strength of the bond and the extent of solvation of the ions produced.

Dissociation and Ionization

  • Dissociation is the separation of ions that already exist in the solid solute, as in NaCl.

  • Ionization is the process in which a neutral molecule splits into charged ions in solution, as in HCl.

  • In this chapter, the two terms are used interchangeably.

docs.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
docs.text:
• Acids taste sour (the word comes from the Latin acidus, meaning sour), turn blue litmus red and liberate H2 on reacting with metals. Example: HCl in gastric juice, acetic acid in vinegar, citric and ascorbic acid in lemon, tartaric acid in tamarind.
  • Bases taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue. Example: washing soda.
  • When acids and bases react in the right proportion, they form salts. Example: NaCl, BaSO4, NaNO3.

docs.title: Arrhenius Concept of Acids and Bases
docs.text:
• According to Arrhenius, acids are substances that dissociate in water to give hydrogen ions, H+(aq), and bases are substances that produce hydroxyl ions, OH-(aq).
\[HX_{(aq)} → H^+_{(aq)} + X^-_{(aq)}\] \[HX_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} → H_3O^+_{(aq)} + X^-_{(aq)}\] \[MOH_{(aq)} → M^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: Hydronium and hydroxyl ions
docs.text:
• A bare proton, H+, is extremely small (about 10-15 m radius) and has an intense electric field. So it cannot exist freely in water.
  • It binds to a lone pair on the oxygen atom of a water molecule to give the trigonal pyramidal hydronium ion, H3O+. In this chapter, H+(aq) and H3O+(aq) mean the same thing, a hydrated proton.
  • In solution, H3O+ is further hydrated to species like H5O2+, H7O3+ and H9O4+. Similarly, OH- is hydrated to H3O2-, H5O3-, H7O4- etc.

docs.title: Limitations of Arrhenius concept
docs.text:
• It applies only to aqueous solutions.
  • It cannot explain the basic nature of substances like ammonia (NH3), which do not contain a hydroxyl group.

docs.title: Brönsted-Lowry Concept of Acids and Bases
docs.text:
• According to Brönsted and Lowry, an acid is a substance that can donate a proton (H+) and a base is a substance that can accept a proton. In short, acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors.

Dissolution of NH3 in water

\[NH_{3(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ NH^+_{4(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\] \[(Base)\ \ \ \ (Acid)\ \ \ \ (Conjugate\ acid)\ \ \ \ (Conjugate\ base)\]

  • Water donates a proton, so it acts as an acid. NH3 accepts a proton, so it acts as a base.

  • In the reverse reaction, NH4+ donates a proton to OH-. So NH4+ is a Brönsted acid and OH- is a Brönsted base.

docs.title: Conjugate acid-base pair
docs.text:
• An acid-base pair that differs only by one proton is called a conjugate acid-base pair.
  • A conjugate acid has one extra proton and a conjugate base has one less proton.
  • In the above example, OH- is the conjugate base of the acid H2O and NH4+ is the conjugate acid of the base NH3.
  • If a Brönsted acid is strong, its conjugate base is weak, and vice-versa.

Ionization of HCl in water

\[HCl_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + Cl^-_{(aq)}\] \[(Acid)\ \ \ \ (Base)\ \ \ \ (Conjugate\ acid)\ \ \ \ (Conjugate\ base)\]
  • Here water accepts a proton, so it acts as a base. Cl- is the conjugate base of HCl and H3O+ is the conjugate acid of H2O.

Conclusion

Water is amphoteric: it acts as a base towards HCl and as an acid towards NH3.

docs.title: Lewis Concept of Acids and Bases
docs.text:
• G.N. Lewis (1923) defined an acid as a species which accepts an electron pair and a base as a species which donates an electron pair.
  • For bases, the Lewis and Brönsted-Lowry concepts are nearly the same, because a base provides a lone pair in both cases.
  • For acids, the Lewis concept is much wider, since many Lewis acids have no proton at all. Example: BF3 has no proton but accepts a lone pair from NH3.
\[BF_3 + :NH_3 → BF_3:NH_3\]
  • Lewis acids: electron deficient species like BF3, AlCl3, Co3+, Mg2+, H+.
  • Lewis bases: species with a lone pair to donate, like H2O, NH3, OH-, F-.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What will be the conjugate bases for the following Brönsted acids: HF, H2SO4 and HCO3-?

A conjugate base has one proton less than the acid. So the conjugate bases are:

  • HF → F-

  • H2SO4 → HSO4-

  • HCO3- → CO32-

Write the conjugate acids for the following Brönsted bases: NH2-, NH3 and HCOO-.

A conjugate acid has one proton more than the base. So the conjugate acids are:

  • NH2- → NH3

  • NH3 → NH4+

  • HCOO- → HCOOH

The species H2O, HCO3-, HSO4- and NH3 can act both as Brönsted acids and bases. For each case give the corresponding conjugate acid and conjugate base.

Species Conjugate acid Conjugate base H2O H3O+ OH- HCO3- H2CO3 CO32- HSO4- H2SO4 SO42- NH3 NH4+ NH2-

Find the conjugate acid/base for the following species: HNO2, CN-, HClO4, F-, OH-, CO32- and S2-.

  • HNO2 is an acid, its conjugate base is NO2-.

  • CN- is a base, its conjugate acid is HCN.

  • HClO4 is an acid, its conjugate base is ClO4-.

  • F- is a base, its conjugate acid is HF.

  • OH- is a base, its conjugate acid is H2O (it can also act as an acid, with conjugate base O2-).

  • CO32- is a base, its conjugate acid is HCO3-.

  • S2- is a base, its conjugate acid is HS-.

Classify the following species into Lewis acids and Lewis bases and show how these act as such: (a) OH- (b) F- (c) H+ (d) BCl3

  • (a) OH- is a Lewis base, as it can donate an electron lone pair (:OH-).

  • (b) F- is a Lewis base, as it can donate any one of its four electron lone pairs.

  • (c) H+ is a Lewis acid, as it can accept a lone pair of electrons from bases like OH- and F-.

  • (d) BCl3 is a Lewis acid, as it can accept a lone pair of electrons from species like ammonia or amines.

Which of the following are Lewis acids? H2O, BF3, H+ and NH4+

  • BF3 and H+ are Lewis acids, as both can accept an electron pair.

  • NH4+ is also listed as a Lewis acid, since it can transfer H+ (an electron pair acceptor) to a base.

  • H2O has two lone pairs on oxygen and acts as a Lewis base.

docs.title: Ionic Equilibrium | Ionic Product of Water and pH
Ionic Equilibrium | Ionic Product of Water and pH
Strong and Weak Acids and Bases
docs.text:
• Acids like perchloric acid (HClO4), hydrochloric acid (HCl), hydrobromic acid (HBr), hydroiodic acid (HI), nitric acid (HNO3) and sulphuric acid (H2SO4) are strong acids, as they are almost completely dissociated in water and act as good proton donors.
  • Bases like LiOH, NaOH, KOH, CsOH and Ba(OH)2 are strong bases, as they are almost completely dissociated in water giving OH- ions.
  • In the Brönsted-Lowry sense, a strong acid is a good proton donor and a strong base is a good proton acceptor.
\[HA_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + A^-_{(aq)}\] \[(Acid)\ \ \ \ (Base)\ \ \ \ (Conjugate\ acid)\ \ \ \ (Conjugate\ base)\]
  • In the above equilibrium, HA and H3O+ compete to donate a proton. If HA is a stronger acid than H3O+, HA donates its proton and the solution mainly contains A- and H3O+.
  • The equilibrium always moves in the direction of formation of the weaker acid and weaker base, because the stronger acid donates a proton to the stronger base.

Conclusion

  • Strong acids have very weak conjugate bases. Example: ClO4-, Cl-, Br-, I-, NO3- and HSO4- are much weaker bases than H2O.

  • Weak acids have very strong conjugate bases. Example: NH2-, O2- and H- are very good proton acceptors and much stronger bases than H2O.

  • Weak acids like nitrous acid (HNO2), hydrofluoric acid (HF) and acetic acid (CH3COOH) are only partially dissociated. Their solutions mainly contain undissociated HA molecules.

docs.title: Acid-base indicators
docs.text:
• Some water-soluble organic compounds like phenolphthalein and bromothymol blue behave as weak acids. They show different colours in their acid form (HIn) and conjugate base form (In-).
\[HIn_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + In^-_{(aq)}\] \[(Colour\ A)\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (Colour\ B)\]
  • Such compounds are used as indicators in acid-base titrations and for finding H+ ion concentration.

docs.title: Ionic Product of Water (K<sub>w</sub>)
docs.text:
• Water can act both as an acid and a base. In pure water, one H2O molecule donates a proton (acid) and another accepts it (base). This is called self-ionization or auto-protolysis of water.
\[H_2O_{(l)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\] \[K = {[H_3O^+][OH^-] \over [H_2O]}\]
  • Water is a pure liquid, so its concentration remains constant and is included in the equilibrium constant. This gives a new constant Kw, called the ionic product of water.
\[K_w = [H^+][OH^-]\]
  • At 298 K, [H+] in pure water is found to be 1.0 × 10-7 M. Since water gives equal numbers of H+ and OH- ions, [OH-] = [H+] = 1.0 × 10-7 M.
\[K_w = (1.0 \times 10^{-7})^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\ M^2\ (at\ 298\ K)\]
  • Kw is an equilibrium constant, so it depends on temperature. Since ionization of water is endothermic, Kw increases with temperature.

docs.title: How much water is ionized?
docs.text:
\[[H_2O] = {1000\ g/L \over 18.0\ g/mol} = 55.55\ M\] \[Ratio\ of\ dissociated\ to\ undissociated\ water = {10^{-7} \over 55.55} = 1.8 \times 10^{-9}\]
  • So only about 2 in 109 water molecules are ionized, i.e., the equilibrium lies mainly towards undissociated water.

docs.title: Acidic, neutral and basic solutions
docs.text: Solution Condition pH at 298 K Acidic [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] > [OH<sup>-</sup>] pH < 7 Neutral [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>-</sup>] pH = 7 Basic [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] < [OH<sup>-</sup>] pH > 7

docs.title: The pH Scale
docs.text:
• The pH of a solution is defined as the negative logarithm (to base 10) of the activity of hydrogen ions, aH+.
  • In dilute solutions (< 0.01 M), activity of H+ is equal in magnitude to its molarity [H+]. Activity has no units.
\[a_{H^+} = {[H^+] \over mol\ L^{-1}}\] \[pH = -log\ a_{H^+} = -log[H^+]\] \[[H^+] = 10^{-pH}\]

Examples

  • An HCl solution with [H+] = 10-2 M has pH = 2.

  • A NaOH solution with [OH-] = 10-4 M has [H+] = 10-10 M, so pH = 10.

  • Pure water at 25°C has [H+] = 10-7 M, so pH = -log(10-7) = 7.

docs.title: Relation between pH and pOH
docs.text:
• Similarly, pOH = -log[OH-] and pKw = -log Kw. Taking negative log of Kw at 298 K:
\[K_w = [H_3O^+][OH^-] = 10^{-14}\] \[-log\ K_w = -log[H_3O^+] - log[OH^-] = -log\ 10^{-14}\] \[pK_w = pH + pOH = 14\]
  • Although Kw changes with temperature, the change in pH is small and is often ignored.
  • The pH scale is logarithmic. A change of 1 unit in pH means [H+] changes by a factor of 10. A change of 2 units means a factor of 100.

docs.title: Measurement of pH
docs.text:
• pH can be found roughly using pH paper, which shows different colours at different pH. pH paper with four strips can measure pH in the range 1–14 with an accuracy of about 0.5.
  • For greater accuracy, a pH meter is used. It measures the pH-dependent electrical potential of the solution to within 0.001.

docs.title: pH of some common substances
docs.text: Fluid pH Fluid pH Saturated solution of NaOH ~15 Black coffee 5.0 0.1 M NaOH solution 13 Tomato juice ~4.2 Lime water 10.5 Soft drinks and vinegar ~3.0 Milk of magnesia 10 Lemon juice ~2.2 Egg white, sea water 7.8 Gastric juice ~1.2 Human blood 7.4 1 M HCl solution ~0 Milk 6.8 Concentrated HCl ~-1.0 Human saliva 6.4

docs.title: pH of Strong Acids and Bases
docs.text:
• A strong acid or base is completely dissociated, so [H+] or [OH-] follows directly from its concentration and the number of H+/OH- it releases.
\[For\ strong\ acid:\ [H^+] = n \times C\] \[For\ strong\ base:\ [OH^-] = n \times C,\ \ pH = 14 - pOH\]

Where, n = number of H+ or OH- per formula unit and C = molar concentration.

  • For very dilute solutions (around 10-6 M or less), the H+ from ionization of water cannot be ignored (see the question on 10-8 M HCl below).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The concentration of hydrogen ion in a sample of soft drink is 3.8 × 10-3 M. What is its pH?

\[pH = -log(3.8 \times 10^{-3})\] \[pH = -\{log(3.8) + log(10^{-3})\} = -\{0.58 - 3.0\} = 2.42\]

Therefore, the pH of the soft drink is 2.42 and it is acidic.

Calculate pH of a 1.0 × 10-8 M solution of HCl.

  • Taking pH = -log(10-8) = 8 would be wrong, because an acid solution cannot be basic. In such a dilute solution, H3O+ from water must also be considered.
\[2H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)},\ \ K_w = 10^{-14}\]

Let x = [OH-] = [H3O+] from water. H3O+ comes from both HCl and water:

\[[H_3O^+] = 10^{-8} + x\] \[K_w = (10^{-8} + x)(x) = 10^{-14}\] \[x^2 + 10^{-8}x - 10^{-14} = 0\] \[[OH^-] = x = 9.5 \times 10^{-8}\ M\] \[pOH = 7.02,\ \ pH = 14 - 7.02 = 6.98\]

The pH of a sample of vinegar is 3.76. Calculate the concentration of hydrogen ion in it.

\[[H^+] = 10^{-pH} = 10^{-3.76}\] \[[H^+] = 1.74 \times 10^{-4}\ M\]

Assuming complete dissociation, calculate the pH of the following solutions: (a) 0.003 M HCl (b) 0.005 M NaOH (c) 0.002 M HBr (d) 0.002 M KOH

\[(a)\ [H^+] = 0.003\ M,\ pH = -log(3 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.52\] \[(b)\ [OH^-] = 0.005\ M,\ pOH = 2.30,\ pH = 14 - 2.30 = 11.70\] \[(c)\ [H^+] = 0.002\ M,\ pH = -log(2 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.70\] \[(d)\ [OH^-] = 0.002\ M,\ pOH = 2.70,\ pH = 14 - 2.70 = 11.30\]

Calculate the pH of the following solutions: (a) 2 g of TlOH dissolved in water to give 2 litre of solution. (b) 0.3 g of Ca(OH)2 dissolved in water to give 500 mL of solution. (c) 0.3 g of NaOH dissolved in water to give 200 mL of solution. (d) 1 mL of 13.6 M HCl is diluted with water to give 1 litre of solution.

(a) Molar mass of TlOH = 204.4 + 17 = 221.4 g/mol

\[[TlOH] = {2 \over 221.4 \times 2} = 4.52 \times 10^{-3}\ M = [OH^-]\] \[pOH = 2.35,\ \ pH = 14 - 2.35 = 11.65\]

(b) Molar mass of Ca(OH)2 = 74 g/mol. Each Ca(OH)2 gives 2 OH-.

\[[Ca(OH)_2] = {0.3 \over 74 \times 0.5} = 8.11 \times 10^{-3}\ M\] \[[OH^-] = 2 \times 8.11 \times 10^{-3} = 1.62 \times 10^{-2}\ M\] \[pOH = 1.79,\ \ pH = 12.21\]

(c) Molar mass of NaOH = 40 g/mol

\[[OH^-] = {0.3 \over 40 \times 0.2} = 0.0375\ M\] \[pOH = 1.43,\ \ pH = 12.57\]

(d) On dilution, M1V1 = M2V2

\[13.6 \times 1 = M_2 \times 1000,\ \ M_2 = 0.0136\ M = [H^+]\] \[pH = -log(0.0136) = 1.87\]

Calculate the hydrogen ion concentration in the following biological fluids whose pH are given below: (a) Human muscle-fluid, 6.83 (b) Human stomach fluid, 1.2 (c) Human blood, 7.38 (d) Human saliva, 6.4

Using [H+] = 10-pH:

\[(a)\ [H^+] = 10^{-6.83} = 1.48 \times 10^{-7}\ M\] \[(b)\ [H^+] = 10^{-1.2} = 6.3 \times 10^{-2}\ M\] \[(c)\ [H^+] = 10^{-7.38} = 4.17 \times 10^{-8}\ M\] \[(d)\ [H^+] = 10^{-6.4} = 3.98 \times 10^{-7}\ M\]

The pH of milk, black coffee, tomato juice, lemon juice and egg white are 6.8, 5.0, 4.2, 2.2 and 7.8 respectively. Calculate the corresponding hydrogen ion concentration in each.

\[Milk:\ [H^+] = 10^{-6.8} = 1.58 \times 10^{-7}\ M\] \[Black\ coffee:\ [H^+] = 10^{-5.0} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[Tomato\ juice:\ [H^+] = 10^{-4.2} = 6.31 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[Lemon\ juice:\ [H^+] = 10^{-2.2} = 6.31 \times 10^{-3}\ M\] \[Egg\ white:\ [H^+] = 10^{-7.8} = 1.58 \times 10^{-8}\ M\]

If 0.561 g of KOH is dissolved in water to give 200 mL of solution at 298 K, calculate the concentrations of potassium, hydrogen and hydroxyl ions. What is its pH?

\[Moles\ of\ KOH = {0.561 \over 56} = 0.01\ mol\] \[[KOH] = {0.01 \over 0.2} = 0.05\ M\] \[[K^+] = [OH^-] = 0.05\ M\] \[[H^+] = {K_w \over [OH^-]} = {10^{-14} \over 0.05} = 2.0 \times 10^{-13}\ M\] \[pH = -log(2.0 \times 10^{-13}) = 12.70\]

The solubility of Sr(OH)2 at 298 K is 19.23 g/L of solution. Calculate the concentrations of strontium and hydroxyl ions and the pH of the solution.

Molar mass of Sr(OH)2 = 87.6 + 34 = 121.6 g/mol

\[[Sr(OH)_2] = {19.23 \over 121.6} = 0.1581\ M\] \[Sr(OH)_2 → Sr^{2+} + 2OH^-\] \[[Sr^{2+}] = 0.1581\ M,\ \ [OH^-] = 2 \times 0.1581 = 0.3162\ M\] \[pOH = -log(0.3162) = 0.50,\ \ pH = 14 - 0.50 = 13.50\]

Ionic product of water at 310 K is 2.7 × 10-14. What is the pH of neutral water at this temperature?

For neutral water, [H+] = [OH-].

\[[H^+]^2 = K_w = 2.7 \times 10^{-14}\] \[[H^+] = 1.64 \times 10^{-7}\ M\] \[pH = -log(1.64 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.78\]

Note that the water is still neutral even though pH < 7, because [H+] = [OH-].

Calculate the pH of the resultant mixtures: (a) 10 mL of 0.2 M Ca(OH)2 + 25 mL of 0.1 M HCl (b) 10 mL of 0.01 M H2SO4 + 10 mL of 0.01 M Ca(OH)2 (c) 10 mL of 0.1 M H2SO4 + 10 mL of 0.1 M KOH

Find the millimoles of H+ and OH- (millimoles = M × V in mL), neutralize, and divide the excess by total volume.

(a) Ca(OH)2 gives 2 OH-:

\[mmol\ OH^- = 2 \times 0.2 \times 10 = 4,\ \ mmol\ H^+ = 0.1 \times 25 = 2.5\] \[Excess\ OH^- = 1.5\ mmol\ in\ 35\ mL,\ \ [OH^-] = {1.5 \over 35} = 0.0429\ M\] \[pOH = 1.37,\ \ pH = 12.63\]

(b) H2SO4 gives 2 H+:

\[mmol\ H^+ = 2 \times 0.01 \times 10 = 0.2,\ \ mmol\ OH^- = 2 \times 0.01 \times 10 = 0.2\]

Complete neutralization, so pH = 7.00.

(c)

\[mmol\ H^+ = 2 \times 0.1 \times 10 = 2,\ \ mmol\ OH^- = 0.1 \times 10 = 1\] \[Excess\ H^+ = 1\ mmol\ in\ 20\ mL,\ \ [H^+] = 0.05\ M\] \[pH = -log(0.05) = 1.30\]

docs.title: Ionic Equilibrium | Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
Ionic Equilibrium | Ionization of Weak Acids and Bases
docs.text: The equilibrium constant for the ionization of a weak acid is called its ionization constant, Ka, and for a weak base is called the base ionization constant, Kb. These constants tell us how strong a weak acid or base is.

docs.title: Ionization Constant of Weak Acids (K<sub>a</sub>)
docs.text:
• Consider a weak acid HX that is partially ionized in water. Let c be its initial concentration and α the degree of ionization (the fraction of HX ionized).
\[HX_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + X^-_{(aq)}\] \[Initial\ concentration\ (M):\ \ c\ \ \ \ \ \ 0\ \ \ \ \ \ 0\] \[Change\ (M):\ \ -cα\ \ \ \ \ \ +cα\ \ \ \ \ \ +cα\] \[Equilibrium\ concentration\ (M):\ \ c - cα\ \ \ \ \ \ cα\ \ \ \ \ \ cα\]
  • The equilibrium constant for this acid dissociation is:
\[K_a = {[H^+][X^-] \over [HX]}\] \[K_a = {c^2α^2 \over c(1-α)} = {cα^2 \over 1-α}\]
  • Ka is called the dissociation or ionization constant of the acid HX.
  • At a given temperature, Ka is a measure of the strength of the acid. The larger the value of Ka, the stronger the acid.
  • Ka is a dimensionless quantity, since the standard state concentration of all species is taken as 1 M.
  • The pH idea is extended to Ka as well:
\[pK_a = -log\ K_a\]
  • A larger Ka means a smaller pKa. So, the smaller the pKa, the stronger the acid.

docs.title: Ostwald's dilution law (approximation)
docs.text:
• For weak acids, α is usually very small, so 1 - α ≈ 1. Then:
\[K_a = cα^2\ \ \ \ or\ \ \ \ α = \sqrt{K_a \over c}\] \[[H^+] = cα = \sqrt{K_a\ c}\] \[pH = {1 \over 2}(pK_a - log\ c)\]
  • So the degree of ionization of a weak electrolyte increases on dilution (as c decreases).
  • This approximation works well when α is less than about 5%. If α comes out larger, solve the full quadratic equation.

docs.title: Ionization constants of some weak acids (298 K)
docs.text: Acid K<sub>a</sub> Hydrofluoric acid (HF) 3.5 × 10<sup>-4</sup> Nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>) 4.5 × 10<sup>-4</sup> Formic acid (HCOOH) 1.8 × 10<sup>-4</sup> Niacin (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NCOOH) 1.5 × 10<sup>-5</sup> Acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) 1.74 × 10<sup>-5</sup> Benzoic acid (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH) 6.5 × 10<sup>-5</sup> Hypochlorous acid (HClO) 3.0 × 10<sup>-8</sup> Hydrocyanic acid (HCN) 4.9 × 10<sup>-10</sup> Phenol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH) 1.3 × 10<sup>-10</sup>

docs.title: Step-wise approach to find the pH of a weak electrolyte
docs.text:
Knowing Ka and the initial concentration c, we can find the concentration of all species, the degree of ionization and the pH:

  • Step 1: Identify the species present before dissociation as Brönsted-Lowry acids/bases.
  • Step 2: Write balanced equations for all possible reactions, including species acting both as acid and base (such as water).
  • Step 3: The reaction with the higher Ka is the primary reaction; the other is a subsidiary reaction.
  • Step 4: For the primary reaction, tabulate (a) initial concentration, (b) change on reaching equilibrium in terms of α, and (c) equilibrium concentration.
  • Step 5: Substitute the equilibrium concentrations in the Ka expression and solve for α.
  • Step 6: Calculate the concentration of each species.
  • Step 7: Calculate pH = -log[H3O+].

docs.title: Percent dissociation
docs.text:
• Another useful measure of the strength of a weak acid is percent dissociation:
\[Percent\ dissociation = {[HA]_{dissociated} \over [HA]_{initial}} \times 100\%\]

docs.title: Ionization Constant of Weak Bases (K<sub>b</sub>)
docs.text:
• A base MOH ionizes as:
\[MOH_{(aq)} ⇌ M^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\] \[K_b = {[M^+][OH^-] \over [MOH]}\]
  • A weak base ionizes only partially, just like a weak acid. Kb is called the base ionization constant.
  • If c is the initial concentration and α the degree of ionization:
\[K_b = {(cα)^2 \over c(1-α)} = {cα^2 \over 1-α}\] \[If\ α \ll 1:\ \ α = \sqrt{K_b \over c},\ \ [OH^-] = \sqrt{K_b\ c}\] \[pK_b = -log\ K_b\]
  • Many organic compounds like amines (derivatives of ammonia in which H atoms are replaced by other groups) are weak bases. Methylamine, codeine, quinine and nicotine are very weak bases due to their very small Kb.
\[NH_{3(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ NH^+_{4(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: Relation between K<sub>a</sub> and K<sub>b</sub>
docs.text:
• For a conjugate acid-base pair, Ka and Kb are related, so if one is known the other can be found. Consider NH4+ and NH3:
\[NH^+_{4(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + NH_{3(aq)},\ \ K_a = {[H_3O^+][NH_3] \over [NH_4^+]} = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}\] \[NH_{3(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ NH^+_{4(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)},\ \ K_b = {[NH_4^+][OH^-] \over [NH_3]} = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\] \[Net:\ 2H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)},\ \ K_w = [H_3O^+][OH^-] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\]
  • The net reaction is the sum of the two reactions, so its equilibrium constant is the product of the two constants:
\[K_a \times K_b = {[H_3O^+][NH_3] \over [NH_4^+]} \times {[NH_4^+][OH^-] \over [NH_3]} = [H_3O^+][OH^-] = K_w\] \[(5.6 \times 10^{-10}) \times (1.8 \times 10^{-5}) = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\]

Conclusion

  • The equilibrium constant for a net reaction obtained by adding two (or more) reactions equals the product of the equilibrium constants of the individual reactions: KNET = K1 × K2 × ...

  • For a conjugate acid-base pair:

\[K_a \times K_b = K_w\] \[pK_a + pK_b = pK_w = 14\ (at\ 298\ K)\]
  • A strong acid has a weak conjugate base and vice-versa.

docs.title: Alternative derivation
docs.text:
• Consider a general base B:
\[B_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ BH^+_{(aq)} + OH^-_{(aq)},\ \ K_b = {[BH^+][OH^-] \over [B]}\]

Multiplying and dividing by [H+]:

\[K_b = {[BH^+][OH^-][H^+] \over [B][H^+]} = [OH^-][H^+] \times {[BH^+] \over [B][H^+]} = {K_w \over K_a}\] \[∴\ K_a \times K_b = K_w\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The ionization constant of HF is 3.2 × 10-4. Calculate the degree of dissociation of HF in its 0.02 M solution. Calculate the concentration of all species present (H3O+, F- and HF) in the solution and its pH.

Possible proton transfer reactions:

\[(1)\ HF + H_2O ⇌ H_3O^+ + F^-,\ \ K_a = 3.2 \times 10^{-4}\] \[(2)\ H_2O + H_2O ⇌ H_3O^+ + OH^-,\ \ K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\]

As Ka >> Kw, reaction (1) is the principal reaction.

\[Initial\ (M):\ HF = 0.02,\ H_3O^+ = 0,\ F^- = 0\] \[Equilibrium\ (M):\ HF = 0.02 - 0.02α,\ H_3O^+ = 0.02α,\ F^- = 0.02α\] \[K_a = {(0.02α)^2 \over 0.02(1-α)} = {0.02α^2 \over 1-α} = 3.2 \times 10^{-4}\] \[α^2 + 1.6 \times 10^{-2}α - 1.6 \times 10^{-2} = 0\]

Solving, α = +0.12 or -0.12. The negative root is not acceptable, so α = 0.12.

\[[H_3O^+] = [F^-] = cα = 0.02 \times 0.12 = 2.4 \times 10^{-3}\ M\] \[[HF] = c(1-α) = 0.02(1 - 0.12) = 17.6 \times 10^{-3}\ M\] \[pH = -log(2.4 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.62\]

The pH of 0.1 M monobasic acid is 4.50. Calculate the concentration of species H+, A- and HA at equilibrium. Also, determine the value of Ka and pKa of the monobasic acid.

\[[H^+] = 10^{-pH} = 10^{-4.50} = 3.16 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[[H^+] = [A^-] = 3.16 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[[HA]_{eqlbm} = 0.1 - (3.16 \times 10^{-5}) ≈ 0.1\ M\] \[K_a = {[H^+][A^-] \over [HA]} = {(3.16 \times 10^{-5})^2 \over 0.1} = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\] \[pK_a = -log(10^{-8}) = 8\]

Calculate the pH of 0.08 M solution of hypochlorous acid, HOCl. The ionization constant of the acid is 2.5 × 10-5. Determine the percent dissociation of HOCl.

\[HOCl_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} ⇌ H_3O^+_{(aq)} + ClO^-_{(aq)}\] \[Equilibrium\ (M):\ HOCl = 0.08 - x,\ H_3O^+ = x,\ ClO^- = x\] \[K_a = {x^2 \over 0.08 - x} = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\]

As x << 0.08, 0.08 - x ≈ 0.08:

\[x^2 = 0.08 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-5} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\] \[x = [H^+] = 1.41 \times 10^{-3}\ M\] \[Percent\ dissociation = {1.41 \times 10^{-3} \over 0.08} \times 100 = 1.76\%\] \[pH = -log(1.41 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.85\]

The pH of 0.004 M hydrazine solution is 9.7. Calculate its ionization constant Kb and pKb.

\[NH_2NH_2 + H_2O ⇌ NH_2NH_3^+ + OH^-\]

From pH, find [H+], then [OH-] using Kw:

\[[H^+] = 10^{-9.7} = 2.0 \times 10^{-10}\ M\] \[[OH^-] = {K_w \over [H^+]} = {1 \times 10^{-14} \over 2.0 \times 10^{-10}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\ M\]

[NH2NH3+] = [OH-]. Both are very small, so the concentration of undissociated base ≈ 0.004 M.

\[K_b = {[NH_2NH_3^+][OH^-] \over [NH_2NH_2]} = {(5.0 \times 10^{-5})^2 \over 0.004} = 6.3 \times 10^{-7}\] \[pK_b = -log(6.3 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.20\]

Determine the degree of ionization and pH of a 0.05 M ammonia solution (Kb = 1.77 × 10-5). Also, calculate the ionization constant of the conjugate acid of ammonia.

\[NH_3 + H_2O ⇌ NH_4^+ + OH^-\] \[K_b = {0.05α^2 \over 1-α}\]

α is small, so 1 - α ≈ 1:

\[α = \sqrt{1.77 \times 10^{-5} \over 0.05} = 0.0188\] \[[OH^-] = cα = 0.05 \times 0.0188 = 9.4 \times 10^{-4}\ M\] \[[H^+] = {10^{-14} \over 9.4 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.06 \times 10^{-11}\ M\] \[pH = -log(1.06 \times 10^{-11}) = 10.97\]

For the conjugate acid NH4+:

\[K_a = {K_w \over K_b} = {10^{-14} \over 1.77 \times 10^{-5}} = 5.64 \times 10^{-10}\]

The ionization constant of HF, HCOOH and HCN at 298 K are 6.8 × 10-4, 1.8 × 10-4 and 4.8 × 10-9 respectively. Calculate the ionization constants of the corresponding conjugate base.

Using Kb = Kw/Ka:

\[F^-:\ K_b = {10^{-14} \over 6.8 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.47 \times 10^{-11}\] \[HCOO^-:\ K_b = {10^{-14} \over 1.8 \times 10^{-4}} = 5.56 \times 10^{-11}\] \[CN^-:\ K_b = {10^{-14} \over 4.8 \times 10^{-9}} = 2.08 \times 10^{-6}\]

The ionization constant of acetic acid is 1.74 × 10-5. Calculate the degree of dissociation of acetic acid in its 0.05 M solution. Calculate the concentration of acetate ion in the solution and its pH.

\[α = \sqrt{K_a \over c} = \sqrt{1.74 \times 10^{-5} \over 0.05} = 1.87 \times 10^{-2}\] \[[CH_3COO^-] = [H^+] = cα = 0.05 \times 1.87 \times 10^{-2} = 9.33 \times 10^{-4}\ M\] \[pH = -log(9.33 \times 10^{-4}) = 3.03\]

It has been found that the pH of a 0.01 M solution of an organic acid is 4.15. Calculate the concentration of the anion, the ionization constant of the acid and its pKa.

\[[H^+] = [A^-] = 10^{-4.15} = 7.08 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[K_a = {[H^+][A^-] \over [HA]} = {(7.08 \times 10^{-5})^2 \over 0.01 - 7.08 \times 10^{-5}} = 5.05 \times 10^{-7}\] \[pK_a = -log(5.05 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.30\]

The degree of ionization of a 0.1 M bromoacetic acid solution is 0.132. Calculate the pH of the solution and the pKa of bromoacetic acid.

\[[H^+] = cα = 0.1 \times 0.132 = 0.0132\ M\] \[pH = -log(0.0132) = 1.88\]

Here α is not small, so use the full expression:

\[K_a = {cα^2 \over 1-α} = {0.1 \times (0.132)^2 \over 1 - 0.132} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\] \[pK_a = -log(2.0 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.70\]

The pH of 0.005 M codeine (C18H21NO3) solution is 9.95. Calculate its ionization constant and pKb.

\[pOH = 14 - 9.95 = 4.05\] \[[OH^-] = 10^{-4.05} = 8.91 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[K_b = {[OH^-]^2 \over c} = {(8.91 \times 10^{-5})^2 \over 0.005} = 1.59 \times 10^{-6}\] \[pK_b = -log(1.59 \times 10^{-6}) = 5.80\]

What is the pH of 0.001 M aniline solution? The ionization constant of aniline is 4.27 × 10-10. Calculate the degree of ionization of aniline in the solution. Also calculate the ionization constant of the conjugate acid of aniline.

\[[OH^-] = \sqrt{K_b\ c} = \sqrt{4.27 \times 10^{-10} \times 0.001} = 6.53 \times 10^{-7}\ M\] \[α = {[OH^-] \over c} = {6.53 \times 10^{-7} \over 0.001} = 6.53 \times 10^{-4}\] \[pOH = 6.19,\ \ pH = 14 - 6.19 = 7.81\]

For the conjugate acid (anilinium ion, C6H5NH3+):

\[K_a = {K_w \over K_b} = {10^{-14} \over 4.27 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.34 \times 10^{-5}\]

The pH of 0.1 M solution of cyanic acid (HCNO) is 2.34. Calculate the ionization constant of the acid and its degree of ionization in the solution.

\[[H^+] = 10^{-2.34} = 4.57 \times 10^{-3}\ M\] \[K_a = {[H^+]^2 \over c} = {(4.57 \times 10^{-3})^2 \over 0.1} = 2.09 \times 10^{-4}\] \[α = {[H^+] \over c} = {4.57 \times 10^{-3} \over 0.1} = 0.0457\]

docs.title: Ionic Equilibrium | Polybasic Acids and Acid Strength
Ionic Equilibrium | Polybasic Acids and Acid Strength
Di- and Polybasic Acids
docs.text:
• Acids like oxalic acid, sulphuric acid and phosphoric acid have more than one ionizable proton per molecule. Such acids are known as polybasic or polyprotic acids.
  • A polybasic acid ionizes in steps, losing one proton at a time. Each step has its own ionization constant.
  • For a dibasic acid H2X:
\[H_2X_{(aq)} ⇌ H^+_{(aq)} + HX^-_{(aq)},\ \ K_{a_1} = {[H^+][HX^-] \over [H_2X]}\] \[HX^-_{(aq)} ⇌ H^+_{(aq)} + X^{2-}_{(aq)},\ \ K_{a_2} = {[H^+][X^{2-}] \over [HX^-]}\]
  • Ka1 and Ka2 are called the first and second ionization constants of H2X.
  • Similarly, a tribasic acid like H3PO4 has three ionization constants: Ka1, Ka2 and Ka3.

Ionization of phosphoric acid

\[H_3PO_4 ⇌ H^+ + H_2PO_4^-,\ \ K_{a_1} = 7.5 \times 10^{-3}\] \[H_2PO_4^- ⇌ H^+ + HPO_4^{2-},\ \ K_{a_2} = 6.2 \times 10^{-8}\] \[HPO_4^{2-} ⇌ H^+ + PO_4^{3-},\ \ K_{a_3} = 4.2 \times 10^{-13}\]
  • For a polybasic acid, the overall constant is the product of the step-wise constants: for H2X ⇌ 2H+ + X2-, K = Ka1 × Ka2.

docs.title: Why is K<sub>a<sub>1</sub></sub> > K<sub>a<sub>2</sub></sub> > K<sub>a<sub>3</sub></sub>?
docs.text:
• The higher order ionization constants are always smaller than the lower order ones.
  • This is because it is more difficult to remove a positively charged proton from a negative ion, due to electrostatic attraction.
  • Example: Removing a proton from uncharged H2CO3 is easier than removing one from negatively charged HCO3-. Similarly, removing a proton from doubly charged HPO42- is harder than from H2PO4-.

Conclusion

  • A solution of a diprotic acid contains a mixture of H2A, HA- and A2-.

  • Since Ka1 >> Ka2, the H3O+ in the solution comes mainly from the first dissociation step. The primary reaction is the dissociation of H2A.

  • For a weak diprotic acid, the concentration of the dianion is approximately equal to Ka2: [A2-] ≈ Ka2 (when no other acid is present).

docs.title: Factors Affecting Acid Strength
docs.text:
• Broadly, the extent of dissociation of an acid H-A depends on the strength and polarity of the H-A bond.
  • When the H-A bond strength decreases (less energy is needed to break it), HA becomes a stronger acid.
  • When the H-A bond becomes more polar (greater electronegativity difference between H and A), there is more charge separation, the bond breaks more easily and acidity increases.

docs.title: 1. Elements in the same group: bond strength decides
docs.text:
• Down a group, the size of A increases and the H-A bond strength decreases. So acid strength increases down the group.
  • Here bond strength is more important than polarity.
\[Size\ of\ A\ increases\ →\] \[HF \ll HCl \ll HBr \ll HI\] \[Acid\ strength\ increases\ →\]
  • Similarly, H2S is a stronger acid than H2O.

docs.title: 2. Elements in the same period: bond polarity decides
docs.text:
• Across a period, the electronegativity of A increases and the H-A bond becomes more polar. So acid strength increases across the period.
\[Electronegativity\ of\ A\ increases\ →\] \[CH_4 < NH_3 < H_2O < HF\] \[Acid\ strength\ increases\ →\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The first ionization constant of H2S is 9.1 × 10-8. Calculate the concentration of HS- ion in its 0.1 M solution. How will this concentration be affected if the solution is 0.1 M in HCl also? If the second dissociation constant of H2S is 1.2 × 10-13, calculate the concentration of S2- under both conditions.

(i) In 0.1 M H2S alone

\[H_2S ⇌ H^+ + HS^-,\ \ K_{a_1} = 9.1 \times 10^{-8}\]

Let [H+] = [HS-] = x. Since Ka1 is small, [H2S] ≈ 0.1 M.

\[K_{a_1} = {x^2 \over 0.1} = 9.1 \times 10^{-8}\] \[x = [HS^-] = \sqrt{9.1 \times 10^{-9}} = 9.54 \times 10^{-5}\ M\]

For the second step, [H+] ≈ [HS-], so they cancel:

\[K_{a_2} = {[H^+][S^{2-}] \over [HS^-]},\ \ [S^{2-}] = K_{a_2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-13}\ M\]

(ii) In presence of 0.1 M HCl

HCl is a strong acid, so [H+] = 0.1 M. The common ion H+ suppresses the ionization of H2S.

\[[HS^-] = {K_{a_1}[H_2S] \over [H^+]} = {9.1 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.1 \over 0.1} = 9.1 \times 10^{-8}\ M\]

For S2-, use the overall equilibrium H2S ⇌ 2H+ + S2-:

\[K_{a_1} \times K_{a_2} = {[H^+]^2[S^{2-}] \over [H_2S]}\] \[[S^{2-}] = {9.1 \times 10^{-8} \times 1.2 \times 10^{-13} \times 0.1 \over (0.1)^2} = 1.09 \times 10^{-19}\ M\]

So in 0.1 M HCl, [HS-] falls from 9.54 × 10-5 M to 9.1 × 10-8 M, and [S2-] falls from 1.2 × 10-13 M to 1.09 × 10-19 M.

Arrange HF, HCl, HBr and HI in increasing order of acid strength and explain.

\[HF < HCl < HBr < HI\]

These elements belong to the same group. Down the group the size of the halogen increases, so the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker. A weaker bond releases H+ more easily, so acid strength increases from HF to HI, even though bond polarity decreases.

Why is HF a stronger acid than H2O, while H2S is a stronger acid than H2O?

  • F and O are in the same period. F is more electronegative than O, so the H-F bond is more polar than the H-O bond. Hence HF is a stronger acid than H2O.

  • O and S are in the same group. S is larger than O, so the H-S bond is weaker than the H-O bond. Hence H2S is a stronger acid than H2O.

Why is the second ionization constant of carbonic acid (5.6 × 10-11) much smaller than its first ionization constant (4.3 × 10-7)?

In the first step, a proton is removed from the neutral H2CO3 molecule. In the second step, a proton must be removed from the negatively charged HCO3- ion. The negative charge holds the positive proton by electrostatic attraction, so the second ionization is much more difficult and Ka2 << Ka1.

docs.title: Solubility of Ionic Salts
docs.text:
• The solubility of ionic solids in water varies a great deal. Some (like calcium chloride) are so soluble that they are hygroscopic and absorb water vapour from the air. Others (like lithium fluoride) have so little solubility that they are commonly called insoluble.
  • Solubility mainly depends on the lattice enthalpy of the salt and the solvation enthalpy of its ions.
  • To dissolve a salt, the strong attractive forces between its ions (lattice enthalpy) must be overcome by ion-solvent interactions. The solvation enthalpy is always negative, i.e., energy is released.
  • In a non-polar (covalent) solvent, the solvation enthalpy is small and cannot overcome the lattice enthalpy. So ionic salts do not dissolve in non-polar solvents.

Conclusion

For a salt to dissolve in a solvent, its solvation enthalpy must be greater than its lattice enthalpy.

  • Each salt has a characteristic solubility which depends on temperature. Salts are classified as:
Category Type Solubility Category I Soluble Solubility > 0.1 M Category II Slightly soluble 0.01 M < Solubility < 0.1 M Category III Sparingly soluble Solubility < 0.01 M

docs.title: Solubility Product Constant (K<sub>sp</sub>)
docs.text:
• Consider solid barium sulphate in contact with its saturated aqueous solution. An equilibrium exists between the undissolved solid and its ions:
\[BaSO_{4(s)} ⇌ Ba^{2+}_{(aq)} + SO^{2-}_{4(aq)}\] \[K = {[Ba^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}] \over [BaSO_4]}\]
  • For a pure solid, the concentration remains constant, so it is included in the constant:
\[K_{sp} = K[BaSO_4] = [Ba^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]\]
  • Ksp is called the solubility product constant or simply solubility product.
  • For BaSO4, Ksp = 1.1 × 10-10 at 298 K. If its molar solubility is S, then [Ba2+] = [SO42-] = S:
\[1.1 \times 10^{-10} = (S)(S) = S^2\] \[S = 1.05 \times 10^{-5}\ mol\ L^{-1}\]

docs.title: Relation between solubility (S) and K<sub>sp</sub>
docs.text:
• A salt may give two or more ions with different charges. Example: zirconium phosphate, (Zr4+)3(PO43-)4, gives 3 Zr4+ and 4 PO43- ions. If its molar solubility is S:
\[[Zr^{4+}] = 3S,\ \ [PO_4^{3-}] = 4S\] \[K_{sp} = (3S)^3(4S)^4 = 6912\ S^7\] \[S = \left({K_{sp} \over 3^3 \times 4^4}\right)^{1/7} = \left({K_{sp} \over 6912}\right)^{1/7}\]
  • In general, for a salt MxXy with molar solubility S:
\[M_xX_{y(s)} ⇌ xM^{p+}_{(aq)} + yX^{q-}_{(aq)},\ \ (x \times p^+ = y \times q^-)\] \[K_{sp} = [M^{p+}]^x[X^{q-}]^y = (xS)^x(yS)^y = x^x\ y^y\ S^{(x+y)}\] \[S = \left({K_{sp} \over x^x\ y^y}\right)^{1/(x+y)}\] Salt type Example Ksp AB AgCl, BaSO4 S2 AB2 or A2B CaF2, Ag2CrO4 4S3 AB3 Fe(OH)3, Al(OH)3 27S4 A2B3 A2X3 108S5 A3B4 Zr3(PO4)4 6912S7

docs.title: Ionic product (Q<sub>sp</sub>) and precipitation
docs.text:
• When the concentrations are not equilibrium concentrations, the same product is called the ionic product, Qsp (it is the reaction quotient for the dissolution).
  • At equilibrium (saturated solution), Ksp = Qsp. Otherwise, comparing Qsp with Ksp tells us whether precipitation or dissolution will occur:

Conclusion

  • Qsp > Ksp: the solution is supersaturated and precipitation occurs.

  • Qsp = Ksp: the solution is saturated, at equilibrium.

  • Qsp < Ksp: the solution is unsaturated, more salt can dissolve and no precipitate forms.

docs.title: Common Ion Effect on Solubility of Ionic Salts
docs.text:
• By Le Chatelier's principle, if the concentration of one of the ions is increased, it combines with the oppositely charged ion and some salt precipitates until once again Ksp = Qsp.
  • Similarly, if the concentration of one of the ions is decreased, more salt dissolves until Ksp = Qsp.
  • So the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt decreases in presence of a common ion.

Applications

  • Purification of common salt: When HCl gas is passed through a saturated solution of NaCl, pure NaCl precipitates due to the increased concentration (activity) of Cl- from HCl. Soluble impurities like sodium and magnesium sulphates stay in solution. (For soluble salts like NaCl, activities are used instead of molarities in Qsp.)

  • Gravimetric analysis: The common ion effect is used for almost complete precipitation of an ion as its sparingly soluble salt. Example: silver as AgCl, ferric ion as its hydroxide (hydrated ferric oxide) and barium as BaSO4.

docs.title: Effect of pH on Solubility
docs.text:
• The solubility of salts of weak acids (like phosphates) increases at lower pH. At lower pH, the anion X- gets protonated to HX, which lowers [X-]. To restore Ksp = Qsp, more salt dissolves.
  • Two equilibria must be satisfied together:
\[K_{sp} = [M^+][X^-]\] \[HX_{(aq)} ⇌ H^+_{(aq)} + X^-_{(aq)},\ \ K_a = {[H^+][X^-] \over [HX]}\] \[{[X^-] \over [HX]} = {K_a \over [H^+]}\]

Taking inverse and adding 1 on both sides:

\[{[HX] \over [X^-]} + 1 = {[H^+] \over K_a} + 1\] \[{[HX] + [X^-] \over [X^-]} = {[H^+] + K_a \over K_a}\]

Taking inverse again, the fraction of the dissolved anion present as X- is:

\[f = {[X^-] \over [X^-] + [HX]} = {K_a \over K_a + [H^+]}\]
  • If S is the solubility of the salt at a given pH, then [M+] = S and [X-] = fS:
\[K_{sp} = [S][fS] = S^2 \left({K_a \over K_a + [H^+]}\right)\] \[S = \sqrt{K_{sp}\left({[H^+] + K_a \over K_a}\right)}\]
  • The fraction f decreases as pH decreases. So, solubility S increases with increase in [H+], i.e., with decrease in pH.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the solubility of A2X3 in pure water, assuming that neither kind of ion reacts with water. The solubility product of A2X3, Ksp = 1.1 × 10-23.

\[A_2X_3 → 2A^{3+} + 3X^{2-}\]

If S is the solubility, [A3+] = 2S and [X2-] = 3S.

\[K_{sp} = [A^{3+}]^2[X^{2-}]^3 = (2S)^2(3S)^3 = 108S^5 = 1.1 \times 10^{-23}\] \[S^5 = 1.0 \times 10^{-25}\] \[S = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}\ mol/L\]

The values of Ksp of two sparingly soluble salts Ni(OH)2 and AgCN are 2.0 × 10-15 and 6 × 10-17 respectively. Which salt is more soluble? Explain.

\[AgCN ⇌ Ag^+ + CN^-,\ \ K_{sp} = [Ag^+][CN^-] = 6 \times 10^{-17}\]

Let [Ag+] = [CN-] = S1:

\[S_1^2 = 6 \times 10^{-17},\ \ S_1 = 7.8 \times 10^{-9}\ M\] \[Ni(OH)_2 ⇌ Ni^{2+} + 2OH^-,\ \ K_{sp} = [Ni^{2+}][OH^-]^2 = 2 \times 10^{-15}\]

Let [Ni2+] = S2, then [OH-] = 2S2:

\[(S_2)(2S_2)^2 = 4S_2^3 = 2 \times 10^{-15}\] \[S_2 = 7.9 \times 10^{-6}\ M\]

S2 > S1, so Ni(OH)2 is more soluble than AgCN. Note that we compare solubilities, not Ksp values directly, since the salts are of different types.

Calculate the molar solubility of Ni(OH)2 in 0.10 M NaOH. The ionic product of Ni(OH)2 is 2.0 × 10-15.

Let the solubility of Ni(OH)2 be S. It gives S mol/L of Ni2+ and 2S mol/L of OH-, but the solution already has 0.10 mol/L of OH- from NaOH.

\[[OH^-] = (0.10 + 2S)\ mol/L\] \[K_{sp} = [Ni^{2+}][OH^-]^2 = (S)(0.10 + 2S)^2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-15}\]

As Ksp is small, 2S << 0.10, so (0.10 + 2S) ≈ 0.10:

\[2.0 \times 10^{-15} = S(0.10)^2\] \[S = 2.0 \times 10^{-13}\ M = [Ni^{2+}]\]

Compare this with 7.9 × 10-6 M in pure water: the common ion OH- reduces the solubility enormously.

Determine the solubilities of silver chromate, barium chromate, ferric hydroxide, lead chloride and mercurous iodide at 298 K from their solubility product constants. Determine also the molarities of individual ions.

Silver chromate, Ag2CrO4 ⇌ 2Ag+ + CrO42-, Ksp = 1.1 × 10-12

\[4S^3 = 1.1 \times 10^{-12},\ \ S = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[[Ag^+] = 2S = 1.30 \times 10^{-4}\ M,\ \ [CrO_4^{2-}] = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}\ M\]

Barium chromate, BaCrO4 ⇌ Ba2+ + CrO42-, Ksp = 1.2 × 10-10

\[S^2 = 1.2 \times 10^{-10},\ \ S = 1.1 \times 10^{-5}\ M = [Ba^{2+}] = [CrO_4^{2-}]\]

Ferric hydroxide, Fe(OH)3 ⇌ Fe3+ + 3OH-, Ksp = 1.0 × 10-38

\[(S)(3S)^3 = 27S^4 = 1.0 \times 10^{-38},\ \ S = 1.39 \times 10^{-10}\ M\] \[[Fe^{3+}] = 1.39 \times 10^{-10}\ M,\ \ [OH^-] = 3S = 4.17 \times 10^{-10}\ M\]

Lead chloride, PbCl2 ⇌ Pb2+ + 2Cl-, Ksp = 1.6 × 10-5

\[4S^3 = 1.6 \times 10^{-5},\ \ S = 1.59 \times 10^{-2}\ M\] \[[Pb^{2+}] = 1.59 \times 10^{-2}\ M,\ \ [Cl^-] = 3.18 \times 10^{-2}\ M\]

Mercurous iodide, Hg2I2 ⇌ Hg22+ + 2I-, Ksp = 4.5 × 10-29

\[4S^3 = 4.5 \times 10^{-29},\ \ S = 2.24 \times 10^{-10}\ M\] \[[Hg_2^{2+}] = 2.24 \times 10^{-10}\ M,\ \ [I^-] = 4.48 \times 10^{-10}\ M\]

The solubility product constant of Ag2CrO4 and AgBr are 1.1 × 10-12 and 5.0 × 10-13 respectively. Calculate the ratio of the molarities of their saturated solutions.

\[Ag_2CrO_4:\ 4S_1^3 = 1.1 \times 10^{-12},\ \ S_1 = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}\ M\] \[AgBr:\ S_2^2 = 5.0 \times 10^{-13},\ \ S_2 = 7.07 \times 10^{-7}\ M\] \[{S_1 \over S_2} = {6.5 \times 10^{-5} \over 7.07 \times 10^{-7}} = 91.9\]

Silver chromate is about 92 times more soluble, even though its Ksp is only about twice that of AgBr, because the two salts are of different types.

Equal volumes of 0.002 M solutions of sodium iodate and cupric chlorate are mixed together. Will it lead to precipitation of copper iodate? (For cupric iodate Ksp = 7.4 × 10-8)

On mixing equal volumes, each concentration is halved:

\[[Cu^{2+}] = [IO_3^-] = 0.001\ M\] \[Cu(IO_3)_2 ⇌ Cu^{2+} + 2IO_3^-\] \[Q_{sp} = [Cu^{2+}][IO_3^-]^2 = (10^{-3})(10^{-3})^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-9}\]

Qsp (1.0 × 10-9) < Ksp (7.4 × 10-8), so no precipitate of copper iodate is formed.

The ionization constant of benzoic acid is 6.46 × 10-5 and Ksp for silver benzoate is 2.5 × 10-13. How many times is silver benzoate more soluble in a buffer of pH 3.19 compared to its solubility in pure water?

In pure water (benzoate hydrolysis neglected):

\[S_0 = \sqrt{K_{sp}}\]

In the buffer:

\[[H^+] = 10^{-3.19} = 6.46 \times 10^{-4}\ M\] \[S = \sqrt{K_{sp}\left({[H^+] + K_a \over K_a}\right)}\] \[{S \over S_0} = \sqrt{[H^+] + K_a \over K_a} = \sqrt{6.46 \times 10^{-4} + 6.46 \times 10^{-5} \over 6.46 \times 10^{-5}} = \sqrt{11} = 3.32\]

Silver benzoate is about 3.32 times more soluble in the buffer of pH 3.19.

What is the maximum concentration of equimolar solutions of ferrous sulphate and sodium sulphide so that when mixed in equal volumes, there is no precipitation of iron sulphide? (For iron sulphide, Ksp = 6.3 × 10-18)

Let the concentration of each solution be c. After mixing equal volumes, [Fe2+] = [S2-] = c/2. For no precipitation, Qsp must not exceed Ksp:

\[\left({c \over 2}\right)^2 = 6.3 \times 10^{-18}\] \[{c \over 2} = 2.5 \times 10^{-9}\ M\]

So the concentration of each ion in the mixture can be at most 2.5 × 10-9 M, i.e., each original solution can be at most 5.0 × 10-9 M.

What is the minimum volume of water required to dissolve 1 g of calcium sulphate at 298 K? (For calcium sulphate, Ksp is 9.1 × 10-6)

\[CaSO_4 ⇌ Ca^{2+} + SO_4^{2-},\ \ S^2 = 9.1 \times 10^{-6}\] \[S = 3.02 \times 10^{-3}\ mol/L\]

Molar mass of CaSO4 = 136 g/mol

\[Solubility\ in\ g/L = 3.02 \times 10^{-3} \times 136 = 0.41\ g/L\] \[Volume\ required\ for\ 1\ g = {1 \over 0.41} = 2.44\ L\]

The concentration of sulphide ion in 0.1 M HCl solution saturated with hydrogen sulphide is 1.0 × 10-19 M. If 10 mL of this is added to 5 mL of 0.04 M solution of the following: FeSO4, MnCl2, ZnCl2 and CdCl2, in which of these solutions precipitation will take place?

Total volume after mixing = 15 mL.

\[[S^{2-}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-19} \times {10 \over 15} = 6.67 \times 10^{-20}\ M\] \[[M^{2+}] = 0.04 \times {5 \over 15} = 1.33 \times 10^{-2}\ M\] \[Q_{sp} = [M^{2+}][S^{2-}] = 1.33 \times 10^{-2} \times 6.67 \times 10^{-20} = 8.9 \times 10^{-22}\]

Compare Qsp with Ksp of each sulphide:

Sulphide Ksp Qsp > Ksp? FeS 6.3 × 10-18 No, no precipitate MnS 2.5 × 10-13 No, no precipitate ZnS 1.6 × 10-24 Yes, precipitate forms CdS 8.0 × 10-27 Yes, precipitate forms

So, using these Ksp values, precipitation takes place in the ZnCl2 and CdCl2 solutions. CdS, with the smallest Ksp, precipitates most readily.

docs.title: Mole Concept | Calculation of Number of Moles for an Ideal Gas
Mole Concept | Calculation of Number of Moles for an Ideal Gas
Ideal Gas Equation
docs.text:
Number of moles of an ideal gas can be calculated by ideal gas equation:

\(PV = nRT\)

Here, P = Pressure V = Volume R = Universal Gas Constant T = Temperature in Kelvin n = Number of moles

docs.title: Units of Pressure
docs.text:
• It should be remembered that the S.I. unit of pressure is Pascal (Pa).

Remember

  • \(1\ atm = 10^5\ Pa\)
  • \(1\ atm = 10^5\ N/m^2\)
  • \(1\ atm = 76\ cm\ of\ Hg_{(l)}\)
  • \(1\ atm = 760\ mm\ of\ Hg_{(l)}\)
  • \(1\ atm = 760\ torr\)
  • \(1\ atm ≈ 1\ bar\)

docs.title: Values of R in different units
docs.text:
Remember

  • \(R = 0.0821\ L\ atm\ mol^{-1}K^{-1}\)
  • \(R = 8.314\ J\ mol^{-1}K^{-1}\)
  • \(R = 2\ calorie\ mol^{-1}K^{-1}\)

Note

  • \(1\ calorie = 4.186\ Joules\)

docs.title: Units of Volume
docs.text:
• It should be remembered that the S.I unit of volume is m3.

Remember

  • \(1\ cm^3 = 1\ mL\)
  • \(1\ L = 10^3\ cm^3\)
  • \(1\ L = 10^{-3}\ m^3\)

docs.title: Volume Occupied by one mole of an Ideal Gas at STP
docs.text:
• STP stands for Standard Temperature and Pressure.
  • At STP, temperature is 273 K and pressure is 1 atm.
  • Using ideal gas equation, let us calculate the volume of one mole ideal gas at STP:
\[PV = nRT\] \[V = {nRT \over P}\] \[V = {{1 \times 0.0821 \times 273} \over {1}}\] \[V = 22.4 L\]
  • Hence, one mole of any ideal gas(NH3, N2, O2, CO2) will occupy 22.4 L at STP.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
An ideal nitrogen gas is kept in a container of 10 litres under 1.5 atm pressure at 300 K. Calculate (a) number of moles of nitrogen gas (b) mass of nitrogen gas. Molecular mass of nitrogen = 28 u.

(a) The number of moles of ideal nitrogen gas can be calculated by ideal gas equation:

\[PV = nRT\] \[1.5 \times 10 = n \times 0.0821 \times 300\] \[n = {{1.5 \times 10} \over {0.0821 \times 300}}\] \[n = {500 \over 821}\]

(b) The mass of nitrogen can be calculated by:

\[Mass = Number\ of\ moles \times molecular\ mass\] \[Mass\ of\ N_2\ gas = {500 \over 821} \times 28\ grams\] \[Mass\ of\ N_2\ gas = {1400 \over 821}\ grams\]

Calculate in 5.6 L ideal N2 gas at STP, (a) number of moles (b) mass.

(a) The number of moles of ideal nitrogen gas can be calculated by:

\[Moles = {5.6 \over 22.4}\] \[Moles = 0.25\ L\]

(b) The mass of nitrogen can be calculated by:

\[Mass = Number\ of\ moles \times molecular\ mass\] \[Mass\ of\ N_2\ gas = 0.25 \times 28\ grams\] \[Mass\ of\ N_2\ gas = 7\ grams\]

docs.title: Calculation of Number of Moles of atoms
Atomic mass:
docs.text:
Atomic mass is defined as mass of one atom. Its unit is a.m.u or gram/mole. For example, if atomic mass of an atom is 'x' a.m.u or gram/mole, then it means that the mass of one mole of this atom is 'x' grams.

Example

Atomic mass of Ca = 40 a.m.u. It means mass of one mole Ca or 6.022 x 1023 Ca atoms is 40 grams.

Note

One mole is numerically equal to Avogadro constant or 6.022 x 1023.

  • We can either use unitary method to calculate the number of moles of atoms or we can use the below formula:
\[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ atoms = {Mass \over Atomic\ mass}\]

docs.title: Calculation of Number of Moles of molecules
Molecular mass:
docs.text:
Molecular mass is defined as mass of one molecule. Its unit is a.m.u or gram/mole. For example, if molecular mass of a molecule is 'x' a.m.u or gram/mole, then it means that the mass of one mole of this molecule is 'x' grams.

Example

Molecular mass of CaCO3 = 100 a.m.u. It means mass of one mole CaCO3 or 6.022 x 1023 CaCO3 molecules is 100 grams.

  • We can either use unitary method to calculate the number of moles of molecules or we can use the below formula:
\[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ molecules = {Mass \over Molecular\ mass}\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the number of moles in 10 grams of Ca. Atomic mass of Ca = 40 u.

For 5 gram of U238, find: (a) number of moles of U (b) Number of atoms of U.

(a) Number of moles of U can be calculated as:

\[238\ gram\ of\ U\ makes\ 1\ mole.\] \[1\ gram\ of\ U\ makes\ {1 \over 238} mole.\] \[5\ gram\ of\ U\ makes\ {1 \times 5 \over 238} moles = {5 \over 238} moles.\]

(b) Number of atoms of U can be calculated as:

\[238\ grams\ of\ U\ has\ 6.022 \times 10^{23} atoms.\] \[1\ gram\ of\ U\ has\ {6.022 \times 10^{23} \over 238} atoms.\] \[5\ gram\ of\ U\ has\ {6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 5 \over 238} = {1.27 \times 10^{22}} atoms.\]

For 10 grams of CaCO3, calculate:(a) Number of moles of CaCO3.(b) Number of molecules of CaCO3.(c) Number of moles of Ca.(d) Number of moles of C.(e) Number of moles of O.(f) Mass of Ca.(g) Mass of C.(h) Mass of O.

(a) Number of moles of CaCO3 is calculated as:

\[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ CaCO_3 = {Mass \over Molecular\ mass} = {10 \over 100} = 0.1\]

(b) Number of molecules of CaCO3 is calculated as:

\[Number\ of\ CaCO_3\ molecules = 0.1 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{22}\]

(c) Number of moles of Ca is calculated as:

\[ 1\ mole\ of\ CaCO_3\ contains\ 1\ mole\ Ca. \] \[∴\ 0.1\ mole\ of\ CaCO_3\ contains\ 0.1\ mole\ Ca.\]

(d) Number of moles of C is calculated as:

\[ 1\ mole\ of\ CaCO_3\ contains\ 1\ mole\ C. \] \[∴\ 0.1\ mole\ of\ CaCO_3\ contains\ 0.1\ mole\ C.\]

(e) Number of moles of O is calculated as:

\[ 1\ mole\ of\ CaCO_3\ contains\ 3\ moles\ O. \] \[∴\ 0.1\ mole\ of\ CaCO_3\ contains\ 0.3\ mole\ O.\]

(f) Mass of Ca is calculated as:

\[Mass\ of\ Ca = moles \times Atomic\ mass = 0.1 \times 40 = 4\ grams\]

(g) Mass of C is calculated as:

\[Mass\ of\ C = moles \times Atomic\ mass = 0.1 \times 12 = 1.2\ grams\]

(h) Mass of O is calculated as:

\[Mass\ of\ O = moles \times Atomic\ mass = 0.3 \times 16 = 4.8\ grams\]

Calculate the mass of 1000 molecules of CaCO3.

\[Mass\ of\ 1\ CaCO_3\ molecule = 100\ u\] \[Mass\ of\ 1000\ CaCO_3\ molecules = 1000 \times 100\ u\] \[Mass\ of\ 1000\ CaCO_3\ molecules = 1000 \times 100 \times {1.67 \times 10^{-24}}\] \[Mass\ of\ 1000\ CaCO_3\ molecules = 1.67 \times 10^{-19} grams\]

Calculate the mass of 1020 molecules of CaCO3.

\[Mass\ of\ 1\ CaCO_3\ molecule = 100\ u\] \[Mass\ of\ 10^{20}\ CaCO_3\ molecules = 10^{20} \times 100\ u\] \[Mass\ of\ 10^{20}\ CaCO_3\ molecules = 10^{20} \times 100 \times {1.67 \times 10^{-24}}\] \[Mass\ of\ 10^{20}\ CaCO_3\ molecules = 1.67 \times 10^{-2} grams\]

Calculate the mass 5.5 moles of CaCO3.

\[Mass\ of\ 5.5\ moles\ of\ CaCO_3 = Moles \times Molecular\ mass\] \[Mass\ of\ 5.5\ moles\ of\ CaCO_3 = 5.5 \times 100 = 550\ grams\]

Calculate the number of molecules in 5 grams of CaCO3.

\[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ CaCO_3 = Moles \times Molecular\ mass\] \[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ CaCO_3 = {5 \over 100} = 0.05 \] \[Number\ of\ molecules\ of\ CaCO_3 = 0.05 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\] \[Number\ of\ molecules\ of\ CaCO_3 = 3.011 \times 10^{22}\]

Calculate the number of moles of O atoms in 10 grams of O2.

\[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ O_2 = Moles \times Molecular\ mass\] \[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ O_2 = {10 \over 32} \] \[1\ mole\ of\ O_2\ contains\ 2\ moles\ of\ O\ atoms.\] \[ {10 \over 32}\ mole\ of\ O_2\ contains\ {2 \times 10 \over 32} = {5 \over 8}\ moles\ of\ O\ atoms.\]

Calculate the number of moles of 10 mL H2O. Density of H2O is 1 g/mL.

Density of H2O is 1 g/mL.

It means 1 mL of H2O has mass = 1 gram.

∴ 10 mL of of H2O has mass = 10 gram.

\[Moles\ of\ H_2O = {Mass \over Molecular\ mass}\] \[Moles\ of\ H_2O = {10 \over 18} = {5 \over 9} \]

Calculate the number of moles of 100 mL ethanol (CH3CH2OH), whose density is 0.9 g/mL. Molecular mass of ethanol = 46 u.

Density of ethanol is 0.9 g/mL.

It means 1 mL of ethanol has mass = 0.9 gram.

∴ 100 mL of of ethanol has mass = 100 x 0.9 = 90 gram.

\[Moles\ of\ ethanol = {Mass \over Molecular\ mass}\] \[Moles\ of\ ethanol = {90 \over 46} = {45 \over 23} \]

Hence, the number of moles of 100 mL ethanol (CH3CH2OH), whose density is 0.9 g/mL is \({45 \over 23}\)

docs.title: Method 1 (Unitary Method)
docs.text: \[1\ mole\ of\ Ca\ has\ mass = 40\ grams.\] \[Number\ of\ moles\ in\ 40\ grams\ Ca = 1\] \[Number\ of\ moles\ in\ 1\ gram\ Ca = {1 \over 40}\] \[Number\ of\ moles\ in\ 10\ grams\ Ca = {1 \times 10 \over 40} = {0.25\ moles}\]

docs.title: Method 2 (Using formula)
docs.text: \[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ Ca\ atoms = {Mass \over Atomic\ mass}\] \[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ Ca\ atoms = {10\ grams \over 40\ grams/mole}\] \[Number\ of\ moles\ of\ Ca\ atoms = 0.25\ moles\]

docs.title: Mole Concept | Concentration Terms
docs.text:
• Concentration terms are used to signify the amount of solute dissolved in a solvent.
  • Concentration does not change on taking out a part of the solution. For example, if the concentration of 10 L of solution is 'c', then the concentration of same 100 mL solution will also be 'c'.
  • Solute + Solvent = Solution. In a solution, solute is in lesser quantity and solvent is in higher quantity.

docs.title: 1. Molarity
docs.text:
• Molarity is defined as the number of moles of solute dissolved per litre of the solution.
  • It is denoted by 'M' and its unit is moles/L.
  • If the molarity of a solution is 3 moles/L, then we say that the solution is 3 molar (3 M).
\[Molarity = {Moles\ of\ solute \over Volume\ of\ solution\ in\ L}\]
  • Since volume changes with the change in temperature, therefore, molarity is temperature dependent.

docs.title: 2. Grams Per Litre
docs.text:
• It is defined as the grams of solute dissolved per litre of the solution.
  • It is denoted by 'g/L' and its unit is g/L.
\[g/L = {Mass\ of\ solute\ in\ grams \over Volume\ of\ solution\ in\ L}\]
  • Since volume changes with the change in temperature, therefore, g/L is temperature dependent.

docs.title: 3. Molality
docs.text:
• Molality is defined as the number of moles of solute dissolved per kilogram of the solvent.
  • It is denoted by 'm' and its unit is moles/Kg.
  • If the molality of a solution is 3 moles/Kg, then we say that the solution is 3 molal (3 m).
\[Molality = {Moles\ of\ solute \over Mass\ of\ solvent\ in\ Kg}\]
  • Since moles and mass both are independent of temperature, therefore, molality is temperature independent.

docs.title: 4.Mole Fraction
docs.text:
• Let us consider a solution/mixture consisting of two components: A and B. Mole fractions of A and B are defined as:
\[Χ_A = {n_A \over n_A + n_B}\] \[Χ_B = {n_B \over n_A + n_B}\]

Here, nA = moles of A, nB = moles of B

  • It is worth noting that:
\[Χ_A + Χ_B = 1\]
  • Similarly, let us consider a mixture consisting of 'n' components: 1, 2, 3, ...i, ... n. Mole fraction of ith component can be defined as:
\[Χ_i = {n_i \over n_1 + n_2 + n_3 + .... + n_n}\] \[Χ_1 + Χ_2 + Χ_3 + ... +\ Χ_i\ + ... + Χ_n = 1\]
  • Mole fraction is a unitless quantity.
  • Mole fraction is temperature independent because mole does not depend on temperature.

docs.title: 5. Parts per million and Parts per billion
docs.text:
• Parts per million (ppm) is defined as:
\[ppm = {Mass\ of\ solute \times 10^6 \over Mass\ of\ solution}\]
  • Parts per billion (ppb) is defined as:
\[ppb = {Mass\ of\ solute \times 10^9 \over Mass\ of\ solution}\]
  • Both ppm and ppb are unitless quantities.
  • Both ppm and ppb are temperature independent because mass does not depend on temperature.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
A 1M H2SO4 solution is taken whose density is 1.1 g/mL. Calculate its molality.

\[Molarity\ of\ H_2SO_4\ solution = 1\ M\] \[Let\ the\ volume\ of\ solution\ be\ 1\ L.\] \[Then,\ the\ moles\ of\ solute(H_2SO_4) = 1\ mole\] \[∴ Mass\ of\ solute(H_2SO_4) = 1\times 98 = 98 grams\] \[Density\ of\ solution = 1.1\ g/mL.\] \[Mass\ of\ solution = 1.1 \times 1000 = 1100\ g\] \[Mass\ of\ solvent = Mass\ of\ solution - Mass\ of\ solute\] \[Mass\ of\ solvent = 1100 - 98 = 1002\ g = 1.002\ Kg\] \[Molality = {Moles\ of\ solute \over Mass\ of\ solvent\ in\ Kg}\] \[Molality = {1 \over 1.002} = {500 \over 501}\]

Two solutions of 100 mL and 200 mL are taken. 100 mL solution containing NaCl has the molarity of 0.2 M while 200 mL solution containing CaCl2 has molarity of 0.5 M. The two solutions are mixed in a beaker and an additional 100 mL water is added to it. Calculate molarity of Cl- ions.

  • For solution 1:
\[Moles\ of\ NaCl = M \times V\] \[Moles\ of\ NaCl = 0.2 \times 100 \times 10^{-3} = 0.02\] \[Moles\ of\ Cl^- = 0.02\]
  • For solution 2:
\[Moles\ of\ CaCl_2 = M \times V\] \[Moles\ of\ CaCl_2 = 0.5 \times 200 \times 10^{-3} = 0.1\] \[Moles\ of\ Cl^- = 2 \times 0.1 = 0.2\]
  • Total moles of Cl- ions:
\[Total\ moles\ of\ Cl^- = 0.02 + 0.2 = 0.22\]
  • Total volume of solution:
\[Total\ volume\ of\ solution = 100 + 200 + 100 = 400\ mL = 0.4\ L\]
  • Molarity of Cl- ions:
\[Molarity\ of\ Cl^- = {0.22 \over 0.4} = 0.54\ M\]

5 M HCl solution is given from which x mL is taken out in a container. Water is added to it such that volume of solution becomes 5 L and molarity becomes 1.5 mL. Find x.

\[Initial\ moles\ of\ HCl\ taken\ out = Final\ moles\ of HCl\ when\ water\ is\ added\] \[5 \times x \times 10^{-3} = 1.5 \times 5\] \[x = 1500 mL\]

docs.title: Mole Concept | Empirical and Molecular Formula
Mole Concept | Empirical and Molecular Formula
Mass Percentage or Percentage by Mass
docs.text:
• Mass percentage represents the relative quantities of each element in a compound.
  • Mass percentage of an element in the compound can be calculated by:
\[Mass\ Percentage = {Mass\ of\ element \times 100 \over Mass\ of\ compound}\]

Example: Let us calculate mass percentage of CaCO3

Please note that any amount of CaCO3, be it 1 molecule or 100 g or 1 mole or 1000 moles, will contain elements having same mass percentages.

Let us take 1 mole of CaCO3.

\[Mass\ of\ 1\ mole\ CaCO_3 = 100\ g\]

Since, 1 mole CaCO3 contains 1 mole Ca, 1 mole C and 3 moles O:

\[Mass\ of\ 1\ mole\ Ca = 40\ g\] \[Mass\ of\ 1\ mole\ C = 12\ g\] \[Mass\ of\ 3\ moles\ O = 48\ g\] \[Mass\ percentage\ of\ Ca = {40 \times 100 \over 100} = 40\] \[Mass\ percentage\ of\ C = {12 \times 100 \over 100} = 12\] \[Mass\ percentage\ of\ O = {48 \times 100 \over 100} = 48\]

docs.title: Molecular and Empirical Formula
docs.text:
• Molecular formula gives the number of each atom in a single molecule of a compound whereas empirical formula gives the simplest ratio of each atom in a single molecule of the compound.
  • Relation between molecular formula and empirical formula can be described as:
\[Molecular\ formula = (Empirical\ formula)_n\]

Example

Let us consider a compound whose molecular formula is C4H10O2. Then, its empirical formula will be C2H5O.

  • Mass percentage of each element in the compound will be same in both empirical and molecular formula.

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
An organic compound having mass percentage of C = 53.33%, mass percentage of H = 11.11%, mass percentage of O = 35.56%. Molecular weight of the organic compound is 90 g/mole. Find its empirical formula and molecular formula.

Let 100 g of that organic compound is taken.

\[Moles\ of\ C = {53.33 \over 12}\] \[Moles\ of\ H = {11.11 \over 1}\] \[Moles\ of\ O = {35.56 \over 16}\] \[Simplest\ ratio\ of\ moles\ of\ C,\ H,\ and\ O = {53.33 \over 12} : {11.11 \over 1} : {35.56 \over 16}\] \[∴ Simplest\ ratio = 2:5:1\]

Hence, the empirical formula is C2H5O.

Let the molecular mass of compound be (C2H5O)n.

\[Molecular\ mass = 12 \times 2n + 1 \times 5n + 16 \times n\] \[90 = 45n\] \[∴n = 2\] \[Hence,\ Molecular\ formula = (C_2H_5O)_n = (C_2H_5O)_2 = C_4H_{10}O_2\]

docs.title: Mole Concept | Introduction
docs.text:
Basic things to remember:

  • Mass of electron = 9.1 x 10-31 Kg
  • Mass of proton = 1.672 x 10-27 Kg
  • Mass of neutron = 1.674 x 10-27 Kg
  • Charge of electron = -1.6 x 10-19 Kg
  • Charge of proton = 1.6 x 10-19 Kg
  • Charge of neutron = 0

docs.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
docs.text:
Any atom can be represented by:

\[X_p^m\]

Here, p = Atomic number and m = Mass number

  • Atomic number represents the number of protons in an atom. If atomic number of two atoms are same, then they represent the same atom although they may be isotopes. For example, \(C_6^{12}\) and \(C_6^{14}\) both represent carbons and are isotopes of carbon.

  • Mass number represents the number of neutrons and protons (together called as nucleons) in an atom. Nucleons are present in the nucleus of an atom.

\[Mass\ number = Number\ of\ protons + Number\ of\ neutrons\]

  • For a neutral atom, number of protons is equal to number of electrons. For example, in \(Ca_{20}^{40}\) number of electrons = number of protons = 40-20 = 20.

  • Mass number and atomic number are dimensionless quantities since they represent numbers. So, atomic number and mass number have no unit.

  • Only nucleons account for the mass of atom. Due to very small value, the mass of electron is neglected while calculating mass of atom. In other words, mass of electron is negligible as compared to mass of proton or neutron.

\[ ∴ Mass\ of\ Cl = Mass\ of\ Cl^-\]
  • Mass of protons plus the mass of neutrons of an atom is always more than the atomic mass due to binding energy. Binding energy account for the stability of nucleus.

If Z = atomic number, mp = mass of proton, mn = mass of neutron, A = mass number, M = Mass of atom, then:

\[Zm_p + (A-Z) m_n = M + B.E \]

where, B.E = Binding energy of atom

docs.title: Mass of one atom
docs.text:
• To measure mass of an atom, a unit has been defined, which is known as atomic mass unit or a.m.u.
\[1\ a.m.u. = {1 \over 12} \times Mass\ of\ one\ C^{12}\ atom\]
  • We know that:
\[Mass\ of\ 6.022\times 10^{23}\ C^{12}\ atoms = 12\ g\] \[Mass\ of\ 1\ C^{12}\ atoms = {12\over 6.022\times 10^{23}} g\] \[Mass\ of\ 1\ C^{12}\ atoms = 1.99 \times 10^{23} g\]
  • Calculating atomic mass unit:
\[1\ a.m.u. = {1 \over 12} \times Mass\ of one\ C^{12} atom\] \[1\ a.m.u. = {1 \over 12} \times 1.99 \times 10^{-23} g\] \[1\ a.m.u = 1.67 \times 10^{-24} g\]
  • Atomic mass unit (a.m.u or u) is the standard unit relative to which mass of every atom can be measured. Thus, mass number is the relative number which says how many times an atom is heavier than \({1 \over 12} \times Mass\ of\ one\ C^{12} atom\).
  • Atomic mass unit (a.m.u or u) is used to measure mass of atom or masses comparable to mass of atoms.

Remember:

\[1\ a.m.u. = {1 \over 12} \times Mass\ of one\ C^{12} atom\] \[1\ a.m.u. = {1 \over 6.022 \times 10^{23}} g = {1 \over {N_A}} g\] \[1\ a.m.u = 1.67 \times 10^{-24} g\]

Here, NA = Avogadro Number = 6.022 x 1023

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
If mass of protons and neutrons are known, why do we not write: Mass of one C12 atom = 6 x Mass of proton + 6 x Mass of neutron?

It is because the sum of masses of all nucleons is greater than the actual mass of atom due to binding energy.

docs.title: Limiting Reagent
docs.text:
• Limiting reagent is the reactant which gets completely consumed in a chemical reaction. It limits the amount of products formed.
  • Limiting reagent does not refer to the reagent present in lesser quantity. Even the reagent present in larger quantity may act like limiting reagent.

docs.title: How to identify Limiting Reagent?
docs.text:
• Divide the number of moles of reactants by their respective stoichiometric coefficient. The lesser value will indicate that the reactant is limiting reagent.
  • After identifying limiting reagent, make all calculations with respect to limiting reagent only.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
For the given chemical reaction, find the mass of SO2 formed: S(10 g) + O2(10 g) → SO2

\[Moles\ of\ S = {10 \over 32}\] \[Moles\ of\ O_2 = {10 \over 32}\]

Dividing these moles by corresponding stoichiometric coefficient, we find that the values are equal for both S and O2. Hence, both are limiting reagents. Both S and O2 will be completely consumed to form SO2.

\[1\ mole\ of\ S\ forms\ 1\ mole\ of\ SO_2.\] \[{10 \over 32} moles\ of\ S\ forms\ {10 \over 32} moles\ of\ SO_2.\] \[Mass\ of\ SO_2 = {10 \over 32} \times 64 = 20\ g\]

For the given chemical reaction, find the mass of CaCl2 formed: Ca(10 g) + Cl2(10 g) → CaCl2

\[Moles\ of\ Ca = {10 \over 40}\] \[Moles\ of\ Cl_2 = {10 \over 71}\]

Dividing these moles by corresponding stoichiometric coefficient, we find that the value for both Cl2 is less. Hence, Cl2 is the limiting reagent.

\[1\ mole\ of\ Cl_2\ forms\ 1\ mole\ of\ CaCl_2.\] \[{10 \over 71} moles\ of\ Cl_2\ forms\ {10 \over 71} moles\ of\ CaCl_2.\] \[Mass\ of\ CaCl_2 = {10 \over 71} \times 111 = {1110 \over 71}\ g\]

For the given chemical reaction, find the mass of PCl5 formed:P4(10 g) + 10Cl2(10 g) → 4PCl5

\[Moles\ of\ P_4 = {10 \over 124}\] \[Moles\ of\ Cl_2 = {10 \over 71}\]

Dividing these moles by corresponding stoichiometric coefficient, we find that the value for both Cl2 is less (\({{10 \over 71} \over 10} < {10 \over 124}\)). Hence, Cl2 is the limiting reagent.

\[10\ moles\ of\ Cl_2\ form\ 4\ moles\ of\ PCl_5.\] \[1\ mole\ of\ Cl_2\ forms\ {4\over 10} moles\ of\ PCl_5.\] \[{10 \over 71} moles\ of\ Cl_2\ forms\ {4 \over 10} \times {10 \over 71} moles\ of\ PCl_5.\] \[Mass\ of\ PCl_5 = {4 \over 10} \times {10 \over 71} \times 208.5 = {834 \over 71}\ g\]

docs.title: Vapour Density
docs.text:
• Density of a gas relative to hydrogen is called its vapour density. Mathematically, it can be expressed as:
\[Vapour\ Density = {ρ_{gas} \over ρ_{H_2}}\]

  • Let us consider that in a container of capacity 'V' litres, we have 'n' moles of H2 gas and in another container of capacity 'V' litres, we have 'n' moles of a gas of molecular mass 'M'.

  • Then, the density of H2 gas is given by:

\[ρ_{H_2} = {Mass \over Volume}\] \[ρ_{H_2} = {n \times 2 \over V}\]
  • And, the density of the gas of molecular mass 'M' is given by:
\[ρ_{gas} = {Mass \over Volume}\] \[ρ_{gas} = {n \times M \over V}\]
  • Calculating vapour density of the gas of molecular mass 'M':
\[Vapour\ Density = {ρ_{gas} \over ρ_{H_2}}\] \[Vapour\ Density = {{n \times M \over V} \over {n \times 2 \over V}}\] \[∴ Vapour\ Density = {M \over 2}\]
  • Vapour Density has no unit. It is a dimensionless quantity.

docs.title: Relative Density of a gas w.r.t another gas
docs.text:
• Let us consider that we have two gases, gas1 and gas2 of molecular masses M1 and M2 respectively.. Then, the relative density of gas1 w.r.t gas2 is given by:
\[Relative\ density\ of\ gas1\ w.r.t\ gas2 = {M_1 \over M_2}\]

Examples

  • \[Relative\ density\ of\ gas\ of\ molecular\ mass\ M\ w.r.t\ O_2 = {M \over 32}\]
  • \[Relative\ density\ of\ gas\ of\ molecular\ mass\ M\ w.r.t\ N_2 = {M \over 28}\]

docs.title: Relative Density of a gas w.r.t air
docs.text:
\[Relative\ density\ of\ gas\ of\ molecular\ mass\ M\ w.r.t\ air = {M \over M_{air}}\]

Here, Mair = Average molecular mass of air

  • Air consists of approximately 20% oxygen and 80% nitrogen. So, calculating average molecular mass of air:
\[Avg.\ molecular\ mass\ of\ air = {(20 \times 32) + (80 \times 28) \over (20 + 80)}\] \[∴ Avg.\ molecular\ mass\ of\ air ≈ 29\ a.m.u\]
  • Therefore, we can write:
\[Relative\ density\ of\ gas\ of\ molecular\ mass\ M\ w.r.t\ air = {M \over 29}\]

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
Density of a gas relative to air is 1.17. Find the molecular mass of the gas. [Mair = 29 g/mole]

\[Relative\ density\ of\ gas\ of\ molecular\ mass\ M\ w.r.t\ air = {M \over M_{air}}\] \[1.17 = {M \over 29}\] \[M = 33.95 ≈ 34\ g/mole\]

docs.title: Redox Reactions | Balancing of Redox Reactions
Redox Reactions | Balancing of Redox Reactions
docs.text:
Two methods are used to balance redox equations:

  • Oxidation number method: based on the change in oxidation number of the reducing agent and the oxidising agent.
  • Half reaction (ion-electron) method: based on splitting the reaction into an oxidation half and a reduction half.

Both methods give the same answer; the choice is a matter of convenience.

docs.title: Oxidation Number Method
docs.text:
• Step 1: Write the correct formula of each reactant and product (the skeletal equation).
  • Step 2: Assign oxidation numbers to all elements and identify the atoms whose oxidation number changes.
  • Step 3: Calculate the increase or decrease in oxidation number per atom and for the whole molecule/ion. If these are not equal, multiply by suitable coefficients to make the total increase equal to the total decrease.
  • Step 4: If the reaction is in water, add H+ (acidic medium) or OH- (basic medium) on the appropriate side so that the total ionic charges on both sides are equal.
  • Step 5: Balance hydrogen atoms by adding H2O molecules. Finally check oxygen atoms; if they are equal on both sides, the equation is balanced.

Note

If you find that two substances are reduced and nothing is oxidised (or vice versa), something is wrong: either the formulas or the oxidation numbers have been assigned incorrectly.

Example 1: Dichromate and sulphite in acidic medium

Write the net ionic equation for the reaction of K2Cr2O7 with Na2SO3 in acid solution to give Cr3+ and sulphate ion.

  • Step 1: Skeletal ionic equation:
\[Cr_2O_7^{2-}{}_{(aq)} + SO_3^{2-}{}_{(aq)} → Cr^{3+}_{(aq)} + SO_4^{2-}{}_{(aq)}\]
  • Step 2: Assign oxidation numbers to Cr and S:
\[\overset{+6}{Cr_2}O_7^{2-} + \overset{+4}{S}O_3^{2-} → \overset{+3}{Cr^{3+}} + \overset{+6}{S}O_4^{2-}\]

Dichromate is the oxidant and sulphite is the reductant.

  • Step 3: Each Cr decreases by 3, so two Cr atoms decrease by 6 in total. Each S increases by 2. To make increase = decrease, take 3 sulphite ions:
\[Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 3SO_3^{2-} → 2Cr^{3+} + 3SO_4^{2-}\]
  • Step 4: Charge on left = -2 - 6 = -8; charge on right = +6 - 6 = 0. In acidic medium, add 8H+ on the left:
\[Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 3SO_3^{2-} + 8H^+ → 2Cr^{3+} + 3SO_4^{2-}\]
  • Step 5: Add 4H2O on the right to balance hydrogen:
\[Cr_2O_7^{2-}{}_{(aq)} + 3SO_3^{2-}{}_{(aq)} + 8H^+_{(aq)} → 2Cr^{3+}_{(aq)} + 3SO_4^{2-}{}_{(aq)} + 4H_2O_{(l)}\]

Oxygen: 7 + 9 = 16 on the left and 12 + 4 = 16 on the right. The equation is balanced.

Example 2: Permanganate and bromide in basic medium

Permanganate ion reacts with bromide ion in basic medium to give manganese dioxide and bromate ion. Write the balanced ionic equation.

  • Step 1: Skeletal ionic equation:
\[MnO_4^-{}_{(aq)} + Br^-_{(aq)} → MnO_{2(s)} + BrO_3^-{}_{(aq)}\]
  • Step 2: Assign oxidation numbers to Mn and Br:
\[\overset{+7}{Mn}O_4^- + \overset{-1}{Br^-} → \overset{+4}{Mn}O_2 + \overset{+5}{Br}O_3^-\]

Permanganate is the oxidant and bromide is the reductant.

  • Step 3: Mn decreases by 3 and Br increases by 6. So take 2MnO4-:
\[2MnO_4^- + Br^- → 2MnO_2 + BrO_3^-\]
  • Step 4: Charge on left = -3; charge on right = -1. In basic medium, add 2OH- on the right:
\[2MnO_4^- + Br^- → 2MnO_2 + BrO_3^- + 2OH^-\]
  • Step 5: Add one H2O on the left to balance hydrogen:
\[2MnO_4^-{}_{(aq)} + Br^-_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} → 2MnO_{2(s)} + BrO_3^-{}_{(aq)} + 2OH^-_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: Half Reaction (Ion-Electron) Method
docs.text:
• In this method, the two half equations are balanced separately and then added together.
  • Step 1: Write the unbalanced equation in ionic form.
  • Step 2: Separate it into an oxidation half and a reduction half.
  • Step 3: Balance atoms other than O and H in each half reaction.
  • Step 4: In acidic medium, add H2O to balance O atoms and H+ to balance H atoms.
  • Step 5: Add electrons to one side of each half reaction to balance the charges. Multiply one or both half reactions by suitable coefficients so that the number of electrons is equal.
  • Step 6: Add the two half reactions and cancel the electrons (and any common species) on both sides.
  • Step 7: Verify that atoms and charges are balanced on both sides.
