Basic medium

First balance the atoms exactly as in acidic medium. Then, for each H+ ion, add an equal number of OH- ions to both sides. Where H+ and OH- appear on the same side, combine them to give H2O.

Example 3: Fe2+ and dichromate in acidic medium

Balance the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ by Cr2O72- (which is reduced to Cr3+) in acidic medium.

  • Step 1: Unbalanced ionic equation:
\[Fe^{2+}_{(aq)} + Cr_2O_7^{2-}{}_{(aq)} → Fe^{3+}_{(aq)} + Cr^{3+}_{(aq)}\]
  • Step 2: Half reactions:
\[Oxidation\ half:\ \overset{+2}{Fe^{2+}} → \overset{+3}{Fe^{3+}}\] \[Reduction\ half:\ \overset{+6}{Cr_2}O_7^{2-} → \overset{+3}{Cr^{3+}}\]
  • Step 3: Fe is already balanced. Multiply Cr3+ by 2:
\[Cr_2O_7^{2-} → 2Cr^{3+}\]
  • Step 4: Add 7H2O on the right to balance O and 14H+ on the left to balance H:
\[Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ → 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O\]
  • Step 5: Balance charges with electrons. The reduction half has +12 on the left and +6 on the right, so add 6e- on the left:
\[Fe^{2+} → Fe^{3+} + e^-\] \[Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6e^- → 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O\]

Multiply the oxidation half by 6 to equalise electrons:

\[6Fe^{2+} → 6Fe^{3+} + 6e^-\]
  • Step 6: Add the two halves and cancel electrons:
\[6Fe^{2+}_{(aq)} + Cr_2O_7^{2-}{}_{(aq)} + 14H^+_{(aq)} → 6Fe^{3+}_{(aq)} + 2Cr^{3+}_{(aq)} + 7H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • Step 7: Charge on each side = +24. Atoms are balanced. The equation is fully balanced.

Example 4: Permanganate and iodide in basic medium

MnO4- in basic solution oxidises I- to I2 and is itself reduced to MnO2. Write the balanced ionic equation.

  • Step 1: Skeletal ionic equation:
\[MnO_4^-{}_{(aq)} + I^-_{(aq)} → MnO_{2(s)} + I_{2(s)}\]
  • Step 2: Half reactions:
\[Oxidation\ half:\ \overset{-1}{I^-} → \overset{0}{I_2}\] \[Reduction\ half:\ \overset{+7}{Mn}O_4^- → \overset{+4}{Mn}O_2\]
  • Step 3: Balance iodine:
\[2I^- → I_2\]
  • Step 4: In the reduction half, add 2H2O on the right for O and 4H+ on the left for H:
\[MnO_4^- + 4H^+ → MnO_2 + 2H_2O\]

Since the medium is basic, add 4OH- to both sides. 4H+ + 4OH- gives 4H2O, and after cancelling water:

\[MnO_4^- + 2H_2O → MnO_2 + 4OH^-\]
  • Step 5: Balance charges with electrons:
\[2I^- → I_2 + 2e^-\] \[MnO_4^- + 2H_2O + 3e^- → MnO_2 + 4OH^-\]

Multiply the oxidation half by 3 and the reduction half by 2:

\[6I^- → 3I_2 + 6e^-\] \[2MnO_4^- + 4H_2O + 6e^- → 2MnO_2 + 8OH^-\]
  • Step 6: Add and cancel electrons:
\[6I^-_{(aq)} + 2MnO_4^-{}_{(aq)} + 4H_2O_{(l)} → 3I_{2(s)} + 2MnO_{2(s)} + 8OH^-_{(aq)}\]
  • Step 7: Charge on each side = -8. Atoms are balanced.

docs.title: Redox Reactions | Introduction
docs.text:
Redox reactions are reactions in which oxidation and reduction take place simultaneously. The word "redox" itself comes from reduction + oxidation.

  • Redox reactions are everywhere: burning of fuels, extraction of reactive metals by electrolysis, manufacture of chemicals like caustic soda, working of dry and wet batteries and corrosion of metals are all redox processes.
  • Biological processes like respiration and photosynthesis, and environmental topics like the hydrogen economy and the ozone hole, also involve redox chemistry.

docs.title: Classical Concept of Oxidation
docs.text:
• Originally, oxidation meant only the addition of oxygen to an element or a compound. Since air contains about 20% dioxygen, many elements combine with it, which is why most elements occur on earth as oxides.
\[2Mg_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} → 2MgO_{(s)}\] \[S_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} → SO_{2(g)}\] \[CH_{4(g)} + 2O_{2(g)} → CO_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • In the combustion of methane, hydrogen of CH4 is replaced by oxygen. This led chemists to include the removal of hydrogen as oxidation as well:
\[2H_2S_{(g)} + O_{2(g)} → 2S_{(s)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • Later, the term was extended to the addition of other electronegative elements (like F, Cl, S) in place of oxygen:
\[Mg_{(s)} + F_{2(g)} → MgF_{2(s)}\] \[Mg_{(s)} + Cl_{2(g)} → MgCl_{2(s)}\] \[Mg_{(s)} + S_{(s)} → MgS_{(s)}\]
  • Finally, the removal of an electropositive element was also counted as oxidation. For example, potassium ferrocyanide is oxidised to potassium ferricyanide because electropositive potassium is removed from it:
\[2K_4[Fe(CN)_6]_{(aq)} + H_2O_{2(aq)} → 2K_3[Fe(CN)_6]_{(aq)} + 2KOH_{(aq)}\]

Conclusion

Oxidation is the addition of oxygen/electronegative element to a substance or removal of hydrogen/electropositive element from a substance.

docs.title: Classical Concept of Reduction
docs.text:
• Reduction was first defined as the removal of oxygen from a compound. Its scope was later broadened in the same way as oxidation.

Conclusion

Reduction is the removal of oxygen/electronegative element from a substance or addition of hydrogen/electropositive element to a substance.

Examples of reduction

\[2HgO_{(s)} \xrightarrow{Δ} 2Hg_{(l)} + O_{2(g)}\ (removal\ of\ oxygen)\] \[2FeCl_{3(aq)} + H_{2(g)} → 2FeCl_{2(aq)} + 2HCl_{(aq)}\ (removal\ of\ chlorine)\] \[CH_2 = CH_{2(g)} + H_{2(g)} → H_3C - CH_{3(g)}\ (addition\ of\ hydrogen)\] \[2HgCl_{2(aq)} + SnCl_{2(aq)} → Hg_2Cl_{2(s)} + SnCl_{4(aq)}\ (addition\ of\ mercury)\]
  • In the last reaction, HgCl2 is reduced, but at the same time SnCl2 is oxidised to SnCl4 by the addition of chlorine.
  • Looking carefully at all such reactions, chemists realised that oxidation and reduction always occur together. Hence the name redox reactions.

docs.title: Electronic Concept of Redox Reactions
docs.text:
• Consider the reactions of sodium with chlorine, oxygen and sulphur:
\[2Na_{(s)} + Cl_{2(g)} → 2NaCl_{(s)}\] \[4Na_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} → 2Na_2O_{(s)}\] \[2Na_{(s)} + S_{(s)} → Na_2S_{(s)}\]
  • Classically, sodium is oxidised (an electronegative element is added to it) and Cl2, O2 and S are reduced (electropositive sodium is added to them).
  • But the products are ionic: Na+Cl-, (Na+)2O2- and (Na+)2S2-. This shows that sodium has lost electrons and the non-metal has gained them.
  • Each reaction can therefore be split into two half reactions, one showing loss of electrons and the other showing gain of electrons. For NaCl:
\[Oxidation\ half:\ 2Na_{(s)} → 2Na^+_{(g)} + 2e^-\] \[Reduction\ half:\ Cl_{2(g)} + 2e^- → 2Cl^-_{(g)}\] \[Overall:\ 2Na_{(s)} + Cl_{2(g)} → 2Na^+Cl^-_{(s)}\]
  • Sodium gives electrons to chlorine and reduces it, so sodium acts as a reducing agent. Chlorine accepts electrons from sodium and oxidises it, so chlorine acts as an oxidising agent.

Electronic definitions

  • Oxidation: Loss of electron(s) by any species.

  • Reduction: Gain of electron(s) by any species.

  • Oxidising agent: Acceptor of electron(s).

  • Reducing agent: Donor of electron(s).

  • A simple way to remember: the oxidising agent is itself reduced, and the reducing agent is itself oxidised.

docs.title: 1. Zinc in copper nitrate solution
docs.text:
• When a zinc strip is placed in aqueous copper nitrate solution for about an hour, it gets coated with reddish metallic copper and the blue colour of the solution (due to Cu2+) disappears.
  • The formation of Zn2+ can be confirmed by passing H2S through the colourless solution (made alkaline with ammonia), which gives white zinc sulphide, ZnS.
\[Zn_{(s)} + Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} → Zn^{2+}_{(aq)} + Cu_{(s)}\] \[Oxidation:\ Zn → Zn^{2+} + 2e^-\] \[Reduction:\ Cu^{2+} + 2e^- → Cu\]
  • Zinc loses electrons and is oxidised; Cu2+ gains those electrons and is reduced.
  • The reverse reaction does not occur: a copper strip in zinc sulphate solution shows no change, and even the very sensitive H2S test (black CuS) cannot detect any Cu2+. So the equilibrium greatly favours the products.

docs.title: 2. Copper in silver nitrate solution
docs.text:
• A copper rod dipped in silver nitrate solution slowly turns the solution blue (Cu2+ formed) and silver deposits on the rod.
\[Cu_{(s)} + 2Ag^+_{(aq)} → Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2Ag_{(s)}\]
  • Here Cu is oxidised to Cu2+ and Ag+ is reduced to Ag. The equilibrium again greatly favours the products.

docs.title: 3. Cobalt in nickel sulphate solution
docs.text:
\[Co_{(s)} + Ni^{2+}_{(aq)} ⇌ Co^{2+}_{(aq)} + Ni_{(s)}\]
  • At equilibrium, both Ni2+ and Co2+ are present at moderate concentrations. Neither the reactants nor the products are greatly favoured.

docs.title: Activity Series
docs.text:
• These experiments show that metals compete with each other to release electrons, just as acids compete to release protons.
  • Zinc releases electrons to copper and copper releases electrons to silver. So the electron releasing tendency is:
\[Zn > Cu > Ag\]
  • Arranging metals in order of their tendency to release electrons gives the metal activity series or electrochemical series.
  • This competition for electrons is the basis of galvanic cells, where a redox reaction becomes a source of electrical energy. See Electrochemical Cells.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
In the reactions given below, identify the species undergoing oxidation and reduction: (i) H2S(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g) + S(s) (ii) 3Fe3O4(s) + 8Al(s) → 9Fe(s) + 4Al2O3(s) (iii) 2Na(s) + H2(g) → 2NaH(s)

  • (i) H2S is oxidised because hydrogen (more electropositive) is removed from sulphur, or equivalently, electronegative chlorine is added to hydrogen. Chlorine is reduced because hydrogen is added to it.

  • (ii) Aluminium is oxidised because oxygen is added to it. Fe3O4 is reduced because oxygen is removed from it.

  • (iii) Using electronegativity, sodium (electropositive) is added to hydrogen, so hydrogen is reduced and sodium is oxidised. Such cases are better explained by electron transfer.

Justify that the reaction 2Na(s) + H2(g) → 2NaH(s) is a redox change.

  • NaH is an ionic compound, Na+H-. So the reaction can be split into two half reactions:
\[Oxidation\ half:\ 2Na_{(s)} → 2Na^+_{(g)} + 2e^-\] \[Reduction\ half:\ H_{2(g)} + 2e^- → 2H^-_{(g)}\]
  • Sodium loses electrons (oxidised) and hydrogen gains electrons (reduced). Hence, the reaction is a redox change.

docs.title: Why do we need Oxidation Number?
docs.text:
• In ionic reactions like the formation of NaCl, electron transfer is easy to see. But many redox reactions form covalent compounds, where no complete transfer of electrons takes place.
\[2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} → 2H_2O_{(l)}\] \[H_{2(g)} + Cl_{2(g)} → 2HCl_{(g)}\] \[CH_{4(g)} + 4Cl_{2(g)} → CCl_{4(l)} + 4HCl_{(g)}\]
  • In H2O, the shared electrons are only shifted towards oxygen; hydrogen does not lose its electron completely. Still, we can think of H going from a zero state in H2 to a positive state in H2O, and O going from zero in O2 to a negative state in H2O.
  • To keep track of such electron shifts, chemists use oxidation number. In this method, we always assume a complete transfer of electrons from the less electronegative atom to the more electronegative atom.
\[2\overset{0}{H_2} + \overset{0}{O_2} → 2\overset{+1}{H_2}\overset{-2}{O}\] \[\overset{0}{H_2} + \overset{0}{Cl_2} → 2\overset{+1}{H}\overset{-1}{Cl}\] \[\overset{-4}{C}\overset{+1}{H_4} + 4\overset{0}{Cl_2} → \overset{+4}{C}\overset{-1}{Cl_4} + 4\overset{+1}{H}\overset{-1}{Cl}\]
  • This assumption is only for book-keeping, but it makes the description of redox reactions very simple.

Definition

Oxidation number denotes the oxidation state of an element in a compound, ascertained according to a set of rules formulated on the basis that the electrons in a covalent bond belong entirely to the more electronegative element.

  • If an element is present more than once in a molecule or ion (e.g. S in Na2S2O3, Cr in Cr2O72-), the oxidation number calculated is the average for all atoms of that element.

docs.title: 1. Free elements
docs.text: • In the free or uncombined state, every atom has an oxidation number of zero. Example: each atom in H2, O2, Cl2, O3, P4, S8, Na, Mg and Al has oxidation number 0.

docs.title: 2. Monoatomic ions
docs.text:
• For an ion made of only one atom, the oxidation number equals the charge on the ion. Example: Na+ = +1, Mg2+ = +2, Fe3+ = +3, Cl- = -1, O2- = -2.
  • In their compounds, alkali metals always have +1, alkaline earth metals have +2 and aluminium has +3.

docs.title: 3. Oxygen
docs.text:
• Oxygen has an oxidation number of -2 in most compounds. There are two exceptions:
  • Peroxides and superoxides: Here oxygen atoms are directly linked to each other. In peroxides (H2O2, Na2O2) each oxygen is -1, and in superoxides (KO2, RbO2) each oxygen is \(-{1 \over 2}\).
  • Compounds with fluorine: Since fluorine is more electronegative, oxygen gets a positive value. In OF2 oxygen is +2 and in O2F2 it is +1.

docs.title: 4. Hydrogen
docs.text: • Hydrogen has an oxidation number of +1, except in binary compounds with metals (metal hydrides) like LiH, NaH and CaH2, where it is -1.

docs.title: 5. Halogens
docs.text:
• Fluorine is -1 in all its compounds.
  • Cl, Br and I are -1 when they occur as halide ions. But when combined with oxygen (in oxoacids and oxoanions), they have positive oxidation numbers.

docs.title: 6. Sum of oxidation numbers
docs.text:
• The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral compound is zero.
  • In a polyatomic ion, the sum equals the charge on the ion. Example: in CO32-, the sum for one C and three O atoms is -2.

Example: Oxidation number of Cr in K2Cr2O7

Let the oxidation number of Cr be x.

\[2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0\] \[2x = 12\] \[x = +6\]

docs.title: Trends in Oxidation Number
docs.text:
• Metals have positive oxidation numbers, while non-metals can have positive or negative oxidation numbers.
  • Transition elements usually show several positive oxidation states.
  • The highest oxidation number of a representative element is equal to its group number for groups 1 and 2, and (group number - 10) for the other groups. So, the highest oxidation number increases across a period:
Group 1 2 13 14 15 16 17 Element Na Mg Al Si P S Cl Compound NaCl MgSO4 AlF3 SiCl4 P4O10 SF6 HClO4 Highest oxidation number +1 +2 +3 +4 +5 +6 +7
  • The term oxidation state is often used interchangeably with oxidation number. In CO2, the oxidation state (and oxidation number) of carbon is +4 and of oxygen is -2.

docs.title: Stock Notation
docs.text:
• In Stock notation (given by German chemist Alfred Stock), the oxidation number of a metal is written as a Roman numeral in parentheses after the symbol of the metal.
  • Examples: aurous chloride = Au(I)Cl, auric chloride = Au(III)Cl3, stannous chloride = Sn(II)Cl2, stannic chloride = Sn(IV)Cl4.
  • It quickly tells us whether a species is in its oxidised or reduced form. Example: Hg2(I)Cl2 is the reduced form of Hg(II)Cl2.

docs.title: Redox Terms in terms of Oxidation Number
docs.text:
Definitions

  • Oxidation: An increase in the oxidation number of an element in a given substance.

  • Reduction: A decrease in the oxidation number of an element in a given substance.

  • Oxidising agent (oxidant): A reagent which can increase the oxidation number of an element in a given substance.

  • Reducing agent (reductant): A reagent which lowers the oxidation number of an element in a given substance.

  • Redox reaction: A reaction which involves change in oxidation number of the interacting species.

docs.title: Fractional Oxidation Number
docs.text:
• Sometimes the oxidation number of an element comes out as a fraction:
\[C_3O_2:\ Oxidation\ number\ of\ C = {4 \over 3}\] \[Br_3O_8:\ Oxidation\ number\ of\ Br = {16 \over 3}\] \[Na_2S_4O_6:\ Oxidation\ number\ of\ S = 2.5\]
  • Electrons are never shared or transferred in fractions. A fractional value is only the average oxidation number; the structure shows that the element is actually present in different oxidation states.

docs.title: 1. Carbon suboxide (C<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub>)
docs.text:
\[O = \overset{+2}{C} = \overset{0}{C} = \overset{+2}{C} = O\]
  • The two terminal carbons are +2 and the middle carbon is 0. Average = \((2 + 0 + 2)/3 = 4/3\).

docs.title: 2. Tribromooctaoxide (Br<sub>3</sub>O<sub>8</sub>)
docs.text: • The two terminal bromines are +6 and the middle bromine is +4. Average = \((6 + 4 + 6)/3 = 16/3\).

docs.title: 3. Tetrathionate ion (S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2-</sup>)
docs.text:
• The two terminal sulphurs are +5 and the two middle sulphurs are 0. Average = \((5 + 0 + 0 + 5)/4 = 2.5\).

Note

Fe3O4, Mn3O4 and Pb3O4 are mixed oxides which also show fractional average oxidation numbers of the metal. However, in O2+ and O2- the oxidation number is genuinely \(+{1 \over 2}\) and \(-{1 \over 2}\) respectively.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Using Stock notation, represent the following compounds: HAuCl4, Tl2O, FeO, Fe2O3, CuI, CuO, MnO and MnO2.

Applying the rules, the oxidation number of the metal in each compound is:

Compound Oxidation number of metal Stock notation HAuCl4 +3 HAu(III)Cl4 Tl2O +1 Tl2(I)O FeO +2 Fe(II)O Fe2O3 +3 Fe2(III)O3 CuI +1 Cu(I)I CuO +2 Cu(II)O MnO +2 Mn(II)O MnO2 +4 Mn(IV)O2

Justify that the reaction 2Cu2O(s) + Cu2S(s) → 6Cu(s) + SO2(g) is a redox reaction. Identify the species oxidised/reduced, the oxidant and the reductant.

  • Assigning oxidation numbers:
\[2\overset{+1}{Cu_2}\overset{-2}{O} + \overset{+1}{Cu_2}\overset{-2}{S} → 6\overset{0}{Cu} + \overset{+4}{S}\overset{-2}{O_2}\]

  • Copper is reduced from +1 to 0 and sulphur is oxidised from -2 to +4. So it is a redox reaction.

  • Cu2O helps sulphur in Cu2S to increase its oxidation number, so Cu(I) is the oxidant.

  • Sulphur of Cu2S helps copper (in both Cu2S and Cu2O) to decrease its oxidation number, so sulphur of Cu2S is the reductant.

docs.title: Redox Reactions | Questions Based on Oxidation Number
Redox Reactions | Questions Based on Oxidation Number
Questions
docs.text:
Assign oxidation number to: (a) P in NaH2PO4 (b) S in NaHSO4 (c) P in H4P2O7 (d) Mn in K2MnO4 (e) O in CaO2 (f) B in NaBH4 (g) S in H2S2O7 (h) S in KAl(SO4)2.12H2O

Let the oxidation number of the required element be x.

\[(a)\ NaH_2PO_4:\ +1 + 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 ⇒ x = +5\] \[(b)\ NaHSO_4:\ +1 + 1 + x + 4(-2) = 0 ⇒ x = +6\] \[(c)\ H_4P_2O_7:\ 4(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0 ⇒ x = +5\] \[(d)\ K_2MnO_4:\ 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 ⇒ x = +6\]
  • (e) CaO2 is a peroxide:
\[+2 + 2x = 0 ⇒ x = -1\]
  • (f) NaBH4 is a metal hydride, so H is -1:
\[+1 + x + 4(-1) = 0 ⇒ x = +3\] \[(g)\ H_2S_2O_7:\ 2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0 ⇒ x = +6\]
  • (h) Water molecules are neutral, so they contribute zero:
\[+1 + 3 + 2x + 8(-2) = 0 ⇒ x = +6\]

What are the oxidation numbers of the following and how do you rationalise your results? (a) I in KI3 (b) S in H2S4O6 (c) Fe in Fe3O4 (d) C in CH3CH2OH (e) C in CH3COOH

  • (a) By formula, the average oxidation number of I is \(-{1 \over 3}\). But KI3 is K+[I2.I-]: two iodine atoms (the I2 molecule) are 0 and one (the I- ion) is -1.

  • (b) The average oxidation number of S is +2.5. In the structure of S4O62-, the two terminal S atoms are +5 and the two middle S atoms are 0.

  • (c) The average oxidation number of Fe is \(+{8 \over 3}\). Fe3O4 is a mixed oxide, FeO.Fe2O3: one Fe is +2 and two Fe are +3.

  • (d) The average oxidation number of C is -2. Counting each C separately (C-C bond contributes 0, each H contributes -1, each O contributes +1):

\[\overset{-3}{C}H_3 - \overset{-1}{C}H_2OH\]
  • (e) The average oxidation number of C is 0. Counting separately:
\[\overset{-3}{C}H_3 - \overset{+3}{C}OOH\]

Justify that the following reactions are redox reactions: (a) CuO(s) + H2(g) → Cu(s) + H2O(g) (b) Fe2O3(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO2(g) (c) 2K(s) + F2(g) → 2K+F-(s) (d) 4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g)

\[(a)\ \overset{+2}{Cu}O + \overset{0}{H_2} → \overset{0}{Cu} + \overset{+1}{H_2}O\]

Cu is reduced (+2 to 0) and H is oxidised (0 to +1).

\[(b)\ \overset{+3}{Fe_2}O_3 + 3\overset{+2}{C}O → 2\overset{0}{Fe} + 3\overset{+4}{C}O_2\]

Fe is reduced (+3 to 0) and C is oxidised (+2 to +4).

\[(c)\ 2\overset{0}{K} + \overset{0}{F_2} → 2\overset{+1}{K}\overset{-1}{F}\]

K is oxidised (0 to +1) and F is reduced (0 to -1).

\[(d)\ 4\overset{-3}{N}H_3 + 5\overset{0}{O_2} → 4\overset{+2}{N}\overset{-2}{O} + 6H_2\overset{-2}{O}\]

N is oxidised (-3 to +2) and O is reduced (0 to -2).

In each reaction, one element is oxidised and another is reduced, so all are redox reactions.

Fluorine reacts with ice: H2O(s) + F2(g) → HF(g) + HOF(g). Justify that this is a redox reaction.

In HOF, fluorine is the most electronegative atom (-1) and H is +1, so oxygen is 0.

\[H_2\overset{-2}{O} + \overset{0}{F_2} → H\overset{-1}{F} + H\overset{0}{O}\overset{-1}{F}\]

Oxygen is oxidised from -2 to 0 and fluorine is reduced from 0 to -1. Hence, it is a redox reaction.

Calculate the oxidation number of sulphur, chromium and nitrogen in H2SO5, Cr2O72- and NO3-. Suggest structures of these compounds. Count for the fallacy.

  • H2SO5: Taking all O as -2:
\[2(+1) + x + 5(-2) = 0 ⇒ x = +8\]

This is impossible because sulphur cannot exceed +6 (it has only six valence electrons). The fallacy is that H2SO5 (peroxomonosulphuric acid, HO-SO2-O-O-H) contains one peroxide (O-O) linkage, where each of the two oxygens is -1:

\[2(+1) + x + 3(-2) + 2(-1) = 0 ⇒ x = +6\]
  • Cr2O72-:
\[2x + 7(-2) = -2 ⇒ x = +6\]

The structure has two CrO3 units joined by a bridging oxygen; there is no peroxide linkage, so +6 is correct and there is no fallacy.

  • NO3-:
\[x + 3(-2) = -1 ⇒ x = +5\]

In the structure, N forms one N=O double bond, one N-O- single bond and one coordinate bond N→O. N cannot form five covalent bonds (no d-orbitals), but its oxidation number is still +5 since all its five valence electrons are counted towards oxygen.

Write formulas for the following compounds: (a) Mercury(II) chloride (b) Nickel(II) sulphate (c) Tin(IV) oxide (d) Thallium(I) sulphate (e) Iron(III) sulphate (f) Chromium(III) oxide

(a) HgCl2 (b) NiSO4 (c) SnO2 (d) Tl2SO4 (e) Fe2(SO4)3 (f) Cr2O3

Suggest a list of substances where carbon can exhibit oxidation states from -4 to +4 and nitrogen from -3 to +5.

Oxidation state Carbon Nitrogen -4 CH4 - -3 C2H6 NH3 -2 CH3Cl N2H4 -1 C2H2 NH2OH 0 CH2Cl2, diamond N2 +1 OHC-CHO (glyoxal) N2O +2 CO, CHCl3 NO +3 H2C2O4 (oxalic acid) N2O3, HNO2 +4 CO2, CCl4 NO2 +5 - N2O5, HNO3

While sulphur dioxide and hydrogen peroxide can act as oxidising as well as reducing agents, ozone and nitric acid act only as oxidants. Why?

  • In SO2, S is +4. Sulphur can range from -2 to +6, so its oxidation number can either increase or decrease. Hence SO2 can act as both a reductant and an oxidant.

  • In H2O2, O is -1. It can increase to 0 (in O2) or decrease to -2 (in H2O), so H2O2 can also act both ways.

  • In HNO3, N is +5, its highest oxidation state. It can only decrease, so HNO3 acts only as an oxidant.

  • In O3, O is 0. Oxygen can decrease to -2 but cannot show positive oxidation states (except with fluorine). Ozone readily gives O2 and an oxygen atom, which is a strong oxidant. So ozone acts only as an oxidant.

The compound AgF2 is unstable. However, if formed, it acts as a very strong oxidising agent. Why?

In AgF2, silver is in the +2 state, which is unstable. Silver strongly tends to accept an electron and return to its stable +1 state. This makes AgF2 a very strong oxidising agent.

Identify the substance oxidised, reduced, oxidising agent and reducing agent: (a) 2AgBr(s) + C6H6O2(aq) → 2Ag(s) + 2HBr(aq) + C6H4O2(aq) (b) HCHO(l) + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → 2Ag(s) + HCOO-(aq) + 4NH3(aq) + 2H2O(l) (c) HCHO(l) + 2Cu2+(aq) + 5OH-(aq) → Cu2O(s) + HCOO-(aq) + 3H2O(l) (d) N2H4(l) + 2H2O2(l) → N2(g) + 4H2O(l) (e) Pb(s) + PbO2(s) + 2H2SO4(aq) → 2PbSO4(s) + 2H2O(l)

Reaction Oxidised (reducing agent) Reduced (oxidising agent) (a) C6H6O2 (hydroquinone) AgBr (Ag: +1 → 0) (b) HCHO (C: 0 → +2) [Ag(NH3)2]+ (Ag: +1 → 0) (c) HCHO (C: 0 → +2) Cu2+ (Cu: +2 → +1) (d) N2H4 (N: -2 → 0) H2O2 (O: -1 → -2) (e) Pb (0 → +2) PbO2 (Pb: +4 → +2)

What information can you draw from the reaction: (CN)2(g) + 2OH-(aq) → CN-(aq) + CNO-(aq) + H2O(l)?

Taking N as -3, the oxidation number of carbon is:

\[(\overset{+3}{C}N)_2 + 2OH^- → \overset{+2}{C}N^- + \overset{+4}{C}NO^- + H_2O\]
  • Carbon in cyanogen (+3) is simultaneously reduced to +2 (cyanide) and oxidised to +4 (cyanate). So this is a disproportionation reaction of cyanogen in alkaline medium.

Consider the elements Cs, Ne, I and F. Identify the element that exhibits: (a) only negative oxidation state (b) only positive oxidation state (c) both positive and negative oxidation states (d) neither negative nor positive oxidation state.

  • (a) F - being the most electronegative element, it shows only -1.

  • (b) Cs - an alkali metal, it shows only +1.

  • (c) I - shows -1 in iodides and +1, +3, +5, +7 in its oxo compounds.

  • (d) Ne - a noble gas, it shows neither.

docs.title: Redox Reactions | Questions Based on Redox Reactions
Redox Reactions | Questions Based on Redox Reactions
Balancing Redox Equations
docs.text:
Balance by the ion-electron method: MnO4-(aq) + I-(aq) → MnO2(s) + I2(s) (in basic medium)

\[Oxidation:\ 2I^- → I_2 + 2e^-\] \[Reduction:\ MnO_4^- + 2H_2O + 3e^- → MnO_2 + 4OH^-\]
  • Multiply the oxidation half by 3 and the reduction half by 2, then add:
\[2MnO_4^-{}_{(aq)} + 6I^-_{(aq)} + 4H_2O_{(l)} → 2MnO_{2(s)} + 3I_{2(s)} + 8OH^-_{(aq)}\]

Balance by the ion-electron method: MnO4-(aq) + SO2(g) → Mn2+(aq) + HSO4-(aq) (in acidic solution)

\[Oxidation:\ SO_2 + 2H_2O → HSO_4^- + 3H^+ + 2e^-\] \[Reduction:\ MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- → Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O\]
  • Multiply the oxidation half by 5 and the reduction half by 2:
\[5SO_2 + 10H_2O → 5HSO_4^- + 15H^+ + 10e^-\] \[2MnO_4^- + 16H^+ + 10e^- → 2Mn^{2+} + 8H_2O\]
  • Add and cancel the common H+ and H2O:
\[2MnO_4^-{}_{(aq)} + 5SO_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} + H^+_{(aq)} → 2Mn^{2+}_{(aq)} + 5HSO_4^-{}_{(aq)}\]

Balance by the ion-electron method: H2O2(aq) + Fe2+(aq) → Fe3+(aq) + H2O(l) (in acidic solution)

\[Oxidation:\ 2Fe^{2+} → 2Fe^{3+} + 2e^-\] \[Reduction:\ H_2O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^- → 2H_2O\] \[Overall:\ H_2O_{2(aq)} + 2Fe^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2H^+_{(aq)} → 2Fe^{3+}_{(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}\]

Balance by the ion-electron method: Cr2O72- + SO2(g) → Cr3+(aq) + SO42-(aq) (in acidic solution)

\[Oxidation:\ 3SO_2 + 6H_2O → 3SO_4^{2-} + 12H^+ + 6e^-\] \[Reduction:\ Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6e^- → 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O\]
  • Add and cancel 12H+ and 6H2O from both sides:
\[Cr_2O_7^{2-}{}_{(aq)} + 3SO_{2(g)} + 2H^+_{(aq)} → 2Cr^{3+}_{(aq)} + 3SO_4^{2-}{}_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)}\]

Balance in basic medium and identify the oxidising and reducing agents: N2H4(l) + ClO3-(aq) → NO(g) + Cl-(aq)

  • Using the oxidation number method:
\[\overset{-2}{N_2}H_4 + \overset{+5}{Cl}O_3^- → \overset{+2}{N}O + \overset{-1}{Cl^-}\]
  • Each N increases by 4, so N2H4 increases by 8. Cl decreases by 6. LCM of 8 and 6 is 24, so take 3N2H4 and 4ClO3-:
\[3N_2H_4 + 4ClO_3^- → 6NO + 4Cl^-\]
  • Charges are already equal (-4 on each side). Balance H by adding 6H2O on the right:
\[3N_2H_{4(l)} + 4ClO_3^-{}_{(aq)} → 6NO_{(g)} + 4Cl^-_{(aq)} + 6H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • Oxidising agent: ClO3-. Reducing agent: N2H4.

Balance in basic medium and identify the oxidising and reducing agents: Cl2O7(g) + H2O2(aq) → ClO2-(aq) + O2(g)

\[\overset{+7}{Cl_2}O_7 + H_2\overset{-1}{O_2} → \overset{+3}{Cl}O_2^- + \overset{0}{O_2}\]
  • Each Cl decreases by 4, so Cl2O7 decreases by 8. Each H2O2 increases by 2. So take 4H2O2:
\[Cl_2O_7 + 4H_2O_2 → 2ClO_2^- + 4O_2\]
  • Charge on left = 0, on right = -2. Add 2OH- on the left. Then balance H with 5H2O on the right:
\[Cl_2O_{7(g)} + 4H_2O_{2(aq)} + 2OH^-_{(aq)} → 2ClO_2^-{}_{(aq)} + 4O_{2(g)} + 5H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • Oxidising agent: Cl2O7. Reducing agent: H2O2.

The Mn3+ ion is unstable in solution and undergoes disproportionation to give Mn2+, MnO2 and H+ ion. Write a balanced ionic equation for the reaction.

\[Oxidation:\ Mn^{3+} + 2H_2O → MnO_2 + 4H^+ + e^-\] \[Reduction:\ Mn^{3+} + e^- → Mn^{2+}\] \[Overall:\ 2Mn^{3+}_{(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → Mn^{2+}_{(aq)} + MnO_{2(s)} + 4H^+_{(aq)}\]

Chlorine is used to purify drinking water. Excess chlorine is removed by treating with sulphur dioxide. Present a balanced equation for this redox change in water.

\[Reduction:\ Cl_2 + 2e^- → 2Cl^-\] \[Oxidation:\ SO_2 + 2H_2O → SO_4^{2-} + 4H^+ + 2e^-\] \[Overall:\ Cl_{2(aq)} + SO_{2(aq)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} → 2Cl^-_{(aq)} + SO_4^{2-}{}_{(aq)} + 4H^+_{(aq)}\]

docs.title: Oxidants, Reductants and Feasibility
docs.text:
Whenever a reaction between an oxidising agent and a reducing agent is carried out, a compound of lower oxidation state is formed if the reducing agent is in excess, and a compound of higher oxidation state is formed if the oxidising agent is in excess. Justify with three illustrations.

\[(i)\ C + O_2\ (limited) → CO\ (C:\ +2),\ \ C + O_2\ (excess) → CO_2\ (C:\ +4)\] \[(ii)\ P_4 + 6Cl_2\ (limited) → 4PCl_3\ (P:\ +3),\ \ P_4 + 10Cl_2\ (excess) → 4PCl_5\ (P:\ +5)\] \[(iii)\ 4Na + O_2\ (limited) → 2Na_2O\ (O:\ -2),\ \ 2Na + O_2\ (excess) → Na_2O_2\ (O:\ -1)\]

In (i) and (ii), the reductant (C, P4) in excess gives the lower oxidation state of the reductant. In (iii), excess oxidant O2 gives Na2O2, where oxygen is in its higher oxidation state (-1 instead of -2).

When concentrated sulphuric acid is added to an inorganic mixture containing chloride, we get colourless pungent HCl gas, but if the mixture contains bromide, we get red vapour of bromine. Why?

  • With chloride, HCl is formed. HCl is a weak reductant and cannot reduce H2SO4:
\[NaCl + H_2SO_4 → NaHSO_4 + HCl\]
  • With bromide, HBr is formed first. HBr is a stronger reductant and reduces H2SO4 to SO2, getting oxidised to red Br2:
\[NaBr + H_2SO_4 → NaHSO_4 + HBr\] \[2HBr + H_2SO_4 → Br_2 + SO_2 + 2H_2O\]

Consider the reactions: 2S2O32-(aq) + I2(s) → S4O62-(aq) + 2I-(aq) S2O32-(aq) + 4Br2(l) + 5H2O(l) → 2SO42-(aq) + 8Br-(aq) + 10H+(aq) Why does the same reductant, thiosulphate, react differently with iodine and bromine?

  • In S2O32-, the average oxidation number of S is +2.

  • Iodine is a weaker oxidant, so it oxidises S only to +2.5 (in S4O62-).

  • Bromine is a stronger oxidant, so it oxidises S all the way to +6 (in SO42-).

Justify giving reactions that among halogens, fluorine is the best oxidant and among hydrohalic compounds, hydroiodic acid is the best reductant.

  • Fluorine has the highest standard reduction potential (2.87 V) and oxidises all other halide ions:
\[F_2 + 2X^- → 2F^- + X_2\ \ (X = Cl,\ Br,\ I)\]
  • Among HX, the H-I bond is the weakest and I- is the largest ion, so it loses its electron most easily. HI can even reduce H2SO4, which HCl cannot:
\[2HI + H_2SO_4 → I_2 + SO_2 + 2H_2O\]

Why does the following reaction occur? XeO64-(aq) + 2F-(aq) + 6H+(aq) → XeO3(g) + F2(g) + 3H2O(l) What conclusion about Na4XeO6 can be drawn from the reaction?

\[\overset{+8}{Xe}O_6^{4-} + 2\overset{-1}{F^-} + 6H^+ → \overset{+6}{Xe}O_3 + \overset{0}{F_2} + 3H_2O\]
  • Xe is reduced from +8 to +6 and F- is oxidised to F2. Since F2 is the strongest common oxidant, XeO64- must be an even stronger oxidant. So Na4XeO6 is a stronger oxidising agent than F2.

Consider the reactions: (a) H3PO2 + 4AgNO3 + 2H2O → H3PO4 + 4Ag + 4HNO3 (b) H3PO2 + 2CuSO4 + 2H2O → H3PO4 + 2Cu + 2H2SO4 (c) C6H5CHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH- → C6H5COO- + 2Ag + 4NH3 + 2H2O (d) C6H5CHO + 2Cu2+ + 5OH- → No change observed. What inference do you draw about the behaviour of Ag+ and Cu2+?

  • H3PO2 is a strong reductant and reduces both Ag+ and Cu2+.

  • Benzaldehyde is a weaker reductant: it reduces Ag+ (Tollens' reagent) but not Cu2+.

  • Hence, Ag+ is a stronger oxidising agent than Cu2+.

Using standard electrode potentials, predict if the reaction between the following is feasible: (a) Fe3+ and I- (b) Ag+ and Cu (c) Fe3+ and Cu (d) Ag and Fe3+ (e) Br2 and Fe2+ Given: E0(Fe3+/Fe2+) = 0.77 V, E0(I2/I-) = 0.54 V, E0(Ag+/Ag) = 0.80 V, E0(Cu2+/Cu) = 0.34 V, E0(Br2/Br-) = 1.09 V

A reaction is feasible if E0cell = E0(species reduced) - E0(species oxidised) is positive.

\[(a)\ 2Fe^{3+} + 2I^- → 2Fe^{2+} + I_2:\ E^0_{cell} = 0.77 - 0.54 = +0.23\ V\ (feasible)\] \[(b)\ 2Ag^+ + Cu → 2Ag + Cu^{2+}:\ E^0_{cell} = 0.80 - 0.34 = +0.46\ V\ (feasible)\] \[(c)\ 2Fe^{3+} + Cu → 2Fe^{2+} + Cu^{2+}:\ E^0_{cell} = 0.77 - 0.34 = +0.43\ V\ (feasible)\] \[(d)\ Ag + Fe^{3+} → Ag^+ + Fe^{2+}:\ E^0_{cell} = 0.77 - 0.80 = -0.03\ V\ (not\ feasible)\] \[(e)\ Br_2 + 2Fe^{2+} → 2Br^- + 2Fe^{3+}:\ E^0_{cell} = 1.09 - 0.77 = +0.32\ V\ (feasible)\]

Arrange the following metals in the order in which they displace each other from the solution of their salts: Al, Cu, Fe, Mg and Zn.

A metal displaces any metal below it in the activity series (more negative E0 means a stronger reductant):

\[Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu\]

Given the standard electrode potentials: K+/K = -2.93 V, Ag+/Ag = 0.80 V, Hg2+/Hg = 0.79 V, Mg2+/Mg = -2.37 V, Cr3+/Cr = -0.74 V. Arrange these metals in increasing order of reducing power.

The lower (more negative) the reduction potential, the greater the reducing power:

\[Ag < Hg < Cr < Mg < K\]

Depict the galvanic cell in which the reaction Zn(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + 2Ag(s) takes place. Show: (i) which electrode is negatively charged (ii) the carriers of current in the cell (iii) the reaction at each electrode.

\[Zn_{(s)}/Zn^{2+}_{(aq)} || Ag^+_{(aq)}/Ag_{(s)}\]

  • (i) The zinc electrode (anode) is negatively charged, because electrons are released there.

  • (ii) Electrons carry the current in the external wire (from Zn to Ag); ions carry it inside the solutions and through the salt bridge.

  • (iii) Electrode reactions:

\[Anode:\ Zn_{(s)} → Zn^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode:\ 2Ag^+_{(aq)} + 2e^- → 2Ag_{(s)}\]

docs.title: Stoichiometry
docs.text:
In Ostwald's process for the manufacture of nitric acid, the first step involves the oxidation of ammonia gas by oxygen gas to give nitric oxide gas and steam. What is the maximum weight of nitric oxide that can be obtained starting only with 10.00 g of ammonia and 20.00 g of oxygen?

\[4NH_{3(g)} + 5O_{2(g)} → 4NO_{(g)} + 6H_2O_{(g)}\] \[Moles\ of\ NH_3 = {10.00 \over 17} = 0.588\ mol\] \[Moles\ of\ O_2 = {20.00 \over 32} = 0.625\ mol\]
  • O2 needed for 0.588 mol NH3:
\[0.588 \times {5 \over 4} = 0.735\ mol\]
  • Only 0.625 mol O2 is available, so O2 is the limiting reagent.
\[Moles\ of\ NO = 0.625 \times {4 \over 5} = 0.500\ mol\] \[Mass\ of\ NO = 0.500 \times 30 = 15.0\ g\]

docs.title: Redox Reactions | Redox Titrations and Electrode Processes
Redox Reactions | Redox Titrations and Electrode Processes
Redox Titrations
docs.text:
• In acid-base titrations, the strength of one solution is found against another using a pH sensitive indicator.
  • Similarly, in a redox titration, the strength of a reductant or oxidant is determined using a redox sensitive indicator.
  • The end point can be detected in three ways, depending on the reagent used.

docs.title: 1. Self indicator: Permanganate titrations
docs.text:
• The permanganate ion, MnO4-, is intensely coloured, so it acts as its own indicator.
  • When the last of the reductant (Fe2+ or C2O42-) is oxidised, the first lasting tinge of pink colour appears. This is visible at an MnO4- concentration as low as 10-6 mol dm-3 (10-6 mol L-1).
  • This ensures only a minimal "overshoot" in colour beyond the equivalence point, i.e. the point where the reductant and oxidant are equal in terms of their mole stoichiometry.

docs.title: 2. External redox indicator: Dichromate titrations
docs.text:
• Cr2O72- is not a self indicator because it gives no dramatic colour change.
  • Instead, an indicator such as diphenylamine is added. Just after the equivalence point, dichromate oxidises diphenylamine to produce an intense blue colour, which signals the end point.

docs.title: 3. Iodometric titrations
docs.text:
• This method is used for reagents that can oxidise I- ions, for example Cu(II):
\[2Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + 4I^-_{(aq)} → Cu_2I_{2(s)} + I_{2(aq)}\]
  • The liberated iodine is then titrated with thiosulphate ions, which is also a redox reaction:
\[I_{2(aq)} + 2S_2O_3^{2-}{}_{(aq)} → 2I^-_{(aq)} + S_4O_6^{2-}{}_{(aq)}\]
  • Iodine is insoluble in water but stays in solution containing KI as KI3.
  • Starch gives an intense blue colour with iodine. This colour disappears as soon as all the iodine is consumed by thiosulphate, so the end point is easy to track. The rest is only stoichiometric calculation.

docs.title: Limitations of the Concept of Oxidation Number
docs.text:
• The concept of redox processes has kept evolving: from addition/removal of oxygen, to electron transfer, to change in oxidation number.
  • In the modern view, oxidation is a decrease in electron density and reduction is an increase in electron density around the atom(s) involved in the reaction.

docs.title: Redox Couple
docs.text:
• When a zinc rod is dipped in copper sulphate solution, electrons are transferred directly from zinc to Cu2+ ions, and heat is evolved.
  • If instead the zinc and copper are kept in separate beakers (zinc in ZnSO4, copper in CuSO4), both the oxidised and reduced forms of the same species are present at each metal-solution interface.

Definition

A redox couple is the oxidised and reduced forms of a substance taking part in an oxidation or reduction half reaction.

  • It is written with the oxidised form first, separated from the reduced form by a vertical line or slash that represents an interface (e.g. solid/solution). Examples: Zn2+/Zn and Cu2+/Cu.

docs.title: Electrode Processes: Daniell Cell
docs.text:
• The two beakers are connected by a salt bridge (a U-tube containing KCl or NH4NO3 solution set in agar-agar jelly), and the two rods are connected by a metallic wire through an ammeter and a switch. This set-up is the Daniell cell.
  • With the switch off, no reaction occurs. With the switch on:
  • Electrons now flow from Zn to Cu2+ indirectly, through the external wire. The direction of current is opposite to the direction of electron flow.
  • Inside the cell, the circuit is completed by migration of ions through the salt bridge.
  • Current flows only because there is a potential difference between the two rods, which are called electrodes.
\[Anode\ (oxidation):\ Zn_{(s)} → Zn^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2e^-\] \[Cathode\ (reduction):\ Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2e^- → Cu_{(s)}\] \[Overall:\ Zn_{(s)} + Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} → Zn^{2+}_{(aq)} + Cu_{(s)}\]
  • So the same redox reaction now produces electrical energy instead of only heat.

docs.title: Electrode Potential and Redox Strength
docs.text:
• The potential associated with each electrode is its electrode potential. When all species are at unit concentration (gases at 1 atm) and 298 K, it is called the standard electrode potential, E0. By convention, E0 of the hydrogen electrode (H+/H2) is 0.00 V.
  • E0 (written as a reduction potential) measures the tendency of a redox couple to stay in the reduced or oxidised form:
  • A negative E0 means the couple is a stronger reducing agent than H+/H2.
  • A positive E0 means the couple is a weaker reducing agent (i.e. a better oxidising agent) than H+/H2.

Some standard reduction potentials at 298 K:

Reaction (Oxidised form + ne- → Reduced form) E0 / V F2(g) + 2e- → 2F- 2.87 MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- → Mn2+ + 4H2O 1.51 Cl2(g) + 2e- → 2Cl- 1.36 Cr2O72- + 14H+ + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O 1.33 Br2 + 2e- → 2Br- 1.09 Ag+ + e- → Ag(s) 0.80 Fe3+ + e- → Fe2+ 0.77 I2(s) + 2e- → 2I- 0.54 Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu(s) 0.34 2H+ + 2e- → H2(g) 0.00 Fe2+ + 2e- → Fe(s) -0.44 Zn2+ + 2e- → Zn(s) -0.76 Al3+ + 3e- → Al(s) -1.66 Mg2+ + 2e- → Mg(s) -2.36 Na+ + e- → Na(s) -2.71 K+ + e- → K(s) -2.93 Li+ + e- → Li(s) -3.05
  • Going up the table, the strength of the oxidising agent (left side) increases. Going down, the strength of the reducing agent (right side) increases.
  • A redox reaction is feasible when the oxidising agent of a couple higher in the table reacts with the reducing agent of a couple lower in the table (i.e. when the resulting E0cell is positive).

Note

The detailed theory of electrode potential, the standard hydrogen electrode, cell EMF and the Nernst equation is covered in the Electrochemistry chapter: Electrode Potential, EMF of a Cell and Nernst Equation.

docs.title: Redox Reactions | Types of Redox Reactions
Redox Reactions | Types of Redox Reactions
docs.text: Redox reactions can be classified into four types: combination, decomposition, displacement and disproportionation reactions. In the equations below, oxidation numbers are written above the atoms.

docs.title: 1. Combination Reactions
docs.text:
• A combination reaction can be written as:
\[A + B → C\]
  • For it to be a redox reaction, either A or B or both must be in the elemental form.
  • All combustion reactions that use elemental dioxygen, and many reactions with other elements, are combination redox reactions.
\[\overset{0}{C}_{(s)} + \overset{0}{O_2}_{(g)} \xrightarrow{Δ} \overset{+4}{C}\overset{-2}{O_2}_{(g)}\] \[3\overset{0}{Mg}_{(s)} + \overset{0}{N_2}_{(g)} \xrightarrow{Δ} \overset{+2}{Mg_3}\overset{-3}{N_2}_{(s)}\] \[\overset{-4}{C}\overset{+1}{H_4}_{(g)} + 2\overset{0}{O_2}_{(g)} \xrightarrow{Δ} \overset{+4}{C}\overset{-2}{O_2}_{(g)} + 2\overset{+1}{H_2}\overset{-2}{O}_{(l)}\]
  • Note that the oxidation number of hydrogen does not change in the combustion of methane; only carbon is oxidised.

docs.title: 2. Decomposition Reactions
docs.text:
• Decomposition is the opposite of combination: a compound breaks down into two or more components, at least one of which must be in the elemental state.
\[2\overset{+1}{H_2}\overset{-2}{O}_{(l)} \xrightarrow{Δ} 2\overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)} + \overset{0}{O_2}_{(g)}\] \[2\overset{+1}{Na}\overset{-1}{H}_{(s)} \xrightarrow{Δ} 2\overset{0}{Na}_{(s)} + \overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)}\] \[2\overset{+1}{K}\overset{+5}{Cl}\overset{-2}{O_3}_{(s)} \xrightarrow{Δ} 2\overset{+1}{K}\overset{-1}{Cl}_{(s)} + 3\overset{0}{O_2}_{(g)}\]
  • In the decomposition of KClO3, the oxidation number of potassium does not change.
  • Not all decomposition reactions are redox. In the decomposition of calcium carbonate, no element changes its oxidation number:
\[\overset{+2}{Ca}\overset{+4}{C}\overset{-2}{O_3}_{(s)} \xrightarrow{Δ} \overset{+2}{Ca}\overset{-2}{O}_{(s)} + \overset{+4}{C}\overset{-2}{O_2}_{(g)}\]

docs.title: 3. Displacement Reactions
docs.text:
• In a displacement reaction, an ion (or atom) in a compound is replaced by an ion (or atom) of another element:
\[X + YZ → XZ + Y\]
  • Displacement reactions are of two types: metal displacement and non-metal displacement.

docs.title: (a) Metal Displacement
docs.text:
• A metal in a compound is displaced by another metal in the uncombined state. These reactions are widely used in metallurgy to obtain pure metals from their ores.
\[\overset{+2}{Cu}SO_{4(aq)} + \overset{0}{Zn}_{(s)} → \overset{0}{Cu}_{(s)} + \overset{+2}{Zn}SO_{4(aq)}\] \[\overset{+5}{V_2}O_{5(s)} + 5\overset{0}{Ca}_{(s)} \xrightarrow{Δ} 2\overset{0}{V}_{(s)} + 5\overset{+2}{Ca}O_{(s)}\] \[\overset{+4}{Ti}Cl_{4(l)} + 2\overset{0}{Mg}_{(s)} \xrightarrow{Δ} \overset{0}{Ti}_{(s)} + 2\overset{+2}{Mg}Cl_{2(s)}\] \[\overset{+3}{Cr_2}O_{3(s)} + 2\overset{0}{Al}_{(s)} \xrightarrow{Δ} \overset{+3}{Al_2}O_{3(s)} + 2\overset{0}{Cr}_{(s)}\]
  • In each case, the displacing metal is a better reducing agent than the metal being displaced, i.e. it has a greater tendency to lose electrons.

docs.title: (b) Non-metal Displacement
docs.text: • These mainly include hydrogen displacement and, rarely, oxygen displacement.

docs.title: Hydrogen displacement from water
docs.text:
• All alkali metals and some alkaline earth metals (Ca, Sr, Ba) are very good reductants and displace hydrogen from cold water:
\[2\overset{0}{Na}_{(s)} + 2\overset{+1}{H_2}O_{(l)} → 2\overset{+1}{Na}OH_{(aq)} + \overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)}\] \[\overset{0}{Ca}_{(s)} + 2\overset{+1}{H_2}O_{(l)} → \overset{+2}{Ca}(OH)_{2(aq)} + \overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)}\]
  • Less active metals like magnesium and iron react with steam to give dihydrogen:
\[\overset{0}{Mg}_{(s)} + 2\overset{+1}{H_2}O_{(l)} \xrightarrow{Δ} \overset{+2}{Mg}(OH)_{2(s)} + \overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)}\] \[2\overset{0}{Fe}_{(s)} + 3\overset{+1}{H_2}O_{(l)} \xrightarrow{Δ} \overset{+3}{Fe_2}O_{3(s)} + 3\overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)}\]

docs.title: Hydrogen displacement from acids
docs.text:
• Many metals which do not react with cold water (and even some like cadmium and tin which do not react with steam) displace hydrogen from acids:
\[\overset{0}{Zn}_{(s)} + 2\overset{+1}{H}Cl_{(aq)} → \overset{+2}{Zn}Cl_{2(aq)} + \overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)}\] \[\overset{0}{Mg}_{(s)} + 2\overset{+1}{H}Cl_{(aq)} → \overset{+2}{Mg}Cl_{2(aq)} + \overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)}\] \[\overset{0}{Fe}_{(s)} + 2\overset{+1}{H}Cl_{(aq)} → \overset{+2}{Fe}Cl_{2(aq)} + \overset{0}{H_2}_{(g)}\]
  • These reactions are used to prepare dihydrogen in the laboratory. The rate of hydrogen evolution reflects reactivity: slowest for Fe and fastest for Mg.
  • Very less active metals like silver and gold, which may occur in the native state, do not react even with hydrochloric acid.

docs.title: Halogen displacement
docs.text:
• The oxidising power of halogens decreases from fluorine to iodine. Fluorine is so reactive that it even displaces oxygen from water:
\[2\overset{+1}{H_2}\overset{-2}{O}_{(l)} + 2\overset{0}{F_2}_{(g)} → 4\overset{+1}{H}\overset{-1}{F}_{(aq)} + \overset{0}{O_2}_{(g)}\]
  • For this reason, displacement reactions of Cl, Br and I using fluorine are generally not carried out in aqueous solution.
  • Chlorine displaces bromide and iodide ions, and bromine displaces iodide ions:
\[\overset{0}{Cl_2}_{(g)} + 2\overset{-1}{Br^-}_{(aq)} → 2\overset{-1}{Cl^-}_{(aq)} + \overset{0}{Br_2}_{(l)}\] \[\overset{0}{Cl_2}_{(g)} + 2\overset{-1}{I^-}_{(aq)} → 2\overset{-1}{Cl^-}_{(aq)} + \overset{0}{I_2}_{(s)}\] \[\overset{0}{Br_2}_{(l)} + 2\overset{-1}{I^-}_{(aq)} → 2\overset{-1}{Br^-}_{(aq)} + \overset{0}{I_2}_{(s)}\]
  • Br2 and I2 are coloured and dissolve in CCl4, so they can be identified from the colour of the solution. This is the basis of the Layer Test for Br- and I- in the laboratory.
  • Recovery of halogens from halides requires oxidation:
\[2X^- → X_2 + 2e^-\]
  • Cl-, Br- and I- can be oxidised by chemical means. But fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent, so there is no chemical way to convert F- to F2. The only way is to oxidise F- electrolytically.

docs.title: 4. Disproportionation Reactions
docs.text:
• In a disproportionation reaction, an element in one oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
  • The reacting substance always contains an element that can exist in at least three oxidation states. It is present in an intermediate state, and both higher and lower states are formed.
  • Decomposition of hydrogen peroxide is a familiar example, where oxygen goes from -1 to 0 (in O2) and to -2 (in H2O):
\[2\overset{+1}{H_2}\overset{-1}{O_2}_{(aq)} → 2\overset{+1}{H_2}\overset{-2}{O}_{(l)} + \overset{0}{O_2}_{(g)}\]
  • Phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine disproportionate in alkaline medium:
\[\overset{0}{P_4}_{(s)} + 3OH^-_{(aq)} + 3H_2O_{(l)} → \overset{-3}{P}H_{3(g)} + 3H_2\overset{+1}{P}O^-_{2(aq)}\] \[\overset{0}{S_8}_{(s)} + 12OH^-_{(aq)} → 4\overset{-2}{S^{2-}}_{(aq)} + 2\overset{+2}{S_2}O^{2-}_{3(aq)} + 6H_2O_{(l)}\] \[\overset{0}{Cl_2}_{(g)} + 2OH^-_{(aq)} → \overset{+1}{Cl}O^-_{(aq)} + \overset{-1}{Cl^-}_{(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • The last reaction forms household bleaching agents. The hypochlorite ion (ClO-) oxidises the colour-bearing stains to colourless compounds.
  • Bromine and iodine behave like chlorine. But fluorine reacts with alkali differently:
\[2F_{2(g)} + 2OH^-_{(aq)} → 2F^-_{(aq)} + OF_{2(g)} + H_2O_{(l)}\]
  • Being the most electronegative element, fluorine cannot show a positive oxidation state, so it does not disproportionate. (Fluorine will also attack water here to produce some oxygen.)

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Which of the following species do not show disproportionation reaction and why? ClO-, ClO2-, ClO3- and ClO4-. Also write the reaction for each species that disproportionates.

  • ClO4- does not disproportionate because chlorine in it is already in its highest oxidation state, +7. It can only be reduced, not oxidised.

  • The other three disproportionate as follows:

\[3\overset{+1}{Cl}O^- → 2\overset{-1}{Cl^-} + \overset{+5}{Cl}O_3^-\] \[6\overset{+3}{Cl}O_2^- \xrightarrow{h\nu} 4\overset{+5}{Cl}O_3^- + 2\overset{-1}{Cl^-}\] \[4\overset{+5}{Cl}O_3^- → \overset{-1}{Cl^-} + 3\overset{+7}{Cl}O_4^-\]

Suggest a scheme of classification of the following redox reactions: (a) N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g) (b) 2Pb(NO3)2(s) → 2PbO(s) + 4NO2(g) + O2(g) (c) NaH(s) + H2O(l) → NaOH(aq) + H2(g) (d) 2NO2(g) + 2OH-(aq) → NO2-(aq) + NO3-(aq) + H2O(l)

  • (a) Nitric oxide is formed by combining the elements nitrogen and oxygen: combination redox reaction.

  • (b) Lead nitrate breaks down into three components (one of them elemental O2): decomposition redox reaction.

  • (c) Hydrogen of water is displaced by the hydride ion as dihydrogen gas: displacement redox reaction.

  • (d) Nitrogen in NO2 (+4) changes to NO2- (+3) and NO3- (+5): disproportionation redox reaction.

Why do the following reactions proceed differently? Pb3O4 + 8HCl → 3PbCl2 + Cl2 + 4H2O Pb3O4 + 4HNO3 → 2Pb(NO3)2 + PbO2 + 2H2O

  • Pb3O4 is actually a stoichiometric mixture of 2 mol PbO and 1 mol PbO2.

  • In PbO2, lead is in the +4 state, whereas its stable state is +2 (as in PbO). So PbO2 acts as an oxidant and can oxidise Cl- of HCl to Cl2. PbO is a basic oxide and simply undergoes an acid-base reaction.

  • So, the reaction with HCl splits into:

\[2PbO + 4HCl → 2PbCl_2 + 2H_2O\ (acid-base\ reaction)\] \[\overset{+4}{Pb}O_2 + 4H\overset{-1}{Cl} → \overset{+2}{Pb}Cl_2 + \overset{0}{Cl_2} + 2H_2O\ (redox\ reaction)\]
  • HNO3 is itself an oxidising agent, so no redox reaction takes place between PbO2 and HNO3. Only the acid-base reaction occurs with PbO:
\[2PbO + 4HNO_3 → 2Pb(NO_3)_2 + 2H_2O\]
  • It is the passive nature of PbO2 towards HNO3 that makes the reaction different from the one with HCl.

docs.title: Solid State | Close Packed Structures and Voids
Solid State | Close Packed Structures and Voids
docs.text: In solids, the constituent particles are close-packed, leaving the minimum vacant space. To understand this, we treat the particles as identical hard spheres and build the structure in three steps: one dimension, two dimensions and three dimensions.

docs.title: Coordination Number
docs.text: The number of nearest neighbours of a particle is called its coordination number.

docs.title: Close Packing in One Dimension
docs.text:
• There is only one way to arrange spheres in one dimension: in a row, each touching the next.
  • Each sphere touches two neighbours. So the coordination number is 2.

docs.title: Close Packing in Two Dimensions
docs.text: A two dimensional layer is made by placing rows of close-packed spheres next to each other. This can be done in two ways.

docs.title: 1. Square Close Packing (AAA type)
docs.text:
• The second row is placed exactly above the first row, so the spheres are aligned both horizontally and vertically.
  • If the first row is called 'A', the second row is also 'A', giving an AAA arrangement.
  • Each sphere touches four neighbours, so the two dimensional coordination number is 4.
  • Joining the centres of these four neighbours gives a square. Hence this is called square close packing.

docs.title: 2. Hexagonal Close Packing (ABAB type)
docs.text:
• The second row is placed in a staggered manner so that its spheres fit into the depressions of the first row. The second row is called 'B'.
  • The third row lines up with the first ('A'), the fourth with the second ('B'), giving an ABAB arrangement.
  • Each sphere touches six neighbours, so the two dimensional coordination number is 6. The centres of these six spheres lie at the corners of a regular hexagon. Hence this is called two dimensional hexagonal close packing.
  • This packing has less free space and is more efficient than square close packing.
  • The layer has triangular voids. In one row the apex of the triangles points upwards and in the next row downwards.

docs.title: Close Packing in Three Dimensions
docs.text: Three dimensional structures are made by stacking two dimensional layers one above the other.

docs.title: 1. From Square Close-Packed Layers
docs.text:
• The second layer is placed exactly above the first, so the spheres of all layers are aligned horizontally and vertically.
  • This gives an AAA... pattern. The lattice formed is a simple cubic lattice and its unit cell is the primitive cubic unit cell.

docs.title: (a) Placing the second layer over the first
docs.text:
• A hexagonal close-packed layer 'A' is taken and a similar layer 'B' is placed over it so that the spheres of layer B sit in the depressions of layer A.
  • Not all triangular voids of the first layer are covered by the second layer. This creates two types of voids:
    • Tetrahedral void: Wherever a sphere of the second layer is directly above a void of the first layer (or vice versa), a void surrounded by four spheres is formed. Joining the centres of these four spheres gives a tetrahedron.
    • Octahedral void: Wherever a triangular void of the second layer lies above a triangular void of the first layer with the triangles pointing in opposite directions (not overlapping), a void surrounded by six spheres is formed. Joining the centres of these six spheres gives an octahedron.
  • If the number of close-packed spheres is N:
\[Number\ of\ octahedral\ voids = N\] \[Number\ of\ tetrahedral\ voids = 2N\]

docs.title: (b) Placing the third layer over the second
docs.text:
There are two possibilities:

(i) Covering tetrahedral voids - hcp structure

  • The spheres of the third layer are placed over the tetrahedral voids of the second layer. They are then exactly above the spheres of the first layer.
  • The pattern repeats in alternate layers: ABAB...
  • This is called the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Examples: Magnesium, zinc.

(ii) Covering octahedral voids - ccp structure

  • The spheres of the third layer are placed over the octahedral voids of the second layer. They are then aligned with neither the first nor the second layer, so this layer is called 'C'.
  • Only the fourth layer lines up with the first. The pattern is ABCABC...
  • This is called the cubic close-packed (ccp) or face-centred cubic (fcc) structure. Examples: Copper, silver.

Conclusion

  • Both hcp and ccp are highly efficient: 74% of the space in the crystal is filled.
  • In both structures, each sphere is in contact with twelve spheres. So the coordination number is 12.
Arrangement Pattern Coordination number One dimension Single row 2 Square close packing (2D) AAA 4 Hexagonal close packing (2D) ABAB 6 Simple cubic (3D) AAA 6 hcp (3D) ABAB 12 ccp or fcc (3D) ABCABC 12

docs.title: Formula of a Compound and Number of Voids Filled
docs.text:
• In ionic solids, the bigger ions (usually anions) form the close-packed structure and the smaller ions (usually cations) occupy the voids.
  • If the cation is small enough, it occupies tetrahedral voids. If it is bigger, it occupies octahedral voids.
  • Not all voids are filled. The fraction of tetrahedral or octahedral voids occupied depends on the chemical formula of the compound.

A compound is formed by two elements X and Y. Atoms of Y (as anions) make ccp and those of X (as cations) occupy all the octahedral voids. What is the formula of the compound?

  • Let the number of Y atoms in ccp = N.
  • Number of octahedral voids = N.
  • All octahedral voids are occupied by X, so number of X atoms = N.
\[X : Y = N : N = 1 : 1\]

Hence, the formula of the compound is XY.

Atoms of element B form hcp lattice and those of element A occupy 2/3rd of tetrahedral voids. What is the formula of the compound formed by A and B?

  • Let the number of B atoms = N.
  • Number of tetrahedral voids = 2N.
\[Number\ of\ A\ atoms = {2 \over 3} \times 2N = {4N \over 3}\] \[A : B = {4N \over 3} : N = 4 : 3\]

Hence, the formula of the compound is A4B3.

docs.title: Locating Voids in a ccp (fcc) Unit Cell
1. Tetrahedral Voids
docs.text:
• Divide the fcc unit cell into eight small cubes.
  • Each small cube has atoms at alternate corners, i.e. 4 atoms. Joining them gives a regular tetrahedron, so there is one tetrahedral void in each small cube.
  • So there are 8 tetrahedral voids per unit cell. Since a ccp unit cell has 4 atoms, the number of tetrahedral voids is twice the number of atoms.

docs.title: 2. Octahedral Voids
docs.text:
• The body-centre of the cube is not occupied, but it is surrounded by six atoms at the face-centres. Joining these gives an octahedron. So there is one octahedral void at the body-centre.
  • There is also an octahedral void at the centre of each of the 12 edges. Each edge is shared between four unit cells, so only 1/4 of each such void belongs to one unit cell.
\[Octahedral\ void\ at\ body\ centre = 1\] \[Octahedral\ voids\ at\ edge\ centres = 12 \times {1 \over 4} = 3\] \[∴\ Total\ octahedral\ voids = 4\]
  • So the number of octahedral voids per ccp unit cell (4) equals the number of atoms (4).

Conclusion

For a ccp (fcc) unit cell with 4 atoms: tetrahedral voids = 8 and octahedral voids = 4.

docs.title: Solid State | Crystal Lattices and Unit Cells
Solid State | Crystal Lattices and Unit Cells
docs.text: The main characteristic of a crystalline solid is a regular and repeating pattern of its constituent particles. If each particle is shown as a point, the resulting regular three dimensional arrangement of points in space is called a crystal lattice.

docs.title: Crystal Lattice
docs.text:
• Each point in a lattice is called a lattice point or lattice site.
  • Each lattice point represents one constituent particle, which may be an atom, a molecule (group of atoms) or an ion.
  • Lattice points are joined by straight lines to bring out the geometry of the lattice.
  • There are only 14 possible three dimensional lattices. These are called Bravais lattices, after the French mathematician who first described them.

docs.title: Unit Cell
docs.text:
A unit cell is the smallest portion of a crystal lattice which, when repeated in different directions, generates the entire lattice.

A unit cell is characterised by six parameters:

  • Its three edge lengths: a, b and c. These edges may or may not be mutually perpendicular.
  • The three angles between the edges:
    • α - angle between edges b and c
    • β - angle between edges a and c
    • γ - angle between edges a and b
\[Unit\ cell\ parameters:\ a,\ b,\ c,\ \alpha,\ \beta,\ \gamma\]

docs.title: 1. Primitive Unit Cell
docs.text: When constituent particles are present only at the corner positions of a unit cell, it is called a primitive (or simple) unit cell.

docs.title: 2. Centred Unit Cells
docs.text:
When a unit cell has one or more particles at positions other than the corners, in addition to those at the corners, it is called a centred unit cell. These are of three types:

  • Body-centred unit cell: One particle at the body-centre, besides the ones at the corners.
  • Face-centred unit cell: One particle at the centre of each face, besides the ones at the corners.
  • End-centred unit cell: One particle at the centre of any two opposite faces, besides the ones at the corners.

docs.title: Seven Crystal Systems
docs.text:
• There are seven types of primitive unit cells, called the seven crystal systems.
  • Some of these systems can also form centred unit cells. Counting all possible primitive and centred variations gives the 14 Bravais lattices.
Crystal system Possible variations Edge lengths Axial angles Examples Cubic Primitive, Body-centred, Face-centred a = b = c α = β = γ = 90° NaCl, Zinc blende, Cu Tetragonal Primitive, Body-centred a = b ≠ c α = β = γ = 90° White tin, SnO2, TiO2, CaSO4 Orthorhombic Primitive, Body-centred, Face-centred, End-centred a ≠ b ≠ c α = β = γ = 90° Rhombic sulphur, KNO3, BaSO4 Hexagonal Primitive a = b ≠ c α = β = 90°, γ = 120° Graphite, ZnO, CdS Rhombohedral or Trigonal Primitive a = b = c α = β = γ ≠ 90° Calcite (CaCO3), HgS (cinnabar) Monoclinic Primitive, End-centred a ≠ b ≠ c α = γ = 90°, β ≠ 90° Monoclinic sulphur, Na2SO4.10H2O Triclinic Primitive a ≠ b ≠ c α ≠ β ≠ γ ≠ 90° K2Cr2O7, CuSO4.5H2O, H3BO3

Number of Bravais lattices in each system

Cubic (3) + Tetragonal (2) + Orthorhombic (4) + Monoclinic (2) + Hexagonal (1) + Rhombohedral (1) + Triclinic (1) = 14

docs.title: Unit Cells of the 14 Bravais Lattices
Number of Atoms in a Unit Cell
docs.text:
• A crystal lattice is made of a very large number of unit cells, and every lattice point is occupied by one particle.
  • A particle at a corner, face or edge is shared between neighbouring unit cells. So only a fraction of it belongs to one unit cell.
Position of atom Shared between Contribution to one unit cell Corner 8 unit cells 1/8 Face-centre 2 unit cells 1/2 Edge-centre 4 unit cells 1/4 Body-centre 1 unit cell (not shared) 1

docs.title: 1. Primitive (Simple) Cubic Unit Cell
docs.text:
• Atoms are present only at the 8 corners. Each corner atom is shared between 8 unit cells.
\[Number\ of\ atoms = 8 \times {1 \over 8} = 1\ atom\]

docs.title: 2. Body-Centred Cubic (bcc) Unit Cell
docs.text:
• Atoms are present at the 8 corners and one atom at the body-centre. The body-centre atom wholly belongs to the unit cell.
\[8\ corners \times {1 \over 8} = 1\ atom\] \[1\ body\ centre\ atom = 1 \times 1 = 1\ atom\] \[∴\ Total\ atoms\ per\ unit\ cell = 2\]

docs.title: 3. Face-Centred Cubic (fcc) Unit Cell
docs.text:
• Atoms are present at the 8 corners and at the centre of all 6 faces. Each face-centre atom is shared between two adjacent unit cells.
\[8\ corners \times {1 \over 8} = 1\ atom\] \[6\ face\ centres \times {1 \over 2} = 3\ atoms\] \[∴\ Total\ atoms\ per\ unit\ cell = 4\]

Conclusion

Unit cell Atoms per unit cell (z) Simple cubic 1 Body-centred cubic 2 Face-centred cubic 4

docs.title: Solid State | Electrical and Magnetic Properties
Solid State | Electrical and Magnetic Properties
docs.text: Solids show an amazing range of electrical conductivities, extending over 27 orders of magnitude, from 10-20 to 107 ohm-1 m-1. Their magnetic behaviour also varies widely. Both properties can be explained from their structure and electronic configuration.

docs.title: Electrical Properties
docs.text:
On the basis of conductivity, solids are classified into three types:

Type Conductivity range (ohm-1 m-1) Examples Conductors 104 to 107 Metals (about 107) Semiconductors 10-6 to 104 Silicon, germanium Insulators 10-20 to 10-10 Glass, rubber
  • A conductor may conduct electricity by movement of electrons (metallic conductors) or ions (electrolytes).

docs.title: Band Theory
docs.text:
• In a metal, the atomic orbitals of metal atoms form molecular orbitals that are so close in energy that they form a band.
  • The filled band of valence electrons is called the valence band. The next higher, unoccupied band is called the conduction band.
  • The energy gap between them is called the forbidden zone or band gap.

docs.title: 1. Conduction of Electricity in Metals
docs.text:
• Metals conduct electricity in solid as well as molten state.
  • Conductivity depends on the number of valence electrons available per atom.
  • If the band is partially filled, or it overlaps with a higher unoccupied conduction band, electrons can flow easily under an applied electric field. So the metal conducts.

docs.title: 2. Insulators
docs.text:
• The gap between the filled valence band and the conduction band is large.
  • Electrons cannot jump to the conduction band, so the substance has very small conductivity.

docs.title: 3. Conduction of Electricity in Semiconductors
docs.text:
• The gap between the valence band and conduction band is small, so some electrons can jump to the conduction band and show some conductivity.
  • Conductivity of semiconductors increases with rise in temperature, since more electrons can jump to the conduction band. (In metals, conductivity decreases with temperature.)
  • Pure substances like silicon and germanium that behave this way are called intrinsic semiconductors.

docs.title: Doping
docs.text:
• The conductivity of intrinsic semiconductors is too low to be of practical use.
  • It is increased by adding an appropriate amount of a suitable impurity. This process is called doping.
  • The impurity can be electron-rich or electron-deficient compared to silicon or germanium. Such impurities introduce electronic defects.

docs.title: 1. n-type Semiconductors (Electron-rich impurities)
docs.text:
• Silicon and germanium belong to group 14 and have four valence electrons. In their crystals each atom forms four covalent bonds with its neighbours.
  • When doped with a group 15 element like P or As (five valence electrons), the impurity atom occupies some lattice sites.
  • Four of its five electrons form four covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms. The fifth electron is extra and becomes delocalised.
  • These delocalised electrons increase the conductivity. Since the conductivity is due to negatively charged electrons, this is called an n-type semiconductor.

docs.title: 2. p-type Semiconductors (Electron-deficit impurities)
docs.text:
• When silicon or germanium is doped with a group 13 element like B, Al or Ga (three valence electrons), the place where the fourth electron is missing is called an electron hole or electron vacancy.
  • An electron from a neighbouring atom can fill the hole, but it leaves a new hole at its original position. So it looks as if the hole is moving in the direction opposite to the electron.
  • Under an electric field, electrons move towards the positive plate through the holes, but it appears as if positively charged holes are moving towards the negative plate. This is called a p-type semiconductor.
Property n-type p-type Dopant Group 15 (P, As) Group 13 (B, Al, Ga) Nature of impurity Electron-rich Electron-deficient Charge carriers Extra electrons Holes

docs.title: Applications of n-type and p-type Semiconductors
docs.text:
• Diode: A combination of n-type and p-type semiconductors, used as a rectifier.
  • Transistors: Made by sandwiching a layer of one type of semiconductor between two layers of the other type. npn and pnp transistors are used to detect or amplify radio or audio signals.
  • Solar cell: An efficient photo-diode used to convert light energy into electrical energy.

docs.title: 13-15 and 12-16 Compounds
docs.text:
• Combinations of groups 13 and 15, or 12 and 16, are prepared to simulate the average valence of four as in Ge or Si.
  • 13-15 compounds: InSb, AlP, GaAs. Gallium arsenide (GaAs) semiconductors have very fast response and have revolutionised the design of semiconductor devices.
  • 12-16 compounds: ZnS, CdS, CdSe, HgTe.
  • In these compounds, the bonds are not perfectly covalent. Their ionic character depends on the electronegativities of the two elements.

docs.title: Electrical Properties of Transition Metal Oxides
docs.text:
• TiO, CrO2 and ReO3 behave like metals. ReO3 is like metallic copper in its conductivity and appearance.
  • VO, VO2, VO3 and TiO3 show metallic or insulating properties depending on temperature.

docs.title: Magnetic Properties
docs.text:
• Every substance has some magnetic property, which originates from its electrons. Each electron behaves like a tiny magnet.
  • The magnetic moment of an electron comes from two types of motion:
    • its orbital motion around the nucleus
    • its spin around its own axis
  • A moving charge acts like a small loop of current, which has a magnetic moment. So each electron has a permanent spin and an orbital magnetic moment.
  • This magnetic moment is very small and is measured in Bohr magneton, μB.
\[1\ \mu_B = 9.27 \times 10^{-24}\ A\ m^2\]

On the basis of magnetic properties, substances are classified into five categories:

docs.title: 1. Paramagnetism
docs.text:
• Paramagnetic substances are weakly attracted by a magnetic field and are magnetised in the same direction as the field.
  • They lose their magnetism when the field is removed.
  • Paramagnetism is due to the presence of one or more unpaired electrons, which are attracted by the magnetic field.
  • Examples: O2, Cu2+, Fe3+, Cr3+.

docs.title: 2. Diamagnetism
docs.text:
• Diamagnetic substances are weakly repelled by a magnetic field and are weakly magnetised in the opposite direction.
  • They have all electrons paired. Pairing cancels their magnetic moments.
  • Examples: H2O, NaCl, C6H6.

docs.title: 3. Ferromagnetism
docs.text:
• Substances like iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium and CrO2 are very strongly attracted by a magnetic field. They can also be permanently magnetised.
  • In the solid state, the metal ions are grouped together into small regions called domains. Each domain acts as a tiny magnet.
  • In an unmagnetised piece, the domains are randomly oriented and their moments cancel.
  • In a magnetic field, all domains orient in the direction of the field and a strong magnetic effect is produced. This ordering persists even after the field is removed, so the substance becomes a permanent magnet.

docs.title: 4. Antiferromagnetism
docs.text:
• Substances like MnO have a domain structure similar to ferromagnetic substances, but their domains are oppositely oriented and cancel each other's magnetic moment.
  • So the net magnetic moment is zero.

docs.title: 5. Ferrimagnetism
docs.text:
• The magnetic moments of the domains are aligned in parallel and anti-parallel directions in unequal numbers, so there is a net magnetic moment.
  • They are weakly attracted by a magnetic field compared to ferromagnetic substances.
  • Examples: Fe3O4 (magnetite) and ferrites like MgFe2O4 and ZnFe2O4.
  • They lose ferrimagnetism on heating and become paramagnetic.

Alignment of magnetic moments in domains

\[Ferromagnetic:\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\] \[Antiferromagnetic:\ \uparrow\ \downarrow\ \uparrow\ \downarrow\ \uparrow\ \downarrow\] \[Ferrimagnetic:\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \downarrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \downarrow\] Type Behaviour in magnetic field Reason Examples Paramagnetic Weakly attracted Unpaired electrons O2, Cu2+, Fe3+, Cr3+ Diamagnetic Weakly repelled All electrons paired H2O, NaCl, C6H6 Ferromagnetic Strongly attracted, permanently magnetised All domains aligned in same direction Fe, Co, Ni, Gd, CrO2 Antiferromagnetic Net moment zero Equal domains aligned opposite MnO Ferrimagnetic Weakly attracted (compared to ferromagnetic) Unequal parallel and anti-parallel domains Fe3O4, MgFe2O4, ZnFe2O4

docs.title: Solid State | Imperfections in Solids
docs.text:
Although crystalline solids have both short range and long range order, real crystals are never perfect. Irregularities in the arrangement of constituent particles are called crystal defects or imperfections.

  • A solid usually consists of a large number of small crystals, which have defects in them. This happens when crystallisation takes place at a fast or moderate rate.
  • Single crystals are formed when crystallisation is extremely slow. Even these are not free of defects.

docs.title: Types of Defects
docs.text:
• Point defects: Irregularities or deviations from ideal arrangement around a point or an atom in a crystal.
  • Line defects: Irregularities or deviations from ideal arrangement in entire rows of lattice points.

Here we discuss only point defects. Point defects are of three types:

  1. Stoichiometric defects
  2. Impurity defects
  3. Non-stoichiometric defects

docs.title: 1. Stoichiometric Defects
docs.text:
• These point defects do not disturb the stoichiometry (ratio of constituent particles) of the solid.
  • They are also called intrinsic or thermodynamic defects.

docs.title: (a) Vacancy Defect
docs.text:
• When some of the lattice sites are vacant, the crystal is said to have a vacancy defect.
  • It decreases the density of the substance, since some mass is missing from the same volume.
  • This defect can also develop when a substance is heated.

docs.title: (b) Interstitial Defect
docs.text:
• When some constituent particles (atoms or molecules) occupy an interstitial site (a position between the normal lattice sites), the crystal is said to have an interstitial defect.
  • It increases the density of the substance.

Note

Simple vacancy and interstitial defects are shown by non-ionic solids. Ionic solids must always remain electrically neutral, so they show these defects as Frenkel and Schottky defects.

docs.title: (c) Frenkel Defect
docs.text:
• The smaller ion (usually the cation) is dislocated from its normal site to an interstitial site.
  • It creates a vacancy defect at the original site and an interstitial defect at the new site. So it is also called a dislocation defect.
  • It does not change the density of the solid, since no ion leaves the crystal.
  • Shown by ionic substances with a large difference in the size of ions. Examples: ZnS, AgCl, AgBr and AgI (due to the small size of Zn2+ and Ag+ ions).

docs.title: (d) Schottky Defect
docs.text:
• It is basically a vacancy defect in ionic solids. To keep the crystal electrically neutral, the number of missing cations and anions is equal.
  • Like a simple vacancy defect, it decreases the density of the substance.
  • The number of such defects is significant. In NaCl there are about 106 Schottky pairs per cm3 at room temperature. Since 1 cm3 has about 1022 ions, there is one Schottky defect per 1016 ions.
  • Shown by ionic substances in which cation and anion are of almost similar sizes. Examples: NaCl, KCl, CsCl and AgBr.

Note

AgBr shows both Frenkel and Schottky defects.

Property Frenkel defect Schottky defect What happens Smaller ion moves to an interstitial site Equal number of cations and anions are missing Effect on density No change Decreases Shown by Ions of very different sizes Ions of almost similar sizes Examples ZnS, AgCl, AgBr, AgI NaCl, KCl, CsCl, AgBr

docs.title: 2. Impurity Defects
docs.text:
• These arise when foreign ions are present in a crystal.
  • If molten NaCl containing a little SrCl2 is crystallised, some Na+ sites are occupied by Sr2+ ions.
  • Each Sr2+ replaces two Na+ ions to keep the crystal neutral. It occupies the site of one ion and the other site remains vacant.
  • So the number of cationic vacancies produced equals the number of Sr2+ ions.
  • Another similar example is the solid solution of CdCl2 in AgCl.
\[One\ Sr^{2+}\ ion\ replaces\ two\ Na^+\ ions\ →\ one\ cation\ vacancy\]

docs.title: 3. Non-Stoichiometric Defects
docs.text:
• Many inorganic solids contain their constituent elements in a non-stoichiometric ratio because of defects in their crystal structures.
  • These defects are of two types: metal excess defect and metal deficiency defect.

docs.title: (i) Due to anionic vacancies
docs.text:
• Shown by alkali halides like NaCl and KCl.
  • When NaCl crystals are heated in an atmosphere of sodium vapour, sodium atoms are deposited on the surface. Cl- ions diffuse to the surface and combine with Na atoms to give NaCl.
  • For this, sodium atoms lose electrons to form Na+ ions. The released electrons diffuse into the crystal and occupy the anionic sites left vacant.
\[Na → Na^+ + e^-\] \[Na^+ + Cl^- → NaCl\]
  • The crystal now has an excess of sodium.
  • The anionic sites occupied by unpaired electrons are called F-centres (from the German word Farbenzenter for colour centre).
  • F-centres give colour to the crystal. The colour is due to excitation of these electrons when they absorb energy from visible light.
Crystal heated with excess of Colour Sodium (NaCl) Yellow Lithium (LiCl) Pink Potassium (KCl) Violet (or lilac)

docs.title: (ii) Due to extra cations at interstitial sites
docs.text:
• Zinc oxide is white at room temperature. On heating, it loses oxygen and turns yellow.
\[ZnO \xrightarrow{heating} Zn^{2+} + {1 \over 2}O_2 + 2e^-\]
  • Now there is excess zinc in the crystal and its formula becomes Zn1+xO.
  • The excess Zn2+ ions move to interstitial sites and the electrons move to neighbouring interstitial sites.

docs.title: (b) Metal Deficiency Defect
docs.text:
• Some solids are difficult to prepare in the stoichiometric composition and contain less metal than the ideal ratio.
  • A typical example is FeO, which is mostly found with the composition Fe0.95O. It may actually range from Fe0.93O to Fe0.96O.
  • In FeO crystals, some Fe2+ cations are missing. The loss of positive charge is made up by the presence of the required number of Fe3+ ions.
\[3\ Fe^{2+}\ ions\ are\ replaced\ by\ 2\ Fe^{3+}\ ions + 1\ cation\ vacancy\]

docs.title: Solid State | Introduction
docs.text:
Solid state is the state of matter in which the constituent particles (atoms, molecules or ions) have fixed positions and can only oscillate about their mean positions. This is why solids have a definite mass, volume and shape.

  • Liquids and gases are called fluids because their particles are free to move about and they can flow.
  • In solids, particles are held at fixed positions, which explains their rigidity.
  • The properties of a solid depend on the nature of its constituent particles and the binding forces between them. This is why the study of the structure of solids is important for designing new materials like superconductors, magnetic materials and biodegradable polymers.

docs.title: General Characteristics of Solid State
docs.text:
• Whether a substance is a solid, liquid or gas at a given temperature and pressure depends on the balance between two opposing factors:
    • Intermolecular forces try to keep the particles close together.
    • Thermal energy tries to keep them apart by making them move faster.
  • At sufficiently low temperature, the thermal energy is low and the intermolecular forces bring the particles so close that they occupy fixed positions. The substance then exists as a solid.

The characteristic properties of the solid state are:

  1. They have definite mass, volume and shape.
  2. Intermolecular distances are short.
  3. Intermolecular forces are strong.
  4. Their constituent particles have fixed positions and can only oscillate about their mean positions.
  5. They are incompressible and rigid.

docs.title: Amorphous and Crystalline Solids
docs.text: On the basis of the order present in the arrangement of their particles, solids are classified as crystalline or amorphous.

docs.title: 1. Crystalline Solids
docs.text:
• A crystalline solid usually consists of a large number of small crystals, each having a definite characteristic geometrical shape.
  • The arrangement of particles is ordered and has long range order, i.e. a regular pattern of arrangement repeats itself periodically over the entire crystal.
  • Examples: Sodium chloride, quartz, metals like iron and copper, sulphur, iodine, naphthalene.
  • They have a sharp melting point.
  • They are anisotropic: physical properties like electrical resistance or refractive index have different values when measured along different directions in the same crystal. This happens because the arrangement of particles is different along different directions.

docs.title: 2. Amorphous Solids
docs.text:
• An amorphous solid (Greek amorphos = no form) consists of particles of irregular shape.
  • The arrangement has only short range order: a regular repeating pattern is seen only over short distances. Such regions are scattered and the arrangement between them is disordered.
  • Examples: Glass, rubber, plastics, quartz glass. Their structure is similar to that of liquids.
  • They soften over a range of temperature and can be moulded and blown into various shapes. On heating, they may become crystalline at some temperature. This is why some glass objects from ancient civilisations look milky.
  • Like liquids, amorphous solids have a tendency to flow, though very slowly. Therefore they are called pseudo solids or super cooled liquids.

Example
