Glass panes fixed in windows of very old buildings are found to be slightly thicker at the bottom than at the top. This is because glass flows down very slowly over the years.

  • They are isotropic: since there is no long range order and the arrangement is irregular in all directions, the value of any physical property is the same in every direction.
  • Uses: Glass, rubber and plastics are used in daily life. Amorphous silicon is one of the best photovoltaic materials for converting sunlight into electricity.

docs.title: Distinction between Crystalline and Amorphous Solids
docs.text: Property Crystalline solids Amorphous solids Shape Definite characteristic geometrical shape Irregular shape Melting point Melt at a sharp and characteristic temperature Gradually soften over a range of temperature Cleavage property When cut with a sharp edged tool, they split into two pieces with plain and smooth surfaces When cut, they split into two pieces with irregular surfaces Heat of fusion Definite and characteristic heat of fusion No definite heat of fusion Anisotropy Anisotropic Isotropic Nature True solids Pseudo solids or super cooled liquids Order in arrangement Long range order Only short range order

docs.title: Classification of Crystalline Solids
docs.text: Crystalline solids are classified into four categories on the basis of the nature of intermolecular forces operating in them: molecular, ionic, metallic and covalent solids.

docs.title: 1. Molecular Solids
docs.text: Molecules are the constituent particles of molecular solids. They are of three types:

docs.title: (a) Non-polar Molecular Solids
docs.text:
• They consist of atoms (like argon, helium) or non-polar molecules (like H2, Cl2, I2).
  • The particles are held by weak dispersion forces or London forces.
  • They are soft, non-conductors of electricity, have low melting points and are usually liquids or gases at room temperature and pressure.

docs.title: (b) Polar Molecular Solids
docs.text:
• They consist of molecules formed by polar covalent bonds, like HCl, SO2.
  • The molecules are held by relatively stronger dipole-dipole interactions.
  • They are soft and non-conductors of electricity. Their melting points are higher than those of non-polar molecular solids, but most of them are still gases or liquids at room temperature. Examples: Solid SO2, solid NH3.

docs.title: (c) Hydrogen Bonded Molecular Solids
docs.text:
• Their molecules contain polar covalent bonds between H and F, O or N atoms, and are held together by strong hydrogen bonds. Example: H2O (ice).
  • They are non-conductors of electricity and are generally volatile liquids or soft solids at room temperature.

docs.title: 2. Ionic Solids
docs.text:
• Ions are the constituent particles. Cations and anions are arranged in three dimensions and are bound by strong coulombic (electrostatic) forces.
  • They are hard, brittle and have high melting and boiling points.
  • In the solid state, ions are not free to move, so they are insulators. In the molten state or in aqueous solution, the ions become free to move and they conduct electricity.
  • Examples: NaCl, MgO, ZnS, CaF2.

docs.title: 3. Metallic Solids
docs.text:
• Metals are an orderly collection of positive ions surrounded by and held together by a sea of free electrons. Each metal atom contributes one or more electrons to this sea.
  • These mobile electrons are responsible for the high electrical and thermal conductivity of metals. When an electric field is applied, the electrons flow through the network of positive ions.
  • The free electrons are also responsible for the lustre and colour of metals.
  • Metals are highly malleable and ductile. Examples: Fe, Cu, Ag, Mg.

docs.title: 4. Covalent or Network Solids
docs.text:
• Non-metal atoms are joined by covalent bonds throughout the crystal. These are also called giant molecules.
  • Covalent bonds are strong and directional, so the atoms are held very strongly at their positions.
  • They are very hard and brittle, have extremely high melting points (and may even decompose before melting), and are insulators.
  • Examples: Diamond, silicon carbide, SiO2 (quartz), AlN.

Graphite: An Exception

  • Graphite is a covalent solid but it is soft and a good conductor of electricity.
  • In graphite, carbon atoms are arranged in layers. Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three neighbouring atoms in the same layer.
  • The fourth valence electron of each atom is present between the layers and is free to move. These free electrons make graphite a good conductor.
  • The layers can slide over one another. This makes graphite soft and a good solid lubricant.

docs.title: Properties of Different Types of Solids
docs.text: Type of solid Constituent particles Attractive forces Examples Physical nature Electrical conductivity Melting point Non-polar molecular Molecules Dispersion or London forces Ar, CCl<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>, I<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub> Soft Insulator Very low Polar molecular Molecules Dipole-dipole interactions HCl, SO<sub>2</sub> Soft Insulator Low Hydrogen bonded molecular Molecules Hydrogen bonding H<sub>2</sub>O (ice) Hard Insulator Low Ionic Ions Coulombic or electrostatic NaCl, MgO, ZnS, CaF<sub>2</sub> Hard but brittle Insulators in solid state, conductors in molten state and in aqueous solution High Metallic Positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons Metallic bonding Fe, Cu, Ag, Mg Hard but malleable and ductile Conductors in solid as well as molten state Fairly high Covalent or network Atoms Covalent bonding SiO<sub>2</sub> (quartz), SiC, C (diamond), AlN Hard Insulators Very high Covalent (graphite) Atoms Covalent bonding C (graphite) Soft Conductor (exception) Very high

docs.title: Solid State | Packing Efficiency and Density of Unit Cell
Solid State | Packing Efficiency and Density of Unit Cell
docs.text:
However the constituent particles are packed, there is always some free space left in the form of voids. Packing efficiency is the percentage of total space filled by the particles.

\[Packing\ efficiency = {Volume\ occupied\ by\ spheres\ in\ unit\ cell \over Total\ volume\ of\ unit\ cell} \times 100\ \%\]

In each case below, 'a' is the edge length of the cubic unit cell and 'r' is the radius of each sphere (atom).

docs.title: 1. Packing Efficiency in hcp and ccp Structures
docs.text:
• Both hcp and ccp are equally efficient. We calculate it for the ccp (fcc) unit cell.
  • In fcc, atoms touch each other along the face diagonal. Let the face diagonal be b.
\[b^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2\] \[b = \sqrt{2}a\]
  • The face diagonal contains one full sphere and two half spheres (from the corners), so its length is 4r.
\[b = 4r = \sqrt{2}a\] \[a = {4r \over \sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}r \quad or \quad r = {a \over 2\sqrt{2}}\]
  • A ccp unit cell has 4 atoms.
\[Volume\ of\ 4\ spheres = 4 \times {4 \over 3}\pi r^3\] \[Volume\ of\ cube = a^3 = (2\sqrt{2}r)^3 = 16\sqrt{2}r^3\] \[Packing\ efficiency = {4 \times {4 \over 3}\pi r^3 \over 16\sqrt{2}r^3} \times 100 = {{16 \over 3}\pi r^3 \over 16\sqrt{2}r^3} \times 100\] \[Packing\ efficiency = 74\ \%\]

docs.title: 2. Packing Efficiency in Body-Centred Cubic (bcc) Structure
docs.text:
• In bcc, the atom at the body-centre touches the two corner atoms that lie along the body diagonal.
  • Let the face diagonal be b and the body diagonal be c.
\[b^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2\] \[c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = a^2 + 2a^2 = 3a^2\] \[c = \sqrt{3}a\]
  • The three spheres along the body diagonal touch each other, so the body diagonal equals 4r.
\[\sqrt{3}a = 4r\] \[a = {4r \over \sqrt{3}} \quad or \quad r = {\sqrt{3} \over 4}a\]
  • A bcc unit cell has 2 atoms.
\[Volume\ of\ 2\ spheres = 2 \times {4 \over 3}\pi r^3\] \[Volume\ of\ cube = a^3 = \left({4 \over \sqrt{3}}r\right)^3 = {64 \over 3\sqrt{3}}r^3\] \[Packing\ efficiency = {{8 \over 3}\pi r^3 \over {64 \over 3\sqrt{3}}r^3} \times 100 = {\sqrt{3}\pi \over 8} \times 100\] \[Packing\ efficiency = 68\ \%\]

docs.title: 3. Packing Efficiency in Simple Cubic Lattice
docs.text:
• In a simple cubic lattice, atoms are only at the corners and they touch each other along the edge of the cube.
\[a = 2r\] \[Volume\ of\ cube = a^3 = (2r)^3 = 8r^3\]
  • A simple cubic unit cell has only 1 atom.
\[Volume\ of\ 1\ sphere = {4 \over 3}\pi r^3\] \[Packing\ efficiency = {{4 \over 3}\pi r^3 \over 8r^3} \times 100 = {\pi \over 6} \times 100\] \[Packing\ efficiency = 52.36\ \% \approx 52.4\ \%\]

Conclusion

Structure Relation between a and r Atoms per unit cell Coordination number Packing efficiency Simple cubic a = 2r 1 6 52.4 % Body-centred cubic \(\sqrt{3}a = 4r\) 2 8 68 % ccp / fcc and hcp \(\sqrt{2}a = 4r\) 4 (fcc) 12 74 %

ccp and hcp structures have the maximum packing efficiency.

docs.title: Density of a Unit Cell
docs.text:
From the unit cell dimensions, we can calculate the volume of the unit cell. Knowing the density, we can calculate the mass of atoms in the unit cell. This is also an accurate method of determining Avogadro's constant.

Let, for a cubic crystal:

  • a = edge length of unit cell (found by X-ray diffraction)
  • z = number of atoms in one unit cell
  • M = molar mass of the substance
  • NA = Avogadro's constant
  • d = density of the substance
\[Volume\ of\ unit\ cell = a^3\] \[Mass\ of\ one\ atom,\ m = {M \over N_A}\] \[Mass\ of\ unit\ cell = z \times m = {zM \over N_A}\] \[Density,\ d = {Mass\ of\ unit\ cell \over Volume\ of\ unit\ cell}\] \[d = {zM \over a^3 N_A}\]
  • The density of the unit cell is the same as the density of the substance.
  • Out of the five quantities d, z, M, a and NA, if any four are known, the fifth can be calculated.

Note

Keep units consistent. If a is in pm, convert it to cm using 1 pm = 10-10 cm (so that d comes in g cm-3 with M in g mol-1), or to m using 1 pm = 10-12 m (so that d comes in kg m-3 with M in kg mol-1).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
An element has a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure with a cell edge of 288 pm. The density of the element is 7.2 g/cm3. How many atoms are present in 208 g of the element?

\[Volume\ of\ unit\ cell = (288\ pm)^3 = (288 \times 10^{-10}\ cm)^3 = 2.39 \times 10^{-23}\ cm^3\] \[Volume\ of\ 208\ g\ element = {mass \over density} = {208 \over 7.2} = 28.88\ cm^3\] \[Number\ of\ unit\ cells = {28.88 \over 2.39 \times 10^{-23}} = 12.08 \times 10^{23}\]
  • Each bcc unit cell contains 2 atoms.
\[Number\ of\ atoms = 2 \times 12.08 \times 10^{23} = 24.16 \times 10^{23}\]

X-ray diffraction studies show that copper crystallises in an fcc unit cell with cell edge of 3.608 x 10-8 cm. In a separate experiment, copper is determined to have a density of 8.92 g/cm3. Calculate the atomic mass of copper.

  • For an fcc lattice, z = 4.
\[d = {zM \over a^3 N_A} \quad ∴ \quad M = {d N_A a^3 \over z}\] \[M = {8.92 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \times (3.608 \times 10^{-8})^3 \over 4}\] \[M = 63.1\ g\ mol^{-1}\]

Hence, the atomic mass of copper is 63.1 u.

Silver forms ccp lattice and X-ray studies of its crystals show that the edge length of its unit cell is 408.6 pm. Calculate the density of silver (Atomic mass = 107.9 u).

  • For a ccp lattice, z = 4.
\[M = 107.9\ g\ mol^{-1} = 107.9 \times 10^{-3}\ kg\ mol^{-1}\] \[a = 408.6\ pm = 408.6 \times 10^{-12}\ m\] \[d = {zM \over a^3 N_A} = {4 \times 107.9 \times 10^{-3} \over (408.6 \times 10^{-12})^3 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}}\] \[d = 10.5 \times 10^3\ kg\ m^{-3} = 10.5\ g\ cm^{-3}\]

An element with molar mass 2.7 x 10-2 kg mol-1 forms a cubic unit cell with edge length 405 pm. If its density is 2.7 x 103 kg m-3, what is the nature of the cubic unit cell?

\[z = {d a^3 N_A \over M}\] \[z = {2.7 \times 10^3 \times (405 \times 10^{-12})^3 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \over 2.7 \times 10^{-2}}\] \[z = {2.7 \times 10^3 \times 6.643 \times 10^{-29} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \over 2.7 \times 10^{-2}} = 4.0\]

Since there are 4 atoms per unit cell, the unit cell is face-centred cubic (fcc) or ccp.

docs.title: Solid State | Questions on Solid State
Solid State | Questions on Solid State
docs.text: In this article, we will solve conceptual and numerical questions on solid state, including classification of solids, voids, packing efficiency, density of unit cells, defects and semiconductors.

docs.title: Conceptual Questions
docs.text:
Why are solids rigid and why do they have a definite volume?

  • The constituent particles of solids are held at fixed positions by strong intermolecular forces and can only oscillate about their mean positions. So they cannot move or flow, which makes solids rigid.
  • Since the particles are closely packed and the intermolecular distances are short and fixed, solids are incompressible and have a definite volume.

Classify the following as amorphous or crystalline solids: Polyurethane, naphthalene, benzoic acid, teflon, potassium nitrate, cellophane, polyvinyl chloride, fibre glass, copper.

  • Amorphous: Polyurethane, teflon, cellophane, polyvinyl chloride, fibre glass.
  • Crystalline: Naphthalene, benzoic acid, potassium nitrate, copper.

Why is glass considered a super cooled liquid?

Glass is an amorphous solid with only short range order, similar to a liquid. Like liquids, it has a tendency to flow, though very slowly. For example, glass panes in old buildings become slightly thicker at the bottom. Hence glass is called a super cooled liquid or pseudo solid.

Refractive index of a solid is observed to have the same value along all directions. Comment on the nature of this solid. Would it show cleavage property?

A solid having the same value of a physical property in all directions is isotropic. So it is an amorphous solid. When cut with a sharp edged tool, it would split into pieces with irregular surfaces, so it will not show a clean cleavage property.

Classify the following solids based on the nature of intermolecular forces: Potassium sulphate, tin, benzene, urea, ammonia, water, zinc sulphide, graphite, rubidium, argon, silicon carbide.

Type of solid Substances Ionic Potassium sulphate, zinc sulphide Metallic Tin, rubidium Molecular (non-polar) Benzene, argon Molecular (hydrogen bonded) Urea, ammonia, water Covalent or network Graphite, silicon carbide

Classify each of the following as ionic, metallic, molecular, network (covalent) or amorphous: P4O10, (NH4)3PO4, SiC, I2, P4, plastic, graphite, brass, Rb, LiBr, Si.

Type of solid Substances Ionic (NH4)3PO4, LiBr Metallic Brass, Rb Molecular P4O10, I2, P4 Network (covalent) SiC, graphite, Si Amorphous Plastic

Solid A is a very hard electrical insulator in solid as well as in molten state and melts at extremely high temperature. What type of solid is it?

It is a covalent or network solid (like diamond or SiC). Its atoms are held by strong covalent bonds throughout the crystal and there are no free electrons or ions to carry current.

Ionic solids conduct electricity in molten state but not in solid state. Explain.

In the solid state, the ions are held at fixed positions by strong electrostatic forces and cannot move, so ionic solids are insulators. In the molten state, the ions become free to move and carry current.

How many lattice points are there in one unit cell of (i) face-centred cubic (ii) face-centred tetragonal (iii) body-centred lattice?

  • (i) Face-centred cubic: 8 corners x 1/8 + 6 face-centres x 1/2 = 4
  • (ii) Face-centred tetragonal: 8 corners x 1/8 + 6 face-centres x 1/2 = 4
  • (iii) Body-centred: 8 corners x 1/8 + 1 body-centre = 2

Explain how much portion of an atom located at (i) corner and (ii) body-centre of a cubic unit cell is part of its neighbouring unit cell.

  • (i) A corner atom is shared by 8 unit cells, so only 1/8 of it belongs to one unit cell and 7/8 belongs to the neighbouring unit cells.
  • (ii) A body-centre atom belongs wholly to its own unit cell and is not shared with any neighbouring unit cell.

What type of defect can arise when a solid is heated? Which physical property is affected by it and in what way?

When a solid is heated, a vacancy defect can arise because some lattice sites become vacant. It decreases the density of the substance.

What type of stoichiometric defect is shown by (i) ZnS (ii) AgBr?

  • (i) ZnS shows Frenkel defect, due to the large difference in size between Zn2+ and S2-.
  • (ii) AgBr shows both Frenkel and Schottky defects.

Explain how vacancies are introduced in an ionic solid when a cation of higher valence is added as an impurity in it.

When NaCl is crystallised with a little SrCl2, each Sr2+ ion replaces two Na+ ions to keep the crystal neutral. It occupies the site of one Na+ and the other site remains vacant. So one cation vacancy is created for every Sr2+ ion added.

Ionic solids which have anionic vacancies due to metal excess defect develop colour. Explain with a suitable example.

When NaCl crystals are heated in sodium vapour, Na atoms deposit on the surface and lose electrons to form Na+. Cl- ions diffuse to the surface and form NaCl with them. The released electrons occupy the anionic vacancies, forming F-centres. These electrons absorb energy from visible light and get excited, giving the crystal a yellow colour.

A group 14 element is to be converted into an n-type semiconductor by doping it with a suitable impurity. To which group should this impurity belong?

The impurity should belong to group 15 (like P or As). It has five valence electrons; four form bonds and the fifth becomes a free, delocalised electron.

What type of substances would make better permanent magnets, ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic? Justify your answer.

Ferromagnetic substances make better permanent magnets. In a magnetic field, all their domains align in the same direction and this alignment persists after the field is removed. In ferrimagnetic substances, domains are aligned in parallel and anti-parallel directions in unequal numbers, so their net magnetism is weaker.

Classify each of the following as being either a p-type or an n-type semiconductor: (i) Ge doped with In (ii) B doped with Si.

  • (i) In belongs to group 13 and has one electron less than Ge (group 14). It creates holes, so it is a p-type semiconductor.
  • (ii) Si belongs to group 14 and has one electron more than B (group 13). It provides extra electrons, so it is an n-type semiconductor.

Non-stoichiometric cuprous oxide, Cu2O, has a copper to oxygen ratio slightly less than 2:1. Account for the fact that this substance is a p-type semiconductor.

Since there is less copper than the ideal ratio, some Cu+ ions are missing (metal deficiency defect). To keep the crystal neutral, some Cu+ ions change to Cu2+. Each Cu2+ ion can accept an electron from a neighbour, which behaves like a positive hole. Conduction takes place through these positive holes, so it is a p-type semiconductor.

docs.title: Questions on Voids and Formula
docs.text:
What is the two dimensional coordination number of a molecule in a square close-packed layer?

In square close packing, each sphere touches 4 neighbours. So the two dimensional coordination number is 4.

A compound forms hexagonal close-packed structure. What is the total number of voids in 0.5 mol of it? How many of these are tetrahedral voids?

\[Number\ of\ particles,\ N = 0.5 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.011 \times 10^{23}\] \[Octahedral\ voids = N = 3.011 \times 10^{23}\] \[Tetrahedral\ voids = 2N = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\] \[Total\ voids = 3N = 9.033 \times 10^{23}\]

A compound is formed by two elements M and N. The element N forms ccp and atoms of M occupy 1/3rd of tetrahedral voids. What is the formula of the compound?

\[Let\ number\ of\ N\ atoms = x\] \[Tetrahedral\ voids = 2x\] \[Number\ of\ M\ atoms = {1 \over 3} \times 2x = {2x \over 3}\] \[M : N = {2x \over 3} : x = 2 : 3\]

Hence, the formula of the compound is M2N3.

Ferric oxide crystallises in a hexagonal close-packed array of oxide ions with two out of every three octahedral holes occupied by ferric ions. Derive the formula of the ferric oxide.

\[Let\ number\ of\ O^{2-}\ ions = x\] \[Octahedral\ voids = x\] \[Number\ of\ Fe^{3+}\ ions = {2 \over 3}x\] \[Fe : O = {2 \over 3}x : x = 2 : 3\]

Hence, the formula is Fe2O3.

A cubic solid is made of two elements P and Q. Atoms of Q are at the corners of the cube and P at the body-centre. What is the formula of the compound? What are the coordination numbers of P and Q?

\[Q\ atoms\ per\ unit\ cell = 8 \times {1 \over 8} = 1\] \[P\ atoms\ per\ unit\ cell = 1\]
  • So the formula is PQ.
  • The P atom at the body-centre is surrounded by 8 Q atoms at the corners, and each Q atom is surrounded by 8 P atoms of the neighbouring unit cells. So the coordination number of both P and Q is 8.

If the radius of the octahedral void is r and radius of the atoms in close-packing is R, derive the relation between r and R.

  • An octahedral void is surrounded by six spheres. Consider the four spheres lying in one plane around the void; their centres form a square of side 2R.
  • The void sphere touches two spheres placed diagonally across this square, so the diagonal of the square = 2R + 2r.
\[Diagonal\ of\ square = \sqrt{2} \times 2R\] \[2R + 2r = 2\sqrt{2}R\] \[r = (\sqrt{2} - 1)R\] \[r = 0.414\ R\]

Which of the following lattices has the highest packing efficiency: (i) simple cubic (ii) body-centred cubic (iii) hexagonal close-packed lattice?

Packing efficiencies are: simple cubic = 52.4%, bcc = 68%, hcp = 74%. Hence, hexagonal close-packed lattice has the highest packing efficiency.

docs.title: Numerical Questions on Unit Cell
docs.text:
Silver crystallises in fcc lattice. If edge length of the cell is 4.07 x 10-8 cm and density is 10.5 g cm-3, calculate the atomic mass of silver.

  • For fcc, z = 4.
\[M = {d a^3 N_A \over z}\] \[M = {10.5 \times (4.07 \times 10^{-8})^3 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \over 4}\] \[M = {10.5 \times 6.742 \times 10^{-23} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \over 4}\] \[M = 106.6\ g\ mol^{-1}\]

Hence, the atomic mass of silver is about 106.6 u.

Niobium crystallises in body-centred cubic structure. If density is 8.55 g cm-3, calculate the atomic radius of niobium using its atomic mass 93 u.

  • For bcc, z = 2.
\[a^3 = {zM \over d N_A} = {2 \times 93 \over 8.55 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}}\] \[a^3 = 3.612 \times 10^{-23}\ cm^3 = 36.12 \times 10^{-24}\ cm^3\] \[a = 3.306 \times 10^{-8}\ cm = 330.6\ pm\]
  • For bcc:
\[r = {\sqrt{3} \over 4}a = 0.433 \times 330.6\] \[r = 143.1\ pm\]

Copper crystallises into an fcc lattice with edge length 3.61 x 10-8 cm. Show that the calculated density is in agreement with its measured value of 8.92 g cm-3. (Atomic mass of Cu = 63.5 u)

  • For fcc, z = 4.
\[d = {zM \over a^3 N_A} = {4 \times 63.5 \over (3.61 \times 10^{-8})^3 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}}\] \[d = {254 \over 4.705 \times 10^{-23} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}} = {254 \over 28.33}\] \[d = 8.97\ g\ cm^{-3}\]

The calculated value (8.97 g cm-3) is in close agreement with the measured value (8.92 g cm-3).

Gold (atomic radius = 0.144 nm) crystallises in a face-centred unit cell. What is the length of a side of the cell?

  • For fcc:
\[a = 2\sqrt{2}r = 2 \times 1.414 \times 0.144\] \[a = 0.407\ nm = 407\ pm\]

Aluminium crystallises in a cubic close-packed structure. Its metallic radius is 125 pm. (i) What is the length of the side of the unit cell? (ii) How many unit cells are there in 1.00 cm3 of aluminium?

  • (i) For ccp (fcc):
\[a = 2\sqrt{2}r = 2 \times 1.414 \times 125 = 353.6\ pm\]
  • (ii) Volume of one unit cell:
\[a^3 = (353.6 \times 10^{-10}\ cm)^3 = 4.42 \times 10^{-23}\ cm^3\] \[Number\ of\ unit\ cells = {1.00 \over 4.42 \times 10^{-23}} = 2.26 \times 10^{22}\]

docs.title: Numerical Questions on Defects
docs.text:
Analysis shows that nickel oxide has the formula Ni0.98O1.00. What fractions of nickel exist as Ni2+ and Ni3+ ions?

  • Let the number of Ni2+ ions = x. Then the number of Ni3+ ions = 0.98 - x.
  • Total positive charge must balance the charge of one O2- ion:
\[2x + 3(0.98 - x) = 2\] \[2.94 - x = 2\] \[x = 0.94\] \[Fraction\ of\ Ni^{2+} = {0.94 \over 0.98} \times 100 = 96\ \%\] \[Fraction\ of\ Ni^{3+} = {0.04 \over 0.98} \times 100 = 4\ \%\]

If NaCl is doped with 10-3 mol % of SrCl2, what is the concentration of cation vacancies?

  • 10-3 mol % means 100 mol of NaCl is doped with 10-3 mol of SrCl2.
\[SrCl_2\ per\ mol\ of\ NaCl = {10^{-3} \over 100} = 10^{-5}\ mol\]
  • Each Sr2+ ion creates one cation vacancy.
\[Cation\ vacancies = 10^{-5} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\] \[Cation\ vacancies = 6.022 \times 10^{18}\ per\ mol\ of\ NaCl\]

docs.title: Azeotropes
docs.text:
• Azeotropes are constant boiling mixtures, ie, these mixtures boil at constant temperature without any change in composition.
  • The composition in liquid phase and vapour phase remains same for an azeotropic mixture.

docs.title: Azeotropic Mixture
docs.text:
• These are the liquid mixtures which cannot be separated by fractional distillation.
  • There are two types of azeotropic mixtures: (a) Maximum boiling azeotropes and (b) Minimum boiling azeotropes

docs.title: Zeotropic Mixture
docs.text:
• These are the liquid mixtures which can be separated by distillation.

Note

The details of azeotropes and zeotropes are beyond the scope of our syllabus. For details, check out these links:

  • Azeotropes: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azeotrope

  • Zeotropic Mixture: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeotropic_mixture

docs.title: Solution | Colligative Properties of Dilute Solution
Solution | Colligative Properties of Dilute Solution
Colligative Properties
docs.text: • Colligative properties are the properties which depend on the number of solute particles present in the solution irrespective of nature of solute.

docs.title: Four colligative properties:
docs.text:
• Relative Lowering of vapour pressure (RLVP)
  • Elevation in boiling point
  • Depression in freezing point
  • Osmotic Pressure

docs.title: 1. Relative Lowering of vapour pressure
docs.text:
• When a non-volatile solute is added to a pure solvent, its vapour pressure decreases. This decrease in vapour pressure is known as lowering of vapour pressure.

Lowering of V.P = po - ps

where, po = V.P of pure solvent

and, ps = V.P of solution

  • Relative lowering of vapour pressure is defined as:
\[RLVP = {p_o - p_s\over p_o}\]
  • Since, ps = poΧsolvent, therefore, we can write:
\[RLVP = {p_o - p_oΧ_{solvent}\over p_o}\] \[RLVP = {1 - Χ_{solvent}}\] \[∴\ RLVP = Χ_{solute} \]
  • Hence, we can conclude that:
\[RLVP = {p_o - p_s\over p_o} = {Χ_{solute}}\]

Remember

Lowering of V.P is not a colligative property. Relative lowering of V.P is a colligative property.

docs.title: 2. Elevation of Boiling Point
docs.text:
• The boiling point of a solution is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of solution becomes equal to the atmospheric pressure or external pressure.

  • Boiling point depends on external pressure. As external pressure changes, boiling point will also change.

  • When a non-volatile solute is added to a solvent, then its boiling point will increase, ie, boiling point of a solution is always greater than pure solvent.

  • This increase in boiling point of pure solvent is known as elevation of boiling point. If Tb is the boiling point of solution and Tob is the boiling point of pure solvent, then elevation of boiling point, ΔTb is given by:

\[ΔT_b = T_b - T^o_b\]
  • Elevation of boiling point is directly proportional to molality of solute in the solution.
\[ΔT_b\ ∝\ m\] \[ΔT_b = {K_b\ m}\] \[where, K_b = {Molal\ elevation\ constant}\]

docs.title: 3. Depression of Freezing Point
docs.text:
• Freezing point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of solid becomes equal to atmospheric pressure.

  • When a non-volatile solute is added to a pure solvent, its freezing point decreases. This decrease in freezing point is known as depression of freezing point.

  • If Tf is the freezing point of solution and Tof is the freezing point of pure solvent, then:

\[ΔT_f = {T^o_f - T_f}\]
  • Depression of freezing point is directly proportional to molality of solute dissolved in the solution.
\[ΔT_f\ ∝\ m\] \[ΔT_f = {K_f\ m}\] \[where, K_f = {Molal\ depression\ constant}\]

docs.title: 4. Osmotic Pressure
docs.text:
• Osmosis: The spontaneous flow of solvent molecules from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a semi-permeable membrane is called osmosis.

  • Osmotic Pressure: The pressure required to stop the movement of solvent molecules from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a semi-permeable membrane is called osmotic pressure. It is directly proportional to concentration of solution and is given by:

\[Π = {CRT}\] \[where, Π = Osmotic\ Pressure\] \[C = concentration\ of\ solution\] \[R = Universal\ Gas\ Constant\] \[T = Temperature\]

  • Reverse Osmosis(RO): If a pressure greater than osmotic pressure is applied, the direction of osmosis is reversed and the process is known as reverse osmosis. This principle is used by water filters.

  • Isotonic Solutions: Two solutions having same osmotic pressure are called isotonic solutions.

  • Hypertonic Solution: The solution having higher osmotic pressure as compared to other solution is known as hypertonic solution.

  • Hypotonic Solution: The solution having lower osmotic pressure as compared to other solution is known as hypotonic solution.

Remember

Hypertonic solution and hypotonic solution are relative terms. A solution X may be hypertonic as compared to another solution Y but may be hypotonic for solution Z.

docs.title: Concentration Terms
docs.text:
• Concentration Terms are used to express the amount of solute dissolved in a solvent.
  • There are different concentration terms like mass percentage, volume percentage, mass by volume percentage, parts per million, molarity, molality, mole fraction
  • We will discuss each one of them in detail.

docs.title: Mass Percentage(w/w)
docs.text:
Mass percentage of a component of a solution is defined as:

\[w/w = {Mass\ of\ component \times 100 \over Total\ mass\ of\ solution}\]

If 10 gram sugar is present in 90 gram water, find its mass percentage.

Here, the mass of solution is (10+90) grams = 100 grams.

\[w/w = {Mass\ of\ component \times 100 \over Total\ mass\ of\ solution}\] \[= {10 \times 100 \over 100}\] \[= {10}\]

docs.title: Volume Percentage(v/v)
docs.text:
Volume percentage of a component of a solution is defined as:

\[v/v = {Volume\ of\ component \times 100 \over Total\ volume\ of\ solution}\]

If 10 ml sugar is present in 90 ml water, find its volume percentage.

Here, the volume of solution is (10+90) ml = 100 ml.

\[v/v = {Volume\ of\ component \times 100 \over Total\ volume\ of\ solution}\] \[= {10 \times 100 \over 100}\] \[= {10}\]

docs.title: Mass by Volume Percentage(w/v)
docs.text:
Mass by volume percentage of a component of a solution is defined as:

\[w/v = {Mass\ of\ component \times 100 \over Total\ volume\ of\ solution}\]

If 10 grams sugar is present in 100 ml solution, find its volume percentage.

Here, the volume of solution is = 100 ml.

\[w/v = {Mass\ of\ component \times 100 \over Total\ volume\ of\ solution}\] \[= {10 \times 100 \over 100}\] \[= {10}\]

docs.title: Parts per million(ppm)
docs.text:
• When solute is present in very small amount, we express its concentration in terms of parts per million.

ppm is calculated using the following formula:

\[ppm = {n \times 10^6 \over N}\]

where, n = Number of parts of component

and, N = Number of parts of all components of solution

  • Parts per million can be expressed as mass to mass, volume to volume and mass to volume.

docs.title: Parts per billion (ppb)
docs.text:
parts per billion(ppb) is defined as:

\[ppb = {n \times 10^9 \over N}\]

where, n = Number of parts of component

and, N = Number of parts of all components of solution

  • Similar to ppm, parts per billion(ppb) is also used when solute is in a very small amount.

docs.title: Mole Fraction (Χ)
docs.text:
• For a solution consisting of A as solute and B as solvent, we define mole fraction of A present in the solution as:
\[Χ_A = {n_A \over n_A + n_B}\]

where, nA = Moles of A

and, nB = Moles of B

  • Similarly, mole fraction of B in the solution is defined as:
\[Χ_B = {n_B \over n_A + n_B}\]
  • Here, we can see that:
\[Χ_A + Χ_B = 1\]
  • Similarly, for a solution containing k components, we can write:
\[Χ_1 = {n_1 \over n_1 + n_2 + n_3 +\ ..... +\ n_k}\] \[Χ_2 = {n_2 \over n_1 + n_2 + n_3 +\ ..... +\ n_k}\] \[Χ_3 = {n_3 \over n_1 + n_2 + n_3 +\ ..... +\ n_k}\]

Similarly,

\[Χ_k = {n_k \over n_1 + n_2 + n_3 +\ ..... +\ n_k}\]

And,

\[Χ_1 + Χ_2 + Χ_3 +\ ......\ + Χ_k = 1\]

docs.title: Molarity(M)
docs.text:
• Molarity is defined as number of moles of solute present in one litre of solution.
\[M = {n_{solute} \over V_{solution} (L)}\]
  • Since molarity is dependent on volume, it changes with change in temperature.

docs.title: Molality(m)
docs.text:
• Molality is defined as number of moles of solute present in one kilogram of solvent.
\[m = {n_{solute} \over mass_{solvent} (Kg)}\]
  • Molality does not change with change in temperature.

docs.title: Differences between Ideal and Non-Ideal Solutions
docs.text: S.No Ideal Solution Non-Ideal Solution 1 The solutions which obey Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration are known as ideal solutions. When a solution does not obey Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration, then it is called non-ideal solution. 2 For binary solution with components A and B, A-A type and B-B type interactions are equal to A-B type interactions. For binary solution with components A and B, A-A type and B-B type interactions are not equal to A-B type interactions. 3 The enthalpy of mixing of the pure components to form the solution is zero (ΔH<sub>mix</sub> = 0). It means that no heat is absorbed or evolved when the components are mixed. The enthalpy of mixing of the pure components to form the solution is not zero (ΔH<sub>mix</sub> ≠ 0), ie, it is either positive or negative. 4 The volume of mixing is also zero (ΔV<sub>mix</sub> = 0). It means the volume of solution would be equal to the sum of volumes of the two components. The volume of mixing is not zero (ΔV<sub>mix</sub> ≠ 0), ie, it is either positive or negative. 5 Examples: Benzene+Toluene, CCl<sub>4</sub>+CS<sub>2</sub> Examples: Benzene+Water, Acetone+Ethanol

docs.title: Types of non-ideal solution
docs.text:
Non-ideal solutions can be further classified into two types: non-ideal solution with positive deviation and non-ideal solution with negative deviation.

S.No Non-Ideal Solution with positive deviation Non-Ideal Solution with negative deviation 1 For binary solution, p > poAΧA + poBΧB For binary solution, p < poAΧA + poBΧB 2 For binary solution with components A and B, A-A type and B-B type interactions are stronger than A-B type interactions. For binary solution with components A and B, A-A type and B-B type interactions are weaker than A-B type interactions. 3 ΔHmix > 0. It means that heat is absorbed when the components are mixed. ΔHmix < 0. It means that heat is evolved when the components are mixed. 4 ΔVmix > 0. It means the volume of solution would be greater than the sum of volumes of the two components. ΔVmix < 0. It means the volume of solution would be less than the sum of volumes of the two components. 5 Example: Cyclohexane+Ethanol Example: Methanol+Water

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• Solutions are homogeneous mixtures of two or more components, i.e, the composition and properties of all the components are uniform throughout the mixture.
  • Single phase containing two or more components is called solution.
  • Solution consists of a solvent and one or more solutes.
  • Generally, the component which has same phase as that of a solution and is present in larger amount is known as solvent.
  • Generally, the component which is present in smaller amount is known as solute.
  • Examples: Solution of H2O + NaCl, Air (Mixture of different gases), Blood (mixture of water, oxygen, haemoglobin etc.).

docs.title: Types of Solutions and Examples

docs.title: Solution | Questions based on Concentration Terms
Solution | Questions based on Concentration Terms
Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the mole fraction of ethylene glycol (C2H6O2) in a solution containing 20% of C2H6O2 by mass.

Let the mass of solution be 100 grams

Then, the mass of C2H6O2 = 20 grams.

And, mass of water = (100 - 20) grams = 80 grams.

Molecular mass of C2H6O2 = 62 grams/mole.

Moles of C2H6O2 = 20/62

Moles of water = 80/18

\[Χ_{C_2H_6O_2} = {n_{C_2H_6O_2} \over n_{C_2H_6O_2} + n_{H_2O}}\] \[Χ_{C_2H_6O_2} = {20/62 \over 20/62 + 80/18} = 0.068\]

Also,

\[Χ_{H_2O} = 1 - 0.068 = 0.932\]

Calculate the molarity of solution containing 5 g of NaOH in 450 mL solution.

\[n_{NAOH} = {5 \over 40} = 0.125\ moles\] \[V_{solution} = {450 \over 1000} = 0.45\ L\] \[M = {n_{NAOH} \over V_{solution}} = {0.125 \over 0.45} = 0.278\ mol/L\]

Calculate the molality of 2.5 g of ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) dissolved in 75 g of benzene (C6H6).

\[Molecular\ mass\ of\ CH_3COOH = 60\ g/mol\] \[n_{CH_3COOH} = {2.5 \over 60} = 0.0417\ moles\] \[m_{solvent} = {75 \over 1000} = 0.075\ Kg\] \[m = {n_{CH_3COOH} \over m_{solvent}}\] \[m = {0.0417 \over 0.075} = 0.556\ mol/Kg\]

Calculate the mass percentage of benzene (C6H6) and carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) if 22 g of benzene is dissolved in 122 g of carbon tetrachloride.

\[Mass\ of\ solution = 22 + 122 = 144\ g\] \[w/w\ of\ benzene = {22\times 100\over 144} = 15.28\] \[w/w\ of\ CCl_4 = {122 \times 100\over 144} = 84.72\]

Calculate the mole fraction of benzene in solution containing 30% by mass in carbon tetrachloride.

Let the mass of solution be 100 g

Then, the mass of benzene = 30 g

And, the mass of carbon tetrachloride = 70 g

Moles of benzene (nC6H6) = 30/78 g/mol

Moles of carbon tetrachloride (nCCl4) = 70/154 g/mol

\[Χ_{C_6H_6} = {n_{C_6H_6} \over n_{C_6H_6} + n_{CCl_4}}\] \[Χ_{C_6H_6} = {30/78 \over 30/78 + 70/154} = 0.459\] \[Χ_{CCl_4} = 1 - 0.459 = 0.541\]

Calculate the molarity of each of the following solutions: (a) 30 g of Co(NO3)2.6H2O in 4.3 L of solution (b) 30 mL of 0.5 M H2SO4 diluted to 500 mL.

(a)

\[Moles\ of\ Co(NO_3)_2.6H_2O = {30 \over 291}\] \[Molarity = {30/291 \over 4.3} = 0.024 mol/L\]

(b) Here the moles of solute will be same even after dilution.

\[n_{H_2SO_4} = M_{H_2SO_4} \times V_{solution} (L)\] \[n_{H_2SO_4} = {0.5 \times 0.3} = 0.15\]

Molarity of diluted solution is given as:

\[M = {n_{H_2SO_4} \over V_{solution} (L)}\] \[M = {0.15 \over 0.5} = 0.03\ mol/L\]

Calculate the mass of urea (NH2CONH2) required in making 2.5 kg of 0.25 molal aqueous solution.

\[Let\ mass\ of\ urea = x\ kg\] \[Molality = 0.25\ m\] \[Mass of solution = 2.5\ kg\] \[Mass of solvent = (2.5 - x)\ kg\] \[Moles of urea = {x\times 1000\over 60}\] \[Molality = {(x\times 1000)/60\over 2.5-x}\] \[=>\ 0.25 = {(x\times 1000)/60\over 2.5-x}\] \[=>\ x = 0.034946\ kg = 34.946\ g\]

Calculate (a) molality (b) molarity and (c) mole fraction of KI if the density of 20% (mass/mass) aqueous KI is 1.202 g/mL.

\[w/w = 20\] \[The\ solvent\ is\ water.\] \[Density\ of\ solution = 1.202\ g/mL\] \[Let\ mass\ of\ solution\ be\ 100\ g\] \[Then,\ mass\ of\ KI = 20\ g\] \[And,\ mass\ of\ solvent = 80\ g\] \[Moles\ of\ solvent = {80\over 18}\] \[Volume\ of\ solution = {100\over1.202} mL\] \[Moles of KI = {20\over166}\] \[molality = {20/166 \over 80/1000} = 1.506\ mol/kg\] \[molarity = {20/166 \over 100/(1.202\times 1000)} = 1.45 mol/L \] \[Χ = {20/166\over (20/166 + 80/18)} = 0.0263\]

docs.title: Raoult's Law to calculate Vapour Pressure
docs.text:
• Raoult's Law states that the partial pressure or vapour pressure of any volatile constituent of solution at a given temperature is equal to the product of vapour pressure of pure constituent and its mole fraction in the solution.
\[p = {p^o\ Χ}\]
  • For a solution containing two volatile liquids A and B, we can write:
\[p_A = {p^o_A\ Χ_A}\] \[p_B = {p^o_B\ Χ_B}\]

where,

pA = partial pressure of A

pB = partial pressure of B

poA = partial pressure of pure liquid A

poB = partial pressure of pure liquid B

ΧA = mole fraction of A in solution

ΧB = mole fraction of B in solution

  • From Dalton's law, we can calculate total pressure, P:
\[P = {p_A + p_B}\] \[P = {p^o_A\ Χ_A + p^o_B\ Χ_B}\] \[P = {p^o_A\ Χ_A + p^o_B\ (1-Χ_A)}\] \[P = {(p^o_A-p^o_B)Χ_A + p^o_B}\]
  • The graph of Raoult's law will be a straight line because it is of the form y = mx+c.

Image credit: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoult's_law

docs.title: Raoult's Law as a special case of Henry's Law
docs.text:
• According to Henry's law, partial pressure of a gas over the surface of a solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction dissolved in the solution and is given by:
\[p = {K_H\ Χ}\]
  • According to Raoult's law, partial pressure of a volatile liquid in gaseous form over the surface of a solution is also directly proportional to its mole fraction dissolved in the solution and is given by:
\[p = {p^o\ Χ}\]

  • From the above two equations, it can be clearly seen that there is a difference in proportionality constant between two equations. If a volatile liquid is dissolved in solution, then KH becomes po.

  • Thus, Raoult's law is the special case of Henry's law where KH = po.

docs.title: Solution | Solubility of Gas in Liquid
Solution | Solubility of Gas in Liquid
Solubility of Gas in Liquid
docs.text:
• All gases are soluble in all liquids to some extent depending on pressure.
  • For example, presence of carbon dioxide in cold drinks, presence of oxygen in blood, presence of oxygen in water.
  • Hydrogen chloride(HCl) gas is highly soluble in water.

docs.title: Factors affecting the solubility of gases in liquids
1. Nature of gas:
docs.text:
• Easily liquifiable gases(CO2, SO2, NH3) are more soluble in common solvents like water as compared to other gases(H2, N2).
  • The gases which can form hydrogen bonds or some other types of attractions with the solvent have higher solubility. Example: NH3 in H2O

docs.title: 2. Temperature:
docs.text:
• The solubility of gases in liquid decreases with increase in temperature because on increasing temperature, gas expands and its kinetic energy increases. Also for hydrogen bonded gases like NH3, H-bonds dissociate on increasing temperature.
  • Cold drinks are kept at low temperature to prevent the escape of CO2 gas.

docs.title: 3. Pressure:
docs.text:
• The effect of pressure on solubility of gases can be explained by Henry's law.
  • Henry's law states that the partial pressure of a gas on the surface of solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction dissolved in the solution.
\[p ∝ Χ_{gas}\] \[p = {K_H Χ_{gas}}\]

where, p = partial pressure of gas above the surface of solution

Χgas = Mole fraction of gas in the solution

KH = Henry's Constant (It is the characteristic of a gas)

  • Graph for Henry's law will be a straight line with slope = KH as shown below:

  • Higher is the value of KH, lower is the solubility of gas.

docs.title: Applications of Henry's Law
docs.text:
• To increase the solubility of CO2 in soft drinks and soda water, the bottle is sealed under high pressure.

  • Scuba drivers use tanks filled with air diluted with helium (Helium is less soluble in blood). This is because when scuba drivers are under water, increased pressure increases the solubility of air in the blood. When the divers come towards surface, the pressure gradually decreases. This releases the dissolved gases and leads to the formation of bubbles of nitrogen in the blood. This blocks capillaries and creates a medical condition known as bends, which are painful and dangerous to life. To avoid this, air is diluted with helium in the tank.

  • The partial pressure of oxygen is less at higher altitudes as compared to ground level, which causes low concentration of oxygen in the blood causing weakness.

docs.title: Solution | Solubility of Solid in Liquid
Solution | Solubility of Solid in Liquid
Solubility
docs.text:
• Solubility of a substance can be defined as its maximum amount that can be dissolved in a specified amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
  • There are many factors affecting solubility of a substance like pressure, temperature and nature of solute and solvent.

docs.title: Solubility of Solid in Liquid
docs.text:
• All solids are not soluble in a given liquid.
  • When a solid is added to the solvent, some solute dissolves and its concentration increases in the solution. This process is known as dissolution.
  • Some solute particles in solution collide with the solid solute particles and get separated out od solution. This process is known as crystallization.
  • At equilibrium, rate of crystallization is equal to rate of dissolution. Under such condition, no more solute can be dissolved in the given solvent at same temperature. This type of solution is known as saturated solution.
\[Solute + Solvent ⇋ Solution\]
  • The solution in which more solute can be added in the solvent without changing temperature is known as unsaturated solution.

docs.title: Solution | Solution of Solids in Liquid
Solution | Solution of Solids in Liquid
Solution of Solids in Liquid
docs.text:
• For non-volatile solute, partial pressure of solution is equal to partial pressure of solvent in vapour phase.

  • Thus, from Raoult's law, we can write:

\[p_s = {p^o_{solvent}\ Χ_{solvent}}\]
  • Since Χsolvent is less than 1, the vapour pressure of a solution containing a non-volatile solute is always less than the vapour pressure of pure solvent.

docs.title: Factors affecting solubility of a solid solute in a liquid
docs.text:
1. Nature of solute:

    • Electrolytes are more soluble while non-electrolytes are less soluble.

  2. Nature of solvent:

    • "Like dissolves like". Polar solvent dissolves polar solute and non-polar solvent dissolves non-polar solute.

  3. Temperature:

    • The solubility of solid solutes in a liquid depends on temperature and can be described on the basis of type of dissolution.
    • For exothermic dissolution(Heat is released), solubility decreases on increasing temperature.
    • For endothermic dissolution(Heat is absorbed), solubility increases on increasing temperature.

docs.title: Solution | Vapour Pressure of Liquid Solution
Vapour Pressure
docs.text:
• The pressure exerted by vapours of a liquid over its liquid surface when the liquid and vapours are in equilibrium is known as vapour pressure.
  • Equilibrium means the state where rate of vaporization is equal to rate of condensation.

Image Credit: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapor_pressure

docs.title: Factors affecting vapour pressure
docs.text:
1. Nature of liquid:
    • The liquid having strong attraction forces between its molecules will have lower vapour pressure as compared to other liquids.
    • Example: water has lower vapour pressure as compared to alcohol due to this reason.
  2. Temperature:
    • On increasing temperature, vapour pressure of liquid will increase and vice-versa.
  3. Surface Area of liquid:
    • Vapour pressure increases with increase in surface area of liquid and vice-versa.
  4. Purity of solution:
    • Vapour pressure of pure liquid will always be greater than the vapour pressure of its solution with a non-volatile solid.
    • For example, vapour pressure of pure water is greater than (water + sugar) solution.

docs.title: Structure of Atom | Atomic Models
docs.text: Atomic models were proposed to explain how the positively and negatively charged particles are distributed inside an atom. Many of these models could not explain the stability of the atom. Two important models were given by J.J. Thomson and Ernest Rutherford.

docs.title: Thomson Model of Atom
docs.text:
• J.J. Thomson (1898) proposed that an atom is a sphere (radius about 10-10 m) in which the positive charge is uniformly distributed.
  • The electrons are embedded in this positive sphere in such a way that the most stable electrostatic arrangement is obtained.
  • The model is also called the plum pudding, raisin pudding or watermelon model. The atom is like a pudding or watermelon of positive charge, with plums or seeds (electrons) embedded in it.
  • An important feature of this model is that the mass of the atom is assumed to be uniformly distributed over the whole atom.
  • The model could explain the overall neutrality of the atom, but it was not consistent with later experiments (Rutherford's scattering experiment).

docs.title: α-Particle Scattering Experiment
docs.text:
• Rutherford and his students (Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden) bombarded a very thin gold foil (thickness about 100 nm) with a stream of high energy α-particles from a radioactive source.
  • A circular fluorescent zinc sulphide screen was placed around the foil. Whenever an α-particle struck the screen, a tiny flash of light was produced at that point.
  • According to the Thomson model, the mass of each gold atom is spread evenly. So all α-particles were expected to pass through, slowing down and changing direction only by small angles.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
1. Most of the α-particles passed through the gold foil undeflected.
  2. A small fraction of the α-particles was deflected by small angles.
  3. A very few α-particles (about 1 in 20,000) bounced back, i.e. were deflected by nearly 180°.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
1. Most of the space in the atom is empty, since most α-particles passed through undeflected.
  2. The few deflections must be due to an enormous repulsive force. So the positive charge is not spread throughout the atom, but is concentrated in a very small volume which repels the positively charged α-particles.
  3. The volume of the nucleus is negligible compared to the volume of the atom. The radius of the atom is about 10-10 m, while that of the nucleus is about 10-15 m. If a cricket ball were the nucleus, the atom would have a radius of about 5 km.

docs.title: Postulates of Rutherford's Nuclear Model
docs.text:
1. The positive charge and most of the mass of the atom is densely concentrated in an extremely small region called the nucleus.
  2. The nucleus is surrounded by electrons that move around it with very high speed in circular paths called orbits. The model resembles the solar system, with the nucleus as the sun and the electrons as the planets.
  3. Electrons and the nucleus are held together by electrostatic forces of attraction.

docs.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
docs.text:
• The positive charge of the nucleus is due to protons. The number of protons in the nucleus is equal to the atomic number (Z).
  • An atom is electrically neutral, so the number of electrons in a neutral atom equals the number of protons.
  • For example, hydrogen has 1 proton and sodium has 11 protons, so their atomic numbers are 1 and 11. They also have 1 and 11 electrons respectively.
\[Atomic\ number\ (Z) = Number\ of\ protons\ in\ the\ nucleus\] \[Atomic\ number\ (Z) = Number\ of\ electrons\ in\ a\ neutral\ atom\]
  • The mass of the nucleus is due to protons and neutrons. Protons and neutrons together are called nucleons.
  • The total number of nucleons is called the mass number (A) of the atom.
\[Mass\ number\ (A) = Number\ of\ protons\ (Z) + Number\ of\ neutrons\ (n)\] \[Number\ of\ neutrons = A - Z\]

docs.title: Isobars and Isotopes
docs.text: • The composition of an atom is written using the element symbol X with the mass number A as a left superscript and the atomic number Z as a left subscript: \(^A_ZX\).

docs.title: 1. Isobars
docs.text:
• Isobars are atoms with the same mass number but different atomic number.
  • Example: \(^{14}_6C\) and \(^{14}_7N\).

docs.title: 2. Isotopes
docs.text:
• Isotopes are atoms with the same atomic number but different mass number. They differ only in the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
  • Isotopes of hydrogen:
Isotope Symbol Protons Neutrons Abundance Protium \(^1_1H\) 1 0 99.985% Deuterium \(^2_1D\) 1 1 0.015% Tritium \(^3_1T\) 1 2 Trace amounts
  • Other examples: carbon atoms with 6, 7 and 8 neutrons (\(^{12}_6C\), \(^{13}_6C\), \(^{14}_6C\)) and chlorine atoms with 18 and 20 neutrons (\(^{35}_{17}Cl\), \(^{37}_{17}Cl\)).

Note

Chemical properties of atoms are controlled by the number of electrons, which is decided by the number of protons. The number of neutrons has very little effect on chemical properties. Therefore, all isotopes of an element show the same chemical behaviour.

How to find protons, neutrons and electrons in a species \(^A_ZX\)

  • Number of protons = Z and number of neutrons = A – Z, whether the species is neutral or an ion.

  • For a neutral atom, number of electrons = Z.

  • For a cation (positive ion), number of electrons is less than Z. For an anion (negative ion), number of electrons is more than Z.

docs.title: 1. Cannot explain stability of the atom
docs.text:
• The Coulomb force between the electron and the nucleus (\(kq_1q_2/r^2\)) is mathematically similar to the gravitational force between the sun and planets (\(Gm_1m_2/r^2\)). So the electrons were expected to move in well defined orbits like planets.
  • However, a body moving in an orbit is always accelerating, because its direction keeps changing.
  • According to Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, an accelerated charged particle emits electromagnetic radiation. (Planets are uncharged, so this does not apply to them.)
  • So an orbiting electron should continuously lose energy, its orbit should keep shrinking and it should spiral into the nucleus in only about 10-8 s. This does not happen.
  • If the electrons were stationary instead, they would be pulled into the nucleus by electrostatic attraction, forming a miniature Thomson model.

docs.title: 2. Says nothing about electronic structure
docs.text: • The model does not tell how the electrons are distributed around the nucleus or what their energies are.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in \(^{80}_{35}Br\).

\[Z = 35,\ A = 80,\ species\ is\ neutral\] \[Number\ of\ protons = Number\ of\ electrons = Z = 35\] \[Number\ of\ neutrons = A - Z = 80 - 35 = 45\]

The number of electrons, protons and neutrons in a species are equal to 18, 16 and 16 respectively. Assign the proper symbol to the species.

  • Atomic number = number of protons = 16. So the element is sulphur (S).
\[Mass\ number = protons + neutrons = 16 + 16 = 32\]
  • The species is not neutral as protons are not equal to electrons. It has 18 – 16 = 2 extra electrons, so it is an anion with charge –2.
\[Symbol:\ ^{32}_{16}S^{2-}\]

How many neutrons and protons are there in the following nuclei? \(^{13}_6C\), \(^{16}_8O\), \(^{24}_{12}Mg\)

Nucleus Protons (Z) Neutrons (A – Z) \(^{13}_6C\) 6 7 \(^{16}_8O\) 8 8 \(^{24}_{12}Mg\) 12 12

An element with mass number 81 contains 31.7% more neutrons as compared to protons. Assign the atomic symbol.

\[Let\ protons = x,\ then\ neutrons = x + 0.317x = 1.317x\] \[x + 1.317x = 81\] \[x = {81 \over 2.317} = 34.96 ≈ 35\]
  • Atomic number 35 corresponds to bromine. Neutrons = 81 – 35 = 46.
\[Symbol:\ ^{81}_{35}Br\]

docs.title: Structure of Atom | Bohr's Model and Hydrogen Spectrum
Structure of Atom | Bohr's Model and Hydrogen Spectrum
Atomic Spectra
docs.text:
• When white light passes through a prism, waves of shorter wavelength bend more than waves of longer wavelength. So the light spreads into a series of coloured bands called a spectrum. Red light (longest wavelength) is deviated least and violet light (shortest wavelength) is deviated most.
  • In the spectrum of white light, violet merges into blue, blue into green and so on, from 7.50 × 1014 Hz (violet) to 4 × 1014 Hz (red). Such a spectrum is called a continuous spectrum. A rainbow is an example.
  • When atoms absorb energy, they move to a higher energy (excited) state, which is unstable. On returning to a lower energy state, they emit radiation.

docs.title: 1. Emission Spectrum
docs.text:
• The spectrum of radiation emitted by a substance that has absorbed energy is called an emission spectrum.
  • Energy is supplied by heating or irradiating the sample and the wavelengths of emitted radiation are recorded.

docs.title: 2. Absorption Spectrum
docs.text:
• A continuum of radiation is passed through a sample. The wavelengths absorbed by the sample are missing and appear as dark spaces in the bright continuous spectrum.
  • An absorption spectrum is like a photographic negative of an emission spectrum.
  • The study of emission or absorption spectra is called spectroscopy.

docs.title: 3. Line Spectrum
docs.text:
• Atoms in the gas phase do not give a continuous spread of wavelengths. They emit light only at specific wavelengths with dark spaces in between. Such spectra are called line spectra or atomic spectra.
  • Every element has a unique line emission spectrum, so line spectra are used like fingerprints to identify unknown atoms.
  • Elements like rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs), thallium (Tl), indium (In), gallium (Ga) and scandium (Sc) were discovered through spectroscopy. Helium was discovered in the sun by the same method.

docs.title: Line Spectrum of Hydrogen
docs.text:
• When an electric discharge is passed through hydrogen gas, H2 molecules dissociate and the excited hydrogen atoms emit radiation of discrete frequencies. The lines form several series named after their discoverers.
  • Balmer (1885) found that the visible lines obey:
\[\bar{\nu} = 109,677 \left({1 \over 2^2} - {1 \over n^2}\right) cm^{-1},\ where\ n = 3, 4, 5, ...\]
  • These lines are called the Balmer series. They are the only lines of hydrogen in the visible region.
  • Rydberg showed that all series of hydrogen can be described by:
\[\bar{\nu} = 109,677 \left({1 \over n_1^2} - {1 \over n_2^2}\right) cm^{-1}\]

Where, n1 = 1, 2, 3, ... and n2 = n1 + 1, n1 + 2, ...

  • The value 109,677 cm-1 is called the Rydberg constant for hydrogen.
Series n1 n2 Spectral Region Lyman 1 2, 3, ... Ultraviolet Balmer 2 3, 4, ... Visible Paschen 3 4, 5, ... Infrared Brackett 4 5, 6, ... Infrared Pfund 5 6, 7, ... Infrared

  • Two features are common to all line spectra: (i) the line spectrum of each element is unique and (ii) there is regularity in the line spectrum of each element. These features are explained by the electronic structure of the atom.

docs.title: Bohr's Model for Hydrogen Atom
docs.text:
Niels Bohr (1913) was the first to explain quantitatively the structure and spectrum of the hydrogen atom. His model is based on the following postulates:

  • Postulate 1: The electron in the hydrogen atom moves around the nucleus in a circular path of fixed radius and energy. These paths are called orbits, stationary states or allowed energy states. They are arranged concentrically around the nucleus.
  • Postulate 2: The energy of an electron in an orbit does not change with time. The electron moves to a higher stationary state when it absorbs the required energy, and moves to a lower one when it emits energy. The energy change is not continuous.
  • Postulate 3: The frequency of radiation absorbed or emitted in a transition between two stationary states differing in energy by ΔE is given by Bohr's frequency rule:
\[ν = {ΔE \over h} = {E_2 - E_1 \over h}\]

Where, E1 and E2 are the energies of the lower and higher energy states.

  • Postulate 4: The angular momentum of an electron in a stationary state is quantized. It is an integral multiple of h/2π:
\[m_evr = n{h \over 2π},\ where\ n = 1, 2, 3, ...\]

Angular Momentum

Angular momentum = I × ω, where I = mer2 is the moment of inertia and ω = v/r is the angular velocity. So angular momentum = mer2 × v/r = mevr.

docs.title: (a) Principal quantum number
docs.text: • The stationary states are numbered n = 1, 2, 3, ... These integers are called principal quantum numbers.

docs.title: (b) Radius of orbits
docs.text:
\[r_n = n^2a_0,\ where\ a_0 = 52.9\ pm\]
  • The radius of the first orbit (n = 1), 52.9 pm, is called the Bohr radius. As n increases, r increases, so the electron is farther from the nucleus.

docs.title: (c) Energy of orbits
docs.text:
\[E_n = -R_H\left({1 \over n^2}\right),\ where\ R_H = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ J\] \[E_1 = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ J,\ \ E_2 = -0.545 \times 10^{-18}\ J\]
  • RH is called the Rydberg constant (in energy units). The lowest energy state (n = 1) is called the ground state.

Why is the energy negative?

  • A free electron at rest, infinitely far from the nucleus (n = ∞), is assigned zero energy. Such an atom is called an ionized hydrogen atom.

  • When the electron is attracted by the nucleus and present in orbit n, energy is released and its energy becomes lower than zero, i.e. negative.

  • As n decreases, En becomes larger in magnitude and more negative. The most negative value (n = 1) corresponds to the most stable orbit.

docs.title: (d) Hydrogen like species
docs.text:
• Bohr's theory also applies to ions with only one electron, like He+, Li2+, Be3+. These are called hydrogen like species.
\[E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left({Z^2 \over n^2}\right) J\] \[r_n = {52.9\ (n^2) \over Z}\ pm\]

Where, Z is the atomic number (2 for He, 3 for Li).

  • As Z increases, energy becomes more negative and radius becomes smaller, so the electron is more tightly bound to the nucleus.

docs.title: (e) Velocity of electron
docs.text: • The velocity of the electron increases with increase in positive charge on the nucleus and decreases with increase in principal quantum number.

docs.title: Explanation of Line Spectrum of Hydrogen
docs.text:
• Radiation is absorbed when the electron moves from an orbit of smaller n to one of higher n, and emitted when it moves from a higher orbit to a lower one.
\[ΔE = E_f - E_i\] \[ΔE = \left(-{R_H \over n_f^2}\right) - \left(-{R_H \over n_i^2}\right)\] \[ΔE = R_H\left({1 \over n_i^2} - {1 \over n_f^2}\right) = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left({1 \over n_i^2} - {1 \over n_f^2}\right) J\]

Where, ni and nf are the initial and final orbits.

  • The frequency and wavenumber of the photon are:
\[ν = {ΔE \over h} = {2.18 \times 10^{-18} \over 6.626 \times 10^{-34}}\left({1 \over n_i^2} - {1 \over n_f^2}\right)\] \[ν = 3.29 \times 10^{15}\left({1 \over n_i^2} - {1 \over n_f^2}\right) Hz\] \[\bar{\nu} = {ν \over c} = {3.29 \times 10^{15} \over 3 \times 10^8}\left({1 \over n_i^2} - {1 \over n_f^2}\right)\] \[\bar{\nu} = 1.09677 \times 10^7\left({1 \over n_i^2} - {1 \over n_f^2}\right) m^{-1}\]
  • In absorption, nf > ni, ΔE is positive and energy is absorbed. In emission, ni > nf, ΔE is negative and energy is released.
  • This expression is the same as the empirical Rydberg formula. Each spectral line corresponds to a particular transition. With a large number of atoms, many transitions occur together, giving many lines. The brightness of a line depends on the number of photons of that wavelength.

Maximum number of spectral lines

When an electron falls from orbit n to the ground state, the maximum number of lines emitted is:

\[Number\ of\ lines = {n(n-1) \over 2}\]

docs.title: Limitations of Bohr's Model
docs.text:
1. It cannot explain the finer details (doublets, i.e. two closely spaced lines) of the hydrogen spectrum seen with sophisticated spectroscopic techniques.
  2. It cannot explain the spectrum of atoms other than hydrogen, even helium which has only two electrons.
  3. It cannot explain the splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) or an electric field (Stark effect).
  4. It cannot explain the ability of atoms to form molecules by chemical bonds.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What are the frequency and wavelength of a photon emitted during a transition from n = 5 state to the n = 2 state in the hydrogen atom?

  • Since ni = 5 and nf = 2, this is a line of the Balmer series in the visible region.
\[ΔE = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left({1 \over 5^2} - {1 \over 2^2}\right) = -4.58 \times 10^{-19}\ J\]
  • The negative sign shows it is emission energy. Taking magnitude:
\[ν = {ΔE \over h} = {4.58 \times 10^{-19} \over 6.626 \times 10^{-34}} = 6.91 \times 10^{14}\ Hz\] \[λ = {c \over ν} = {3.0 \times 10^8 \over 6.91 \times 10^{14}} = 434\ nm\]

Calculate the energy associated with the first orbit of He+. What is the radius of this orbit?

\[E_n = -{2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times Z^2 \over n^2}\ J\ atom^{-1}\] \[For\ He^+,\ n = 1,\ Z = 2\] \[E_1 = -{2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 2^2 \over 1^2} = -8.72 \times 10^{-18}\ J\] \[r_n = {0.0529\ n^2 \over Z}\ nm = {0.0529 \times 1^2 \over 2} = 0.02645\ nm\]

docs.title: Structure of Atom | Dual Nature of Matter and Uncertainty Principle
Structure of Atom | Dual Nature of Matter and Uncertainty Principle
docs.text:
To overcome the shortcomings of Bohr's model, a more general model of the atom was needed. Two important developments led to it:

  1. Dual behaviour of matter.
  2. Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

docs.title: Dual Behaviour of Matter: de Broglie Relation
docs.text:
• The French physicist de Broglie (1924) proposed that matter, like radiation, shows dual behaviour, i.e. both particle and wave like properties.
  • Just as a photon has momentum as well as wavelength, an electron should also have momentum as well as wavelength.
  • He gave the following relation between wavelength (λ) and momentum (p) of a material particle:
\[λ = {h \over mv} = {h \over p}\]

Where, m is the mass of the particle, v is its velocity and p is its momentum.

  • de Broglie's prediction was confirmed when an electron beam was found to undergo diffraction, a property of waves.
  • This is used in the electron microscope, which uses the wave like behaviour of electrons just as an ordinary microscope uses the wave nature of light. It can magnify about 15 million times.
  • Every moving object has a wave character. But the wavelengths of ordinary objects are so short (because of their large mass) that their wave properties cannot be detected. For electrons and other sub-atomic particles (very small mass), the wavelengths can be detected.

Useful forms of de Broglie equation

\[K.E. = {1 \over 2}mv^2 = {p^2 \over 2m}\] \[λ = {h \over \sqrt{2m \times K.E.}}\]

docs.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
docs.text:
• Werner Heisenberg (1927) stated the uncertainty principle, which is a consequence of the dual behaviour of matter and radiation.
  • It is impossible to determine simultaneously the exact position and exact momentum (or velocity) of an electron.
\[Δx \times Δp_x ≥ {h \over 4π}\] \[Δx \times Δ(mv_x) ≥ {h \over 4π}\] \[Δx \times Δv_x ≥ {h \over 4πm}\]

Where, Δx is uncertainty in position and Δpx (or Δvx) is uncertainty in momentum (or velocity).

  • If the position is known very accurately (Δx is small), the velocity will be uncertain (Δvx is large), and vice versa.

Example

Suppose you try to measure the thickness of a sheet of paper with an unmarked metrestick. The result will be meaningless. You need an instrument graduated in units smaller than the thickness of the paper.

Similarly, to locate an electron we must use "light" with a wavelength smaller than the size of the electron. But such light has high momentum (p = h/λ). Its photons collide with the electron and change its energy. We may find the position, but we would know very little about the velocity after the collision.

docs.title: Significance of Uncertainty Principle
docs.text:
• It rules out the existence of definite paths or trajectories of electrons and similar particles.
  • The trajectory of an object is fixed by its position and velocity at different moments. Since both cannot be known exactly at the same time for an electron, we cannot talk of its trajectory.
  • The effect is significant only for microscopic objects and negligible for macroscopic objects.

Macroscopic vs microscopic objects

For an object of mass 1 milligram (10-6 kg):

\[Δv.Δx = {h \over 4πm} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \over 4 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-6}} ≈ 10^{-28}\ m^2\ s^{-1}\]

This is extremely small and of no real consequence.

For an electron of mass 9.11 × 10-31 kg:

\[Δv.Δx = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \over 4 \times 3.1416 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31}} ≈ 10^{-4}\ m^2\ s^{-1}\]

If we try to locate the electron within 10-8 m, then:

\[Δv = {10^{-4}\ m^2\ s^{-1} \over 10^{-8}\ m} ≈ 10^4\ m\ s^{-1}\]

This is so large that the classical picture of electrons moving in fixed Bohr orbits cannot hold.

Conclusion

The precise statements of position and momentum of electrons have to be replaced by statements of probability that the electron has a given position and momentum. This is the basis of the quantum mechanical model of the atom.

docs.title: Reasons for the Failure of Bohr Model
docs.text:
• In Bohr's model, the electron is a charged particle moving in a well defined circular orbit. The wave character of the electron is ignored.
  • An orbit is a clearly defined path, which can be defined only if both position and velocity of the electron are known exactly at the same time. This is not possible according to the uncertainty principle.
  • So the Bohr model ignores the dual behaviour of matter and also contradicts Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. There was no point extending it to other atoms.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What will be the wavelength of a ball of mass 0.1 kg moving with a velocity of 10 m s-1?

\[λ = {h \over mv} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ J\ s \over 0.1\ kg \times 10\ m\ s^{-1}}\] \[λ = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ m\ \ (J = kg\ m^2\ s^{-2})\]

This wavelength is far too small to be detected.

The mass of an electron is 9.1 × 10-31 kg. If its K.E. is 3.0 × 10-25 J, calculate its wavelength.

\[K.E. = {1 \over 2}mv^2\] \[v = \sqrt{2 \times K.E. \over m} = \sqrt{2 \times 3.0 \times 10^{-25} \over 9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = 812\ m\ s^{-1}\] \[λ = {h \over mv} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \over 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 812}\] \[λ = 8.967 \times 10^{-7}\ m = 896.7\ nm\]

Calculate the mass of a photon with wavelength 3.6 Å.

\[λ = 3.6\ Å = 3.6 \times 10^{-10}\ m\] \[Velocity\ of\ photon = c = 3 \times 10^8\ m\ s^{-1}\] \[m = {h \over λc} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \over 3.6 \times 10^{-10} \times 3 \times 10^8}\] \[m = 6.135 \times 10^{-33}\ kg\]

Calculate the wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 2.05 × 107 m s-1.

\[λ = {h \over mv} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \over 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.05 \times 10^7}\] \[λ = 3.55 \times 10^{-11}\ m\]

If the velocity of the electron in Bohr's first orbit is 2.19 × 106 m s-1, calculate the de Broglie wavelength associated with it.

\[λ = {h \over mv} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \over 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.19 \times 10^6}\] \[λ = 3.32 \times 10^{-10}\ m = 332\ pm\]

A microscope using suitable photons is employed to locate an electron in an atom within a distance of 0.1 Å. What is the uncertainty involved in the measurement of its velocity?

\[Δx Δp = {h \over 4π}\ \ or\ \ Δx\ mΔv = {h \over 4π}\] \[Δv = {h \over 4πΔx\ m}\] \[Δv = {6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ J\ s \over 4 \times 3.14 \times 0.1 \times 10^{-10}\ m \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ kg}\] \[Δv = 0.579 \times 10^7\ m\ s^{-1} = 5.79 \times 10^6\ m\ s^{-1}\]

A golf ball has a mass of 40 g and a speed of 45 m/s. If the speed can be measured within an accuracy of 2%, calculate the uncertainty in the position.

\[Δv = 45 \times {2 \over 100} = 0.9\ m\ s^{-1}\] \[Δx = {h \over 4πmΔv} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \over 4 \times 3.14 \times 40 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.9}\] \[Δx = 1.46 \times 10^{-33}\ m\]

This is about 1018 times smaller than the diameter of a typical atomic nucleus. So for large particles, the uncertainty principle sets no meaningful limit on the precision of measurement.

docs.title: Structure of Atom | Electromagnetic Radiation and Planck's Quantum Theory
Structure of Atom | Electromagnetic Radiation and Planck's Quantum Theory
docs.text: Niels Bohr improved Rutherford's model using two developments: (i) the dual character of electromagnetic radiation, i.e. radiation has both wave like and particle like properties, and (ii) atomic spectra, which can be explained only by assuming quantized electronic energy levels.

docs.title: Wave Nature of Electromagnetic Radiation
docs.text:
• James Maxwell (1870) suggested that when an electrically charged particle moves under acceleration, alternating electric and magnetic fields are produced and transmitted. These are transmitted as waves called electromagnetic waves or electromagnetic radiation.
  • Newton thought light was made of particles (corpuscles). The wave nature of light was established only in the 19th century.

docs.title: Properties of Electromagnetic Waves
docs.text:
1. The oscillating electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation of the wave. Both have the same wavelength, frequency, speed and amplitude.
  2. Unlike sound or water waves, electromagnetic waves do not need a medium and can travel in vacuum.
  3. There are many types of electromagnetic radiation which differ in wavelength (or frequency). Together they form the electromagnetic spectrum.
  4. Different units are used to represent electromagnetic radiation.

docs.title: Regions of the Electromagnetic Spectrum
docs.text:
Region Approximate frequency Use / Example Radio frequency ~106 Hz Broadcasting Microwave ~1010 Hz Radar Infrared ~1013 Hz Heating Visible ~1015 Hz The only part our eyes can detect Ultraviolet ~1016 Hz Component of sun's radiation
  • In increasing order of frequency: radio waves < microwaves < infrared < visible < ultraviolet < X-rays < γ-rays.
  • The visible spectrum extends from violet (about 400 nm) to red (about 750 nm).

docs.title: 1. Frequency (ν)
docs.text:
• Frequency is the number of waves that pass a given point in one second.
  • SI unit is hertz (Hz, s-1).

docs.title: 2. Wavelength (λ)
docs.text: • Wavelength is the distance between two successive crests (or troughs) of a wave. SI unit is metre (m), but smaller units like nm and Å are commonly used.

docs.title: 3. Speed of Light (c)
docs.text:
• In vacuum, all types of electromagnetic radiation travel at the same speed, c = 3.0 × 108 m s-1 (2.997925 × 108 m s-1 to be precise).
\[c = ν λ\]

docs.title: 4. Wavenumber (\(\bar{\nu}\))
docs.text:
• Wavenumber is the number of wavelengths per unit length. Its SI unit is m-1, but cm-1 is commonly used.
\[\bar{\nu} = {1 \over λ}\]

docs.title: Particle Nature of Electromagnetic Radiation: Planck's Quantum Theory
docs.text:
Some phenomena could not be explained by the wave nature of light (classical physics):

  1. Emission of radiation from hot bodies (black body radiation).
  2. Ejection of electrons from a metal surface when radiation strikes it (photoelectric effect).
  3. Variation of heat capacity of solids with temperature.
  4. Line spectra of atoms, especially hydrogen.

docs.title: Black Body Radiation
docs.text:
• When an iron rod is heated, it first turns dull red, then more and more red, then white and finally blue at very high temperature. So the emitted radiation goes from lower to higher frequency as temperature rises.
  • An ideal body which emits and absorbs radiation of all frequencies is called a black body, and the radiation emitted by it is called black body radiation.
  • The intensity versus frequency curve of a black body depends only on its temperature. At a given temperature, intensity increases with decrease of wavelength, reaches a maximum and then decreases.

docs.title: Planck's Quantum Theory
docs.text:
• Max Planck (1900) suggested that atoms and molecules can emit or absorb energy only in discrete quantities and not continuously.
  • The smallest quantity of energy that can be emitted or absorbed as electromagnetic radiation is called a quantum.
  • The energy of a quantum is proportional to the frequency of radiation:
\[E = hν = {hc \over λ}\]

Where, h = Planck's constant = 6.626 × 10-34 J s

  • Using this theory, Planck could explain the intensity distribution of black body radiation at different temperatures.

docs.title: Photoelectric Effect
docs.text: • H. Hertz (1887) observed that electrons are ejected when certain metals (like potassium, rubidium, caesium) are exposed to a beam of light. This is called the photoelectric effect.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
1. Electrons are ejected as soon as light strikes the surface. There is no time lag.
  2. The number of electrons ejected is proportional to the intensity (brightness) of light.
  3. For each metal, there is a minimum frequency ν0, called the threshold frequency, below which no photoelectric effect is seen. For ν > ν0, electrons come out with some kinetic energy.
  4. The kinetic energy of ejected electrons increases with the frequency of light, but does not depend on its intensity.

Example

Red light (ν = 4.3 to 4.6 × 1014 Hz) of any brightness may shine on potassium for hours and no electrons are ejected. But even a very weak yellow light (ν = 5.1 to 5.2 × 1014 Hz) ejects electrons, because the threshold frequency of potassium is 5.0 × 1014 Hz.

  • According to classical physics, the energy of light depends on its brightness, so both the number and the kinetic energy of electrons should depend on brightness. This was not observed.

docs.title: Einstein's Explanation
docs.text:
• Einstein (1905) explained the effect using Planck's theory. A beam of light is a stream of particles called photons, each with energy hν.
  • When a photon of enough energy strikes an electron, it transfers its energy instantly and the electron is ejected without delay.
  • The minimum energy needed to eject an electron is hν0, called the work function (W0). The remaining energy appears as kinetic energy of the photoelectron:
\[hν = hν_0 + {1 \over 2}m_ev^2\] \[K.E. = {1 \over 2}m_ev^2 = h(ν - ν_0)\]
  • A more intense beam has more photons, so more electrons are ejected.
Metal Li Na K Mg Cu Ag W0 / eV 2.42 2.3 2.25 3.7 4.8 4.3

docs.title: Dual Behaviour of Electromagnetic Radiation
docs.text:
• The particle nature of light explains black body radiation and the photoelectric effect, but the wave nature is needed to explain interference and diffraction.
  • So light has dual behaviour: it behaves as a wave or as a stream of particles depending on the experiment.
  • When radiation interacts with matter it shows particle like properties, and when it propagates it shows wave like properties.
  • Microscopic particles like electrons also show this wave-particle duality.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
The Vividh Bharati station of All India Radio, Delhi, broadcasts on a frequency of 1,368 kHz. Calculate the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation emitted. Which part of the spectrum does it belong to?

\[λ = {c \over ν} = {3.00 \times 10^8\ m\ s^{-1} \over 1368 \times 10^3\ s^{-1}}\] \[λ = 219.3\ m\]

This is a characteristic radiowave wavelength.

The visible spectrum extends from violet (400 nm) to red (750 nm). Express these wavelengths in frequencies (Hz).

\[ν_{violet} = {c \over λ} = {3.00 \times 10^8 \over 400 \times 10^{-9}} = 7.50 \times 10^{14}\ Hz\] \[ν_{red} = {3.00 \times 10^8 \over 750 \times 10^{-9}} = 4.00 \times 10^{14}\ Hz\]

So the visible spectrum extends from 4.0 × 1014 Hz to 7.5 × 1014 Hz.

Calculate (a) wavenumber and (b) frequency of yellow radiation having wavelength 5800 Å.

\[λ = 5800\ Å = 5800 \times 10^{-10}\ m\] \[\bar{\nu} = {1 \over λ} = {1 \over 5800 \times 10^{-10}\ m} = 1.724 \times 10^6\ m^{-1}\] \[ν = {c \over λ} = {3 \times 10^8 \over 5800 \times 10^{-10}} = 5.17 \times 10^{14}\ s^{-1}\]

Calculate energy of one mole of photons of radiation whose frequency is 5 × 1014 Hz.

\[E = hν = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 5 \times 10^{14} = 3.313 \times 10^{-19}\ J\] \[Energy\ of\ 1\ mole\ photons = 3.313 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\] \[= 199.51\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]
