A 100 watt bulb emits monochromatic light of wavelength 400 nm. Calculate the number of photons emitted per second by the bulb.

\[Power = 100\ W = 100\ J\ s^{-1}\] \[E = {hc \over λ} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8 \over 400 \times 10^{-9}} = 4.969 \times 10^{-19}\ J\] \[Number\ of\ photons = {100\ J\ s^{-1} \over 4.969 \times 10^{-19}\ J} = 2.012 \times 10^{20}\ s^{-1}\]

When electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 300 nm falls on the surface of sodium, electrons are emitted with a kinetic energy of 1.68 × 105 J mol-1. What is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from sodium? What is the maximum wavelength that will cause a photoelectron to be emitted?

\[E = {hc \over λ} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8 \over 300 \times 10^{-9}} = 6.626 \times 10^{-19}\ J\] \[Energy\ of\ 1\ mole\ photons = 6.626 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.99 \times 10^5\ J\ mol^{-1}\] \[Minimum\ energy\ per\ mole = (3.99 - 1.68) \times 10^5 = 2.31 \times 10^5\ J\ mol^{-1}\] \[Minimum\ energy\ per\ electron = {2.31 \times 10^5 \over 6.022 \times 10^{23}} = 3.84 \times 10^{-19}\ J\] \[λ_{max} = {hc \over E} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8 \over 3.84 \times 10^{-19}} = 517\ nm\]

This corresponds to green light.

The threshold frequency ν0 for a metal is 7.0 × 1014 s-1. Calculate the kinetic energy of an electron emitted when radiation of frequency ν = 1.0 × 1015 s-1 hits the metal.

\[K.E. = h(ν - ν_0)\] \[K.E. = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times (10.0 \times 10^{14} - 7.0 \times 10^{14})\] \[K.E. = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{14} = 1.988 \times 10^{-19}\ J\]

A photon of wavelength 4 × 10-7 m strikes a metal surface, the work function of the metal being 2.13 eV. Calculate (i) the energy of the photon (eV), (ii) the kinetic energy of the emission and (iii) the velocity of the photoelectron (1 eV = 1.6020 × 10-19 J).

\[E = {hc \over λ} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8 \over 4 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.97 \times 10^{-19}\ J\] \[E = {4.97 \times 10^{-19} \over 1.602 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.10\ eV\] \[K.E. = 3.10 - 2.13 = 0.97\ eV = 1.55 \times 10^{-19}\ J\] \[v = \sqrt{2 \times K.E. \over m_e} = \sqrt{2 \times 1.55 \times 10^{-19} \over 9.11 \times 10^{-31}}\] \[v = 5.84 \times 10^5\ m\ s^{-1}\]

docs.title: Structure of Atom | Electronic Configuration
docs.text: The filling of electrons into the orbitals of different atoms follows the Aufbau principle, which is based on Pauli's exclusion principle, Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity and the relative energies of the orbitals.

docs.title: Aufbau Principle
docs.text:
• 'Aufbau' is a German word meaning 'building up'. Here it means the filling up of orbitals with electrons.
  • In the ground state of an atom, the orbitals are filled in order of their increasing energies. Electrons first occupy the lowest energy orbital available, and enter higher energy orbitals only after the lower ones are filled.
  • The order of filling (based on the (n + l) rule) is:
\[1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, ...\]
  • This order can be remembered using the diagram below. Starting from the top, follow the arrows from right top to bottom left.

docs.title: Pauli Exclusion Principle
docs.text:
• Given by the Austrian scientist Wolfgang Pauli (1926).
  • No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers.
  • It can also be stated as: Only two electrons may exist in the same orbital and these electrons must have opposite spin.
  • So two electrons in the same orbital have the same n, l and ml, but opposite ms.
  • This principle fixes the capacity of each sub-shell: s can hold 2, p can hold 6, d can hold 10 and f can hold 14 electrons.
\[Maximum\ electrons\ in\ a\ shell = 2n^2\] \[Maximum\ electrons\ in\ a\ sub\text{-}shell = 2(2l + 1)\]

docs.title: Hund's Rule of Maximum Multiplicity
docs.text:
• This rule deals with filling electrons into orbitals of the same sub-shell, i.e. orbitals of equal energy, called degenerate orbitals.
  • Pairing of electrons in the orbitals belonging to the same sub-shell (p, d or f) does not take place until each orbital of that sub-shell has got one electron each, i.e. it is singly occupied.
  • Since there are three p, five d and seven f orbitals, pairing starts with the entry of the 4th, 6th and 8th electron respectively.
  • Half filled and completely filled degenerate sets of orbitals have extra stability.

docs.title: Writing Electronic Configurations
docs.text: The electronic configuration can be represented in two ways:

docs.title: 1. s<sup>a</sup>p<sup>b</sup>d<sup>c</sup> notation
docs.text: • Each sub-shell is written with its letter, and the number of electrons is shown as a superscript. The principal quantum number is written before the sub-shell. Example: 1s22s22p3.

docs.title: 2. Orbital diagram
docs.text: • Each orbital is shown as a box and each electron as an arrow: ↑ for positive spin and ↓ for negative spin. This shows all four quantum numbers.

docs.title: Elements Hydrogen to Neon
docs.text:
• Hydrogen has one electron in 1s: 1s1. Helium: 1s2, the two electrons having opposite spins.
  • The third electron of lithium cannot go into 1s (Pauli exclusion principle), so it goes into 2s: 1s22s1. Beryllium: 1s22s2.
  • In the next six elements, 2p orbitals are filled progressively, following Hund's rule:
Element Z Configuration 2p orbital diagram B 5 1s22s22p1 ↑, –, – C 6 1s22s22p2 ↑, ↑, – N 7 1s22s22p3 ↑, ↑, ↑ O 8 1s22s22p4 ↑↓, ↑, ↑ F 9 1s22s22p5 ↑↓, ↑↓, ↑ Ne 10 1s22s22p6 ↑↓, ↑↓, ↑↓

docs.title: Core and Valence Electrons
docs.text:
• From sodium (1s22s22p63s1) to argon (1s22s22p63s23p6), the 3s and 3p orbitals fill in the same pattern as Li to Ne.
  • The first two shells can be written as [Ne]. So Na is [Ne]3s1 and Ar is [Ne]3s23p6.
  • Electrons in completely filled shells are called core electrons. Electrons added to the outermost shell (highest n) are called valence electrons.

docs.title: Elements beyond Argon
docs.text:
• In potassium and calcium, 4s is lower in energy than 3d, so it is filled first: K is [Ar]4s1 and Ca is [Ar]4s2.
  • From scandium (Sc) to zinc (Zn), the 3d orbitals are filled, since 3d is lower in energy than 4p.
  • From gallium (Ga) to krypton (Kr), 4p is filled. Rubidium (Rb) to xenon (Xe) fill 5s, 4d and 5p in a similar way.
  • Caesium (Cs) and barium (Ba) fill 6s. From lanthanum (La) to mercury (Hg), 4f and 5d are filled. Then 6p, 7s, and finally 5f and 6d are filled.
  • Elements after uranium (U) are short-lived and are produced artificially.

docs.title: Stability of Completely Filled and Half Filled Sub-shells
docs.text:
• The ground state configuration of an atom always corresponds to the lowest total electronic energy.
  • In some elements like Cr and Cu, the 4s and 3d sub-shells differ only slightly in energy. An electron shifts from 4s to 3d if this makes the 3d sub-shell exactly half filled or completely filled.
  • Configurations like p3, p6, d5, d10, f7, f14 are more stable.

Exceptional configurations

\[Cr\ (Z = 24):\ [Ar]3d^54s^1\ and\ not\ [Ar]3d^44s^2\] \[Cu\ (Z = 29):\ [Ar]3d^{10}4s^1\ and\ not\ [Ar]3d^94s^2\]

docs.title: 1. Symmetrical distribution of electrons
docs.text:
• Symmetry leads to stability. Completely filled or half filled sub-shells have a symmetrical distribution of electrons.
  • Electrons in the same sub-shell have equal energy but different spatial distribution. So they shield one another relatively little and are more strongly attracted by the nucleus.

docs.title: 2. Exchange energy
docs.text:
• When two or more electrons with the same spin are present in degenerate orbitals, they tend to exchange their positions. The energy released by this exchange is called exchange energy.
  • The number of possible exchanges is maximum when the sub-shell is half filled or completely filled. So exchange energy, and hence stability, is maximum.
  • For a d5 configuration, electron 1 can make 4 exchanges, electron 2 can make 3, electron 3 can make 2 and electron 4 can make 1. Total = 10 exchanges.
  • Exchange energy is the basis of Hund's rule: electrons entering degenerate orbitals keep parallel spins as far as possible.

Conclusion

The extra stability of half filled and completely filled sub-shells is due to: (i) relatively small shielding, (ii) smaller coulombic repulsion energy and (iii) larger exchange energy.

docs.title: Importance of Electronic Configuration
docs.text: The electronic configuration explains many questions that Dalton's model could not, such as why atoms combine to form molecules, why some elements are metals and others non-metals, and why helium and argon are unreactive while halogens are reactive.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Write the electronic configurations of the following ions: (a) H– (b) Na+ (c) O2– (d) F–

\[(a)\ H^-\ (2\ electrons):\ 1s^2\] \[(b)\ Na^+\ (10\ electrons):\ 1s^22s^22p^6\] \[(c)\ O^{2-}\ (10\ electrons):\ 1s^22s^22p^6\] \[(d)\ F^-\ (10\ electrons):\ 1s^22s^22p^6\]

Which atoms are indicated by the following configurations? (a) [He]2s1 (b) [Ne]3s23p3 (c) [Ar]4s23d1

  • (a) 2 + 1 = 3 electrons: Lithium (Li)

  • (b) 10 + 5 = 15 electrons: Phosphorus (P)

  • (c) 18 + 3 = 21 electrons: Scandium (Sc)

An atom of an element contains 29 electrons and 35 neutrons. Deduce (i) the number of protons and (ii) the electronic configuration of the element.

  • For a neutral atom, number of protons = number of electrons = 29. The element is copper (Cu).

  • Due to the extra stability of a completely filled 3d sub-shell:

\[Cu:\ 1s^22s^22p^63s^23p^63d^{10}4s^1\]

Indicate the number of unpaired electrons in: (a) P (b) Si (c) Cr (d) Fe (e) Kr

Element Configuration Unpaired electrons P [Ne]3s23p3 3 Si [Ne]3s23p2 2 Cr [Ar]3d54s1 6 Fe [Ar]3d64s2 4 Kr [Ar]3d104s24p6 0

docs.title: Structure of Atom | Introduction and Sub-atomic Particles
Structure of Atom | Introduction and Sub-atomic Particles
docs.text:
The idea of atoms is very old. Early Indian and Greek philosophers (around 400 B.C.) believed that if matter is divided again and again, we finally reach a particle that cannot be divided further. The word 'atom' comes from the Greek word 'a-tomio', meaning 'uncut-able' or 'non-divisible'.

  • John Dalton (1808) gave the first scientific atomic theory, called Dalton's atomic theory, which treated the atom as the ultimate indivisible particle of matter.
  • Experiments at the end of the nineteenth century showed that atoms are actually made up of smaller sub-atomic particles: electrons, protons and neutrons.
  • After these discoveries, scientists had to answer some important questions:
    • Why is the atom stable even though it contains charged particles?
    • Why do different elements show different physical and chemical properties?
    • How do atoms combine to form different molecules?
    • What is the origin of the radiation absorbed or emitted by atoms?

docs.title: Sub-atomic Particles
docs.text: Dalton's theory could explain the law of conservation of mass, the law of constant composition and the law of multiple proportions. However, it could not explain why substances like glass or ebonite produce electricity when rubbed with silk or fur. This pointed to the existence of charged particles inside the atom.

docs.title: Discovery of Electron
docs.text:
• Michael Faraday (1830) showed that when electricity is passed through a solution of an electrolyte, matter is liberated and deposited at the electrodes. This suggested that electricity itself is made of particles.
  • In the mid 1850s, Faraday and others studied electrical discharge through partially evacuated glass tubes called cathode ray discharge tubes.
  • A cathode ray tube is a glass tube with two thin metal electrodes sealed in it. Discharge through the gas is seen only at very low pressure and very high voltage.
  • When high voltage is applied, a stream of particles moves from the negative electrode (cathode) to the positive electrode (anode). These are called cathode rays or cathode ray particles.
  • When a hole is made in the anode and the tube behind it is coated with zinc sulphide (a phosphorescent material), a bright spot appears on the coating where the rays strike it.

docs.title: Properties of Cathode Rays
docs.text:
1. Cathode rays start from the cathode and move towards the anode.
  2. The rays themselves are invisible. Their behaviour is observed with the help of fluorescent or phosphorescent materials that glow when hit by them. Old television picture tubes work on this principle.
  3. In the absence of an electric or magnetic field, cathode rays travel in straight lines.
  4. In the presence of an electric or magnetic field, they behave like negatively charged particles. These negatively charged particles are called electrons.
  5. The characteristics of cathode rays do not depend on the material of the electrodes or the gas present in the tube.

Conclusion

Since the properties of cathode rays are the same whatever the electrode material or gas used, electrons must be a basic constituent of all atoms.

docs.title: Charge to Mass Ratio of Electron
docs.text:
• In 1897, J.J. Thomson measured the ratio of charge (e) to mass (me) of the electron. He applied electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the path of the electrons.
  • The deviation of the particles from their path depends on:
    • Magnitude of charge: greater the charge, greater the interaction with the field and greater the deflection.
    • Mass of the particle: lighter the particle, greater the deflection.
    • Strength of the field: deflection increases with the voltage across the electrodes or the strength of the magnetic field.
  • With only the electric field applied, the electrons hit the screen at one point (A). With only the magnetic field, they hit another point (C). By balancing the two fields, the electrons can be brought back to their original path (point B).
  • From these deflections Thomson found:
\[{e \over m_e} = 1.758820 \times 10^{11}\ C\ kg^{-1}\]

Where, me is mass of electron in kg and e is magnitude of charge on electron in coulomb (C).

  • Since electrons are negatively charged, the charge on an electron is written as –e.

docs.title: Charge on the Electron: Millikan's Oil Drop Method
docs.text:
• R.A. Millikan (1906–14) found the charge on an electron using the oil drop experiment.
  • Fine oil droplets from an atomiser enter an electrical condenser through a tiny hole in its upper plate. Their fall is watched through a telescope fitted with a micrometer eye piece.
  • The air in the chamber is ionised by X-rays. The oil droplets pick up charge by colliding with the gaseous ions.
  • By changing the voltage on the plates, the fall of a charged droplet can be slowed down, speeded up or stopped. From this, the charge on the droplet is calculated.
  • Millikan found that the charge q on any droplet is always an integral multiple of a fundamental charge e:
\[q = ne,\ where\ n = 1, 2, 3, ...\]
  • Millikan's value of charge was –1.6 × 10-19 C. The present accepted value is –1.6022 × 10-19 C.
  • Combining this with Thomson's e/me value gives the mass of the electron:
\[m_e = {e \over e/m_e} = {1.6022 \times 10^{-19}\ C \over 1.758820 \times 10^{11}\ C\ kg^{-1}}\] \[m_e = 9.1094 \times 10^{-31}\ kg\]

docs.title: Discovery of Protons and Neutrons
docs.text:
• Electrical discharge in a modified cathode ray tube produced rays of positively charged particles called canal rays (or anode rays).
  • Properties of these positively charged particles:
    1. Unlike cathode rays, they depend on the nature of the gas in the tube. They are simply positively charged gaseous ions.
    2. Their charge to mass ratio depends on the gas from which they are formed.
    3. Some of them carry a multiple of the fundamental unit of charge.
    4. Their behaviour in electric or magnetic fields is opposite to that of electrons.
  • The smallest and lightest positive ion was obtained from hydrogen. It was called the proton and was characterised in 1919.
  • Chadwick (1932) bombarded a thin sheet of beryllium with α-particles. Electrically neutral particles with mass slightly greater than that of protons were emitted. He named them neutrons.

docs.title: Properties of Fundamental Particles
docs.text:
Name Symbol Absolute charge/C Relative charge Mass/kg Mass/u Approx. mass/u Electron e –1.6022 × 10-19 –1 9.10939 × 10-31 0.00054 0 Proton p +1.6022 × 10-19 +1 1.67262 × 10-27 1.00727 1 Neutron n 0 0 1.67493 × 10-27 1.00867 1

Note

  • X-rays: Röentgen (1895) found that when electrons strike a material in a cathode ray tube, rays are produced that cause fluorescence. He called them X-rays. They are produced most effectively when electrons strike a dense metal anode (called a target). X-rays are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, have very high penetrating power and very short wavelength (~0.1 nm).

  • Radioactivity: Becquerel observed that certain elements emit radiation on their own. This is called radioactivity and such elements are called radioactive elements. Three kinds of rays are emitted: α-rays (high energy particles with two units of positive charge and four units of atomic mass, i.e. helium nuclei), β-rays (negatively charged particles similar to electrons) and γ-rays (high energy neutral radiation like X-rays, not made of particles).

  • Penetrating power: α-particles are the least penetrating, β-rays are about 100 times and γ-rays about 1000 times as penetrating as α-particles.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Calculate the number of electrons which will together weigh one gram. Also calculate the mass and charge of one mole of electrons.

\[Mass\ of\ one\ electron = 9.10939 \times 10^{-31}\ kg = 9.10939 \times 10^{-28}\ g\] \[Number\ of\ electrons\ in\ 1\ g = {1 \over 9.10939 \times 10^{-28}} = 1.098 \times 10^{27}\] \[Mass\ of\ 1\ mole\ electrons = 9.10939 \times 10^{-31} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 5.486 \times 10^{-7}\ kg\] \[Charge\ on\ 1\ mole\ electrons = 1.6022 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 9.648 \times 10^4\ C\]

In Millikan's experiment, static electric charge on an oil drop is found to be –1.282 × 10-18 C. Calculate the number of electrons present on it.

\[Number\ of\ electrons = {q \over e} = {1.282 \times 10^{-18} \over 1.6022 \times 10^{-19}}\] \[Number\ of\ electrons = 8\]

docs.title: Structure of Atom | Quantum Mechanical Model of Atom
Structure of Atom | Quantum Mechanical Model of Atom
docs.text:
• Classical mechanics (based on Newton's laws) describes macroscopic objects like a falling stone or orbiting planets very well. It fails for microscopic objects like electrons, atoms and molecules because it ignores dual behaviour of matter and the uncertainty principle.
  • Quantum mechanics is a theoretical science that deals with the study of the motions of microscopic objects that have both observable wave like and particle like properties.
  • When quantum mechanics is applied to macroscopic objects (where wave properties are insignificant), it gives the same results as classical mechanics.
  • Quantum mechanics was developed independently in 1926 by Werner Heisenberg and Erwin Schrödinger.

docs.title: Schrödinger Equation
docs.text:
• The fundamental equation of quantum mechanics, developed by Schrödinger, incorporates the wave-particle duality of matter. For a system whose energy does not change with time, it is written as:
\[\hat{H}ψ = Eψ\]

Where, \(\hat{H}\) is a mathematical operator called the Hamiltonian, E is the total energy and ψ is the wave function.

  • The Hamiltonian is built from the total energy of the system: kinetic energies of all particles (electrons and nuclei), attraction between electrons and nuclei, and repulsion among electrons and among nuclei.
  • Solving this equation gives E and ψ.

docs.title: Hydrogen Atom and the Schrödinger Equation
docs.text:
• For the hydrogen atom, the solution gives the allowed energy levels and the corresponding wave functions (ψ) of the electron.
  • These quantized energy states are characterised by three quantum numbers: principal quantum number n, azimuthal quantum number l and magnetic quantum number ml. They arise naturally from the solution.
  • The wave function is a mathematical function of the electron's coordinates and has no physical meaning by itself.
  • Wave functions of hydrogen or hydrogen like species (one electron systems) are called atomic orbitals.
  • The probability of finding an electron at a point is proportional to |ψ|2 at that point.
  • For multi-electron atoms, the Schrödinger equation cannot be solved exactly, but approximate methods show that their orbitals are similar to hydrogen orbitals, only somewhat contracted due to higher nuclear charge. Unlike hydrogen, their orbital energies depend on both n and l.

docs.title: Important Features of the Quantum Mechanical Model
docs.text:
1. The energy of electrons in atoms is quantized, i.e. it can only have certain specific values.
  2. Quantized energy levels are a direct result of the wave like properties of electrons and are allowed solutions of the Schrödinger equation.
  3. The exact position and exact velocity of an electron cannot be found simultaneously. So the path of an electron can never be known, and we only talk of the probability of finding the electron at different points.
  4. An atomic orbital is the wave function ψ for an electron in an atom. An orbital cannot contain more than two electrons. In a multi-electron atom, electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy. All information about the electron is stored in its orbital wave function.
  5. The probability of finding an electron at a point is proportional to |ψ|2, which is called the probability density and is always positive. From |ψ|2 at different points, we can predict the region where the electron will most probably be found.

Orbit vs Orbital

Orbit Orbital A circular path around the nucleus in which electron moves (Bohr). A quantum mechanical concept: the one electron wave function ψ in an atom. Its exact description is impossible due to uncertainty principle, so it has no real meaning. Characterised by three quantum numbers n, l and ml. Cannot be demonstrated experimentally. ψ has no physical meaning, but ψ2 gives the probability density, which has physical meaning.

docs.title: Quantum Numbers
docs.text: Orbitals are distinguished by their size, shape and orientation. These are described by quantum numbers. Each orbital is designated by three quantum numbers n, l and ml.

docs.title: 1. Principal Quantum Number (n)
docs.text:
• It is a positive integer: n = 1, 2, 3, ...
  • It determines the size and, to a large extent, the energy of the orbital. For hydrogen and hydrogen like species, energy and size depend only on n.
  • It identifies the shell. The number of orbitals in a shell is n2.
n 1 2 3 4 Shell K L M N
  • As n increases, the electron is located farther from the nucleus and its energy increases.

docs.title: 2. Azimuthal Quantum Number (l)
docs.text:
• It is also called the orbital angular momentum or subsidiary quantum number. It defines the three dimensional shape of the orbital.
  • For a given n, l can have n values: l = 0, 1, 2, ..., (n – 1).
  • Each shell contains one or more sub-shells (sub-levels). The number of sub-shells in a shell equals n.
Value of l 0 1 2 3 4 5 Sub-shell notation s p d f g h Number of orbitals 1 3 5 7 9 11 n l Sub-shell 1 0 1s 2 0, 1 2s, 2p 3 0, 1, 2 3s, 3p, 3d 4 0, 1, 2, 3 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f

docs.title: 3. Magnetic Quantum Number (m<sub>l</sub>)
docs.text:
• It gives the spatial orientation of the orbital with respect to a standard set of coordinate axes.
  • For a given l, there are (2l + 1) values of ml:
\[m_l = -l, -(l-1), ..., 0, ..., (l-1), +l\]
  • For l = 0, ml = 0 (one s orbital). For l = 1, ml = –1, 0, +1 (three p orbitals). For l = 2, ml = –2, –1, 0, +1, +2 (five d orbitals).
  • Values of l are derived from n, and values of ml are derived from l. For example, n = 2, l = 1, ml = 0 is an orbital in the p sub-shell of the second shell.

docs.title: 4. Electron Spin Quantum Number (m<sub>s</sub>)
docs.text:
• The three quantum numbers above could not explain why some lines in spectra of multi-electron atoms appear as doublets or triplets. This suggested more energy levels.
  • George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit (1925) proposed a fourth quantum number, the electron spin quantum number (ms).
  • An electron spins around its own axis, like the earth. Its spin angular momentum can have two orientations relative to a chosen axis, given by ms = +½ (spin up, ↑) or –½ (spin down, ↓).
  • An orbital cannot hold more than two electrons, and the two must have opposite spins.

Summary of quantum numbers

  • n defines the shell and determines the size and, to a large extent, the energy of the orbital.

  • l identifies the sub-shell and determines the shape of the orbital. There are n sub-shells in the nth shell. To some extent l also determines energy in multi-electron atoms.

  • ml designates the orientation of the orbital. There are (2l + 1) orbitals in a sub-shell.

  • ms refers to the orientation of the spin of the electron.

docs.title: Shapes of Atomic Orbitals
docs.text:
• According to Max Born, ψ2 at a point gives the probability density of the electron at that point.
  • For a 1s orbital, the probability density is maximum at the nucleus and decreases sharply away from it.
  • For a 2s orbital, the probability density first decreases sharply to zero, then increases to a small maximum, and then approaches zero again.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
• The region where the probability density reduces to zero is called a nodal surface or simply a node.
\[Radial\ nodes = n - l - 1\] \[Angular\ nodes = l\] \[Total\ nodes = n - 1\]
  • An ns orbital has (n – 1) radial nodes: one for 2s, two for 3s and so on.

docs.title: Boundary Surface Diagrams
docs.text:
• In charge cloud diagrams, the density of dots in a region represents the electron probability density there.
  • A boundary surface diagram is a surface of constant probability density that encloses the region where the probability of finding the electron is very high (about 90%).
  • We cannot draw a boundary enclosing 100% probability, because |ψ|2 has some value, however small, at any finite distance from the nucleus.

docs.title: 1. s-Orbitals
docs.text:
• All s orbitals are spherically symmetric: the probability of finding the electron at a given distance is the same in all directions.
  • Size of s orbitals increases with n: 4s > 3s > 2s > 1s.

docs.title: 2. p-Orbitals
docs.text:
• Each p orbital consists of two lobes on either side of a plane passing through the nucleus. The probability density is zero on this plane.
  • For l = 1 there are three values of ml, so there are three p orbitals with mutually perpendicular axes: px, py and pz. Their size, shape and energy are identical; they differ only in orientation.
  • There is no simple relation between the values of ml (–1, 0, +1) and the x, y, z directions.
  • p orbitals increase in size and energy with n: 4p > 3p > 2p.
  • Number of radial nodes = n – 2: one for 3p, two for 4p.

docs.title: 3. d-Orbitals
docs.text:
• For l = 2, the orbital is a d orbital. The minimum value of n is 3, since l cannot be greater than n – 1.
  • There are five ml values (–2, –1, 0, +1, +2), so there are five d orbitals: dxy, dyz, dxz, dx2–y2 and dz2.
  • The first four have similar shapes (four lobes). dz2 is different, but all five 3d orbitals have equal energy.
  • 4d, 5d, ... orbitals have similar shapes to 3d but differ in size and energy.

docs.title: Angular Nodes (Nodal Planes)
docs.text:
• Besides radial nodes, p and d orbitals have zero probability density on planes passing through the nucleus. These are angular nodes.
  • For pz, the xy-plane is a nodal plane. For dxy, there are two nodal planes passing through the origin and bisecting the xy plane containing the z-axis.
  • Number of angular nodes = l: one for p orbitals, two for d orbitals.

docs.title: 1. Hydrogen Atom
docs.text:
• The energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom depends only on n:
\[1s < 2s = 2p < 3s = 3p = 3d < 4s = 4p = 4d = 4f < ...\]
  • Orbitals having the same energy are called degenerate. The 1s orbital is the most stable, called the ground state. An electron in 2s, 2p or higher orbitals is in an excited state.

docs.title: 2. Multi-electron Atoms
docs.text:
• The energy depends on both n and l. For a given n, s, p, d, f have different energies.
  • The reason is the mutual repulsion among electrons. In hydrogen there is only attraction between the electron and the nucleus.
  • Inner shell electrons partially screen the outer electrons from the nucleus. This is called shielding of outer shell electrons by inner shell electrons. The net positive charge felt by an electron is called the effective nuclear charge (Zeffe).
  • Being spherical, an s orbital shields more effectively than p, and p more than d. Also, an s electron spends more time near the nucleus than p, and p more than d.
  • So for a given n, Zeff decreases with increase in l. The s orbital is more tightly bound than p, and p more than d. Energies follow s < p < d < f within a shell.

(n + l) Rule

  • The lower the value of (n + l) for an orbital, the lower is its energy.

  • If two orbitals have the same (n + l), the one with lower n has lower energy.

Orbital n l n + l Comment 1s 1 0 1 2s 2 0 2 2p 2 1 3 2p (n = 2) is lower than 3s 3s 3 0 3 3p 3 1 4 3p (n = 3) is lower than 4s 4s 4 0 4 3d 3 2 5 3d (n = 3) is lower than 4p 4p 4 1 5
  • Energies of orbitals in the same sub-shell decrease with increase in atomic number (Zeff). For example: E2s(H) > E2s(Li) > E2s(Na) > E2s(K).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What is the total number of orbitals associated with the principal quantum number n = 3?

  • For n = 3, l = 0, 1 and 2.

  • One 3s orbital (l = 0, ml = 0), three 3p orbitals (l = 1, ml = –1, 0, +1) and five 3d orbitals (l = 2, ml = –2, –1, 0, +1, +2).

\[Total\ orbitals = 1 + 3 + 5 = 9\]

The same result is obtained from n2 = 32 = 9.

Using s, p, d, f notations, describe the orbital with the following quantum numbers: (a) n = 2, l = 1 (b) n = 4, l = 0 (c) n = 5, l = 3 (d) n = 3, l = 2

Option n l Orbital (a) 2 1 2p (b) 4 0 4s (c) 5 3 5f (d) 3 2 3d

docs.title: Structure of Atom | Questions Based on Structure of Atom
Structure of Atom | Questions Based on Structure of Atom
Questions on Photons and Photoelectric Effect
docs.text:
Yellow light emitted from a sodium lamp has a wavelength (λ) of 580 nm. Calculate the frequency (ν) and wavenumber of the yellow light.

\[ν = {c \over λ} = {3 \times 10^8 \over 580 \times 10^{-9}} = 5.17 \times 10^{14}\ s^{-1}\] \[\bar{\nu} = {1 \over λ} = {1 \over 580 \times 10^{-9}} = 1.72 \times 10^6\ m^{-1}\]

Find energy of each of the photons which (i) correspond to light of frequency 3 × 1015 Hz (ii) have wavelength of 0.50 Å.

\[(i)\ E = hν = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{15} = 1.988 \times 10^{-18}\ J\] \[(ii)\ E = {hc \over λ} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8 \over 0.50 \times 10^{-10}} = 3.98 \times 10^{-15}\ J\]

What is the number of photons of light with a wavelength of 4000 pm that provide 1 J of energy?

\[E = {hc \over λ} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8 \over 4000 \times 10^{-12}} = 4.97 \times 10^{-17}\ J\] \[Number\ of\ photons = {1 \over 4.97 \times 10^{-17}} = 2.01 \times 10^{16}\]

Electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 242 nm is just sufficient to ionise the sodium atom. Calculate the ionisation energy of sodium in kJ mol-1.

\[E = {hc \over λ} = {6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8 \over 242 \times 10^{-9}} = 8.21 \times 10^{-19}\ J\] \[Ionisation\ energy = 8.21 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 4.94 \times 10^5\ J\ mol^{-1}\] \[Ionisation\ energy = 494\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\]

Electrons are emitted with zero velocity from a metal surface when it is exposed to radiation of wavelength 6800 Å. Calculate threshold frequency (ν0) and work function (W0) of the metal.

  • Since electrons are emitted with zero velocity, the photon energy just equals the work function.
\[ν_0 = {c \over λ_0} = {3 \times 10^8 \over 6800 \times 10^{-10}} = 4.41 \times 10^{14}\ s^{-1}\] \[W_0 = hν_0 = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 4.41 \times 10^{14} = 2.92 \times 10^{-19}\ J\]

docs.title: Questions on Bohr's Model and Hydrogen Spectrum
docs.text:
What is the wavelength of light emitted when the electron in a hydrogen atom undergoes transition from an energy level with n = 4 to an energy level with n = 2?

\[ΔE = 2.18 imes 10^{-18}\left({1 \over 2^2} - {1 \over 4^2} ight) = 2.18 imes 10^{-18} imes {3 \over 16}\] \[ΔE = 4.09 imes 10^{-19}\ J\] \[λ = {hc \over ΔE} = {6.626 imes 10^{-34} imes 3 imes 10^8 \over 4.09 imes 10^{-19}} = 4.86 imes 10^{-7}\ m = 486\ nm\]

How much energy is required to ionise a H atom if the electron occupies n = 5 orbit? Compare your answer with the ionization enthalpy of H atom (energy required to remove the electron from n = 1 orbit).

\[E_5 = -{2.18 imes 10^{-18} \over 5^2} = -8.72 imes 10^{-20}\ J\] \[Energy\ required\ (n = 5 → ∞) = 0 - (-8.72 imes 10^{-20}) = 8.72 imes 10^{-20}\ J\] \[Energy\ required\ (n = 1 → ∞) = 2.18 imes 10^{-18}\ J\] \[{2.18 imes 10^{-18} \over 8.72 imes 10^{-20}} = 25\]

So, 25 times more energy is needed to remove the electron from n = 1 than from n = 5.

What is the maximum number of emission lines when the excited electron of a H atom in n = 6 drops to the ground state?

\[Number\ of\ lines = {n(n-1) \over 2} = {6 imes 5 \over 2} = 15\]

(i) The energy associated with the first orbit in the hydrogen atom is –2.18 × 10-18 J atom-1. What is the energy associated with the fifth orbit? (ii) Calculate the radius of Bohr's fifth orbit for hydrogen atom.

\[(i)\ E_5 = -{2.18 imes 10^{-18} \over 5^2} = -8.72 imes 10^{-20}\ J\] \[(ii)\ r_5 = n^2 a_0 = 25 imes 52.9\ pm = 1322.5\ pm = 1.3225\ nm\]

Calculate the wavenumber for the longest wavelength transition in the Balmer series of atomic hydrogen.

  • Longest wavelength means smallest energy gap. In the Balmer series, this is n = 3 to n = 2.
\[ ar{ u} = 109677\left({1 \over 2^2} - {1 \over 3^2} ight) = 109677 imes {5 \over 36}\] \[ ar{ u} = 15233\ cm^{-1} = 1.523 imes 10^6\ m^{-1}\]

The electron energy in hydrogen atom is given by En = (–2.18 × 10-18)/n2 J. Calculate the energy required to remove an electron completely from the n = 2 orbit. What is the longest wavelength of light in cm that can be used to cause this transition?

\[ΔE = E_∞ - E_2 = 0 - \left(-{2.18 imes 10^{-18} \over 4} ight) = 5.45 imes 10^{-19}\ J\] \[λ = {hc \over ΔE} = {6.626 imes 10^{-34} imes 3 imes 10^8 \over 5.45 imes 10^{-19}} = 3.65 imes 10^{-7}\ m\] \[λ = 3.65 imes 10^{-5}\ cm\]

What transition in the hydrogen spectrum would have the same wavelength as the Balmer transition n = 4 to n = 2 of He+ spectrum?

\[For\ He^+:\ ar{ u} = R Z^2\left({1 \over 2^2} - {1 \over 4^2} ight) = R imes 4 imes {3 \over 16} = {3R \over 4}\] \[For\ H:\ R\left({1 \over n_1^2} - {1 \over n_2^2} ight) = {3R \over 4}\] \[\left({1 \over n_1^2} - {1 \over n_2^2} ight) = {3 \over 4} = {1 \over 1^2} - {1 \over 2^2}\]

So the transition is n = 2 to n = 1 (first line of Lyman series).

Calculate the energy required for the process: He+(g) → He2+(g) + e–. The ionization energy for the H atom in the ground state is 2.18 × 10-18 J atom-1.

\[E_n = -2.18 imes 10^{-18} imes {Z^2 \over n^2}\] \[For\ He^+,\ Z = 2,\ n = 1:\ E_1 = -2.18 imes 10^{-18} imes 4 = -8.72 imes 10^{-18}\ J\] \[Energy\ required = 8.72 imes 10^{-18}\ J\]

Emission transitions in the Paschen series end at orbit n = 3 and start from orbit n, and can be represented as ν = 3.29 × 1015 (Hz) [1/32 – 1/n2]. Calculate the value of n if the transition is observed at 1285 nm. Find the region of the spectrum.

\[ν = {c \over λ} = {3 imes 10^8 \over 1285 imes 10^{-9}} = 2.335 imes 10^{14}\ Hz\] \[{1 \over 9} - {1 \over n^2} = {2.335 imes 10^{14} \over 3.29 imes 10^{15}} = 0.0710\] \[{1 \over n^2} = 0.1111 - 0.0710 = 0.0401\] \[n^2 = 24.9 ≈ 25,\ so\ n = 5\]

The radiation of 1285 nm lies in the infrared region.

docs.title: Questions on Quantum Numbers
docs.text:
What is the lowest value of n that allows g orbitals to exist?

  • For g orbitals, l = 4. Since l can be at most (n – 1), n – 1 = 4, so n = 5.

An electron is in one of the 3d orbitals. Give the possible values of n, l and ml for this electron.

\[n = 3,\ l = 2,\ m_l = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2\]

Explain, giving reasons, which of the following sets of quantum numbers are not possible. (a) n = 0, l = 0, ml = 0, ms = +½ (b) n = 1, l = 0, ml = 0, ms = –½ (c) n = 1, l = 1, ml = 0, ms = +½ (d) n = 2, l = 1, ml = 0, ms = –½ (e) n = 3, l = 3, ml = –3, ms = +½ (f) n = 3, l = 1, ml = 0, ms = +½

  • (a) Not possible, because n cannot be zero.

  • (b) Possible (1s orbital).

  • (c) Not possible, because for n = 1, l can only be 0.

  • (d) Possible (2p orbital).

  • (e) Not possible, because for n = 3, l can be 0, 1 or 2 only.

  • (f) Possible (3p orbital).

How many electrons in an atom may have the following quantum numbers? (a) n = 4, ms = –½ (b) n = 3, l = 0

  • (a) For n = 4, total electrons = 2n2 = 32. Half of them have ms = –½. So, 16 electrons.

  • (b) n = 3, l = 0 is the 3s orbital, which can hold 2 electrons.

(a) How many sub-shells are associated with n = 4? (b) How many electrons will be present in the sub-shells having ms value of –½ for n = 4?

  • (a) For n = 4, l = 0, 1, 2, 3. So there are 4 sub-shells: 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f.

  • (b) Number of orbitals = n2 = 16. Each orbital has one electron with ms = –½. So, 16 electrons.

Which of the following are isoelectronic species, i.e. those having the same number of electrons? Na+, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, S2–, Ar

Species Na+ K+ Mg2+ Ca2+ S2– Ar Electrons 10 18 10 18 18 18

  • Na+ and Mg2+ are isoelectronic (10 electrons).

  • K+, Ca2+, S2– and Ar are isoelectronic (18 electrons).

docs.title: Adsorption Isotherm
docs.text: The variation in the amount of gas adsorbed by the adsorbent with pressure at constant temperature can be expressed by means of a curve termed as adsorption isotherm.

docs.title: Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm
docs.text:
• In 1909, Freundlich gave an empirical relationship between the quantity of gas adsorbed by unit mass of solid adsorbent and pressure, at a particular temperature:
\[ {x \over m} = k.P^{1/n}\ \ (n > 1)\]

Where, x = mass of gas adsorbed on mass m of the adsorbent at pressure P; k and n are constants which depend on the nature of the adsorbent and the gas at a particular temperature.

  • The relationship is shown by plotting mass of gas adsorbed per gram of adsorbent (x/m) against pressure (P):

  • At a fixed pressure, x/m decreases with increase in temperature (195 K > 244 K > 273 K). This shows physisorption decreases with rise in temperature.
  • The curves always approach saturation at high pressure.

docs.title: Linear form of Freundlich isotherm
docs.text:
• Taking logarithm of the Freundlich equation:
\[log{x \over m} = log\ k + {1 \over n}log\ P\]
  • This is the equation of a straight line (y = c + mx). If log(x/m) is plotted on the y-axis against log P on the x-axis and a straight line is obtained, the Freundlich isotherm is valid.
\[Slope = {1 \over n}\] \[Intercept\ on\ y\ axis = log\ k\]

docs.title: Limitations of Freundlich isotherm
docs.text:
• Freundlich isotherm explains adsorption only approximately.
  • The factor 1/n can have values between 0 and 1 (probable range 0.1 to 0.5). So the equation holds good only over a limited range of pressure.
\[When\ {1 \over n} = 0:\ {x \over m} = k\ (constant),\ adsorption\ is\ independent\ of\ pressure\] \[When\ {1 \over n} = 1:\ {x \over m} = kP,\ i.e.,\ {x \over m} ∝ P\]
  • Both conditions are supported by experiment. However, the experimental isotherms always approach saturation at high pressure, which Freundlich isotherm cannot explain. Thus, it fails at high pressure.

docs.title: Adsorption from Solution Phase
docs.text:
Solids can adsorb solutes from solutions also.

Examples

  • When a solution of acetic acid in water is shaken with charcoal, part of the acid is adsorbed and its concentration in solution decreases.

  • Litmus solution shaken with charcoal becomes colourless.

  • The precipitate of Mg(OH)2 becomes blue when precipitated in the presence of magneson reagent, due to adsorption of magneson.

  • Observations for adsorption from solution:
    • The extent of adsorption decreases with an increase in temperature.
    • The extent of adsorption increases with an increase of surface area of the adsorbent.
    • The extent of adsorption depends on the concentration of the solute in solution.
    • The extent of adsorption depends on the nature of the adsorbent and the adsorbate.
  • The exact mechanism is not known. Freundlich's equation approximately describes it, with concentration in place of pressure:
\[ {x \over m} = kC^{1/n}\] \[log{x \over m} = log\ k + {1 \over n}log\ C\]

Where, C is the equilibrium concentration (when adsorption is complete).

  • A plot of log(x/m) against log C gives a straight line. This can be checked by adding equal volumes of acetic acid solutions of different concentrations to equal amounts of charcoal in different flasks. The difference between the initial and final concentration in each flask gives x.

docs.title: 1. Production of high vacuum
docs.text: The remaining traces of air in a vessel evacuated by a vacuum pump can be adsorbed by charcoal to give a very high vacuum.

docs.title: 2. Gas masks
docs.text: Gas masks contain activated charcoal (or a mixture of adsorbents) which adsorbs poisonous gases. They are used for breathing in coal mines.

docs.title: 3. Control of humidity
docs.text: Silica gel and aluminium gel are used as adsorbents to remove moisture and control humidity.

docs.title: 4. Removal of colouring matter from solutions
docs.text: Animal charcoal removes colours of solutions by adsorbing coloured impurities.

docs.title: 5. Heterogeneous catalysis
docs.text: Adsorption of reactants on the solid catalyst surface increases the rate of reaction. Examples: manufacture of NH3 using iron, manufacture of H2SO4 by contact process, and hydrogenation of oils using finely divided nickel.

docs.title: 6. Separation of inert gases
docs.text: Noble gases are adsorbed to different extents by coconut charcoal at different temperatures, so a mixture of noble gases can be separated.

docs.title: 7. In curing diseases
docs.text: Many drugs kill germs by getting adsorbed on them.

docs.title: 8. Froth floatation process
docs.text: A low grade sulphide ore is concentrated by separating it from silica and other earthy matter using pine oil and a frothing agent.

docs.title: 9. Adsorption indicators
docs.text: Surfaces of precipitates like silver halides adsorb dyes such as eosin and fluorescein, giving a characteristic colour at the end point.

docs.title: 10. Chromatographic analysis
docs.text: Chromatography is based on adsorption and has many applications in analytical and industrial fields.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What is an adsorption isotherm? Describe Freundlich adsorption isotherm.

The variation in the amount of gas adsorbed by the adsorbent with pressure at constant temperature, expressed as a curve, is called an adsorption isotherm.

Freundlich gave the empirical relation:

\[ {x \over m} = kP^{1/n}\ \ (n > 1)\]

Taking logarithm:

\[log{x \over m} = log\ k + {1 \over n}log\ P\]

A plot of log(x/m) vs log P is a straight line with slope 1/n and intercept log k. Since 1/n lies between 0 and 1, the isotherm holds only over a limited range of pressure and fails at high pressure, where adsorption reaches saturation.

What are the factors which influence the adsorption of a gas on a solid?

  • Nature of the gas: Easily liquefiable gases (high critical temperature) are adsorbed more in physisorption. In chemisorption, gases that can react with the adsorbent are adsorbed.
  • Nature of the adsorbent: Porous and finely divided solids like charcoal and silica gel adsorb more.
  • Surface area of the adsorbent: Greater the surface area, greater the adsorption.
  • Pressure: Adsorption increases with pressure (x/m = kP1/n) until saturation.
  • Temperature: Physisorption decreases with rise in temperature; chemisorption first increases and then decreases.

Discuss the effect of pressure and temperature on the adsorption of gases on solids.

  • Effect of pressure: At constant temperature, x/m increases with pressure. At low pressure x/m is nearly proportional to P, at intermediate pressure x/m = kP1/n, and at high pressure x/m becomes independent of pressure (saturation).

  • Effect of temperature: Adsorption is exothermic. So by Le Chatelier's principle, physisorption decreases with rise in temperature. Chemisorption needs activation energy, so it first increases with temperature and then decreases at still higher temperature.

Why are substances like platinum and palladium often used for carrying out electrolysis of aqueous solutions?

Platinum and palladium are chemically inert. They are not attacked by the electrolyte or by the products of electrolysis, so they act only as surfaces for electron transfer. They are also good adsorbents of gases like hydrogen and oxygen, which helps the electrode reactions occur easily on their surface.

docs.title: Surface Chemistry | Adsorption
docs.text: Surface chemistry deals with phenomena that occur at the surfaces or interfaces. The accumulation of molecular species at the surface rather than in the bulk of a solid or liquid is termed adsorption.

docs.title: Surface Chemistry
docs.text:
• An interface (or surface) is the boundary that separates two bulk phases. It is written with a hyphen or a slash between the phases, e.g., solid-gas or solid/gas.
  • Gases mix completely with each other, so there is no interface between two gases.
  • An interface is usually only a few molecules thick, but its area depends on the size of the particles of the bulk phases.
  • Many important processes take place at interfaces: corrosion, electrode processes, heterogeneous catalysis, dissolution and crystallisation.
  • To study surfaces properly, a really clean surface is needed. Under very high vacuum (10-8 to 10-9 pascal), ultra clean metal surfaces can be obtained. Such surfaces must be stored in vacuum, otherwise they get covered by O2 and N2 from air.
  • The three main topics of surface chemistry are adsorption, catalysis and colloids.

docs.title: Adsorption
docs.text:
• The surface of a solid has a tendency to attract and retain molecules of the phase with which it comes into contact. These molecules stay only at the surface and do not go deeper into the bulk.
  • The substance which concentrates or accumulates at the surface is called the adsorbate.
  • The material on whose surface adsorption takes place is called the adsorbent.
  • Solids in finely divided state have a large surface area. Hence, charcoal, silica gel, alumina gel, clay, colloids and finely divided metals are good adsorbents.
  • The process of removing an adsorbed substance from the surface is called desorption.

Adsorption in action

  • When a gas like O2, H2, CO, Cl2, NH3 or SO2 is kept in a closed vessel with powdered charcoal, the pressure of the gas decreases because gas molecules get adsorbed on the charcoal surface.

  • When animal charcoal is shaken with a solution of an organic dye like methylene blue, the filtrate turns colourless. The dye molecules are adsorbed on the charcoal.

  • An aqueous solution of raw sugar becomes colourless when passed over beds of animal charcoal, as the colouring substances are adsorbed.

  • Air becomes dry in the presence of silica gel because water molecules get adsorbed on the surface of the gel.

docs.title: Adsorption vs Absorption
docs.text:
• In adsorption, the substance is concentrated only at the surface and does not penetrate into the bulk of the adsorbent.
  • In absorption, the substance is uniformly distributed throughout the bulk of the solid.

Examples

  • Chalk dipped in ink: The surface retains the colour of the ink due to adsorption of coloured molecules, while the solvent goes deeper into the stick due to absorption. On breaking the chalk, it is white from inside.

  • Water vapour: Water vapours are absorbed by anhydrous calcium chloride but adsorbed by silica gel.

  • Both adsorption and absorption can take place simultaneously. The term sorption is used to describe both processes together.

docs.title: Mechanism of Adsorption
docs.text:
• Inside the adsorbent, every particle is surrounded by similar particles on all sides, so all the forces acting on it are balanced.
  • Particles at the surface are not surrounded on all sides. They have unbalanced or residual attractive forces.
  • These residual forces attract the adsorbate particles onto the surface.
  • The extent of adsorption increases with the increase of surface area per unit mass of the adsorbent at a given temperature and pressure.

docs.title: Thermodynamics of adsorption
docs.text:
• During adsorption, the residual forces of the surface decrease, i.e., the surface energy decreases. This energy appears as heat. Hence, adsorption is always exothermic, i.e., ΔH is always negative.
  • When a gas is adsorbed, the freedom of movement of its molecules becomes restricted. So the entropy decreases, i.e., ΔS is negative.
  • For a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure, ΔG must be negative:
\[ΔG = ΔH - TΔS\] \[ΔH < 0,\ ΔS < 0\ (so,\ -TΔS > 0)\]
  • ΔG becomes negative only when ΔH is sufficiently negative to outweigh the positive -TΔS term.
  • As adsorption proceeds, ΔH becomes less and less negative. Finally ΔH = TΔS and ΔG = 0. At this stage, adsorption equilibrium is attained.

docs.title: 1. Physical adsorption (Physisorption)
docs.text: When a gas accumulates on the surface of a solid due to weak van der Waals' forces, the adsorption is called physical adsorption or physisorption.

docs.title: 2. Chemical adsorption (Chemisorption)
docs.text:
When gas molecules or atoms are held to the solid surface by chemical bonds (covalent or ionic), the adsorption is called chemical adsorption or chemisorption. It needs high activation energy, so it is also called activated adsorption.

  • Sometimes both processes occur together. Physisorption at low temperature may pass into chemisorption as temperature increases.
  • Example: H2 is first adsorbed on nickel by van der Waals' forces. The H2 molecules then dissociate into hydrogen atoms, which are held on the surface by chemisorption.

docs.title: Characteristics of Physisorption
docs.text:
• Lack of specificity: van der Waals' forces are universal, so a surface does not prefer any particular gas.
  • Nature of adsorbate: Easily liquefiable gases (higher critical temperature) are adsorbed more, because van der Waals' forces are stronger near the critical temperature.

Example

1 g of activated charcoal adsorbs more SO2 (critical temperature 630 K) than CH4 (critical temperature 190 K), which in turn is adsorbed more than H2 (critical temperature 33 K, about 4.5 mL).

  • Reversible nature: Physisorption is generally reversible:
\[Solid + Gas ⇌ Gas/Solid + Heat\]
  • By Le Chatelier's principle, increasing pressure (which decreases the volume of gas) increases adsorption, and decreasing pressure removes the gas.
  • Since the process is exothermic, physisorption occurs readily at low temperature and decreases with increasing temperature.
  • Surface area: Adsorption increases with surface area. Finely divided metals and porous substances are good adsorbents.
  • Enthalpy of adsorption: It is low, 20–40 kJ mol-1, because only weak van der Waals' forces are involved.

docs.title: Characteristics of Chemisorption
docs.text:
• High specificity: It occurs only if chemical bonding is possible between adsorbent and adsorbate. Example: O2 is adsorbed on metals due to oxide formation, and H2 is adsorbed by transition metals due to hydride formation.
  • Irreversibility: As a compound is formed, chemisorption is usually irreversible.
  • Effect of temperature: It is exothermic, but very slow at low temperature due to high activation energy. Like most chemical changes, it often increases with rise in temperature. High pressure is also usually favourable.
  • Surface area: Like physisorption, it increases with increase of surface area.
  • Enthalpy of adsorption: It is high, 80–240 kJ mol-1, as chemical bonds are formed.

docs.title: Comparison of Physisorption and Chemisorption
docs.text: Physisorption Chemisorption Arises due to van der Waals' forces Caused by chemical bond formation Not specific in nature Highly specific in nature Reversible in nature Irreversible Depends on nature of gas; easily liquefiable gases adsorbed readily Depends on nature of gas; gases which can react with adsorbent show it Enthalpy of adsorption is low (20–40 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) Enthalpy of adsorption is high (80–240 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) Favoured by low temperature; decreases with increase of temperature Favoured by high temperature; increases with increase of temperature No appreciable activation energy needed High activation energy sometimes needed Increases with increase of surface area Also increases with increase of surface area Forms multimolecular layers under high pressure Forms a unimolecular layer

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Distinguish between the meaning of the terms adsorption and absorption. Give one example of each.

In adsorption, the substance concentrates only at the surface of the adsorbent and does not penetrate into the bulk. In absorption, the substance is uniformly distributed throughout the bulk of the solid.

  • Adsorption: Water vapour is adsorbed by silica gel.
  • Absorption: Water vapour is absorbed by anhydrous calcium chloride.

Why does physisorption decrease with the increase of temperature?

Physisorption is exothermic and reversible:

\[Solid + Gas ⇌ Gas/Solid + Heat\]

According to Le Chatelier's principle, increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium backward, so gas is desorbed. Also, at higher temperature the molecules have more kinetic energy and the weak van der Waals' forces cannot hold them on the surface.

Why are powdered substances more effective adsorbents than their crystalline forms?

Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, and its extent increases with surface area. A powdered (finely divided) substance has a much larger surface area per unit mass than its crystalline form, so it provides more surface for the adsorbate and is a more effective adsorbent.

Why is adsorption always exothermic?

The surface particles of an adsorbent have unbalanced residual forces. When adsorbate particles get attached, these residual forces decrease, i.e., surface energy decreases, and the energy is released as heat. So ΔH is negative.

Also, adsorption decreases the entropy of the adsorbate (ΔS < 0). For adsorption to be spontaneous, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS must be negative, which is possible only when ΔH is negative. Hence, adsorption is always exothermic.

What do you understand by activation of adsorbent? How is it achieved?

Activation of an adsorbent means increasing its adsorbing power by increasing its effective surface area. It is achieved by:

  • Subdividing the adsorbent into a fine powder.
  • Making the surface rough or porous.
  • Heating the adsorbent (in vacuum or in steam) to remove gases and impurities already adsorbed on it, so that the free surface becomes available. For example, charcoal is activated by heating it in steam.

docs.title: Catalyst and Catalysis
docs.text:
Substances which alter the rate of a chemical reaction and themselves remain chemically and quantitatively unchanged after the reaction are known as catalysts, and the phenomenon is known as catalysis.

  • The term catalyst was suggested by Berzelius in 1835, who first studied the effect of foreign substances on reaction rates systematically.

Example

Potassium chlorate decomposes slowly to give oxygen in the temperature range 653–873 K:

\[2KClO_3 → 2KCl + 3O_2\]

When a little MnO2 is added, the decomposition takes place at a much lower temperature (473–633 K) and at a much faster rate. The MnO2 remains unchanged in mass and composition.

docs.title: Promoters and Poisons
docs.text:
• Promoters are substances that enhance the activity of a catalyst.
  • Poisons are substances that decrease the activity of a catalyst.
  • Example: In Haber's process for the manufacture of ammonia, molybdenum acts as a promoter for iron, which is the catalyst.
\[N_{2(g)} + 3H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Fe(s),\ Mo(s)} 2NH_{3(g)}\]

docs.title: 1. Homogeneous catalysis
docs.text:
When the reactants and the catalyst are in the same phase (liquid or gas), the process is called homogeneous catalysis.

Examples

  • Oxidation of SO2 to SO3 with oxides of nitrogen as catalyst in the lead chamber process (all in gas phase):
\[2SO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{NO(g)} 2SO_{3(g)}\]
  • Hydrolysis of methyl acetate catalysed by H+ ions from hydrochloric acid (all in liquid phase):
\[CH_3COOCH_{3(l)} + H_2O_{(l)} \xrightarrow{HCl(l)} CH_3COOH_{(aq)} + CH_3OH_{(aq)}\]
  • Hydrolysis of sugar catalysed by H+ ions from sulphuric acid (all in solution):
\[C_{12}H_{22}O_{11(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4(l)} C_6H_{12}O_{6(aq)}\ (glucose) + C_6H_{12}O_{6(aq)}\ (fructose)\]

docs.title: 2. Heterogeneous catalysis
docs.text:
When the reactants and the catalyst are in different phases, the process is called heterogeneous catalysis.

Examples

  • Oxidation of SO2 to SO3 in the presence of Pt (gas reactants, solid catalyst):
\[2SO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Pt(s)} 2SO_{3(g)}\]
  • Formation of ammonia using finely divided iron in Haber's process (gas reactants, solid catalyst):
\[N_{2(g)} + 3H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Fe(s)} 2NH_{3(g)}\]
  • Oxidation of ammonia to nitric oxide using platinum gauze in Ostwald's process (gas reactants, solid catalyst):
\[4NH_{3(g)} + 5O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Pt(s)} 4NO_{(g)} + 6H_2O_{(g)}\]
  • Hydrogenation of vegetable oils using finely divided nickel (one reactant liquid, other gas, catalyst solid):
\[Vegetable\ oil_{(l)} + H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Ni(s)} Vegetable\ ghee_{(s)}\]

docs.title: Adsorption Theory of Heterogeneous Catalysis
docs.text:
• Old adsorption theory: Reactants (gases or solutions) are adsorbed on the surface of the solid catalyst. The increase in concentration of reactants at the surface increases the rate. Also, the heat released during adsorption (exothermic) helps increase the rate.
  • Modern adsorption theory combines the old adsorption theory with the intermediate compound formation theory. The catalytic activity is localised on the surface of the catalyst.
  • The surface of the catalyst, unlike its bulk, has free valencies. These provide the seat for chemical forces of attraction. Gas molecules coming in contact with the surface are held there by loose chemical combination.
  • When different molecules are adsorbed side by side, they react to form new molecules, which then leave the surface for fresh reactant molecules.

docs.title: Steps of the mechanism
docs.text:
• Step 1: Diffusion of reactants to the surface of the catalyst.
  • Step 2: Adsorption of reactant molecules on the surface of the catalyst.
  • Step 3: Chemical reaction on the catalyst surface through formation of an intermediate.
  • Step 4: Desorption of products from the catalyst surface, making the surface available again.
  • Step 5: Diffusion of products away from the catalyst surface.
\[Catalyst\ surface + A + B → A\ and\ B\ adsorbed → Intermediate → Catalyst + A-B\]
  • This theory explains why the catalyst remains unchanged in mass and chemical composition at the end of the reaction and why it is effective even in small quantities.
  • However, it does not explain the action of catalytic promoters and catalytic poisons.

docs.title: 1. Activity
docs.text:
• The activity of a catalyst depends largely on the strength of chemisorption.
  • Reactants must be adsorbed reasonably strongly for the catalyst to be active, but not so strongly that they become immobilised and leave no space for other reactants.
  • For hydrogenation reactions, catalytic activity increases from Group 5 to Group 11 metals, with maximum activity shown by Group 7–9 elements.
\[2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Pt} 2H_2O_{(l)}\]

docs.title: 2. Selectivity
docs.text:
The selectivity of a catalyst is its ability to direct a reaction to yield a particular product. Starting with the same reactants, H2 and CO, different catalysts give different products:

\[CO_{(g)} + 3H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Ni} CH_{4(g)} + H_2O_{(g)}\] \[CO_{(g)} + 2H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Cu/ZnO-Cr_2O_3} CH_3OH_{(g)}\] \[CO_{(g)} + H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Cu} HCHO_{(g)}\]
  • So a catalyst is highly selective: a substance which catalyses one reaction may fail to catalyse another.

docs.title: Shape-Selective Catalysis by Zeolites
docs.text:
The catalytic reaction that depends upon the pore structure of the catalyst and the size of the reactant and product molecules is called shape-selective catalysis.

  • Zeolites are good shape-selective catalysts because of their honeycomb-like structures.
  • They are microporous aluminosilicates with a three-dimensional network of silicates in which some silicon atoms are replaced by aluminium atoms, giving an Al–O–Si framework.
  • Reactions in zeolites depend on the size and shape of reactant and product molecules, and on the pores and cavities of the zeolite.
  • Zeolites occur in nature and are also synthesised for catalytic selectivity.
  • They are widely used in petrochemical industries for cracking of hydrocarbons and isomerisation.
  • ZSM-5 is an important zeolite catalyst in the petroleum industry. It converts alcohols directly into gasoline (petrol) by dehydrating them to give a mixture of hydrocarbons.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What role does adsorption play in heterogeneous catalysis?

In heterogeneous catalysis, the reactant molecules are first adsorbed on the surface of the solid catalyst through free valencies. This increases the concentration of reactants at the surface, weakens their bonds, and brings the molecules close together, so they react through an intermediate. The heat of adsorption also helps increase the rate. The products are then desorbed, leaving the surface free for fresh reactants.

Why is it necessary to remove CO when ammonia is obtained by Haber's process?

CO acts as a poison for the iron catalyst used in Haber's process. It gets strongly adsorbed on the catalyst surface and blocks the active sites, so the activity of the catalyst decreases. Hence, CO must be removed.

Why is the ester hydrolysis slow in the beginning and becomes faster after sometime?

\[CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O → CH_3COOH + C_2H_5OH\]

The acid (CH3COOH) formed in the reaction furnishes H+ ions, which catalyse the hydrolysis. In the beginning, very little acid is present, so the reaction is slow. As more acid is formed, the reaction becomes faster. Such a reaction, where a product acts as a catalyst, is called autocatalysis.

What is the role of desorption in the process of catalysis?

After the reaction on the catalyst surface, the products must leave the surface (desorption). This makes the surface free again for fresh reactant molecules to be adsorbed, so the catalyst can continue its action.

What do you mean by activity and selectivity of catalysts?

  • Activity: It is the ability of a catalyst to increase the rate of a reaction. It depends on the strength of chemisorption; reactants must be adsorbed reasonably strongly but not so strongly that they get immobilised. Example: Pt catalyses 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

  • Selectivity: It is the ability of a catalyst to direct a reaction to yield a particular product. Example: CO and H2 give CH4 with Ni, CH3OH with Cu/ZnO-Cr2O3 and HCHO with Cu.

What is shape selective catalysis? Describe some features of catalysis by zeolites.

A catalytic reaction that depends on the pore structure of the catalyst and the size of the reactant and product molecules is called shape-selective catalysis.

Features of zeolites:

  • They are microporous aluminosilicates with an Al–O–Si framework and a honeycomb-like structure.
  • Reactions depend on the size and shape of reactant and product molecules and on the pores and cavities of the zeolite.
  • They are used for cracking of hydrocarbons and isomerisation in petrochemical industries.
  • ZSM-5 converts alcohols directly into gasoline by dehydration.

Give four examples of heterogeneous catalysis.

\[2SO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Pt(s)} 2SO_{3(g)}\] \[N_{2(g)} + 3H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Fe(s)} 2NH_{3(g)}\] \[4NH_{3(g)} + 5O_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Pt(s)} 4NO_{(g)} + 6H_2O_{(g)}\] \[Vegetable\ oil_{(l)} + H_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{Ni(s)} Vegetable\ ghee_{(s)}\]

docs.title: Surface Chemistry | Colloids and their Classification
Surface Chemistry | Colloids and their Classification
Colloids
docs.text:
A colloid is a heterogeneous system in which one substance is dispersed (dispersed phase) as very fine particles in another substance called dispersion medium.

  • Solutions are homogeneous, while a suspension (like sand stirred in water) slowly settles down. Colloids lie between these two extremes.
  • The essential difference between a solution and a colloid is particle size.
  • In a solution, the particles are ions or small molecules. In a colloid, the dispersed phase may be a single macromolecule (like a protein or synthetic polymer) or an aggregate of many atoms, ions or molecules.
  • Colloidal particles are larger than simple molecules but small enough to remain suspended. Their diameter lies between 1 and 1000 nm (10-9 to 10-6 m).
Property True solution Colloid Suspension Particle size Less than 1 nm 1 nm to 1000 nm More than 1000 nm Nature Homogeneous Heterogeneous Heterogeneous Settling Does not settle Does not settle (remains suspended) Settles down with time

docs.title: Large surface area of colloids
docs.text:
Colloidal particles have an enormous surface area per unit mass because of their small size.

Example

A cube of 1 cm side has a total surface area of 6 cm2. If it is divided equally into 1012 cubes, each cube becomes the size of a large colloidal particle and the total surface area becomes 60,000 cm2 or 6 m2.

\[Side\ of\ each\ small\ cube = {1\ cm \over 10^4} = 10^{-4}\ cm\] \[Total\ area = 10^{12} \times 6 \times (10^{-4})^2 = 6 \times 10^4\ cm^2\]

This huge surface area is the reason for many special properties of colloids.

docs.title: Classification of Colloids
docs.text:
Colloids are classified on the basis of:

  • Physical state of dispersed phase and dispersion medium.
  • Nature of interaction between dispersed phase and dispersion medium.
  • Type of particles of the dispersed phase.

docs.title: 1. Classification Based on Physical State
docs.text:
• The dispersed phase and the dispersion medium can each be a solid, liquid or gas, so eight types of colloidal systems are possible.
  • A gas mixed with another gas forms a homogeneous mixture, so it is not a colloid.
Dispersed phase Dispersion medium Type of colloid Examples Solid Solid Solid sol Some coloured glasses and gem stones Solid Liquid Sol Paints, cell fluids Solid Gas Aerosol Smoke, dust Liquid Solid Gel Cheese, butter, jellies Liquid Liquid Emulsion Milk, hair cream Liquid Gas Aerosol Fog, mist, cloud, insecticide sprays Gas Solid Solid sol Pumice stone, foam rubber Gas Liquid Foam Froth, whipped cream, soap lather
  • The most common types are sols (solids in liquids), gels (liquids in solids) and emulsions (liquids in liquids).
  • Many familiar things are colloids: whipped cream is a foam (gas in liquid), firefighting foams are colloids, and most biological fluids are aqueous sols. Inside a cell, proteins and nucleic acids are colloidal-sized particles dispersed in an aqueous solution of ions and small molecules.
  • If the dispersion medium is water, the sol is called an aquasol or hydrosol. If the dispersion medium is alcohol, it is called an alcosol, and so on.

docs.title: 2. Classification Based on Nature of Interaction
docs.text: Depending on the interaction between dispersed phase and dispersion medium, sols are lyophilic (solvent attracting) or lyophobic (solvent repelling). If water is the medium, the terms are hydrophilic and hydrophobic.

docs.title: (a) Lyophilic colloids
docs.text:
• 'Lyophilic' means liquid-loving.
  • Sols formed directly by mixing substances like gum, gelatine, starch, rubber, etc. with a suitable liquid are lyophilic sols.
  • If the dispersion medium is removed (say by evaporation), the sol can be formed again simply by remixing with the medium. So these are also called reversible sols.
  • They are quite stable and cannot be easily coagulated.

docs.title: (b) Lyophobic colloids
docs.text:
• 'Lyophobic' means liquid-hating.
  • Substances like metals and their sulphides do not form a colloid when simply mixed with the medium. Their sols are prepared only by special methods.
  • They are readily precipitated (coagulated) by adding small amounts of electrolytes, by heating or by shaking. Hence, they are not stable.
  • Once precipitated, they do not give back the sol by simply adding the dispersion medium. So these are also called irreversible sols.
  • Lyophobic sols need stabilising agents for their preservation.
Lyophilic sols Lyophobic sols Formed by direct mixing with medium Prepared only by special methods Reversible Irreversible Quite stable Unstable; need stabilising agents Not easily coagulated Easily coagulated by small amounts of electrolyte Examples: gum, gelatine, starch, rubber Examples: metals, metal sulphides

docs.title: 3. Classification Based on Type of Particles
(a) Multimolecular colloids
docs.text:
• On dissolution, a large number of atoms or small molecules aggregate together to form species with size in the colloidal range. These are multimolecular colloids.
  • Examples: A gold sol contains particles of various sizes having many atoms. A sulphur sol consists of particles containing a thousand or more S8 molecules.

docs.title: (b) Macromolecular colloids
docs.text:
• Macromolecules in suitable solvents form solutions in which the size of the macromolecules is in the colloidal range. These are macromolecular colloids.
  • They are quite stable and resemble true solutions in many respects.
  • Natural examples: starch, cellulose, proteins and enzymes. Man-made examples: polythene, nylon, polystyrene, synthetic rubber, etc.

docs.title: (c) Associated colloids (Micelles)
docs.text:
• Some substances behave as normal strong electrolytes at low concentration, but at higher concentration they form aggregates and show colloidal behaviour. These aggregated particles are called micelles or associated colloids.
  • Micelles form only above a particular temperature called the Kraft temperature (Tk) and above a particular concentration called the critical micelle concentration (CMC).
  • On dilution, they revert back to individual ions.
  • Surface active agents such as soaps and synthetic detergents belong to this class. For soaps, the CMC is 10-4 to 10-3 mol L-1.
  • They have both lyophobic and lyophilic parts. A micelle may contain 100 or more molecules.

docs.title: Mechanism of Micelle Formation
docs.text:
• Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a higher fatty acid, represented as RCOO-Na+. Example: sodium stearate, CH3(CH2)16COO-Na+.
  • In water it dissociates into RCOO- and Na+ ions.
  • The RCOO- ion has two parts:
    • A long hydrocarbon chain R, the non-polar tail, which is hydrophobic.
    • A polar group COO-, the polar-ionic head, which is hydrophilic.
  • At low concentration, the RCOO- ions stay at the surface of water with the COO- head in water and the hydrocarbon tail pointing away from it (figure a).
  • At the critical micelle concentration, the anions are pulled into the bulk and aggregate into a sphere, with the hydrocarbon chains pointing towards the centre and the COO- heads on the outer surface (figure b). This aggregate is called an ionic micelle. It may contain as many as 100 such ions.
  • Detergents like sodium laurylsulphate, CH3(CH2)11SO4-Na+, form micelles in the same way. Here the polar head is -SO4-.

docs.title: Cleansing Action of Soaps
docs.text:
• Soap molecules form a micelle around an oil (grease) droplet. The hydrophobic tails of the stearate ions dissolve in the oil droplet and the hydrophilic heads project outwards like bristles.
  • Since the polar heads interact with water, the oil droplet surrounded by stearate ions is pulled into water and removed from the dirty surface.
  • The negatively charged sheath around the globules prevents them from coming together and forming aggregates.
  • Thus, soap helps in emulsification and washing away of oils and fats.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
How are colloids classified on the basis of (i) physical states of components (ii) nature of dispersion medium and (iii) interaction between dispersed phase and dispersion medium?

  • (i) Physical states of components: Eight types — solid sol, sol, aerosol (solid in gas), gel, emulsion, aerosol (liquid in gas), solid sol (gas in solid) and foam.
  • (ii) Nature of dispersion medium: If the medium is water, the sol is a hydrosol (aquasol); if alcohol, an alcosol; if benzene, a benzosol; if gas, an aerosol.
  • (iii) Interaction between phases: Lyophilic (solvent loving, e.g., starch, gelatine) and lyophobic (solvent hating, e.g., gold sol, As2S3 sol).

What are lyophilic and lyophobic sols? Give one example of each type. Why are hydrophobic sols easily coagulated?

Lyophilic sols are formed directly by mixing substances like gum, gelatine or starch with a suitable liquid; they are reversible and stable. Example: starch sol.

Lyophobic sols cannot be formed by direct mixing and are prepared by special methods; they are irreversible and unstable. Example: gold sol.

Hydrophobic sols are stable only because of the charge on their particles; they are not protected by a layer of solvent (no solvation). When an electrolyte is added, the charge is neutralised easily, the particles come together and coagulate.

What is the difference between multimolecular and macromolecular colloids? Give one example of each. How are associated colloids different from these two types of colloids?

  • Multimolecular colloids are formed by aggregation of a large number of atoms or small molecules into particles of colloidal size. Example: sulphur sol (aggregates of S8 molecules).
  • Macromolecular colloids are formed by single large molecules (macromolecules) whose size itself is in the colloidal range. Example: starch, proteins.
  • Associated colloids behave as normal strong electrolytes at low concentration but form aggregates (micelles) at higher concentration, above the Kraft temperature and CMC. They revert to ions on dilution. Example: soap solution.

What are micelles? Give an example of a micellar system.

Micelles are aggregated particles formed by surface active agents (like soaps and detergents) in solution above the Kraft temperature and above the critical micelle concentration. Each micelle has a hydrophobic core of hydrocarbon chains and an outer surface of polar heads. Example: sodium stearate (soap) in water.

Action of soap is due to emulsification and micelle formation. Comment.

Soap anions (RCOO-) have a hydrophobic tail and a hydrophilic head. Around an oil or grease droplet, the tails dissolve in the oil and the heads face the water, forming a micelle. This pulls the oil droplet into water as an emulsion. The negative charge on the surface of such droplets keeps them apart, so they do not combine again and are washed away. Thus, the cleansing action of soap is due to emulsification and micelle formation.

Explain the terms with suitable examples: (i) Alcosol (ii) Aerosol (iii) Hydrosol.

  • (i) Alcosol: A sol with alcohol as the dispersion medium. Example: sol of cellulose nitrate in ethyl alcohol (collodion).
  • (ii) Aerosol: A colloid with a gas as the dispersion medium. Example: smoke (solid in gas), fog (liquid in gas).
  • (iii) Hydrosol: A sol with water as the dispersion medium. Example: starch sol, gold sol.

Comment on the statement that 'colloid is not a substance but a state of substance'.

Whether a substance behaves as a colloid depends only on its particle size (1–1000 nm), not on its chemical nature. The same substance can form a true solution or a colloid under different conditions. For example, NaCl forms a true solution in water but a colloid in benzene, and soap behaves as an electrolyte at low concentration but forms micelles (colloid) at high concentration. Hence, colloid is a state of a substance rather than a separate kind of substance.

docs.title: Surface Chemistry | Emulsions and Colloids Around Us
Surface Chemistry | Emulsions and Colloids Around Us
Emulsions
docs.text:
Emulsions are liquid-liquid colloidal systems, i.e., the dispersion of finely divided droplets of one liquid in another liquid.

  • When a mixture of two immiscible or partially miscible liquids is shaken, a coarse dispersion of one liquid in the other is obtained. This is called an emulsion.
  • Generally, one of the two liquids is water.

docs.title: 1. Oil in water (O/W type)
docs.text:
• Oil is the dispersed phase and water is the dispersion medium.
  • Examples: milk (liquid fat dispersed in water) and vanishing cream.

docs.title: 2. Water in oil (W/O type)
docs.text:
• Water is the dispersed phase and oil is the dispersion medium.
  • Examples: butter and cream.
Property Oil in water (O/W) Water in oil (W/O) Dispersed phase Oil Water Dispersion medium Water Oil Examples Milk, vanishing cream Butter, cream Emulsifying agents Proteins, gums, natural and synthetic soaps Heavy metal salts of fatty acids, long chain alcohols, lampblack

docs.title: Emulsifying Agents
docs.text:
• Emulsions of oil in water are unstable and sometimes separate into two layers on standing.
  • To stabilise an emulsion, a third component called an emulsifying agent (emulsifier) is added.
  • The emulsifying agent forms an interfacial film between the suspended droplets and the medium.
  • Principal emulsifying agents for O/W emulsions are proteins, gums, natural and synthetic soaps, etc. For W/O emulsions, they are heavy metal salts of fatty acids, long chain alcohols, lampblack, etc.
  • The process of making an emulsion is called emulsification.

docs.title: Properties of Emulsions
docs.text:
• Emulsions can be diluted with any amount of the dispersion medium. But if the dispersed liquid is added, it forms a separate layer.
  • The droplets in emulsions are often negatively charged and can be precipitated by electrolytes.
  • Emulsions show Brownian movement and Tyndall effect.
  • Emulsions can be broken into their constituent liquids by heating, freezing, centrifuging, etc. This process is called demulsification.

docs.title: Colloids Around Us
docs.text: Most substances we come across in daily life are colloids: the food we eat, the clothes we wear, wooden furniture, houses and newspapers are largely made of colloids.

docs.title: 1. Blue colour of the sky
docs.text: Dust particles along with water suspended in air scatter blue light, which reaches our eyes, so the sky looks blue.

docs.title: 2. Fog, mist and rain
docs.text:
• When a large mass of air containing dust particles is cooled below its dew point, moisture condenses on the surfaces of these particles, forming fine droplets. These colloidal droplets float in air as mist or fog.
