  • Clouds are aerosols of small water droplets suspended in air. In the upper atmosphere, the droplets grow bigger by condensation until they fall as rain. Sometimes rain occurs when two oppositely charged clouds meet.
  • Artificial rain can be caused by throwing electrified sand or spraying a sol carrying charge opposite to that on the clouds from an aeroplane.

docs.title: 3. Food articles
docs.text: Milk, butter, halwa, ice creams, fruit juices, etc. are all colloids in one form or the other.

docs.title: 4. Blood
docs.text: Blood is a colloidal solution of an albuminoid substance. The styptic action of alum and ferric chloride solution is due to coagulation of blood, forming a clot which stops further bleeding.

docs.title: 5. Soils
docs.text: Fertile soils are colloidal in nature, with humus acting as a protective colloid. Due to their colloidal nature, soils adsorb moisture and nourishing materials.

docs.title: 6. Formation of delta
docs.text: River water is a colloidal solution of clay. Sea water contains many electrolytes. When river water meets sea water, these electrolytes coagulate the clay, which gets deposited to form a delta.

docs.title: 1. Electrical precipitation of smoke
docs.text:
• Smoke is a colloidal solution of solid particles such as carbon, arsenic compounds, dust, etc. in air.
  • Before it leaves the chimney, smoke is passed through a chamber containing plates with a charge opposite to that of the smoke particles. A high voltage electrode (30000 volts or more) is used for this.
  • The particles lose their charge on contact, get precipitated and settle on the floor of the chamber. Gases free from carbon particles come out.
  • This precipitator is called the Cottrell precipitator.

docs.title: 2. Purification of drinking water
docs.text: Water from natural sources often contains suspended impurities. Alum is added to coagulate these impurities and make the water fit for drinking.

docs.title: 3. Medicines
docs.text:
• Most medicines are colloidal in nature. Colloidal medicines are more effective because they have a large surface area and are easily assimilated.
  • Examples: argyrol (a silver sol) is used as an eye lotion; colloidal antimony is used in curing kalaazar; colloidal gold is used for intramuscular injection; milk of magnesia, an emulsion, is used for stomach disorders.

docs.title: 4. Tanning
docs.text: Animal hides are colloidal, with positively charged particles. When a hide is soaked in tannin, which has negatively charged colloidal particles, mutual coagulation takes place and the leather hardens. This is called tanning. Chromium salts are also used in place of tannin.

docs.title: 5. Cleansing action of soaps and detergents
docs.text: Soaps and detergents clean by forming micelles around oil and grease droplets and emulsifying them in water.

docs.title: 6. Photographic plates and films
docs.text: These are prepared by coating an emulsion of light sensitive silver bromide in gelatin over glass plates or celluloid films.

docs.title: 7. Rubber industry
docs.text: Latex is a colloidal solution of negatively charged rubber particles. Rubber is obtained by coagulation of latex.

docs.title: 8. Industrial products
docs.text: Paints, inks, synthetic plastics, rubber, graphite lubricants, cement, etc. are all colloidal solutions.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What are emulsions? What are their different types? Give example of each type.

Emulsions are liquid-liquid colloidal systems in which fine droplets of one liquid are dispersed in another liquid. They are of two types:

  • Oil in water (O/W): Oil is dispersed in water. Example: milk, vanishing cream.
  • Water in oil (W/O): Water is dispersed in oil. Example: butter, cream.

What is demulsification? Name two demulsifiers.

The process of breaking an emulsion into its constituent liquids is called demulsification. It can be done by heating, freezing, centrifuging, etc. Two common demulsifiers are:

  • Heating (or freezing)
  • Addition of an electrolyte, which neutralises the charge on the droplets

Give four uses of emulsions.

  • Cleansing action of soaps and detergents is based on emulsification of oil and grease.
  • Milk, butter and cream are emulsions used as food.
  • Milk of magnesia, an emulsion, is used as a medicine for stomach disorders.
  • Photographic films are coated with an emulsion of silver bromide in gelatin.

How is a delta formed at the mouth of a river?

River water is a colloidal solution of negatively charged clay particles. Sea water contains many electrolytes like NaCl and MgCl2. When river water meets sea water, the ions from these electrolytes neutralise the charge on the clay particles, causing coagulation. The coagulated clay settles down, and over time this deposit forms a delta.

Why does alum or ferric chloride stop bleeding from a cut?

Blood is a colloidal solution of negatively charged albuminoid particles. Alum and FeCl3 provide Al3+ and Fe3+ ions, which have high coagulating power (Hardy-Schulze rule). They coagulate the blood and form a clot, which stops further bleeding.

docs.title: Enzymes
docs.text:
Enzymes are complex nitrogenous organic compounds produced by living plants and animals which act as very effective catalysts. They are termed biochemical catalysts and the phenomenon is known as biochemical catalysis.

  • Enzymes are actually protein molecules of high molecular mass. They form colloidal solutions in water.
  • Numerous reactions in the bodies of animals and plants that maintain the life process are catalysed by enzymes.
  • Many enzymes have been obtained in pure crystalline state from living cells. The first enzyme was synthesised in the laboratory in 1969.

docs.title: 1. Inversion of cane sugar
docs.text:
The enzyme invertase converts cane sugar into glucose and fructose.

\[C_{12}H_{22}O_{11(aq)}\ (cane\ sugar) + H_2O_{(l)} \xrightarrow{Invertase} C_6H_{12}O_{6(aq)}\ (glucose) + C_6H_{12}O_{6(aq)}\ (fructose)\]

docs.title: 2. Conversion of glucose into ethyl alcohol
docs.text:
The enzyme zymase converts glucose into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide.

\[C_6H_{12}O_{6(aq)} \xrightarrow{Zymase} 2C_2H_5OH_{(aq)} + 2CO_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: 3. Conversion of starch into maltose
docs.text:
The enzyme diastase converts starch into maltose.

\[2(C_6H_{10}O_5)_{n(aq)}\ (starch) + nH_2O_{(l)} \xrightarrow{Diastase} nC_{12}H_{22}O_{11(aq)}\ (maltose)\]

docs.title: 4. Conversion of maltose into glucose
docs.text:
The enzyme maltase converts maltose into glucose.

\[C_{12}H_{22}O_{11(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} \xrightarrow{Maltase} 2C_6H_{12}O_{6(aq)}\]

docs.title: 5. Decomposition of urea
docs.text:
The enzyme urease decomposes urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.

\[NH_2CONH_{2(aq)} + H_2O_{(l)} \xrightarrow{Urease} 2NH_{3(g)} + CO_{2(g)}\]

docs.title: 6. Digestion of proteins
docs.text: In the stomach, pepsin converts proteins into peptides, while in the intestine, pancreatic trypsin converts proteins into amino acids by hydrolysis.

docs.title: 7. Conversion of milk into curd
docs.text: It is an enzymatic reaction brought about by lacto bacilli enzyme present in curd.

docs.title: Summary of some enzymatic reactions
docs.text: Enzyme Source Enzymatic reaction Invertase Yeast Sucrose → Glucose and fructose Zymase Yeast Glucose → Ethyl alcohol and CO<sub>2</sub> Diastase Malt Starch → Maltose Maltase Yeast Maltose → Glucose Urease Soyabean Urea → Ammonia and CO<sub>2</sub> Pepsin Stomach Proteins → Amino acids

docs.title: 1. Most highly efficient
docs.text: One molecule of an enzyme may transform one million molecules of the reactant per minute.

docs.title: 2. Highly specific nature
docs.text: Each enzyme is specific for a given reaction, i.e., one enzyme cannot catalyse more than one reaction. For example, urease catalyses the hydrolysis of urea only and not of any other amide.

docs.title: 3. Highly active under optimum temperature
docs.text:
• The rate of an enzyme reaction is maximum at a definite temperature, called the optimum temperature. On either side of it, enzyme activity decreases.
  • The optimum temperature range for enzymatic activity is 298–310 K. Human body temperature (310 K) is suited for enzyme-catalysed reactions.

docs.title: 4. Highly active under optimum pH
docs.text: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is maximum at a particular pH called the optimum pH, which is between pH 5–7.

docs.title: 5. Increasing activity in presence of activators and co-enzymes
docs.text:
• Co-enzymes: When a small non-protein (vitamin) is present along with an enzyme, its catalytic activity increases considerably.
  • Activators: These are generally metal ions such as Na+, Mn2+, Co2+, Cu2+, etc. When weakly bonded to enzyme molecules, they increase catalytic activity. For example, amylase in presence of NaCl (Na+ ions) is catalytically very active.

docs.title: 6. Influence of inhibitors and poisons
docs.text: Like ordinary catalysts, enzymes are inhibited or poisoned by certain substances. These interact with the active functional groups on the enzyme surface and reduce or completely destroy the catalytic activity. Many drugs work by acting as enzyme inhibitors in the body.

docs.title: Mechanism of Enzyme Catalysis
docs.text:
• The surface of colloidal enzyme particles has many cavities of characteristic shape. These contain active groups such as -NH2, -COOH, -SH, -OH, etc., which are the active centres.
  • The reactant (substrate) molecules having a complementary shape fit into these cavities just like a key fits into a lock (lock and key model).
  • Due to the active groups, an activated complex is formed, which then decomposes to give the products.
  • The reaction proceeds in two steps:
\[Step\ 1\ (binding\ of\ enzyme\ to\ substrate):\ E + S → ES^{\ne}\] \[Step\ 2\ (decomposition\ of\ activated\ complex):\ ES^{\ne} → E + P\]

docs.title: Catalysts in Industry
docs.text:
Process Catalyst and conditions Haber's process for manufacture of ammonia Finely divided iron, molybdenum as promoter; 200 bar pressure and 723–773 K Ostwald's process for manufacture of nitric acid Platinised asbestos; 573 K Contact process for manufacture of sulphuric acid Platinised asbestos or vanadium pentoxide (V2O5); 673–723 K

Haber's process

\[N_{2(g)} + 3H_{2(g)} → 2NH_{3(g)}\]

Ostwald's process

\[4NH_{3(g)} + 5O_{2(g)} → 4NO_{(g)} + 6H_2O_{(g)}\] \[2NO_{(g)} + O_{2(g)} → 2NO_{2(g)}\] \[4NO_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} + O_{2(g)} → 4HNO_{3(aq)}\]

Contact process

\[2SO_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} → 2SO_{3(g)}\] \[SO_{3(g)} + H_2SO_{4(aq)} → H_2S_2O_{7(l)}\ (oleum)\] \[H_2S_2O_{7(l)} + H_2O_{(l)} → 2H_2SO_{4(aq)}\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
What are enzymes? Write in brief the mechanism of enzyme catalysis.

Enzymes are complex nitrogenous organic compounds (proteins of high molecular mass) produced by living plants and animals, which catalyse biochemical reactions.

Mechanism (lock and key): The surface of an enzyme has cavities of characteristic shape containing active groups like -NH2, -COOH, -SH and -OH. The substrate molecule with a complementary shape fits into the cavity like a key in a lock and forms an activated complex, which then decomposes into products, releasing the enzyme.

\[E + S → ES^{\ne}\] \[ES^{\ne} → E + P\]

Name the enzymes that convert (i) cane sugar into glucose and fructose (ii) glucose into ethyl alcohol (iii) urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.

  • (i) Invertase
  • (ii) Zymase
  • (iii) Urease

Why are enzymes most effective at about 310 K and pH 5–7?

Enzyme activity is maximum at an optimum temperature (298–310 K) and an optimum pH (5–7). Away from these values, the enzyme activity decreases. Human body temperature is about 310 K and body fluids have pH in this range, which is why enzyme-catalysed reactions proceed efficiently in the body.

docs.title: Surface Chemistry | Preparation and Purification of Colloids
Surface Chemistry | Preparation and Purification of Colloids
docs.text: In this article, we will discuss the important methods for preparing colloidal solutions and the methods used to purify them.

docs.title: 1. Chemical methods
docs.text:
• Colloidal solutions can be prepared by chemical reactions such as double decomposition, oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis.
  • These reactions form molecules which then aggregate to form sols.
\[Double\ decomposition:\ As_2O_3 + 3H_2S → As_2S_3\ (sol) + 3H_2O\] \[Oxidation:\ SO_2 + 2H_2S → 3S\ (sol) + 2H_2O\] \[Reduction:\ 2AuCl_3 + 3HCHO + 3H_2O → 2Au\ (sol) + 3HCOOH + 6HCl\] \[Hydrolysis:\ FeCl_3 + 3H_2O → Fe(OH)_3\ (sol) + 3HCl\]

docs.title: 2. Electrical disintegration or Bredig's arc method
docs.text:
• This method involves both dispersion and condensation.
  • It is used to prepare colloidal sols of metals such as gold, silver, platinum, etc.
  • An electric arc is struck between two electrodes of the metal immersed in the dispersion medium, which is kept cold in an ice-bath.
  • The intense heat of the arc vaporises the metal, and the vapours condense in the cold medium to form particles of colloidal size.

docs.title: 3. Peptization
docs.text:
Peptization may be defined as the process of converting a precipitate into colloidal sol by shaking it with dispersion medium in the presence of a small amount of electrolyte. The electrolyte used for this purpose is called a peptizing agent.

  • It is generally used to convert a freshly prepared precipitate into a colloidal sol.
  • During peptization, the precipitate adsorbs one of the ions of the electrolyte on its surface. This develops a positive or negative charge on the precipitate, and the like charges make it break up into smaller particles of colloidal size.

Example

A freshly prepared precipitate of ferric hydroxide is converted into a sol by shaking it with a small amount of FeCl3 solution. The precipitate adsorbs Fe3+ ions and breaks up into positively charged colloidal particles.

docs.title: Purification of Colloidal Solutions
docs.text:
The process used for reducing the amount of impurities to a requisite minimum is known as purification of colloidal solution.

  • Freshly prepared colloidal solutions usually contain excess electrolytes and other soluble impurities.
  • Traces of electrolyte are essential for the stability of the colloid, but larger quantities coagulate it. So the impurities must be reduced to a minimum.

docs.title: 1. Dialysis
docs.text:
It is a process of removing a dissolved substance from a colloidal solution by means of diffusion through a suitable membrane.

  • Ions and small molecules of a true solution can pass through animal membrane (bladder), parchment paper or cellophane sheet, but colloidal particles cannot.
  • The apparatus used is called a dialyser.
  • A bag of the membrane containing the colloidal solution is suspended in a vessel through which fresh water flows continuously.
  • The molecules and ions (crystalloids) diffuse through the membrane into the outer water, and the pure colloidal solution is left behind in the bag.

docs.title: 2. Electro-dialysis
docs.text:
• Ordinary dialysis is quite slow. It can be made faster by applying an electric field, if the dissolved impurity is only an electrolyte. This is called electrodialysis.
  • The colloidal solution is placed in a bag of membrane and pure water is taken outside. Electrodes are fitted in the outer compartment.
  • The ions in the colloidal solution migrate out towards the oppositely charged electrodes, while the colloidal particles stay in the bag.

docs.title: 3. Ultrafiltration
docs.text:
Ultrafiltration is the process of separating the colloidal particles from the solvent and soluble solutes present in the colloidal solution by specially prepared filters, which are permeable to all substances except the colloidal particles.

  • Colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper because its pores are too large.
  • The pores can be made smaller by impregnating the filter paper with colloidion solution. The usual colloidion is a 4% solution of nitrocellulose in a mixture of alcohol and ether.
  • An ultra-filter paper is made by soaking filter paper in colloidion solution, hardening it with formaldehyde and then drying it.
  • Ultrafiltration is slow. To speed it up, pressure or suction is applied.
  • The colloidal particles left on the ultra-filter paper are stirred with fresh dispersion medium to get a pure colloidal solution.
Method Principle Speed Dialysis Diffusion of ions and small molecules through a membrane Slow Electro-dialysis Migration of ions through a membrane under an electric field Faster (only for electrolyte impurities) Ultrafiltration Filtration through filter paper with very fine pores Slow; speeded up by pressure or suction

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Explain the term dialysis.

Dialysis is the process of removing a dissolved substance (ions or small molecules) from a colloidal solution by diffusion through a suitable membrane such as parchment paper, animal bladder or cellophane. The colloidal solution is kept in a bag of the membrane, which is placed in flowing water. The crystalloids diffuse out into the water while colloidal particles, being too big, remain inside. Thus, a pure colloidal solution is obtained.

What is peptization? Explain with an example.

Peptization is the conversion of a freshly prepared precipitate into a colloidal sol by shaking it with the dispersion medium in presence of a small amount of electrolyte (peptizing agent). The precipitate adsorbs ions of the electrolyte, gets charged, and breaks into colloidal particles. For example, freshly precipitated Fe(OH)3 forms a positively charged sol on shaking with a little FeCl3 solution, because Fe3+ ions are adsorbed.

Give the chemical reactions for preparing (i) arsenious sulphide sol (ii) sulphur sol (iii) gold sol (iv) ferric hydroxide sol.

\[(i)\ As_2O_3 + 3H_2S → As_2S_3\ (sol) + 3H_2O\] \[(ii)\ SO_2 + 2H_2S → 3S\ (sol) + 2H_2O\] \[(iii)\ 2AuCl_3 + 3HCHO + 3H_2O → 2Au\ (sol) + 3HCOOH + 6HCl\] \[(iv)\ FeCl_3 + 3H_2O → Fe(OH)_3\ (sol) + 3HCl\]

Why is it essential to wash the precipitate with water before estimating it quantitatively?

Some amount of the electrolytes mixed during the formation of the precipitate gets adsorbed on its surface. These adsorbed impurities would add to the mass of the precipitate and give a wrong result. Also, they may cause peptization of the precipitate. So the precipitate is washed with water to remove the adsorbed electrolytes before estimation.

docs.title: Surface Chemistry | Properties of Colloids
docs.text: Colloidal solutions show characteristic colligative, optical, mechanical and electrical properties such as Tyndall effect, Brownian movement, charge on particles, electrophoresis and coagulation.

docs.title: 1. Colligative Properties
docs.text:
• Colloidal particles are big aggregates, so the number of particles in a colloidal solution is much smaller than in a true solution of the same concentration.
  • Hence, the values of colligative properties (osmotic pressure, lowering of vapour pressure, depression in freezing point and elevation in boiling point) are of small order compared to true solutions at the same concentration.

docs.title: 2. Tyndall Effect
docs.text:
• A true solution kept in the dark appears clear when seen along the direction of light, and perfectly dark when viewed at right angles to the beam.
  • A colloidal solution looks clear by transmitted light, but when viewed at right angles to the beam, the path of the beam is illuminated by a bluish light.
  • This effect was first observed by Faraday and later studied in detail by Tyndall. It is called the Tyndall effect. The bright cone of light is called the Tyndall cone.
  • It is due to the scattering of light in all directions by colloidal particles.

Example

In a cinema hall, the path of the projected beam is visible due to scattering of light by dust and smoke particles.

Conditions for Tyndall effect

  • The diameter of the dispersed particles is not much smaller than the wavelength of the light used.

  • The refractive indices of the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium differ greatly in magnitude.

  • Tyndall effect is used to distinguish between a colloidal solution and a true solution.

docs.title: Ultramicroscope
docs.text:
• In 1903, Zsigmondy used the Tyndall effect to build the ultramicroscope.
  • An intense beam of light is focussed on the colloidal solution, and the focus is observed through a microscope at right angles to the beam. The particles appear as bright stars against a dark background.
  • The ultramicroscope does not show the actual particles, only the light scattered by them. So it gives no information about the size and shape of colloidal particles.

docs.title: 3. Colour
docs.text:
• The colour of a colloidal solution depends on the wavelength of light scattered by the dispersed particles, which in turn depends on the size and nature of the particles.
  • Colour also depends on how the observer receives the light. For example, a mixture of milk and water appears blue by reflected light and red by transmitted light.
  • The finest gold sol is red. As the particle size increases, it appears purple, then blue and finally golden.

docs.title: 4. Brownian Movement
docs.text:
• Under a powerful ultramicroscope, colloidal particles are seen in continuous zig-zag motion all over the field of view. This was first observed by the botanist Robert Brown and is called Brownian movement.
  • It is independent of the nature of the colloid but depends on the size of particles and the viscosity of the solution. Smaller the size and lower the viscosity, faster the motion.
  • It is due to the unbalanced bombardment of the particles by the molecules of the dispersion medium.
  • Brownian movement has a stirring effect which does not let the particles settle. So it is responsible for the stability of sols.

docs.title: 5. Charge on Colloidal Particles
docs.text:
Colloidal particles always carry an electric charge. All particles in a given sol carry the same type of charge, either positive or negative.

Positively charged sols Negatively charged sols Hydrated metallic oxides: Al2O3.xH2O, CrO3.xH2O, Fe2O3.xH2O Metals: copper, silver, gold sols Basic dye stuffs: methylene blue sol Metallic sulphides: As2S3, Sb2S3, CdS sols Haemoglobin (blood) Acid dye stuffs: eosin, congo red sols Oxides: TiO2 sol Sols of starch, gum, gelatin, clay, charcoal

docs.title: Origin of charge
docs.text:
• The charge may arise due to electron capture during electrodispersion of metals, preferential adsorption of ions from solution, and/or formation of an electrical double layer.
  • Preferential adsorption of ions is the most accepted reason. When two or more ions are present, the ion common to the colloidal particle is usually adsorbed.

Examples

  • AgNO3 added to KI solution: AgI adsorbs I- (KI in excess), giving a negative sol, AgI/I-.

  • KI added to AgNO3 solution: AgI adsorbs Ag+ (AgNO3 in excess), giving a positive sol, AgI/Ag+.

  • FeCl3 added to excess hot water: adsorption of Fe3+ gives a positive sol, Fe2O3.xH2O/Fe3+.

  • FeCl3 added to NaOH: adsorption of OH- gives a negative sol, Fe2O3.xH2O/OH-.

docs.title: Electrical double layer and zeta potential
docs.text:
• The charged layer on the particle attracts counter ions from the medium, forming a second layer, e.g., AgI/I- K+ and AgI/Ag+ I-.
  • The combination of these two layers of opposite charges is called the Helmholtz electrical double layer.
  • The first layer is firmly held and is called the fixed layer. The second layer is mobile and is called the diffused layer.
  • The potential difference between the fixed layer and the diffused layer is called the electrokinetic potential or zeta potential.
  • The similar charge on all particles makes them repel each other, which prevents them from coalescing. This is largely responsible for the stability of the sol.

docs.title: 6. Electrophoresis
docs.text:
• When an electric potential is applied across two platinum electrodes dipped in a colloidal solution, the colloidal particles move towards one or the other electrode.
  • The movement of colloidal particles under an applied electric potential is called electrophoresis. It confirms the presence of charge on colloidal particles.
  • Positively charged particles move towards the cathode and negatively charged particles move towards the anode.

  • In the set-up shown, a negatively charged sol is placed in a U-tube with water above it. On applying the potential, the negative particles move up towards the positive electrode (anode) and collect there, and the level of the sol falls on the other side.

  • When the movement of particles is prevented by some suitable means, the dispersion medium itself begins to move in the electric field. This is called electroosmosis.

docs.title: 7. Coagulation or Precipitation
docs.text:
The process of settling of colloidal particles is called coagulation or precipitation of the sol.

  • The stability of lyophobic sols is due to the charge on the particles. If the charge is removed, the particles come together, form aggregates and settle under gravity.

docs.title: Methods of coagulation of lyophobic sols
docs.text:
• By electrophoresis: The particles move to the oppositely charged electrode, get discharged and precipitate.
  • By mixing two oppositely charged sols: Mixed in nearly equal proportions, they neutralise each other's charges and precipitate. Example: hydrated ferric oxide (+ve sol) with arsenious sulphide (-ve sol). This is called mutual coagulation.
  • By boiling: Increased collisions with molecules of the medium disturb the adsorbed layer, reduce the charge and cause settling.
  • By persistent dialysis: Prolonged dialysis removes even the traces of electrolyte needed for stability, so the colloid coagulates.
  • By addition of electrolytes: Excess electrolyte neutralises the charge on the particles. The ion that neutralises the charge is called the coagulating ion. A negative ion coagulates a positive sol, and a positive ion coagulates a negative sol.

docs.title: Hardy-Schulze Rule
docs.text:
Generally, the greater the valence of the flocculating ion added, the greater is its power to cause precipitation. This is known as the Hardy-Schulze rule.

\[For\ a\ negative\ sol:\ Al^{3+} > Ba^{2+} > Na^+\] \[For\ a\ positive\ sol:\ [Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} > PO_4^{3-} > SO_4^{2-} > Cl^-\]

docs.title: Coagulating value
docs.text:
• The minimum concentration of an electrolyte in millimoles per litre required to cause precipitation of a sol in two hours is called the coagulating value.
  • The smaller the coagulating value, the higher the coagulating power of the ion.
\[Coagulating\ power ∝ {1 \over Coagulating\ value}\]

docs.title: Coagulation of lyophilic sols
docs.text:
• Two factors stabilise lyophilic sols: the charge and the solvation of the colloidal particles.
  • To coagulate them, both must be removed: (i) by adding an electrolyte and (ii) by adding a suitable solvent.
  • Solvents like alcohol and acetone dehydrate the dispersed phase of hydrophilic sols. Then a small amount of electrolyte can bring about coagulation.

docs.title: Protection of Colloids
docs.text:
• Lyophilic sols are more stable than lyophobic sols because their particles are extensively solvated, i.e., covered by a sheath of the dispersion medium.
  • When a lyophilic sol is added to a lyophobic sol, the lyophilic particles form a layer around the lyophobic particles and protect them from electrolytes.
  • Lyophilic colloids used for this purpose are called protective colloids. Example: gelatin protecting a gold sol.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Explain what is observed (i) when a beam of light is passed through a colloidal sol (ii) an electrolyte, NaCl is added to hydrated ferric oxide sol (iii) electric current is passed through a colloidal sol?

  • (i) The path of the beam becomes visible as a bright cone when viewed at right angles, due to scattering of light by colloidal particles (Tyndall effect).
  • (ii) Hydrated ferric oxide sol is positively charged. The Cl- ions of NaCl neutralise the positive charge on the particles, and the sol gets coagulated (precipitated).
  • (iii) The colloidal particles move towards the oppositely charged electrode (electrophoresis). Positive particles move to the cathode and negative particles move to the anode, where they get discharged and coagulate.

Explain the terms: (i) Electrophoresis (ii) Coagulation (iii) Tyndall effect.

  • (i) Electrophoresis: The movement of colloidal particles towards an oppositely charged electrode under an applied electric potential. It confirms that colloidal particles are charged.
  • (ii) Coagulation: The process of settling of colloidal particles as a precipitate, generally by neutralising their charge, e.g., by adding an electrolyte.
  • (iii) Tyndall effect: The scattering of light by colloidal particles, due to which the path of a light beam through a colloidal solution becomes visible as a bright cone when viewed at right angles.

What modification can you suggest in the Hardy-Schulze law?

Hardy-Schulze law considers only the charge (valence) of the coagulating ion. It should also take into account the size of the ion. A smaller ion has a higher charge density and is adsorbed more easily, so it is a better coagulant than a larger ion of the same charge. So the law can be modified as: coagulating power depends on both the valence and the size of the flocculating ion.

Arrange the following in increasing order of coagulating power for a negatively charged As2S3 sol: NaCl, BaCl2, AlCl3.

The sol is negative, so the cations are the coagulating ions. By the Hardy-Schulze rule, coagulating power increases with the valence of the cation.

\[NaCl\ (Na^+) < BaCl_2\ (Ba^{2+}) < AlCl_3\ (Al^{3+})\]

Why are lyophilic colloids called protective colloids?

When a lyophilic sol is added to a lyophobic sol, its particles form a protective layer around the lyophobic particles. This layer shields them from the electrolyte, so the lyophobic sol does not coagulate easily. Hence, lyophilic colloids are called protective colloids.

docs.title: 1. Isochoric Process
docs.text:
• In an isochoric process, volume remains constant.
\[V = constant\] \[dV = 0\] \[So,\ work\ done\ by\ gas:\] \[W = 0\] \[Using\ first\ law\ of\ thermodynamics:\] \[ΔU = q + W\] \[q = ΔU\]

docs.title: 2. Isobaric Process
docs.text:
• In an isobaric process, pressure remains constant.
\[P = constant\] \[W = - \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} P_{ext} dV\] \[Since,\ P_{ext}\ is\ constant:\] \[W = -P_{ext} (V_2 - V_1) = -P_{ext}ΔV\] \[Using\ first\ law\ of\ thermodynamics:\] \[ΔU = q + W\] \[ΔU = q - P_{ext}ΔV\]

docs.title: 3. Isothermal Process
docs.text:
• In an isothermal process, temperature remains constant.
\[T = constant\] \[dT = 0\] \[Change\ in\ internal\ energy,\ ΔU:\] \[ΔU = \int nC_vdT = 0\] \[Using\ first\ law\ of\ thermodynamics:\] \[ΔU = q + W\] \[0 = q + W\] \[q = -W\]

It means that heat absorbed = work done by the system or work done on the system = heat released.

  • Work done by gas in isothermal reversible process:
\[W_{rev} = - \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} P_{ext}dV\] \[W_{rev} = - \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} {nRT \over V}dV\] \[W_{rev} = - nRT \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} {1 \over V}dV\] \[W_{rev} = -nRT\ ln{V_2 \over V_1}\]

We know that P is inversely proportional to V. So, we can also write:

\[W_{rev} = -nRT\ ln{P_1 \over P_2}\]
  • Work done by gas in isothermal irreversible process:
\[W_{irr} = -P_{ext} (V_2 - V_1)\] \[W_{irr} = -P_{ext} ({nRT \over P_2} - {nRT \over P_1})\] \[W_{irr} = -P_{ext}nRT ({1 \over P_2} - {1 \over P_1})\]

docs.title: 4. Adiabatic Process
docs.text:
• An adiabatic process is a process in which there is no exchange of heat between system and surrounding.
\[q = 0\] \[Using\ first\ law\ of\ thermodynamics:\] \[ΔU = q + W\] \[ΔU = 0 + W\] \[ΔU = W\]
  • Work done for an adiabatic Process:
\[W = ΔU\] \[W = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} nC_vdT\] \[W = nC_v(T_2 - T_1)\]

If the process is irreversible, we can also calculate work done as:

\[W = -P_{ext}(V_2 - V_1)\] \[W = -P_{ext}({nRT_2 \over P_2} - {nRT_1 \over P_1})\]
  • Equation of state for an adiabatic Process:

The equation of state of an adiabatic process can be expressed in three forms as given below -

\[PV^{γ} = constant\ (First\ Form)\] \[Since,\ V = {nRT \over P}\] \[V ∝ {T \over P}\] \[P({T \over P})^γ = constant\] \[P^{1-γ}T^γ = constant\ (Second\ form)\] \[Since,\ P = {nRT \over V}\] \[P ∝ {T \over V}\] \[PV^γ = constant\] \[ {T \over V} V^γ = constant\] \[TV^{γ-1} = constant\ (Third\ form)\]
  • Joule Thomson Effect: A gas on adiabatic expansion shows cooling. In other words, the temperature of a gas or a system decreases if the gas is expanded adiabatically.

Proof

In case of expansion, work done is negative:

\[W < 0\]

Since, it is an adiabatic process, q = 0. So, W = ΔU

\[ΔU < 0\] \[nC_v(T_2 - T_1) < 0\] \[T_2 < T_1\]

Thus, final temperature, T2 is less than initial temperature T1. Hence, a gas on adiabatic expansion shows cooling.

docs.title: 5. Free Expansion
docs.text:
• Expansion against zero external pressure is known as free expansion.
  • In free expansion, work done is zero.
\[W = - \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2}P_{ext}dV\] \[W = 0\ (Since,\ P_{ext} = 0)\]
  • No heat is supplied or released during free expansion.
\[q = 0\]
  • Applying first law of thermodynamics, we can calculate change in internal energy as:
\[ΔU = q + W\] \[ΔU = 0\] \[ \int\limits_{T_2}^{T_1} nC_vdT = 0\] \[nC_v(T_2 - T_1) = 0\] \[T_2 = T_1\]

Thus, final temperature = initial temperature

So, in free expansion, temperature does not change.

docs.title: Thermodynamics | Carnot Cycle and Second Law of Thermodynamics
Thermodynamics | Carnot Cycle and Second Law of Thermodynamics
Carnot Cycle
docs.text:
• Carnot cycle is based on first law of thermodynamics. It tells about conversion of heat energy into work.
  • Carnot cycle also helps us in defining second law of thermodynamics.
  • A Carnot cycle consists of following components: (a) sink, (b) source, (c) insulated stand, (d) gas cylinder (system).
  • Sink: A sink can absorb any amount of heat released by the system.
  • Source: A source has infinite thermal conductivity and any amount of heat can be taken from it.
  • Insulated stand: An insulated stand is a diathermic substance, ie, no heat can be transferred to or taken from it.
  • A carnot cycle consists of four steps: (a) isothermal reversible expansion (b) adiabatic reversible expansion (c) isothermal reversible compression (d) adiabatic reversible compression.
  • Carnot cycle is a cyclic process.

docs.title: Graphical Representation of carnot cycle
docs.text:
Image credit: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnot_cycle

In the above graph, process 1→2 is reversible isothermal expansion with constant temperature T1. Process 2→3 is reversible adiabatic expansion. Process 3→4 is reversible isothermal expansion with constant temperature T2. Process 4→1 is reversible adiabatic compression. Let's assume Q1 heat is absorbed from source during process 1→2 and Q2 heat is released to sink during process 3→4.

docs.title: Step 1. Reversible Isothermal Expansion (Process 1→2)
docs.text:
• Let pressure and volume at state 1 be (P1, V1) and at state 2 be (P2, V2).

  • Change in internal energy(ΔU) is zero because it is isothermal process.

  • Work done, W12 is given by:

\[W_{12} = -nRT_1ln{V_2 \over V_1}\]
  • Heat absorbed Q1 can be calculated from first law of thermodynamics:
\[ΔU = q + W_{12}\] \[0 = Q_1 - nRT_1ln{V_2 \over V_1}\] \[Q_1 = nRT_1ln{V_2 \over V_1}\]

Q1 will be positive because V2 > V1, which also indicates that heat is absorbed during this process.

docs.title: Step 2. Reversible Adiabatic Expansion (Process 2→3)
docs.text:
• Let pressure and volume at state 3 be (P3, V3).

  • Change in internal energy(ΔU) is given by:

\[ΔU = nC_v(T_2 - T_1)\]

  • Since, it is an adiabatic process, no heat is absorbed or released.

  • Work done, W23 is calculated from first law of thermodynamics:

\[ΔU = q + W_{23}\] \[nC_v(T_2 - T_1) = 0 + W_{23}\] \[W_{23} = nC_v(T_2 - T_1)\]

docs.title: Step 3. Reversible Isothermal Compression (Process 3→4)
docs.text:
• Let pressure and volume at state 4 be (P4, V4).

  • Change in internal energy(ΔU) is zero because it is isothermal process.

  • Work done, W34 is given by:

\[W_{34} = -nRT_2ln{V_4 \over V_3}\]
  • Heat absorbed Q2 can be calculated from first law of thermodynamics:
\[ΔU = q + W_{34}\] \[0 = Q_2 - nRT_2ln{V_4 \over V_3}\] \[Q_2 = nRT_2ln{V_4 \over V_3}\]

Q2 will be negative because V4 < V3, which also indicates that heat is released during this process.

docs.title: Step 4. Reversible Adiabatic Compression (Process 4→1)
docs.text:
• Change in internal energy(ΔU) is given by:
\[ΔU = nC_v(T_1 - T_2)\]

  • Since, it is an adiabatic process, no heat is absorbed or released.

  • Work done, W23 is calculated from first law of thermodynamics:

\[ΔU = q + W_{41}\] \[nC_v(T_1 - T_2) = 0 + W_{41}\] \[W_{41} = nC_v(T_1 - T_2) \] \[W_{41} = -nC_v(T_2 - T_1)\]

docs.title: Total Work done in Carnot cycle
docs.text:
• Total work done is given by:
\[W = W_{12} + W_{23} + W_{34} + W_{41}\] \[W = -nRT_1ln{V_2 \over V_1} + nC_v(T_2 - T_1) - nRT_2ln{V_4 \over V_3} - nC_v(T_2 - T_1)\] \[W = -nR(T_1ln{V_2 \over V_1} + T_2ln{V_4 \over V_3})\]

docs.title: Efficiency of carnot cycle
docs.text:
• For adiabatic reversible expansion process 2->3, we can write:
\[T_1V_2^{γ-1} = T_2V_3^{γ-1}\]
  • For adiabatic reversible compression process 4->1, we can write:
\[T_1V_1^{γ-1} = T_2V_4^{γ-1}\]
  • Dividing above two equations, we get:
\[ {V_2 \over V_1} = {V_3 \over V_4}\]
  • Efficiency, η of carnot cycle in terms of temperatures T1 and T2 can be calculated as:
\[η = {|Work\ done| \over Heat\ absorbed}\] \[η = {nR(T_1ln{V_2 \over V_1} + T_2ln{V_4 \over V_3}) \over nRT_1ln{V_2 \over V_1}}\] \[η = {T_1ln{V_2 \over V_1} - T_2ln{V_3 \over V_4} \over T_1ln{V_2 \over V_1}}\] \[Since,\ {V_2 \over V_1} = {V_3 \over V_4},\ we\ can\ write:\] \[η = {T_1 - T_2 \over T_1}\]

Here, T1 = Temperature of source and T2 = Temperature of sink

  • Efficiency, η of carnot cycle in terms of Q1 and Q2 can be calculated as:
\[η = {|Work\ done| \over Heat\ absorbed}\] \[η = {nR(T_1ln{V_2 \over V_1} + T_2ln{V_4 \over V_3}) \over nRT_1ln{V_2 \over V_1}}\] \[η = {Q_1 - Q_2 \over Q_1}\]
  • Let us estimate the value of efficiency, η:
\[η = {T_1 - T_2 \over T_1}\] \[η = 1 - {T_2 \over T_1}\]

Here, T2 = Temperature of sink and T1 = Temperature of source.

Also, temperature of source, T1 is always greater than temperature of sink, T2.

So, value of η lies between 0 and 1 but it is never 1.

\[0 < η < 1\]

It means only a part of heat absorbed is converted into work. This will help us in defining second law of thermodynamics.

docs.title: Entropy change in Carnot Cycle
docs.text: • Since entropy is a state function and carnot cycle is a cyclic process, so entropy change in carnot cycle will be zero.

docs.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics
docs.text:
Claussius Statement

It is impossible to convey heat from a cooler body to a hotter body without the help of any external agent.

Kelvin-Planck Statement

It is impossible to build an engine which can convert heat completely into work in a complete cycle.

docs.title: Degree of freedom
docs.text:
• Degree of freedom is the number of independent ways by which a system can exchange energy.

  • There are three types of degree of freedom:

  • Translational degree of freedom (ftr)
  • Rotational degree of freedom (fr)

  • Vibrational degree of freedom (fv)

  • At room temperature, vibrational degree of freedom of a gas is zero.

  • At high temperature where vibrational degree of freedom is non-zero, total degree of freedom, f = 3N (where, N = atomicity of a gas). For monoatomic gas like He, N = 1, for diatomic gas like O2, N = 2 and for triatomic gas like O3, N = 3.

  • Cv is related to degree of freedom, f as:

\[C_v = {fR \over 2}\] \[Poisson's\ ratio,\ γ = {C_p \over C_v}\] \[γ = {C_v + R \over C_v}\] \[γ = {{fR \over 2} + R \over {fR \over 2}}\] \[γ = 1 + {2 \over f}\]

docs.title: Degree of freedom for monoatomic gas
docs.text:
• Translational degree of freedom: A monoatomic gas can translate in all three directions: x, y and z. So, ftr = 3

  • Rotational degree of freedom: A monoatomic gas cannot rotate because it does not have any external axis. However, it spins about its own axis. So, fr = 0.

  • Vibrational degree of freedom: At room temperature, vibrational degree of freedom, fv = 0.

  • Total degree of freedom, f at room temperature for monoatomic gas:

\[f = f_{tr} + f_r + f_v = 3 + 0 + 0 = 3\] \[C_v = {fR \over 2} = {3R \over 2}\] \[C_p = C_v + R = {{3R \over 2} + R} = {5R \over 2}\] \[Poisson's\ ratio,\ γ = {C_p \over C_v} = {5 \over 3}\]

docs.title: Degree of freedom for diatomic gas
docs.text:
• Translational degree of freedom: A diatomic gas can also traverse in three directions x, y and z. So, ftr = 3.
  • Rotational degree of freedom: A diatomic gas has two external axes. So, its rotational degree of freedom, fr = 2.

Note that Fig (a) and Fig (b) may look different but they actually represent the same axis because rotation about these axes produce same rotation with one atom at rest and other in motion.

  • Vibrational degree of freedom: At room temperature, vibrational degree of freedom, fv = 0.

  • Total degree of freedom, f at room temperature for diatomic gas:

\[f = f_{tr} + f_r + f_v = 3 + 2 + 0 = 5\] \[C_v = {fR \over 2} = {5R \over 2}\] \[C_p = C_v + R = {5R \over 2} + R = {7R \over 2}\] \[Poisson's\ ratio,\ γ = {C_p \over C_v} = {7 \over 5}\]

docs.title: Degree of freedom for triatomic linear gas
docs.text:
• Translational degree of freedom: A triatomic gas can traverse in all three directions. So, ftr = 3.

  • Rotational degree of freedom: In a triatomic linear gas, there are two external axes, so fr = 2.

  • Vibrational degree of freedom: At room temperature, vibrational degree of freedom, fv = 0.

  • Total degree of freedom, f at room temperature for triatomic linear gas:

\[f = f_{tr} + f_r + f_v = 3 + 2 + 0 = 5\] \[C_v = {fR \over 2} = {5R \over 2}\] \[C_p = C_v + R = {5R \over 2} + R = {7R \over 2}\] \[Poisson's\ ratio,\ γ = {C_p \over C_v} = {7 \over 5}\]

docs.title: Degree of freedom for triatomic non-linear gas
docs.text:
• Translational degree of freedom: A triatomic gas can traverse in all three directions. So, ftr = 3.

  • Rotational degree of freedom: In a triatomic non-linear gas, there are three external axes, so fr = 3.

  • Vibrational degree of freedom: At room temperature, vibrational degree of freedom, fv = 0.

  • Total degree of freedom, f at room temperature for triatomic non-linear gas:

\[f = f_{tr} + f_r + f_v = 3 + 3 + 0 = 6\] \[C_v = {fR \over 2} = {6R \over 2} = 3R\] \[C_p = C_v + R = 3R + R = 4R\] \[Poisson's\ ratio,\ γ = {C_p \over C_v} = {4 \over 3}\]

docs.title: Calculation of Vibrational degree of freedom at high temperature
docs.text:
• For any gas, at sufficiently high temperature when vibrational degree of freedom cannot be ignored:
\[Total\ degree\ of\ freedom,\ f = 3N\] \[where\ N = atomicity of gas\]
  • Vibrational degree of freedom, fv is given by:
\[f_v = f - (f_{tr} + f_r) = 3N - (f_{tr} + f_r)\] \[where\ f_{tr} = translational\ degree\ of\ freedom\] \[and,\ f_r = rotational\ degree\ of\ freedom\]
  • For monoatomic gas:
\[f_v = 3N - (f_{tr} + f_r) = 3 \times 1 - (3 + 0) = 0 \]
  • For diatomic gas:
\[f_v = 3N - (f_{tr} + f_r) = 3 \times 2 - (3 + 2) = 1 \]
  • For triatomic linear gas:
\[f_v = 3N - (f_{tr} + f_r) = 3 \times 3 - (3 + 2) = 4 \]
  • For triatomic non-linear gas:
\[f_v = 3N - (f_{tr} + f_r) = 3 \times 3 - (3 + 3) = 3 \]

docs.title: Enthalpy (H)
docs.text:
• The heat content of a system at constant pressure is called enthalpy.
  • Enthalpy of a system can be represented as a function of pressure, P and temperature, T.
\[H = f(P,\ T)\] \[Partially\ differentiating\ both\ sides:\] \[dH = {({dH \over dP})}_T dP + {({dH \over dT})}_P dT\] \[Here, {({dH \over dP})}_T = Change\ in\ H\ w.r.t\ P\ at\ constant\ temperature\] \[Here, {({dH \over dT})}_P = Change\ in\ H\ w.r.t\ T\ at\ constant\ pressure\] \[Since,\ pressure\ is\ constant.\ So,\ dP = 0\] \[dH = {({dH \over dT})}_P dT\] \[For\ 1\ mole\ of\ ideal\ gas:\] \[dH = C_pdT\] \[For\ n\ moles\ of\ ideal\ gas:\] \[dH = nC_pdT\] \[Integrating\ both\ sides:\] \[ \int\limits_{H_1}^{H_2} dH = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} nC_pdT\] \[H_2 - H_1 = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} nC_pdT\] \[ΔH = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} nC_pdT\] \[Here,\ C_p = Molar\ heat\ capacity\ at\ constant\ pressure\]
  • If ΔH is negative, then heat is released and reaction is exothermic.
  • If ΔH is positive, then heat is absorbed and reaction is endothermic.

docs.title: Relation between Internal Energy (U) and Enthalpy (H)
docs.text:
• The relation between U and H is given by the following equation:
\[H = U + PV\] \[Differentiating\ both\ sides:\] \[dH = dU + d(PV)\]
  • If pressure P is constant (isobaric process), we can write:
\[dH = dU + d(PV)\] \[dH = dU + PdV\] \[Integrating\ both\ sides:\] \[\int\limits_{H_1}^{H_2} dH = \int\limits_{U_1}^{U_2} dU + P \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} dV\] \[H_2 - H_1 = (U_2 - U_1) + P(V_2 - V_1)\] \[ΔH = ΔU + P ΔV\]
  • If Volume V is constant (isochoric process), we can write:
\[dH = dU + d(PV)\] \[dH = dU + VdP\] \[Integrating\ both\ sides:\] \[\int\limits_{H_1}^{H_2} dH = \int\limits_{U_1}^{U_2} dU + V \int\limits_{P_1}^{P_2} dP\] \[H_2 - H_1 = (U_2 - U_1) + V(P_2 - P_1)\] \[ΔH = ΔU + V ΔP\]
  • For a gaseous phase chemical reaction containing ideal gases:
\[dH = dU + d(PV)\] \[dH = dU + d(nRT)\]

Since, most chemical reactions occur at constant temperature:

\[dH = dU + RT(dn)\] \[Integrating\ both\ sides:\] \[\int\limits_{H_1}^{H_2} dH = \int\limits_{U_1}^{U_2} dU + RT \int\limits_{n_1}^{n_2} dn\] \[H_2 - H_1 = (U_2 - U_1) + RT (n_2 - n_1)\] \[ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT\]

Here, Δng = Gaseous moles of products - Gaseous moles of reactants

docs.title: Entropy
docs.text:
• The measure of degree of randomness of a system is known as its entropy.
  • Entropy is an extensive property. Thus, more is the number of molecules, more is the randomness or entropy.
  • Entropy of gas is greater than that of liquid or solid. Similarly, entropy of liquid is greater than that of the solid.
  • Entropy is a state function, ie, its value depends only on initial and final states.
  • Mathematically, entropy (S) can be expressed as:
\[dS = {dq_{rev} \over T}\] \[ \int dS = \int {dq_{rev} \over T}\] \[ ΔS = \int {dq_{rev} \over T}\] \[ ΔS = \int {nC_pdT \over T}\]

Here, qrev = Heat exchanged by the system reversibly and T = temperature

  • For a spontaneous process, change in entropy will be positive (ΔS > 0).
  • Entropy of a system is maximum at equilibrium.
  • Entropy gives the quantitative idea about the unavailable energy of a system, ie, the energy which cannot be used for performing useful work.

docs.title: Calculation of change in entropy for an ideal gas
docs.text:
\[dS = {dq_{rev} \over T}\]

By first law of thermodynamics, dqrev = dU - W

\[dS = {dU - dW \over T}\] \[dS = {dU - (-PdV) \over T}\] \[dS = {dU + PdV \over T}\]

Since, dU = nCvdT, we can write:

\[dS = {nC_vdT + PdV \over T}\]

Integrating both sides:

\[ \int\limits_{S_1}^{S_2}dS = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2}{nC_v \over T}dT + \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2}{P \over T}dV\] \[ S_2 - S_1 = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2}{nC_v \over T}dT + \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2}{nRT \over VT}dV\] \[ΔS = nC_v \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2}{1 \over T}dT + nR \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2}{1 \over V}dV\] \[ {ΔS = nC_vln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{V_2 \over V_1}}\]

Let's derive the formula for ΔS in terms of Cp:

\[ΔS = n(C_p-R)ln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{V_2 \over V_1}\] \[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1} - nRln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{V_2 \over V_1}\] \[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{V_2T_1 \over T_2V_1}\]

Since, P ∝ (T/V):

\[ {ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{P_1 \over P_2}}\]

Case 1. For an isochoric process

In an isochoric process, volume remains constant. So, V1 = V2.

\[ΔS = nC_vln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{V_2 \over V_1}\] \[ΔS = nC_vln{T_2 \over T_1}\]

Case 2. For an isobaric process

In an isobaric process, pressure remains constant. So, P1 = P2.

\[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{P_1 \over P_2}\] \[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1}\]

Case 3. For an isothermal Process

In an isothermal process, temperature remains constant. So, T1 = T2.

\[ΔS = nC_vln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{V_2 \over V_1}\] \[ΔS = nRln{V_2 \over V_1}\] \[Or,\ ΔS = nRln{P_1 \over P_2}\]

Case 4. When two gases are mixed at same temperature in a container

  • Let us consider two gases A and B with moles nA and nB be mixed together in a container of volume V.

  • For gas A, let initial pressure, P1 = (nART / V) and final pressure P2 = ((nA + nB)RT / V)

\[ΔS_A = n_ARln{P_1 \over P_2}\] \[ΔS_A = n_ARln{{n_ART \over V} \over {(n_A + n_B)RT \over V}}\] \[ΔS_A = n_ARln{n_A \over n_A + n_B}\]

We know that nA / (nA + nB) = mole fraction of A (ΧA).

\[ΔS_A = n_ARlnΧ_A\]
  • Similarly for gas B, entropy change is given by:
\[ΔS_B = n_BRlnΧ_B\]
  • Total entropy change is given by:
\[ΔS_{total} = ΔS_A + ΔS_B\] \[ {ΔS_{total} = n_ARlnΧ_A + n_BRlnΧ_B} \]
  • Total molar entropy (entropy per mole) is given by:
\[ΔS_m = {n_A \over n_A + n_B}RlnΧ_A + {n_B \over n_A + n_B}RlnΧ_B\] \[ {ΔS_m = Χ_ARlnΧ_A + Χ_BRlnΧ_B} \]

docs.title: Change in entropy of system, surrounding and universe
docs.text:
• Let the change in entropy of universe be denoted by ΔStotal.
\[ ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{system} + ΔS_{surrounding} \]

Case 1. For a reversible process

For a reversible process, total entropy change, ΔStotal is zero.

\[ ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{system} + ΔS_{surrounding} = 0 \] \[ ΔS_{system} = - ΔS_{surrounding} \]

Case 2. For an irreversible process

  • For an irreversible process, entropy change of surrounding (ΔSsurrounding) is given by:
\[ΔS_{surrounding} = {-q_{irr} \over T}\]

where, qirr = heat absorbed by the surrounding during irreversible process

  • Total entropy change or entropy change of universe is given by:
\[ ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{system} + ΔS_{surrounding} \] \[ ΔS_{total} = {{1 \over T} \int dq_{rev}} - {q_{irr} \over T} \] \[ ΔS_{total} = {q_{rev} \over T} - {q_{irr} \over T} \]
  • It is worth noting that all irreversible processes (or, natural processes) are spontaneous processes. So, ΔStotal will always be positive.
\[ ΔS_{total} > 0\] \[ {q_{rev} \over T} - {q_{irr} \over T} > 0\] \[ {q_{rev} \over T} > {q_{irr} \over T} \] \[ q_{rev} > q_{irr} \]
  • For an adiabatic irreversible process, qirr = 0 because surrounding does not exchange heat with the system. So, ΔSsurrounding = 0.

So, for an adiabatic irreversible process:

\[ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{system}\]

Case 3. For free expansion

  • In free expansion, W = 0, q = 0 and ΔU = 0.

  • Surrounding exchange no heat with the system. So, qirr = 0. Therefore, ΔSsurrounding = 0.

  • Total entropy change is given by:

\[ ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{system} + ΔS_{surrounding} \] \[ S_{total} = ΔS_{system} \]

docs.title: Thermal Death of Universe
docs.text:
• All natural processes are irreversible and spontaneous. So, change in entropy of natural processes will always be greater than zero.
  • In other words, the entropy of the universe is constantly increasing for irreversible processes.
  • Entropy is constantly increasing, ie, unavailable energy is constantly increasing. This leads to the conclusion that a time will come when no energy will be available for doing work. This is known as thermal death of universe.

docs.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
docs.text:
• Whenever the state of a system changes, there will be change in its internal energy.
  • This change in its internal energy can be done by two ways: (a) by doing work on the system or work is done by the system (b) by supplying heat to the system or heat is released by the system.
  • This is known as First Law of Thermodynamics. It is based on energy conservation principle.
  • Mathematically, we can express first law of thermodynamics as:
\[ΔU = q + W\]

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
A gas contained in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston expands against a constant external pressure of 1 atm from volume 4 L to 14 L. In doing so, it absorbs 800 J from surrounding. Calculate the change in internal energy of the system.

\[W = - \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} P_{ext}dV\]

Since Pext is constant, we can write this as:

\[W = -P_{ext} (V_2 - V_1)\] \[W = -1 (14 - 4)\] \[W = -10\ atm L \] \[W = -10 \times 101.3\ J\ (Since,\ 1\ atm\ L = 101.3\ J)\] \[W = -1013\ J\]

Now, calculating ΔU from first law of thermodynamics:

\[ΔU = q + W\] \[ΔU = 800\ J + (-1013)\ J\] \[ΔU = -213\ J\]
  • Please note that we have used heat absorbed by the system as +800 J in the question as per sign convention.

docs.title: Thermodynamics | Gibbs Free Energy and Third Law of Thermodynamics
Thermodynamics | Gibbs Free Energy and Third Law of Thermodynamics
Gibbs Free Energy (G)
docs.text:
• There are two types of energy in a system: (a) Entropy (Waste energy) and (b) Gibbs free energy (Useful energy).
  • The energy in the system which can be converted to useful work is known as Gibbs Free energy.
  • It is a state function. So, its value depends only on initial and final state of the system.
  • It is an extensive property.

docs.title: Mathematical Definition of Gibbs Free Energy
docs.text:
• Mathematically, we can define Gibbs Free Energy, G as:
\[G = H - TS\]

Here, H = Enthalpy of the system

T = Temperature and S = Entropy of the system

\[dG = dH - TdS - SdT\]
  • If the process is isothermal:
\[dG = dH - TdS\]

Integrating both sides, we get:

\[ΔG = ΔH - TΔS\]
  • This equation is also known as Gibbs Helmoltz Equation.

Spontaneity of a process

  • Case 1: If ΔG < 0, process will be spontaneous.
  • Case 2: If ΔG > 0, process will be non-spontaneous.
  • Case 3: If ΔG = 0, system will be in equilibrium.

docs.title: Standard Change in Gibbs Free Energy (ΔG<sup>o</sup>)
docs.text:
Change in Gibbs Free Energy at 1 bar pressure and 298 K temperature is known as standard change in Gibbs Free Energy (ΔGo).

At standard conditions:

\[ΔG^o = ΔH^o - TΔS^o\]

Here, ΔHo = Change in enthalpy of the system at 1 bar pressure and 298 K

and, ΔSo = Change in entropy of the system at 1 bar pressure and 298 K

docs.title: Change in Gibbs Free Energy for isothermal reversible process
docs.text:
Mathematical definition of G is given by:

\[G = H - TS\] \[dG = dH - TdS\] \[dG = d(U + PV) - TdS\] \[dG = dU + PdV + VdP - TdS\]

At constant temperature, dU = 0.

\[dG = PdV + VdP - TdS\]

For an isothermal reversible process, we can write using first law of thermodynamics:

\[dU = dq + dW\] \[0 = dq - PdV\] \[PdV = dq = TdS\]

Putting this value of PdV in the expression of dG:

\[dG = TdS + VdP - TdS\] \[dG = VdP\]

Integrating both sides, we get:

\[ \int\limits_{G_1}^{G_2} dG = \int\limits_{P_1}^{P_2} VdP\] \[ (G_2 - G_1) = \int\limits_{P_1}^{P_2}{nRT \over P}dP\] \[ΔG = nRTln{P_2 \over P_1}\]

Since, pressure is inversely proportional to volume, we can write:

\[ΔG = nRTln{V_1 \over V_2}\]

docs.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Reaction Quotient
docs.text:
• Mathematically, Gibbs Free Energy is related to reaction quotient by the following equation:
\[ΔG = ΔG^o + RTlnQ_c\]

Here, ΔG = Change in Gibbs Free Energy

ΔGo = Change in Standard Gibbs Free Energy

T = Temperature

R = Universal Gas Constant

Qc = Reaction Quotient

  • At equilibrium, ΔG = 0 and Q = Kc (equilibrium constant):
\[0 = ΔG^o + RTlnK_c\] \[ΔG^o = -RTlnK_c\]

docs.title: Third Law of Thermodynamics
docs.text:
• The third law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of a solid approaches zero at absolute zero temperature (0 K).

  • In other words, the entropy of a perfect crystalline substance becomes zero at absolute zero temperature (0 K).

\[S_0 = 0\]
  • The third law of thermodynamics can be used to calculate the absolute entropy of a substance at a given temperature.

At any temperature T:

\[ΔS = S_T - S_0\] \[ΔS = S_T - 0\] \[Or,\ S_T = ΔS\]

Here, ST = entropy at temperature T

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Note

Please note that in all the questions discussed below, we should assume that the process is reversible because only in case of reversible process, we can calculate work done by finding area under P-V curve (because Pext will be approximately equal to Pgas).

In the process shown in the form of graph where a gas expands from 1 L to 10 L, if heat supplied to the gas is 100 J, calculate the change in internal energy. (Take 1 atm L = 100 J)

We know that work done can be calculated by finding area under P-V curve.

Since, this is expansion, work done will be negative.

\[W = - Area\ under\ P-V\ curve\] \[W = - (10 \times (10-1))\] \[W = -10 \times 9 = 90\ atm\ L\] \[W = -90 \times 100 = -9000\ J\]

Change in internal energy, ΔU can be calculated by first law of thermodynamics. Here, q will be positive because heat is supplied.

\[ΔU = q + W\] \[ΔU = (100 - 9000)\ J\] \[ ΔU = -8900\ J \]

In the process shown in the form of graph, if change in internal energy is 100 J, calculate q for the process.

We know that work done can be calculated by finding area under P-V curve.

Since, this is expansion, work done will be negative.

\[W = - Area\ under\ P-V\ curve\] \[W = - (Area\ of\ triangle + Area\ of\ rectangle)\] \[W = - ({1 \over 2} \times 10 \times 5 + 10 \times 5)\] \[W = -75 J\]

q can be calculated using first law of thermodynamics:

\[ΔU = q + W\] \[100 = q - 75\ J\] \[ q = 175\ J \]

For the process shown below, calculate: (a) W (b) ΔU (c) q.

We know that work done can be calculated by finding area under P-V curve.

Since, this is a cyclic process and graph is clockwise, work done will be negative. (It is because area under expansion curve from A to B is greater than the area under compression curve from B to A).

\[W = - Area\ under\ P-V\ curve\] \[W = - π \times 4^2\] \[W = -16π\ J\]

Since, this is a cyclic process, ΔU = 0 (because internal energy is a state function)

q can be calculated from first law of thermodynamics:

\[ΔU = q + W\] \[0 = q - 16π\ J\] \[ q = 16π\ J \]

For the process shown below, calculate: (a) W (b) ΔU (c) q.

We know that work done can be calculated by finding area under P-V curve.

Work done in the path AB is 0 because it is isochoric process:

\[W_{AB} = 0\]

Work done in path BC (expansion):

\[W_{BC} = - Area\ of\ curve\ V_1BCV_2\] \[W_{BC} = - {1 \over 2} (P_2 - P_1) (V_2 - V_1) - (V_2 - V_1) P_1\] \[W_{BC} = - {1 \over 2} (V_2 - V_1) (P_2 - P_1 + P_1)\] \[W_{BC} = - {1 \over 2} (V_2 - V_1) P_2\]

Work done in the path CD is 0 because it is isochoric process:

\[W_{CD} = 0\]

Work done in path DA (compression):

\[W_{DA} = Area\ of\ curve\ V_2DAV_1\] \[W_{DA} = {1 \over 2} (P_2 - P_1) (V_2 - V_1) - (V_2 - V_1) P_1\] \[W_{DA} = {1 \over 2} (V_2 - V_1) (P_2 - P_1 + P_1)\] \[W_{DA} = {1 \over 2} (V_2 - V_1) P_2\]

Total work done in the process:

\[W_{total} = W_{AB} + W_{BC} + W_{CD} + W{DA}\] \[W_{total} = 0 - {1 \over 2} (V_2 - V_1) P_2 + 0 + {1 \over 2} (V_2 - V_1) P_2\] \[W_{total} = 0\]

docs.title: Heat Capacity
docs.text:
• We can define heat capacity as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a given mass of substance by 1 Kelvin (or 1 ℃).
  • It is denoted by C and is an extensive property, ie, it depends on the amount of matter present in the substance.
\[C = {dq \over dT}\] \[where,\ q = heat\ and\ T = temperature\]

docs.title: Specific Heat Capacity
docs.text:
• Specific heat capacity is defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 K.
  • It can also be defined as the heat capacity per unit gram of mass.
  • It is an intensive property because it does not depend on amount of matter present in the substance (it is expressed as per unit gram of mass).
  • It is denoted by the symbol S.
\[S = {C \over m}\] \[where,\ C = Heat\ capacity\ and\ m = mass\ in\ gram\] \[S = {dq \over mdT}\]

docs.title: Molar Heat Capacity
docs.text:
• Molar heat capacity is defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 mole of a substance by 1 K.
  • It is defined as heat capacity per unit mole.
  • It is an intensive property, ie it does not depend on amount of matter present in the substance.
  • It is denoted by Cm.
\[C_m = {C \over n}\] \[where,\ C = heat\ capacity\ and\ n = moles\] \[C_m = {dq \over ndT}\] \[Also,\ dq = nC_mdT\]

Let's put substitute values in the equation of Cm.

\[C_m = {dq \over ndT}\]

Using first law of thermodynamics, dq = dU - dW:

\[C_m = {(dU - dW) \over ndT}\] \[C_m = {dU \over ndT} - {dW \over ndT}\] \[C_m = {nC_vdT \over ndT} - {(-PdV) \over ndT}\] \[C_m = C_v + {PdV \over ndT}\]
  • Molar heat capacity at constant volume is denoted by Cv.
  • Molar heat capacity at constant pressure is denoted by Cp.

docs.title: Relation between C<sub>p</sub> and C<sub>v</sub>
docs.text:
• The relation between Cp and Cv is given as:
\[C_p - C_v = R\]

  • Let's try to prove this relation.

  • At constant pressure:

\[dH = dU + PdV\] \[dH = dU - dW\] \[dU = dH + dW\] \[By\ first\ law\ of\ thermodynamics:\] \[dU = dq + dW\] \[Hence,\ at\ constant\ pressure,\ we\ can\ write:\] \[dq = dH\] \[dq = nC_pdT\ (Since,\ dH = nC_pdT)\]
  • Also, we know that:
\[dU = nC_vdT\]
  • Applying first law of thermodynamics at constant pressure:
\[dU = dq + dW\] \[nC_vdT = nC_pdT - PdV\] \[n(C_v - C_p) dT = -PdV\] \[n(C_v - C_p) dT = -nRdT\] \[C_v - C_p = -R\] \[C_p - C_v = R\]

docs.title: Poisson's Ratio
docs.text:
Poisson's ratio is defined as the ratio of molar heat capacity at constant pressure (Cp) to molar heat capacity at constant volume (Cv).

\[γ = {C_p \over C_v}\]

docs.title: Calculation of molar heat capacity and Poisson's ratio for a mixture of gases
docs.text:
• Let us consider a container containing a mixture of three gases A, B and C whose moles are n1, n2 and n3 respectively. Let their molar heat capacity at constant volume be Cv1, Cv2 and Cv3 respectively.

  • We can calculate Cv(mix) of mixture of these gases as:

\[C_{v(mix)} = {n_1C_{v1} + n_2C_{v2} + n_3C_{v3} \over n_1 + n_2 + n_3}\]
  • Cp(mix) can be calculated as:
\[C_{p(mix)} = C_{v(mix)} + R\]
  • Poisson's ratio, γmix is given by:
\[γ_{mix} = {C_{p(mix)} \over C_{v(mix)}}\]

Important formula to remember from this article

  • dU = nCvdT

  • dq = nCpdT

  • Cp - Cv = R

  • γ = Cp / Cv

Here, U = internal energy, Cv = molar heat capacity at constant volume, Cp = molar heat capacity at constant pressure, n = moles, q = heat, T = temperature, γ = Poisson's ratio

docs.title: Thermodynamics | Heat, Work and Internal Energy
Thermodynamics | Heat, Work and Internal Energy
Heat (q)
docs.text:
• Heat is a form of energy, which flows due to difference in temperature.
  • It flows from high temperature to low temperature.
  • Heat is a path function, ie, it depends on the path followed by the system to reach to the current state.
  • Sign convention: Heat absorbed by the system is taken as positive and heat released by the system is taken as negative.

docs.title: Work (W)
docs.text:
• Work is a mode of transfer of energy. Work can be done either through expansion or compression.

  • Work is a path function, ie, it depends on the actual path followed by the system to reach the current state.

  • Sign convention: Work done by the system is negative and work done on the system is positive.

  • In expansion, work is done by the system, so work done is negative. In compression, work is done on the system, so work done is positive.

  • Work done by the system is calculated as:
\[dW = -Fdx\]

Here, we have negative sign because direction of external force, F and displacement dx is opposite.

\[Since,\ F = Pressure \times Area\] \[dW = -PAdx\] \[dW = -PdV\] \[Integrating\ both\ sides:\] \[\int dW = -\int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} PdV\] \[W = -\int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} PdV\]

Here, since P is the external pressure, we can say that work done by the system is:

\[W = -\int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} P_{ext}dV\]
  • Since the geometrical meaning of integration is finding area under curve, so we can also calculate work done by finding area under P-V curve (for a reversible process in which Pext is approximately equal to Pgas). We will discuss reversible process later.

docs.title: Internal Energy (U)
docs.text:
• The sum of all possible kinds of energy present in the system is called its internal energy.
  • Thus, internal energy constitutes kinetic energy, potential energy, electronic energy, nuclear energy, rotational energy, vibrational energy etc.
  • Internal energy is a state function, ie, it depends only on initial and final state of the system.
  • For a cyclic process, ΔU = 0
  • It is an extensive property, ie, it depends on amount of matter present in the system.

docs.title: Calculation of internal energy
docs.text:
• Internal energy can be expressed as a function of volume and temperature.
\[U = f(V,T)\] \[dU = {({dU \over dV})}_TdV + {({dU \over dT})}_VdT\] \[where,\ {({dU \over dV})}_T = Change\ in\ U\ w.r.t\ V\ at\ constant\ T\] \[and,\ {({dU \over dT})}_V = Change\ in\ U\ w.r.t\ T\ at\ constant\ V\]
  • For an ideal gas, volume cannot be changed at constant temperature because there is no force of attraction or repulsion existing between two ideal gas molecules.
\[So,\ {({dU \over dV})}_T = 0\]
  • Thus, for an ideal gas, we can write:
\[dU = {({dU \over dV})}_T dT\]
  • For one mole of ideal gas:
\[C_v = {({dU \over dV})}_T\] \[Hence,\ dU = C_vdT\]
  • For n moles of ideal gas:
\[dU = nC_vdT\] \[Integrating\ both\ sides:\] \[ΔU = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} nC_vdT\] \[If\ C_v\ is\ independent\ of\ temperature:\] \[ΔU = nC_v(T_2 - T_1)\] \[where,\ C_v = Molar\ heat\ capacity\ at\ constant\ volume\]

Note

  • For a cyclic process, ΔU = 0.
  • For an isothermal process, ΔU = 0 (Since, T2 = T1).

docs.title: Thermodynamics | Introduction
docs.text: Thermodynamics is the branch of chemistry which deals with study of the interrelationships among heat, work, and the energy content of a system.

docs.title: Some common terms related to thermodynamics
docs.text:
System

The part of universe which is taken into consideration for thermodynamics investigation is known as a system. There are three types of system: open system, closed system and isolated system.

Surrounding

The part of the universe except system is known as surrounding.

Boundary

  • Boundary is also known as wall. Boundary is defined as anything which separates system and surrounding. It can be real or imaginary. The point or place where the impact of system ends defines an imaginary boundary.

  • There are two types of boundary or wall: (a) Diathermic wall, which allows the passage of energy through it and (b) Adiabatic wall which does not allow the passage of energy through it.

docs.title: Types of System
docs.text:
• Open System: An open system can exchange both matter and energy with its surrounding.
  • Closed System: A closed system can exchange only energy with its surrounding. Exchange of matter is not possible.
  • Isolated System: An isolated system does not allow exchange of energy and matter with its surrounding. It is very difficult to design an ideal isolated system in real world.

Image Credit: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isolated_system

docs.title: Intensive and extensive properties
docs.text:
• Intensive Property: The property of a system which is independent of size of system and the amount of matter present in the system is known as intensive property. For example, if we take one glass of water from a container, then also temperature of water in both container and glass is same. Therefore, temperature is an intensive property. Other examples of intensive properties are temperature, molarity, molality, density, refractive index etc.

  • Extensive Property: The property of a system which depends on size of system and the amount of matter present in the system is known as extensive property. Volume, mass, moles, internal energy are some examples of extensive property.

docs.title: Characteristics of intensive and extensive properties
docs.text:
• Intensive properties are non-additive while extensive properties are additive. For example, let's consider we have two 100 mL solutions of lemon juice of equal concentration. If we mix these two, then the concentration will remain same but volume of new solution will be 200 mL.

  • If E1 and E2 are two extensive properties, then E1/E2 becomes an intensive property. Example: density = mass/volume Thus, an extensive property expressed per unit mole, per unit volume or per unit Kg becomes an intensive property.

  • Extensive property multiplied by intensive property yields an extensive property.

docs.title: State variables and state of a system
docs.text:
• The variables which define the state of a system are known as state variables or state parameters. Examples: pressure, volume, temperature, number of moles.

  • When all the state parameters have a definite value, then the system is said to be in a definite state. If any one of the parameters changes, then the state of a system changes.

docs.title: State Functions and Path Functions
docs.text:
• State Function: The function whose value depends on initial and final state of a system and is independent of the path followed to change the state of a system is called state function. Displacement is a state function and distance is a path function. Other examples of path function are enthalpy, internal energy, entropy, Gibbs Free energy etc.

  • Path Function: The function whose value depends on the path followed to change the state of the system is known as path function. Heat and work are path functions.

docs.title: Polytropic Process
docs.text:
• Polytropic process is a process which follows the equation:
\[PV^x = k\]

where, x = polytropic index and k = constant

Special Cases:

  1. If x = 0 ⇒ P = constant ⇒ Isobaric process
  2. If x = 1 ⇒ PV = constant ⇒ Isothermal process
  3. If x = γ ⇒ PVγ = constant ⇒ Adiabatic process

docs.title: Work done in a polytropic process
docs.text:
For a reversible polytropic process, work done can be calculated as:

\[W = - \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} P_{ext}dV\] \[W = - \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} P_{gas}dV\] \[W = - \int\limits_{V_1}^{V_2} {k \over V^x}dV\] \[W = {-k(V_2^{1-x} - V_1^{1-x}) \over 1-x}\]

docs.title: Calculation of molar heat capacity
docs.text:
• Molar heat capacity is defined as heat capacity per unit mole.
\[C_m = {dq \over ndT}\] \[C_m = {dU - dW \over ndT}\] \[C_m = {dU - (-PdV) \over ndT}\] \[C_m = {dU \over ndT} + {PdV \over ndT}\] \[C_m = {nC_vdT \over ndT} + {PdV \over ndT}\] \[C_m = C_v + {PdV \over ndT}\]
  • Let's calculate dV/dT so that it can be used in above expression.
\[PV^x = k\] \[ {T \over V}V^x = k\] \[TV^{x-1} = k\]

Differentiating both sides:

\[V^{x-1}dT + T(x-1)V^{x-2}dV = 0\] \[ {dV \over dT} = {V \over T(1-x)}\]

Putting in the expression of Cm:

\[C_m = C_v + {PV \over nT(1-x)}\]

Since, PV = nRT (ideal gas equation), we can write:

\[C_m = C_v + {nRT \over nT(1-x)}\] \[C_m = C_v + {R \over (1-x)}\]

docs.title: Questions based on Polytropic Process
docs.text:
For a monoatomic ideal gas, the ratio of pressure and square of volume is 3. How much heat should be supplied to increase the temperature of 5 moles of the gas by 50oC?

\[ {P \over V^2} = 3\] \[ PV^{-2} = constant\]

This is a polytropic process with x = -2.

Molar heat capacity is given by:

\[C_m = C_v + {R \over (1-x)}\] \[C_m = C_v + {R \over (1-(-2))}\] \[C_m = {3R \over 2} + {R \over 3}\] \[C_m = {11R \over 6}\]

Also, molar heat capacity is given by:

\[C_m = {dq \over ndT}\] \[dq = nC_mdT\] \[q = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} nC_mdT\] \[q = nC_m(T_2 - T_1)\] \[q = nC_mΔT\] \[q = 5 \times {11R \over 6} \times 50\] \[q = {1375R \over 3}\] \[q = {1375 \times 8.314 \over 3}\] \[q = 3810.58\ J\]

The molar heat capacity of a gas (at room temperature) for which pressure and volume are equal is 7R/2. What will be the rotational degree of freedom for this gas? Also, predict the atomicity of gas.

\[Given:\ P = V\] \[PV^{-1} = constant\]

This is a polytropic process with x = -1.

Molar heat capacity is given by:

\[C_m = C_v + {R \over (1-x)}\] \[⇒{7R \over 2} = C_v + {R \over (1-(-1))}\] \[⇒{7R \over 2} = C_v + {R \over 2}\] \[⇒C_v = 3R\]

Thus, it is a triatomic gas.

\[C_v = {fR \over 2}\] \[⇒3R = {fR \over 2}\] \[⇒f = 6\]

Thus, total degree of freedom = 6

Let ftr = Translational degree of freedom and fr = Rotational degree of freedom. Then, At room temperature:

\[f_{tr} + f_r = f\] \[3 + f_r = 6\] \[f_r = 3\]

Thus, rotational degree of freedom is 3.

Calculate the molar heat capacity of monoatomic gas for which the ratio of pressure and volume is 1.

\[Given:\ {P \over V} = 1\] \[PV^{-1} = constant\]

This is a polytropic process with x = -1.

Molar heat capacity is given by:

\[C_m = C_v + {R \over (1-x)}\]

Since, Cv = 3R/2 for a monoatomic gas, we can write:

\[C_m = {3R \over 2} + {R \over (1-(-1))} \] \[C_m = {3R \over 2} + {R \over 2}\] \[C_m = 2R\]

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
For an ideal gas Cp = 2.5R, calculate the change in entropy when 3 moles of this gas is heated from 300 K to 600 K at: (a) Constant pressure (b) Constant volume.

\[Given\ values: n = 3,\ C_p = 2.5R,\ T_1 = 300\ K,\ T_2 = 600\ K\] \[C_v = C_p - R = 2.5R - R = 1.5R\]

(a) Change in entropy at constant pressure:

\[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{P_1 \over P_2}\] \[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1}\] \[ΔS = 3 \times 2.5R \times ln{600 \over 300}\] \[ΔS = 7.5 \times 8.314 \times ln2\] \[ΔS = 43.22\ JK^{-1}\]

(b) Change in entropy at constant volume:

\[ΔS = nC_vln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{V_2 \over V_1}\] \[ΔS = nC_vln{T_2 \over T_1}\] \[ΔS = 3 \times 1.5R \times ln{600 \over 300}\] \[ΔS = 4.5 \times 8.314 \times ln2\] \[ΔS = 25.93\ JK^{-1}\]

Calculate the change in entropy when 3 moles of an ideal gas is heated and compressed simultaneously from 300 K, 1 atm to 400 K, 5 atm. (Cp = 7R/2)

Applying the formula of ΔS:

\[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{P_1 \over P_2}\] \[ΔS = 3 \times {7R \over 2} ln{400 \over 300} + 3 \times R ln{1 \over 5}\] \[ΔS = 3 \times 3.5 \times 8.314 \times ln{4 \over 3} + 3 \times 8.314 \times ln{1 \over 5}\] \[ΔS = -15.03\ JK^{-1}\]

Since, ΔS is negative, this process is non-spontaneous.

By how much does the entropy of 3 moles of an ideal gas change if pressure is reduced from 2 bar to 1 bar without any change in temperature?

\[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{P_1 \over P_2}\]

Since, temperature is constant, we can write:

\[ΔS = nRln{P_1 \over P_2}\] \[ΔS = 3 \times 8.314 \times ln{2 \over 1}\] \[ΔS = 17.288\ JK^{-1}\]

Evaluate the change in entropy when 3 moles of an ideal gas is heated from 27oC to 727oC at constant pressure of 1 atm. (Cp = 23.7 J K-1mol-1)

\[Given:\ T_1 = (27 + 273) = 300\ K\] \[and,\ T_2 = (727 + 273) = 1000\ K\] \[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{P_1 \over P_2}\]

Since, pressure is constant, we can write:

\[ΔS = nC_pln{T_2 \over T_1}\] \[ΔS = 3 \times 23.7 \times ln{1000 \over 300}\] \[ΔS = 85.6\ JK^{-1}\]

Nitrogen is heated from 300 K to 600 K at constant pressure of 1 atm. Calculate the change in molar entropy if Cp = 20 + 10 T, where T = temperature.

\[ΔS = \int {dq_{rev} \over T}\] \[ΔS = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} {nC_pdT \over T}\]

Molar change in entropy means change in entropy per mole. So, molar entropy change ΔS_m is given by:

\[ΔS_m = {ΔS \over n}\] \[ΔS_m = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} {C_pdT \over T}\] \[ΔS_m = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} {20 + 10T \over T}dT\] \[ΔS_m = \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} {20 \over T}dT + \int\limits_{T_1}^{T_2} {10T \over T}dT\] \[ΔS_m = 20 ln{T_2 \over T_1} + 10(T_2 - T_1)\] \[ΔS_m = 20 ln{600 \over 300} + 10(600 - 300)\] \[ΔS_m = 20 ln2 + 10 \times 300\] \[ΔS_m = 3013.863\ JK^{-1}mol^{-1}\]

A five litre container is divided so that 1 L of O2 gas at 1 atm and 4 L of N2 gas at 2 atm are on the two sides of the thin membrane. The membrane is then broken, allowing the gas to mix up at 300 K. Calculate the entropy of mixing for this process.

  • Moles of O2 gas is given by:
\[n_{O_2} = {PV \over RT}\] \[n_{O_2} = {1 \times 1 \over 0.0821 \times 300} = 0.0406\]
  • Moles of N2 gas is given by:
\[n_{N_2} = {PV \over RT}\] \[n_{N_2} = {2 \times 4 \over 0.0821 \times 300} = 0.3248\]
  • When two gases are mixed, mole fractions of O2 and N2 are:
\[Χ_{O_2} = {n_{O_2} \over n_{O_2} + n_{N_2}}\] \[Χ_{O_2} = {0.0406 \over 0.0406 + 0.3248} = 0.11\] \[Χ_{N_2} = {n_{N_2} \over n_{O_2} + n_{N_2}} = 0.89\]
  • Entropy change for O2:
\[ΔS_{O_2} = n_{O_2}RlnΧ_{O_2}\] \[ΔS_{O_2} = 0.0406 \times 8.314 \times ln(0.11) = -0.745\ JK^{-1}\]
  • Entropy change for N2:
\[ΔS_{N_2} = n_{N_2}RlnΧ_{N_2}\] \[ΔS_{N_2} = 0.3248 \times 8.314 \times ln(0.89) = -0.315\ JK^{-1}\]
  • Total entropy change or entropy of mixing is given by:
\[ΔS = ΔS_{O_2} + ΔS_{N_2}\] \[ΔS = (-0.745) + (-0.315) = -1.06\ JK^{-1}\]

Derive the condition to obtain maximum molar entropy change if two gases are mixed to form a binary mixture.

  • Let the two gases be denoted by A and B. Let the mole fraction of A = ΧA and mole fraction of B = 1 - ΧA. Molar entropy change of mixing of these two gases:
\[ΔS_m = Χ_AlnΧ_A + (1 - Χ_A) ln (1 - Χ_A)\] \[ΔS_m = Χ_AlnΧ_A + ln (1 - Χ_A) - Χ_A ln (1 - Χ_A)\]
  • Differentiating with respect to χA:
\[ {d(ΔS_m) \over dΧ_A} = ln {Χ_A \over (1 - Χ_A)} \]
  • For maximum value of ΔSm:
\[ {d(ΔS_m) \over dΧ_A} = 0 \] \[ ln {Χ_A \over (1 - Χ_A)} = 0 \] \[ {Χ_A \over (1 - Χ_A)} = 1 \] \[ 2Χ_A = 1 \] \[ Χ_A = 0.5 \]
  • Hence, to obtain maximum molar entropy change by mixing two gases A and B, mole fraction of A, ΧA = 0.5 and mole fraction of B, ΧB = 0.5, ie, A and B should be equimolar or they should have same number of moles.

One mole of an ideal gas is expanded isothermally at 298 K until its volume is tripled. Find ΔSgas and ΔStotal under following conditions: (a) Expansion is reversible (b) Expansion is irreversible where 836.8 J less heat is absorbed than in the first (c) Free expansion

  • Let's calculate the entropy change for the system or gas.
\[ ΔS_{gas} = nRln{V_2 \over V_1} \] \[ ΔS_{gas} = nRln{3V \over V} \] \[ ΔS_{gas} = nRln(3) \] \[ ΔS_{gas} = 1 \times 8.314 \times ln(3) \] \[ ΔS_{gas} = 9.134\ JK^{-1} \]

This is the value of ΔSgas for all three cases mentioned in the question.

  • (a) Since, the process is reversible, ΔStotal = 0. So, ΔSsurrounding = -ΔSgas = -9.134 JK-1

  • (b) ΔSsurrounding for irreversible process is given by:

\[ΔS_{surrounding} = {-q_{irr} \over T}\] \[ΔS_{surrounding} = {-(q_{rev} - 836.8) \over T}\]

ΔStotal is given by:

\[ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{gas} + ΔS_{surrounding}\] \[ ΔS_{total} = {q_{rev} \over T} + {-(q_{rev} - 836.8) \over T}\] \[ ΔS_{total} = {836.8 \over T}\] \[ ΔS_{total} = {836.8 \over 298} = 2.808\ JK^{-1}\]
  • (c) For free expansion, ΔSsurrounding = 0.
\[So,\ ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{gas} = 9.134\ JK^{-1}\]

Calculate the entropy change when 0.5 L of an ideal gas (Cv = 12.6 JK-1mol-1) at 300 K and 1 atm pressure is allowed to expand to double its volume and simultaneously heated to 373 K.

Number of moles, n can be calculated by ideal gas equation:

\[n = {PV \over RT}\] \[n = {1 \times 0.5 \over 0.0821 \times 300} = 0.02\]

Change in entropy, ΔS is given by:

\[ΔS = nC_vln{T_2 \over T_1} + nRln{V_2 \over V_1}\] \[ΔS = 0.02 \times 12.6 \times ln{373 \over 300} + 0.02 \times 8.314 \times ln{2V_1 \over V_1}\] \[ΔS = 0.17\ JK^{-1}\]

The temperature of an ideal monoatomic gas is raised from 25oC to 250oC. What must be the accompanying pressure change in order that the entropy of gas may be unaffected by the complete process?

Given values: T1 = 25 + 273 = 298 K, T2 = 250 + 273 = 523 K

As per the question, ΔS = 0.
